quote_verbatim: Of course, it's per-share intrinsic value, not book value, that counts. Book value is an accounting term that measures the capital, including retained earnings, that has been put into a business. Intrinsic value is a present-value estimate of the cash that can be taken out of a business during its remaining life. At most companies, the two values are unrelated.
concept: Intrinsic value is the discounted cash a business can yield over its life; book value only measures capital put in, and the two usually have no relation.
evolution_notes: The opening section of the letter carries no section title; the letter's own title line is used as the heading. Same paragraph goes on to say Berkshire is an exception where book value tracks intrinsic value.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Chairman's Letter - 1993

quote_verbatim: From 1991 to 1993, Coke and Gillette increased their annual operating earnings per share by 38% and 37% respectively, but their market prices moved up only 11% and 6%. In other words, the companies overperformed their stocks, a result that no doubt partly reflects Wall Street's new apprehension about brand names. Whatever the reason, what will count over time is the earnings performance of these companies.
concept: Judge a holding by the business's earnings over time, not by the stock's move; the two diverge in the short run.
evolution_notes: Preceded by: market price and intrinsic value arrive at about the same destination over time but diverge in the short run; followed by the Graham voting-machine/weighing-machine quotation.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Chairman's Letter - 1993

quote_verbatim: At Berkshire, we have no view of the future that dictates what businesses or industries we will enter. Indeed, we think it's usually poison for a corporate giant's shareholders if it embarks upon new ventures pursuant to some grand vision. We prefer instead to focus on the economic characteristics of businesses that we wish to own and the personal characteristics of managers with whom we wish to associate - and then to hope we get lucky in finding the two in combination.
concept: No top-down vision of which industries to enter; look for good business economics and good managers together, one case at a time.
evolution_notes: Just before: 'Five years ago we had no thought of getting into shoes ... So much for strategic plans.'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Dexter Shoe

quote_verbatim: Since I have a huge percentage of my net worth committed for life to Berkshire shares - and since the company will issue me neither restricted shares nor stock options - my gain-loss equation will always match that of all other owners.
concept: The manager's own money in the stock, with no options or restricted shares, aligns his outcome with every owner's.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Dexter Shoe

quote_verbatim: Finally, and of paramount importance, Harold and Peter can be sure that they will get to run their business - an activity they dearly love - exactly as they did before the merger. At Berkshire, we do not tell .400 hitters how to swing.
concept: Acquired managers who love their business keep running it as before; Berkshire does not direct able operators.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Dexter Shoe

quote_verbatim: In the past, we've criticized the managerial practice of shooting the arrow of performance and then painting the target, centering it on whatever point the arrow happened to hit. We will instead risk embarrassment by painting first and shooting later.
concept: State the performance goal in advance and be held to it, rather than defining success after the result.
evolution_notes: The goal stated is look-through earnings of about $1.85 billion by 2000, to match 15% intrinsic value growth.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: "Look-Through" Earnings

quote_verbatim: In the meantime, we'll try to resist the temptation to do something marginal simply because we are long on cash. There's no use running if you're on the wrong road.
concept: Idle cash is no reason to make a marginal purchase; wait for sensible terms.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: "Look-Through" Earnings

quote_verbatim: Charlie and I would follow a buy-and-hold policy even if we ran a tax-exempt institution. We think it the soundest way to invest, and it also goes down the grain of our personalities. [...] What this little tale tells us is that tax-paying investors will realize a far, far greater sum from a single investment that compounds internally at a given rate than from a succession of investments compounding at the same rate.
concept: Buy and hold; deferred tax makes one long-held compounder worth far more than a succession of equal-rate investments.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Taxes

quote_verbatim: To oversimplify the matter somewhat, the total of the funds prepaid by policyholders and the funds earmarked for incurred-but-not-yet-paid claims is called "the float." [...] Our cost of float is determined by our underwriting loss or profit.
concept: Float is premiums prepaid plus claims reserved but unpaid; its cost is the underwriting loss, or negative when there is an underwriting profit.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Insurance Operations

quote_verbatim: A company writing at the same combined ratio now as in the 1980's today has a far less attractive business than it did then. Only by making an analysis that incorporates both underwriting results and the current risk-free earnings obtainable from float can one evaluate the true economics of the business that a property-casualty insurer writes. [...] The value of float funds - in effect, their transfer price as they move from the insurance operation to the investment operation - should be determined simply by the risk-free, long-term rate of interest.
concept: Judge an insurer's underwriting economics by underwriting result plus float valued at the long-term risk-free rate; investment results are a separate analysis.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Insurance Operations

quote_verbatim: It would be fallacious, however, to conclude from this single-year result that the super-cat business is a wonderful one, or even a satisfactory one. A simple example will illustrate the fallacy: Suppose there is an event that occurs 25 times in every century. If you annually give 5-for-1 odds against its occurrence that year, you will have many more winning years than losers. Indeed, you may go a straight six, seven or more years without loss. You also will eventually go broke.
concept: A run of profitable years in catastrophe risk proves nothing; underpriced odds win most years and still end in ruin.
evolution_notes: Followed by: 'there is no way for us - or anyone else - to calculate the true odds on super-cat coverages. In fact, it will take decades for us to find out whether our underwriting judgment has been sound.'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Insurance Operations

quote_verbatim: Better than anyone else, these giants understand that the test of a reinsurer is its ability and willingness to pay losses under trying circumstances, not its readiness to accept premiums when things look rosy.
concept: A reinsurer is judged by whether it can and will pay in a catastrophe, not by its appetite for premium in good times.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Insurance Operations

quote_verbatim: But we are now seeing signs of price deterioration. If this trend continues, we will resign ourselves to much-reduced volume, keeping ourselves available, though, for the large, sophisticated buyer who requires a super-cat insurer with large capacity and a sure ability to pay losses.
concept: When insurance prices fall, accept much lower volume rather than write underpriced business.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Insurance Operations

quote_verbatim: But we continue to think that it is usually foolish to part with an interest in a business that is both understandable and durably wonderful. Business interests of that kind are simply too hard to replace. [...] In our view, what makes sense in business also makes sense in stocks: An investor should ordinarily hold a small piece of an outstanding business with the same tenacity that an owner would exhibit if he owned all of that business.
concept: Do not sell a piece of an understandable, durably wonderful business; hold it as tenaciously as an owner of the whole would.
evolution_notes: Between the two sentences: the CEO who would never sell his 'crown jewel' subsidiary yet trades his own portfolio on a broker's 'You can't go broke taking a profit.'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Common Stock Investments

quote_verbatim: Charlie and I decided long ago that in an investment lifetime it's just too hard to make hundreds of smart decisions. That judgment became ever more compelling as Berkshire's capital mushroomed and the universe of investments that could significantly affect our results shrank dramatically. Therefore, we adopted a strategy that required our being smart - and not too smart at that - only a very few times.
concept: Make few decisions and make them well; a strategy needing only a handful of smart calls in a lifetime.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Common Stock Investments

quote_verbatim: We believe that a policy of portfolio concentration may well decrease risk if it raises, as it should, both the intensity with which an investor thinks about a business and the comfort-level he must feel with its economic characteristics before buying into it. In stating this opinion, we define risk, using dictionary terms, as "the possibility of loss or injury."
concept: Risk is the possibility of loss or injury; concentration can lower it by forcing deeper thought and higher comfort before buying.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Common Stock Investments

quote_verbatim: In their hunger for a single statistic to measure risk, however, they forget a fundamental principle: It is better to be approximately right than precisely wrong. For owners of a business - and that's the way we think of shareholders - the academics' definition of risk is far off the mark, so much so that it produces absurdities. For example, under beta-based theory, a stock that has dropped very sharply compared to the market - as had Washington Post when we bought it in 1973 - becomes "riskier" at the lower price than it was at the higher price.
concept: Beta as risk is precise and wrong: it calls a business riskier when it gets cheaper; prefer approximate rightness.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Common Stock Investments

quote_verbatim: In fact, the true investor welcomes volatility. [...] The more manic-depressive this chap is, the greater the opportunities available to the investor. That's true because a wildly fluctuating market means that irrationally low prices will periodically be attached to solid businesses. It is impossible to see how the availability of such prices can be thought of as increasing the hazards for an investor who is totally free to either ignore the market or exploit its folly.
concept: Volatility is opportunity, not hazard, for an investor free to ignore or exploit the market's prices.
evolution_notes: The elided words introduce Graham's 'Mr. Market' from Chapter 8 of The Intelligent Investor; Graham is named by Buffett here.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Common Stock Investments

quote_verbatim: In contrast, we'll happily forgo knowing the price history and instead will seek whatever information will further our understanding of the company's business. After we buy a stock, consequently, we would not be disturbed if markets closed for a year or two. We don't need a daily quote on our 100% position in See's or H. H. Brown to validate our well-being. Why, then, should we need a quote on our 7% interest in Coke?
concept: Study the business, not the price history; a part-owner needs no daily quote any more than a whole owner does.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Common Stock Investments

quote_verbatim: In our opinion, the real risk that an investor must assess is whether his aggregate after-tax receipts from an investment (including those he receives on sale) will, over his prospective holding period, give him at least as much purchasing power as he had to begin with, plus a modest rate of interest on that initial stake. [...] The primary factors bearing upon this evaluation are: 1) The certainty with which the long-term economic characteristics of the business can be evaluated; 2) The certainty with which management can be evaluated, both as to its ability to realize the full potential of the business and to wisely employ its cash flows; 3) The certainty with which management can be counted on to channel the rewards from the business to the shareholders rather than to itself; 4) The purchase price of the business; 5) The levels of taxation and inflation that will be experienced and that will determine the degree by which an investor's purchasing-power return is reduced from his gross return.
concept: Real risk is failing to get back purchasing power plus modest interest after tax; judged by certainty about the business, the managers' ability and honesty, the price, and tax and inflation.
evolution_notes: Elided: 'Though this risk cannot be calculated with engineering precision, it can in some cases be judged with a degree of accuracy that is useful.' Followed by the Justice Stewart 'I know it when I see it' comparison.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Common Stock Investments

quote_verbatim: The might of their brand names, the attributes of their products, and the strength of their distribution systems give them an enormous competitive advantage, setting up a protective moat around their economic castles. The average company, in contrast, does battle daily without any such means of protection.
concept: A moat is the brand, product and distribution strength that protects an economic castle; most companies fight daily without one.
evolution_notes: Context: Coke and Gillette 'have actually increased their worldwide shares of market in recent years'; Peter Lynch's warning label on commodity-like products follows.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Common Stock Investments

quote_verbatim: The theoretician bred on beta has no mechanism for differentiating the risk inherent in, say, a single-product toy company selling pet rocks or hula hoops from that of another toy company whose sole product is Monopoly or Barbie. But it's quite possible for ordinary investors to make such distinctions if they have a reasonable understanding of consumer behavior and the factors that create long-term competitive strength or weakness. Obviously, every investor will make mistakes. But by confining himself to a relatively few, easy-to-understand cases, a reasonably intelligent, informed and diligent person can judge investment risks with a useful degree of accuracy.
concept: Tell a fad (pet rock) from a durable franchise (Barbie) by understanding consumers and competitive strength; confine yourself to few, easy cases.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Common Stock Investments

quote_verbatim: In many industries, of course, Charlie and I can't determine whether we are dealing with a "pet rock" or a "Barbie." We couldn't solve this problem, moreover, even if we were to spend years intensely studying those industries. Sometimes our own intellectual shortcomings would stand in the way of understanding, and in other cases the nature of the industry would be the roadblock. For example, a business that must deal with fast-moving technology is not going to lend itself to reliable evaluations of its long-term economics. [...] We'll stick instead with the easy cases. Why search for a needle buried in a haystack when one is sitting in plain sight?
concept: Where the industry or the analyst's limits make long-term economics unknowable, such as fast-moving technology, pass and stick to easy cases.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Common Stock Investments

quote_verbatim: Of course, some investment strategies - for instance, our efforts in arbitrage over the years - require wide diversification. If significant risk exists in a single transaction, overall risk should be reduced by making that purchase one of many mutually-independent commitments. Thus, you may consciously purchase a risky investment - one that indeed has a significant possibility of causing loss or injury - if you believe that your gain, weighted for probabilities, considerably exceeds your loss, comparably weighted, and if you can commit to a number of similar, but unrelated opportunities.
concept: Risky individual bets are acceptable only with a favourable probability-weighted payoff and many independent such bets, like a casino.
evolution_notes: Continues: 'adopt the outlook of the casino that owns a roulette wheel ... but will refuse to accept a single, huge bet.'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Common Stock Investments

quote_verbatim: Another situation requiring wide diversification occurs when an investor who does not understand the economics of specific businesses nevertheless believes it in his interest to be a long-term owner of American industry. That investor should both own a large number of equities and space out his purchases. By periodically investing in an index fund, for example, the know-nothing investor can actually out-perform most investment professionals. Paradoxically, when "dumb" money acknowledges its limitations, it ceases to be dumb.
concept: An investor who cannot judge businesses should diversify widely and buy an index fund periodically.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Common Stock Investments

quote_verbatim: On the other hand, if you are a know-something investor, able to understand business economics and to find five to ten sensibly-priced companies that possess important long-term competitive advantages, conventional diversification makes no sense for you. It is apt simply to hurt your results and increase your risk. I cannot understand why an investor of that sort elects to put money into a business that is his 20th favorite rather than simply adding that money to his top choices - the businesses he understands best and that present the least risk, along with the greatest profit potential.
concept: An investor who can find five to ten sensibly priced advantaged businesses should concentrate in his best-understood choices, not diversify.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Common Stock Investments

quote_verbatim: In that case, I believe directors should behave as if there is a single absentee owner, whose long-term interest they should try to further in all proper ways. Unfortunately, "long-term" gives directors a lot of wiggle room. If they lack either integrity or the ability to think independently, directors can do great violence to shareholders while still claiming to be acting in their long-term interest.
concept: Directors should act for a single absentee owner; 'long-term' is the cover under which directors without integrity harm owners.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Corporate Governance

quote_verbatim: The requisites for board membership should be business savvy, interest in the job, and owner-orientation. Too often, directors are selected simply because they are prominent or add diversity to the board. That practice is a mistake. Furthermore, mistakes in selecting directors are particularly serious because appointments are so hard to undo: The pleasant but vacuous director need never worry about job security.
concept: Directors should be chosen for business savvy, interest and owner-orientation, not prominence; bad choices are hard to undo.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Corporate Governance

quote_verbatim: If change does not come, and the matter is sufficiently serious, the outside directors should resign. Their resignation will signal their doubts about management, and it will emphasize that no outsider is in a position to correct the owner/manager's shortcomings.
concept: Where a controlling owner-manager will not change, outside directors' only remedy on a serious matter is to resign.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Corporate Governance

quote_verbatim: At Berkshire, we believe that the company's money is the owners' money, just as it would be in a closely-held corporation, partnership, or sole proprietorship. Therefore, if funds are to be given to causes unrelated to Berkshire's business activities, it is the charities favored by our owners that should receive them. We've yet to find a CEO who believes he should personally fund the charities favored by his shareholders. Why, then, should they foot the bill for his picks?
concept: Company money is the owners' money; a CEO should not spend it on his own charitable choices.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Shareholder-Designated Contributions

quote_verbatim: At the time of our purchase, we knew that the economic prospects of the company were good. But equally important, Charlie and I concluded that Kay would prove to be an outstanding manager and would treat all shareholders honorably. That latter consideration was particularly important because The Washington Post Company has two classes of stock, a structure that we've seen some managers abuse.
concept: Good economics plus a manager judged able and honorable to all holders; honour matters most where dual-class stock allows abuse.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: A Few Personal Items

quote_verbatim: The two of them took hold of a company that had stagnated during the previous decade and moved it from $4.4 billion of market value to $58 billion in less than 13 years. What a difference a pair of managers like this makes, even when their product has been around for 100 years.
concept: Management can transform even a century-old franchise that had stagnated; the managers are part of the case.
evolution_notes: Just before: impressions of Don Keough formed as a neighbour in 1958 were 'a factor in my decision' to buy Coca-Cola in 1988-89.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: A Few Personal Items

quote_verbatim: because they lend themselves to the use of unusual amounts of leverage and they’re sometimes not completely understood by the people involved. And any time you combine ignorance and borrowed money — (laughter) — you can get some pretty interesting consequences. (Laughter) Particularly when the numbers get vague. [...] And it — the ability to borrow enormous amounts of money combined with a chance to get either very rich or very poor very quickly, has historically been a recipe for trouble at some point.
concept: Leverage joined to instruments the users do not understand, with vague numbers, is a recipe for trouble.
evolution_notes: Example given: P&G going 'from selling soap to writing puts on bonds'. Munger asked if Berkshire does anything approaching derivatives: 'No.'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 11. Derivatives: dangerous combination of “ignorance and borrowed money”

quote_verbatim: We could conceivably buy a business — I don’t think we would be likely to — but we could we could conceivably buy a business that had no current after-tax cash flow. But, we would have to think it had a tremendous future. [...] But if we think the present value of the future earning power is attractive enough compared to the purchase price, we would not be overwhelmed by what the first year’s figure would be.
concept: The test is present value of future earning power against price, not the current year's cash flow, though current figures are usually representative.
evolution_notes: GEICO cited as bought while losing significant money.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 13. Unlikely we’d buy company with no current cash flow

quote_verbatim: Yeah. We don’t care what we report in the first year or two of — after buying anything.
concept: Reported results in the first year or two after a purchase do not matter.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 13. Unlikely we’d buy company with no current cash flow

quote_verbatim: Well, I would say that in a world of 7 percent long-term bond rates that we would certainly want to think we were discounting future after-tax streams of cash at at least a 10 percent rate. But that will depend on the certainty we feel about the business. The more certain we feel about a business, the closer we are willing to play it. We have to feel pretty certain about any business before we’re even interested at all. But there are still degrees of certainty, and — If we thought we were getting a stream of cash over the next 30 years that we felt extremely certain about, we would use a discount rate that would be somewhat less than if it was one where we thought we might get some surprises in five or 10 years — possibility existed.
concept: Discount rate set above the long bond and varied by certainty: the surer the cash stream, the closer to the bond rate; pretty high certainty is the entry ticket.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 13. Unlikely we’d buy company with no current cash flow

quote_verbatim: And I think that the table in the report that shows you what our cost to float has been over the years, and also what the trend of float has been over the years, would, unless you thought that table had no validity for the future, I think that that table would tend to the point you in the direction of saying the insurance business does have a very significant excess of intrinsic value over carrying value. Very hard number to put something on. But — and you don’t want to extrapolate that table out.
concept: An insurer's value over book is read from the history of its cost of float and the growth of float, without extrapolating it.
evolution_notes: Ties to L1993-009 and L1993-010 (the letter's float table and float definition).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 14. Insurance business intrinsic value is well above book value

quote_verbatim: I think the idea of carving ownerships in an enterprise into little, tiny $20 pieces is almost insane. And it’s quite inefficient to service a $20 account and I don’t see why there shouldn’t be a minimum as a condition of joining some enterprise.
concept: No stock split: ownership should not be carved into tiny pieces.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 15. Why Berkshire doesn’t split its stock

quote_verbatim: And you can start with the As and work through to the Zs and you’ll — every company in the New York Stock Exchange, one way or another, has attracted some constituency of shareholders. [...] I mean, we have — we don’t think we can improve on this group, and we followed certain policies that we think attracted certain types of shareholders and actually pushed away others.
concept: A company's policies select its shareholders; choose policies that attract long-term owners and repel the rest.
evolution_notes: Continues at line 173: a policy that draws buyers 'for the wrong reason' only replaces someone already in the room.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 15. Why Berkshire doesn’t split its stock

quote_verbatim: Well, I think you judge management by two yardsticks. One is how well they run the business and I think you can learn a lot about that by reading about both what they’ve accomplished and what their competitors have accomplished, and seeing how they have allocated capital over time. You have to have some understanding of the hand they were dealt when they themselves got a chance to play the hand. [...] And then the second thing you want to figure out is how well that they treat their owners.
concept: Judge managers by how well they play the hand dealt, against competitors and in capital allocation, and by how they treat owners.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 18. “Two yardsticks” for judging management

quote_verbatim: It’s interesting how often the ones that, in my view, are the poor managers also turn out to be the ones that really don’t think that much about the shareholders, too. The two often go hand in hand. [...] I mean they come about by reading reports rather than any intimate personal knowledge or — and knowing them personally at all. So it — you know, read the proxy statements, see what they think of — see how they treat themselves versus how they treat the shareholders, look at what they have accomplished, considering what the hand was that they were dealt when they took over compared to what is going on in the industry.
concept: Managers can be judged from reports and proxy statements: how they treat themselves versus owners; poor operators and poor stewards tend to coincide.
evolution_notes: Also in this answer: 'you don’t have to make a hundred correct judgments in this business or 50 correct judgments. You only have to make a few.' Compare L1993-015.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 18. “Two yardsticks” for judging management

quote_verbatim: Charlie and I have two jobs. We have to identify and keep good managers interested after we’ve figured out who they are. And that often is a little different here, because I would say a majority of our managers are financially independent, so that they don’t go to work because they are worried about putting kids through school or putting food on the table. So they have to have some reason to go to work aside from that.
concept: The chairman's jobs are to find and keep good managers, many of them rich, who must have a reason beyond money to work; and to allocate capital.
evolution_notes: At line 215: 'the important thing we do with managers, generally, is to find the .400 hitters and then not tell them how to swing, as I put in the report. The second thing we do is allocate capital.' Compare L1993-005.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 19. How Berkshire keeps great managers

quote_verbatim: We have no company-wide compensation plan. We wouldn’t dream of having some compensation expert or consultant come in and screw it up. (Laughter) [...] People, generally, are compensated relating in some manner that relates to how their business does as opposed to — there’s no reason to pay anybody based on how Berkshire does, because no one has responsibility for Berkshire except for Charlie and me. And we try to make them responsible for their own units, compensated based on how those units do.
concept: Pay each manager on his own unit's results under a plan fitted to that business, never a company-wide formula.
evolution_notes: Between the two sentences: some businesses need much capital, some none; 'it would be crazy to have some huge framework ... where one size would fit all.'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 19. How Berkshire keeps great managers

quote_verbatim: Well, I’ve got nothing to add, but I think that concept of treating the other fellow the way you’d like to be treated if the roles were reversed — it’s so simple, when you stop to think about it, but —
concept: Treat managers as you would want to be treated if the roles were reversed.
evolution_notes: Munger adds at line 223: 'we like our businesses — our relationships — to be more than a business relationship'.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 19. How Berkshire keeps great managers

quote_verbatim: We think our stock is more likely to be rationally priced over time following the present policies than if we were to split it in some major way. And we don’t think the average price would necessarily be higher. We think that the volatility would probably be somewhat greater, and we see no way that volatility helps our shareholders as a group.
concept: A company should seek a rationally priced stock; volatility in its own shares does not help its owners as a group.
evolution_notes: Pulls against L1993-018 ('the true investor welcomes volatility'): there volatility in a stock one buys is opportunity; here volatility in Berkshire's own stock helps no shareholder group. The two may be reconciled by buyer versus existing-owner standpoint; the speaker does not reconcile them here.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 25. Stock split wouldn’t raise long-term average price

quote_verbatim: If you talk to one person, you’d hear one thing, and you’d talk to another — you really should not make decisions in securities based on what other people think. If you’re doing that, you should think about doing something else, because it’s — A public opinion poll will just — it will not get you rich on Wall Street. So you really want to stick with businesses that you feel you can somehow evaluate yourself. [...] You cannot get rich with a weather vane.
concept: Decide on your own evaluation of a business, never on others' opinions, forecasts or analysts' views.
evolution_notes: Elided: 'Charlie and I, we don’t read anything about what business is going to be — the economy is going to do, or the market’s going to do'.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 27. Don’t pay attention to what people say about stocks

quote_verbatim: We certainly like it, if we were to own a bank, we would — or own shares in a bank — we would like the idea of the bank repurchasing its stock at a price that we thought was attractive. We would think that they probably knew more about their own bank than some other bank they were going to buy and that if the numbers are right, it’s an attractive way to use capital.
concept: Buying back stock at an attractive price is a sound use of capital, since management knows its own company better than an acquisition target.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 28. Judge bank stock buybacks on case-by-case basis

quote_verbatim: at Berkshire, it absolutely makes no difference to us what accounting treatment we get on something. We are interested in the economics of a transaction. [...] We don’t care what accounting — we sort of rewrite the accounting for any business that we’re looking at, because in our heads we want to have, in effect, a standardized way of looking at businesses.
concept: Judge a transaction by its economics, not its accounting; recast every business's accounts to a common basis.

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 29. We don’t pay attention to accounting of a transaction

The figures are frequently quite silly on a functional basis. [...] But, I think it’s just a place to start thinking about economic reality. By their nature, they can’t tie perfectly — they can’t even tie very well — to economic reality.
concept: Published accounts are a starting point for economic analysis and cannot tie well to economic reality.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 29. We don’t pay attention to accounting of a transaction

quote_verbatim: We regard it is a negative when we find a management that’s preoccupied with accounting considerations. But, we find it so frequent that we can’t afford to use it as a total exclusionary factor. [...] If you find a management that doesn’t care about the accounting but does explain to you in clear terms what’s going on, I think you should regard that as a plus in owning a security.
concept: A management preoccupied with accounting is a negative though not disqualifying; one that explains clearly and ignores accounting cosmetics is a plus.
speaker: BUFFETT
