speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 3. Breaking up Berkshire wouldn’t help

quote_verbatim: Berkshire is incredibly decentralized, in the — in terms of power and decisions resting in the operating divisions. In terms of the marketable securities, it’s incredibly centralized.
concept: Operating decisions sit with the operating units; investment of surplus capital is held at the centre.
evolution_notes: Munger adds: 'Eventually we will reach the penalty' of size. Heading 24 of this session develops the same split for capital allocation.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 3. Breaking up Berkshire wouldn’t help

quote_verbatim: We think the management of General Dynamics has done an absolutely sensational job. Obviously, also it isn’t the kind of business, basically, that we have a 20-year view on, or something of the sort.
concept: Excellent management does not by itself make a business one to hold for twenty years; the business's own durability sets the holding view.
evolution_notes: Said while declining to explain a partial sale. Consistent with L1993-014, which reserves tenacious holding for durably wonderful businesses.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 4. “Absolutely sensational job” by General Dynamics management

quote_verbatim: Our best way to handle that is to give all the information we can to shareholders and prospective shareholders, and follow policies that we think will induce the investment-oriented with long time horizons to join us, and not to encourage other people. [...] Which, you know, has always struck me as like having a house that you like, and you’re living in, and, you know, it’s worth $100,000 and you tell your broker, you know, if anybody ever comes along and offers 90, you want to sell it.
concept: Full information and owner-minded policies attract long-horizon holders; a stop-loss on a business you like is as senseless as one on the house you live in.
evolution_notes: Restates M1994-007 (policies select shareholders) and M1994-013 (rational price, not volatility, is the aim for one's own stock).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 5. No encouragement for short-term stockholders

quote_verbatim: But A, we do generate cash in considerable amounts, so that we will not husband cash, simply because we think the market’s going to go down, in order to buy something. [...] But it isn’t like we can change around the whole portfolio then, because that doesn’t gain us anything. I mean, we’d be selling things at lower prices to buy things at lower prices. [...] But if you asked us next month whether Berkshire would be better off if the whole stock market were down 50 percent or where it is now, we would be better off if it was down 50 percent, whether we had any cash on hand now or not, because we would be generating cash to buy things.
concept: Do not hoard cash against a market fall; a falling market helps a steady net buyer, and rotating the existing portfolio in a fall gains nothing.
evolution_notes: Extends M1994-036 (a net buyer welcomes falling prices) and M1994-049 (cash is a residue, not an allocation).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 6. Berkshire benefits when the stock market falls

quote_verbatim: The trick is to pay them only when you’re getting very big results for the owners. I mean, it — there’s no way you’re going to pay numbers that look like numbers in other industries, and get great results for owners. But if you pay these big numbers, I think you should be getting very good results for owners.
concept: Where big pay is the norm, tie it to very big results for the owners; big pay without them is the failure.
evolution_notes: Heading 20 of this session: Munger on a Salomon target 'hellishly hard to hit', 'if that happens, you’ll be very glad to pay the money'. Compare M1994-011 (pay on the unit's own results).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 7. Salomon’s compensation: “Far from ideal”

quote_verbatim: But we’re better off, probably — if we like something well enough to write a put on it, we’re probably better off buying the security itself, and particularly since we can’t do it in the kind of quantities that really would make it meaningful to Berkshire. [...] And on balance, I don’t think it’s as useful a way to spend my time as just looking for securities to buy outright.
concept: If you like a security enough to write a put on it, buy the security; time is better spent finding outright purchases.
evolution_notes: Buffett notes the 1993 Coke puts earned about 7.5 million dollars but says Berkshire is unlikely to do much of it again.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 8. Unlikely to write put options on Coca-Cola again

quote_verbatim: I don’t think people should be buying stocks because they’re reading in the paper that we’re buying something.
concept: Do not buy a stock because Berkshire is reported to be buying it.
evolution_notes: Buffett says well over half such press reports have been wrong and Berkshire never corrects them, since correcting the false ones would identify the true. Compare M1994-014 (decide on your own evaluation).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 9. Don’t believe reports on what we’re buying or selling

quote_verbatim: We are willing to put a lot of money into a single security. When I ran the partnership, the limit I got to was about 40 percent in a single stock. [...] Because, no, we’re not going to do that unless we think we understand the business very well, and we think the nature of the business, what we’re paying for it, the people running it, and all of that lead up to virtually no risk, and — But you find those things, occasionally. And we would put — assuming it were that much more attractive than the second, and third, and fourth choices — we would put a big percentage of our net worth in it.
concept: Put a large share of net worth in one security when the business is well understood and business, price and people together leave virtually no risk, and it beats the next choices by a wide margin.
evolution_notes: Munger confirms he too exceeded 40 percent in one holding. Restates L1993-026 (concentrate in best-understood businesses) and L1993-016 (concentration can lower risk).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 11. Diversify if you don’t understand businesses

quote_verbatim: but we would only advise you to do it, if you’re doing it based on your conclusions about — your own ideas of value, and something that you really feel you know enough to buy the whole business, if your funds were sufficient, and it was being offered to you. You ought to really understand the business. [...] So it’s not crazy, if you understand the business well, and if the price is sufficiently attractive, to put a very significant percentage of your net worth in. If you don’t understand businesses, then you’re better off diversifying and fairly widely diversifying.
concept: Concentrate only on your own idea of value, in something you know well enough to buy the whole business; if you do not understand businesses, diversify widely.
evolution_notes: Buffett notes people routinely put most of their net worth into a farm or filling station. Munger follows with the story of an heir who refused a trust officer's advice to diversify out of Berkshire (not rowed: an anecdote with no stated principle). Restates L1993-025.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 11. Diversify if you don’t understand businesses

quote_verbatim: But the one thing I can assure you is that, probably, if you spend a relatively small amount of time on it, the facts that you will have available to you for making a decision on that question will be just as good, essentially, as the facts you’d get if you’d worked at the Coca-Cola Company for 20 years, or if you were a food and beverage analyst in Wall Street or anything of the sort. That’s the kind of businesses we like to look at, are things that we think we can understand that way.
concept: A preferred business is one whose public reports, read briefly, give an outsider facts as good as an insider's twenty years.
evolution_notes: Buffett opens: 'You really have to come to your own conclusion' and closes 'we don’t like you to give you our answers', restating M1994-014. Compare M1994-027 and M1994-052.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 12. We don’t like to “give you our answers” on Coca-Cola

quote_verbatim: But it is a disadvantage. Size is a disadvantage, you’re absolutely correct in the basic point, both in buying and in selling. And we don’t know any way around that. We allow for it, in terms of what we expect, you know, the kind of possibilities we need to see.
concept: Size hurts in both buying and selling and cannot be engineered away; allow for it in the opportunities required.
evolution_notes: Heading 3 of this session: 'your universe of opportunity shrinks' with size, and Munger's 'Eventually we will reach the penalty'. Buffett adds that selling so rarely keeps it from being a crusher.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 14. “Size is a disadvantage” in buying and selling

quote_verbatim: We have no key man insurance. It really doesn’t — it wouldn’t be material. [...] And basically, the math of intelligently selling insurance is better than the math of intelligently buying insurance.
concept: Do not buy insurance against immaterial risks; the arithmetic favours the intelligent seller of insurance over the buyer.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 15. No key man insurance for Buffett and Munger

quote_verbatim: If you own Coca-Cola, you own a bunch of foreign bonds with coupons on them, denominated in local currencies, that go on forever.
concept: Owning a business with foreign earnings is owning perpetual coupons of unknown size paid in foreign currencies.
evolution_notes: Ties to M1994-047 and heading 22 of this session: value is the discounted stream of cash.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 17. Berkshire doesn’t hedge currencies

quote_verbatim: We basically don’t think it’s worth it. We don’t think our opinion on currencies is any good. [...] we do not know more than the market does about currencies. So there are costs to hedging. [...] But we see no reason to incur those costs with what we regard as a — totally, a 50-50 proposition. [...] But if you take that — the way we look at businesses, being the discounted flow of future cash out between now and Judgment Day, we can’t really hedge that kind of a risk anyway.
concept: No currency hedging: no edge over the market on currencies, a cost for a 50-50 bet, and a perpetual cash stream cannot be hedged anyway.
evolution_notes: Buffett adds they would slightly prefer dollar earnings and would dislike very weak currencies. Compare M1994-035 and M1994-037 (no market or macro opinion).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 17. Berkshire doesn’t hedge currencies

quote_verbatim: Obviously, it’s easier to understand the future of a Coca-Cola than it is a Salomon. But that doesn’t mean it’s a better buy.
concept: A more understandable future does not by itself make the better purchase; price can favour the harder business.
evolution_notes: Pulls against M1994-027 (prefer easy-to-understand businesses), M1994-071 (heading 12) and M1994-078 (heading 22: more concerned with certainty than with the cheapest-looking number). Buffett adds that Salomon is still volatile and carries the systemic risk of any investment or commercial bank, and that holdings reflect when money was available as much as preference. He does not reconcile the two statements.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 21. Salomon is a “better company than it was some years back”

quote_verbatim: But the economic value of any asset, essentially, is the present value, the appropriate interest rate, of all the future streams of cash going in or out of the business. And there are all kinds of businesses that Charlie and I don’t think we have the faintest idea what that future stream will look like. And if we don’t have the faintest idea what the future stream is going to look like, we don’t have the faintest idea what it’s worth, now.
concept: Economic value is the discounted future cash in and out; where the stream cannot be foreseen, the value is unknown.
evolution_notes: Buffett points to the 1992 report for the fuller discussion and calls pricing a stock without a view of the cash stream 'cognitive dissonance'. Restates M1994-047 and L1993-001.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 22. Calculating intrinsic value

quote_verbatim: So we are looking for things where we feel — fairly high degree of probability — that we can come within a range of looking at those numbers out over a period of time, and then we discount them back. And we are more concerned with the certainty of those numbers than we are with getting the one that looks absolutely the cheapest, but based upon numbers that we don’t have any — we don’t have great confidence in.
concept: Seek businesses whose cash can be estimated within a range with high probability; prefer certainty of the numbers over the cheapest-looking number resting on weak confidence.
evolution_notes: Compare M1994-004 (discount rate varied by certainty). In tension with M1994-076 (heading 21).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 22. Calculating intrinsic value

quote_verbatim: The numbers in any accounting report mean nothing, per se, as to economic value. They are guidelines to tell you something about how to get at economic value. [...] And to figure out that answer, you have to understand something about business. You don’t have to understand a lot about mathematics. [...] And of course, if we find numbers where it looks like people are taking the most optimistic interpretation of things that they can under GAAP and all of that, we get very worried about people who look like they massage the numbers in any way.
concept: Accounts are guidelines to value read with business understanding, not answers; the most optimistic reading of GAAP is a warning about the people.
evolution_notes: Buffett likens the work to buying an apartment house or a farm: what is laid out, what comes back, how certain, against alternatives. Restates M1994-017 and M1994-018.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 22. Calculating intrinsic value

quote_verbatim: We are willing to — [...] — buy companies that aren’t going to grow at all. [...] It — assuming we get enough for our money when we do it.
concept: Growth is not required; a business with none is acceptable if the price gives enough for the money.
evolution_notes: The elisions cover the questioner's interjections; the sentence is Buffett's across three lines.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 23. Growth alone doesn’t make a company a good investment

quote_verbatim: But you can certainly have a situation where there’s absolutely no growth in the business, and it’s a much better investment than some company that’s going to grow at very substantial rates, particularly if they’re going to need capital in order to grow. There’s a huge difference in the business that grows and requires a lot of capital to do so, and the business that grows, and doesn’t require capital. And I would say that, generally, financial analysts do not give adequate weight to the difference in those. [...] Our — some of our best businesses that we own outright don’t grow. But they throw off lots of money, which we can use to buy something else. And therefore, our capital is growing, without physical growth being in the business.
concept: Ask whether growth consumes capital; growth needing much capital can be worth less than no growth that throws off cash for redeployment.
evolution_notes: Munger: 'it’s fairly simple, but it’s not so simple it can all be explained in one sentence.' Buffett: 'A lot of managements don’t understand that very well, actually.' Compare M1994-051 (rising share alone does not make a wonderful business).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 23. Growth alone doesn’t make a company a good investment

quote_verbatim: And we allocate all the capital ourselves. I mean, that is our job. [...] And so many CEOs, when they get there, think they can solve it by either having a staff that does it, or by hiring consultants, or whatever it may be. [...] And in our view, that is — and that’s a terrible mistake, because it’s — it is, if not the key function of the CEO, it’s one of two or three key functions at say 80 or 90 percent of all companies. And if you can’t do it yourself, you’re going to make a lot of mistakes.
concept: Capital allocation is a chief executive's own job and is not delegated to staff or consultants.
evolution_notes: Compare M1994-062 (Munger: centralized securities) and M1994-008 (managers judged on capital allocation).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 24. Capital allocation shouldn’t be delegated

quote_verbatim: And if you take a CEO that’s in a job for 10 years, and he has a business that earns, say, 12 percent on equity, and he’s — and he pays out a third, that means he’s got 8 percent per year of equity. I mean, when you think of his tenure in office, how much capital he’s allocated, it’s an enormous factor over time. And yet, probably relatively few chief executives are either trained for, or are selected on, the basis of their ability to allocate capital.
concept: Retained earnings over a CEO's tenure make allocation an enormous factor, yet few CEOs are chosen or trained for it; ask whether this one can do it.
evolution_notes: Buffett's image: a lifelong pianist handed a violin at Carnegie Hall.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 24. Capital allocation shouldn’t be delegated

quote_verbatim: And Charlie and I take responsibility for all capital allocation decisions, other than just, sort of, routine expenditures at the operating businesses. And we don’t get into those at all. [...] We think those people know how to allocate the money that relates to the actual operations of their business. We think, in terms of the capital that is generated above that, that that’s our job.
concept: Operating managers allocate the capital their operations need without review; the surplus above that is allocated at the top.
evolution_notes: No headquarters staff; Munger: 'we have practically nobody at headquarters in Omaha.' Same split as M1994-062.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 24. Capital allocation shouldn’t be delegated

quote_verbatim: But Keynes started off with the wrong theory, I would say, in the ’20s and essentially tried to predict business cycles in markets, and then shifted to fundamental analysis of businesses in the ’30s, and did extremely well.
concept: Predicting cycles and markets failed Keynes; fundamental analysis of businesses succeeded.
evolution_notes: A third party's mistake narrated with its lesson, not the speaker's own. Buffett also recommends the General Theory chapter on market psychology and Keynes's letters, and says Keynes diversified far less than Graham (named by Buffett; not quoted here). Compare M1994-035 and M1994-038.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 25. Keynes: Great “wisdom” about investing

quote_verbatim: The problem is not that what has worked in the past will cease to work in the future.  To the contrary, we believe that our formula - the purchase at sensible prices of businesses that have good underlying economics and are run by honest and able people - is certain to produce reasonable success.
concept: The method in one line: buy at sensible prices businesses with good underlying economics run by honest and able people.
evolution_notes: The opening section carries no section title; the letter's own title line is the heading, as the 1994 AM unit set. Followed by: a fat wallet is the enemy of superior results.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Chairman's Letter - 1994

quote_verbatim: A fat wallet, however, is the enemy of superior investment results. [...] Though there are as many good businesses as ever, it is useless for us to make purchases that are inconsequential in relation to Berkshire's capital. [...] We now consider a security for purchase only if we believe we can deploy at least $100 million in it.
concept: Size of capital handicaps returns; a purchase too small to matter to the whole is not worth making.
evolution_notes: Munger quoted inside: 'If something is not worth doing at all, it's not worth doing well.' Compare M1994-072 (size a disadvantage).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Chairman's Letter - 1994

quote_verbatim: Nevertheless, we will stick with the approach that got us here and try not to relax our standards. [...] Charlie and I agree and will try to wait for opportunities that are well within our own "happy zone."
concept: Do not relax standards under pressure of size; wait for the pitch inside one's own zone.
evolution_notes: The elided text is Ted Williams on waiting for a good ball to hit; the book title is broken across lines 38-40 in the source, left out of the quote for that reason.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Chairman's Letter - 1994

quote_verbatim: We will continue to ignore political and economic forecasts, which are an expensive distraction for many investors and businessmen. [...] Imagine the cost to us, then, if we had let a fear of unknowns cause us to defer or alter the deployment of capital.  Indeed, we have usually made our best purchases when apprehensions about some macro event were at a peak.  Fear is the foe of the faddist, but the friend of the fundamentalist.
concept: Ignore macro and political forecasts; macro fear is the time to buy, not to wait.
evolution_notes: Followed (lines 64-68): 'A different set of major shocks is sure to occur in the next 30 years. We will neither try to predict these nor to profit from them. If we can identify businesses similar to those we have purchased in the past, external surprises will have little effect on our long-term results.'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Chairman's Letter - 1994

quote_verbatim: If you suffer, we will suffer; if we prosper, so will you.  And we will not break this bond by introducing compensation arrangements that give us a greater participation in the upside than the downside. [...] We will not ask you to invest with us and then put our own money elsewhere.
concept: Managers' pay and personal wealth should share owners' downside as well as upside, with their own money in the same stock.
evolution_notes: Repeats L1993-004 (no options or restricted shares, net worth in Berkshire).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Chairman's Letter - 1994

quote_verbatim: It's far better to own a significant portion of the Hope diamond than 100% of a rhinestone, and the companies just mentioned easily qualify as rare gems.
concept: A part interest in an outstanding business beats full control of a mediocre one.
evolution_notes: The gems named just before are Coca-Cola, Gillette and Wells Fargo, each expressed as Berkshire's proportional share of servings, blade sales and bank earnings.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Chairman's Letter - 1994

quote_verbatim: We define intrinsic value as the discounted value of the cash that can be taken out of a business during its remaining life.  Anyone calculating intrinsic value necessarily comes up with a highly subjective figure that will change both as estimates of future cash flows are revised and as interest rates move.  Despite its fuzziness, however, intrinsic value is all-important and is the only logical way to evaluate the relative attractiveness of investments and businesses.
concept: Intrinsic value is discounted future cash; it is subjective and moves with estimates and rates, but it is the only logical yardstick.
evolution_notes: Restates L1993-001 and M1994-077. Section opens: intrinsic value is 'a number that is impossible to pinpoint but essential to estimate.'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Book Value and Intrinsic Value

quote_verbatim: First, we must estimate the earnings that the graduate will receive over his lifetime and subtract from that figure an estimate of what he would have earned had he lacked his education.  That gives us an excess earnings figure, which must then be discounted, at an appropriate interest rate, back to graduation day.  The dollar result equals the intrinsic economic value of the education. [...] In all cases, what is clear is that book value is meaningless as an indicator of intrinsic value.
concept: Cost put in (book value) and discounted future output (intrinsic value) are different things; the first says nothing about the second.
evolution_notes: The college-education analogy; the cost includes earnings foregone.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Book Value and Intrinsic Value

quote_verbatim: You might expect that Scott Fetzer's success could only be explained by a cyclical peak in earnings, a monopolistic position, or leverage.  But no such circumstances apply.  Rather, the company's success comes from the managerial expertise of CEO Ralph Schey, of whom I'll tell you more later.
concept: Before crediting a high return on equity, rule out a cyclical peak, a monopoly position and leverage as its source.
evolution_notes: Just before (lines 239-245): no leverage added, debt reduced to virtually none, no sale-leasebacks, no sold receivables; a 'conservatively-financed and liquid enterprise'. Also excludes bankruptcy debt-forgiveness windfalls from the return-on-equity ranking.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Book Value and Intrinsic Value

quote_verbatim: These charges have no effect on cash or the taxes we pay, and are not, in our view, an economic cost (though many accountants would disagree with us).
concept: Amortization of an acquisition premium is a bookkeeping charge, not an economic cost.
evolution_notes: Followed by: carrying value of Scott Fetzer halved while its earnings doubled, so intrinsic value grew while book value was marked down.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Book Value and Intrinsic Value

quote_verbatim: Ben Graham taught me 45 years ago that in investing it is not necessary to do extraordinary things to get extraordinary results.  In later life, I have been surprised to find that this statement holds true in business management as well.  What a manager must do is handle the basics well and not get diverted.  That's precisely Ralph's formula.  He establishes the right goals and never forgets what he set out to do.  On the personal side, Ralph is a joy to work with.  He's forthright about problems and is self-confident without being self-important.
concept: A good manager handles the basics, sets the right goals, stays undiverted, and is candid about problems without self-importance.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Book Value and Intrinsic Value

quote_verbatim: At Berkshire, we look to performance, not to the calendar.
concept: No mandatory retirement; managers are kept on performance, not age.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Book Value and Intrinsic Value

quote_verbatim: Understanding intrinsic value is as important for managers as it is for investors.  When managers are making capital allocation decisions - including decisions to repurchase shares - it's vital that they act in ways that increase per-share intrinsic value and avoid moves that decrease it.  This principle may seem obvious but we constantly see it violated.
concept: Every capital allocation decision, buybacks included, is judged by whether it raises per-share intrinsic value.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Intrinsic Value and Capital Allocation

quote_verbatim: In corporate transactions, it's equally silly for the would-be purchaser to focus on current earnings when the prospective acquiree has either different prospects, different amounts of non-operating assets, or a different capital structure.  At Berkshire, we have rejected many merger and purchase opportunities that would have boosted current and near-term earnings but that would have reduced per-share intrinsic value.
concept: Whether a deal is accretive to current earnings per share is the wrong test; reject deals that lift near-term earnings but cut per-share value.
evolution_notes: Illustrated by the MBA student merging with a day laborer; followed by Gretzky, 'Go to where the puck is going to be.'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Intrinsic Value and Capital Allocation

quote_verbatim: But, alas, they usually reduce the wealth of the acquirer's shareholders, often to a substantial extent.  That happens because the acquirer typically gives up more intrinsic value than it receives.
concept: Most big acquisitions destroy the buyer's value because it gives more intrinsic value than it gets.
evolution_notes: Just before: acquisitions are a bonanza for the acquiree's holders, raise acquirer management's income and status, and are a honey pot for bankers. Medlin: 'a chain letter in reverse.'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Intrinsic Value and Capital Allocation

quote_verbatim: Over time, the skill with which a company's managers allocate capital has an enormous impact on the enterprise's value.  Almost by definition, a really good business generates far more money (at least after its early years) than it can use internally.  The company could, of course, distribute the money to shareholders by way of dividends or share repurchases.  But often the CEO asks a strategic planning staff, consultants or investment bankers whether an acquisition or two might make sense.  That's like asking your interior decorator whether you need a $50,000 rug.
concept: A good business throws off more cash than it can use; what management does with the surplus decides much of its value, and advisers paid on deals are the wrong people to ask.
evolution_notes: Compare M1994-082 and M1994-083 (capital allocation is the CEO's job; CEOs rarely chosen for it).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Intrinsic Value and Capital Allocation

quote_verbatim: The acquisition problem is often compounded by a biological bias:  Many CEO's attain their positions in part because they possess an abundance of animal spirits and ego.  If an executive is heavily endowed with these qualities - which, it should be acknowledged, sometimes have their advantages - they won't disappear when he reaches the top.
concept: Expect ego and animal spirits in a CEO to drive deal-making; the trait that got him the job keeps operating.
evolution_notes: Followed by the insurer CEO's 'Aw, fellas, all the other kids have one.'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Intrinsic Value and Capital Allocation

quote_verbatim: As a first step, these managers will look for ways to deploy their earnings advantageously in their businesses.  What's left, they will send to Charlie and me.  We then will try to use those funds in ways that build per-share intrinsic value.  Our goal will be to acquire either part or all of businesses that we believe we understand, that have good, sustainable underlying economics, and that are run by managers whom we like, admire and trust.
concept: Buy all or part of businesses that are understood, have good sustainable economics, and are run by managers liked, admired and trusted.
evolution_notes: Same structure as M1994-084 (operating capital local, surplus central). Compare L1994-001.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Intrinsic Value and Capital Allocation

quote_verbatim: In setting compensation, we like to hold out the promise of large carrots, but make sure their delivery is tied directly to results in the area that a manager controls.  When capital invested in an operation is significant, we also both charge managers a high rate for incremental capital they employ and credit them at an equally high rate for capital they release.
concept: Pay managers on results they control, and charge and credit them a high rate for capital used and released.
evolution_notes: Just before: Schey paid on Scott Fetzer's results, not Berkshire's, since a Berkshire-linked bonus would be 'totally capricious'. After: the bonus is symmetrical, so it pays him to send unusable cash to Omaha.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Compensation

quote_verbatim: In our book, alignment means being a partner in both directions, not just on the upside. Many "alignment" plans flunk this basic test, being artful forms of "heads I win, tails you lose."
concept: Alignment of management with owners means sharing the downside as well as the upside.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Compensation

quote_verbatim: A common form of misalignment occurs in the typical stock option arrangement, which does not periodically increase the option price to compensate for the fact that retained earnings are building up the wealth of the company.  Indeed, the combination of a ten-year option, a low dividend payout, and compound interest can provide lush gains to a manager who has done no more than tread water in his job.
concept: A fixed-price option rewards a manager for retained earnings piling up, not for performance; low payout makes it worse.
evolution_notes: Continues: 'when payments to owners are held down, the profit to the option-holding manager increases.' The point is never spelled out in proxy statements.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Compensation

quote_verbatim: In all instances, we pursue rationality.  Arrangements that pay off in capricious ways, unrelated to a manager's personal accomplishments, may well be welcomed by certain managers.  Who, after all, refuses a free lottery ticket?  But such arrangements are wasteful to the company and cause the manager to lose focus on what should be his real areas of concern.
concept: Pay unrelated to a manager's own accomplishments is waste and costs him focus.
evolution_notes: Also: the Schey arrangement took five minutes without lawyers or consultants and has never been changed; 'irrational behavior at the parent may well encourage imitative behavior at subsidiaries.'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Compensation

quote_verbatim: Our intent is to supply you with the financial information that we would wish you to give us if our positions were reversed.
concept: Report to owners what you would want reported to you if roles were reversed.
evolution_notes: Purchase-premium charges are shown separately so the businesses' earnings appear as if not acquired.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Sources of Reported Earnings

quote_verbatim: As we calculate them, look-through earnings consist of: (1) the operating earnings reported in the previous section, plus; (2) the retained operating earnings of major investees that, under GAAP accounting, are not reflected in our profits, less; (3) an allowance for the tax that would be paid by Berkshire if these retained earnings of investees had instead been distributed to us. [...] If our intrinsic value is to grow at our target rate of 15%, our look-through earnings, over time, must also increase at about that pace.
concept: Look-through earnings add the retained earnings of investees, less the tax on distribution, and are the measure value growth must track.
evolution_notes: Operating earnings here exclude capital gains, special items and major restructuring charges; Buffett warns the figures are 'necessarily very rough'. Compare L1993-006.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: "Look-Through" Earnings

quote_verbatim: As we've explained in past reports, what counts in our insurance business is, first, the amount of "float" we develop and, second, its cost to us.  Float is money we hold but don't own. [...] An insurance business is profitable over time if its cost of float is less than the cost the company would otherwise incur to obtain funds.  But the business has a negative value if the cost of its float is higher than market rates for money.
concept: An insurer is judged by the size of its float and its cost against the market cost of money; costly float means negative value.
evolution_notes: Restates L1993-009 and L1993-010; adds the explicit negative-value case.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Insurance Operations

quote_verbatim: There's not much sense in paying premiums for coverage that will evaporate precisely when it is needed.  So the certainty that Berkshire will be both solvent and liquid after a catastrophe of unthinkable proportions is a major competitive advantage for us.
concept: In catastrophe reinsurance, the advantage is certain solvency and liquidity after the disaster, since that is what the buyer is paying for.
evolution_notes: Compare L1993-012. Second advantage named: writing single policies of a size no one else will consider, quoted the same day.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Insurance Operations

quote_verbatim: By writing coverages in large lumps, we obviously expose Berkshire to lumpy financial results.  That's totally acceptable to us:  Too often, insurers (as well as other businesses) follow sub-optimum strategies in order to "smooth" their reported earnings. By accepting the prospect of volatility, we expect to earn higher long-term returns than we would by pursuing predictability.
concept: Accept lumpy reported results for higher long-term returns; smoothing earnings leads to worse strategies.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Insurance Operations

quote_verbatim: Given the risks we accept, Ajit and I constantly focus on our "worst case," knowing, of course, that it is difficult to judge what this is, since you could conceivably have a Long Island hurricane, a California earthquake, and Super Cat X all in the same year.  Additionally, insurance losses could be accompanied by non-insurance troubles. [...] If you are not comfortable with this level of exposure, the time to sell your Berkshire stock is now, not after the inevitable mega-catastrophe.
concept: Size risk by the worst case, including several catastrophes at once and losses elsewhere that move with them, and state it to owners in advance.
evolution_notes: The elided text gives the correlated example (a Southern California quake hitting See's, Wells Fargo and Freddie Mac) and the worst case of about $600 million after tax; line 806 prints 'insurance' alone on a broken line, left inside the elision. Also (lines 814-818): capital will 'chase premiums, irrespective of their adequacy', so volume will fall; compare L1993-013.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Insurance Operations

quote_verbatim: Our investments continue to be few in number and simple in concept:  The truly big investment idea can usually be explained in a short paragraph.  We like a business with enduring competitive advantages that is run by able and owner-oriented people.  When these attributes exist, and when we can make purchases at sensible prices, it is hard to go wrong (a challenge we periodically manage to overcome).
concept: A big idea fits in a short paragraph: enduring competitive advantage, able owner-oriented managers, a sensible price.
evolution_notes: Third statement of the triad in this letter; compare L1994-001 and L1994-006.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Common Stock Investments

quote_verbatim: Investors should remember that their scorecard is not computed using Olympic-diving methods:  Degree-of-difficulty doesn't count. If you are right about a business whose value is largely dependent on a single key factor that is both easy to understand and enduring, the payoff is the same as if you had correctly analyzed an investment alternative characterized by many constantly shifting and complex variables.
concept: Prefer businesses whose value rests on one easy, enduring factor; difficulty earns no extra reward.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Common Stock Investments

quote_verbatim: We try to price, rather than time, purchases.  In our view, it is folly to forego buying shares in an outstanding business whose long-term future is predictable, because of short-term worries about an economy or a stock market that we know to be unpredictable.  Why scrap an informed decision because of an uninformed guess? [...] In each case, we pondered what the business was likely to do, not what the Dow, the Fed, or the economy might do.
concept: Buy on price, not timing; judge what the business will do, not the market, the Fed or the economy.
evolution_notes: Transcription artifact: lines 875-879 break 'price,' and 'time,' onto their own lines (italics lost in extraction); the quote reads them in sequence. Elided: the five whole businesses bought in the years they became available at acceptable prices. Compare L1994-004.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Common Stock Investments

quote_verbatim: Before looking at new investments, we consider adding to old ones.  If a business is attractive enough to buy once, it may well pay to repeat the process.
concept: Consider adding to existing holdings before buying something new.
evolution_notes: 1994 adds were Coca-Cola and American Express.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Common Stock Investments

quote_verbatim: Nevertheless, I find that a long-term familiarity with a company and its products is often helpful in evaluating it.
concept: Long familiarity with a company and its products helps in judging it.
evolution_notes: Illustrated by GEICO, the Washington Post, Coca-Cola ('The real money was in the syrup') and American Express/IDS.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Common Stock Investments

quote_verbatim: Mistakes occur at the time of decision.  We can only make our mistake-du-jour award, however, when the foolishness of the decision become obvious.
concept: A mistake is made when the decision is made, even if it shows only later.
evolution_notes: 'become' is as printed. First nominee: selling Cap Cities at $63 in 1993, after an earlier sale at $4.30 in 1978-80; 'Now I've become a repeat offender.' No lesson is stated for that one, so it is not rowed separately.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Mistake Du Jour

quote_verbatim: Rather, this was a case of sloppy analysis, a lapse that may have been caused by the fact that we were buying a senior security or by hubris. [...] Before this purchase, I simply failed to focus on the problems that would inevitably beset a carrier whose costs were both high and extremely difficult to lower. [...] eventually a fundamental rule of economics prevailed:  In an unregulated commodity business, a company must lower its costs to competitive levels or face extinction.  This principle should have been obvious to your Chairman, but I missed it.
concept: USAir: a senior security and hubris led him to ignore high, sticky costs; in an unregulated commodity business costs must fall to competitive levels or the firm dies.
evolution_notes: Elided: regulation once let airlines pass high costs through; after deregulation the problem stayed hidden while low-cost capacity was small, and 'non-sustainable' costs became further embedded. Compare M1994-032.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Mistake Du Jour

quote_verbatim: Whatever the outcome, we will heed a prime rule of investing:  You don't have to make it back the way that you lost it.
concept: A loss need not be recovered in the same investment that caused it.
evolution_notes: The 1995 meeting heading 11 takes this as its title.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Mistake Du Jour

quote_verbatim: Additionally, Dan and Carl prepared well for their departure and left their companies in outstanding hands.
concept: Part of a CEO's record is preparing a succession that leaves the company in good hands.
evolution_notes: Just before: both managed through tough industry conditions to record earnings.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Miscellaneous

quote_verbatim: You can be sure that Charlie and I will not use these shares without being completely satisfied that we are receiving as much in intrinsic value as we are giving.
concept: Issue shares in a deal only when the intrinsic value received at least equals the value given.
evolution_notes: On the preferred-stock authorization; the meeting's heading 3 is the motion. Acquisition criteria are in an appendix (page 21) of the report, which this unit's order line does not include.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Miscellaneous

quote_verbatim: WARREN BUFFETT: Only if we receive less in value than we give. That’s the key to it. I mean, if we issue $200 million worth of preferred and we receive a business that’s only worth 150 million, there’s no question you’re worse off than before. [...] If we give 200 million of cash for a business that’s worth a 150 million, we are worse off. We may not have issued a share of stock. But we have diluted the value of your stock if we do that. As long as we get value received, in terms of whether — of cash, common stock, or preferred stock — then you are not diluted in terms of value.
concept: Dilution means giving more value than is received, whatever the currency; issuing shares at fair value does not dilute, overpaying in cash does.
evolution_notes: Same answer: companies issuing stock worth more than they receive run Medlin's 'chain letter in reverse'. Line 91: 'We’re not going to give 120 percent of X if we’re only willing to pay a hundred percent of X, just because the form of a deal changes.' Compare L1994-038 and L1994-015.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 3. Motion authorizing preferred stock

quote_verbatim: Because a management can build an empire just by issuing these little pieces of paper, which they feel don’t cost them anything.
concept: Watch for managers who treat their own stock as costless currency for empire-building.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 3. Motion authorizing preferred stock

quote_verbatim: CHARLIE MUNGER: There was a particular bank where one of the officers wanted stock options, pointed out to the management that they could issue all these shares and it didn’t cost anything. Now, imagine hiring a manager who thinks that way and paying them money — (laughter) — to behave like Judas in your very midst.
concept: A manager who thinks issuing shares or options costs nothing is betraying the owners who pay him.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 3. Motion authorizing preferred stock

quote_verbatim: WARREN BUFFETT: We have had conversations with managers — (laughter) — where they tell us how fortunate they feel because the stock is down and they can issue options cheaper. Now, if they were issuing those to the third parties, you know, I’m not sure whether they’d have exactly the same attitude. But we have no feeling that we’re getting richer when we issue shares. We have a feeling we’re getting richer when we get at least as much value in a business as the shares are worth that we issue.
concept: A manager pleased to issue options cheaply after a price fall shows he does not see them as a cost to owners.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 3. Motion authorizing preferred stock

quote_verbatim: But borrowing money is not necessarily at all harmful to shareholders — although certainly, if it’s carried to excess, it is. And the preferred is a form of quasi-borrowed money that does rank ahead of the common shareholder. But then, at the same time, we’re adding a business which we think is going to benefit the shareholder, if we issue that. So that’s the tradeoff.
concept: Debt or preferred placed ahead of common is a tradeoff against the business acquired; harmful when carried to excess.
evolution_notes: Just before: any change to the capital structure shifts the position of each layer; Berkshire has borrowed a couple of times to buy a business.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 3. Motion authorizing preferred stock

quote_verbatim: CHARLIE MUNGER: We probably wouldn’t try and be that cute. (Laughter)
concept: Avoid overly clever structures that try to win on both sides of the tax rules.
evolution_notes: Answer to a question on a preferred whose dividend would be deductible to the issuer and qualify for the dividends-received deduction to the holder.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 3. Motion authorizing preferred stock

quote_verbatim: And that is of absolutely no consequence to us. We care not a wit about the accounting treatment that we receive. We feel that we have a shareholder body that’s intelligent enough to understand the economic reality of a transaction. [...] We would rather do whatever makes the most sense for us and for the seller, and then explain to you whatever accounting peculiarities may arise out of the transaction.
concept: Structure a deal for its economics, not its accounting treatment, and explain the accounting to owners afterward.
evolution_notes: 'not a wit' as printed. Context: other companies choose consideration to get pooling rather than purchase accounting. 'And it probably helps us make a deal, occasionally.'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 3. Motion authorizing preferred stock

quote_verbatim: But we have a structure that’s about as good as you can do, in terms of people knowing what they’re getting into when they make a deal with us and being able to count on the conditions that prevail at the time of the deal, continuing for a long period in the future. [...] But what you do run into is the company that’s the acquiring company, itself, either being acquired or some new management coming along, or some new management consultant coming along, and saying, “Well, this doesn’t fit our strategic plan anymore, so let’s dump this division.” And people that join in with Berkshire can be relatively, I think, comfortable about nothing like that happening.
concept: Offer sellers a permanent, stable owner whose terms at the deal will hold for the long term; do not later dump divisions.
evolution_notes: Just before: family directors are there so a concentrated, stable ownership will persist after his death; a seller cares 'who you deliver thousands of people that have joined you' to, not only the price. Heading 30 returns to not selling businesses.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 5. Buffetts on the board adds stability

quote_verbatim: So, we believe in managers knowing that money costs money. And I would say that, just generally, my experience in business is that most managers, when using their own money, understand that money costs money. But sometimes managers, when using other people’s money, start thinking of it a little bit like free money. And that’s a habit we don’t want to encourage around Berkshire.
concept: Charge managers for capital so they treat other people's money as costly; rates set between 14 and 20 percent.
evolution_notes: Expands L1994-019. Rates 14 to 20 percent, LIBOR for seasonal needs, credit at the same rate for capital released (lines 217-219).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 7. Managers need to know “money costs money”

quote_verbatim: Our managers don’t mind being measured, and they like getting a — I think they enjoy seeing a batting average posted. And a batting average that does not include a cost of capital is a phony batting average.
concept: A performance measure that ignores the cost of capital is false.
evolution_notes: Just before: Buffett does not see capital budgets from wholly owned subsidiaries and there is no headquarters staff to review them; the capital charge is the guide instead. Munger: 'Well, I certainly agree.'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 7. Managers need to know “money costs money”

quote_verbatim: As a general matter, there are only two reasons for buying insurance. One is to protect yourself against a loss that you are unable or unwilling to bear yourself. [...] Or the second reason, which occasionally comes up, is if you think the insurance company is actually selling you a policy that’s too cheap, so that you really expect, over a period of time, to have a mathematical advantage by buying insurance. Well, we try to avoid selling the second kind and to concentrate on selling the first kind.
concept: Insurance is rightly bought only for losses one cannot or will not bear, or because it is underpriced; sell only the first kind.
evolution_notes: Line 237: 'we really don’t want to insure someone for a loss that they can afford themselves', since it may mean their loss expectancy exceeds the premium.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 8. The two reasons for buying insurance

quote_verbatim: For example, a manager that’s terribly worried that his board of directors may second-guess him if he has an uninsured loss, is going to buy a lot more protection, probably, than the company really needs. [...] So, he may do something that is very unintelligent from the company’s standpoint merely to protect his own position.
concept: Managers may spend company money to protect their own position from second-guessing rather than the company.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 8. The two reasons for buying insurance

quote_verbatim: There are certain companies that are exposing themselves in this country to losses which would wipe them out. And they prefer not to buy reinsurance because it’s, quote, “expensive.” But what they’re really doing is betting on something that won’t happen very often, happening not at all. [...] And if you’re a 63-year-old CEO and you figure, “I’m going to retire in a couple of years,” you know, the odds are pretty good that it won’t happen on your watch. But the — it will happen on somebody’s watch.
concept: Look for firms exposed to a ruinous rare loss whose managers skip protection because the event is unlikely in their own tenure.
evolution_notes: Compare L1993-011 (an event 25 times a century: many winning years, then broke).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 8. The two reasons for buying insurance

quote_verbatim: Because if you start an insurance company to write earthquake insurance in California and you raise a few hundred million dollars, you’ll either have essentially have no losses or, if you write enough of it, you’ll go broke. And most years, you’ll have no losses. [...] The only thing that may restrict that is that if the buyer is sophisticated enough to question the viability of that company under really extreme conditions, which is the only conditions that count when you’re buying catastrophe insurance, that may restrict it.
concept: Easy entry into catastrophe insurance produces good early records that end in ruin; the only test that counts is solvency under extreme conditions.
evolution_notes: 'essentially have no losses' as printed. Compare L1994-026 and L1993-012.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 9. “We can sustain shocks … that others can’t”

quote_verbatim: So we can sustain shocks, and we will sustain shocks, I should add, that others can’t. And we try to get paid appropriately for that. [...] If the rates — if there were enough capacity at really ridiculous rates, I mean, in the end, we wouldn’t be writing that business at that time. But I don’t think that will happen. It certainly hasn’t happened so far. And if it happens, you know, so be it. We’ll all play golf until the loss occurs.
concept: Get paid for capacity to absorb shocks; when rates become ridiculous, stop writing and wait.
evolution_notes: Between: the largest insurers and reinsurers come to Berkshire 'because they know that we’ll pay'. Compare L1993-013. Munger: 'Nothing to add.'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 9. “We can sustain shocks … that others can’t”

quote_verbatim: We try not to get into things we — that we don’t understand. And if we’re going to lose your money, we want to be able to come before you, you know, next year and tell you we lost your money because we thought this and it turned out to be that. We don’t want to say, you know, somebody wrote us a report saying if, you know, “This is what’s going to happen,” in some field that we don’t understand and that, therefore, we lost your money by following someone else’s advice.
concept: Stay out of what you do not understand; a loss should come from your own stated reasoning, not from relying on someone else's report.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 10. Graham’s principles for high-tech stocks?

quote_verbatim: I think he would have a margin of safety principle that might be a little different because there’s essentially more risk in a high-tech company. But he would still have the margin of safety principle on a — sort of adjusted for the mathematical risk of loss in his mind. He would have — he would look at it as a business, not as a stock. You know, he would not buy it on borrowed money.
concept: The same principles apply in any field one understands: a margin of safety sized to the risk of loss, a business not a stock, no borrowed money.
evolution_notes: Said of Bill Gates judging a business he understands; Buffett holds Graham's principles 'perfectly valid when applied to high-tech companies' but says he does not know how to do it.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 10. Graham’s principles for high-tech stocks?

quote_verbatim: But our circle of things we understand is really unlikely to enlarge, maybe a tiny bit here or there. But if the capital doesn’t get too large, the circle’s OK. And — but we will not —if we have trouble finding things within our circle, we will not enlarge the circle. You know, we’ll wait. That’s our approach.
concept: When nothing is found inside the circle of competence, wait rather than widen the circle.
evolution_notes: 'not —if' spacing as printed. Compare L1994-003 (wait within the happy zone).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 10. Graham’s principles for high-tech stocks?

quote_verbatim: Because it is true that a very important principle in investing is you don’t have to make it back the way you lost it. And in fact, it’s usually a mistake to make — try and make it back the way that you lost it.
concept: Trying to recover a loss in the same position that caused it is usually a mistake.
evolution_notes: Restates L1994-036 and strengthens it from 'don't have to' to 'usually a mistake'.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 11. USAir: “You don’t have to make it back the way you lost it”

quote_verbatim: And we know that there’s an extra cost involved to us if we should try to sell, or it may be impossible. And that’s not of great importance with us because we don’t buy things to sell, but it’s of some importance.
concept: A privately placed security carries a known cost of illiquidity; it matters little to a buyer who does not buy to sell, but it is not nothing.
evolution_notes: Line 293: board seats give inside knowledge, so 'dealing with anything where we’ve got fiduciary obligations is, maybe, not practical at all'.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 11. USAir: “You don’t have to make it back the way you lost it”

quote_verbatim: CHARLIE MUNGER: I’d like to repeat that business about not having to get it back the way you lost it. You know, that’s the reason so many people are ruined by gambling. They get behind and then they feel they have to get it back the way they lost it. It’s a deep part of the human nature. And it’s very smart just to lick it by will, and little phrases like that are very useful.
concept: The urge to win back a loss where it was lost is deep in human nature and ruins gamblers; overcome it by will, with the help of short maxims.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 11. USAir: “You don’t have to make it back the way you lost it”

quote_verbatim: WARREN BUFFETT: Yeah, one of the important things in stocks is that the stock does not know that you own it. You know, you have all these feelings about it. You know, and — (laughter) — you remember what you paid, you know? (Laughter) [...] And it — you know, it doesn’t give a damn, you know? (Laughter) It just sits there. And it — you know, a stock at 50, somebody’s paid a hundred, they feel terrible. Somebody else paid 10, they feel wonderful. All these feelings, and it has no impact whatsoever.
concept: The price paid and one's feelings about a stock are irrelevant to what it is worth now.
evolution_notes: Continues: a businessman who built a business goes into 'a mathematically disadvantageous game', starts losing and tries to make it back 'not only the way they lost it, but that night'; 'it’s a great mistake.'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 11. USAir: “You don’t have to make it back the way you lost it”

quote_verbatim: But I really don’t think you need that sort of thing. I mean, I do not think it’s that complicated to figure out, you know, where it makes sense to put money. You can make mistakes doing it. But in terms of the mental manipulations you go through, I don’t think it’s a very complicated subject. And I don’t think that — I think that the people marketing one or another fad in management tend to make them a little more complicated than needed so that you have to call in the high priest.
concept: Deciding where to put money is not mentally complicated; formal systems like EVA are made complex so that experts must be hired.
evolution_notes: On economic value added, which Buffett says has flaws but 'generally comes out with the right answers'. Munger (line 323): the concept has some merit but 'the exact formal methods, I don’t believe we use'; (line 329) 'It’s way less silly than the capital assets pricing model.' Line 331: fads also run through investing and investment bankers 'create product to satisfy the demand'.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 12. Beware of complicated fads and “high priests”

quote_verbatim: We would obviously care very much about the counterparty, because that transaction is just a little piece of paper between two people. [...] And therefore, you want to be sure that that person will be both willing and able to write the check. And so, we’re probably more concerned about counterparty risk than most people might be.
concept: A derivative is only as good as the counterparty's willingness and ability to pay at the end.
evolution_notes: Berkshire has two kinds of derivative transactions of modest size and would use more 'if the conditions were right'. Compare L1994-026 (insurance worth only certain payment).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 13. Derivatives: “Potential for mistakes and mischief”

quote_verbatim: Last year and the year before, I think I said that derivatives often combine borrowed money with ignorance, and that that is a rather dangerous combination. [...] They involved a creation of risk, not the transfer of risk, you know, not the moderation of risk, but the creation of risk on a huge scale.
concept: Borrowed money plus ignorance is dangerous; many derivatives create risk rather than transfer or reduce it.

Not rowed separately: a view on how the world should be run.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 13. Derivatives: “Potential for mistakes and mischief”

Now the — and the tough part is assessing over a longer period of time whether — because of volatility, it’s much harder to assess whether — what the average returns might be from a business. [...] But the question is what the average return on capital will be. And we knew that was difficult to predict when we went in. And we found out it’s even more difficult to predict than we thought.
concept: Volatile businesses make average returns on capital hard to estimate; Salomon proved even harder to predict than expected.

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 14. Salomon’s murky future

And we will — the other thing about options is you don’t make a decision on them until you have to make a decision.

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 14. Salomon’s murky future

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 16. Cards are key to future of American Express

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 17. “Corruption won” in stock option accounting rule

heading: ### 25. Economics of the moat and the castle

quote_verbatim: And then our — then what we have to decide is — all moats are subject to attack in a capitalistic system, so everybody is going to try and — if you’ve got a big castle in there, people are going to be trying to figure out how to get to it. How much do they depend on the genius of the lord in the castle? And then if we feel good about the moat, then we try to figure out whether, you know, the lord is going to try to take it all for himself, whether he’s likely to do something stupid with the proceeds, et cetera.
concept: Every moat is under attack and most are worthless; ask why the castle still stands, what keeps it standing for 5 to 20 years, how permanent that is, how much rests on the manager, then whether the manager will take it for himself or waste the proceeds.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 25. Economics of the moat and the castle

So you’re — by and large, you’re talking scale advantages and low agency costs.
concept: In economists' terms the honest lord is low agency cost, and the moat is mostly scale advantage, including scale of intelligence.

heading: ### 25. Economics of the moat and the castle

heading: ### 31. Focus on Graham’s three principles

quote_verbatim: In other words, there’s three important aspects to it. You know, one is your attitude toward the stock market. [...] Second principle is the margin of safety, which again, gives you an enormous edge, and actually has applicability far beyond just the investment world. And then the third is just looking at stocks as businesses, which gives you an entirely different view than most people that are in the market. And with those three sort of philosophical benchmarks, the exact — the evaluation technique you use is not really that important.

heading: ### 31. Focus on Graham’s three principles

quote_verbatim: CHARLIE MUNGER: Yeah. To the extent that the method of estimating future cash flow requires projections, I would say that projections, while they’re logically required by the circumstances, on average, do more harm than good in America. Most of them are put together by people who have an interest in a particular outcome. [...] And a projection prepared in America by anybody with a commission, or an executive trying to justify a particular course of action, will frequently be a lie. It’s not a deliberate lie, in most cases. The man has gotten to believe it himself. And that’s the worst kind.

heading: ### 9. Comparing investing styles of Ben Graham and Phil Fisher

heading: ### 14. “Not too likely” we’ll buy a business outside the U.S.

quote_verbatim: And the growth in capital has been greater than the growth rate in premium volume and in invested assets, so that achieving the same success on underwriting and achieving the same success on investments will produce a lower return on capital unless they buy in stock, which they have done fairly significantly. [...] It’s a very good business. But it’s not a business where, if you double the capital, you can double the earnings easily.

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 16. Decline in GEICO’s return on equity

We get a lot of speculation on that, but it’s of no use to Berkshire to be talking about purchases or sales. [...] And it — we are not in the business of giving investment advice, basically. We’ll talk about our principles.
concept: Talk about principles, never about what is being bought or sold; disclosure follows the legal requirement and a dollar threshold.

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 17. No comment on Guinness investment

quote_verbatim: It earns good returns on invested capital or we wouldn’t be buying into it. We always look for good returns on capital. And a lot of companies in the jewelry business do not get good returns on capital. [...] It takes unusual sales per square foot compared to competitors to succeed in that, and we have one operation that does that in spades at Borsheims, and then a different type of operation that does it at Helzberg’s.
concept: Good returns on capital are required; in an industry where most participants are not prosperous, look for the operator with an unusual measurable edge such as sales per square foot.
evolution_notes: Same heading: retailing is a business 'where you have to stay smart over time' (M1995-040) and the manager's record is extremely good. Buffett declines to give Helzberg's figures.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 21. Helzberg has unusually good sales for jewelry retailer

quote_verbatim: Yeah, we frequently find that owners of entire businesses have schizophrenia. [...] And I think over time, we’ve made acquisitions that were fair on both sides, and averaged out, they’ve worked well for Berkshire. And I think a company that behaves that way is giving the best long-term value to the private owner who wants to sell. You do not want to sell your business for stock to a firm that likes issuing stock.
concept: Buy on terms fair to both sides; a seller taking stock should avoid a buyer that likes issuing stock, since that dilutes the stock received.
evolution_notes: The elided part: sellers want a little more than their business is worth in tax-free stock, and want the buyer to make 'just one dumb acquisition — theirs'. Compare L1994-038 and M1995-001 to M1995-003 on issuing shares.

heading: ### 21. Helzberg has unusually good sales for jewelry retailer

quote_verbatim: There is a lot more to — there’s more to intrinsic value, as we’ve discussed earlier, than just adding up what you think you can sell the pieces for at any given time, because it is a prospective figure. It is future cash discounted back to the present. And capital allocation is a good part of that. What you expect the float to do, for example, over time, would not — that would lead to a large swing in possible numbers relative to value.
concept: Intrinsic value is prospective, future cash discounted to the present, not the sale value of the pieces; future capital allocation and the path of float swing it widely.
evolution_notes: Earlier in the heading Buffett says there are 'important factors besides P/E', calls the float page 'as important a page as there is in the report', and declines to state Berkshire's value. He adds that National Indemnity's 1967 value, had the float's growth been foreseen, was many multiples of what most thought, 'and probably what we thought at the time.'
