speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 22. Insurance float important in estimating intrinsic value

quote_verbatim: There’s no chance we’ll be in businesses we don’t understand, and I won’t understand it. [...] Well, if you made an exception, he would be a good guy to make — a very good guy — to make an exception with. But I don’t think I’ll make an exception.
concept: No investment in a business not understood, even where the manager is a trusted friend; no exception for the person.
evolution_notes: Buffett bought 100 Microsoft shares personally to receive the reports. Compare M1995-016 and M1994-039.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 24. Buffett doesn’t understand Microsoft, despite his friendship with Gates

quote_verbatim: So, I think you can learn a lot from other people. In fact, I think, if you learn reasonably well from other people, you don’t have to get any new ideas or do much on your own. You can just apply the best of what you see.
concept: Learn from others and apply the best of what you see; original ideas are not required.
evolution_notes: Munger next: 'It’s extraordinary how resistant some people are to learning anything.' Buffett: Graham was much read and little followed, 'this incredible resistance to thinking or change', and Munger asks how much Berkshire has been copied.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 25. Business schools should study Mrs. B’s success

quote_verbatim: She didn’t invent something that the world had never seen before. She didn’t have a lock on some piece of real estate that protected her from competition. You know, all of these — and yet, she accomplished something that virtually no one has accomplished. [...] It’s a very smart woman, but it’s not something that’s incapable of being replicated in the habits and the way of thinking.
concept: A great success in a competitive business can rest on neither invention nor a protected position but on habits and ways of thinking that can be replicated; study it.
evolution_notes: Buffett contrasts business schools teaching EVA (compare M1995-023) with no page on Mrs. B, started with 500 dollars in 1937. Sits against M1995-039's account of the moat as mostly scale advantage: here the advantage is the operator's habits.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 25. Business schools should study Mrs. B’s success

quote_verbatim: I mean, there aren’t that many years around, so you ought to be doing what you like at the present time, and Charlie and I have always followed that pretty well.
concept: Do work you like now rather than tolerate disliked work for more money and a better job later.
evolution_notes: A personal rule, not an investment rule. Buffett: he never believed the theory of 'I’ll take this job I don’t like now, and I’ll get one I like later on'. Heading 15 says the same of fame: 'I do what I like to do.'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 26. Do what you like now, not later

quote_verbatim: It would be a big mistake, with businesses with as many different economic characteristics, or as varying economic characteristics existing, as they do at Berkshire, to try and have some formula approach that paid managers in all of these different businesses based on a simple formula of one kind. [...] If they use a lot of capital, they’re going to have a capital charge, is what it amounts to. [...] The best managers, we aren’t going to change their behavior much by the compensation thing. [...] So we try to have a system that rewards the things that we want to have rewarded, and treats them fairly in a way that they understand they’re treated fairly.
concept: No single pay formula across different businesses; charge for capital where much is used; pay rewards what is wanted and is visibly fair, since pay changes the best managers little.
evolution_notes: Restates M1994-011 and M1995-009. Buffett: no capital charge where capital is unimportant, 'We don’t believe in going through a lot of machinations if it’s going to involve peanuts at the end', and thresholds differ for easy and tough businesses.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 27. “We let .400 hitters swing the way they want to swing”

quote_verbatim: We don’t have any budgets that come up to headquarters. We let .400 hitters swing the way they want to swing. [...] And they feel, and we want them to feel, like they own their own business. [...] So, what we have to do is create a situation, or maintain a situation, where they are having more fun doing what they’re doing than anything else they can do in life, and that’s what’s we’re designing for.
concept: Proven managers run their businesses their own way, with no budgets sent to headquarters; the design goal is that they enjoy the work more than any alternative.
evolution_notes: Buffett: an independently wealthy seller told how to swing 'would tell us what we could do with it very quickly'. Compare L1993-005 and M1994-010.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 27. “We let .400 hitters swing the way they want to swing”

quote_verbatim: I look — I usually know ahead of time, but I mean, I would first look at the size. And if the size isn’t right — and it isn’t going to be virtually any time — I don’t look any further, because there’s just no time to be looking at all kinds of smaller opportunities. I do think, if you’re working with very small amounts of money, that there almost always are some significant inefficiency someplace — to find things.
concept: Screen first on size the capital can use and stop there if it fails; small sums, by contrast, can almost always find some inefficiency in less-followed companies.
evolution_notes: Earlier in the answer: 'you run into companies that are less followed as you get smaller.' Compare L1994-002 and M1994-072 on size.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 29. We don’t look for small stock bargains anymore, but they exist

quote_verbatim: I’ve mentioned to some people, when I started out, I actually went through all of the Moody’s manuals and the Standard and Poor’s manuals page by page. And you know, it was probably 20,000 pages, but there were a lot of things that popped out, and none of them were in any brokerage report or anything of the sort. They were just plain overlooked, and you had to — You could find out about them, but nobody was going to tell you about them.
concept: Overlooked bargains are found by reading every page of the reference manuals oneself; nobody will point them out.
evolution_notes: Buffett guesses it 'continues to be true, but not on anything like the scale it was then.'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 29. We don’t look for small stock bargains anymore, but they exist

quote_verbatim: So, you know, I use that sometimes as an example of efficient markets, because somebody called me and offered me a share of it, and those things, you know — is that an efficient market or not? You know, 29,000 for 20,000 of cash, plus 11,000 of royalty income at 25 cent gas and $3 oil? I don’t think so. You can find things out there.
concept: Test the efficient-market claim against a concrete case: a share priced near its cash with large royalty income on top shows bargains exist.
evolution_notes: The Delta Duck Club (Atled): 98 shares, about 20,000 a share cash and about 7,000 after-tax earnings against a 29,000 price, 'a long-lived field'. Munger calls it scavenging for cigar butts.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 30. Early Buffett cigar butt: Delta Duck Club

quote_verbatim: Grant McFayden treats his employees right, his customers right, everybody right. “When he gets involved with somebody who’s a little nuts, he gets up from his desk, and walks to where they are, and extricates himself as soon as he can.” [...] Now, my father was trying to teach me, and I must say it worked beautifully, because I decided that I would adopt the Grant McFayden approach.
concept: Treat everyone right, and when entangled with someone unreasonable, get out at once; that is how legal trouble is minimized.
evolution_notes: Munger's father contrasted McFayden with client X, 'a walking minefield of continuous legal troubles'. Munger: 'Warren independently reached the same approach very early in life. Boy has that saved us a lot of trouble.' Earlier in the heading Buffett: if sued frivolously, do not pay and make life comparably difficult for the other party.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 31. Secret to avoiding lawsuits: “You can’t make a good deal with a bad person”

quote_verbatim: we basically have the attitude that you can’t make a good deal with a bad person. And you can — that means we just forget about it. I mean, we don’t try and protect ourselves by contracts, or getting into all kinds of, you know, due diligence, or — We just forget about it. We can do fine over time, dealing with people that we like, and admire, and trust.
concept: No good deal is possible with a bad person; do not try to protect against one with contracts or due diligence, just walk away and deal with people you like, admire and trust.
evolution_notes: Buffett continues: the bad actor 'will tend to try and tantalize you', 'you won’t win. It just pays to avoid them', and 'maybe one or two experiences have convinced us, even more so'. Compare M1995-066 (Lloyd's) and M1995-045, M1995-046.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 31. Secret to avoiding lawsuits: “You can’t make a good deal with a bad person”

quote_verbatim: You have to figure out what you’re good at and who you really can offer something special to. Borsheims offers something very special to people, but in part, it comes about through being at one location. [...] And that gives you operating costs that are many — oh, 20 percentage points — off of what somebody else will be doing without that pulling power. And that, in turn, enables you to offer the lower prices, which keeps the circle going. I mean, it’s very hard to replicate something like that.
concept: Know what you are good at and for whom; an advantage that runs in a circle (selection draws volume, volume lowers cost, low cost allows low prices) is hard to replicate and may not survive being spread across many sites.
evolution_notes: Just before: Sol Price said part of his success was 'figuring out the customer he didn’t want', and 'Borsheims can’t be Helzberg’s, and Helzberg’s can’t be Borsheims.' Buffett adds it is a question to keep asking: 'McDonald’s certainly did well by deciding to open a second store.' Compare M1995-071 and M1995-076.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 32. Why there’s just one Borsheims store

quote_verbatim: So if you — anything you do that tends to pull down equity, if it doesn’t change your ability to do the same sales volume — it’s leveraged American business, in effect, by putting the health liabilities on the balance sheet. It may be wrong. It may be that business can earn 15 percent or so. But I think competitive factors tend to, over time, keep pushing that number down, somewhat.
concept: A higher return on equity can come from shrinking the equity rather than better business; competition tends to push aggregate returns back down over time.
evolution_notes: Buffett would pick 12 to 13 percent for American business over ten years and calls that 'not bad at all' at 7 percent interest rates. Compare L1994-009 (rule out leverage before crediting a high return on equity) and M1995-069.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 33. Factors boosting reported return on equity

quote_verbatim: Yeah. I think all of those published averages overstate what’s earned anyway. They’re the biggest companies, they’re the winners, they’re the ones whose stock sells at high multiples, so they can issue it to other people for high-earning assets. And many of the low-return people are constantly being dropped out of the figures.
concept: Published return averages overstate what business earns because they cover the winners and drop the low-return companies.
evolution_notes: Munger: 'it would be remarkable to me if, on average, American business earned 13 percent on capital after taxes.'
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 33. Factors boosting reported return on equity

quote_verbatim: They don’t show as a cost, for example, the cost of stock options. And the American shareholders pay that, so the American shareholder has not gotten the returns on equity shown by those numbers, although it’s not a huge factor. [...] If you let me omit my costs, I can show a very high return on equity.
concept: Reported returns that omit the cost of stock options overstate what shareholders earned; returns are only as good as the costs they include.
evolution_notes: Buffett guesses two or three tenths of a percent for options alone. Restates M1995-030.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 33. Factors boosting reported return on equity

quote_verbatim: There’s no question, in a business that earns a high rate on capital, that doesn’t have natural ways to employ that money within the business, that we actually may contribute significantly to the long-term results of that business by taking the capital out. Because if they don’t have a place to use it, nevertheless, they might well use it someplace. And we have the whole universe to spread that money over.
concept: A parent adds value by taking out capital a high-return business cannot use, before it is spent badly, and by supplying capital to a business that can grow faster than its own equity.
evolution_notes: Buffett continues: a company earning 20 percent on equity but able to grow 25 percent 'is going to feel equity strains', and Berkshire would supply capital that earns 20 percent. Compare M1994-084 and M1995-055.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 34. Return on capital at Berkshire subsidiaries

quote_verbatim: Yeah. I think our chief contribution to the businesses we acquire is what we don’t do.
concept: The owner's main contribution to an acquired business is what it refrains from doing to it.
evolution_notes: Followed by a break in the recording. Buffett just before: no committee and directors' meeting 'show-and-tell stuff', 'we really free them up to spend a hundred percent of the time thinking about what is good for the business over time.' Compare M1995-079.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 34. Return on capital at Berkshire subsidiaries

quote_verbatim: We cannot compound money at 23 percent from a $12 billion base. We don’t know how to do that, and it would be a mistake for anybody to think that we could come close to that.
concept: Past compounding rates cannot be projected from a much larger base; expecting them is a mistake.
evolution_notes: Buffett: 'we’ve never seen anybody in the world compound numbers like that, at that rate.' Compare L1994-002 and M1994-072 on size.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 35. “Advanced math is of no use” in investing

quote_verbatim: advanced math is of no use in the investment process. And understanding a mathematical relationship, sort of an ability to quantify — a numeracy, as they call it, I think that’s generally helpful in investments because something that tells you when things make sense or don’t make sense, or sort of how an item in one area relates to something someplace else. But that doesn’t really require any great mathematical ability.
concept: Investing needs numeracy, a sense of whether figures make sense and how they relate, not advanced mathematics.
evolution_notes: Compare M1994-046 (plain probability over modern finance theory) and M1995-023.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 35. “Advanced math is of no use” in investing

quote_verbatim: I mean, I think Charlie and I probably, when we read about one business, we’re always thinking of it against a screen of dozens of businesses — it’s just sort of automatic, and — [...] And it’s always in your mind, you are prioritizing and selecting in some manner. My own feeling about the best way to apply that is just to read everything in sight. You know, I mean, if you’re reading a few hundred annual reports a year and you’ve read Graham, and Fisher, and a few things, you’ll soon see whether it kind of falls into place or not.
concept: Judge each business against a mental screen of dozens of others, always ranking; build that screen by reading everything, a few hundred annual reports a year.
evolution_notes: The elided analogy is a baseball scout weighing one player against an alternative. Later in the heading: without a mosaic of statistics 'you wouldn’t know whether a .300 hitter was a good hitter or not.'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 35. “Advanced math is of no use” in investing

quote_verbatim: Yeah. I think the set of numbers — the one set of numbers in America that are the best quick guide to measuring one business against another are the Value Line numbers. [...] I can’t imagine anybody being in the investment business involving common stocks without that thing on the shelf. [...] By the way, I pay no attention to their timeliness ratings, or stock ratings.
concept: Compare businesses on long statistical histories (Value Line's fifteen years on log paper) and ignore the publisher's ratings and timeliness calls.
evolution_notes: Buffett agrees: 'none of that means anything', 'it’s the statistical material'. Munger wishes the series went back further; Buffett saves the old ones.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 35. “Advanced math is of no use” in investing

quote_verbatim: I like a lot of historical background on things, just to, sort of, get it in my head as to how the business has evolved over time, and what’s been permanent and what hasn’t been permanent, and all of that. [...] But I think it is — I think if you think about if — we’re trying to buy businesses we want to own forever, you know, and if you’re thinking that way you might as well see what it’s been like to own them forever, and look back a ways.
concept: To buy a business to own forever, read its long history to see what has been permanent and what has not.
evolution_notes: Buffett's example: reading 1930s Fortune articles on Coca-Cola; he says he does it 'probably more for fun than for actually decision making'. Compare L1994-033 (long familiarity helps) and M1995-052 (judge by the past record).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 35. “Advanced math is of no use” in investing

quote_verbatim: So, they were different — they were certainly different than the typical banker. And then the question was, is how much did that difference make, in terms of how they would run the place? And they ran into some very heavy seas, subsequently. And I think, probably, the difference — I probably think those human differences that were perceived earlier are what enabled them to come through as well as they did.
concept: In a bank, ask how far its managers differ from the typical banker and how much that difference will matter when the seas get heavy.
evolution_notes: Buffett knew Reichardt and Hazen from meeting them and 'from having read a lot of things they said'. He closes: 'if we hadn’t gone a little further, though, than just looking at numbers, we would not have been able to make that decision.' Compare M1994-021 and L1993-032.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 36. Management made the difference for Wells Fargo

quote_verbatim: So, we were basically betting that their real estate lending was way better than average. And indeed, it was. And they also handled it on the way down, way better than average. So, you can argue that everybody else was looking at this horrible concentration of real estate loans and this sea of troubles in the real estate field, and in bankers to the real estate field. And they just assumed that Wells Fargo was going to go broke.
concept: Where the crowd prices a concentrated lender for average losses, the bet is on whether its loan quality and collection are well above average; average losses would have broken it.
evolution_notes: Munger: the real-estate collapse was 'the biggest collapse in 40 or 50 years in that field', and 'since their loans were way higher quality, and their loan collection methods were way higher quality than others, that it would be all right.'
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 36. Management made the difference for Wells Fargo

quote_verbatim: I don’t think there’s anything magic about whether shareholder equity is positive or negative. [...] And there is nothing magic about a company having a positive shareholders’ equity. [...] And it’s just a fiction, as to the numbers between the two organizations.
concept: Book equity, positive or negative, is an accounting figure; a business with large intangible value and sound credit can carry negative equity after buybacks.
evolution_notes: Buffett's example: Coca-Cola's 5 billion equity against about 75 billion market value; buying in 10 billion would leave negative equity with sound credit. He notes state law may prohibit such repurchases. Compare L1994-008 (book value and intrinsic value are different things).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 37. Nothing “magic” about a positive shareholders’ equity

quote_verbatim: You should buy in your stock when you don’t have a use for the money. And that could be management specific. [...] But once a company has attended to the things that are required or advantageous for the present business, we think reacquisition of stock is a very logical thing to consider, as long as you don’t think you’re paying more than the intrinsic value of the business in doing it. And obviously, the bigger the discount from intrinsic value, the more compelling that particular use of money is.
concept: After the present business's needs, buy back stock when there is no better use for the money and the price is below intrinsic value; the bigger the discount, the stronger the case.
evolution_notes: The elided sentence: a management with a wide field of capital allocation may have a use for the money where a specialized one does not. Restates M1994-033 and M1994-053; compare M1995-054 and M1995-067.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 37. Nothing “magic” about a positive shareholders’ equity

quote_verbatim: Generally speaking, maybe Coca-Cola can have a negative equity, but I don’t think it would be a good idea for General Motors. I think there is something to be said for a positive shareholders’ equity.
concept: Negative equity may suit a business with great intangible earning power but not a capital-heavy one; a positive equity has value.
evolution_notes: Pulls against M1995-098 (Buffett: nothing magic about positive equity), immediately before. Munger prefaces 'I’ve got nothing to add.'
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 37. Nothing “magic” about a positive shareholders’ equity

quote_verbatim: The question is, is who’s got the edge in it? Because everybody is going to want to be in it, and they already are. [...] But you better have some way of playing one part of the game better than others or natural capitalistic forces are going to grind you down. [...] So, the growth aspects overall of the market were not a big — are not a big factor with us. It’s really a question of figuring out who’s going to win what game, and who’s going to lose what game.
concept: A market's growth matters little; ask who has an edge in some segment, since without one competition grinds a participant down where customers switch freely.
evolution_notes: Buffett: people 'are quite willing to shift cards' for a small advantage. Compare M1994-051 (lowest-cost performer wins; rising share alone is not enough) and M1994-080 (growth not required).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 38. Looking for winners in competitive credit card business

quote_verbatim: You’re certainly seeing the value of bank branches diminish significantly. It used to be a point of enormous pride with managements, in how many branches they had. [...] And there are a lot of people that have their eye on that market, including Microsoft, as you mention. It may be to their advantage to hook up with the present players. I mean, I know it’s certainly something that gets explored. But they may figure out a way to go around the present players, too. And that’s one investment consideration.
concept: An incumbent's prized asset (bank branches) can lose value; ask whether newcomers will join the incumbents or find a way around them.
evolution_notes: Buffett expects little change in banking in five years but major change over 20 to 30, with winners and losers 'a very tough question'. Munger: Merrill Lynch went around the banks with cash management accounts, 'I don’t think it’s the only innovation that’ll come along.' Compare M1995-061 (technology as a curse to incumbents).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 39. Expect big changes in banking over next 20 years

quote_verbatim: so I would say you would look at those in a general way very much as you’d look at banking operations first. And then you’d try and figure out what are the specific strengths or weaknesses of both organizations.
concept: Judge a company first by the economics of its industry in general, then by its own specific strengths and weaknesses.
evolution_notes: Said while declining to comment on specific holdings (M1995-070); 'I don’t want to spoil the fun for you.'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 40. No comment on SunTrust and PNC moats

quote_verbatim: Berkshire owes 7 or 800 million — or whatever it is now, in debt, and we owe another 3 billion-some of float. You know, those numbers would’ve sounded very big to me 25 years ago, but — and yet we’re one of the most conservatively financed operations you’ll find. [...] I mean, you can’t talk about debt levels without relating it to the ability to pay debt.
concept: Debt is judged against the ability to pay it, not by its absolute size; then ask how stable the income is and to whom the debt is owed.
evolution_notes: Said of the national debt and of Berkshire. Earlier in the heading: 'if I had to look at one single statistic, I would look at that ratio, just like I would look at a ratio of debt to income for an individual. Then you’d get into the question of the stability of the income and to whom it is owed.' The rest of the heading is a view on national finances and is not rowed. Munger's 'Serpico effect', 'where you start rewarding what you don’t want more of', is said of the country.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 42. National debt isn’t scary now, when compared to GDP

quote_verbatim: We bought more last year, and it’s not a bad measuring stick against buying other things. [...] if I’m going to look at another business I will say, you know, “Why would I rather have this than more Coca-Cola?” [...] I mean, the only reason to put the money in there is if they’ve measured against what they’re already doing.
concept: Measure every new purchase against adding to the best holding already owned; an allocation not measured against present holdings makes no sense.
evolution_notes: Buffett calls it 'slightly nuts' for institutions to put 3 or 4 percent in international or emerging equities 'because everybody else is doing it'. Compare L1994-032 (consider adding to existing holdings first) and M1994-049.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 43. Coca-Cola as “measuring stock” to evaluate alternatives

quote_verbatim: For an ordinary individual the best thing you have easily available is your measuring stick. If it isn’t — if the new thing isn’t better than what you already know is available, it hasn’t met your threshold, then that screens out, you know, 99 percent of what you see, and it’s an enormous thought conserver. [...] And all Warren says is, deciding whether to do something, just compare the best opportunity you have.
concept: Use the best opportunity already available as the threshold; anything not better is screened out, which removes most candidates and saves thought.
evolution_notes: Munger: institutions 'are deliberately using a technique that takes away the best mental tool they have', and business schools teach it; Nietzsche's man who thought he walked better with a lame leg. Compare M1995-093 (screen against dozens of businesses).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 43. Coca-Cola as “measuring stock” to evaluate alternatives

quote_verbatim: if you buy Berkshire, you should only think about buying it for a very long period of time. We have no idea what Berkshire is going to do, either intrinsically or in the market, in the next year. And you know, we care about the intrinsic part of it. We don’t care about the market aspect. We do care about building intrinsic value.
concept: Buy a share of a business only for a very long period; one year's outcome is unknowable, and only the growth of intrinsic value is cared about.

heading: OWNER-RELATED BUSINESS PRINCIPLES

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: OWNER-RELATED BUSINESS PRINCIPLES

quote_verbatim: Because of this two-pronged approach to business ownership and because of the limitations of conventional accounting, consolidated reported earnings may reveal relatively little about our true economic performance. Charlie and I, both as owners and managers, virtually ignore such consolidated numbers. However, we will also report to you the earnings of each major business we control, numbers we consider of great importance.
concept: Consolidated reported earnings may say little about economic performance; the earnings of each major business are what matter.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: OWNER-RELATED BUSINESS PRINCIPLES

quote_verbatim: Accounting consequences do not influence our operating or capital-allocation decisions. When acquisition costs are similar, we much prefer to purchase $2 of earnings that is not reportable by us under standard accounting principles than to purchase $1 of earnings that is reportable.

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: OWNER-RELATED BUSINESS PRINCIPLES

quote_verbatim: We rarely use much debt and, when we do, we attempt to structure it on a long-term fixed-rate basis. We will reject interesting opportunities rather than over-leverage our balance sheet. This conservatism has penalized our results but it is the only behavior that leaves us comfortable, considering our fiduciary obligations to policyholders, depositors, lenders and the many equity holders who have committed unusually large portions of their net worth to our care. (As one of the Indianapolis "500" winners said: "To finish first, you must first finish.")
concept: Little debt, long-term and fixed-rate; pass up opportunities rather than over-leverage, accepting lower results to be sure of finishing.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: OWNER-RELATED BUSINESS PRINCIPLES

We will only do with your money what we would do with our own, weighing fully the values you can obtain by diversifying your own portfolios through direct purchases in the stock market.
concept: Management does with owners' money only what it would do with its own, measured against what owners could buy for themselves in the market.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: OWNER-RELATED BUSINESS PRINCIPLES

concept: Retention is justified only if each dollar kept produces at least a dollar of market value, checked on a five-year rolling basis.

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: OWNER-RELATED BUSINESS PRINCIPLES

And — But we look for people that know their businesses, love their businesses, love their shareholders, want to treat them as partners. And we still look to the underlying business, though.

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 3. “A lot of mediocrity” among CEOs

quote_verbatim: And we like people that have batted .350 or .360, in terms of predicting that they’re going to bat over .300 in the future. And some guy says, you know, “I batted .127 last year. But I’ve got a new bat or a new batting coach,” you know, some management consultant has come in and told them how to do it, supposedly. We’re very suspicious of that. So we don’t like banjo hitters who suddenly proclaim that they can become power hitters. And then we try to figure out what their attitude is toward shareholders.

evolution_notes: Buffett: 'there’s an enormous difference in the talent of American business managers'; 'We still want them to be in a good business, though. I would emphasize that.' Compare M1995-052 (judge by the past record) and M1994-008.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 3. “A lot of mediocrity” among CEOs

quote_verbatim: In terms of building the business, he only built it when it made sense, not when it did something for his ego or to make it larger alone. He did it when it was in his shareholders’ interests. And they’re not all Tom Murphys. But when you find them, and they’re in a decent business, you want to bet very heavily and not make the same mistake I made by selling out once or twice, too. (Laughter)
concept: A manager who grows the business only when it serves shareholders, not ego or size, in a decent business, warrants a very heavy bet; selling out of such a holding was a mistake.
evolution_notes: Tom Murphy at Cap Cities, 'you could see it in 50 different ways'. Compare L1995-032 (selling part of a holding run by an exceptional manager was a costly error) and M1994-042 (managers gain from size alone).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 3. “A lot of mediocrity” among CEOs

quote_verbatim: You know, we think diversification is — as practiced generally — makes very little sense for anyone that knows what they’re doing. Diversification is a protection against ignorance. I mean, if you want to make sure — (laughter) — that nothing bad happens to you relative to the market, you own everything. There’s nothing wrong with that. I mean, that is a perfectly sound approach for somebody who does not feel they know how to analyze businesses.
concept: Diversification protects against ignorance: owning everything is sound for someone who cannot analyse businesses and makes little sense for someone who can.
evolution_notes: Just before: 'We like to put a lot of money in things that we feel strongly about.' Restates L1993-025 and L1993-026.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 4. “Diversification is a protection against ignorance”

quote_verbatim: If you know how to analyze businesses and value businesses, it’s crazy to own 50 stocks or 40 stocks or 30 stocks, probably, because there aren’t that many wonderful businesses that are understandable to a single human being, in all likelihood. And to have some super-wonderful business and then put money in number 30 or 35 on your list of attractiveness and forego putting more money into number one, just strikes Charlie and me as madness. And it’s conventional practice, and it may — you know, if you all you have to achieve is average, it may preserve your job. But it’s a confession, in our view, that you don’t really understand the businesses that you own.
concept: For one who can value businesses, money goes to the top of the ranked list rather than to the thirtieth idea; wide holdings confess that the owner does not understand the businesses.
evolution_notes: 'if you all you have to achieve' is as printed. Compare M1995-105 (measure every new purchase against adding to the best holding) and L1994-032 (consider adding to existing holdings first).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 4. “Diversification is a protection against ignorance”

quote_verbatim: But three wonderful businesses is more than you need in this life to do very well. [...] I mean, if you had — a really wonderful business is very well protected against the vicissitudes of the economy over time and the competition. I mean, you know, we’re talking about businesses that are resistant to effective competition. And three of those will be better than 100 average businesses. And they’ll be safer, incidentally. I mean, there is less risk in owning three easy-to-identify, wonderful businesses than there is in owning 50 well-known, big businesses.
concept: A wonderful business is one resistant to effective competition and protected against economic swings; three such businesses carry less risk than fifty well-known big ones.
evolution_notes: The elided middle: fortunes were built on one wonderful business such as Coca-Cola, and 'there aren’t 50 Coca-Colas'. Munger: much of modern corporate finance 'is twaddle'; Buffett on modern portfolio theory: 'It has no utility. But you know, it will tell you how to do average.' Later (line 819): 'If you find three wonderful businesses in your life, you’ll get very rich. And if you understand them — bad things aren’t going to happen to those three.' Compare L1993-016 and M1995-108.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 4. “Diversification is a protection against ignorance”

quote_verbatim: We want, at Berkshire, to do everything as efficiently as we can. Part of that, in a big way, is not taking on a lot of people we don’t need. A lot of the mistakes that are being corrected now are because people got very fat. And their businesses got very fat in the past and took on all kinds of people they don’t need. [...] We don’t want to take on more people than we need in any of our businesses, because we don’t want to lay people off, either.
concept: Do not hire beyond need, so that layoffs are never needed; today's downsizing corrects bloat that prosperity let grow.
evolution_notes: The elided middle: oil companies' employment per barrel fell dramatically, which 'just means that they weren’t being run that well 20 years ago'. Earlier in the heading Buffett hopes to avoid businesses, like New England textiles, that require layoffs.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 5. Downsizing is sometimes needed to correct excessive hiring in the past

quote_verbatim: Well, if you put it in reverse, you’d say, name a business that has been ruined because it was over-downsized. I cannot think of a single one. But if you asked me to name businesses that were half-ruined, or ruined, by bloat, I mean, I could just rattle off name after name after name.
concept: Invert the question: bloat has ruined many businesses and over-downsizing none, so bloat is the danger to watch.
evolution_notes: Buffett adds: 'You’re very likely to compete against some guy, at some point, who doesn’t have more people around than needed in the business, too.' Compare M1996-005 (work backwards from the outcome to avoid).

heading: ### 5. Downsizing is sometimes needed to correct excessive hiring in the past

quote_verbatim: But there has been capital come in, and that is negative for our business. I mean, because any capital that’s brought in, basically, will get employed. [...] And if you’ve got a lot of capital in this business, or if you attracted a lot of capital, you will do something. You might like to do something smart, but if need be, you’ll do something dumb. You’ll rationalize it, so you think it’s smart. But you will do it.
concept: New capital in an industry will be employed, dumbly if need be, and rationalized as smart; inflows of capital are a warning of price cutting.

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 6. No layoffs at insurance operations due to reduced volume

quote_verbatim: We have promised people, at all of our insurance operations, that we will never have layoffs because of a drop in volume. We do not want the people who run our insurance business to feel they have to write X dollars in order to keep everybody there. [...] What we can’t afford are people feeling some internal compulsion to keep writing business in order to keep their job.
concept: Remove the incentive to write business for its own sake: no layoffs for a fall in volume, accepting some idle overhead, so staff never write to keep their jobs.
evolution_notes: Compare L1993-013 (accept much lower volume when prices fall) and M1995-015. Tension of emphasis with this heading's predecessor (no more people than needed, heading 5) is noted, not rowed: idle insurance overhead is accepted on purpose.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 6. No layoffs at insurance operations due to reduced volume

quote_verbatim: It’s a lot like investments. If you feel you have to invest every day, you’re going to make a lot of mistakes. It just — it isn’t that kind of a business. You have to wait until you get the fat pitch. And in insurance, it’s similar. You do not — if we had a budget for premium volume for our insurance companies, it would be the dumbest thing we could do, because they would meet the budget. They could meet any budget I set out.
concept: Wait for the fat pitch in insurance as in investing; a volume budget would be met and paid for for decades, so none is set.
evolution_notes: Continues (line 873): a budget to write 500 million would be met 'and I would be paying the bills for decades to come'; GEICO, the low-cost operator, is the exception that grows under almost any circumstances. Compare L1994-003 and M1995-079 (no budgets).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 6. No layoffs at insurance operations due to reduced volume

quote_verbatim: And the management of GEICO is focused. I love focused management. [...] And when they lose that focus — as, actually, did Coke and Gillette both, at one point 20 to 30 years ago somewhat — it shows up. [...] GEICO actually started — they started fooling around in a number of things in the early ’80s, and they paid a price to do it. They paid a very big price. They paid a direct price, in terms of the cost of those things, because they almost all worked out badly. And then they paid an additional price in the loss of focus on the main business.
concept: Look for management focused on the main business; diversifying moves cost twice, once directly and again through lost focus on the core.
evolution_notes: GEICO is kept out of other countries while the home opportunity is huge. At line 897: 'So, we like focus. We love focus.' Compare L1994-011 (a good manager stays undiverted).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 7. International expansion for GEICO would be dangerous distraction

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 10. Newspapers may evolve, but won’t disappear entirely

quote_verbatim: Now, if I were asked, would I trade that for $7 billion and not have to pay tax on the gain that would result if I did that, but I would then have to stay out of the insurance business forever — total forever non-compete clause of any kind in insurance — would I accept that? And the answer is no. Now, that is not because I would rather have 7 billion of float than 7 billion of net proceeds of free money. It’s because I expect the 7 billion to grow.
concept: Value an insurance business by asking whether you would trade its float for the same sum in tax-free cash plus a permanent non-compete; refusing means the value lies in the float's expected growth.
evolution_notes: Buffett defines float in the same breath: 'the money we’re holding that belongs to someone else but that we have the use of'. Compare L1995-014, M1996-022 and M1996-023.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 11. Why $7B of insurance float is better than $7B of cash

quote_verbatim: WARREN BUFFETT: That’s probably true in this case. I’m not sure about other cases. But it would’ve been a terrible mistake. It would’ve been a mistake to do it 10 or 12 years ago with 300 million. [...] So as Charlie says, that is not the answer that we would’ve given some time back. But it’s a very valuable business. It has to be run right. [...] And it’s not automatic. But they have the people, the distribution structure, the reputation, the capital strength, the competitive advantages. They have those in place.

speaker: BUFFETT

quote_verbatim: which is that the borrower has the option of calling off the deal tomorrow or retaining it for 30 years. And that is a very disadvantageous contract to enter into, if you lend money. They have done quite an intelligent job of attacking that by callable debt and various things. But you can’t address a problem like that totally. quote_verbatim: But in general terms, unless you find the prices of a great company really offensive, if you feel you’ve identified it — And by definition, a great company is one that’s going to remain great for 30 years. If it’s going to be a great company for three years, you know, it ain’t a great company. [...] So, you really want to go along with the idea of something that, if you were going to take a trip for 20 years, you wouldn’t feel bad leaving the money in with no orders with your broker and no power of attorney or anything, and you just go on the trip. And you know you come back, and it’s going to be a terribly strong company. I think it’s better just to own them.
concept: A great company is one that stays great for 30 years, one you could leave untouched through a 20-year trip; once identified, own it unless the price is really offensive.

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 13. Don’t wait for downturn to buy a great company

quote_verbatim: So, to sit there and hope that you buy them in the throes of some panic, you know, that you sort of take the attitude of a mortician, you know, waiting for a flu epidemic or something, I mean — (laughter) — it — I’m not sure that will be a great technique.
concept: Waiting for a panic to buy an identified great business is a poor technique; the extremes are rarely captured except by an accidental sum of money.
evolution_notes: At line 981: 'you never get the benefits of those extremes anyway, unless you just come into some accidental sum of money at some time. So, I think the main thing to do is find wonderful businesses.' At line 985: 'So, we’ve had our share of flu epidemics. But you don’t want to spend your life — (laughs) — waiting around for them.' Compare M1995-057 and M1994-065.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 13. Don’t wait for downturn to buy a great company

quote_verbatim: You know, I think, if you like the business, and you like the person that’s coming to you, and the price sounds reasonable, and you really know the business, I think, probably, the thing to do is to take it and don’t worry about how it’s quoted. It won’t be quoted tomorrow, or next week, or next month. You know, I think people’s investment would be more intelligent, you know, if stocks were quoted about once a year.
concept: Treat a stock as a share in a private hometown business: like the business, like the person, find the price reasonable, know the business, then buy and ignore the quotation.
evolution_notes: Set up at line 983 by the case of the best business in your hometown whose owner offers his dead brother's 20 percent. Compare M1994-034 and L1993-019.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 13. Don’t wait for downturn to buy a great company

quote_verbatim: If you have something you think you understand that looks very attractive to you, we think it’s smart to do what you understand. If — we’ve been unable to find companies that fit our slender talents. We well might have been in the Pfizers and Microsofts and so forth. But we’ve never had to revert to it. We don’t sneer at it. Other people with more talent have found that a wonderful course of action.
concept: Do what you understand; others with different talents may rightly own businesses one cannot judge oneself.
evolution_notes: Compare M1994-055 (more than one sound method) and M1995-074.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 14. “Change is likely to work against us”

quote_verbatim: WARREN BUFFETT: We generally look at businesses — we feel change is likely to work against us. We do not have great ability — we do not think we have great ability to predict where change is going to lead. We think we have some ability to find businesses where we don’t think change is going to be very important.
concept: Assume change works against the investor; seek businesses where change is not going to be very important rather than predict where change leads.
evolution_notes: At line 1001: 'We don’t think it’s an opportunity at all. I mean, we — it scares the hell out of us. Because we don’t know how things are going to change.' Compare L1993-023 and M1996-019.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 14. “Change is likely to work against us”

quote_verbatim: They wouldn’t have that same credibility someplace else. But in the shaving field, they have it. Those are assets that can’t be built. And they’re very hard to destroy. So change — we think we know, in a general way, what the soft drink industry or the shaving industry or the candy business is going to look like 10 or 20 years from now. We think Microsoft is a sensational company run by the best of managers. But we don’t have any idea what that world is going to look like in 10 or 20 years. [...] I mean, in the end, we want to understand, ourselves, where we think a business is going.
concept: Credibility in a field (Gillette in shaving), backed by distribution and outspending rivals on improvement, is an asset that cannot be built and is hard to destroy; the test is whether one understands oneself where the industry will be in 10 or 20 years.
evolution_notes: Before: Gillette will spend 'many multiples the money on developing better shaving systems' than anyone else; 'They’ve got the distribution system. They’ve got the believability.' A great manager (Gates) does not substitute: 'I don’t want to bet on anybody else.' At line 1003: 'why going around trying to bet on things we don’t know, when we can bet on the simple things?'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 14. “Change is likely to work against us”

quote_verbatim: So, we will not disclose, in the way of our security holdings, more than we feel we have to disclose in order to be fair about things that can be material to the company. And we certainly have no interest in disclosing them to people who, essentially, want to use the information to try and figure out where our buying power may be, subsequently, or something of the sort.
concept: Disclose holdings only as far as fairness on material matters requires; supplying investment ideas does not benefit the owners.

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 15. We don’t reveal more about our stocks than we have to

quote_verbatim: Most of the things — we try to be in businesses that are fairly simple and that can’t get all messed up. And by and large, I think that we’ve got an unusual portfolio of those. And when it gets to our investees, you know, they’re going to worry about those problems themselves. We really worry about allocating money around Berkshire and having the right managers in place. That — if we can do those two right, everything else’ll take care of itself.
concept: Own simple businesses that cannot get badly messed up; the centre does capital allocation and choosing managers, and leaves operating problems to the operators.
evolution_notes: Munger: 'The Nebraska Furniture Mart would be full of furniture and know the customers. I don’t think a computer crash is going to do us in.' Restates M1996-032 and M1994-062.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 16. Buffett isn’t worrying about the Y2K computer problem

quote_verbatim: I think ours are way easier to predict. There are fair — they tend to be fundamental things, fairly simple. Rate of change is not fast, so I feel pretty comfortable. [...] Whereas, if you — if we were to buy — if we owned a base metals business or many retailing businesses I can think of, or an auto business, I’m not sure I’d know where we would stand in the competitive pecking order five or 10 years from now. I would not want to try and come in and displace See’s Candies, for example, in the business it does, or the Furniture Mart.
concept: Predictability rests on fundamental, simple products with a slow rate of change; ask whether you know where the business will stand in its competitive pecking order in five or ten years, and whether you would want to try to displace it.
evolution_notes: Peter Bevelin asked whether See's, furniture, jewelry and shoes are hard to predict. Buffett expects 'one surprise' in five years, 'But there won’t be a series of them.' Compare M1994-026 and L1995-008 (retailers).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 17. Berkshire businesses are “way easier to predict”

quote_verbatim: So the question is, 10 years from now, what place in the mind — because it’s a share of mind. You know, they call it share of market, but it starts with share of mind — and what place in the mind of billions of children around the world, and their parents, does Disney itself have, and their characters, relative to that owned by other organizations and other characters?
concept: Share of market starts with share of mind; judge a consumer franchise by the place it will hold in customers' minds ten years out relative to rivals.
evolution_notes: Buffett calls Eisner 'by far, the most important factor in Disney’s success' and describes the films-parks-merchandise circle 'which feeds on itself'; he expects more competition, 'But I would rather start with Disney’s hand than anyone else’s, by some margin.' Line 1065: recycling Snow White every seven or eight years is 'kind of like having an oil field' that seeps back in. Compare M1995-085 (self-reinforcing circle).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 18. Eisner is “most important factor” in Disney’s success

quote_verbatim: Well, I think it helps to do the simple arithmetic. Suppose you have a billion children of low-middle income 20 years from now. And suppose you could make $10 per year per child, after taxes, from your position. It gets into very large numbers.
concept: Size a franchise with simple arithmetic: a small profit per customer across a very large future customer base.
evolution_notes: Munger adds that his grandchildren want to see Disney 'over and over and over again'. Compare M1995-092 (numeracy).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 18. Eisner is “most important factor” in Disney’s success

quote_verbatim: And if you’re buying the local brain surgeon, you would not pay any real multiple of earnings because he’s going to have this revelation, several days later, that it’s really him and not you there, with your little stock certificate, that’s producing the earnings. [...] But whoever owns the Mayo Clinic has an asset that is independent of the attitude of any one person in the place the next day. Wall Street has a mix of both. And there are some businesses that are more — where the value resides more in the institution. And there are some where the value resides more in the individuals.
concept: Ask whether the value resides in the institution (Mayo Clinic) or in individuals (the local brain surgeon); where the people produce the earnings, the owner of the certificate does not really own them and should pay no real multiple.
evolution_notes: Line 1081: Wall Street is 'not an easy business to predict, unless you have a business that’s very institutional in character, and there aren’t many of those in Wall Street.' Compare M1995-043 (businesses where employees claim the returns) and M1995-056.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 19. Why Wall Street businesses are “tough” to manage

quote_verbatim: I mean, we are not trying to predict markets. We never will try and predict markets. We’re trying to find wonderful businesses. And the fact that a part of the market is kind of screwy, you know, that’s unimportant to us. We tried, a few times, shorting some of those things in our innocence of youth. And it’s very tough to make money shorting even the obvious frauds.
concept: Never try to predict markets; a mispriced corner of the market is irrelevant to finding wonderful businesses, and shorting even obvious frauds rarely pays.
evolution_notes: Before: 'there have always been hundreds of cases, or thousands of cases, of things that are ridiculously priced, and phony stock promotions'. Compare M1994-035 and M1994-038.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 20. Not important if part of the market is “kind of screwy”

quote_verbatim: we don’t look at indicia from stocks in general, or from P/Es, or price-sales ratios, or what other things are doing. We really just focus on businesses. We don’t care if there’s a stock market. I mean, would we want to own Coca-Cola, the 8 percent we own of Coca-Cola, or the 11 percent or Gillette, if they said, you know, “We’re just going to delist the stock and we’re never — you know, we’ll open it again in 20 years?” It’s fine with us, you know. And if it goes down on the news, we’ll buy more of it. So we care about what the business does.
concept: Ask whether you would be content to own the business if its stock were delisted for 20 years; market-wide indicators are ignored and only what the business does counts.
