evolution_notes: He gives it as one reason to seek owners with long-term horizons.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: The Relationship of Intrinsic Value to Market Price

quote_verbatim: Because Charlie and I wished to minimize the issuance of Berkshire shares, the transaction we structured gave FlightSafety shareholders a choice of cash or stock but carried terms that encouraged those who were tax-indifferent to take cash.
concept: Pay in cash where possible; minimise issuing your own shares in an acquisition.
evolution_notes: Compare L1995-028 and R1995-010 on issuing only for equal value.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Acquisitions of 1996

quote_verbatim: He will run operations just as he has in the past:  We never fool with success. [...] The real explanation, however, is self-interest:  It's difficult to teach a new dog old tricks.
concept: Leave a successful manager to run the business as before, regardless of age; experience is what is being bought.
evolution_notes: Said of Al Ueltschi, 79, of FlightSafety; he adds that many Berkshire managers past 70 still perform as they did when young.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Acquisitions of 1996

quote_verbatim: To begin with, float is money we hold but don't own.  In an insurance operation, float arises because premiums are received before losses are paid.  Secondly, the premiums that an insurer takes in typically do not cover the losses and expenses it eventually must pay.  That leaves it running an "underwriting loss," which is the cost of float.  An insurance business has value if its cost of float over time is less than the cost the company would otherwise incur to obtain funds.  But the business is an albatross if the cost of its float is higher than market rates for money.
concept: Float is money held but not owned; an insurer has value only if its cost of float is below the market cost of money.
evolution_notes: Restates L1995-014 and L1995-016. Just before, he says what counts is first the amount of float and second its cost, and that float is a major component of intrinsic value not reflected in book value.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Insurance Operations - Overview

quote_verbatim: What you must understand, however, is that a truly terrible year in the super-cat business is not a possibility - it's a certainty. [...] If you would tend to react that way, you should not own Berkshire shares now, just as you should entirely avoid owning stocks if a crashing market would lead you to panic and sell.  Selling fine businesses on "scary" news is usually a bad decision.
concept: Expect the certain bad year in advance; whoever would panic-sell on scary news should not own the stock at all.
evolution_notes: Followed by Woodruff on when to sell Coke: "I don't know.  I've never sold any."
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Super-Cat Insurance

quote_verbatim: Gyrations in Berkshire's earnings don't bother us in the least:  Charlie and I would much rather earn a lumpy 15% over time than a smooth 12%. [...] We are most comfortable with that thinking, however, when we have shareholder/partners who can also accept volatility, and that's why we regularly repeat our cautions.
concept: Prefer higher lumpy returns to lower smooth ones, and warn owners so they can accept the volatility.
evolution_notes: Repeats L1995-017 almost word for word, adding the condition that the shareholders accept volatility too.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Super-Cat Insurance

quote_verbatim: First, the parties buying reinsurance from us know that we both can and will pay under the most adverse of circumstances. [...] Indeed, one reason we never "lay off" part of the risks we insure is that we have reservations about our ability to collect from others when disaster strikes.
concept: In reinsurance the advantage is certainty of payment in the worst case; do not rely on collecting from others then.
evolution_notes: The second and third advantages named: capacity reserved for long-standing clients after a catastrophe, and cover of a size no one else offers.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Super-Cat Insurance

quote_verbatim: We don't know - nor do we think computer models will help us, since we believe the precision they project is a chimera.  In fact, such models can lull decision-makers into a false sense of security and thereby increase their chances of making a really huge mistake.
concept: Precise risk models give false security and raise the chance of a huge mistake.
evolution_notes: Cites portfolio insurance in the 1987 crash.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Super-Cat Insurance

quote_verbatim: Even if perfection in assessing risks is unattainable, insurers can underwrite sensibly.  After all, you need not know a man's precise age to know that he is old enough to vote nor know his exact weight to recognize his need to diet.  In insurance, it is essential to remember that virtually all surprises are unpleasant [...] The super-cat business is just like the investment business in that it often takes a long time to find out whether you knew what you were doing.
concept: Judge risk roughly but soundly without precision; assume surprises are bad; results take a long time to show skill.
evolution_notes: The elided part prices super-cat so that about 90% of premiums are eventually paid out in losses and expenses.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Super-Cat Insurance

quote_verbatim: In this respect, as in others, we try to "reverse engineer" our future at Berkshire, bearing in mind Charlie's dictum:  "All I want to know is where I'm going to die so I'll never go there." [...] If we can't tolerate a possible consequence, remote though it may be, we steer clear of planting its seeds. That is why we don't borrow big amounts and why we make sure that our super-cat business losses, large though the maximums may sound, will not put a major dent in Berkshire's intrinsic value.
concept: Invert: avoid any intolerable consequence, however remote; hence little borrowing and capped catastrophe losses.
evolution_notes: Munger's dictum is quoted by Buffett; the row's speaker is Buffett. The preceding paragraph aggregates the exposure: a California quake would also hit See's, Wells Fargo and Freddie Mac.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Super-Cat Insurance

quote_verbatim: There's nothing esoteric about GEICO's success:  The company's competitive strength flows directly from its position as a low-cost operator.  Low costs permit low prices, and low prices attract and retain good policyholders.  The final segment of a virtuous circle is drawn when policyholders recommend us to their friends.
concept: A low-cost position is a competitive strength when it feeds a circle: low price, good customers, referrals, lower cost.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Insurance - GEICO and Other Primary Operations

quote_verbatim: Our goal, however, is not to widen our profit margin but rather to enlarge the price advantage we offer customers.
concept: Use a cost advantage to widen the customer's price advantage, not the margin.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Insurance - GEICO and Other Primary Operations

quote_verbatim: Nonetheless, the economies of scale we enjoy should allow us to maintain or even widen the protective moat surrounding our economic castle. [...] GEICO's sustainable cost advantage is what attracted me to the company way back in 1951, when the entire business was valued at $7 million.
concept: A sustainable cost advantage from scale is the moat; it survives new competitors entering.
evolution_notes: Compare L1995-013 (castles behind unbreachable moats). The same advantage justified paying $2.3 billion for the remaining 49%.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Insurance - GEICO and Other Primary Operations

quote_verbatim: The GEICO plan exemplifies Berkshire's incentive compensation principles:  Goals should be (1) tailored to the economics of the specific operating business; (2) simple in character so that the degree to which they are being realized can be easily measured; and (3) directly related to the daily activities of plan participants.  As a corollary, we shun "lottery ticket" arrangements, such as options on Berkshire shares, whose ultimate value - which could range from zero to huge - is totally out of the control of the person whose behavior we would like to affect.
concept: Incentive goals: specific to the business, simple to measure, tied to daily work; no options whose payoff the person cannot control.
evolution_notes: GEICO's bonuses rest on two variables: growth in voluntary auto policies and underwriting profit on seasoned business.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Insurance - GEICO and Other Primary Operations

quote_verbatim: Furthermore, at Berkshire, we never greet good work by raising the bar.
concept: Do not raise targets in response to good results.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Insurance - GEICO and Other Primary Operations

quote_verbatim: We think it foolish for an insurance company to pay bonuses that are tied to overall corporate results when great work on one side of the business - underwriting or investment - could conceivably be completely neutralized by bad work on the other.
concept: Pay each person on the results of their own side of the business, not on the overall total.
evolution_notes: Lou Simpson is paid on four-year investment performance.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Insurance - GEICO and Other Primary Operations

quote_verbatim: This procedure lets you view the earnings of our businesses as they would have been reported had we not purchased them.  For the reasons discussed on pages 65 and 66, this form of presentation seems to us to be more useful to investors and managers than one utilizing generally-accepted accounting principles (GAAP), which require purchase-premiums to be charged off business-by-business.
concept: Look at a bought business's earnings before purchase-accounting charges; that view is more useful than GAAP's.
evolution_notes: Pages 65 and 66 are the Owner's Manual's intrinsic-value and goodwill discussion, reprinted in the report.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Sources of Reported Earnings

quote_verbatim: Not that we mind this division of money, since on balance we regard the undistributed earnings of investees as more valuable to us than the portion paid out.  The reason is simple: Our investees often have the opportunity to reinvest earnings at high rates of return.  So why should we want them paid out?
concept: Retained earnings are worth more than dividends when the business can reinvest them at high rates of return.
evolution_notes: Opens with 'Reported earnings are a poor measure of economic progress at Berkshire', because only dividends from investees appear in them. Compare R1995-009 (dollar retained, dollar created).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: "Look-Through" Earnings

quote_verbatim: To depict something closer to economic reality at Berkshire than reported earnings, though, we employ the concept of "look-through" earnings.  As we calculate these, they consist of: (1) the operating earnings reported in the previous section, plus; (2) our share of the retained operating earnings of major investees that, under GAAP accounting, are not reflected in our profits, less; (3) an allowance for the tax that would be paid by Berkshire if these retained earnings of investees had instead been distributed to us.
concept: Look-through earnings: own operating earnings plus share of investees' retained earnings, less the tax that a distribution would cost.
evolution_notes: He warns the figures 'can be no more than approximate, since they are based on a number of judgment calls'.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: "Look-Through" Earnings

quote_verbatim: Inactivity strikes us as intelligent behavior. [...] The art of investing in public companies successfully is little different from the art of successfully acquiring subsidiaries.  In each case you simply want to acquire, at a sensible price, a business with excellent economics and able, honest management.  Thereafter, you need only monitor whether these qualities are being preserved.
concept: Buy a stock as you would a whole business (excellent economics, able and honest management, sensible price), then only monitor that those qualities persist; inactivity is intelligent.
evolution_notes: Preceded by 'We continue to make more money when snoring than when active.' The elided sentences compare trading minority positions to trading subsidiaries on discount-rate predictions.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Common Stock Investments

quote_verbatim: When carried out capably, an investment strategy of that type will often result in its practitioner owning a few securities that will come to represent a very large portion of his portfolio. [...] To suggest that this investor should sell off portions of his most successful investments simply because they have come to dominate his portfolio is akin to suggesting that the Bulls trade Michael Jordan because he has become so important to the team.
concept: Do not trim the best holdings merely because they have grown to dominate the portfolio.
evolution_notes: The elided illustration: buying 20% of the future earnings of college basketball stars.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Common Stock Investments

quote_verbatim: In studying the investments we have made in both subsidiary companies and common stocks, you will see that we favor businesses and industries unlikely to experience major change.  The reason for that is simple:  Making either type of purchase, we are searching for operations that we believe are virtually certain to possess enormous competitive strength ten or twenty years from now.  A fast-changing industry environment may offer the chance for huge wins, but it precludes the certainty we seek.
concept: Favour businesses unlikely to change, because the aim is near-certain competitive strength in ten or twenty years.
evolution_notes: Same thought as M1996-058 (change likely to work against us) the year before.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Common Stock Investments

quote_verbatim: As investors, however, our reaction to a fermenting industry is much like our attitude toward space exploration:  We applaud the endeavor but prefer to skip the ride.
concept: Welcome innovation as a citizen; avoid investing in a fermenting industry.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Common Stock Investments

quote_verbatim: But the reasons why people today buy boxed chocolates, and why they buy them from us rather than from someone else, are virtually unchanged from what they were in the 1920s when the See family was building the business.  Moreover, these motivations are not likely to change over the next 20 years, or even 50.
concept: The test of stability is whether the reasons customers buy, and buy from you, are unchanged and will stay so, even if products and machinery change.
evolution_notes: He then applies the same test to Coke: the fundamentals behind 'competitive dominance and stunning economics' have stayed constant.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Common Stock Investments

quote_verbatim: Companies such as Coca-Cola and Gillette might well be labeled "The Inevitables." [...] In the end, however, no sensible observer - not even these companies' most vigorous competitors, assuming they are assessing the matter honestly - questions that Coke and Gillette will dominate their fields worldwide for an investment lifetime.
concept: An 'Inevitable' is a company that even honest competitors agree will dominate its field for an investment lifetime.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Common Stock Investments

quote_verbatim: Obviously many companies in high-tech businesses or embryonic industries will grow much faster in percentage terms than will The Inevitables.  But I would rather be certain of a good result than hopeful of a great one.
concept: Prefer certainty of a good result to hope of a great one.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Common Stock Investments

quote_verbatim: Leadership alone provides no certainties:  Witness the shocks some years back at General Motors, IBM and Sears, all of which had enjoyed long periods of seeming invincibility.  Though some industries or lines of business exhibit characteristics that endow leaders with virtually insurmountable advantages, and that tend to establish Survival of the Fattest as almost a natural law, most do not.  Thus, for every Inevitable, there are dozens of Impostors, companies now riding high but vulnerable to competitive attacks.
concept: Leadership is not durability; only some industries give leaders insurmountable advantages, and most leaders are impostors vulnerable to attack.
evolution_notes: He adds that he and Munger can identify only a few Inevitables and so add 'a few "Highly Probables."'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Common Stock Investments

quote_verbatim: You can, of course, pay too much for even the best of businesses. The overpayment risk surfaces periodically and, in our opinion, may now be quite high for the purchasers of virtually all stocks, The Inevitables included.  Investors making purchases in an overheated market need to recognize that it may often take an extended period for the value of even an outstanding company to catch up with the price they paid.
concept: Even the best business can be overpaid for; an overpayment may take years for value to catch up.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Common Stock Investments

quote_verbatim: A far more serious problem occurs when the management of a great company gets sidetracked and neglects its wonderful base business while purchasing other businesses that are so-so or worse. [...] Loss of focus is what most worries Charlie and me when we contemplate investing in businesses that in general look outstanding.  All too often, we've seen value stagnate in the presence of hubris or of boredom that caused the attention of managers to wander.
concept: The chief worry in an outstanding business is management losing focus on the base business and buying mediocre ones.
evolution_notes: Example given: shrimp farming at Coke and oil exploration at Gillette decades earlier.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Common Stock Investments

quote_verbatim: Most investors, both institutional and individual, will find that the best way to own common stocks is through an index fund that charges minimal fees.  Those following this path are sure to beat the net results (after fees and expenses) delivered by the great majority of investment professionals.
concept: For most investors a minimal-fee index fund is the best way to own stocks.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Common Stock Investments

quote_verbatim: Intelligent investing is not complex, though that is far from saying that it is easy.  What an investor needs is the ability to correctly evaluate selected businesses. Note that word "selected":  You don't have to be an expert on every company, or even many.  You only have to be able to evaluate companies within your circle of competence.  The size of that circle is not very important; knowing its boundaries, however, is vital.
concept: Circle of competence: evaluate only selected businesses you can judge; the size of the circle matters less than knowing its edges.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Common Stock Investments

quote_verbatim: To invest successfully, you need not understand beta, efficient markets, modern portfolio theory, option pricing or emerging markets. You may, in fact, be better off knowing nothing of these. [...] In our view, though, investment students need only two well-taught courses - How to Value a Business, and How to Think About Market Prices.
concept: Investing needs only valuing a business and thinking rightly about market prices, not modern finance theory.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Common Stock Investments

quote_verbatim: Your goal as an investor should simply be to purchase, at a rational price, a part interest in an easily-understandable business whose earnings are virtually certain to be materially higher five, ten and twenty years from now.  Over time, you will find only a few companies that meet these standards - so when you see one that qualifies, you should buy a meaningful amount of stock.  You must also resist the temptation to stray from your guidelines:  If you aren't willing to own a stock for ten years, don't even think about owning it for ten minutes.
concept: Buy at a rational price an easily understood business whose earnings are virtually certain to be much higher in 5, 10 and 20 years; buy meaningfully when found; hold for ten years or not at all.
evolution_notes: Followed by: 'Put together a portfolio of companies whose aggregate earnings march upward over the years, and so also will the portfolio's market value.'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Common Stock Investments

quote_verbatim: Though it's seldom recognized, this is the exact approach that has produced gains for Berkshire shareholders:  Our look-through earnings have grown at a good clip over the years, and our stock price has risen correspondingly.  Had those gains in earnings not materialized, there would have been little increase in Berkshire's value.
concept: Market value follows the growth of look-through earnings; without the earnings growth there is no value growth.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Common Stock Investments

quote_verbatim: We will try to build earnings by running our present businesses well - a job made easy because of the extraordinary talents of our operating managers - and by purchasing other businesses, in whole or in part, that are not likely to be roiled by change and that possess important competitive advantages.
concept: Grow earnings by running what is owned well and buying, whole or part, businesses unlikely to be roiled by change and with important competitive advantages.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Common Stock Investments

quote_verbatim: But my analysis of USAir's business was both superficial and wrong. I was so beguiled by the company's long history of profitable operations, and by the protection that ownership of a senior security seemingly offered me, that I overlooked the crucial point:  USAir's revenues would increasingly feel the effects of an unregulated, fiercely-competitive market whereas its cost structure was a holdover from the days when regulation protected profits.  These costs, if left unchecked, portended disaster, however reassuring the airline's past record might be.  (If history supplied all of the answers, the Forbes 400 would consist of librarians.)
concept: A long profit history and a senior security do not protect against a cost structure that no longer fits a deregulated, competitive market; the past record is not the answer.
evolution_notes: Compare L1995-025 (preferreds not loss-proof). He adds that fixing the costs needed labor concessions airlines rarely get short of bankruptcy, that he twice tried to sell the preferred cheaply, and that the one thing he got right was a penalty-dividend clause on arrearages.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: USAir

quote_verbatim: (In the securities business, whatever can be sold will be sold.)
concept: Expect the securities industry to sell whatever it can, whatever the buyer's interest.
evolution_notes: Said of the threatened unit trusts that would have marketed Berkshire look-alikes on its non-repeatable record.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Financings

quote_verbatim: Overall, we tried to make sure that the B stock would be purchased only by investors with a long-term perspective.
concept: Design an issue so that it attracts long-term owners and repels short-term buyers.
evolution_notes: The means: a 1.5% commission to blunt broker enthusiasm and an open-ended amount to repel buyers seeking a hype-and-scarcity spurt. Compare L1995-029.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Financings

quote_verbatim: That's dead wrong.  We have paid a great many fees over the last 30 years [...] and we are delighted to make payments that are commensurate with performance.
concept: Fees are fine when commensurate with performance.
evolution_notes: Answering the claim that he and Munger dislike all investment-banking fees. He praises Salomon bankers for proposing terms against their own financial interest.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Financings

quote_verbatim: We will always "post" these reports on a Saturday so that anyone interested will have ample time to digest the information before trading begins.
concept: Release information so all holders can digest it before trading, none ahead of others.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Miscellaneous

quote_verbatim: Charlie and I hope that you do not think of yourself as merely owning a piece of paper whose price wiggles around daily and that is a candidate for sale when some economic or political event makes you nervous. We hope you instead visualize yourself as a part owner of a business that you expect to stay with indefinitely, much as you might if you owned a farm or apartment house in partnership with members of your family.
concept: A share is part ownership of a business to be held indefinitely, not paper to be sold when nervous.
evolution_notes: Commentary added in the 1996 Owner's Manual to the first principle (R1995-001). Compare M1996-003 (share as part of a farm).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: OWNER-RELATED BUSINESS PRINCIPLES

quote_verbatim: As owners of, say, Coca-Cola or Gillette shares, we think of Berkshire as being a non-managing partner in two extraordinary businesses, in which we measure our success by the long-term progress of the companies rather than by the month-to-month movements of their stocks. [...] If we have good long-term expectations, short-term price changes are meaningless for us except to the extent they offer us an opportunity to increase our ownership at an attractive price.
concept: Measure a holding by the company's long-term progress; short-term price moves matter only as chances to buy more cheaply.
evolution_notes: The elided sentence: they would not care if several years went by with no trading or quotation in those stocks.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: OWNER-RELATED BUSINESS PRINCIPLES

quote_verbatim: Charlie and I cannot promise you results. But we can guarantee that your financial fortunes will move in lockstep with ours for whatever period of time you elect to be our partner. We have no interest in large salaries or options or other means of gaining an "edge" over you. We want to make money only when our partners do and in exactly the same proportion.
concept: Managers should gain only as owners gain, in the same proportion, with no salary or option edge.
evolution_notes: Commentary on the eat-our-own-cooking principle (R1995-002): Munger's family has 90% or more of its net worth in Berkshire, Buffett's more than 99%.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: OWNER-RELATED BUSINESS PRINCIPLES

quote_verbatim: Operating with large amounts of capital as we do today, we cannot come close to performing as well as we once did with much smaller sums. The best rate of gain in intrinsic value we can even hope for is an average of 15% per annum, and we may well fall far short of that target. Indeed, we think very few large businesses have a chance of compounding intrinsic value at 15% per annum over an extended period of time.
concept: Very few large businesses can compound intrinsic value at 15% for long; size lowers the attainable rate.
evolution_notes: Same reality as L1996-002. | ERRATUM 2026-10-04: not reprinted in the FY2013 report
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: OWNER-RELATED BUSINESS PRINCIPLES

quote_verbatim: Overall, Berkshire and its long-term shareholders benefit from a sinking stock market much as a regular purchaser of food benefits from declining food prices. So when the market plummets - as it will from time to time - neither panic nor mourn. It's good news for Berkshire.
concept: A net buyer gains from falling prices; a market plunge is good news, not a cause for panic.
evolution_notes: The preceding paragraph: 'The challenge for us is to generate ideas as rapidly as we generate cash', and a depressed market lowers prices of whole companies and pieces and helps investees that buy back their own shares.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: OWNER-RELATED BUSINESS PRINCIPLES

quote_verbatim: Charlie and I pay a great deal of attention to how well our businesses are doing, and we also work to understand the environment in which each business is operating. For example, is one of our businesses enjoying an industry tailwind or is it facing a headwind?  Charlie and I need to know exactly which situation prevails and to adjust our expectations accordingly.
concept: Separate a business's own performance from the industry tailwind or headwind it is enjoying or facing.
evolution_notes: The letter applies it to USAir: performance 'helped significantly by an industry tailwind that may be cyclical' (L1996-040 context).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: OWNER-RELATED BUSINESS PRINCIPLES

quote_verbatim: In other words, we believe in telling you how we think so that you can evaluate not only Berkshire's businesses but also assess our approach to management and capital allocation.
concept: Managers should explain how they think so owners can judge their management and capital allocation, not only the businesses.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: OWNER-RELATED BUSINESS PRINCIPLES

quote_verbatim: This pleasant result has occurred because most of our investees are engaged in truly outstanding businesses that can often employ incremental capital to great advantage, either by putting it to work in their businesses or by repurchasing their shares. Obviously, every capital decision that our investees have made has not benefitted us as shareholders, but overall we have garnered far more than a dollar of value for each dollar they have retained.
concept: Retained earnings count fully only when the business can employ incremental capital to advantage, in the business or in buybacks.
evolution_notes: Same thought as L1996-022 in the letter.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: OWNER-RELATED BUSINESS PRINCIPLES

quote_verbatim: The financial calculus that Charlie and I employ would never permit our trading a good night's sleep for a shot at a few extra percentage points of return. I've never believed in risking what my family and friends have and need in order to pursue what they don't have and don't need.
concept: Never risk what one has and needs to gain what one does not have and does not need.
evolution_notes: Commentary on the debt principle (R1995-007).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: OWNER-RELATED BUSINESS PRINCIPLES

quote_verbatim: Neither item, of course, is equity; these are real liabilities. But they are liabilities without covenants or due dates attached to them. In effect, they give us the benefit of debt - an ability to have more assets working for us - but saddle us with none of its drawbacks.
concept: Deferred taxes and float are real liabilities but act as leverage without covenants or due dates, so long as their cost stays near zero.
evolution_notes: Before it: float is cost-free 'as long as we can break even in our insurance underwriting'. After it: 'there is no guarantee that we can obtain our float in the future at no cost.'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: OWNER-RELATED BUSINESS PRINCIPLES

quote_verbatim: Charlie and I are interested only in acquisitions that we believe will raise the per-share intrinsic value of Berkshire's stock. The size of our paychecks or our offices will never be related to the size of Berkshire's balance sheet.
concept: Acquire only to raise per-share intrinsic value; keep managers' pay unrelated to size.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: OWNER-RELATED BUSINESS PRINCIPLES

quote_verbatim: If we reach the point that we can't create extra value by retaining earnings, we will pay them out and let our shareholders deploy the funds.
concept: When retention no longer creates extra value, pay the earnings out.
evolution_notes: Commentary on the dollar-retained test (R1995-009). | ERRATUM 2026-10-04: not reprinted in the FY2013 report
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: OWNER-RELATED BUSINESS PRINCIPLES

quote_verbatim: Shock should have registered instead had we issued shares when our stock was undervalued. Managements that say or imply during a public offering that their stock is undervalued are usually being economical with the truth or uneconomical with their existing shareholders' money
concept: A management that issues stock while calling it undervalued is either shading the truth or wasting existing owners' money.
evolution_notes: Cut before the next clause, where the file prints a garbled cents sign ('80›' for 80 cents). Commentary on the issuance principle (R1995-010).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: OWNER-RELATED BUSINESS PRINCIPLES

quote_verbatim: True, we closed our textile business in the mid-1980's after 20 years of struggling with it, but only because we felt it was doomed to run never-ending operating losses. We have not, however, given thought to selling operations that would command very fancy prices nor have we dumped our laggards, though we focus hard on curing the problems that cause them to lag.
concept: Close a business only when it is doomed to endless losses; otherwise keep laggards and work to cure them.
evolution_notes: Commentary on R1995-011 (never sell good businesses; avoid gin rummy behavior).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: OWNER-RELATED BUSINESS PRINCIPLES

quote_verbatim: At Berkshire you will find no "big bath" accounting maneuvers or restructurings nor any "smoothing" of quarterly or annual results. We will always tell you how many strokes we have taken on each hole and never play around with the scorecard. When the numbers are a very rough "guesstimate," as they necessarily must be in insurance reserving, we will try to be both consistent and conservative in our approach.
concept: No big baths, no smoothing; where figures must be estimates, be consistent and conservative.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: OWNER-RELATED BUSINESS PRINCIPLES

quote_verbatim: In all of our communications, we try to make sure that no single shareholder gets an edge:  We do not follow the usual practice of giving earnings "guidance" or other information of value to analysts or large shareholders. Our goal is to have all of our owners updated at the same time.
concept: No guidance and no private information to analysts or large holders; all owners informed at once.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: OWNER-RELATED BUSINESS PRINCIPLES

quote_verbatim: To the extent possible, we would like each Berkshire shareholder to record a gain or loss in market value during his period of ownership that is proportional to the gain or loss in per-share intrinsic value recorded by the company during that holding period. [...] As that implies, we would rather see Berkshire's stock price at a fair level than a high level. evolution_notes: Compare M1996-028 to M1996-031. Munger (line 597): 'Warren lives one of the most rational lives I’ve ever seen.'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 33. Buffett describes a “normal” day

quote_verbatim: On the subject of options, I would say that most options are constructed poorly, from the standpoint of the owner, but they’re constructed very well from the standpoint of the person who receives them, which is not entirely unexplainable because the — it’s a very strange form of negotiation when the beneficiary is the one that also really does all the design and hires the experts to come in and tell him what is good for the company when the expert knows that the guy who signs the check would be quite interested also in hearing what’s good for him.
concept: Check who designed the options: when the beneficiary designs them and hires the experts, they favour him over the owners.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 34. Abuse of stock options as executive compensation

quote_verbatim: We feel that if you want a typist to type 100 words a minute, that you ought to pay for typing 100 words a minute, not what the earnings per share were last year. [...] So we believe in tying incentive comp to performance for which you have responsibility.
concept: Pay incentives on the performance a person is responsible for; only those responsible for the whole should be paid on the whole.
evolution_notes: Same principle as L1996-018 and L1996-020. Line 615: Chuck Huggins at See's is paid on the candy business, not on Berkshire.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 34. Abuse of stock options as executive compensation

quote_verbatim: With a company that pays no dividend like Berkshire, if you’re going to leave all your capital in every year, for me to get a fixed-price option for ten years would mean that I was getting a royalty on money that you left with me. [...] So I think any option should have a step-up in price that reflects the fact that money is reinvested by the shareholders annually. [...] I think options ought to be granted, basically, at the fair value of the business at the time they’re granted.
concept: A fixed-price option on a company that retains earnings is a royalty on time; options need a step-up for retained capital and a grant price at fair business value.
evolution_notes: Line 609: the savings-account illustration. Line 619: managers 'ought to get paid for really making it, not simply because the shareholders reinvest money with them.'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 34. Abuse of stock options as executive compensation

quote_verbatim: Certainly the management of a company would not give an option on their business to some third party at a market price they felt was way too low, so I find it a little disingenuous when managements say that they’re — when they get a takeover bid, they say that the company’s really worth twice that much, but they’re perfectly willing to issue options to themselves at this price which they say is totally inadequate, when the owners get the option elsewhere.
concept: A management that calls a bid price inadequate but grants itself options at that price is disingenuous.
evolution_notes: Compare R1996-013 (issuing while calling the stock undervalued).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 34. Abuse of stock options as executive compensation

quote_verbatim: In terms of overall level of compensation, the real sin is having a mediocre manager. I mean, that is what costs owners very significant amounts of money over time. And if a mediocre manager is paid a relatively small sum, it’s still a great mistake. And if they’re paid huge sums, it’s a travesty. And that happens sometimes. It’s almost impossible to pay the outstanding manager a sum that’s disproportion to the value of that outstanding manager, when you get a large enterprise.
concept: The costly error is a mediocre manager at any pay; an outstanding manager of a large enterprise can hardly be overpaid.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 34. Abuse of stock options as executive compensation

quote_verbatim: It had stagnated during the previous decade under an earlier management, despite having the same product and those great Mean Joe Greene commercials you saw [...] I mean, having the right person in place is just enormously important.
concept: The same great product can stagnate under one management and compound under another; the person in charge matters enormously.
evolution_notes: Coca-Cola at a $4 billion market value when Goizueta took over. Pulls against M1996-037 (great business needs no management) and L1996-024; noted in the note, not rowed as a tension.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 34. Abuse of stock options as executive compensation

quote_verbatim: If something is so wonderful as a standard technique of compensation, why does it have to be masked under weak, corrupt, and contemptible accounting? [...] And you can get, if you overuse stock options, where the whole thing is sort of a chain letter.
concept: A practice that must be hidden by accounting is suspect; heavy option use flatters income while nothing is expensed.
evolution_notes: Line 621: present option accounting is 'weak, corrupt, and contemptible'. He prefers stock to options and supports sharing with people doing important work down the organisation.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 34. Abuse of stock options as executive compensation

quote_verbatim: But such is the envy effect that the practice spreads to everybody else. And then the taxi driver and everybody starts thinking the system is irrational, unfair, crazy. [...] And I would argue that the Tom Murphy attitude is the right attitude.
concept: Envy spreads pay excess; leaders with power and wealth should exercise restraint, as Tom Murphy did.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 34. Abuse of stock options as executive compensation

concept: Leaders who argue black is white for their own pay, as on option accounting, degrade the whole organisation and forfeit credibility.
evolution_notes: Line 635: managers agree options are compensation and compensation is expense, yet lobbied Congress against expensing them; he compares it to legislating pi to 3.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 34. Abuse of stock options as executive compensation

quote_verbatim: If we could see, you know, looking at any business, what its future cash inflows or outflows from the business to the owners — or from the owners — would be over the next, we’ll call it, a hundred years, or until the business is extinct, and then could discount that back at the appropriate interest rate, which I’ll get to in a second, that would give us a number for intrinsic value. [...] Businesses have coupons that are going to develop in the future, too. The only problem is they aren’t printed on the instrument. And it’s up to the investor to try to estimate what those coupons are going to be over time.
concept: Intrinsic value is the discounted cash to and from owners over the life of the business; a business is a bond whose coupons are not printed and must be estimated.
evolution_notes: Same coupon image as M1994-074.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 2. How to buy a business

quote_verbatim: When we get into businesses where we think we can understand them reasonably well, we are trying to print the coupons out. We are trying to figure out what businesses are going to be worth in ten or 20 years. When we bought See’s Candy in 1972, we had to come to the judgment as to whether we could figure out the competitive forces that would operate, the strengths and weaknesses of the company, and how that would look over a ten or 20 or 30-year period.
concept: The test before buying is whether the competitive forces, strengths and weaknesses can be figured over ten to thirty years.
evolution_notes: Same ten-year horizon as the morning's M1997-021.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 2. How to buy a business

quote_verbatim: The only reason for putting cash into any kind of an investment now is because you expect to take cash out. Not by selling it to somebody else, because that’s just a game of who beats who, but, in a sense, by what the asset, itself, produces. [...] If you’re a speculator, you’re primarily focusing on what the price of the object is going to do independent of the business. And that’s not our game. So we figure if we’re right about the business, we’re going to make a lot of money. And if we’re wrong about the business, we don’t have any hopes — we don’t expect to make money.
concept: Investment means cash out from what the asset produces, not from resale; speculation watches price apart from the business; the return rides on being right about the business.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 2. How to buy a business

quote_verbatim: There are a number of filters which say to us we don’t know what that business is going to be worth in ten or 20 years. And we can’t even make an educated guess. Obviously, we don’t think we know to three decimal places, or two decimal places, or anything like that, precisely what’s going to be produced. But we have a high degree of confidence that we’re in the ballpark with certain kinds of businesses. The filters are designed to make sure we’re in those kinds of businesses. We, basically, use long-term, risk-free government bond-type interest rates to think back in terms of what we should discount at.
concept: The filters screen out businesses whose value in ten or twenty years cannot even be guessed; for the rest, ballpark confidence, discounted at the long risk-free government rate.
evolution_notes: Compare M1996-025 on the government bond rate and the threshold of understanding.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 2. How to buy a business

quote_verbatim: We give you the information that, if the positions were reversed, we would want to get from you.
concept: Report to owners what you would want to be told if the positions were reversed.
evolution_notes: Same answer: the report carries the factors Buffett and Munger look at themselves.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 2. How to buy a business

quote_verbatim: I would argue that one filter that’s useful in investing is the simple idea of opportunity cost. If you have one opportunity that you already have available in large quantity, and you like it better than 98 percent of the other things you see, well, you can just screen out the other 98 percent because you already know something better. [...] With this attitude, you get a concentrated portfolio, which we don’t mind.
concept: Opportunity cost is a filter: anything worse than the best idea already available in quantity is screened out, which yields concentration.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 2. How to buy a business

quote_verbatim: if somebody shows us a business, you know, the first thing that goes through our head is would we rather own this business than more Coca-Cola? Would we rather own it than more Gillette? It’s crazy not to compare it to things that you’re very certain of. [...] If every management, before they bought a business in some unrelated deal that they might not have even heard of, you know, more than a short time before that’s being promoted to them, if they said, “Is this better than buying in our own stock, you know? Is this better than even buying, you know, buying Coca-Cola stock or something,” there’d be a lot fewer deals done.
concept: Every new purchase is measured first against more of the most certain business already owned, and against buying in one's own stock.
evolution_notes: Buffett follows at line 675: "we try to measure against what we regard as close to perfection as we can get."
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 2. How to buy a business

quote_verbatim: Well, no matter how bad the management, if you’re buying at 50 percent of asset value or 30 percent or so on down, you have a lot going for you. And as the world has wised up and as stocks have behaved so well for people, good stocks, generally, have gone to higher and higher prices. That game gets much harder. Now, to find something at a discount from intrinsic value, those simple systems, ordinarily, don’t work.
concept: Buying far below liquidating value once worked whatever the management; as the world wised up those simple systems stopped working.
evolution_notes: Not a personal error but a method outgrown; kind chosen because the lesson is narrated against the old practice. Followed by M-row on Warren's kind of thinking (line 679).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 2. How to buy a business

quote_verbatim: You’ve got to get into Warren’s kind of thinking. And that is a lot harder. I think you can predict the future in a few places best if you understand a few basic ideas that come from a good general education. [...] In other words, Coca-Cola’s a simple company if it’s stripped down and analyzed in terms of some elemental forces.
concept: The future can be predicted in a few places by stripping a business down to elemental forces using a few basic ideas from a general education.
evolution_notes: Munger adds at line 683: "You just have to know a few simple things and really know them."
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 2. How to buy a business

quote_verbatim: When Charlie talks about “liquidating value,” he’s not talking about closing up the enterprise. But he’s talking about what somebody else would pay for that stream of cash, too, I mean —
concept: Liquidating value here means what another buyer would pay for the stream of cash, not the value of closing the enterprise.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 2. How to buy a business

quote_verbatim: But part of investing and calculating intrinsic values is if you get the wrong answer when you get through — in other words, if it says don’t buy, you can’t buy just because somebody else thinks it’s going to up or because your friends have made a lot of easy money lately or anything of the sort. You just — you have to be able to walk away from anything that doesn’t work. And very few things work these days.
concept: When the calculation says don't buy, walk away whatever others think or earn.
evolution_notes: Buffett continues at line 691: "You also have to walk away from anything you don’t understand which, in my case, is a big handicap."
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 2. How to buy a business

quote_verbatim: Part of it being harder now, too, is the amount of the capital we run. I mean, if we were running $100,000, our prospects for returns would be — and we really needed the money — our prospects for return would be considerably better than they are running Berkshire. It’s very simple. Our universe of possible ideas would expand by a huge factor.
concept: Size of capital shrinks the universe of possible ideas and so the prospective return.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 2. How to buy a business

quote_verbatim: And if interest rates go higher, the valuation goes down automatically. And more importantly, if the returns on equity of American industry — which are historic highs, and which sort of classical economics would tell you would be hard to maintain — if those returns go down, on average, that also would pull it down.
concept: The market's value rests on two inputs, interest rates and returns on equity; record returns are hard to maintain.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 3. Stocks look high, but not as high as they look

quote_verbatim: After a while, as I mentioned earlier, people get captivated simply by the notion of rising prices without going back to the underlying rationale. And that’s when you get very dangerous conditions in terms of possible bubbles.
concept: A bubble is prices rising on the notion of rising prices, cut loose from the underlying rationale.
evolution_notes: Buffett closes at line 719: "It’s just people behave in extreme ways in markets. And over time, that’s very good for people that keep their heads."
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 3. Stocks look high, but not as high as they look

quote_verbatim: One of the intelligent things, possibly, could be to buy in our own stock. But that would imply that our own stock was cheaper relative to value than anything else we could find among possible opportunities. And the chances are we could find things that were more attractive.
concept: A buyback must beat every other opportunity on price relative to value, not merely be cheap.
evolution_notes: Munger closes the answer at line 733: "We don’t have any rule against it. Opportunity cost is the game around here." Compare M1996-013.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 4. When Berkshire is cheap, other things are usually cheaper

quote_verbatim: And so there shouldn’t be anybody in this room that owns the stock that would not find it palatable, if not become positively enthusiastic, about the stock going down 50 percent. It would not bother Charlie. It wouldn’t bother me, because we would have very intelligent things, then, to do with whatever capital we came into.
concept: A buyer of capital should welcome a fifty percent fall, since it brings intelligent uses for the money.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 4. When Berkshire is cheap, other things are usually cheaper

quote_verbatim: But if Coca-Cola were domiciled in Amsterdam, or Gillette were domiciled in London, they had the same basic businesses, we would be attracted to them to virtually the same degree we are as having them domiciled in Atlanta and Boston.
concept: The business attracts, not the country of domicile.
evolution_notes: Repeats M1996-068.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 5. International earnings in the United States

quote_verbatim: And if you can sell Coca-Cola, you know, do you really want to get into steel in Malaysia or something? (Laughter)
concept: Foreign growth is best owned through a franchise that sells abroad, against the opportunity cost of a worse business there.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 5. International earnings in the United States

quote_verbatim: Some things travel very well. And some things don’t. I mean, Gillette travels. Disney travels. McDonalds travels. Coke travels. You know, See’s Candy doesn’t travel as well. It might if you spent 50 years working on it.
concept: Whether a brand travels across countries is a property of the business to be checked, not assumed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 5. International earnings in the United States

quote_verbatim: Sometimes in the insurance business, you have a choice between being a good business or a big business. [...] On the other hand, I think it’s tough to compete against Don because he brings an element of knowledge and personal attention to the account and factors of that sort that a really large company would have trouble duplicating.
concept: Good and big can be a choice; a small specialist whose knowledge and attention a large rival cannot duplicate is hard to compete against.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 6. Businesses with “natural limits” welcomed at Berkshire

quote_verbatim: There’s a huge class of businesses in America which are very strong and will throw out large amounts of cash in relation to their size but which can’t rationally be expanded very much. And if you try and expand certain kinds of businesses, you’re throwing money down the rat hole. The beauty of the Berkshire Hathaway system is that such businesses are very welcome here because the cash comes into headquarters and is allocated there.
concept: A strong cash-throwing business that cannot rationally expand should not be forced to; its cash goes to headquarters for allocation.
evolution_notes: Compare M1996-074 (best businesses need no capital).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 6. Businesses with “natural limits” welcomed at Berkshire

quote_verbatim: Part the reason they have a moat around them is that they’re of a size and have specialized skills that other organizations just can’t get into it. [...] They have a distribution system that works wonders. But you can’t pump two or three times the volume through that distribution system. And if you could pump it through, there would’ve been more competition.
concept: A moat can come from the very smallness and specialization that keeps others out; the limit on volume is what keeps competition away.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 6. Businesses with “natural limits” welcomed at Berkshire

quote_verbatim: So there are businesses that have certain natural limits that, you know, you want to be careful that you don’t talk yourself into thinking a business that has limits and find out that it really has way more potential. I mean, it would’ve been a shame if Mr. [Asa Griggs] Candler decided that Coca-Cola only appealed to people in Atlanta or something of the sort. So you have to be a little careful on that.
concept: Accepting natural limits carries the opposite risk of mistaking a business with far more potential for a limited one.
evolution_notes: Pulls against M1997-070 (Munger: such businesses cannot rationally be expanded) in the same answer. The sentence is printed as garbled; kept as printed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 6. Businesses with “natural limits” welcomed at Berkshire

quote_verbatim: But we — a fellow like Don will be very good at understanding, you know, where his competitive advantages can take him and where they don’t take him.
concept: A good manager knows where his competitive advantages reach and where they stop.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 6. Businesses with “natural limits” welcomed at Berkshire

quote_verbatim: I don’t think we’ve ever owned an airline stock, common stock. [...] I don’t think we’ve ever owned a paper company common stock. And we’ve only had a very limited amount of investment in the investment banking businesses. Those are industries that we don’t feel that we’ve got the same kind of long-term economic advantage that we have in something like a Coke or a Gillette. So those are not natural places for us to be common shareholders.
concept: Industries without a long-term economic advantage are held, if at all, as senior securities, not as common stock.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 7. Debt deals vs. buying stock

quote_verbatim: As a digression, you know, people in the insurance business thought that — they all had these models — and some of them were prepared by reinsurance brokers and some of them by various research institutes — as how much they would lose under certain kinds of circumstances. And they couldn’t have been further off with an Andrew, or with the Northridge earthquake. Fortunately, we don’t rely on those.
concept: Do not rely on the industry's catastrophe-loss models; they were far off when the catastrophes came.
evolution_notes: Buffett adds: "I don’t know what exactly we do rely on, but we don’t rely on those. (Laughter)"
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 9. We know our super-cat insurance risks, but many others don’t

quote_verbatim: So every three, or five, or seven years, or who knows what, we will lose significant money in the super-cat business. And we expect that over 20 or 25 years, we will make more money than we lose. [...] It only makes sense for us to be in it when the premium prices are right. But when they are appropriate, we will — we’re more than willing to step up and take on a fair amount of risk.
concept: Accept lumpy large losses if the long-run sum is positive, and write the risk only when the price is right.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 9. We know our super-cat insurance risks, but many others don’t

quote_verbatim: Our exposures are limited to a given dollar amount. That dollar amount may be large. But at least we know what it is. And we take risks — that we’re willing to take risks when we think we’re appropriately paid. There’s a mentality to bring to the super-cat business that’s somewhat akin to what you bring to the investment business.
concept: Take only risks whose maximum is known and for which one is appropriately paid; the mindset is the investor's.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 9. We know our super-cat insurance risks, but many others don’t

quote_verbatim: A billion dollars would be, what, 2 1/2 percent, or less, of the liquid assets and securities around Berkshire. And so that’s irritating, but it — (laughter) — it’s not going to destroy the enterprise. Whereas, if you have an unwitting super-cat exposure that you don’t even recognize you have, it could destroy your company.
concept: A known loss sized against resources irritates; an unrecognized exposure can destroy the company.
evolution_notes: Munger continues at line 829 on Twentieth Century: "they had no idea they had a super-cat exposure in what they thought was a simple, little direct writing insurance operation."
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 9. We know our super-cat insurance risks, but many others don’t

quote_verbatim: You can really get fooled in this business. [...] It’s not — you get a lot of surprises in that field. And the surprises in insurance are never symmetrical. They’re all bad. (Laughs)
concept: Insurance loss estimates run low; surprises in insurance are all bad, never symmetrical.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 9. We know our super-cat insurance risks, but many others don’t

quote_verbatim: Obviously, if you understood a business perfectly — the future of a business — you would need very little in the way of a margin of safety. So the more volatile the business is — or possibility is — but assuming you still want invest in it, the larger the margin of safety.
concept: Understanding and margin of safety are bound: the less certain the business, the larger the margin required.
evolution_notes: Compare M1995-017 and M1996-084.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 10. “You need a large margin of safety”

quote_verbatim: So it depends on the nature of the underlying risk. We don’t get the margin of safety now that we got in a 1973-4 period, for example. The biggest thing to do is understand the business. If you understand the business, and get into the kind of the businesses where surprises — by their nature — surprises are few.
concept: The margin needed depends on the risk underneath; above all understand the business and pick ones where surprises are few.
evolution_notes: Follows the truck-and-bridge image in the same paragraph.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 10. “You need a large margin of safety”

quote_verbatim: So our approach is really to try and learn vicariously.
concept: Learn from other people's mistakes rather than one's own.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 11. Learn from the mistakes of others

quote_verbatim: The biggest one, probably — or the biggest category over time — is being reluctant to pay up a little for a business I knew was really outstanding, or to continue to buy it at higher prices when I knew it was outstanding. So the cost of that has been many, many billions. And I’ll probably keep making that mistake. There are — the mistakes are made when there are businesses you can understand and they’re attractive and you don’t do something about it. [...] I don’t worry at all about the mistakes that come about because when I met Bill Gates, I didn’t buy Microsoft or something. That’s not my game. But the mistakes are made when you — most of our mistakes have been mistakes of omission rather than commission.
concept: The costliest repeated mistake is refusing to pay up for an outstanding business one understands; omissions inside the circle count, those outside it do not.
evolution_notes: Same lesson as the morning's M1997-003 ("incredibly price conscious").
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 11. Learn from the mistakes of others

quote_verbatim: I think most people get very few, what I call, no-brainer opportunities, where it’s just so damned obvious that this is going to work. And since they are very few and they may be separated by periods of years, I think people have to learn to have the courage and the intelligence to step up in a major way when those rare opportunities come by.
concept: Obvious opportunities are rare and years apart; step up in a major way when one comes.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 11. Learn from the mistakes of others

quote_verbatim: You got to be willing to take a really big bite. And it’s crazy if you don’t. And it’s crazy if you dabble around at the edges, so you’re not prepared to take a big bite when the time comes.
concept: Do not dabble at the edges; keep ready to take a big bite.
evolution_notes: Buffett answering Munger's M1997-085. | ERRATUM 2026-10-04: Munger's row is M1997-084, not M1997-085 (the 1997 PM note)
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 11. Learn from the mistakes of others

quote_verbatim: The risk-free rate is used merely to equate one item to another. In other words, we’re looking for whatever’s the most attractive. But in terms of present valuing anything, we’re going to use a number. And, obviously, we can always buy the government bonds. So that becomes the yardstick rate. It doesn’t mean we want to buy government bonds. [...] But it’s the appropriate yardstick, in our view, to simply use to compare across all kinds of investment opportunities, oil wells, farms, whatever it may be. Now, it gets into degree of certainty, too. But it’s the yardstick rate.
concept: The risk-free rate is a constant yardstick to compare all opportunities, not a hurdle met; certainty enters separately.
evolution_notes: Develops M1997-053; the question proposed a 12 or 15 percent opportunity-cost rate instead.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 12. Treasury bonds are yardstick to compare investments

quote_verbatim: Investments usually play second fiddle to the insurance business at most companies that are in the insurance business. We look at them as being of equal importance. [...] And we run them as two distinct businesses. We do whatever makes the most sense on the investment side, whatever makes the most sense on the insurance side. We never do anything on the investment side that will impinge on our business on the insurance side.
concept: Insurance and investing are run as two equal, distinct businesses, and investing never impinges on underwriting.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 13. Insurance and investing are equal, but distinct, businesses

quote_verbatim: GEICO has entirely different characteristics than the super-cat business. They both call themselves insurance. They both develop float. But in economic terms and in terms of competitive strengths and that sort of thing, they’re two very different businesses.
concept: Judge each insurer by its own economics and competitive strengths, not by the shared label or the shared float.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 13. Insurance and investing are equal, but distinct, businesses

quote_verbatim: So one opportunity cost of buying the stock is to compare it with a bond. But you may find that half the stocks in America, you’re so fearful about or know so little about or think so poorly of, that you’d rather have the government bond. So on an opportunity cost basis, they’re taken out of the filter. Now, you start finding corporations where you like the stocks way better than government bonds. You got to compare them one against the other. And when you find one that you regard as the best opportunity, that you can understand as the best opportunity, now you’ve got one to buy. It’s a very simple idea. [...] It’s child’s play as a mental process. Now, it’s hard to make the business appraisals. But the mental process is a cinch.
concept: Filter every stock first against the government bond, then rank the survivors against each other; buy the best one understood.
evolution_notes: Munger closes at line 879: "I think life is a whole series of opportunity costs." Compare M1997-055.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 14. Munger on choosing your spouse

quote_verbatim: If Charlie and I were forced — told we had a choice of buying stock A, B, C or D and all 2,500 or 3,000, or whatever it may be, listed on the New York Stock Exchange, or buying a ten-year government bond and we had to hold the stock for ten years or the bond for ten years, probably in at least 80 percent of the cases, we’d take the ten-year Government, you know. In many cases, because we didn’t understand the business well enough elsewhere. Or secondly, we may understand it and still prefer the 10 percent Government. So — but we would measure everything that way.
concept: Desert-island test: hold this stock or the ten-year government bond for ten years; most stocks lose to the bond.
