evolution_notes: The float definition and the lemon test that follow (lines 392-405) repeat L1996-008, L1997-011 and L1997-012 and are not rowed again. Compare L1994-025, L1995-014 (amount and cost, without the outlook).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: The Economics of Property-Casualty Insurance

quote_verbatim: Impressive as the growth in our float has been -- 25.4% compounded annually -- what really counts is the cost of this item. If that becomes too high, growth in float becomes a curse rather than a blessing.
concept: Float growth is only good if its cost stays low; costly float growing fast is a curse.
evolution_notes: Continues: "As long as we can continue to achieve an underwriting profit, float will continue to outrank net worth in value" (lines 433-434); compare L1997-013.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: The Economics of Property-Casualty Insurance

quote_verbatim: Charlie and I have the easy jobs at Berkshire: We do very little except allocate capital. And, even then, we are not all that energetic. We have one excuse, though: In allocating capital, activity does not correlate with achievement. Indeed, in the fields of investments and acquisitions, frenetic behavior is often counterproductive. Therefore, Charlie and I mainly just wait for the phone to ring.
concept: In capital allocation activity does not produce results; frenetic dealing hurts, so wait for opportunities to come.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Sources of Reported Earnings

quote_verbatim: Naturally, they want to be paid fairly for their efforts, but pay alone can't explain their extraordinary accomplishments. Instead, each is primarily motivated by a vision of just how far his or her business can go -- and by a desire to be the one who gets it there.
concept: The best managers are driven by the business itself, not by pay.
evolution_notes: Compare line 323 of the same letter on Santulli: "he has no economic need whatsoever to work", and R1996-025.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Sources of Reported Earnings

quote_verbatim: Here, I need to make a confession (ugh): The portfolio actions I took in 1998 actually decreased our gain for the year. In particular, my decision to sell McDonald's was a very big mistake. Overall, you would have been better off last year if I had regularly snuck off to the movies during market hours.
concept: Trimming and selling holdings during the year cost money; inaction would have done better.
evolution_notes: The lesson is left implicit in the movies line; compare L1998-017 (activity does not correlate with achievement).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Investments

quote_verbatim: Cash never makes us happy. But it's better to have the money burning a hole in Berkshire's pocket than resting comfortably in someone else's.
concept: Idle cash is unwelcome, but holding it beats handing it to others to manage while waiting for a large use.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Investments

quote_verbatim: General Re subsequently eliminated its positions in about 250 common stocks, incurring $935 million of taxes in the process. This "clean sweep" approach reflects a basic principle that Charlie and I employ in business and investing: We don't back into decisions.
concept: Inherited positions are not kept by default; each holding must be a decision made afresh, even at a tax cost.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Investments

quote_verbatim: Our never-comment-even-if-untrue policy in regard to investments may disappoint "piggybackers" but will benefit owners: Your Berkshire shares would be worth less if we discussed what we are doing.
concept: Do not disclose investment activity beyond what law requires, because disclosure costs owners value.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Investments

quote_verbatim: This Alice-in-Wonderland outcome occurs because existing accounting principles ignore the cost of stock options when earnings are being calculated, even though options are a huge and increasing expense at a great many corporations. [...] Though options, if properly structured, can be an appropriate, and even ideal, way to compensate and motivate top managers, they are more often wildly capricious in their distribution of rewards, inefficient as motivators, and inordinately expensive for shareholders.
concept: Options are a real expense that accounting hides; properly built they can suit top managers, but usually they reward capriciously and cost owners heavily.
evolution_notes: Compare L1997-032 (options are a cost).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Accounting -- Part 1

quote_verbatim: Think for a moment of that $190 million we are going to spend for advertising at GEICO this year. Suppose that instead of paying cash for our ads, we paid the media in ten-year, at-the-market Berkshire options. Would anyone then care to argue that Berkshire had not borne a cost for advertising, or should not be charged this cost on its books?
concept: Test an accounting treatment by changing the payee: paying any supplier in options would plainly be a cost.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Accounting -- Part 1

quote_verbatim: Charlie and I, however, have trouble being philosophical about unrecorded costs. When we consider investing in an option-issuing company, we make an appropriate downward adjustment to reported earnings, simply subtracting an amount equal to what the company could have realized by publicly selling options of like quantity and structure. Similarly, if we contemplate an acquisition, we include in our evaluation the cost of replacing any option plan. Then, if we make a deal, we promptly take that cost out of hiding.
concept: Before investing, cut reported earnings by the market value of options issued; before acquiring, charge the cost of replacing the option plan.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Accounting -- Part 1

quote_verbatim: But there's an offset to these points: Options issued to employees are often repriced, a transformation that makes them much more costly than the public variety. [...] Giving an employee a company car that can only be used for certain purposes diminishes its value to the employee, but does not in the least diminish its cost to the employer.
concept: The cost of compensation is measured by what the employer gives up, not by what the employee can do with it.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Accounting -- Part 1

quote_verbatim: The earning revisions that Charlie and I have made for options in recent years have frequently cut the reported per-share figures by 5%, with 10% not all that uncommon. On occasion, the downward adjustment has been so great that it has affected our portfolio decisions, causing us either to make a sale or to pass on a stock purchase we might otherwise have made.
concept: The options adjustment is large enough to change buy and sell decisions.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Accounting -- Part 1

quote_verbatim: "If options aren't a form of compensation, what are they? If compensation isn't an expense, what is it? And, if expenses shouldn't go into the calculation of earnings, where in the world should they go?"
concept: Three questions that test any claim that options are not a cost.
evolution_notes: Introduced as asked "a few years ago" in these pages (line 668).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Accounting -- Part 1

quote_verbatim: In recent years, probity has eroded. Many major corporations still play things straight, but a significant and growing number of otherwise high-grade managers -- CEOs you would be happy to have as spouses for your children or as trustees under your will -- have come to the view that it's okay to manipulate earnings to satisfy what they believe are Wall Street's desires. Indeed, many CEOs think this kind of manipulation is not only okay, but actually their duty. These managers start with the assumption, all too common, that their job at all times is to encourage the highest stock price possible (a premise with which we adamantly disagree).
concept: Otherwise decent managers manipulate earnings when they believe their job is to maximise the stock price; that premise is the warning sign.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Accounting -- Part 2

quote_verbatim: Rationalizing this behavior, these managers often say that their shareholders will be hurt if their currency for doing deals -- that is, their stock -- is not fully-priced, and they also argue that in using accounting shenanigans to get the figures they want, they are only doing what everybody else does. Once such an everybody's-doing-it attitude takes hold, ethical misgivings vanish. Call this behavior Son of Gresham: Bad accounting drives out good.
concept: Everybody-does-it reasoning dissolves ethical restraint, and bad accounting spreads by displacing good.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Accounting -- Part 2

quote_verbatim: The distortion du jour is the "restructuring charge," an accounting entry that can, of course, be legitimate but that too often is a device for manipulating earnings. In this bit of legerdemain, a large chunk of costs that should properly be attributed to a number of years is dumped into a single quarter, typically one already fated to disappoint investors.
concept: Treat restructuring charges with suspicion: they often shift multi-year costs into one bad quarter to flatter the rest.
evolution_notes: Illustrated by the golf-score parable (lines 720-735).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Accounting -- Part 2

quote_verbatim: Unfortunately, CEOs who use variations of these scoring schemes in real life tend to become addicted to the games they're playing -- after all, it's easier to fiddle with the scorecard than to spend hours on the practice tee -- and never muster the will to give them up.
concept: Accounting games once started become habits that managers do not abandon.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Accounting -- Part 2

quote_verbatim: In the acquisition arena, restructuring has been raised to an art form: Managements now frequently use mergers to dishonestly rearrange the value of assets and liabilities in ways that will allow them to both smooth and swell future earnings. Indeed, at deal time, major auditing firms sometimes point out the possibilities for a little accounting magic (or for a lot). Getting this push from the pulpit, first-class people will frequently stoop [...] to third-class tactics.
concept: Mergers are a favoured occasion for rearranging balance sheets to manufacture future earnings, often with auditors' encouragement.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Accounting -- Part 2

quote_verbatim: Berkshire has kept entirely clear of these practices: If we are to disappoint you, we would rather it be with our earnings than with our accounting. In all of our acquisitions, we have left the loss reserve figures exactly as we found them. After all, we have consistently joined with insurance managers knowledgeable about their business and honest in their financial reporting. When deals occur in which liabilities are increased immediately and substantially, simple logic says that at least one of those virtues must have been lacking -- or, alternatively, that the acquirer is laying the groundwork for future infusions of "earnings."
concept: Never reset acquired reserves; a big reserve increase at deal time means the seller was ignorant or dishonest, or the buyer is storing future earnings.
evolution_notes: Preceded by the p-c example: "it is uncanny how often an actuarial 'revelation' of this kind coincides with the inking of a deal" (lines 754-755). Followed by the bank CEO: "We'll make it bigger than that -- that's why we're doing the deal" (lines 769-770).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Accounting -- Part 2

quote_verbatim: Though auditors should regard the investing public as their client, they tend to kowtow instead to the managers who choose them and dole out their pay. ("Whose bread I eat, his song I sing.")
concept: Auditors serve whoever pays them, so their blessing is no guarantee of honest figures.
evolution_notes: Compare line 403-404: "at times I have been amazed by the numbers that big-name auditors have implicitly blessed" (rowed in L1997-012 in its 1997 form).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Accounting -- Part 2

quote_verbatim: At Berkshire, we regard the holder of one share of B stock as the equal of our large institutional investors. [...] But if it is "earnings guidance" or the like that shareholders or analysts seek, we will simply guide them to our public documents.
concept: Treat the smallest owner as the equal of institutions; give no earnings guidance beyond public documents.
evolution_notes: Lines 799-801 restate the two reporting goals (positions reversed; simultaneous access), already rowed as L1994-023, L1995-021, L1997-040.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Reports to Shareholders

quote_verbatim: We will not engage in unfriendly takeovers. We can promise complete confidentiality and a very fast answer -- customarily within five minutes -- as to whether we're interested. We prefer to buy for cash, but will consider issuing stock when we receive as much in intrinsic business value as we give.
concept: Cash is the preferred currency for acquisitions; stock is offered only when the value received equals the value given.
evolution_notes: The six criteria (lines 1174-1185) repeat R1997-001 with the size floor raised from $25 million to $50 million of pre-tax earnings, and a new sentence seeking acquisitions "in the $5-20 billion range" (lines 1187-1188). The cash preference is new to the criteria; compare R1995-010 and L1997-028 (tilt consideration toward cash), L1997-029 (issuing stock cost owners). The collies passage (lines 1195-1198) repeats R1995-015.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ACQUISITION CRITERIA

quote_verbatim: Charlie and I feel totally comfortable with this eggs-in-one-basket situation because Berkshire itself owns a wide variety of truly extraordinary businesses. Indeed, we believe that Berkshire is close to being unique in the quality and diversity of the businesses in which it owns either a controlling interest or a minority interest of significance.
concept: Concentrating personal wealth in one holding is acceptable when that holding itself owns many extraordinary businesses.
evolution_notes: Under principle 2, "We eat our own cooking" (line 3554). Compare L1998-005 (99% of net worth). The rest of the reprinted manual repeats rows R1995-001 to R1995-013 and R1996-001 to R1996-025 and is not rowed again.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: OWNER-RELATED BUSINESS PRINCIPLES

quote_verbatim: At that juncture, the Buffett family will not be involved in managing the business, only in picking and overseeing the managers who do. [...] Essentially my job will be split into two parts, with one executive becoming responsible for investments and another for operations. If the acquisition of new businesses is in prospect, the two will cooperate in making the decisions needed. Both executives will report to a board of directors who will be responsive to the controlling shareholder, whose interests will in turn be aligned with yours.
concept: Succession separates investing from operating, with the controlling owner picking and overseeing managers rather than managing.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: THE MANAGING OF BERKSHIRE

quote_verbatim: Well, we don’t — Charlie and I don’t think about the market. And Ben didn’t very much. I think he made a mistake to occasionally try and place a value on it. We look at individual businesses. And we don’t think of stocks as little items that wiggle around on the paper and that have charts attached to them. We think of them as parts of businesses.
concept: Ignore the level of the market; value individual businesses and treat stocks as parts of them.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 6. We buy businesses and don’t predict stock moves

quote_verbatim: We do know that we will only buy things that we think make sense, in terms of the value that we receive for Berkshire. And when we can’t find things, the money piles up. And when we find — when we do find things, we pile in. But the stock market — I know of no one that has been successful at — and really made a lot of money predicting the actions of the market itself. I know a lot of people who have done well picking businesses and buying them at sensible prices.
concept: Buy only on value received; let cash accumulate when nothing qualifies and commit heavily when something does; market prediction does not make money.
evolution_notes: Same answer: "we do not find bargains in this market among the larger companies that are our universe. That is not a stock market forecast in any way, shape, or form" (line 65).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 6. We buy businesses and don’t predict stock moves

quote_verbatim: But that, I would say, the incremental value today, because it’s under the Berkshire umbrella, is zero. Because we are bringing nothing to the party that Gen Re’s own investment people would not have brought to the party. We obviously think that there will be important incremental value over a long period of time. We — but when that value will appear or how much of it develops, is a matter that’s out of our hands.
concept: Credit no immediate synergy to an acquisition when the owner brings nothing the existing managers lack.
evolution_notes: Compare L1998-013 (freedom, not skill).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 7. Expecting slow short-term growth of Gen Re’s float

quote_verbatim: But the title is right, you only have to get rich once. And why do people, very bright people, risk losing something that’s very important to them, to gain something that’s totally unimportant? The added money has no utility whatsoever. And the money that was lost had enormous utility.
concept: Never risk what you have and need for what you do not need; the utility of loss and gain is asymmetric.
evolution_notes: Compare R1996-009 (a good night's sleep) and R1995-007.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 10. LTCM: Smart people’s dumb risks with derivatives

quote_verbatim: Whenever a bright person, a really bright person, goes broke that has a lot of money, it’s because of leverage. It — you simply — you basically can’t — it would be almost impossible to go broke without borrowed money being in the equation.
concept: Ruin for the able and wealthy almost always runs through borrowed money.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 10. LTCM: Smart people’s dumb risks with derivatives

quote_verbatim: And as you know, at Berkshire, we’ve never used any real amount of borrowed money. Now, if we’d used somewhat more, you know, we’d be really rich. But if we’d used a whole lot more, we might have gotten in trouble some times. And there’s just no upside to it, you know? What’s two percentage points more, you know, on a given year, that year? And run the risk of real failure.
concept: Forgo leverage even though it would have raised returns, because a few extra points do not justify a chance of real failure.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 10. LTCM: Smart people’s dumb risks with derivatives

quote_verbatim: And that leads to trouble. You know, 99 percent of the time it works. But, you know, 83 and a thirds percent of the time, it works to play Russian roulette with one bullet in there and six chambers. But neither 83 1/3 percent or 99 percent is good enough when there is no gain to offset the risk of loss.
concept: A high probability of success is not enough when failure is ruin and success adds nothing that matters.
evolution_notes: Earlier in the answer: "if you hand me a revolver with six bullets — or six chambers — and one bullet and you say, 'Pull it once for a million dollars,' and I say, 'No.' And then you say, 'What is your price?' The answer is there is no price" (line 117).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 10. LTCM: Smart people’s dumb risks with derivatives

quote_verbatim: I would argue that there is a second factor that makes the situation dangerous. And that is that the accounting for being actively engaged in derivatives, interest rate swaps, et cetera is very weak. [...] So, you get an irresponsible clearing system, irresponsible accounting — this is not a good combination.
concept: Derivatives are dangerous where no clearing system exists and the accounting lets traders book profits early.
evolution_notes: Munger at line 113: "the general system of finance in America involving derivatives is irresponsible ... There’s no clearing system, as there is in a commodities market."
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 10. LTCM: Smart people’s dumb risks with derivatives

quote_verbatim: And this is absolutely standard. You know, it’s GAAP accounting. But it front-ends profits. And if you front-end profits and you pay people a percentage of the profits, you’re going to get some very interesting results, sometimes.
concept: Pay tied to profits that accounting books up front invites bad behaviour.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 10. LTCM: Smart people’s dumb risks with derivatives

quote_verbatim: Investment is the process of putting out money today to get more money back at some point in the future. And the question is, how far in the future, how much money, and what is the appropriate discount rate to take it back to the present day and determine how much you pay?
concept: Investment is money out now for more back later; value turns on how much, how far off, and the discount rate.
evolution_notes: Endorsing a questioner's model: look-through earnings grown and discounted to a present value; "you have the right approach".
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 11. “Right approach” to estimating Berkshire’s intrinsic value

quote_verbatim: We would probably use a lower discount factor in evaluating any business now, under present-day interest rates. Now, that doesn’t mean we would pay that figure once we use that discount number. But we would use that to establish comparability across investment alternatives. So, if we were looking at 50 companies and making the sort of calculation that you just talked about, we would use a — we would probably use the long-term government rate to discount it back. But we wouldn’t pay that number after we discounted it back. We would look for appropriate discounts from that figure.
concept: Discount every business at the long-term government rate for comparability, then buy only at a discount to that value.
evolution_notes: Continues: "it doesn’t really make any difference whether you use a higher figure and then look across them or use our figure and look for the biggest discount" (line 135). Compare M1996-024, M1997-126, M1998-150, M1998-151.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 11. “Right approach” to estimating Berkshire’s intrinsic value

quote_verbatim: And it really is the success with which we invest those retained earnings and growth and float that will have an important fact — that will be an important factor — in how fast our intrinsic value grows. And to an important extent, the — what happens there is out of our control. I mean, it does depend on the markets in which we operate.
concept: For a business that retains everything, value growth depends on the reinvestment rate available, which external markets largely set.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 11. “Right approach” to estimating Berkshire’s intrinsic value

quote_verbatim: But anytime we buy into a business, and anytime that we’ve bought in for some time, we have tried to think of what that business is going to look like in five, or 10, or 15 years. And we recognize that the internet, in many forms of retailing, is likely to pose such a threat that we simply wouldn’t want to get into the business.
concept: Picture the business ten or fifteen years out before buying; a credible threat to that picture is reason enough to stay out.
evolution_notes: Later in the answer: "if I were to buy into any retailing business, whether I was buying a stock of it or buying a whole business, I would think very hard about what people are going to be trying to do to that business through the internet" (line 159). Compare M1998-088.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 12. Internet will have a huge impact, but hard to predict winners

quote_verbatim: But I would say that because of their name — brand names are going to mean very, very much when you have literally, you know, thousands and thousands of choices. People can’t — they have to trust somebody.
concept: When choices multiply, a trusted brand gains value because buyers must trust someone.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 12. Internet will have a huge impact, but hard to predict winners

quote_verbatim: When I was young, the department stores had a bunch of, sort of, monopolistic advantages. [...] And they lost all three of those advantages. And yet, they’ve done well, a lot of them, for many decades since. At other times, you get a change and you just get destroyed.
concept: Losing an advantage to change does not always destroy a business, and sometimes it does; the outcome is hard to call.
evolution_notes: Opens: "I think it is tricky predicting the technological change. Either it will or won’t destroy some business." Closes (line 165): "We agree, it’s a big risk. But it’s not easy to make predictions in which you have great confidence."
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 12. Internet will have a huge impact, but hard to predict winners

quote_verbatim: Yeah, if you go down to 16th and Farnam, where the streetcar tracks used to cross, that was the best real estate in town. And people signed 100-year, 50-year leases on it. And it looked like there was nothing more safe, because they weren’t going to move the streetcar lines. The only thing was that they moved the streetcars.
concept: An advantage that looks permanent can rest on a condition that disappears.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 12. Internet will have a huge impact, but hard to predict winners

quote_verbatim: Because we have bought existing businesses. And we have tampered as little as possible with their cultures after we buy them. [...] Now, it is true that if we — if there’s a stock option plan at a company, we will substitute a plan that is performance-based, which ties much more clearly to the performance of the business than any option plan could. And we will have a — we will design one that has an expectable cost that’s equal to the expectable cost of the option plan.
concept: Leave acquired cultures and pay systems alone, except replace option plans with performance plans of equal expected cost.
evolution_notes: Compare the letter's General Re option replacement (L1998-023 context, lines 614-617 of the 1998 letter).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 14. Different compensation plans with the same goal

quote_verbatim: We do like the idea of paying for performance. I mean, that is kind of a fundamental tenant. Everybody says they like that. But then they design systems that payoff no matter what happens, in many cases. And we’ve been reluctant to do that.
concept: Pay for performance means pay that does not arrive regardless of results; check whether a plan pays off no matter what.
evolution_notes: "tenant" as printed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 14. Different compensation plans with the same goal

quote_verbatim: Yeah, I think it’s important for the shareholders to realize that we are probably more decentralized, in terms of personnel practices, than any company of our size, or bigger, in America. We don’t have a headquarters culture that’s forced on the operating businesses. The operating businesses have their own cultures. And I think in every case I can think of, it’s a wonderful culture. And we just leave them alone.
concept: No headquarters culture is imposed; each subsidiary keeps its own and is left alone.
evolution_notes: Buffett follows (line 209): "we don’t try and cross-fertilize ... we just assume they’ll do best if left to their own initiative."
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 14. Different compensation plans with the same goal

quote_verbatim: Yeah, well, the best form of financing for us is cheap float. Now, most insurance companies don’t generate cheap float. So, I mean, there are plenty of companies in the insurance business who have a cost of float that makes it unattractive, actually, to expand their businesses. [...] But we would not just quit when we ran out of money from float. We would go ahead and borrow moderate amounts of money. We would never borrow huge amounts of money, though.
concept: Cheap float is the best financing; most insurers' float is too costly to grow; beyond float, borrow only moderately.
evolution_notes: Compare M1999-006 (no real amount of borrowed money) and L1998-016.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 15. Low-cost float generates money for investing

quote_verbatim: If you start with A and you go through and you look at everything and you find small securities in your area of competence that you can understand the business, I think you — and occasionally find little arbitrage situations or little wrinkles here and there in the market — I think, working with a very small sum, that there is an opportunity to earn very high returns. But that advantage disappears very rapidly as the money compounds.
concept: Very high returns are available on small sums by exhaustive search of small, understandable securities; the edge vanishes as capital grows.
evolution_notes: Compare L1998-003 (size caps returns).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 16. Big returns are easier with small amounts of money

quote_verbatim: We had it very easy, compared to you. It can still be done. But it’s harder now. You have to know more. I mean, just sifting through the manuals until you find something that’s selling at two times earnings, that won’t work for you.
concept: Mechanical cheapness screens no longer find bargains; more knowledge is needed now.
evolution_notes: Buffett replies: "It’ll work. It’s just you won’t find any." (line 245).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 16. Big returns are easier with small amounts of money

quote_verbatim: I love that, when they, you know, they say, “Well, you know, we earned a dollar a share in total last year, but look at the two dollars a share that we tell you we really earned. The other dollar a share doesn’t count.” And then they throw in mistakes of the past or mistakes of the future. And every three or four years, ask you to forget this as if it doesn’t mean anything. We’ve never had a charge like that that we’ve set forth in Berkshire and we never will. It isn’t that we don’t have things we do that cost us money in moving around. But we do not ask you to forget about those costs.
concept: Recurring 'special' charges are real costs; never ask owners to ignore them.
evolution_notes: Compare L1998-031 and R1996-015.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 17. “Surprisingly high” return on equity

quote_verbatim: And there’s a real question in a capitalistic society whether if long-term rates are 5 1/2 percent, whether return on equity can be, across the board, some number like 18 or 20 percent. There’re an awful lot of companies out there that are implicitly promising you, either by what they say their growth in earnings will be, or various other ways, that they’re going to earn at these rates of 20 percent-plus. And, you know, I’m dubious about those claims.
concept: Be sceptical of growth promises that imply returns on equity far above what competition allows economy-wide.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 17. “Surprisingly high” return on equity

quote_verbatim: But we try to figure out what the average option issuance is going to be. And then we say to ourselves, “How much could the company have received for those options if they’d sold them as warrants to the public?” [...] So, we say that the cost to the shareholder of issuing the options is about what could be received if they sold — turned those options into warrants — and sold them public or sold them as options.
concept: Option cost: average annual issuance (over about five years) valued at what the company could get selling them as public warrants.
evolution_notes: Compare L1998-025 (the same method in the letter); this adds the five-year averaging "because the grants are irregular".
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 18. Corporations hooked on “corrupt” stock option accounting

quote_verbatim: And just try going to a company that’s had a lot of options grants every year and tell them you’re going to quit giving the options and pay people the same amount of money. They’ll say, “You took away part of my earnings.” And we say, if you’ve taken away part of the earnings, then let’s show it in the income account and show it as a cost. Because it is a cost.
concept: If replacing options with cash would reduce earnings, the options were a cost all along.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 18. Corporations hooked on “corrupt” stock option accounting

quote_verbatim: We are going to — in evaluating a business, whether we’re going to buy the entire business or whether we’re going to buy part of it — we’re going to figure out how much it’s costing us to issue — and when the company issues those options every year. quote_verbatim: The line separating investment and speculation, which is never bright and clear, becomes blurred still further when most market participants have recently enjoyed triumphs. Nothing sedates rationality like large doses of effortless money. [...] Therefore, the giddy participants all plan to leave just seconds before midnight. There's a problem, though: They are dancing in a room in which the clocks have no hands.
concept: After easy gains, investors drift into speculation planning to leave before the end, but no one can see when the end comes.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Investments

quote_verbatim: We readily acknowledge that there has been a huge amount of true value created in the past decade by new or young businesses, and that there is much more to come. But value is destroyed, not created, by any business that loses money over its lifetime, no matter how high its interim valuation may get.
concept: A business that loses money over its life destroys value whatever its interim market valuation.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Investments

quote_verbatim: What actually occurs in these cases is wealth transfer, often on a massive scale. [...] The fact is that a bubble market has allowed the creation of bubble companies, entities designed more with an eye to making money off investors rather than for them. Too often, an IPO, not profits, was the primary goal of a company's promoters.
concept: A company whose promoters aim at the IPO rather than at profits is built to make money off investors; the gains are transfers, not created value.
evolution_notes: Lines 810-812: the 'business model' was 'the old-fashioned chain letter'; compare M2000-008.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Investments

quote_verbatim: But a pin lies in wait for every bubble. And when the two eventually meet, a new wave of investors learns some very old lessons: First, many in Wall Street  a community in which quality control is not prized  will sell investors anything they will buy. Second, speculation is most dangerous when it looks easiest.
concept: Two old lessons: Wall Street will sell whatever investors will buy, and speculation is most dangerous when it looks easiest.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Investments

quote_verbatim: At Berkshire, we make no attempt to pick the few winners that will emerge from an ocean of unproven enterprises. We're not smart enough to do that, and we know it. Instead, we try to apply Aesop's 2,600-year-old equation to opportunities in which we have reasonable confidence as to how many birds are in the bush and when they will emerge [...] Obviously, we can never precisely predict the timing of cash flows in and out of a business or their exact amount. We try, therefore, to keep our estimates conservative and to focus on industries where business surprises are unlikely to wreak havoc on owners. Even so, we make many mistakes: I'm the fellow, remember, who thought he understood the future economics of trading stamps, textiles, shoes and second-tier department stores.
concept: Skip unproven enterprises; apply the formula only where the cash is reasonably foreseeable, keep estimates conservative, and prefer industries where surprises do little harm, knowing mistakes still come.
evolution_notes: The closing sentence names Buffett's own misjudged industries (trading stamps, textiles, shoes, second-tier department stores) as the reason for conservatism.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Investments

quote_verbatim: Lately, the most promising "bushes" have been negotiated transactions for entire businesses, and that pleases us. You should clearly understand, however, that these acquisitions will at best provide us only reasonable returns. Really juicy results from negotiated deals can be anticipated only when capital markets are severely constrained and the whole business world is pessimistic. We are 180 degrees from that point.
concept: Returns on negotiated purchases depend on the climate: only constrained capital markets and general pessimism produce juicy prices.
evolution_notes: Compare L1997-035 (pessimism drives prices to attractive levels).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Investments

quote_verbatim: In our shoe businesses generally, our attempt to keep the bulk of our production in domestic factories has cost us dearly. [...] I clearly made a mistake in paying what I did for Dexter in 1993. Furthermore, I compounded that mistake in a huge way by using Berkshire shares in payment. Last year, to recognize my error, we charged off all the remaining accounting goodwill that was attributable to the Dexter transaction. We may regain some economic goodwill at Dexter in the future, but we clearly have none at present.
concept: Buffett's own error: overpaying for Dexter, compounded by paying in Berkshire shares; the economic goodwill is gone.
evolution_notes: Earlier: L1999-016 (Dexter's shortfall from industry economics, not management), L1999-014 (stock-for-stock the worst structure).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Sources of Reported Earnings

quote_verbatim: Anyone who thinks that the annual charges for depreciation don't reflect a real cost  every bit as real as payroll or raw materials  should get an internship at a simulator company. Every year we spend amounts equal to our depreciation charge simply to stay in the same economic place  and then spend additional sums to grow.
concept: Depreciation is a real cost; spending equal to it only keeps the business in place, and growth needs more on top.
evolution_notes: Earlier: R1996-023, M1998-127, L1999-024 (two kinds of business needs).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Sources of Reported Earnings

quote_verbatim: When Charlie and I read reports, we have no interest in pictures of personnel, plants or products. References to EBITDA make us shudder  does management think the tooth fairy pays for capital expenditures? We're very suspicious of accounting methodology that is vague or unclear, since too often that means management wishes to hide something. And we don't want to read messages that a public relations department or consultant has turned out. Instead, we expect a company's CEO to explain in his or her own words what's happening.
concept: Reading a report: EBITDA ignores capital spending, vague accounting suggests something hidden, and the CEO should explain in his own words.
evolution_notes: The preceding paragraph (lines 985-989, information we would want if positions were reversed) repeats L1994-023 and L1995-021; simultaneous release (lines 997-1002) repeats L1995-034 and L1997-040.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Full and Fair Reporting

quote_verbatim: Charlie and I think it is both deceptive and dangerous for CEOs to predict growth rates for their companies. [...] It's fine for a CEO to have his own internal goals and, in our view, it's even appropriate for the CEO to publicly express some hopes about the future, if these expectations are accompanied by sensible caveats. But for a major corporation to predict that its per-share earnings will grow over the long term at, say, 15% annually is to court trouble.
concept: A CEO should not publicly predict a long-term growth rate such as 15%; internal goals and caveated hopes are fine.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Full and Fair Reporting

quote_verbatim: That's true because a growth rate of that magnitude can only be maintained by a very small percentage of large businesses. Here's a test: Examine the record of, say, the 200 highest earning companies from 1970 or 1980 and tabulate how many have increased per-share earnings by 15% annually since those dates. You will find that only a handful have.
concept: Check a growth claim against the base rate: very few of the largest earners have compounded per-share earnings at 15% for decades.
evolution_notes: Lines 1031-1032: Buffett would wager that fewer than 10 of the 200 most profitable companies of 2000 will grow EPS 15% a year over the next 20 years.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Full and Fair Reporting

quote_verbatim: The problem arising from lofty predictions is not just that they spread unwarranted optimism. Even more troublesome is the fact that they corrode CEO behavior. Over the years, Charlie and I have observed many instances in which CEOs engaged in uneconomic operating maneuvers so that they could meet earnings targets they had announced. Worse still, after exhausting all that operating acrobatics would do, they sometimes played a wide variety of accounting games to "make the numbers." These accounting shenanigans have a way of snowballing: Once a company moves earnings from one period to another, operating shortfalls that occur thereafter require it to engage in further accounting maneuvers that must be even more "heroic." These can turn fudging into fraud.
concept: Announced targets corrode behavior: uneconomic moves, then accounting games that snowball from fudging into fraud.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Full and Fair Reporting

quote_verbatim: Charlie and I tend to be leery of companies run by CEOs who woo investors with fancy predictions. A few of these managers will prove prophetic -- but others will turn out to be congenital optimists, or even charlatans. Unfortunately, it's not easy for investors to know in advance which species they are dealing with.
concept: A CEO who woos investors with fancy predictions is a warning sign, since the prophet cannot be told in advance from the optimist or charlatan.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Full and Fair Reporting

quote_verbatim: During the decade before, I had enjoyed  make that loved  analyzing, buying and selling stocks. But my results were no better than average. Beginning in 1951 my performance improved. No, I hadn't changed my diet or taken up exercise. The only new ingredient was Ben's ideas. Quite simply, a few hours spent at the feet of the master proved far more valuable to me than had ten years of supposedly original thinking.
concept: Buffett's own decade of average results from 'original thinking' ended when he learned from a master; borrowed sound ideas beat self-invented ones.
evolution_notes: Earlier: L1994-011 (what Ben Graham taught). The Schey passage just above (lines 1108-1110, companies 'focused on the calendar rather than ability') repeats L1994-012 and is not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Miscellaneous

quote_verbatim: Well, Berkshire would like very much to buy businesses of the same quality, and with managements of the same quality, and at prices consistent with the eight businesses that we’ve bought over the last 16 or 18 months. Our first preference is, and has been for many decades — although I would say most observers didn’t seem to realize it — but our first preference has always to been — to be buying outstanding operating businesses.
concept: The first preference is to buy whole outstanding operating businesses, with good managers, at sensible prices; marketable securities come second.
evolution_notes: Same line: the climate 'has not been as friendly toward making money out of marketable securities.' Line 67: hope to add about 40 businesses, keep every one owned, and not issue an appreciable number of shares; the letter states the same three means in L2000-001.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 2. Four-year-old and Buffett look ahead to Berkshire’s future

quote_verbatim:
CHARLIE MUNGER: Personally, I think that the future of the pharmaceutical industry was easier to predict than the future of the high-technology sector. In the pharmaceutical sector, almost everybody did well, and some companies did extremely well. In the other sector, why, there are many permanent casualties in the high-tech sector.

WARREN BUFFETT: Yeah, I would say that there’s certainly nothing obvious to us about the fact that the tech sector — as a group — viewed in aggregate — would be a good buy or be undervalued. Whereas we should have had enough sense to recognize that the pharmaceutical industry, as a group, was undervalued. But the pharmaceutical industry has a far, far better record of returns on large amounts of equity over time, and with a high percentage of the participants having those returns, than the tech industry.
concept: A sector bet works only where the future is predictable and most participants earn high returns on large equity; an industry with many permanent casualties does not qualify.
evolution_notes: Two-speaker exchange, Munger then Buffett, one row under Munger. Buffett's 'we should have had enough sense' names the 1993 pharmaceutical omission. Compare L2000-026 (new businesses and rapidly changing industries are speculative).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 3. Tech sector not comparable to pharmaceuticals

quote_verbatim: Yeah, I think almost all good businesses have occasions where they’re making today look a little worse than today would otherwise be, to help tomorrow. So I regard these transactions as very much the friends of the shareholders.
concept: Good businesses sometimes accept a worse reported today to help tomorrow; such choices serve owners.
evolution_notes: Buffett at line 121: the first-year loss 'you should regard as different than any other type of underwriting loss that we experience, because we willingly enter into these.' The letter's version is L2000-010.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 6. “Pain today, gain tomorrow” insurance transactions

quote_verbatim: The mistakes that have been most extreme in Berkshire’s history are mistakes of omission. They don’t show up in our figures. They show up in opportunity costs. In other words, we have opportunities, we almost do it. In retrospect, we can tell that we were very much mistaken not to do it. In terms of the shareholders, those are the ones in our history that it really cost the most. And very few managements do much thinking or talking about opportunity costs.
concept: The costliest mistakes are omissions, which appear only as opportunity cost and are seldom considered by managements.
evolution_notes: Buffett interjects at line 141: 'Billions and billions and billions.'
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 7. “What really costs … are the blown opportunities”

quote_verbatim: But practically everywhere in life, and in corporate life, too, what really costs, in comparison with what easily might have been, are the blown opportunities. I mean, it just — it’s an awesome amount of money. When I was somewhat younger, I was offered 300 shares of Belridge Oil. Any idiot could’ve told there was no possibility of losing money, and a large possibility of making money. I bought it. The guy called me back three days later, and offered me 1,500 more shares. But this time, I had to sell something to buy the damn Belridge Oil. That mistake, if you traced it through, has cost me $200 million. And I — it was all because I had to go to a slight inconvenience and sell something. Berkshire does that kind of thing, too.
concept: Munger's own error: declining a no-lose, large-upside purchase to avoid the inconvenience of selling something else cost about $200 million.
evolution_notes: Resumes Munger's line-139 statement on omissions across Buffett's interjections at lines 141-145.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 7. “What really costs … are the blown opportunities”

quote_verbatim: I might add that when we speak of errors of omission, of which we’ve had plenty, and some very big ones, we don’t mean not buying some stock where we — a friend runs it, or we know the name and it went from one to 100. That doesn’t mean anything. It’s only — We only regard errors as being things that are within our circle of competence. So if somebody knows how to make money in cocoa beans, or they know how to make money in a software company or anything, and we miss that, that is not an error, as far as we’re concerned. What’s an error is when it’s something we understand, and we stand there and stare at it, and we don’t do anything.
concept: An error of omission counts only inside the circle of competence: something understood and not acted on; missing what lies outside it is no error.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 7. “What really costs … are the blown opportunities”

quote_verbatim: Or worse yet, what really gets me is when we do something very small with it. We do an eyedropper’s worth of it, when we could do it very big. Charlie refers to that elegantly when I do that sort of thing as when I’m sucking my thumb. (Laughter) And there really — I mean, we have been thumbsuckers at times with businesses that we understood well. And it may have been because we started buying, and the price moved up a little, and we waited around hoping we would get more at the price we originally started — there could be a lot of things. But those are huge mistakes. Conventional accounting, of course, does not pick those up at all. But they’re in our scorebook.
concept: Buffett's own recurring error: buying an eyedropper's worth of something well understood, often by waiting for the original price after it rose; such misses are huge and kept in the scorebook.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 7. “What really costs … are the blown opportunities”

quote_verbatim: And it’s — we are conscious in buying into businesses, and we have passed up some businesses, because we were worried about the product liability potential. [...] So it’s a very real concern in any business we get into, in terms of trying to evaluate product liability.
concept: Product-liability exposure is evaluated in every purchase and has caused businesses to be passed up.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 8. Not worried “at all” about product liability involving sugar

quote_verbatim: We make our decisions in insurance and in buying businesses with a very pessimistic attitude toward the chances of that particular ill that Charlie described being even moderated. I mean, we think if — we would project out that the trend would accelerate, but that’s just our natural way of building in a margin of safety in decisions.
concept: Assume an adverse legal trend will accelerate, not moderate; that pessimism is how a margin of safety is built into decisions.
evolution_notes: Follows Munger at line 165 on the plaintiffs' bar, a political view not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 8. Not worried “at all” about product liability involving sugar

quote_verbatim: But we, obviously, are looking every day for ways to deploy cash. And we would never have cash around just to have cash. I mean, we would never think that we should have a cash position of X percent. And I — frankly, I think these asset allocation things that tacticians in Wall Street put out, you know, about 60 percent stocks and 30 — we think that’s total nonsense. [...] Because we want money employed, but we’ll never employ it just to employ it. [...] We don’t like lots of leverage, and we never will.
concept: No target cash percentage or asset allocation: cash is held only because nothing decent is available, never deployed merely to deploy it, and never replaced with heavy borrowing.
evolution_notes: Line 185: 'you will find us quite unhappy over time if cash just keeps building up.'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 9. We don’t “have cash around just to have cash”

quote_verbatim: But we don’t have any notions as to what we want to buy based on how their costs are segmented. What we really are looking for is an enduring competitive advantage. I mean, that’s what’s going through our mind all the time. And then we want, obviously, top-notch people running the place, because we’re not going to run them ourselves. So those are the two factors we look at. We want to understand the cost structure, but Charlie and I can understand the cost structure of many companies — there’s many we can’t — but we can understand a good many companies. And we don’t really care whether we’re buying into a people-intensive business, a raw materialintensive business, a rent-intensive business. We do want to understand it and understand why it’s got an edge against its competitors.
concept: Two factors decide a purchase: an enduring competitive advantage and top-notch managers; the cost structure must be understood, but its mix does not matter.
evolution_notes: 'raw materialintensive' printed as one word in the transcript. Compare M2000-018 (moat as primary criterion).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 10. Costs vary by type of business

quote_verbatim: Yeah, basically, to some extent we’re like the hedgehog that knows one big thing. If you generate float at 3 percent per annum and buy businesses that earn 13 percent per annum with the proceeds of the float, we have actually figured out that that’s a pretty good position to be in.
concept: Berkshire's one big idea: raise float cheaply and invest it in businesses earning much more than its cost.
evolution_notes: Buffett at line 203: 'It took us a long time.' Compare L2000-011 (float judged by cost and deployment).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 10. Costs vary by type of business

quote_verbatim: The real problem is when you’re in the airline business and your wage rates are out of line with your competitors. [...] As long as you’re more efficient than your competitor, and your costs are not higher than your competitor, people will continue to fly. [...] So if you’re running a big airline at Delta or United or whatever, if your costs are on parity or less — labor costs — than your other major competitors, that is much more important to you than the absolute level. [...] Big thing in — you just can’t take labor costs that are materially higher than your competitor in a business that has commodity-like characteristics such as airline seats. You just can’t do it over time. And you can get away with it for a while. But sooner or later, the nature of a capitalist society is that the guy with the lower cost comes in and kills you.
concept: In a commodity-like business, costs relative to competitors matter more than their absolute level; a higher-cost operator is eventually killed by the lower-cost one.
evolution_notes: The USAir example (lines 215-217): about 12 cents a seat mile against Southwest's below 8, 'you’re going to get killed, eventually.' Compare L2000-017.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 11. Airlines must keep costs in line with competitors

quote_verbatim: Yes, fractional ownership is not a commodity business. I mean, the people care enormously about service and the assurance of safety. And I don’t think that, you know, I don’t think if you were buying a parachute you’d want to take the — necessarily take the low bid, and —
concept: A product is not a commodity where customers care enormously about service and safety and will not take the low bid.
evolution_notes: Munger at line 221: 'We hope that our services are preferred by customers more than one airline seat is preferred compared to another.' Line 227: commercial airline passengers assume 'quite a similarity in both service and safety.'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 11. Airlines must keep costs in line with competitors

quote_verbatim: But if you’re in a business that cannot take a long strike, you’re basically playing a game of chicken, you know, with your labor unions. Because they’re going to lose their jobs, too, if you close down. [...] To some extent, you know, the weaker you are, the better your bargaining position is. [...] But it is of — it is no fun being in a business where you cannot take a strike.
concept: A business that cannot survive a long strike is perpetually playing chicken with its unions, a structural weakness to weigh.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 11. Airlines must keep costs in line with competitors

quote_verbatim: But the second one was, we wanted to meet with the key union leaders, and we wanted to tell them, “Lookit, if you ever strike us for any length of — significant length of time — we’re out of business. “You know, you can make our investment valueless. So we really want to look you in the eye and see what kind of people you are before we write this check.”
concept: Where a strike could make the investment valueless, judge the people who could call it before buying.
evolution_notes: The Buffalo News purchase; the 1981 strike that followed (lines 231-233) showed the outcome was 'out of my hands'. Quote keeps the transcript's stray opening quotation mark before 'You know'.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 11. Airlines must keep costs in line with competitors

quote_verbatim: But people will do stupid things in the future. Even — there’s no question. I mean, I will guarantee you sometime in the next 20 years that people will do some exceptionally stupid things in equity markets. And then the question is, you know, are we in a position to do something about that when that happens?
concept: Markets will at some point behave very stupidly; the test is whether one is positioned to act when it happens.
evolution_notes: Munger at line 249: 'This is not a hog heaven period for Berkshire. The investment game is getting more and more competitive.' Buffett's advantages listed at line 245 (preferred purchaser, checks clear, stable ownership, 'under no pressure to do anything dumb') and size as the biggest disadvantage at line 247 (see L1997-004).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 12. Berkshire’s advantages, and one big disadvantage

quote_verbatim: So, our position is that there is no such thing as growth stocks or value stocks, the way Wall Street generally portrays them as being contrasting asset classes. Growth, usually, is a chance to — growth, usually, is a positive for value, but only when it means that by adding capital now, you add more cash availability later on, at a rate that’s considerably higher than the current rate of interest. So, there is no — we don’t — we calculate into any business we buy what we expect to have happen, in terms of the cash that’s going to come out of it, or the cash that’s going to go into it.
concept: Growth adds value only when capital added now yields later cash at a rate well above the current interest rate; every purchase is calculated as cash in and cash out.
evolution_notes: Earlier: M2000-001, L2000-023 (the letter's version of the same point).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 13. “There is no such thing as growth stocks or value stocks”

quote_verbatim: So we’re putting $130 million above depreciation into that business. Now that can be good or bad. I mean, it’s growth. [...] But whether that’s good or bad depends on what we earn on that incremental $130 million over time. So if you tell me that you own a business that’s going to grow to the sky, and isn’t that wonderful, I don’t know whether it’s wonderful or not until I know what the economics are of that growth. [...] But growth has been a curse in the airline business because more and more capital has been put into the business at inadequate returns. Now, growth is wonderful at See’s Candy, because it requires relatively little incremental investment to sell more pounds of candy.
concept: Judge growth by the return on the incremental capital it needs: airlines' growth was a curse, See's growth needs little capital and is wonderful.
evolution_notes: Compare L1999-017 (growth with little capital at See's) and M2000-065 (incremental returns).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 13. “There is no such thing as growth stocks or value stocks”

quote_verbatim: we are especially partial to laying out large sums of money under circumstances where we won’t have to be smart again. In other words, if we buy good businesses run by good people at reasonable prices, there’s a good chance that you people will prosper us for many decades without more intelligence at headquarters. And you can say, in a sense, that’s growth stock investing.
concept: Prefer large commitments that need no further cleverness: good businesses, good people, reasonable prices, held for decades.
evolution_notes: Buffett at line 267: 'we’re trying to put out cash now to get more cash back later on ... you can call that value or you can call it growth. But they’re not two different categories.'
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 13. “There is no such thing as growth stocks or value stocks”

quote_verbatim: I mean, I would pay any bright student probably $50,000 for 10 percent of his future earnings the rest of his life. So he’s a $500,000 asset just standing there. And what you do with that $500,000 asset, in terms of developing your mind and your talents, is hugely important. The best investment you can make, at an early age, is in yourself.
concept: A person's future earning power is a large capital asset; the best early investment is in developing one's own mind and talents.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 14. Advice to young people: Invest in yourself

quote_verbatim: If all you succeed in doing in your life is to get early rich from passive holding of little bits of paper, and you get better and better at only that for all your life, it’s a failed life. Life is more — (applause) — than being shrewd at passive wealth accumulation.
concept: Skill at passive wealth accumulation alone makes a failed life.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 14. Advice to young people: Invest in yourself

quote_verbatim: CHARLIE MUNGER: Well, Warren, you and I were once engaged in the credit and delivery grocery business. And it was a terrible business. It barely supported one family for a hundred years with all of them working 90 hours a week. And somebody actually got the idea that was the wave of the future and turned it into a great internet idea. That can only be described as mania. [...] WARREN BUFFETT: [...] But when we started driving around the trucks and hauling the stuff off and everything, you know, we ran into the same costs that Webvan is running into now. What the internet offered was a chance for people to monetize the hopes of others, in effect. [...] But there’s been very little money created by pure internet businesses so far.
concept: A new channel does not change a terrible business's underlying costs; enthusiasm for it monetizes hopes and transfers money to promoters rather than creating it.
evolution_notes: Two-speaker exchange, Munger then Buffett, one row under Munger. Buffett at line 299: many internet ideas 'were turned into wealth by promoting them to the public. But very few have been turned into wealth by actually producing cash results over time.' Compare L2000-030.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 15. Internet “was a chance for people to monetize the hopes of others”

quote_verbatim: We don’t have a master plan. We don’t — Charlie and I do not sit around and strategize or talk about the future of various industries or do anything of that sort. It just doesn’t happen. We don’t have any reports. We don’t have any staff. We don’t have any of that. We try to look at what comes in — we try to survey the whole financial field. We try to look at what comes in and look for things we understand, where we think they have a durable, competitive advantage, where we like the management, and where the price is sensible.
concept: No master plan or industry strategy: each opportunity is screened for understandability, a durable competitive advantage, liked management and a sensible price.
evolution_notes: Line 321: 'the bigger you are, the fewer the opportunities you’re likely to get.' Munger at line 323: the annual rate of progress 'will go way down'. Compare L2000-003.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 16. “We don’t have a master plan”

quote_verbatim: Now, if that’s your assumption and you’re already capitalizing those profits at a pretty good multiple, then you have to say that you have to come to the conclusion that the value of American business will grow at a relationship that’s not much greater than the growth in GDP. [...] And of course, now if you buy stocks you get 1 1/2 percent, if you’re the American public, before the frictional cost. So that the same rate of growth produces a way smaller aggregate return. And some — You know, I think stocks are a perfectly decent way to make 6 or 7 percent a year over the next 15 or 20 years. But I think anybody that expects to make 15 percent per year, or expects their broker or investment advisor to make that kind of money, is living in a dream world.
concept: With profits capped near a share of GDP and already richly capitalized, business value grows about with GDP; the return is that growth plus the starting yield, so 15% a year is a dream.
evolution_notes: Line 347: corporate profits historically 4 to 6 percent of GDP. Earlier: L1999-022 (profits tied to GDP). The return figures are a forecast; the row is for the method of building expected return from yield plus growth.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 18. Unrealistic investment expectations for pension funds

quote_verbatim: And now when the prospects are way poorer, most pension funds are using — building into their calculations — returns of 9 percent or better on investments. I don’t know how they’re going to get 9 percent or better on investments. But I also know that they change the investment assumption down, it will change the charge to earnings substantially. And they don’t want to do that. So, they continue to use investment assumptions which I think are quite unrealistic. And with companies with a big pension component in their financial situation, and therefore in their income statement, that can be quite significant.
concept: Check a company's assumed pension return against what bonds, mortgages and stocks can deliver; an unrealistic assumption inflates earnings and matters where pensions are large.
evolution_notes: Line 359: the 9 percent assumption stands while long-term governments are below 6 and high-grade corporates near 7; 'it would cause their earnings to go down if they change their investment assumption.'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 18. Unrealistic investment expectations for pension funds

heading: ### 27. Buffett: Giving and getting love is true success

[...] And one of the reasons we didn’t walk is while we were making this wonderful decision we weren’t going to pay a dime more, Ira Marshall said to us, “You guys are crazy. heading: ### 32. “Fretful disposition” will hurt your long-term performance

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 33. Triple-A rating won’t “cause us to do anything stupid”

So we leave a — we would leave a significant margin of safety and would want to buy at a — what would be a clear-cut, to us, discount from the lower levels of intrinsic value we might calculate.

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 35. Berkshire buyback is possible, but not likely

concept: Munger: performance fees weigh most on the conscientious manager who hates to disappoint.

heading: ### 37. Why Buffett doesn’t get a performance fee

concept: The manager to admire gets rich with his shareholders, not off them.

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 37. Why Buffett doesn’t get a performance fee

quote_verbatim: But there are some things in the financial world that are better thought of before they happen, even if they’re low probabilities. And we’re thinking about low probabilities all the time, in terms of Berkshire. I mean, we don’t want anything to go wrong in a big way at Berkshire.
concept: Low-probability disasters are thought through before they happen; nothing may go wrong in a big way.
evolution_notes: The meeting form of the letter's L2002-019. Line 581: a 'low, but not insignificant' probability that derivatives accentuate a systemic problem; line 591: 'it’s not a prediction, it’s a warning.'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 38. “Mild wakeup call” on derivatives

quote_verbatim: Yeah, in engineering, people put big margins of safety into systems — atomic power plants being the extreme example. And in the financial world, in derivatives, it’s as though nobody gave a damn about safety. And they just let it balloon, and balloon, and balloon in usage, and number of trades, and size of trades. And that ballooning is aided by this false accounting, where people are pretending to make money they’re not really making.
concept: Munger: a financial system needs the margins of safety engineers build in; false accounting lets risk balloon instead.
evolution_notes: His forecast of 'some significant blow-up' within five or ten years (line 587) is not part of the row.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 38. “Mild wakeup call” on derivatives

quote_verbatim: But when the Coca-Cola Company starts laying those off, and every other company in the world — major company — does with just a relatively few players, you have now intensified the risk that exists in the system. You have not shed risk at all, you have transferred it, and you have transferred it to very few players. And those players have huge interdependencies with each other
concept: Hedging does not remove risk from the system; it moves it to a few interdependent dealers and concentrates it.
evolution_notes: Line 589 before: derivatives 'have long crossed the point where they decrease risk to the system, and now they enhance risk.' The letter makes the macro point at letter lines 842-855 (not rowed there).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 38. “Mild wakeup call” on derivatives

quote_verbatim: And when you start concentrating risks in institutions which are highly leveraged, and who intersect with a few other institutions like that — all bearing same risks, all having the same motivations in the trading departments — to take on more and more esoteric things because they can book more and more immediate profits, you are courting danger.
concept: Leverage, interlinked counterparties and trading incentives to book immediate profits together court disaster.
evolution_notes: Follows the Salomon too-big-to-fail remark (lines 589-591). Compare the letter's L2002-014 and L2002-017.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 38. “Mild wakeup call” on derivatives

quote_verbatim: And when we’re buying a business we have to ask ourselves, “Do they love the money or do they love the business?” If they love the money, there’s nothing wrong with that, but they probably wouldn’t be running the business for us a year or two down the road.
concept: Ask of a seller-manager whether he loves the money or the business; only the second keeps running it.
evolution_notes: Restates M1998-061, M2000-053 and M2000-098. Line 599: founders on average have more passion than hired managers who plan to resell. Line 609: incompetent but passionate managers are 'weeded out a long time ago', so the weeding left is of 'the ones who want to cash a big paycheck'.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 39. Do managers love the business or the money?

quote_verbatim: I just got one in the other day, something from an investment banker on somebody that wants to resell a business they bought a few years ago. Well you know, the chances that they haven’t doctored up the figures in some way or are trying to sell, I mean, you know, they’re — it’s a piece of meat to them. And if it’s a piece of meat to them, you know, what am I going to do with it?
concept: A business bought to resell is a piece of meat to its owner, likely dressed up for sale; it brings no manager who will stay.

speaker: BUFFETT

concept: A manager measures himself daily by the business, not the stock price or outside opinion.

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 39. Do managers love the business or the money?

concept: Munger: in a manager, passion for the business probably matters more than brainpower.
evolution_notes: Buffett answers at line 609 that competence is already a filter by the time a business reaches Berkshire. 'borne' is as printed.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 39. Do managers love the business or the money?
