But we would regard a number of other countries as virtually equivalent to the U.S. And there’s others that would have been marked down some, and then we’d have a whole bunch we wouldn’t go into under any circumstances because we just don’t understand them well enough. But, you know, we think we understand something like the oil business in China reasonably well. And at a price relative to what we think the future cash generation is, we would make a decision on something like that.
concept: Countries are ranked by how well their tax laws and corporate cultures are understood; some are marked down and some excluded, and within the rest price is set against future cash generation.
evolution_notes: Lead-in, same line: 'We don’t make any great judgment about China ... We simply look at investments around the world and we try to buy into things that we think offer the most value.' Compare M2000-141.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 21. PetroChina investment not a “big deal”

quote_verbatim: The ideal business is one that earns very high returns on capital and could keep using lots of capital at those high returns. I mean that becomes a compounding machine. [...] That you could keep redeploying capital at these same returns over time. But there are very, very, very few businesses like that.
concept: The ideal business earns very high returns on capital and can keep reinvesting at those returns, a compounding machine; very few exist.
evolution_notes: The elision is the arithmetic: 20 percent on 100 million, then on 120 million and 144 million. Restates M2002-024.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 23. Many great businesses can’t boost profits by spending more capital

quote_verbatim: The really — unfortunately, the good businesses, you know, take a Coca-Cola or a See’s Candy, they don’t require much capital. And incremental capital doesn’t produce anything like the returns that this fundamental return that’s produced by some great intangible. [...] There are a lot of promises of those businesses, but we’ve practically never seen one. There’ve been a few. Most of the great businesses generate lots of money. They do not generate lots of opportunities to earn high returns on incremental capital.
concept: Great businesses built on an intangible need little capital and earn little on more; promises of high returns on large incremental capital are seldom kept.
evolution_notes: Line 989: 'we can deploy X at See’s and earn a lot of money, but if we put 5X in we don’t earn any more money to speak of', and the same of The Buffalo News. Compare R1996-008.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 23. Many great businesses can’t boost profits by spending more capital

quote_verbatim: Now, the one good thing about our structure at Berkshire is that we can take those businesses that earn good returns in their business but don’t have the opportunity for returns of those similar magnitude on incremental money, and we can move that money around to buy more businesses. [...] We can move money anyplace that it makes sense, and that’s an advantage of our structure.
concept: Cash from good businesses that cannot reinvest at high returns is moved to wherever it makes sense, not confined to the industry that produced it.
evolution_notes: The elision is newspapers: buying other papers meant 'a very fancy price', and owners felt their options limited to media. Line 993: See's produced 'probably a billion dollars pretax' that would have earned 'terrible returns' kept in candy. Same line: 'whether we do a good job of it or not’s another question'.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 23. Many great businesses can’t boost profits by spending more capital

quote_verbatim: And if you take a business that is a good business, but not a fabulous business, they tend to fall into two categories. One is the business where the whole reported profit just sits there in surplus cash at the end of the year. [...] The second business is one that reports the 12 percent on capital but there’s never any cash. [...] And there are an awful lot of businesses like that, where just to keep going, to stay in place, there’s never any cash. Now, that business doesn’t enable headquarters to drag out all the cash and invest it elsewhere. We hate that kind of a business.
concept: Munger: among merely good businesses, ask whether the reported profit appears as removable cash or must stay in the business just to keep it in place; the second kind is hated.
evolution_notes: The second elision is John Anderson's used construction equipment: 'every year you make a profit, and there it is, sitting in the yard.' Compare M2002-061 and L2000-035.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 23. Many great businesses can’t boost profits by spending more capital

quote_verbatim: There’s no way they can deploy the money they make in the razor and blade business to keep putting more money in that kind of business. It just doesn’t take that kind of capital. They have to deploy some money of it, but it’s peanuts compared to the profits. And the temptation then is to go out and buy other businesses, and of course that’s what Charlie and I do when we face that, but we don’t think that, overall, the batting average of American industry in redeploying capital has been great.
concept: A great business throwing off more cash than it can use is tempted to buy other businesses, and American industry's record at redeploying capital is poor.
evolution_notes: Line 999: 'In a sense, we sort of knock the very procedure that has gotten us to where we are.' Munger, line 1001: 'I don’t like being an example of an activity where most people who try and follow it will get terrible results.' Stands beside the redeployment advantage at line 991 (rowed in this batch); see Tensions seen.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 23. Many great businesses can’t boost profits by spending more capital

quote_verbatim: I don’t do — I don’t make requests of my friends, basically, for anything. And I just — I would spend the rest of my life doing it. They would feel — I would never know — (applause) — you know, what they were doing — you know, I would never know what they were doing because I was asking, versus what they really felt.
concept: Make no requests of friends: a yes given to the asker cannot be told from what the friend really thinks.
evolution_notes: Line 1019: 'I just don’t want to use my friendship for that purpose, frankly. And I don’t do it, even for things that I strongly believe in, myself.' A rule of personal conduct, not of investing; rowed as a stated way of acting, see note.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 24. Buffett: I don’t ask my friends for favors

quote_verbatim: But I do think that there’s something unattractive about a very rich guy that pops off on everything. [...] but I do try to hold myself in check, somewhat, because there’s a little bit of, you know, this, “I’m rich, therefore I’m right”- type stuff that I don’t think sits very well.
concept: Wealth or celebrity confers no authority outside one's field; hold back from pronouncing on everything.
evolution_notes: Line 1027: 'when I see it in other people I don’t like it that, you know, “I’m a celebrity therefore, you know, you got to listen to me on everything that I say.”' A rule of personal conduct; the topics he names (campaign finance, taxes) are left out.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 25. “There’s something unattractive about a very rich guy that pops off on everything”

quote_verbatim: Where a business requires practically no capital, we tend to reward the management based on the earnings. The minute the business starts requiring capital we tend to put a capital factor into this compensation system. We don’t have any one standard system. They’re all different, based on accidents of history and circumstances.
concept: Munger: pay on earnings where little capital is used; add a capital charge as soon as the business requires capital; no single standard system.
evolution_notes: Restates M1995-078. Buffett at line 1055: 'When capital is an important part of the business, we stick a charge for capital in. If it’s an unimportant part of the business, we don’t stick it in.'
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 27. Simple compensation plans and no consultants

quote_verbatim: We don’t believe in making things more complex than needed. So, we don’t try for little — all kinds of little refinements — which a compensation consultant would come in and tell you was needed, because that’s how he would justify a large bill. And he would also come in and tinker with it a little the following year, and the following year, and so on. We have very simple systems on comp.
concept: Keep pay systems simple; the consultant's refinements and yearly tinkering exist to justify his bill.
evolution_notes: Line 1065 repeats it: 'can you imagine a consultant coming around and saying, “I’ve got a one-paragraph compensation arrangement for you?” ... So, they’ve got to make things complicated, and we don’t believe in that.' Compare M2000-092 and the morning's M2003-022.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 27. Simple compensation plans and no consultants

quote_verbatim: But some of our businesses are terrific businesses, and so we have very high standards of performance before people get performance bonuses. Some of our businesses are very tough businesses, and the threshold is much lower, but the managerial talent needed to reach that threshold is just as much as in the — with the higher threshold in other businesses.
concept: Set the bonus threshold by the economics of the business: high in a terrific business, lower in a tough one where reaching it takes as much talent.
evolution_notes: Continues: 'compensation is not rocket science'; proxy statements 'are thicker than the annual reports because they’re talking about the compensation of people.'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 27. Simple compensation plans and no consultants

quote_verbatim: And then they create a whole department that spends all their time attending conferences about, you know, compensation methods, and they have consultants in, and it becomes an industry. And it isn’t going to break itself up. I mean you — when you get those — when you get a huge bureaucracy involved in making all kinds of pay determinations and everything, it’s never going to go away unless you do something about it. But that’s true of any bureaucracy we run into.
concept: A bureaucracy, once built, never dismantles itself; it goes only if someone acts.
evolution_notes: Line 1057 gives the cause: 'I see all of the time and effort put in because, frankly, it pays off for the CEO to do it.' Same line: 'We don’t have much bureaucracy at Berkshire'.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 27. Simple compensation plans and no consultants

quote_verbatim: Yeah. And on EVA, there are ideas implicit in that that we use. For instance, hurdle rates by — based on opportunity costs. Perfectly reasonable concept. But to us, that system, with all its labels and lingo, has a lot of baggage that we don’t need. We just use the implicit, simple stuff that’s buried in EVA.
concept: Munger: keep EVA's implicit idea of opportunity-cost hurdle rates and drop its labelled system and lingo.
evolution_notes: Buffett at line 1055: 'We would not dream of using something like that, although I think actually a few of our subsidiaries may use it in some way.' Compare M2000-125 and Munger's opportunity cost at M2003-117.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 27. Simple compensation plans and no consultants

quote_verbatim: The main reason we get good results out of our managers is that, you know, they like hitting .400. They like hitting .400 and being fairly paid, but they — the fact that they batted .400 is the biggest thing to them, in life. [...] Now, it shouldn’t be incidental to our managers. It’s got to be fair or they’re going to — nobody wants to work in an environment where they feel they’re being treated unfairly, but — That is not a complicated procedure.
concept: The managers worth having are driven by the record itself; pay must be fair, not elaborate, because unfairness drives them out.
evolution_notes: The elision: 'It’s, you know, it’s sort of the way we feel. If we get a good batting average in our business performance, the pay is incidental.'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 27. Simple compensation plans and no consultants

quote_verbatim: And we do make them very specific to the enterprise that’s under their control. We do not pay the people of See’s Candy based on how The Buffalo News does or vice versa. And I can show you a lot of crazy compensation systems in corporate America where that really is the ultimate effect of what’s happening.
concept: Pay each manager on the enterprise under his own control, never on another unit's results.
evolution_notes: Restates the morning's M2003-019 and L1994-022.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 27. Simple compensation plans and no consultants

quote_verbatim: Anytime you have financial institutions that interrelate in many ways, and have big receivables and payables, balances with everything, you’ve always got the danger of domino effects. And that’s a factor in the insurance business. It’s a factor in banking business. I think it’d be less in the brokerage business.
concept: Wherever financial institutions are bound by large receivables and payables to one another, domino failure is possible.
evolution_notes: Compare L2002-017 (minimize links, chain reaction).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 28. Buffett OK with large brokerages holding his stocks

quote_verbatim: But if somebody has got the right to repledge your securities and they get in trouble themselves, I don’t know any more what the SIPC — there’s a SIPC protection, but I’m — [...] Yeah, I think that’s true. And no, I would think twice between having all my securities rehypothecated by somebody else. A cash account.
concept: Hold securities in a segregated cash account; think twice before giving a broker the right to repledge them.
evolution_notes: The elision crosses Munger's interjection at line 1079, 'It’s not unlimited. You’re liable.'; Buffett resumes the same thought. Line 1075: a cash account with a large stock exchange firm 'wouldn’t worry me'.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 28. Buffett OK with large brokerages holding his stocks

quote_verbatim: I mean, the intrinsic value of any financial asset, you know, is the stream of cash that it’ll produce between now and Judgment Day, discounted by an interest rate that equates between all the different possible assets. That’s true of an oil royalty, a farm, an apartment house, an equity, a business operation, you know, a lemonade stand.
concept: Intrinsic value of any financial asset is its cash until Judgment Day discounted at a rate common to all assets.
evolution_notes: Restates M2002-020 and R1996-018; compare this afternoon's M2003-073.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 30. Intrinsic value: “fuzzy,” but essential

quote_verbatim: And that — you have to decide what sort of businesses that you think you can understand well enough to make a — some kind of reasonable calculation. It’s not scientific, but it is the intrinsic value. I mean the fact that it’s fuzzy to calculate doesn’t mean that it’s not the proper way to think about it.
concept: Choose businesses understood well enough for a reasonable calculation; fuzziness does not make intrinsic value the wrong way to think.
evolution_notes: Restates in substance M2003-074 from heading 5 this afternoon.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 30. Intrinsic value: “fuzzy,” but essential

quote_verbatim: And at Berkshire, you’ve got two questions. You’ve got the question of what the businesses we own now are worth. And then, since we redeploy all the capital they generate, you have to figure out what you’re willing to assume about what we do with the capital.
concept: Valuing a company that retains all its cash asks two questions: what the present businesses are worth, and what the retained capital will be made to earn.
evolution_notes: Line 1109: 'we’re in a whole different game now with huge amounts of capital', and whether the billions 'will be deployed in a way that creates lots more cash later on' is something 'we can’t give any prediction on'.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 30. Intrinsic value: “fuzzy,” but essential

quote_verbatim: When we buy anything, we are attempting to look out into the economic future and say, “What kind of cash can this business generate over time? How sure do we feel about it? And how does the purchase price compare with that?” And if we feel we’re getting a — we have to feel fairly good about our projections. Won’t feel perfect, because we — no one knows the answer precisely. We have to feel pretty good about our projections, and then we have to have a purchase price that’s rational in relation to those.
concept: Three questions on every purchase: what cash the business can generate over time, how sure one is, and how the price compares.
evolution_notes: Names McLane and Clayton as instances. 'Our projections' here are Berkshire's own estimates; the projections refused at M2003-065 are other people's. Listed under Tensions seen, not rowed as a tension.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 30. Intrinsic value: “fuzzy,” but essential

quote_verbatim: I’ve — I mean it’s sort of infuriating to see specious shareholder suits raised on, you know, any kind of a deal, just because there’s a lot of DO — D&O insurance — and they know people will pay off rather than go through the nuisance of a suit. And we never — we don’t pay off — but corporate America does.
concept: Do not pay off specious suits for the sake of avoiding nuisance.
evolution_notes: The tort-reform question and the plaintiffs' lawyers' 'clout' are political and left out of the quote.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 31. Munger: Tort lawsuit system is “crazy”

quote_verbatim: I just wish the people paid rather than the D&O carriers, because when a D&O carrier pays, or when a company pays, it — the costs get socialized, and the people that did the wrong things seldom pay out of their own pockets.
concept: Where an insurer or the company pays for a director's wrong, the cost is socialized and the wrongdoer has no stake; look at who actually pays.
evolution_notes: Lead-in: 'It usually doesn’t come out of their own pocket, so it gets back to that — the lack of parity in the interest of the people on both sides.' Munger at line 1137: 'there would be a great improvement, net, in Omaha — in America — if there were no D&O insurance. Zero. I think people — (applause) — would behave a lot better.' Compare L2002-035 (no D&O insurance) and M2003-021 (no parity of concern).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 31. Munger: Tort lawsuit system is “crazy”

quote_verbatim: In California, Costco has about one-third of its employees and two-thirds of its workmen’s compensation expense. [...] And they put this enormous burden on business. And of course, eventually the jobs will leave. I had a friend who took a plant away from Texas where he had workmen’s compensation expense of 30-odd percent, and took it to Ogden, Utah, where it went to 2 percent. So fraud, allowed to run, builds on itself.
concept: Munger: a jurisdiction's tolerated claims fraud is a large cost borne by the business located there, and fraud allowed to run grows.
evolution_notes: Rowed under the brief's clarification that a general rule inside a political answer is rowed without the politics: the elision is 'California is an institutionalized fraud. Fraudulent chiropractors, fraudulent lawyers, fraudulent what have you.' Continues with lawyers and lobbyists who like the fraud and a forecast of reform. Compare M2002-102 (quitclaim tort-exposed areas).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 31. Munger: Tort lawsuit system is “crazy”

quote_verbatim: Now really, when we submit that bid of 500-and-some-odd million, our bid has to remain outstanding for a good many months. So in effect, by making that bid, I get back to the earlier statements I made about option value. For $14 million, we were telling the creditors of Burlington that, for a period of maybe four months or five months, that they could sell us that business for our number or, for a considerable period, they could get more money for it. Now that is a very low price, in my view, for a put.
concept: A fixed bid left open for months is a put sold to the seller, and a breakup fee is its price.
evolution_notes: Buffett ties it to the morning's option discussion (M2003-012, any option has value). Line 1147: 'what I would call a put fee'.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 32. “It’s tough to buy things out of bankruptcy”

quote_verbatim: But we would never agree to that sort of a sum for that sort of exposure, outside of bankruptcy. It just doesn’t make any sense. The world changes too much. If you look at the value of businesses, as measured on the New York Stock Exchange, you’ll see fluctuations of a hundred percent in a year. [...] We would not — we will not participate in a procedure where we’re going to bid hundreds of millions of dollars and where our bid has to remain outstanding.
concept: Do not leave a large fixed-price bid outstanding for months for a small fee; business values move too much in that time.
evolution_notes: The elision: 2 or 3 percent to commit at a fixed price 'for a business in a tough industry ... does not make a lot of sense. I did it, so — but it got rejected.' Line 1149 names the risks while the bid sits: a World Trade Center disaster, a California earthquake, a suspension of trading. Line 1151: 'we will not be making many bids.'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 32. “It’s tough to buy things out of bankruptcy”

quote_verbatim: Yeah, we like to go in heavy. I mean, if we want to invest in a business through the stock market, we want to put a lot of money in. You know, we do not believe in a little of this and a little of that. So, at our present size, we’re limited primarily by the availability of the quantity we want, rather than restricting ourselves based on some percentage of a total portfolio.
concept: Commit heavily to a chosen stock, limited by the quantity available rather than by a portfolio percentage.
evolution_notes: Munger at line 1167: 'Well, we ordinarily don’t like small positions.' Buffett continues: 'we almost never want to quit', and Munger at line 1171: 'Well, not unless the price goes up.'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 33. “We like to go in heavy” when buying a stock

quote_verbatim: Yeah. And of course that’s where we made our big mistakes. I mean we have — or I’ve made the big mistakes, actually. I — There have been a couple of things that we knew enough to buy, that were in our circle of competence, where we could have bought lots of stock, except it went up a little bit and then we faded because of price. We didn’t fade because we didn’t want to put more than X dollars in. If we find an idea that we want to put $500 million in, we probably would be even happier if we could put 3 or 4 billion in. Good ideas are too scarce to be parsimonious with once you find them.
concept: The big mistakes were stopping purchases of understood ideas when the price rose a little; good ideas are too scarce to be bought sparingly.
evolution_notes: Buffett's own mistake. Compare the morning's M2003-047 (stopped buying Walmart, $8 billion).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 33. “We like to go in heavy” when buying a stock

quote_verbatim: Yeah, having narrowly averted the mistake of being unwilling to pay up at See’s Capital [Candies], we’ve gone on and made the same damn mistake several times, with respect to marketable securities. We evidently learn very slowly. (Laughter) [...] Those are opportunity cost billions. They don’t show up on the financial statements, but the amount of money that’s been blown by dumb decisions at headquarters at Berkshire Hathaway is awesome. (Laughter)
concept: Munger: unwillingness to pay up, nearly made at See's, was repeated in stocks; the cost is opportunity-cost billions that never appear in the accounts.
evolution_notes: The elision crosses Buffett's one-line 'It’s cost us many, many, many billions of dollars, too.' (line 1177); Munger resumes the same thought. 'See’s Capital [Candies]' is printed with the transcriber's bracket, kept as printed. Compare M2001-004 (omissions as opportunity cost) and M2003-039.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 33. “We like to go in heavy” when buying a stock

quote_verbatim: The question on discount rates, we use the same discount — I mean in theory — we would use the same discount rate across all securities, because if you really knew the cash they were going to produce, you know, that would take care of it. We may be more conservative in estimating the returns of cash from some, but the discount rate we would use is a constant.
concept: One constant discount rate across all securities; uncertainty is handled by more conservative cash estimates, not by changing the rate.
evolution_notes: Compare M1999-011 and M1999-103. Questioned at heading 36 by a shareholder citing covariance in modern finance; Munger's answer there is in the row on line 1243 in this batch.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 34. Short-term rates don’t affect investment decisions

quote_verbatim: Now, in terms of where we commit, you know, we don’t want to use the fact that short-term rates are 1 1/4 percent to think that something that yields us 3 percent or 4 percent is a good deal. So we sort of have a minimum threshold in our mind about which we’re — below which — we’re unwilling to commit money. [...] We don’t regard what we can get on shortterm rates now as adequate, but we’ll still sit in — rather than bend a little bit and start settling for lower rates for 30 years because rates for 30 days are so low, we would rather just sit it out and wait a while.
concept: Low short rates do not lower the minimum return demanded for a long commitment; rather wait than lock in low returns for decades.
evolution_notes: The elision: the threshold holds 'whether interest rates are 6 or 7 percent, or whether they’re 3 or 4 percent', 'a whole lot higher than present Government rates', and 'when we’re looking at a business, we’re looking at holding it forever.' 'shortterm' is printed without the hyphen.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 34. Short-term rates don’t affect investment decisions

quote_verbatim: And we quit on buying — we don’t want to buy equities where our real expectancy is below 10 percent. Now, that’s true whether short rates are 6 percent or whether short rates are 1 percent. We just feel that it would get very sloppy to start dipping below that. [...] So, there’s just a point at which we drop out of the game. And it’s arbitrary. There’s no — we have no scientific studies or anything.
concept: No equity is bought below a 10 percent expectancy whatever short rates are; the line is admittedly arbitrary but keeps the discipline from going sloppy.
evolution_notes: Restates the same year's letter, L2002-020 (10% pre-tax or sidelines). The elision: 'we will get opportunities that are at least at that level, and perhaps substantially above.'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 36. Why Berkshire wants at least a 10 percent return

quote_verbatim: Now, once you find a group of equities in that range, and leaving aside the problem of huge sums of money, which we have, then we just buy the most attractive. That usually means the ones we feel the surest about, I mean, as a practical matter. There’s just some businesses that possess economic characteristics that make their future prospects, far out, far more predictable than others. There’s all kinds of businesses that you just can’t remotely predict what they’ll earn, and you just have to forget about them.
concept: Among equities clearing the threshold, buy the ones one is surest about; businesses whose earnings cannot be predicted are forgotten.
evolution_notes: Line 1227: 'we have, over time, gotten very partial to the businesses where we think the predictability is high.' Restates M2003-074 and M2003-078 from this afternoon.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 36. Why Berkshire wants at least a 10 percent return

quote_verbatim: Yeah. The — I think in the last analysis, everything we do comes back to opportunity cost. But it, to some extent — in fact, to some considerable extent — we are guessing at our future opportunity cost. [...] And if interest rates were to more or less permanently settle at 1 percent or something like that, and Warren were to reappraise his notions of future opportunity cost, he would change the numbers.
concept: Munger: the hurdle is a guess at future opportunity cost, and it would change if that guess changed, for instance under permanently low rates.
evolution_notes: The elision: Buffett 'is guessing that he’ll have opportunities in due course to put out money at pretty attractive rates of return, and therefore, he’s not going to waste a lot of firepower now at lower returns.' Munger quotes Keynes on changing conduct when the view of the facts changes. Sits against Buffett's 'whether short rates are 6 percent or whether short rates are 1 percent' (line 1225); Munger reconciles it in the same answer, so it is listed under Tensions seen.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 36. Why Berkshire wants at least a 10 percent return

quote_verbatim: And we’re making a decision, as Charlie says, that it’s better to take 200 million for a while, on the theory that we’ll find something that gives us 10 percent or better, than to commit to the 800 million a year and then find that, in a year or thereabouts, when the better opportunities came along, that what we had committed to had a big principal loss in it.
concept: Accept a low yield on cash rather than lock into long bonds that would carry a principal loss when better opportunities arrive.
evolution_notes: Lead-in: 16 billion at 1 1/4 percent is 200 million a year against roughly 5 percent on 20-year Governments. Ends: 'it’s not terribly scientific. But it — all I can tell you is, in practice, it seems to work pretty well.'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 36. Why Berkshire wants at least a 10 percent return

quote_verbatim: And we won’t give up a lot in expectable return for smoothness, but if you give us a choice of having money come in every week and the same present value of money coming in in very lumpy ways that we wouldn’t know about, we would choose the smooth. But if you give us a choice of a higher present value for the lumpiness, we will take the lumpiness. [...] And other people value smoothness so highly that we do get a spread, in our view, for lumpy returns.
concept: Prefer smooth cash at equal present value, but take lumpy cash for a higher present value; others overpay for smoothness, which leaves a spread.
evolution_notes: Answers the covariance question. Restates in substance L1994-027, L1995-017 and L1996-010 (lumpy 15% over smooth 12%). Munger at line 1233: the partnerships' event arbitrage paid off when the market was in the tank, 'doing what this academic theory prescribes ... but we didn’t use the modern lingo.'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 36. Why Berkshire wants at least a 10 percent return

quote_verbatim: We’re willing to assume that for a payment, and very, very few people in the world are. Even those that can afford it. We would even assume it for 2 1/2 billion, present value. We’d want more proportionally to assume it for that, but Charlie and I, I think, would agree that we would take that on if we got paid well enough for it. We wouldn’t do it for 25 billion, but we will do things, and therefore, you know, we get the calls on that sort of thing. And that is more profitable business, over time, than bread and butter business.
concept: Take single large risks that few will accept, within a ceiling and at a price that rises more than proportionally with size; that willingness brings the calls and the better business.
evolution_notes: Lead-in, line 1239: 'we don’t mind paying out $250 million as long as we get paid appropriately for us. And that would create bad cash flow that particular week.'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 37. Berkshire insures $1B Pepsi contest

quote_verbatim: Yeah, once you’re talking about opportunity cost that’s personal to yourself and your own situation and your own abilities, you’ve departed from modern finance, totally. And that’s what we’ve done. We’re intelligently making these guesses, as best we can, based on our own circumstances and our own abilities. I think it’s crazy to do it based on somebody else’s circumstances and somebody else’s abilities.
concept: Munger: the hurdle rate is an opportunity cost personal to one's own circumstances and abilities, not a market-wide figure from modern finance.
evolution_notes: Printed under heading 37 but answers the covariance question of heading 36. Compare M2003-117 and M2001-086.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 37. Berkshire insures $1B Pepsi contest

quote_verbatim: Most companies are saddled with institutional constraints. A company's history, for example, may commit it to an industry that now offers limited opportunity. A more common problem is a shareholder constituency that pressures its manager to dance to Wall Street's tune. Many CEOs resist, but others give in and adopt operating and capital-allocation policies far different from those they would choose if left to themselves.
concept: Ask whether a company's history or its shareholders' pressure is pushing its manager into operating and capital-allocation choices he would not make if left alone.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: BERKSHIRE HATHAWAY INC.

quote_verbatim: When valuations are similar, we strongly prefer owning businesses to owning stocks. During most of our years of operation, however, stocks were much the cheaper choice. We therefore sharply tilted our asset allocation in those years toward equities [...] If stocks become significantly cheaper than entire businesses, we will buy them aggressively. If selected bonds become attractive, as they did in 2002, we will again load up on these securities. Under any market or economic conditions, we will be happy to buy businesses that meet our standards.
concept: Whole businesses are preferred at similar valuations, but capital goes to whichever of businesses, stocks or bonds is significantly cheaper at the time.
evolution_notes: The order of preference restates the Owner's Manual's fourth principle (R1996-005); the new element is the condition 'When valuations are similar' and the tilt to whichever is cheaper. The elision skips the acquisitions discussion and the earnings-growth table (lines 166-219).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Operating Earnings

quote_verbatim: (Investment managers often profit far more from piling up assets than from handling those assets well. So when one tells you that increased funds won't hurt his investment performance, step back: His nose is about to grow.)
concept: A manager paid on assets gains from size, so his claim that more money will not hurt his performance should be disbelieved.
evolution_notes: Said of Berkshire's own case just before: 'a difficulty greatly accentuated by the mushrooming of the funds we must deploy' (lines 166-167).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Operating Earnings

quote_verbatim: But first we need to warn you that growth-rate presentations can be significantly distorted by a calculated selection of either initial or terminal dates. For example, if earnings are tiny in a beginning year, a long-term performance that was only mediocre can be made to appear sensational. [...] Picking a terminal year that is particularly buoyant will also favorably bias a calculation of growth.
concept: Check the start and end years of any growth-rate figure: a near-breakeven base or a buoyant final year makes mediocre growth look sensational.
evolution_notes: Buffett then applies it to Berkshire: 1964 earnings were 'so close to breakeven that any calculation of earnings growth from that base would be meaningless' (lines 189-190), and he presents several base years 'so that you can decide for yourself which period is most meaningful' (lines 196-197).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Operating Earnings

quote_verbatim: Our capital is underutilized now, but that will happen periodically. It's a painful condition to be in � but not as painful as doing something stupid. (I speak from experience.)
concept: Idle capital is accepted as a periodic cost because a foolish purchase costs more.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Operating Earnings

quote_verbatim: knowledge I acquired after earlier making the mistake of buying some distressed junk debt of Oakwood Homes, one of the industry's largest companies. At the time of that purchase, I did not understand how atrocious consumer-financing practices had become throughout most of the manufactured housing industry. But I learned: Oakwood rather promptly went bankrupt.
concept: Buying distressed debt without understanding an industry's lending practices was a mistake, and the knowledge it gave later informed the Clayton purchase.
evolution_notes: The meeting form of the industry's credit failure is M2003-004. Buffett says the Clayton offer rested on 'what I had learned from the Oakwood experience' (line 273).

heading: Acquisitions

quote_verbatim: Progress in design and construction was not matched, however, by progress in distribution and financing. Instead, as the years went by, the industry's business model increasingly centered on the ability of both the retailer and manufacturer to unload terrible loans on naive lenders. When "securitization" then became popular in the 1990s, further distancing the supplier of funds from the lending transaction, the industry's conduct went from bad to worse. Much of its volume a few years back came from buyers who shouldn't have bought, financed by lenders who shouldn't have lent. [...] A different business model is required, one that eliminates the ability of the retailer and salesman to pocket substantial money up front by making sales financed by loans that are destined to default.
concept: Where the seller is paid up front and the loan's loss falls on a distant lender, volume comes from bad loans; the model is unsound until that is removed.
evolution_notes: Related to M2003-004 and M2003-005. Buffett names the sound model: 'one requiring significant down payments and shorter-term loans' (lines 287-288). The elision skips Clayton's conduct and the deal's genesis (lines 264-282).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Acquisitions

quote_verbatim: we looked at the record of fund directors in respect to the two key tasks board members should perform � whether at a mutual fund business or any other. These two all-important functions are, first, to obtain (or retain) an able and honest manager and then to compensate that manager fairly.
concept: A board of any company has two essential jobs: get an able and honest manager, and pay that manager fairly.
evolution_notes: L2002-026 stated the two responsibilities for fund directors (best manager, lowest fee); here they are extended to 'any other' board.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Corporate Governance

quote_verbatim: Why in the world don't the directors of those funds simply select whomever they think is best among the bidding organizations and sign up with that party directly? The winner would consequently be spared a huge "payoff" to the former manager who, having flouted the principles of stewardship, deserves not a dime. Not having to bear that acquisition cost, the winner could surely manage the funds in question for a far lower ongoing fee than would otherwise have been the case. Any truly independent director should insist on this approach to obtaining a new manager.
concept: When a fund manager that has betrayed shareholders sells itself, directors should hire the best bidder directly so no payoff reaches the offender and the fee falls.
evolution_notes: Follows L2002-026 and L2002-027 on fund directors.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Corporate Governance

quote_verbatim: Why not simply affirm in each annual report that "(1) We have looked at other management companies and believe the one we have retained for the upcoming year is among the better operations in the field; and (2) we have negotiated a fee with our managers comparable to what other clients with equivalent funds would negotiate." [...] Certainly these directors would satisfy themselves on both matters were they handing over a large chunk of their own money to the manager. If directors are unwilling to make these two declarations, shareholders should heed the maxim "If you don't know whose side someone is on, he's probably not on yours."
concept: Ask fund directors to declare that the manager is among the better ones and the fee is what others would negotiate; refusal shows whose side they are on.
evolution_notes: The maxim repeats L2002-030; the two declarations are new. Buffett adds that he would 'enthusiastically make the two declarations' for some funds, 'including some that charge above-average fees' (lines 484-485).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Corporate Governance

quote_verbatim: True independence � meaning the willingness to challenge a forceful CEO when something is wrong or foolish � is an enormously valuable trait in a director. It is also rare. The place to look for it is among high-grade people whose interests are in line with those of rank-and-file shareholders � and are in line in a very big way.
concept: A director's independence means willingness to challenge a forceful CEO, and it is found in high-grade people with a very large shareholder-aligned stake.
evolution_notes: Where to look restates L2002-033 (directors with huge and true ownership interests); the definition is new. Buffett adds the limit at lines 520-522: 'This structure does not guarantee perfect behavior, however: I've sat on boards of companies in which Berkshire had huge stakes and remained silent as questionable proposals were rubber-stamped' (the confession of L2002-025).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Berkshire Governance

quote_verbatim: In addition to being independent, directors should have business savvy, a shareholder orientation and a genuine interest in the company. The rarest of these qualities is business savvy � and if it is lacking, the other two are of little help. Many people who are smart, articulate and admired have no real understanding of business. That's no sin; they may shine elsewhere. But they don't belong on corporate boards.
concept: Of a director's three qualities, business savvy is the rarest and the one without which the others count for little.
evolution_notes: The three requisites restate L1993-028; the ranking of business savvy is new. Buffett applies it to himself: on a medical or scientific board 'I could be replaced, without loss, by a potted plant' (line 531).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Berkshire Governance

quote_verbatim: One warning: When analyzing Berkshire, be [...] sure to remember that the company should be viewed as an unfolding movie, not as a still photograph. Those who focused in the past on only the snapshot of the day sometimes reached erroneous conclusions.
concept: Judge a company by how it is developing over time, not by one moment's figures.
evolution_notes: The elision skips only the printed page number '10' (line 572) between 'be' and 'sure'; no words are omitted.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Sector Results

quote_verbatim: Insurers sell a non-proprietary piece of paper containing a non-proprietary promise. Anyone can copy anyone else's product. No installed base, key patents, critical real estate or natural resource position protects an insurer's competitive position. Typically, brands do not mean much either. The critical variables, therefore, are managerial brains, discipline and integrity.
concept: Where nothing structural protects a business (no installed base, patents, real estate, resources or brand), results depend on management's brains, discipline and integrity.
evolution_notes: The meeting called P-C insurance 'a commodity business to too big a degree' (M2003-009). Just before: 'Our results have been exceptional for one reason: We have truly exceptional managers' (line 626).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Insurance

quote_verbatim: We should point out again that in any given year a company writing long-tail insurance (coverages giving rise to claims that are often settled many years after the loss-causing event takes place) can report almost any earnings that the CEO desires. Too often the industry has reported wildly inaccurate figures by misstating liabilities. Most of the mistakes have been innocent. Sometimes, however, they have been intentional, their object being to fool investors and regulators. Auditors and actuaries have usually failed to prevent both varieties of misstatement.
concept: A long-tail insurer's reported earnings are whatever its liability estimates make them, and auditors and actuaries rarely catch the error or the deceit.
evolution_notes: Buffett says he is repeating himself ('point out again'); compare L2001-022 (insurance accounting as 'a self-graded exam') and L2002-012 (estimate-based earnings overstated). Rowed for the new element, that auditors and actuaries 'usually failed to prevent both varieties'. The Gen Re underreserving confession that follows (lines 722-725) repeats L2001-015 and is not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Insurance

quote_verbatim: The size of this debt (which is not now, nor will it be, an obligation of Berkshire) is entirely appropriate. MidAmerican's diverse and stable utility operations assure that, even under harsh economic conditions, aggregate earnings will be ample to very comfortably service all debt.
concept: Debt is appropriate when diverse, stable earnings would very comfortably service it even under harsh economic conditions.
evolution_notes: Earlier in the letter Buffett asks readers to 'understand the limited circumstances under which we will use debt, since typically we shun it' (lines 567-568).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Regulated Utility Businesses

quote_verbatim: Though far from foolproof, these transactions involve no credit risk and are conducted in exceptionally liquid securities. We therefore finance the positions almost entirely with borrowed money. As the assets are reduced, so also are the borrowings.
concept: Borrowing to carry positions is used only where they carry no credit risk and are exceptionally liquid, and the borrowing shrinks with the assets.
evolution_notes: Said of 'a few opportunistic strategies in AAA fixed-income securities' (line 842).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Finance and Financial Products

quote_verbatim: And now it's confession time: I'm sure I could have saved you $100 million or so, pre-tax, if I had acted more promptly to shut down Gen Re Securities. Both Charlie and I knew at the time of the General Reinsurance merger that its derivatives business was unattractive. Reported profits struck us as illusory, and we felt that the business carried sizable risks that could not effectively be measured or limited. Moreover, we knew that any major problems the operation might experience would likely correlate with troubles in the financial or insurance world that would affect Berkshire elsewhere. In other words, if the derivatives business were ever to need shoring up, it would commandeer the capital and credit of Berkshire at just the time we could otherwise deploy those resources to huge advantage. [...] Charlie would have moved swiftly to close down Gen Re Securities � no question about that. I, however, dithered. As a consequence, our shareholders are paying a far higher price than was necessary to exit this business.
concept: A business whose troubles would correlate with the rest of the firm's, and would draw capital just when it is most valuable, should be closed promptly; delay cost about $100 million.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the 1974 parenthesis (lines 889-897: a major insurance fraud kept funds in cash when stocks were 'extraordinarily cheap') and the page number between. L2002-011 named Gen Re Securities as easy to enter and impossible to exit; correlation in a crisis is L2002-016 and M2003-034.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Finance and Financial Products

quote_verbatim: We are in no hurry to record income, have enormous balance-sheet strength, and believe that over the long-term the economics of holding our consumer paper are superior to what we can now realize through securitization. So Clayton has begun to retain its loans. We believe it's appropriate to finance a soundly-selected book of interest-bearing receivables almost entirely with debt (just as a bank would).
concept: Keep loans whose long-term economics are better than selling them, even at the cost of later reported income, and fund sound receivables with debt as a bank would.
evolution_notes: Securitization had produced the 'front-ending' of income, 'a result dictated by GAAP' (lines 943-944).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Finance and Financial Products

quote_verbatim: You may wonder why we borrow money while sitting on a mountain of cash. It's because of our "every tub on its own bottom" philosophy. We believe that any subsidiary lending money should pay an appropriate rate for the funds needed to carry its receivables and should not be subsidized by its parent. Otherwise, having a rich daddy can lead to sloppy decisions.
concept: Each subsidiary pays a proper rate for its own funds, because a parent's subsidy breeds sloppy decisions.
evolution_notes: Berkshire lends to Clayton 'at our cost plus one percentage point' (lines 952-956).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Finance and Financial Products

quote_verbatim: We own pieces of excellent businesses � all of which had good gains in intrinsic value last year � but their current prices reflect their excellence. The unpleasant corollary to this conclusion is that I made a big mistake in not selling several of our larger holdings during The Great Bubble. If these stocks are fully priced now, you may wonder what I was thinking four years ago when their intrinsic value was lower and their prices far higher. So do I.
concept: Holding excellent businesses through a bubble when price far exceeded value was a big mistake by Buffett's own account.
evolution_notes: Buffett draws no rule from it; the lesson is implied by the comparison of value and price four years apart. Compare the bubble rows L2000-030 and L2000-031.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Investments

quote_verbatim: When we can't find anything exciting in which to invest, our "default" position is U.S. Treasuries, both bills and repos. No matter how low the yields on these instruments go, we never "reach" for a little more income by dropping our credit standards or by extending maturities. Charlie and I detest taking even small risks unless we feel we are being adequately compensated for doing so.
concept: Idle money sits in Treasury bills and repos, and low yields never justify lowering credit standards or lengthening maturities; no risk without adequate pay.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Investments

quote_verbatim: But these advantages paled when they were measured against damage done loyal associates who had with great personal effort built businesses of their own. Indeed, Charlie and I see nothing charitable in harming decent, hard-working people just so we and other shareholders can gain some minor tax efficiencies.
concept: A minor gain to shareholders does not justify harm to the people who depend on the company's businesses.
evolution_notes: Rowed as a rule of ownership for the synthesis to keep or drop; the occasion was the abortion-related boycott that hurt Pampered Chef's independent associates (lines 1276-1288), and the politics are left out of the quote.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Designated Gifts Program

quote_verbatim: We are certain that the rate of per-share progress will diminish in the future -- a greatly enlarged capital base will see to that. But we will be disappointed if our rate does not exceed that of the average large American corporation.
concept: The yardstick for per-share progress, as size slows it, is to beat the average large American corporation.
evolution_notes: The third principle's reprint changed this year: the sentences of R1996-004 (the hoped-for 15% and the falling short) do not appear in this file, and these take their place. The rest of the reprint repeats earlier R rows.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: OWNER-RELATED BUSINESS PRINCIPLES

[...] And the trick, as I’ve said, is really to have the auditors more worried about the audit committee than they are worried about the management. [...] Because once on the record, it means the auditors — it means they’re on the line.
concept: Put the auditors' answers on the record so that they fear the audit committee more than management.
evolution_notes: Restates L2002-036 and L2002-037 (the four questions) from the FY2002 letter. Buffett adds that auditors are 'hired by the management' and see it regularly, so 'it’s tempting to listen a little bit more to management than the audit committee' (line 29).

And we try to write everything in plain English at Berkshire, and we try to explain things within the body of the letter that might give people the wrong impression if they simply looked at the figures, or that they might not be able to discern.
concept: Footnotes a careful reader cannot understand fail the owner; report in plain English and explain what the figures alone would mislead on.

And I have seen a lot of that. It’s deceptive. I like the statement that the two fellows at Google made the other day where they essentially said that if numbers are lumpy or peculiar when they get to them, they’re going to be lumpy or peculiar when they get to the public. [...] But the one thing they shouldn’t do is start playing games from quarter to quarter or year to year in terms of moving numbers around.
concept: Report numbers as lumpy as they come and explain them; shifting results between periods is deception.

There’s been no — there’s been no use of our positions to, in effect, extract money for our own personal causes, either in the charitable area or the political area.
concept: Managers do not use their positions to extract money from employees or vendors for their own causes.

The real job of the directors is to come up with the right CEO for a company and prevent him or her for overreaching. If they do that job well, the rest takes care of itself. [...] And, of course, that’s fine until a red balloon comes down the line and then you get a big pop and the machine has followed its little guidelines but it’s not slicing apples anymore.

I mean, it’s almost absurd, and somebody doesn’t understand proportionality at all when they come to that sort of conclusion.

quote_verbatim: The best thing is to have a lot of earning power of your own. If you’re the best brain surgeon in town, or even the best lawyer in town, you will retain purchasing power, in terms of your income, no matter what happens
concept: The surest protection against inflation is one's own earning power.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct as much as investing; the investment answer follows on the same line ('In the investment world, it’s tougher').
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 9. Surviving inflation

quote_verbatim: But Charlie and I think the best answer is to own fine businesses that will be able to price in inflationary terms and will not have huge capital investment that is required to handle the larger dollar volume of sales. [...] Unfortunately, most businesses will not come out well in real terms during inflation. Their earnings may go up a fair amount over time, but they’re compelled to put more and more dollars into the business just to stay in the same place. You know, the worst kind of a business is one that’s — makes you put more money on the table all the time and doesn’t give you greater earnings. So you really want a business that can have pricing that reflects inflation and does not have very much capital investment that reflects inflation. But inflation is the enemy of the investor, in terms of real returns.
concept: In inflation, own businesses that can raise prices without needing ever more capital; the worst business demands more money without more earnings.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the See's Candy reference to an earlier annual report. 'Inflation is the enemy of the investor' restates M2003-024. Buffett then calls TIPS 'not a bad investment for people that have worries about inflation heating up' (line 177).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 9. Surviving inflation

quote_verbatim: Yeah, most people are going to get a very small real return from investment after considering inflation and taxes. I think that’s an iron law of the world and if, for a brief period, some of us do better than that, we ought to be very thankful. One of the great defenses to being worried about inflation is not having a lot of silly needs in your life.
concept: Expect a very small real return after inflation and taxes; few needs are a defense against inflation.
evolution_notes: The last sentence is personal conduct, for the synthesis to keep or drop. Compare M2002-096 (6 or 7 percent is not wrong in low inflation).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 9. Surviving inflation

quote_verbatim: Many corporations have a huge amount of effort spent in talking to groups of analysts. One of Berkshire’s strengths has been that we don’t spend time in that way. That’s a very time-consuming process. And it does give some shareholders some advantage over others. We try and be more egalitarian in events like this and the way we write the annual report, et cetera.
concept: No private analyst meetings: they cost management time and give some shareholders an advantage over others.
evolution_notes: Restates L1998-036 and the Owner's Manual's twelfth principle (no single shareholder gets an edge). Buffett had said just before that any such meeting should be 'open to everybody' (line 197).

heading: ### 10. Reluctance to hold special meetings for analysts

concept: Test a shareholder report by asking whether it tells what the writers would want to know if positions were reversed.

quote_verbatim: Our failure here illustrates the importance of a guideline � stay with simple propositions � that we usually apply in investments as well as operations. If only one variable is key to a decision, and the variable has a 90% chance of going your way, the chance for a successful outcome is obviously 90%. But if ten independent variables need to break favorably for a successful result, and each has a 90% probability of success, the likelihood of having a winner is only 35%. In our zinc venture, we solved most of the problems. But one proved intractable, and that was one too many. Since a chain is no stronger than its weakest link, it makes sense to look for � if you'll excuse an oxymoron � mono-linked chains.
concept: The zinc-recovery write-off teaches simple propositions: every additional independent condition that must go right multiplies down the chance of success, so prefer decisions that hang on one variable.

quote_verbatim: Insurers have generally earned poor returns for a simple reason: They sell a commodity-like product. Policy forms are standard, and the product is available from many suppliers, some of whom are mutual companies ("owned" by policyholders rather than stockholders) with profit goals that are limited. Moreover, most insureds don't care from whom they buy. Customers by the millions say "I need some Gillette blades" or "I'll have a Coke" but we wait in vain for "I'd like a National Indemnity policy, please." Consequently, price competition in insurance is usually fierce. Think airline seats.

quote_verbatim: But we instead consistently priced to make a profit, not to match our most optimistic competitor. We never left customers � but they left us. quote_verbatim: Another way to prosper in a commodity-type business is to be the low-cost operator. Among auto insurers operating on a broad scale, GEICO holds that cherished title. For NICO, as we have seen, an ebb-and-flow business model makes sense. But a company holding a low-cost advantage must pursue an unrelenting foot-to-the-floor strategy.
concept: In a commodity business there are two ways to prosper: price discipline that lets volume ebb and flow, or a low-cost position that must be pressed for growth without let-up.

speaker: BUFFETT

quote_verbatim: But after my friend and hero Lorimer Davidson retired as CEO in 1970, his successors soon made a huge mistake by under-reserving for losses. This produced faulty cost information, which in turn produced inadequate pricing. By 1976, GEICO was on the brink of failure. [...] Subsequently, the company embarked on some unwise diversification moves. This shift of emphasis away from its extraordinary core business stunted GEICO's growth
concept: GEICO's under-reserving gave false cost figures and so false prices, nearly ruining it; its later diversification away from a great core business stunted growth.
evolution_notes: The mistakes are those of GEICO's managements after 1970, with the lesson drawn by Buffett. The same self-deception is named in the 'institutional imperative' row from lines 337-346. Restates in part L2003-015 (long-tail earnings at the CEO's discretion).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Insurance

quote_verbatim: Investors should understand that in all types of financial institutions, rapid growth sometimes masks major underlying problems (and occasionally fraud). The real test of the earning power of a derivatives operation is what it achieves after operating for an extended period in a no-growth mode. You only learn who has been swimming naked when the tide goes out.
concept: In a financial institution, judge earning power after a long spell without growth, because rapid growth can hide problems and fraud.
evolution_notes: Said of the Gen Re Securities wind-down: 'Like Hell, derivative trading is easy to enter but difficult to leave.' (lines 642-643), which restates L2002-011; marks that set annual bonuses and 'phantom profits' (lines 645-650) restate L2002-014. The tide line also closes L2001-018.

quote_verbatim: Some people may look at this table and view it as a list of stocks to be bought and sold based upon chart patterns, brokers' opinions, or estimates of near-term earnings. Charlie and I ignore such distractions and instead view our holdings as fractional ownerships in businesses. This is an important distinction. Indeed, this thinking has been the cornerstone of my investment behavior since I was 19.

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Investments

Unfortunately, however, it's the windshield through which investors must peer, and that glass is invariably fogged. [...] Nevertheless, I can properly be criticized for merely clucking about nose-bleed valuations during the Bubble rather than acting on my views. Though I said at the time that certain of the stocks we held were priced ahead of themselves, I underestimated just how severe the overvaluation was. I talked when I should have walked.
concept: Not acting on a view of gross overvaluation during the Bubble was a mistake, though hindsight makes such swings look easier to catch than they are.
evolution_notes: The same mistake is L2003-021, which gives no lesson ('So do I.'); this passage adds the hindsight caveat and 'I talked when I should have walked.' quote_verbatim: And, again, our usual caveat: macro-economics is a tough game in which few people, Charlie and I included, have demonstrated skill. We may well turn out to be wrong in our currency judgments. [...] If so, our mistake will be very public. The irony is that if we chose the opposite course, leaving all of Berkshire's assets in dollars even as they declined significantly in value, no one would notice our mistake. [...] From a reputational standpoint, Charlie and I run a clear risk with our foreign-exchange commitment. But we believe in managing Berkshire as if we owned 100% of it ourselves. And, were that the case, we would not be following a dollar-only policy.

evolution_notes: The second elision skips Keynes, quoted by Buffett: 'Worldly wisdom teaches that it is better for reputation to fail conventionally than to succeed unconventionally.' and Buffett's lemming gloss (lines 1215-1217). The first skips 'the fact that so many pundits now predict weakness for the dollar makes us uneasy' (line 1211). The 100%-owner standard is the one given to managers in L1998-010. The currency view itself (lines 1081-1206) is a macro view and is not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT

quote_verbatim: Two post-bubble governance reforms have been particularly useful at Berkshire, and I fault myself for not putting them in place many years ago. The first involves regular meetings of directors without the CEO present. I've sat on 19 boards, and on many occasions this process would have led to dubious plans being examined more thoroughly. In a few cases, CEO changes that were needed would also have been made more promptly. There is no downside to this process, and there are many possible benefits. [...] The issues raised are usually not of a type discoverable by audit, but relate instead to personnel and business practices. Berkshire would be more valuable today if I had put in a whistleblower line decades ago.
concept: Directors should meet regularly without the CEO, and employees need a reprisal-free line to the chairman and audit committee; Buffett faults himself for adopting both late.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the description of the whistleblower line and Berkshire's decentralization (lines 1278-1283). Related to the boardroom atmosphere of L2002-024, which makes it hard to raise whether the CEO should be replaced.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Miscellaneous

quote_verbatim: Charlie and I love the idea of shareholders thinking and behaving like owners. [...] Usually, they've focused on minutiae and ignored the three questions that truly count. First, does the company have the right CEO? Second, is he/she overreaching in terms of compensation? Third, are proposed acquisitions more likely to create or destroy per-share value? [...] On such questions, the interests of the CEO may well differ from those of the shareholders. Directors, moreover, sometimes lack the knowledge or gumption to overrule the CEO. Therefore, it's vital that large owners focus on these three questions and speak up when necessary.
concept: An owner judges a company on three questions where the CEO's interest may differ from his: the right CEO, overreaching pay, and whether acquisitions create or destroy per-share value.
evolution_notes: The first elision skips 'Sometimes that requires them to be pro-active. And in this arena large institutional owners should lead the way. So far, however, the moves made by institutions have been less than awe-inspiring.' (lines 1288-1291); the second is placed only to skip the printed page number 22 (line 1296). speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Miscellaneous

Their open-market purchases in recent years had meanwhile been nominal, even though the stock had sold far below the acquisition price proposed. In other words, these directors didn't want the shareholders to be offered X even though they had consistently declined the opportunity to buy stock for their own account at a fraction of X. [...] Neither the shareholders nor I will ever know what motivated the dissenters. Indeed they themselves will not likely know, given that self-interest inevitably blurs introspection.
concept: Set directors' stance on an offer against their own buying: refusing owners a price far above what they would pay themselves points to fee income, and self-interest hides even from the director himself.
evolution_notes: The case is 'a recent acquisition proposal (not from Berkshire)' scuttled by directors receiving 'about $100,000 annually' in fees (lines 1348-1357), 'based upon circumstantial evidence' (line 1348); at the same meeting 'the board voted itself a significant increase in directors' fees' (lines 1371-1372). Restates in part L2002-034 (fee-dependent directors); the 'treasure' definition of independence (lines 1314-1325) restates L2003-011 and is not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Miscellaneous

quote_verbatim: no one � neither the FASB, nor investors generally, nor I � are talking about restricting the use of options in any way. Indeed, my successor at Berkshire may well receive much of his pay via options, albeit logically-structured ones in respect to 1) an appropriate strike price, 2) an escalation in price that reflects the retention of earnings, and 3) a ban on his quickly disposing of any shares purchased through options. We cheer arrangements that motivate managers, whether these be cash bonuses or options. And if a company is truly receiving value for the options it issues, we see no reason why recording their cost should cut down on their use.
concept: Options are acceptable pay if logically structured: an appropriate strike price, a strike that rises with retained earnings, and no quick sale of the shares; and their cost is recorded.
evolution_notes: The meeting form of the escalating strike is M1999-030 ('it should reflect the cost of capital'). Buffett then says certain CEOs fight expensing because their pay 'would be far more rationally determined' and their stock would sell lower, using funds that 'are instead put up by their shareholders' (lines 1396-1401). The call to write to Congress (lines 1403-1405) is political and not quoted.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Miscellaneous

quote_verbatim: Now, investment gains or losses: we don’t give a thought as to the timing of those. We take all investment actions based on what we think makes the most economic sense, and whether it results in a gain or a loss for quarter is just totally meaningless to us.
concept: Investment decisions follow economic sense alone; whether a quarter shows a realized gain or loss is ignored.
evolution_notes: Restates M2003-006. Buffett then calls the coming accounting gain on the Gillette-for-P&G exchange 'meaningless' because 'we’ve just swapped our Gillette stock for Procter and Gamble stock, which we expect to hold for a very long time' (lines 39-41).

heading: ### 5. Preliminary Q1 earnings

quote_verbatim: But we really want to buy from somebody who doesn’t want to sell. And they certainly don’t want to leave the business. So we are looking for people that have a passion that extends beyond their paycheck every week or every month for their business. Because if we hand somebody a hundred million or a billion dollars for their business, they have no financial need to work. They have to want to work. And we can’t stand there with a whip. We don’t have any contracts at Berkshire. They don’t work, as far as I’m concerned. So we hope that they love their business and then we do everything possible to avoid extinguishing, or in any way dampening, that love. [...] Then we need to look into their eyes and say, do they love the money or do they love the business?
concept: A seller-manager made rich by the sale stays only for love of the business; ask whether he loves the money or the business, use no contracts, and do nothing to dampen that love.
evolution_notes: Restates M1997-039, M1998-061, M2000-053, M2000-098 and M2003-060. Buffett calls passion 'The most important factor, subject to this one caveat' (line 63). The elision skips the intelligence-energy-integrity passage rowed from line 65 in this batch.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 8. What Buffett looks for in managers

quote_verbatim: I tell students that what we’re looking for when we hire somebody, beyond this passion, we’re looking for intelligence. We’re looking for energy. And we’re looking for integrity. And we tell them, if they don’t have the last, the first two will kill you. Because if you hire somebody without integrity, you really want them to be dumb and lazy, don’t you? I mean, the last thing in the world you want is that they are smart energetic.
concept: Hire for intelligence, energy and integrity; without integrity the first two make a person more dangerous.
evolution_notes: Restates M1997-115 and M1998-062. Munger's only comment: 'The interesting thing is how well it’s worked over a great many decades and how few people copy it.' (line 69).

heading: ### 9. Buffett on beer industry and its history

quote_verbatim: What we’re looking for is businesses with a durable competitive advantage. I don’t think there’s any question that Anheuser has a very, very strong consumer position. [...] But the other thing about it is, of course, in beer you do not see the prevalence of private labels or generic products that you see in a great many consumer products that are being — that had strong positions over the years, that are being attacked . That’s a small plus. But beer consumption per capita is going no place.
concept: Look for a durable competitive advantage; for a consumer brand, check whether private labels and generics attack it, and weigh that against flat category demand.

speaker: BUFFETT
