quote_verbatim: And I actually terminated a partnership back at the end of 1969 because I felt that that the money was coming out, you know, of the woodwork. There were all kinds of people that wanted to use it and compete, and I just didn’t feel we could do intelligent things. Within four years, I saw the greatest opportunities that I’ve ever seen in my lifetime. [...] Now, people were just as smart then. They had all these people with 150 IQs running around, and they actually had money. But the world became paralyzed for a short period. [...] You don’t need to do that very many times in a lifetime. [...] But things do happen that change the landscape dramatically, I mean really dramatically, in financial markets from time to time.
concept: When too much money chases deals to do intelligent things, stand aside; markets full of able, funded people still freeze and misprice from time to time, and a few such chances suffice.
evolution_notes: The elisions skip the 1998 on-the-run and off-the-run Treasury spread (lines 103-105) and the 2002 high-yield table, bonds bought at '25 percent to 60 or 70 percent yield' and sold at 6 percent (line 105). Buffett says that just before: 'it looked like there was so much money sloshing around that it would be impossible to do intelligent things with money' (line 101), and of now: 'we are positioned very badly in terms of buying businesses' (line 107).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 10. Competition from hedge funds

quote_verbatim: A lot of the buying by private equity funds in both real estate and stocks, and for companies, is fee-motivated. In other words, the investment manager will rationalize any price paid because he likes the extra fees for managing the extra assets. [...] He sent a lot of money back, and stopped soliciting money from his clients in certain activities where the opportunities went away. That’s the right way to behave, but it’s not normal.
concept: Munger: a manager paid on assets will rationalize any price; the right conduct, rare, is to return money when opportunities go away.
evolution_notes: The returner is Howard Marks, named by Munger in the elided lines ('I think Howard Marks is here today.'). The meeting form of the letter's 'His nose is about to grow' (L2003-003).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 10. Competition from hedge funds

quote_verbatim: So he was looking at businesses that he didn’t understand with the hope that he can place the money. Charlie and I are at a disadvantage in buying businesses because we have almost all of our net worth in the downside as well as the upside. You know, if we had a 2 percent fee and 20 percent of the profits and a goodbye kiss for the losses, you know, that’s a different equation than exists at Berkshire. We run it as if it’s 100 percent our money, which it is close to 100 percent of our net worth. And we will own the downside. And we don’t get paid for spending the money, we get paid for making money.
concept: Ask how a buyer is paid: one paid to deploy money, with no share of losses, buys what he does not understand; capital is run as one's own, owning the downside and paid only for making money.
evolution_notes: The case is a caller who would lose a 2 percent fee on unspent funds after the sign-up period (line 111). The 100-percent standard is the letter's L2004-012 and L1998-010. Buffett: 'we’ve seen no deal anybody else has made the last year that we wish we had made' (line 117).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 10. Competition from hedge funds

quote_verbatim: But the advice I would give is to read everything in sight. And to start very young. It’s a huge advantage in almost any field to start young. If that’s where your interest lies, and you start young, and you read a lot, you’re going to you’re going to do well. I mean there are no secrets in this business that only the priesthood knows.
concept: Read everything on the subject and start young; nothing in investing is secret.
evolution_notes: Restates M2004-033. The doubled 'you’re going to you’re going to' is as printed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 11. Buffett’s early interest in stocks

quote_verbatim: It’s a simple business. It’s not — it requires qualities of temperament way more than it requires qualities of intellect. I mean, if you’ve got more than 125 IQ, you can throw away the rest of the points or give them to your other members of the family or do something because you don’t need it in investing. But you do need a certain temperament that enables you to think for yourself.
concept: Investing needs a temperament for independent thought far more than intellect beyond a moderate level.
evolution_notes: Restates M2004-035 and M2002-041.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 11. Buffett’s early interest in stocks

quote_verbatim: And then you have to develop a framework — and I developed it from reading Ben Graham, I didn’t come up with it myself — very simple framework. And then you have to look for opportunities that fit within that framework as you go through life, and you can’t do something every day. You know, you can learn every day, but you can’t act every day. And I talked about reading the annual reports of Anheuser-Busch for 25 years, but I’ve read the reports of Coca-Cola and Gillette and all kinds of companies long before we invested in them.
concept: Hold a simple framework, learn daily, and act only on the occasional opportunity that fits it, often after reading a company's reports for years.
evolution_notes: The years of reading before buying are the practice behind M1996-101 and the 100 shares held 'so I can get the reports promptly and directly' (line 77). Munger adds Keynes's view that 'money management is sort of a low calling' (line 133), a view not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 11. Buffett’s early interest in stocks

quote_verbatim: I think the corporate types — the corporate managers — ought to study investing better because they’d be better managers. And I think that everyone who thinks through the investment process learns more about how the world really works.
concept: Munger: corporate managers should study investing, because thinking it through teaches how the world works and makes better managers.
evolution_notes: Munger goes on to dislike the share of GDP and of 'the nation’s brainpower' going to money management (line 137), a view not rowed.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 12. CEOs should know more about investing

quote_verbatim: I will have friends who are CEOs of companies and they’ll have somebody else handle their money. If you say to them, you know, should you buy Coca-Cola or Gillette or something like that, they’ll say that’s much too tough. I don’t understand that sort of thing. What do I know about investing? And then some investment banker walks in the next day with the idea they buy a $3 billion company, which is just buying a lot of shares of stock in one company, and they’ll run through some little two-hour presentation and turn it over to a strategic planning group and think that they are then the ones that should make that decision as to whether to buy multibillion-dollar businesses when they really don’t feel they’re qualified to make $10,000 decisions with their own money.
concept: An acquisition is an investment decision; a CEO who would not trust himself to pick a stock with his own money is not equipped to approve a multibillion-dollar purchase on a banker's presentation.

speaker: BUFFETT

heading: ### 14. Profit margins squeezed by rising commodity prices

[...] You can learn a lot about — you learn a lot about the durability of the economics of a business by observing the behavior of — the price behavior.

heading: ### 15. Tax rate not a factor in Berkshire dividend calculus

heading: ### 17. Housing market bubbles and irrationality

quote_verbatim: And you can say, how can you go crazy about farmland? It’s going to produce about 45 bushels an acre of soybeans, about 120 bushels an acre of corn. And there’s no way you could dream about a tripling, or the internet causing, you know, cornmeals to go up or something of the sort. But people went crazy on it. [...] People go crazy in economics, periodically, in all different kinds of ways. [...] But when you get prices increasing at far, far greater rates than construction costs or inflationary factors, sometimes there can be some pretty serious consequences.
concept: Even an asset with plain, fixed output can be bid far above it in a periodic mania; prices rising far faster than replacement cost or inflation warn of serious consequences.
evolution_notes: The case: a farm near Omaha sold for about $2000 an acre around 1980, bought by Buffett from the FDIC a few years later 'for $600 an acre' (lines 265-267), with 'lots of banks failing in this area' (line 267). Buffett adds that housing 'will not behave, necessarily, the same as other markets' because people live in the houses (lines 267-269).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 17. Housing market bubbles and irrationality

quote_verbatim: It can have all kinds of secondary and tertiary effects that you might not think of initially. So, we find when there’s trouble, everything correlates.
concept: In a catastrophe, insurance, operating businesses and investments are hit together through secondary effects; when there is trouble everything correlates.
evolution_notes: Restates M2003-034 and L2002-016. The example: a major California earthquake would hit National Indemnity and General Re and 'might very well have a severe effect on See’s Candy. It might very well have a severe effect on Wells Fargo.' (line 293).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 18. Catastrophe insurance: “everything correlates”

quote_verbatim: And it’s — part of my job is to have at least a general idea of the sort of risk that the various enterprises might be running operationally, and then integrate that into my own notion of the risk that we run, in terms of investments, in terms of all kinds of things. [...] But that — my job is to think absolutely in terms of worst case. [...] Everything will — everything that can happen, will happen. [...] And it’s Berkshire’s job to be prepared, absolutely, for the very worst.
concept: The head of the company integrates operating and investment risks and plans for the absolute worst case, assuming over centuries that anything that can happen will.
evolution_notes: Restates L1994-028 and L1995-018. The elisions skip the hurricane and quake exposures (line 295) and Long Island and the New Madrid quakes (line 297); Buffett wants 'no matter what happens, you know, I don’t lose sleep that night' (line 295).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 18. Catastrophe insurance: “everything correlates”

quote_verbatim: But in the end, we’re willing to lose a lot of money in one day, but we’re not willing to do anything that causes us any discomfort, in terms of writing checks the following morning. [...] But we would regard ourselves as vulnerable to extinction, as a company, if we did not have nuclear, chemical, and biological risks excluded from virtually all of our policies, although we intentionally take on the risk periodically, but only in an amount that we feel we can handle. We do not write it and give it away for free. And we do not want to write it promiscuously, because there could be events happen that would make it impossible for our checks to clear the next day, and we’re not going to get ourselves in that position.
concept: Accept a very large one-day loss but never one that strains paying the next morning; exclude risks that could cause extinction and take them only in priced, bounded amounts.
evolution_notes: Restates L2001-014 and M2002-014; compare L2001-012 (Buffett saw the terrorism exposure and did not limit it). The elision skips the book and tape recommendation on nuclear terrorism (lines 301-303). Examples before it: the airport policy of $500 million excess of $2 1/2 billion and the Final Four cancellation cover (lines 299-301).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 18. Catastrophe insurance: “everything correlates”

quote_verbatim: We’re likely to do better than most other people in dealing with what concerns you. We care more about it, that kind of correlation. We just naturally have minds that think about tidal waves in California, where they’ve never had one in modern California civilization. [...] There’s nothing physically impossible in having a 60-foot tidal wave in an earthquake zone, which California is in. But it’s never happened in modern history. But it’s the kind of thing that we do think about.
concept: Munger: think about events that are physically possible though absent from modern history, not only those in the record.
evolution_notes: Compare M2003-082 (institutions die in gaps the models call near impossible) and M2004-061 (recency distorts rare events).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 18. Catastrophe insurance: “everything correlates”

quote_verbatim: I mean, what you have here is, individually, we probably worry more about the downside than that just about any manager you can find. [...] We’ve never used a lot of borrowed money. Back when I started out, I mean, I had $10,000. But I just didn’t want to borrow any significant amount of money. There’s no reason to. You know, we’re living fine. We were living fine when I had $10,000. And the idea that you risk what you need and is important to you for something that you don’t need and it is unimportant, is just craziness. And we try to run Berkshire that way.
concept: Avoid significant borrowing even when small: never risk what you need for what you do not need.
evolution_notes: Restates R1996-009 and M2004-065. Buffett continues with his aunt, who 'had everything she had in Berkshire', and the craziness of risking her return to Social Security 'to try and add a few dollars to my net worth, or a few percentage points to the record' (lines 307-309), with 'maybe if I had a two-and-twenty percent arrangement with my Aunt Katie, I’d be — differently, but I hope not.' (line 309); compare M2005-008.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 18. Catastrophe insurance: “everything correlates”

quote_verbatim: Generally, the more the asset class becomes inflated, the less a prudent banker will lend. But of course, in this country, now you have mortgages intermediated in a way that the person buying the mortgage, in the case of — I’m thinking of Freddie [Mac] and Fannie [Mae] and other forms like that, so we’re talking about the lower-priced houses — but the mortgage buyer does not need to care about what kind of mortgage — what kind of a financial transaction the purchase is. All they have to do is look at the guarantee, and they look at that rather than whether somebody’s put any money down, or anything of the sort.
concept: A prudent lender lends less as an asset class inflates; when a guarantee stands between lender and borrower, the lender stops looking at the loan itself.
evolution_notes: Just before: 'terms have become easier and easier as prices have increased. Now, that is absolutely counter to, you know, how people think about lending in general.' (line 355). Compare L2003-007 (the distant lender who bears the loss).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 21. Zero-down mortgages fueling housing price bubble

quote_verbatim: They started saying a farm was an asset appreciation investment, not an income investment. And once you talk about something that’s an asset appreciation investment, ignoring the underlying economics of what you’re lending on, you’re really talking about the bigger-fool game. You’re saying, you know, this is a silly price but there’ll be a bigger fool that comes along. And that actually can be a profitable game for a while. But it’s nothing that bankers should engage in.
concept: Lending or buying on expected appreciation rather than the asset's income is the bigger-fool game, profitable for a while and not for a prudent lender.
evolution_notes: Of the 1980 farm bubble, when small-town banks 'lent amounts that the farm itself could never repay' (line 357); the farm itself is the case rowed from lines 267-269. Compare M1998-158 and M2002-080.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 21. Zero-down mortgages fueling housing price bubble

quote_verbatim: But you can have an accidental aggregation of behavior that somewhat leads to the same effect. I mean, if you keep marking up something, and in the process, the payment for the marked up price comes from someone else who feels they are bearing no risk because they’ve got the government guarantee in between, the money can just flood in and everybody feels very happy for a long time.
concept: When the payer of a marked-up price feels no risk because a guarantee sits between, money floods in and the markup can run for a long time.
evolution_notes: Concludes the illustration of an Omaha whose fixed population resells houses to each other every year at higher prices, financed by guaranteed mortgages bought 'in New York or Tokyo' (lines 363-365). Munger agrees: 'You have varied Ponzi effects in various parts of any modern economy.' (line 367).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 21. Zero-down mortgages fueling housing price bubble

quote_verbatim: So we would much prefer a — some asset that is going to be useful whether the currency is worth what it is today, or 10 percent of what it is today, or whether people are using seashells in order to transact business. Because people will go on eating and they’ll go on drinking and doing various things. And their preferences will translate, in real dollars, into more or less the same economics for us. And we would not trade the ownership of those kind of assets for us for a hunk of yellow metal, which has very little real utility
concept: Against currency debasement, prefer productive assets whose real economics hold whatever the currency, like See's real price per pound, over gold with little utility.
evolution_notes: Restates M2000-119 and M2002-075. Buffett: 'if the dollar goes down 50 percent, we will be selling See’s candy for double the present price. We’ll be getting the same real price' (line 375); the 1940 gold at $35 an ounce compounded to 'a little over $400' is 'not something that causes me to salivate' (line 381).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 22. “Not enthused” about gold

quote_verbatim: If you have the opportunities of Berkshire Hathaway, averaged out, gold is a dumb investment.
concept: Munger: judge gold against the average of one's other opportunities; against good ones it is a poor investment.
evolution_notes: Munger's earlier form is M2002-076 (rates matter to stocks, gold does not).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 22. “Not enthused” about gold

quote_verbatim: We try to have a culture that minimizes that. And I think we do have a culture that minimizes that. We — it’s very important, in our view, to have the right incentives. And many places, we think, have incentives that aren’t so good. I mean, when I get on an airplane, and we own the company, like NetJets, the last thing in the world I want to tell the pilot is that I’m running late and I hope we can get to New York a little faster. [...] But you should not have a system that causes people to, for example, worry about quarterly earnings. None of our — our managers do not submit budgets into Omaha. I have no idea what we’re going to earn next quarter. And I have no implicit body language out there, or anything of the sort, to our managers that I’m hoping to earn X dollars per share in the quarter.
concept: Set incentives so no one is pushed to hurry what must be done carefully; no budgets sent up, no quarterly earnings hopes signalled, even by body language.
evolution_notes: No budgets restates M1995-079. The worry stated first: 'we’ve got 180,000 people out there, and I’ll guarantee you something is going wrong someplace, as we talk.' (line 389). The elision skips companies that 'incent people ... some of the wrong things' (line 391).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 23. The danger of earnings expectations

quote_verbatim: Because in the insurance business particularly, you can report any numbers, basically, that you want to, if you write long-tail business for a short period of time. [...] Let’s assume at the start of the year I asked everybody to submit budgets and then I went on Wall Street and preached a bunch of numbers. Even if their compensation didn’t depend on it, the managers would feel, you know, we don’t want to let Warren down on this. So, you know, we’ll take an optimistic view of reserves, and that’s easy to do, at the end of the quarter and we won’t let him down and then he won’t look like a jerk in front of Wall Street.
concept: A publicly announced number pressures managers to meet it through estimates such as reserves, from loyalty alone even without pay attached.
evolution_notes: Compare L2003-015 (long-tail earnings at the CEO's discretion) and L2000-039 (announced targets corrode behavior). The elision skips the $45 billion of loss reserves where 'who knows whether the right figure is 45 billion or 46 or 44?' (line 393).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 23. The danger of earnings expectations

quote_verbatim: Well, if you stop to think about it, the history of much of which we don’t like in modern corporate capitalism comes from an unreasonable expectation, communicated from headquarters, that earnings have to go up with no volatility and great regularity — corporate earnings, I mean. That kind of an expectation from headquarters is not just the kissing cousin of evil. It’s the blood brother of evil. And we just don’t need that blood brother in our headquarters.
concept: Munger: headquarters must never communicate an expectation of smooth, regularly rising earnings, the source of much corporate misconduct.
evolution_notes: Compare M2004-029 (from hedging to smoothing for analysts to lying) and L1994-027.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 23. The danger of earnings expectations

quote_verbatim: Businesses do not meet expectations quarter after quarter and year after year. It just isn’t in the nature of running businesses. And, in our view, people that predict precisely what the future will be are either kidding investors, or they’re kidding themselves, or they’re kidding both. [...] But setting up a system that either exerts financial or psychological pressure on the people around you to do things that they probably really don’t even want to do, in order to avoid disappointing you, I mean, I just think that that’s — it’s a terrible mistake.
concept: A management that predicts precise results is kidding investors, itself or both; a system of financial or psychological pressure to meet such predictions is a terrible mistake.
evolution_notes: Restates L2000-037 and M2001-047. The elision skips boards where 'the ego of the CEO became very involved in meeting predictions which were impossible' (line 399).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 23. The danger of earnings expectations

quote_verbatim: And we have dodged it, largely, over the years by actually buying businesses from people where we’ve seen the record. [...] And I don’t think we’ve had much success, but we also haven’t tried very much, to identify people before they’ve had a record, to try and identify the ones that are superstars. Instead, we’ve taken the easy way, and we go — and if somebody comes to us with a business that’s done phenomenally for 10 or 15 or 20 years, or maybe for 50 years, and we’ve seen how — what their batting average is — we’ve actually seen they batted .350, or whatever it may be, in the major leagues. And we just make the assumption that we won’t screw it up by hiring them.
concept: Judge managers by long records already made rather than trying to pick future stars, which Buffett says he cannot do well.
evolution_notes: Restates M1996-038, M1997-039 and M1998-168. The question quotes the FY2004 letter's 'extraordinary business ability is largely innate' (letter line 453, not rowed). The elision skips the MBA class he could not rank and the practice tee (line 405).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 24. We look for managers with great track records

quote_verbatim: And they took grades in school and whether they got MBAs and all that sort of thing, and they found that the best correlation was with the age at which they started their own business first. [...] And I do think there’s a lot to wiring. I think there’s also a lot to working with the wiring you have and developing it over time. I don’t think that it’s all innate, and I don’t think you can’t improve. I know you can improve on what you’re given at birth, but I do think an awful lot of it is wiring, more so than I would have thought 30 or 40 years ago.
concept: Business ability is largely inborn wiring that can be developed; an early start in business predicts success better than grades or degrees.
evolution_notes: Buffett flags the study himself: 'I wish I could remember where I saw this study and it may not even be a valid study' (line 409). He continues that he has 'never heard him — Charlie say anything dumb about business' and the same of Tony Nicely (line 411).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 24. We look for managers with great track records

quote_verbatim: Yeah. Part of it is intelligence and part of it is temperament. [...] I think sensible people with the right temperament and the right intelligence, if they live long enough in our system, will get rich. But temperament is, I think to some extent, inherited, too.
concept: Munger: business success needs intelligence and temperament, partly inherited; sensible people with both get rich given time.
evolution_notes: The elision skips his classmate Bill Ginn, whom he knew at 14 'would be rich' (line 413). Compare M2005-010 and M2004-034.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 24. We look for managers with great track records

quote_verbatim: They got very carried away with delivering promised rates of growth. I remember reading in the Freddie Mac report some years ago, where they talked about delivering in the mid-teens or low-teens or something like that. And I thought to myself, you know, that this is madness, because you can’t do that when you’re running a big carry trade operation. Interest rate — the slope of the curve will develop. There’s no way to lend money for 30 years to somebody who can pay you off 30 seconds later, to actually match assets and liabilities in a way that’s risk-free. [...] But the GSEs got caught up with delivering increasing earnings all the time to Wall Street. So they first enlarged their portfolios and later, as we’ve seen, they got involved in some accounting shenanigans
concept: A promise of steady mid-teens growth from an inherently mismatched carry trade is madness; the pressure to deliver it leads first to more risk, then to accounting shenanigans.
evolution_notes: Restates M2004-025 and M2003-081. Freddie Mac's and Fannie Mae's mistake, lesson drawn by Buffett. He later calls it a blank check to 'two institutions that are trying to produce annual gains in earnings per share of 15 percent, and doing it by accounting means when they ran out of the ability to do it by other means' (line 455). The $5 billion and $9 billion mismarks in opposite directions (line 463) restate M2004-026 and are not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 27. Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and the home mortgage mess

quote_verbatim: But there — we would feel very comfortable with lots of U.K. businesses. And, you know, they’d have — it’d be the same criteria we applied over here: a durable competitive advantage, and a management that we like and trust, and a reasonable price.
concept: A foreign business is judged by the same three criteria as a domestic one: durable competitive advantage, trusted management, reasonable price.
evolution_notes: Restates M2001-024. The U.K. 3 percent disclosure rule is 'a deterrent, but it’s not an overwhelming deterrent' (line 483), a practice not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 28. UK reporting requirements are a deterrent

I mean, you’ve got to — you have to deflate that by the growth in population.
concept: Compare economic growth figures per capita, deflating by population growth, before concluding one economy outgrows another.

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 28. UK reporting requirements are a deterrent

quote_verbatim: I think it’s very tough for individuals to either select individual stocks, select individual times to enter the market, select currencies. I mean, I just think that’s a game that they tend to get interested in at the wrong time. There’s some adverse selection, in terms of when people who do not follow stocks carefully get interested in stocks.
concept: Individuals who do not follow stocks closely tend to become interested at the wrong time; selecting stocks, timing or currencies is hard for them.
evolution_notes: The letter's third cause of poor returns, untimely entries and exits, is L2004-001.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 30. Invest in yourself and ignore asset allocation

quote_verbatim: I think that, you know, the best investment you can have, for most people, is in your own abilities. I mean, when I talk to students, you know, I would pay a student — in many cases, I would be glad to, you know, pay them $100,000, cash up front, for 10 percent of all their future earnings. So, I’m willing to pay 100,000 for 10 percent of them, I’m valuing the whole person at a million dollars, just capital value standing there in front of me. And those — anything you do to develop your own abilities is probably going to be — or your own business — is probably going to be more productive for you than starting to think about individually making commitments into foreign exchange.
concept: For most people the best investment is in their own abilities or business, a capital asset worth more than currency bets.
evolution_notes: Restates M2001-021. Shares its printed line with the adverse-selection row of this batch, which precedes it on that line.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 30. Invest in yourself and ignore asset allocation

We are looking for opportunities and we don’t much care what category they’re in, and we certainly don’t want to have our search for opportunities governed by some predetermined artificial bunch of categories. In this sense, we’re totally out of step with modern investment management, but we think they’re wrong. [...] And I want you to remember one of my favorite sayings as you do this asset allocation. “If a thing’s not worth doing at all, it’s not worth doing well.”
concept: Munger: search for opportunities whatever their category; predetermined asset-allocation categories are not worth doing at all.
evolution_notes: Restates M1994-049, M2001-010 and M2004-019. The elision crosses Buffett's interjections (lines 519, 523, 527) and Munger's own question 'When have you done a big asset allocation strategy?' (line 521); Munger resumes the same thought at line 529.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 30. Invest in yourself and ignore asset allocation

quote_verbatim: We end up with peculiar asset mixes. I mean, if the junk bond thing had gone on a little longer, instead of having 7 billion in there, we might have had 30 billion in. But we were doing that simply based on the fact that it was screaming at us. And we do the same thing with equities. I mean, back — for many years, we had more than the net worth of Berkshire in equity positions. But they were cheap.
concept: Asset mix is the residue of buying whatever is screamingly cheap, in size, not a target.
evolution_notes: Restates L2003-002 and M2004-041. Buffett answers Munger's 'When have you done a big asset allocation strategy?' with 'Never.' (lines 521-523).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 30. Invest in yourself and ignore asset allocation

quote_verbatim: But inflation destroys value, but it destroys it very unequally. The best business to have during inflation is one that retains its earning power in real dollars without commensurate investment to, in effect, fund the inflation-produced nominal growth. The worst kind of business is where you have to keep putting more and more money into a lousy business. [...] So the best protection is a very good business that does not require big capital investment.
concept: Inflation hurts businesses unequally: the best keeps real earning power without matching new investment, the worst must keep pouring money into a lousy business.
evolution_notes: Restates M2004-008. The elided example is the airlines, which 'have to keep buying new planes' at far higher cost with inadequate returns; See's is given later in the answer (line 553) as the business that 'does not have huge capital investments that have to be made in current dollars'.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 2. We’ll “do pretty well” when inflation is high

quote_verbatim: if you’re the leading brain surgeon in town or the leading lawyer in town or the — whatever it may be — you don’t have to keep re-educating yourself to be that in current terms. You bought your expertise when you went to medical school or law school in old dollars, and you don’t have to keep reinvesting. And you retain your earning power in current dollars.
concept: The best inflation protection is a skill bought once in old dollars that keeps its earning power in current dollars without reinvestment.
evolution_notes: Restates M2004-007 (one's own earning power). Personal finance; the same test as the business-level row on line 549, applied to a person.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 2. We’ll “do pretty well” when inflation is high

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 2. We’ll “do pretty well” when inflation is high

quote_verbatim: the public utility business, for example — it costs a lot more money to maintain capital expenditures now in dollar terms than it would’ve 30 years ago. So you have to keep putting more and more money into a public utility. And you’d better hope that the rate of return allowed is commensurate in times of high inflation the same way that it might have been in low inflation with a lower rate of return.
concept: A capital-hungry regulated business survives inflation only if its allowed return rises with inflation; check that before relying on it.
evolution_notes: Contrasted in the same sentence run with See's, which needs no large capital in current dollars.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 2. We’ll “do pretty well” when inflation is high

quote_verbatim: Now, would I rather have grocery prices go up or down if I’m going to be buying groceries tomorrow and next week and next month and next year? And the answer is obviously, if I’m a net buyer, I would — I will do better if prices are lower.
concept: A permanent net buyer of businesses and securities does better when their prices fall.
evolution_notes: Restates M1999-070. Opens with 'if the market gets cheaper, we will have many more opportunities to do intelligent things with money' (line 573).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 3. Buffett: Don’t bet against America

quote_verbatim: But we don’t have much — we don’t spend any time — Charlie and I spend no time — thinking or talking about what the stock market is going to do, because we don’t know. We do know, sometimes, that we’re getting very good value for our money when we buy some stocks or some bonds, as it may be. But we are not operating on the basis of any kind of macro forecast about stocks. And there’s always a list of reasons — you gave a few — there’s always a list of reasons why the country will have problems tomorrow. But there’s always a list of opportunities which don’t get mentioned quite as often.
concept: Spend no time forecasting the market; what can sometimes be known is good value in a particular purchase, and the list of reasons for trouble is always matched by unmentioned opportunities.
evolution_notes: Restates M1999-081, M2004-101 and M2005-023. Buffett then sets out the 1790-to-2005 record of the country and says 'it does not make sense to bet against America' (line 581), which is a view of the country and is not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 3. Buffett: Don’t bet against America

quote_verbatim: I have seen more people pass up opportunities because they get focused on a single economic variable or a single problem that the country faces, and they forget about the good things. I mean, if you can buy very good businesses at attractive prices, it’s crazy to say, “I think I’ll sit this out because it might get a little cheaper next year,” or something of the sort, and because the world’s going to go to hell. We just — we’ve never operated that — we’ve never decided not to buy a business we liked because of a macro view.
concept: Never pass up a very good business at an attractive price because of one economic variable, a macro worry or the hope it gets cheaper.
evolution_notes: Restates M1998-024 and M2004-102. Munger answers 'Have we?' with 'Not yet.' (line 587). Munger's 'we are at or near the apex of a great civilization' (line 583) is a forecast and is not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 3. Buffett: Don’t bet against America

quote_verbatim: I mean, just imagine if Ford or General Motors had signed contracts that made them pay several thousand dollars a ton more for steel than their competitors did. I mean, it would — people would immediately feel that was untenable. [...] And when you get all through with it, if they have huge advantages on the health care and the annuity side, it’s not going to be a fair fight.
concept: Treat a contractual legacy cost such as retiree pensions and health care like an above-market input price: if competitors do not bear it, the fight is not fair.
evolution_notes: The elided sentences say GM and Ford are committed 'to pay sums for retired, particularly, workers in both the annuity field and in the health field that are staggeringly high compared to some of their competitors', who buy steel, aluminum and rubber at the same price. Buffett returns to the steel comparison at line 605.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 4. GM and Ford haunted by past commitments

quote_verbatim: But they’re in a similar situation because the contracts they voluntarily signed. And part of the reason they signed those — and undoubtedly — was that they bore no accounting consequences at the time. It’s a terrible mistake for managers not to think in terms of reality rather than the accounting numbers. But back in the ’60s, you did not have to account for pensions on an accrual basis. [...] And so people said, “Well, if we don’t have to count it, it isn’t real.” Well, believe me, it’s real.
concept: Past auto managers signed retiree commitments because they carried no accounting cost; managers must think in reality, not in what the accounting counts.
evolution_notes: The mistake is that of earlier GM and Ford managements; Buffett says the present CEOs were 'handed, by managers of the past, extremely difficult hands to play' (line 601). Restates M2003-110, M2003-111 and M2003-112 on pension and retiree-medical liabilities; L1998-010 tells Berkshire's managers to ignore accounting effects on decisions.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 4. GM and Ford haunted by past commitments

quote_verbatim: I think — just because it hasn’t happened yet doesn’t mean that the problem isn’t real. If you jump out of the window on the 42nd floor, and you’re still doing fine on the way down as you pass the 20th — (laughter) — it doesn’t mean you don’t have a serious problem. (Laughter) If I were the governor of Michigan, or the president of the United States, or a director of General Motors or Ford, or a family member of Ford, I would want to address the problem right now.
concept: Munger: a problem whose consequences have not yet arrived is still real; a director should face it now rather than wait.
evolution_notes: Munger opens: 'Warren gave a very optimistic prognosis'; he closes: 'I think it would be better faced.' Answers the GM and Ford legacy contracts rowed at lines 601-607.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 4. GM and Ford haunted by past commitments

quote_verbatim: And generally, the experiences were not very good when they got outside of their own fields. But I think when those companies bought businesses, they really thought they were going to take them over and run them themselves. And Charlie and I are under no illusions that we can run the businesses that we buy as well as, or nearly as well as, the people that have been running them over time.
concept: Diversifiers failed outside their fields because they meant to run what they bought; a buyer should assume the sellers run the business better than he could.
evolution_notes: The mistake is the diversifiers': Gillette's '20-some businesses', Coke in the 1960s, the cigarette and oil companies (line 635). Buffett admits Berkshire did the same buying, with 'the motivations ... somewhat different' and 'some notable failures'.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 6. Our successors will provide the “same wonderful lack of oversight”

quote_verbatim: We don’t have companies that were run one way and then we’re going to run them entirely differently, and have them reporting in all kinds of special ways to us, and have a human relations department and a public relations department, then the legal department — all kinds of things in Omaha — telling them how to run their businesses. We think that destroys — can destroy — many good businesses — certainly can destroy the incentive of the people that have already gotten rich to stay around and make us rich in turn.
concept: Headquarters directives, special reporting and staff departments can destroy good businesses and the incentive of already-rich sellers to stay.
evolution_notes: Restates L1998-009, M1997-113 and M1999-135. Same answer as the diversifiers' mistake at lines 635-637.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 6. Our successors will provide the “same wonderful lack of oversight”

quote_verbatim: It’s come from our lack of oversight of the subsidiary companies. [...] And if you’re not going to use a lot of oversight, you’ve got to be very careful in what you bring into your corporate family. And you’ve got to be very careful in treating, honorably and well, the people who are running the businesses over which you’re not giving any oversight to speak of.
concept: Munger: little oversight works only if great care goes into what is admitted and the people left in charge are treated honorably and well.
evolution_notes: Munger's sentence begins at line 641 ('I don’t agree with you that the success at Berkshire has come from our oversight of the subsidiary —'), Buffett interjects 'No.' (line 643), and Munger resumes with '— companies.' The quote starts after that resumption. Restates M1999-019 and M1999-135. Munger adds that GE's system 'works very well for them' but is not 'the only system'.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 6. Our successors will provide the “same wonderful lack of oversight”

quote_verbatim: We take people that know how to play their game very well, and we let them play the game. [...] The bigger worry would be that the culture would get tampered with in some way and people would try to oversteer, basically.
concept: Let people who play their game well play it; the danger to such a system is a successor who tampers with the culture and oversteers.
evolution_notes: Buffett says Berkshire is 'a conglomerate' and has succeeded not through 'great complicated systems or some magic formulas' but 'simplicity itself' (line 647).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 6. Our successors will provide the “same wonderful lack of oversight”

quote_verbatim: And we don’t require growth potential as part of a business. If a business makes good money and we can use it to buy other businesses, one of the advantages of the Berkshire system is we have a tax efficient and kind of frictionless way of moving money to the best opportunities.
concept: Growth potential is not required of a business that earns good money, when the money can be moved without friction to the best opportunities elsewhere.
evolution_notes: Follows See's, which 'doesn’t contribute a huge percentage of our net income now, but it provided income that let us buy other things in the past' (line 657). Related to R1996-024 (excess cash sent to the centre).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 7. Berkshire’s best-ever investments: GEICO and Ajit Jain

quote_verbatim: And I think it’s a terrible mistake for people to get hooked on revolving credit at high interest rates. And I — that’s the first thing I tell students is that, if they don’t remember anything else I say, just, you know, don’t fool around with charge cards and run up balances that keep getting larger and larger.
concept: Do not carry growing revolving balances at high interest rates.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct (personal finance). Restates M2004-125. Said while showing the GEICO credit card: 'I still advise you to pay off your account before it starts revolving.'
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 7. Berkshire’s best-ever investments: GEICO and Ajit Jain

quote_verbatim: Now the search expenses that brought us Ajit Jain, now there was an investment that really paid a dividend. I can think of no higher return investment that we’ve ever made that was better than that one. (Applause) And I think that’s a good life lesson. In other words, getting the right people into your system can frequently be more important than anything else.
concept: Munger: getting the right people into the system can matter more than anything else; the search cost of a great manager is the highest-return investment.
evolution_notes: Buffett named Munger as partner and the first half of GEICO for $40 million as the best investments (line 657). Related to M2001-031 (talented managers are the scarce resource).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 7. Berkshire’s best-ever investments: GEICO and Ajit Jain

quote_verbatim: And the enemy of investment performance is activity. And the creator of profit in a profit-minded exchange is activity. [...] I mean, you know, the profit of an exchange, the profit of the people working on them, in a sense that’s the frictional cost of capitalism. That’s coming out of the earnings of the businesses. And, you know, IBM or General Motors or General Electric will not earn more money because their stock turns over more frequently.
concept: Activity is the enemy of investment performance; trading profits are a frictional cost taken from the businesses' earnings, which turnover never raises.
evolution_notes: Restates M2000-006, M2003-025 and M2004-088. The surrounding view that the NYSE should stay 'not-for-big-profit' is a view on the exchange's structure and is not rowed. Munger's 'duty as an exemplar' for the exchange's governors (line 687) is not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 8. NYSE should not being trying to earn a profit

quote_verbatim: Well, financial companies are more difficult to analyze than many companies. I mean, the — it is more — if you take the insurance business, you know, the biggest single element that is very difficult to evaluate, even if you own the company, is the loss and loss adjustment expense reserve. And that has a huge impact on reported earnings of any given period. And the shorter the period, the more the impact can be from just small changes in assumptions.
concept: Financial companies are harder to analyze; an insurer's loss reserve is hard to judge even for its owner and small changes in assumptions move short-period earnings greatly.
evolution_notes: Restates L2001-022, L2003-015 and M2001-066. Buffett gives Berkshire's own 45 billion of reserves, which 'could just as easily' be 45 1/2 or 44 1/2, and says of banks 'it basically is whether the loans are any good' (line 727).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 10. Don’t blame the ratings agencies

quote_verbatim: if you’re analyzing something like WD-40, you know, or See’s Candy, or our brick business, or whatever, you know, they may have good or bad prospects but you’re not likely to be fooling yourself much about what’s going on currently. But with financial institutions, it’s much tougher. Then you add — throw in derivatives on top of it, and, you know, it’s — no one probably knows, you know, perfectly, what some of the — or even within a reasonable range — the exact condition of some of the biggest, you know, banks in the world.
concept: In a simple business the current condition is known even if prospects are not; in a financial institution, more so with derivatives, even the current condition may be unknowable.
evolution_notes: Restates M2004-025 and M2004-027. Buffett adds that 'very smart — financially smart — people' on the Freddie and Fannie boards were not negligent (line 729).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 10. Don’t blame the ratings agencies

quote_verbatim: So I just think you have to accept the fact that insurance, banking, finance companies — we’ve seen all kinds of finance company — both frauds and just big mistakes over time — of just one after another over the years. And the — it’s just a more dangerous field to analyze. It doesn’t mean you can’t make money in it. We’ve made a lot of money on it. But it’s difficult. Now, obviously a GEICO, where you’re insuring pretty much the same thing — auto drivers — and you get — your statistics are much more valid in something like that than they will be if you’re taking something that — like asbestos liability — you’re subject to far greater errors in estimation.
concept: Finance is a more dangerous field to analyze though money can be made in it; within insurance, homogeneous risks give valid statistics and long-tail liabilities give large estimation errors.
evolution_notes: Continues the answer at lines 727-729. Buffett adds he would bet the 20 largest insurers' asbestos estimates 'are way off, but I don’t know in which direction' (line 733).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 10. Don’t blame the ratings agencies

quote_verbatim: where you’ve got complexity, which by its very nature provides better opportunities to be mistaken and not have it come to notice, or to be fraudulent and have it not be found out, you’re going to get more fraud and mistakes than you are if you’re selling a business where you shovel sand out of the river and sell it by the truckload. [...] So, if you don’t like the lack of perfect accounting in financial institutions, you’re in the wrong world.
concept: Munger: complexity breeds undetected mistakes and fraud, so expect more of both in financial institutions than in a simple business.
evolution_notes: Restates M2002-121 and M2004-105. The elided sentences compare natural gas and sand and add that government-owned banks report worst of all.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 10. Don’t blame the ratings agencies

quote_verbatim: We’re not unhappy with anything we own. We’re not happy with putting more money in, so we’re in a zone in some of those securities that — where we wouldn’t buy and we wouldn’t sell. [...] But we would face significant costs — including taxes, but on top of taxes — in trying to go in and out of the big positions we have. And basically we like the businesses. [...] But there is a zone, which because of size, because of taxes, where we would neither be a buyer nor a seller.
concept: Between the price at which one would buy and the price at which one would sell lies a zone, widened by size and taxes, in which a liked business is simply held.
evolution_notes: Related to M1997-144 and L1993-014. Buffett adds that common stocks are a lower share of Berkshire's intrinsic value than at almost any time since the 1969 partnership liquidation (line 753). Munger's remarks on size limiting the 'nimble moneymaking record of the past' (lines 757-765) describe Berkshire and are not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 11. We like our stocks but aren’t buying more now

quote_verbatim: I would say that gold would be way down on my list as a store of value. I mean, I would much prefer owning a hundred acres of land near here in Nebraska, or an apartment house, or an index fund. [...] You know, it has — a farm has utility, an apartment house has utility, a business, you know, will produce earnings. And some businesses will produce them in real terms as they go along.
concept: As a store of value prefer assets with utility or earnings, land, an apartment house, a business, an index fund, over gold, which produces nothing.
evolution_notes: Restates M2000-119, M2002-075 and M2005-033. The elision covers Buffett's arithmetic: $20 gold in 1900 to $400, the Dow from 66 to 11- or 12,000 'and paid you dividends'. He closes: 'it doesn’t do much along the way, for anybody' (line 785).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 12. “I don’t see gold as a store of value”

quote_verbatim: Well, I think gold was — and similar items — that was a great thing to have if you were a well-to-do Jewish family in Vienna in 1935, because you had hazards where that gold had enormous utility to you. But for Berkshire Hathaway sitting here in 2005, it just doesn’t interest us at all.
concept: Munger: gold's worth depends on the holder's hazards; it has utility to someone facing persecution or flight, none to Berkshire.
evolution_notes: Restates M2005-034 and M2002-076.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 12. “I don’t see gold as a store of value”

quote_verbatim: Every now and then — I mean, and I agree — very infrequently, you probably can say something intelligent about markets as a whole. I mean, that you do see circumstances that are extreme enough that you can make a statement that is likely to look reasonably intelligent five or 10 years later. [...] Most of the time, you know, you’re in some in between zone. [...] I mean, I knew in a general way that I was going to be right, particularly in certain aspects of the market, but I didn’t know when, and then I didn’t know how right or anything of the sort.
concept: Only at rare extremes can anything intelligent be said about the market as a whole, and even then the direction is known, not the timing or the degree.
evolution_notes: Buffett names 1969, 1974 and the summer 1999 Sun Valley talk as the times he spoke out. Sits beside M1999-081 and M2005-054 (no market forecasts); the same answer limits the exception to extremes. Closes: 'I don’t think it’s an extreme enough period that you can speak out in some very definitive way about the outlook' (line 799).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 13. No stock bubble right now, but no bargains, either

quote_verbatim: I think that if you had to make a choice between owning long-term bonds, which are now yielding — the Treasury — only a little over 4 1/2 percent, or owning equities for the next 20 years, and you couldn’t make — change that decision, I would certainly prefer equities.
concept: Compare a locked-in twenty-year holding of equities with the long Treasury yield; at a little over 4 1/2 percent, equities are preferred.
evolution_notes: Repeated at line 799 ('if you told me I had to go away for 20 years and choose between what’s obtainable in an index fund of equities or be committed to long-term bonds, I would rather take equities'). The expectation of 6 or 7 percent is in the next row, from the same line.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 13. No stock bubble right now, but no bargains, either

quote_verbatim: But I think people that have expectations that they can earn more than 6 or 7 percent in equities, and certainly when they start expecting double digits, I think the degree to what they have expectations, they can do that or that they can find somebody else to do it for them, I think they’re making a big mistake. But 6 or 7 percent is not the end of the world at all.
concept: Expecting more than 6 or 7 percent from equities, or a manager who will deliver double digits, is a big mistake.
evolution_notes: Restates M2001-025 and M2003-025. Shares line 797 with the bond comparison row just before it. Buffett adds: 'I think you will get a chance to do something that is more screamingly intelligent in not too many years' (line 799), a forecast, not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 13. No stock bubble right now, but no bargains, either

quote_verbatim: I would say, number one, that in a corporation like Berkshire, that’s taxable under subchapter C of the Internal Revenue Code, owning real estate is grossly disadvantaged compared to owning it directly by individuals such as yourself. [...] Name me a lot of C corporations that have been passive holders in real estate and have done well over a whole lot of years. It’s almost a null class.
concept: Munger: a taxable corporation is grossly disadvantaged as a passive holder of real estate against individuals; such holders that did well are almost a null class.
evolution_notes: Restates M2002-106 and M2002-107. The elided sentences: real estate 'is having bubble valuation problems of its own right now', and rich friends selling their worst properties get bids 'higher than their highest expectations'.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 14. “Bubble valuation problems” for real estate

quote_verbatim: At that time they were selling at discounts to the values of properties. And those values of properties were much more conservatively figured than today. Today, you have very fancy prices on real estate. And on top of that, you have the REITs often selling at a premium, though. So, I regard REITs as quite unattractive now, certainly compared to five or six years ago.
concept: Judge a holding vehicle by its price against conservatively figured underlying asset values; a premium on top of fancy asset prices is doubly unattractive.
evolution_notes: Buffett had his small outside portfolio 'all in REITs' when the NASDAQ was near its high (line 813). Munger then asks whether it is 'that much more so' for a corporation, and Buffett agrees (lines 815-821).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 14. “Bubble valuation problems” for real estate

quote_verbatim: REITs were very unpopular five or six years ago. Now they’re popular. It’s better to pay attention to something that is being scorned than something that’s being championed.
concept: Look at what is scorned rather than what is championed.
evolution_notes: Munger adds 'And the REITs have phony accounting.' (line 823), not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 14. “Bubble valuation problems” for real estate

quote_verbatim: I mean, [investor] Peter Lynch has always said, you know, “Buy a business that’s so good that an idiot can run it, because sooner or later one will.” (Laughter) We’ve got a country that’s so good that we can have policies that are counterproductive — (applause) — and we’ll still come out OK.
concept: Buy a business good enough that an idiot can run it, because one eventually will.
evolution_notes: Buffett quotes Peter Lynch at this meeting and applies the line to the country; the country half is a view and is in the quote only because it is the same sentence run. Related to M1999-106 and M2000-071 (a structural advantage making management nearly irrelevant).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 16. “Unwise” economic policies, but no “Armageddon”

quote_verbatim: They may create, you know, very severe dislocations in financial markets from time to time. But that’s been the history of this country. I mean, we have had very dramatic things happen in financial markets over the years. And the country survives despite that. And sometimes there’s great opportunity in those dislocations.
concept: Severe financial dislocations recur and the economy survives them; they are often where the great opportunities lie.
evolution_notes: Restates M2004-128 (a crisis is a time to buy). Buffett says he is 'not an Armageddon type at all on the economy' while 'we’re following policies that are unwise' (line 853).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 16. “Unwise” economic policies, but no “Armageddon”

quote_verbatim: Yeah, we don’t have any great record as macroeconomic predictors. And I don’t see any reason why we should really start now.
concept: Munger: having no record as macroeconomic predictors, do not start predicting.
evolution_notes: Restates M1999-081 and M1999-116. Munger adds that 'there are more chances for convulsion now' but 'Apart from knowing that, we have no contribution to make.'
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 16. “Unwise” economic policies, but no “Armageddon”

quote_verbatim: But as you turn it over to fund managers who think their job is to beat the S&P in — on a short-term basis — you are getting very short time horizons on huge amounts of money. And those people may think they are operating independently in one sense. But they’re responding to the same stimuli. And they can, as they did in the fall of 1998, they can all head for the exits — or try to head for the exits — at one time. And the thing about financial instruments is there is no exit. I mean, the only way that you get rid of a financial — the only way you leave your seat in a burning theatre in financial markets is to find somebody else to take the seat. And that is not always easy.
concept: Money held by short-horizon managers responding to the same stimuli is on a hair trigger; in a rush there is no exit, only a buyer to take your seat.
evolution_notes: Restates M2004-028. Contrasted with Buffett's early clients buying utility stocks 'a hundred shares at a time in Omaha', money 'not on a hair-trigger basis' (line 861).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 16. “Unwise” economic policies, but no “Armageddon”

quote_verbatim: And he got in the habit of picking up easy money with the credit systems of the world. He kept selling naked puts secured by his account, including puts on a whole lot of internet stocks. And in due time, he didn’t have the $5 million of securities, and he didn’t have the house, and he now works in a restaurant. That kind of self-destruction wasn’t possible before we created all these wonderful trading opportunities involving credit.
concept: Munger: picking up easy money by writing naked puts on credit led a comfortable man to lose everything; credit-financed trading enables self-destruction.
evolution_notes: The mistake is a third party's, a man known to one of Munger's children. Restates M2004-065 and M2004-128 on leverage. Munger's view that single-stock futures and listed options should not have been allowed and that legalizing gambling was 'not a smart thing for this country to do' is political and left out of the quote.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 16. “Unwise” economic policies, but no “Armageddon”

quote_verbatim: The real problem that you can face, and may often face, is when you’re dealing with mediocrity. I mean, if you have a baseball team and you have a .240 hitter in the majors, a .240 hitter in the majors is still a pretty good baseball player. But if your job is to have a winning team, you get rid of him. And you find somebody that can bat .280 or .290 and field just as well. In business, the tough part is to get rid of something a notch or two above mediocrity, but not the best one that could be found.
concept: A director's hardest case is a chief executive a notch above mediocre but not the best obtainable; a board that wants to win replaces him.
evolution_notes: Restates M2004-005 (the directors' real job is the right CEO). Buffett goes on to the social instincts and fee dependence that make a charge against 'this guy at the head of the table' very difficult (line 891).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 17. Why Berkshire’s board is better

quote_verbatim: And we believe that, you know, independence is — it’s a state of mind. I mean, it — and it’s a willingness, but not the eagerness, to challenge the ideas of others.
concept: A director's independence is a state of mind: willingness, not eagerness, to challenge others' ideas.
evolution_notes: Restates L2003-011.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 17. Why Berkshire’s board is better

quote_verbatim: the group around you, in terms of social behavior, can only tolerate a certain amount of obnoxiousness on the part of yourself. You have to sort of ration it out. And so you save yourself for big ones.
concept: A director's capacity to object is limited by the group's tolerance, so ration it and save it for the big issues.
evolution_notes: Related to L2002-025 (Buffett's own silence as a director). Buffett says of major acquisitions proposed on boards he sat on, 'a significant percentage of them I wouldn’t do myself', but 'I wouldn’t get the votes probably anyway' and a bullet fired 'usually it doesn’t do any good'.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 17. Why Berkshire’s board is better

quote_verbatim: But we have real owners on our board. And what they make for being board members is really inconsequential, as I get reminded occasionally — (laughter) — compared to their investment. [...] But the people that want — who make their evaluations by checklist, you know, whether — either in terms of diversity or in terms of supposed independence — although I don’t know how anybody that’s getting half their income from board memberships can be independent — you know, we don’t — we may not stack up so well.
concept: Judge a board by whether its directors are real owners whose fees are inconsequential beside their investment, not by checklist independence.
evolution_notes: Restates M2003-001, M2004-005 and L2002-034. Munger opened the heading: Berkshire's directors 'are rich and they own a lot of stock' and get no liability insurance from Berkshire (line 887). The answer is cut off by the tape change (heading 18).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 17. Why Berkshire’s board is better

quote_verbatim: Charlie and I, in managing Berkshire, try to do things — put money in things — that we understand. And when I mean understand, I mean, that we — where we think we know, in a reasonable way, what the economics will look like in five or 10 or 20 years. And Bill [Gates] is a lot smarter about a whole lot of things than I am. But it’s still Charlie and I that have the responsibility for managing the money. And we’ll stick in what we consider to be our circle of competence. And the fact that somebody else’s circle is wider or different, you know, that’s the way the world is.
concept: To understand a business means to know reasonably what its economics will be in five, ten or twenty years; stay inside one's own circle whatever the width of others'.
evolution_notes: Restates M2003-092, M2002-092 and M2002-093. The question is lost in the tape change (heading 18); the answer begins '(Laughter) No, the answer is'.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 19. Gates is smart but we must stock to our “circle of competence”

quote_verbatim: A director getting $150,000 a year from a company, who needs it, is not an independent director. That director automatically becomes an inside director.
concept: Munger: a director who needs his fee is in effect an inside director.
evolution_notes: Restates L2002-034. Munger's following 'it’s a typical government intervention' is political and left out.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 20. If corporate directors need the money, they’re not independent

quote_verbatim: Yeah, I have never — I’ve been on 19 boards — I have never seen a director, where the directors’ fees were important to them, object to an acquisition proposal, object to a compensation arrangement of the CEO. It’s just never happened, you know — in my experience. And you know, they do not — they frequently do not — behave as they would if they owned the place. And basically we want people that behave as if they own the place.
concept: Directors to whom the fees matter never object to an acquisition or a CEO's pay; want directors who behave as owners.
evolution_notes: Restates L2002-034 and M2003-001; follows Munger's row at line 907. Buffett later tells of a Berkshire director 'removed twice from compensation committees' for questioning the pay proposed: 'they’re looking for Chihuahuas, and not Great Danes and Dobermans' (line 913).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 20. If corporate directors need the money, they’re not independent

quote_verbatim: And if Elihu Root didn’t approve of something the government asked him to do, he could always go back and be the most sought after lawyer in the world. He had an identity to go back to and he didn’t need the government’s salary. And I think that ought to be more the test in corporate directorships. Is a man really fit to make tough calls who isn’t perfectly willing to leave the office at any time? My answer is no.
concept: Munger: a director is fit to make tough calls only if he has an identity to return to and is perfectly willing to leave at any time.
evolution_notes: Munger calls it 'the Elihu Root system': 'no man was fit to hold public office who wasn’t perfectly willing to leave it at any time'.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 20. If corporate directors need the money, they’re not independent

quote_verbatim: Well, I would say that the financial returns, achieved in a way that we want them to be achieved, are the determinant of whether we’ve made an intelligent commitment. Now, we don’t get rid of companies that don’t meet our original expectations. [...] We say that if a business is going to permanently lose money, we’ll get rid of it. If it has major labor problems over a period of time, we might get rid of it. But we are not going to engage in what we call gin-rummy type management where we pick up one card and discard another.
concept: Returns achieved in the right way judge a commitment, but an owned business that disappoints is not sold for a better use of the money; only permanent losses or lasting labor trouble justify selling.
evolution_notes: Restates M2000-052 and M2001-097. Buffett refers to 'a section in the back of our annual report on the economic principles' as the source of the policy.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 21. Why we keep companies despite disappointing results

quote_verbatim: And so we will not — if a business has been disappointing to us, but we like the people there and we’re not having — not because of labor problems — and we’re not going to have to put money in incessantly, we will stay with it when business school theory and management theory would say get rid of it and do something else. [...] And we don’t — we just — we want the shareholders to know that we have this mindset that may produce slightly suboptimal returns because of our attitude. But that’s the way we’re going to play it, and we tell people ahead of time that that’s the way we’re going to play it.
concept: A policy that may cost some return, such as keeping disappointing businesses with good people, is told to shareholders in advance.
evolution_notes: Continues the gin-rummy passage at line 927. The elision includes 'if we owned 100 percent of Berkshire we wouldn’t do it that way', i.e. the policy would not change for a sole owner.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 21. Why we keep companies despite disappointing results

quote_verbatim: But the people that have gone in with us have stuck with us in times like that. And our attitude is we’ll stick with them. So to the — I would say that how the people behave with us after we buy the business is an important part of how we feel about, you know, the whole relationship as well as the returns achieved.
concept: Beyond returns, judge an acquisition by how its people behave toward the owner after the purchase.
evolution_notes: Answers the question whether there are criteria 'beyond purely financial returns' (line 925).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 21. Why we keep companies despite disappointing results

quote_verbatim: We will own stocks of companies where we wouldn’t want to own the whole business. I mean, you know, you can — I’m not sure that the logic is perfect on that, but we would not have trouble owning stock in a cigarette company. We wouldn’t want to manufacture cigarettes, you know.

If we are delighting customers, eliminating unnecessary costs and improving our products and services, we gain strength. But if we treat customers with indifference or tolerate bloat, our businesses will wither. On a daily basis, the effects of our actions are imperceptible; cumulatively, though, their consequences are enormous. When our long-term competitive position improves as a result of these almost unnoticeable actions, we describe the phenomenon as "widening the moat."
concept: Widening the moat means the daily, individually invisible acts (delighting customers, cutting needless cost, improving products) that cumulatively strengthen a business's competitive position.

quote_verbatim: And doing that is essential if we are to have the kind of business we want a decade or two from now. We always, of course, hope to earn more money in the short-term. quote_verbatim: From a risk standpoint, it is far safer to have earnings from ten diverse and uncorrelated utility operations that cover interest charges by, say, a 2:1 ratio than it is to have far greater coverage provided by a single utility. A catastrophic event can render a single utility insolvent � witness what Katrina did to the local electric utility in New Orleans � no matter how conservative its debt policy.

Maybe so. But many of Berkshire's hundreds of thousands of investors have a large portion of their net worth in our stock (among them, it should be emphasized, a large number of our board and key managers) and a disaster for the company would be a disaster for them. Moreover, there are people who have been permanently injured to whom we owe insurance payments that stretch out for fifty years or more. To these and other constituencies we have promised total security, whatever comes
concept: Refuse the extra profit moderate leverage would bring when owners have much of their net worth in the company and claimants depend on it for decades.

quote_verbatim: Humans age at greatly varying rates � but sooner or later their talents and vigor decline. Some managers remain effective well into their 80s � Charlie is a wonder at 82 � and others noticeably fade in their 60s. When their abilities ebb, so usually do their powers of self-assessment. Someone else often needs to blow the whistle.
concept: A manager's self-assessment fails as his abilities fade, so the decision to replace an aging manager must come from someone else.

heading: ### 12. Don’t let your fear overcome your logic

quote_verbatim: Now, if there were suddenly a crisis now, there would be 500 firms that would be studying it intensely, each having capital that they could commit on a hair trigger. In our day, we would frequently be all alone. [...] Well, when you have a huge convulsion, which is like a big fire in this auditorium right now, you know, you get a lot of weird behavior. (Laughter) And if you — (Laughter) — and if you can — [...] — and if you can be wise when everybody else is going crazy, sure, there will still be opportunities. But that may give you long, dull stretches, if that’s your strategy.
concept: Munger: with many more competitors, bargains now come mainly in convulsions; being wise when others go crazy still finds them, at the price of long dull stretches between.
evolution_notes: A two-speaker exchange. The first elision crosses Buffett's 'But in 2002 —', Munger's 'We’d be the only buyer.' and Buffett's reply on 2002 (lines 855-859); the second crosses Buffett's 'Particularly at the head table. (Laughter)' (line 863); Munger resumes the same thought each time. Munger's competition point and Buffett's 2002 reply pull apart, and Munger reconciles them in the same answer ('there will still be opportunities'), so no tension row. Related M2001-042 (few competitors on small opportunities).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 12. Don’t let your fear overcome your logic

quote_verbatim: Three years ago — two — three years ago you could find a number of securities in Korea, population 50 million, advanced society, strong balance sheets, strong industry positions, at three or so times earnings. Now — [...] — five years earlier. And plenty of smart people in Korea in the investment business, plenty of smart people here scouring — the information was all available. You can go to the internet and get information about Korean companies that’s just as good as you get it from the SEC. And there they were, dozens of companies at very, very, very cheap prices.
concept: Freely available information and many smart competitors do not prevent gross mispricing; strong businesses can sit at three times earnings years after the convulsion that caused it.
evolution_notes: A two-speaker exchange; the elision crosses Munger's 'But that took a convulsion to create that, a real — a big convulsion.' and Buffett's 'Yeah. But the convulsion happened three or four years earlier —' and Munger's 'Yeah.' (lines 869-873). Munger closes: 'It did happen. But if I asked you to name 20 more like it, you would have great difficulty' (line 881); Buffett: 'if I have 20 more like it, I’m not going to name them. (Laughter)' (line 883). Buffett answers Munger's point in heading 13 (line 891).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 12. Don’t let your fear overcome your logic

quote_verbatim: And Charlie says you can’t find 20 of them, but you don’t have to find 20 of them; you only have to find one, really. You do not have to have tons of good ideas in this business, you just have a good idea that’s worth a ton, occasionally.
concept: An investor needs only an occasional single idea worth a great deal, not many good ideas.
evolution_notes: Answers Munger's 'name 20 more like it' under heading 12 (line 881). Restates M2003-068 (right on a very few decisions) and M2001-085 (good ideas are rare).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 13. If we were starting out again …

quote_verbatim: And in securities, we would be doing the same thing, which would probably mean smaller stocks — it would mean smaller stocks — because we would find things that could have an impact on a small portfolio that will have no impact on a portfolio the size of Berkshire. If we were trying to buy businesses, we’d have a tough time. We would have no reputation, so people would not be coming to us. [...] But the basic principles wouldn’t be different.
concept: A small investor applies the same principles to smaller stocks, where a find can matter to a small portfolio; buying whole businesses needs a reputation a beginner lacks.
evolution_notes: The elision skips Munger's start in real estate development, where 'brain power and energy could magnify small amounts of capital in a huge way' (line 893). Restates M1995-080, M1999-021, M1999-091 and M2001-042 on small sums.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 13. If we were starting out again …

quote_verbatim: You know, I think if I’d been running a partnership a couple of years ago with a small amount of money, I think I’d have probably been 100 percent in Korea. And, you know, I would be looking around for something that was very mispriced and which — and that I understood. And every now and then, that’s going to happen.
concept: With small capital, look for something very mispriced that one understands, and concentrate in it heavily when it appears.
evolution_notes: Munger qualifies: 'He wouldn’t have quite done that when he had the partnership, but he would have been way more concentrated than is conventional' (line 901). Related M1996-041 (money to the top of the ranked list).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 13. If we were starting out again …

quote_verbatim: The concept that you’re likely to find just one thing where it will make 20 percent per annum and you just sit back for the next 40 years, that tends to be dreamland. And in the real world, you have to find something that you can understand that’s the best you have available. And once you’ve found the best thing, then you measure everything against that because it’s your opportunity cost. That’s the way small sums of money should be invested. And the trick, of course, is getting enough expertise that your opportunity cost — meaning your default option, which is still pretty good — is very high.
