[...] Most people aren’t going to find thousands of things that are equally good; they’re going to find a few things where one or two of them are way better than anything else they know. And the right way to think about investing is to act thinking about your best opportunity cost.
concept: Munger: find the best understood opportunity, measure everything else against it as the opportunity cost, and build expertise so that default option is high; a few things will be far better than the rest.
evolution_notes: The elision crosses 'That’s why modern portfolio theory is so asinine. (Laughter)' (line 897) and Buffett's 'It really is, folks.' (line 899); Munger resumes the same thought. He adds 'that’s in the freshman course in economics everywhere in the basic textbook; it just hasn’t made its way into modern portfolio theory' (line 905). Restates M1997-055, M1997-147, M2001-081, M2001-086 and M2003-117.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 13. If we were starting out again …

quote_verbatim: Well, Ben Graham said long ago that you’re neither right nor wrong because people agree with you or disagree with you. In other words, being contrarian has no special virtue over being a trend follower. You’re right because your facts and reasoning are right. So all you do is you try to make sure that the facts you have are correct. [...] And then once you have the facts, you’ve got to think through what they mean. And you don’t take a public opinion survey.
concept: A judgment is right because its facts and reasoning are right, not because others agree or disagree; contrarianism earns nothing in itself.
evolution_notes: Graham's maxim spoken by Buffett; the source is Ben Graham. The elision skips 'And that’s usually pretty easy to do in this country. I mean, information is available on all kinds of things. Internet makes it even easier' (line 935). Related M1994-014 and M1999-093 (do not wait for agreement).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 15. “Things are really screwed up if you’re getting calls on Sunday”

quote_verbatim: You don’t pay attention to things that are unimportant. I mean, what you’re looking for is something — things that are important and knowable. If something’s important but unknowable, forget it. [...] In focusing on business and investment decisions, you try to think — you narrow it down to the things that are knowable and important, and then you decide whether you have information of sufficient value that — you know, compared to price and all that — that will cause you to act. What others are doing means nothing.
concept: Narrow a decision to what is important and knowable, then ask whether the information, against the price, is enough to act on; what others do means nothing.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the nuclear-weapon example and 'there are all kinds of things are that knowable but are unimportant' (line 935). Restates M1997-143, M1998-023 and M2000-043.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 15. “Things are really screwed up if you’re getting calls on Sunday”

quote_verbatim: It’s what Graham writes in Chapter 8 of “The Intelligent Investor,” that the market is there to serve you and not to instruct you. That’s of enormous importance. When people talk about momentum in stocks or charting or any kind of things like that, they’re saying that the market is instructing you. The market doesn’t instruct us; the market is there to serve us. If it does something silly, we get a chance to do something because it’s doing something silly. We do it. But it doesn’t tell us anything. It just tells us prices. And if the price is out of line where the facts and reasoning lead you, then you — then action is called for. And if it doesn’t, you forget it and go play bridge that day and the next day, see whether there’s something new.
concept: The market gives prices, not instructions; momentum and charting treat it as instructing; act only when the price departs from where one's facts and reasoning lead.
evolution_notes: Graham's Chapter 8 spoken by Buffett; the source is Ben Graham. Restates M1997-012 and M2003-046.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 15. “Things are really screwed up if you’re getting calls on Sunday”

quote_verbatim: Now, I will tell you that if — you can make a lot of money on Sunday. You may not get a chance very often, but any calls you get on Sunday you’re probably going to make money on. (Laughter) Things are really screwed up if you’re getting calls on Sunday. And all you have to do is make sure that you’re the callee and not the caller — (laughs) on Sunday.
concept: Distressed sellers calling out of hours signal the best opportunities; be the one called, never the one who must call.
evolution_notes: Said of the LTCM crisis in 1998: 'We were getting calls on Sunday from people that had portfolios that were in trouble' (line 939). Related M2002-105 (big mispricing needs a forced seller).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 15. “Things are really screwed up if you’re getting calls on Sunday”

quote_verbatim: You never get in a position, obviously, where the other fellow can call your tune. You have to be able to play out your hand under all circumstances. But if you can play out your hand, and you’ve got the right facts, and you reason by yourself, and you let the market serve you and not instruct you, you can’t miss.
concept: Never be in a position where another can force your hand; with staying power, right facts and independent reasoning, the market's prices serve you.
evolution_notes: Munger: 'Well, I would say some of you probably can miss. (Laughter)' (line 943). Related L2005-020 and L2005-021 (no significant debt; a single zero).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 15. “Things are really screwed up if you’re getting calls on Sunday”

quote_verbatim: We try to — and we take it very seriously — we try to put everything in that report that we would want to know if the positions were reversed. If I were sitting with all of my net worth in Berkshire and had been on a desert island for a year and I — and the manager was reporting to me about the business, we’d try to have that same information that I would want from him. [...] I mean, there’s — you can drown people in information that really doesn’t make much difference.
concept: Report to owners what you would want if positions were reversed, without drowning them in information that makes no difference.
evolution_notes: The elision skips 'And we would try to present it to you in a way that’s understandable. And we don’t leave out things that we think are important. We try not to put — I mean, there’s — it runs about 76, I think, or maybe even 80 pages this year' (line 957). Restates L1994-023, R1995-012, M1997-054, M1998-125, M2003-071 and M2004-012.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 16. How to read Berkshire’s annual report

quote_verbatim: Thinking about: what is there? What are these guys going to do with it? What are they trying to attempt? What are the odds they’re going to be successful in that attempt? What are they —? You know, what is it worth if they don’t succeed very well in deploying additional capital? What might be the case if they were successful in deploying excess capital and incremental capital? But I can tell you that, obviously, we think it’s very important. What counts is the kind of businesses we have, the kind of managers we have running those businesses, what those businesses are likely to earn over time — and we’ve expressed ourselves a little on that — And then what are the resources that are available to keep adding to that collection of businesses?
concept: Value a capital-allocating company by what it holds, what it will do with its excess capital and the odds of success, the value if it fails or succeeds in redeploying, and the businesses, managers and earning power it has.
evolution_notes: Said of Berkshire itself. Related L2005-002 (does the holding company bring anything to the party).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 16. How to read Berkshire’s annual report

quote_verbatim: Charlie and I, if we had to stick a number down on a piece of paper right now as to some pinpoint number — we wouldn’t do it because we know that’s impossible. But if we had to stick a number down, it would be a different number between the two of us. It would be a different number if I did it today from tomorrow, probably. But we’d be in the same ballpark, and we’d be looking at the same things.
concept: Intrinsic value cannot be a pinpoint number; two careful people, or one on different days, reach different figures in the same ballpark from the same factors.
evolution_notes: Lead-in: 'you don’t carry it out to four decimal places' (line 961). He then names the factors for Berkshire's value ten years out: annual earnings developed, 'the quality of those earnings, the possibilities going forward from that point of those businesses, and the liquid assets we have' (line 961). Restates M1996-009 and M1995-115; L2005-001 in this year's letter.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 16. How to read Berkshire’s annual report

quote_verbatim: Yeah. I generally try and approach a complex task, like the one you presented, by quickly disposing of what I call the no-brainer decisions and — meaning the easy ones. [...] But I would go at it in that sequence: taking the no-brainers first.
concept: Munger: attack a complex valuation by disposing of the easy, no-brainer parts first, leaving the hard parts for last.
evolution_notes: The elision skips his application to Berkshire: the operating businesses outside insurance are 'the easiest valuation process in Berkshire', with insurance and the redeployment of excess cash the harder parts (line 965). The printed 'all the operating insurance that don’t involve surplus cash' appears to mean operating businesses; left as printed.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 16. How to read Berkshire’s annual report

quote_verbatim: I mean, it’s a question of making judgments about whether you’re getting paid enough. And if we have a lot of money, you know, 30 years from now, it will mean that our judgments overall were decent. And if we have a big loss on one this year, it does not mean that our judgment’s wrong because it — it’s going to lead to peaks and valleys.
concept: Catastrophe underwriting is judging whether one is paid enough; the judgment is graded over decades, not by one year's big loss.
evolution_notes: Restates M2006-033 (one year proves nothing). Before it: 'we talk about what we think the probabilities are of $50 billion events and up, or $20 billion events and up' (line 975).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 17. Buffett’s key insurance question

quote_verbatim: I would feel that the earthquake experience of the last 100 or 200 years has more validity than the windstorm or the hurricane experience of the last hundred or 200 years. I don’t know that for sure, but I would bet real money that way, and we have.
concept: Judge which loss histories still describe the risk: a long record is valid where the generating conditions are stable and less so where they may be changing.
evolution_notes: He adds 'what will hurricane experience be like 10 years from now [...] You know, I don’t know. But I’ll keep thinking about it every day' (line 977). Restates M2006-030 (a hundred-year history book) and L2005-007.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 17. Buffett’s key insurance question

quote_verbatim: So I think we’d be out of our minds if we wrote weather-related insurance on the theory that global warming would have no effect at all. And the natural reaction is to raise your prices, as the risks go up. And whether you’ve raised them enough, and carefully controlled your risks enough, that’s the art of the business.
concept: Munger: when the risk may be rising, price for it and control exposure; judging whether prices and controls are enough is the art of insurance.
evolution_notes: Lead-in: 'the laws of thermodynamics are such that if the oceans get warmer — I think they are getting warmer — the weather is going to be — have more highenergy uproar in it' (line 979; 'highenergy' as printed). Related L2005-007 (mega-cat prices far higher, capped exposure) and M2005-028.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 17. Buffett’s key insurance question

quote_verbatim: Yeah. And you have this possibility that, you know, 1 percent changes or 2 percent changes in something can produce 100 percent of probabilistic changes in cost. It’s an explosive sort of equation that you’re dealing with. And, you know, but that’s the game we’re in, and we don’t have to play it ever. If we don’t like what we’re being offered — and we didn’t like what we were being offered a while back in many areas — somebody else can take our place in line. We’ll be happy to have them.
concept: Where small changes in an input can double the expected cost, the safeguard is freedom to decline: write nothing when the price offered is not liked, and let others take the place.
evolution_notes: Related M1998-035 (hold price, accept lower volume).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 17. Buffett’s key insurance question

quote_verbatim: It’s a very, very complex field with a lot of change, a lot of technological differences. And in terms of investments, I think the policy has generally been that it all goes into the too hard pile.
concept: Munger: a very complex field with much technological change goes, for investment, into the too-hard pile.
evolution_notes: Said of health care. Buffett: 'it is a very, very tough problem on which I have no particular insights' (line 1005). Restates M2006-013, M2005-099 and M2006-062 (the too-hard pile); related L1993-023 and M1999-075.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 18. Health care is in Berkshire’s “too hard” pile

quote_verbatim: And a complicated bankruptcy can offer opportunities for profit. Now, there’s so many people looking at bankruptcies currently, or potential bankruptcies, it’s a field that I would say does not have a lot of promise right now, but it has had promise in the past. [...] So anytime there’s something big, complicated, there’s certainly a good chance of mispricing. Now, lately the mispricing may be more on the high side than on the low side. But, over time, you’re going to find some — there will be some attractive things to do in bankruptcy situations. [...] It’s something to understand if you’re in the business of buying investments or businesses.
concept: Big, complicated situations such as bankruptcies are likely to be mispriced, though a field crowded with lookers loses its promise and its mispricing can run high as well as low.
evolution_notes: The first elision skips Fruit of the Loom bonds, Enron and the Penn Central (lines 1019-1021); the second skips being outbid at Burlington and Seitel (line 1021). Later: the Ospreys 'considerably more than tripled our money' (line 1023). Related M2001-078 (a distressed bond covered by the assets in bankruptcy).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 19. “A complicated bankruptcy can offer opportunities for profit”

quote_verbatim: And the courts in that case, I would say, abused the senior creditors horribly. And so you could have read a law book and reached one conclusion, and if you’d bought the wrong securities, why, you would have found out you’d guessed wrong.
concept: Munger: in a bankruptcy the legal priority in the book may not decide the outcome; courts weigh employees and communities, so seniority alone is not a safe basis for buying.
evolution_notes: Said of the Eastern Airlines bankruptcy, where 'a lot of employees [...] and communities [...] would’ve been affected' (line 1025). Buffett follows with the Penn Central judge who set the priorities aside: 'it wasn’t what the book said would be done [...] Judges can determine things in a very big way' (line 1027). Munger's earlier view of courts bidding for bankruptcy business (line 1017) is not rowed.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 19. “A complicated bankruptcy can offer opportunities for profit”

quote_verbatim: So I think the struggle between the manufacturers of brands and retailers will go on and on and on and become more intensified. So I would think, if I were on either side of that equation, I would want to be strengthening my hand.
concept: Where brand makers and concentrating retailers contend for the margin, each side should strengthen its bargaining hand; judge a brand's position against the retailer's growing power.
evolution_notes: Lead-in: 'the big retailers are becoming — and more so all the time — brands of their own [...] and there’s more and more concentration going on' (line 1041). He judges P&G and Gillette 'better as a combined enterprise' for that reason. On P&G's pharmaceutical business: 'I don’t know a thing about that' and Munger 'That makes two of us. (Laughter)' (lines 1047-1049).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 20. Buffett endorses Procter & Gamble-Gillette merger

quote_verbatim: And they almost — well, they invariably, I would say — auction the business. They seek what they call a strategic buyer. A strategic buyer is some guy that pays too much. (Laughter) Because — you know, and he wants to justify it, so he says it’s strategic. I mean, I have never understood being a strategic buyer.
concept: A 'strategic' purchase is the label a buyer gives a price too high to justify on the business's own figures.
evolution_notes: Said of financial groups that buy a business and resell it 'fairly quickly' (line 1059). He adds 'I hang up faster than Charlie would' when called as 'the logical strategic buyer'. Related L1995-004 and M1998-015 (no strategic plan).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 21. “A strategic buyer is some guy that pays too much”

quote_verbatim: But the idea that we’re going to find a business to buy from some guy who, from the moment he bought it a few years ago, has been thinking, “How do I get out of this thing?” You know, “What do I do to make it earn — have those figures for a couple years look a certain way so that I can get the maximum amount in a couple years?” You know, that — we’re just not going to make any attractive buys there. We won’t trust the figures. You know, we — it just — it’s — what we like is a business that — where the guy before was running with the idea of running it a hundred years, and taking care of the business in every way possible and was not contemplating sale, but, for one reason or another, finally needs to monetize the company. We won’t — we will not get any sensible buys, really, from the resellers.
concept: A seller who bought planning to exit has shaped the figures for the sale and they cannot be trusted; buy from owners who ran the business to last and sell only from need.
evolution_notes: Lead-in: 'I’m not talking to the specifics of this one at all because I really don’t know on Oriental Trading' (line 1061). Restates L2000-008, M2000-099 and M2006-003 on sellers; related L2005-006 (we buy to keep).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 21. “A strategic buyer is some guy that pays too much”

quote_verbatim: Some of these things, literally, you know, Fund A is selling to Fund B to Fund C. I mean, I’ve seen some that have changed hands three or four times. They’re just marking them up, and everybody’s getting two — they’re getting 20 percent of the profit so they mark it up. And probably Fund C or Fund D may be owned by the same pension funds that own Fund A, except that everybody’s just taking a big 20 percent slice out of it every time they move it from one place to another. We’re not buyers of anything the financial buyers have been in in recent — you know, and currently own.
concept: Businesses passed between funds are marked up for the managers' profit share at each sale, often between the same ultimate owners; do not buy from financial buyers.
evolution_notes: Munger: in the 1930s 'you could borrow more against the real estate than you could sell it for. And I think that’s happened in some of these private equity deals [...] This is not our field. (Laughter)' (line 1065), a remark. Related L2005-016 to L2005-018 (owners earn what businesses earn, less frictions).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 21. “A strategic buyer is some guy that pays too much”

quote_verbatim: Well, gambling, I think — I think the distinction that usually is made is that gambling involves creating risks that don’t need to be created. [...] So there’s a transfer of — in the case of cat coverage — large existing risks as opposed to the creation of a risk that is not required. I mean, you can watch a football game without betting on it. But you can’t live in a house, you know, on a Florida coast without having a risk that your entire investment disappears.
concept: Gambling creates a risk that need not exist; insurance transfers a large risk that already exists, and the question is who bears it.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the roulette wheel and the coastal home 'the risk is there [...] and then the question is who bears it' (line 1097). He ends: 'I hope you’re right that the house wins in both cases. (Laughter)'.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 23. Key distinction between insurance and gambling

quote_verbatim: The whole concept of house advantage is a very interesting one in modern commerce. A lot of the investment management operations, which were not ordinarily spoken of in the past in croupier terms — but the terms of a lot of private equity investment now — I think the proprietors of the partnerships are taking a house edge that looks a lot like the rake of the croupier in Monte Carlo, except it’s bigger. (Laughter)
concept: Munger: read an investment manager's fee terms as a house edge; in much private equity the proprietors' take exceeds a casino croupier's rake.
evolution_notes: Buffett: 'Is there anyone we’ve forgotten to insult? (Laughter)' (line 1101). Restates M2006-045 (2 and 20 cannot work) and L2005-017 (heads-tails fees).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 23. Key distinction between insurance and gambling

quote_verbatim: There’s nothing evil, per se, about — in my view — about selling things short. I would say that it’s a very, very tough way to make a living. It’s not only often painful financially, it’s very painful emotionally because it — a stock that you sell short — a stock that you buy at 20 can go down 20 points, and a stock that you sell short at 20 can go up an infinite amount.
concept: Short selling is not wrong but is a very tough living: the loss on a long is capped at the price, the loss on a short is unlimited, and the strain is emotional as well as financial.
evolution_notes: Before it, of Berkshire: 'The more shorts, the better, because they have to buy the stock later on' (line 1109). Restates M2001-091, M2001-093 and M2002-090.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 24. Selling short isn’t unethical, but it’s tough to make money

quote_verbatim: Short sellers — the situations in which there have been huge short interests very often — very often have been later revealed to be frauds or semi-frauds.
concept: A very large short interest has often marked a company later shown to be a fraud or semi-fraud.
evolution_notes: Pulls against M1999-089 ('Trading activity in the stock, including short interest, is irrelevant'); listed under the note's Tensions seen. Followed by the hundred short ideas at lines 1113-1115. | ERRATUM 2026-10-04: The pull against M1999-089 named above does not hold on reading that row: M1999-089 says shorting of Berkshire's own stock does not hurt it ('What counts is the intrinsic value of Berkshire'), not that short interest carries no information about another company. No tension is listed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 24. Selling short isn’t unethical, but it’s tough to make money

quote_verbatim: But the — the batting average — I mean, I’ve — over the years, I’ve probably had a hundred ideas of things that should be shorted, and I would say that almost every one of them have turned out to be correct. And I’ll bet if I’d tried to do it and make money out of it, I probably would have lost money, I would have had no fun, and the opportunity cost, as Charlie said, would have been enormous. Because if somebody’s running something that’s semi-fraudulent, they’re probably pretty good at it and they’re working full time at it and they’ve succeeded for a while and they may keep succeeding. [...] I would never put any money with a short fund, but not because I would think it would be ethically wrong. I just think they’re unlikely to make money.
concept: Being right that a company is a fraud does not make shorting it pay: the promoter works full time and may keep succeeding, and the opportunity cost is large; do not invest in short funds.
evolution_notes: The elision skips 'if you go in at X and it goes to 5X [...] It’s a very tough psychological game to play. Few people may be well-suited for it' (line 1113). Restates M1996-066, M2001-095 and M2002-082.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 24. Selling short isn’t unethical, but it’s tough to make money

quote_verbatim: Well, I think you’re absolutely right there — in the sense that it’s — that would be one of the most irritating experiences in the world, to figure out something is crooked and foolish and so forth and then short it at X and have it go to 3X. Now you’re watching all these happy crooks splashing around in your money while you’re meeting margin calls. (Laughter) Why would you want to go in hailing distance of an experience like that?
concept: Munger: stay well away from shorting even what is plainly crooked, since the stock can triple while you meet margin calls.
evolution_notes: Agrees with Buffett's hundred short ideas at lines 1113-1115. Restates M2002-081.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 24. Selling short isn’t unethical, but it’s tough to make money

quote_verbatim: Sitting in those seats, we both grew skeptical about the ability of big entities of any type to function well. Size seems to make many organizations slow-thinking, resistant to change and smug.
concept: Be skeptical that a big organization of any type functions well; size tends to make it slow-thinking, resistant to change and smug.
evolution_notes: Followed by Churchill, "We shape our buildings, and afterwards our buildings shape us", and the fact that of the ten largest non-oil companies by market capitalization in 1965 only one made the 2006 list (lines 163-166). Then the balance: "In fairness, we've seen plenty of successes as well" (line 173). New in the letters read so far.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: BERKSHIRE HATHAWAY INC.

quote_verbatim: Charlie and I measure Berkshire's progress and evaluate its intrinsic value in a number of ways. No single criterion is effective in doing these jobs, and even an avalanche of statistics will not capture some factors that are important. [...] There are two statistics, however, that are of real importance. The first is the amount of investments (including cash and cash-equivalents) that we own on a per-share basis. [...] Using our funds for these purchases has both slowed our growth in investments and accelerated our gains in pre-tax earnings from non-insurance businesses, the second yardstick we use.
concept: No single measure captures a business's value and some important factors cannot be counted; for Berkshire the two numbers that matter are investments per share and pre-tax non-insurance earnings per share.
evolution_notes: The uncountable factor named is succession: "it's essential that we have managers much younger than I available to succeed me [...] but I can't prove it to you with numbers" (lines 191-193). The second elision skips the first table and the shift from securities to operating businesses (lines 199-216). Related to the intrinsic-value rows L1994-007 and R1996-019; the two-statistic yardstick is new in the letters read so far.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Yardsticks

quote_verbatim: It's a business without magic except for that imparted by the people who run it. But Eitan, Jacob and their associates are true managerial magicians who constantly develop tools that make their customers' machines more productive. The result: ISCAR makes money because it enables its customers to make more money. There is no better recipe for continued success.
concept: A business that makes money by making its customers more money has the best recipe for lasting success.
evolution_notes: Earlier in the passage, Eitan Wertheimer's letter "made the quality of the company and the character of its management leap off the page" (lines 257-258). New in the letters read so far.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Acquisitions

quote_verbatim: Charlie and I love it when we can acquire businesses that can be placed under managers, such as John Holland at Fruit, who have already shown their stuff at Berkshire. [...] In effect, we leverage the managerial talent already with us by these tuck-in deals. We will make many more.
concept: Buy businesses that can be put under managers already proven inside the group; tuck-in deals leverage managerial talent already owned.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the MiTek example: 14 acquisitions since 2001, with results "far in excess of what he had predicted" (lines 314-316). Then: "We continue, however, to need "elephants"" (line 320). New in the letters read so far.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Acquisitions

quote_verbatim: We remain prepared to lose $6 billion in a single event, if we have been paid appropriately for assuming that risk. We are not willing, though, to take on even very small exposures at prices that don't reflect our evaluation of loss probabilities. Appropriate prices don't guarantee profits in any given year, but inappropriate prices most certainly guarantee eventual losses. Rates have recently fallen because a flood of capital has entered the super-cat field. We have therefore sharply reduced our wind exposures. Our behavior here parallels that which we employ in financial markets: Be fearful when others are greedy, and be greedy when others are fearful.
concept: Take any size of risk that is properly paid for and no risk, however small, that is not; right prices do not guarantee a year's profit but wrong prices guarantee eventual losses, so cut exposure when capital floods in and prices fall.
evolution_notes: Lead-in: "Neither Ajit Jain, who manages our super-cat operation, nor I know what lies ahead. We do know that it would be a huge mistake to bet that evolving atmospheric changes are benign in their implications for insurers" (lines 421-423). The willingness to lose a large sum if paid restates L2001-013; the fearful/greedy line restates L2004-001, there advice to investors who time the market, here applied to underwriting. The appropriate-versus-inappropriate prices sentence is new in the letters read so far.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Insurance

quote_verbatim: When an industry's underlying economics are crumbling, talented management may slow the rate of decline. Eventually, though, eroding fundamentals will overwhelm managerial brilliance. (As a wise friend told me long ago, "If you want to get a reputation as a good businessman, be sure to get into a good business.")
concept: Talented management can slow but not stop an industry whose economics are eroding; the business, not the manager, decides the outcome.
evolution_notes: Lead-in: "Not all of our businesses are destined to increase profits" (line 617). Applied to the newspaper industry and the Buffalo News (lines 620-622). The maxim is an unnamed friend's, spoken by Buffett. Meeting rows on good businesses over good managers, e.g. M1996-023 and M2003-115, are related; new in the letters read so far.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Manufacturing, Service and Retailing Operations

quote_verbatim: Advertisers preferred the paper with the most circulation, and readers tended to want the paper with the most ads and news pages. This circularity led to a law of the newspaper jungle: Survival of the Fattest. Thus, when two or more papers existed in a major city (which was almost universally the case a century ago), the one that pulled ahead usually emerged as the stand-alone winner. After competition disappeared, the paper's pricing power in both advertising and circulation was unleashed.
concept: Where advertisers and readers each want the paper the other wants, the leader becomes the sole survivor, and with competition gone its pricing power is unleashed: how a newspaper franchise formed.
evolution_notes: Before it: newspapers "were the primary source of information" and their ads "the easiest way to find job opportunities" (lines 629-632); after it: "For owners this was economic heaven" (line 645). The meeting row M2006-064 speaks of the "monopoly newspaper"; the circularity mechanism is new in the letters read so far.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Manufacturing, Service and Retailing Operations

quote_verbatim: Newspaper properties, moreover, continued to sell as if they were indestructible slot machines. In fact, many intelligent newspaper executives who regularly chronicled and analyzed important worldwide events were either blind or indifferent to what was going on under their noses. [...] Simply put, if cable and satellite broadcasting, as well as the internet, had come along first, newspapers as we know them probably would never have existed.
concept: Intelligent insiders can miss the erosion of their own franchise; ask whether the business would exist at all if its substitutes had come first.
evolution_notes: The mistake is the newspaper industry's (executives and buyers), not Buffett's; he cites his own 1991 warning that media businesses "will prove considerably less marvelous than I, the industry, or lenders thought" (lines 649-651). Restates in a letter the meeting row M2006-064 (owners resisting "seeing what's right in front of them").
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Manufacturing, Service and Retailing Operations

quote_verbatim: However, the economic potential of a newspaper internet site � given the many alternative sources of information and entertainment that are free and only a click away � is at best a small fraction of that existing in the past for a print newspaper facing no competition. [...] Aspiring press lords should be careful, however: There's no rule that says a newspaper's revenues can't fall below its expenses and that losses can't mushroom. Fixed costs are high in the newspaper business, and that's bad news when unit volume heads south.
concept: A business facing free substitutes a click away has a fraction of a protected one's potential, and high fixed costs turn falling volume into mushrooming losses.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the non-economic appeal of owning a paper, "prominence" and "power and influence" (lines 672-678). After it: "Unless we face an irreversible cash drain, we will stick with the News" (line 685), which restates R1995-011. New in the letters read so far.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Manufacturing, Service and Retailing Operations

quote_verbatim: The "optional" contracts and "teaser" rates that have been popular have allowed borrowers to make payments in the early years of their mortgages that fall far short of covering normal interest costs. Naturally, there are few defaults when virtually nothing is required of a borrower. As a cynic has said, "A rolling loan gathers no loss." But payments not made add to principal, and borrowers who can't afford normal monthly payments early on are hit later with above-normal monthly obligations.
concept: A low early default rate means nothing when the borrower is asked to pay almost nothing; unpaid interest builds into larger later obligations.
evolution_notes: Followed by the Scarlett O'Hara line and "For many home owners, "tomorrow" has now arrived" (lines 744-745). The cynic's line is a third party's maxim spoken by Buffett. Related to L2003-007 and the meeting rows M2006-024 and M2006-025 on dumb lending and accrued unpaid interest.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Regulated Utility Business

quote_verbatim: The answer is that derivatives, just like stocks and bonds, are sometimes wildly mispriced. For many years, accordingly, we have selectively written derivative contracts � few in number but sometimes for large dollar amounts. [...] I manage them personally, and they are free of counterparty credit risk.
concept: Any instrument, derivatives included, can be wildly mispriced; write a few, large, selected contracts that carry no counterparty credit risk and keep them under the principal's own control.
evolution_notes: The question it answers: "Why, you may wonder, are we fooling around with such potentially toxic material?" (line 979), after "heard me talk of the systemic problems that could result from the enormous growth in the use of derivatives" (lines 978-979). Buffett reconciles the two in the same passage, so no tension row; compare L2002-011, L2002-018 and L2002-019. The elision skips "We currently have 62 contracts outstanding" (line 983).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Investments

quote_verbatim: It's not hard, of course, to find smart people, among them individuals who have impressive investment records. But there is far more to successful long-term investing than brains and performance that has recently been good. Over time, markets will do extraordinary, even bizarre, things. A single, big mistake could wipe out a long string of successes. We therefore need someone genetically programmed to recognize and avoid serious risks, including those never before encountered. Certain perils that lurk in investment strategies cannot be spotted by use of the models commonly employed today by financial institutions.
concept: Judge an investment manager not by brains or a recent record but by an inborn ability to recognize and avoid serious risks, including unprecedented ones that standard models cannot detect.
evolution_notes: Context: the plan to hire a younger chief investment officer (lines 1003-1005). "A single, big mistake could wipe out a long string of successes" restates L2005-021 ("multiplied by a single zero"); distrust of models restates L1996-012. The manager test is new in the letters read so far.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Investments

quote_verbatim: Temperament is also important. Independent thinking, emotional stability, and a keen understanding of both human and institutional behavior is vital to long-term investment success. I've seen a lot of very smart people who have lacked these virtues.
concept: Long-term investing needs temperament as well as intelligence: independent thinking, emotional stability and an understanding of human and institutional behavior.
evolution_notes: Then the retention problem: "we can retain our choice, even though he or she could leave and make much more money elsewhere" (lines 1022-1023), and Lou Simpson, who stayed although "If money alone had been the object" he would have left (lines 1030-1032). Temperament is a theme of meeting rows such as M2000-096 and M2004-034; new in the letters read so far.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Investments

quote_verbatim: Over the years I've been queried many times about potential directors and have yet to hear anyone ask, "Does he think like an intelligent owner?" The questions I instead get would sound ridiculous to someone seeking candidates for, say, a football team, or an arbitration panel or a military command. In those cases, the selectors would look for people who had the specific talents and attitudes that were required for a specialized job. At Berkshire, we are in the specialized activity of running a business well, and therefore we seek business judgment.
concept: Choose a director by the one question that matters, whether the person thinks like an intelligent owner, and seek business judgment as one would seek the specific talent for any specialized job.
evolution_notes: Before it, the four criteria "owner-oriented, business-savvy, interested and truly independent" and the fee-dependent "independent" director (lines 1056-1064), which restate L1993-028, L2002-034 and L2003-012 and are not rowed separately; the passage also sets the question against selecting for a category, "It sometimes sounds as if the mission is to stock Noah's ark" (lines 1067-1069). The meeting row M1996-028 uses "intelligent owner"; the question as a director test is new in the letters read so far.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Some Changes on Berkshire's Board

quote_verbatim: Corporate bigwigs often complain about government spending, criticizing bureaucrats who they say spend taxpayers' money differently from how they would if it were their own. But sometimes the financial behavior of executives will also vary based on whose wallet is getting depleted.
concept: Executives spend differently when the money is not their own; watch whose wallet is being depleted.
evolution_notes: Illustrated by the Salomon barber: when free haircuts ended, one top executive went from weekly to once every three weeks (lines 1105-1108). Before it, Berkshire's headquarters payroll and "We're careful when spending your money" (line 1100). Related to L2002-031 (spend as if the money were theirs); the observation about executives is new in the letters read so far.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: This and That

quote_verbatim: The existence of foundation ownership will in no way influence our board's decisions about dividends, repurchases, or the issuance of shares. We will follow exactly the same rule that has guided us in the past: What action will be likely to deliver the best result for shareholders over time?
concept: Decide dividends, repurchases and share issuance by one question: what will likely give shareholders the best result over time, regardless of who the holders are.
evolution_notes: Before it, the aim that Berkshire sell "at neither a large discount nor large premium to intrinsic value" and that "incoming shareholders don't overpay" (lines 1216-1220), which restates principle 14 (R1996-017). The single-question form is new in the letters read so far.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: This and That

quote_verbatim: Following a strategy that involved no real risk � defined as permanent loss of capital � Walter produced results over his 47 partnership years that dramatically surpassed those of the S&P 500.
concept: Real risk is permanent loss of capital.
evolution_notes: Of Walter Schloss, who "took not a dime unless his investors made money" (line 1264) and selected securities "by certain simple statistical methods Walter learned while working for Ben Graham" (lines 1272-1273); Edwin Schloss: "We try to buy stocks cheap" (line 1274). Compare the risk definitions L1993-016 and L1993-020; the four-word definition is new in the letters read so far.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: This and That

quote_verbatim: It's particularly noteworthy that he built this record by investing in about 1,000 securities, mostly of a lackluster type. A few big winners did not account for his success. It's safe to say that had millions of investment managers made trades by a) drawing stock names from a hat; b) purchasing these stocks in comparable amounts when Walter made a purchase; and then c) selling when Walter sold his pick, the luckiest of them would not have come close to equaling his record. There is simply no possibility that what Walter achieved over 47 years was due to chance.
concept: Test whether a record is skill or luck: a long record built from many ordinary holdings, not a few big winners, beats what the luckiest of millions of random pickers would achieve.
evolution_notes: Follows the row on lines 1277-1278 (risk defined as permanent loss of capital). New in the letters read so far.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: This and That

quote_verbatim: And what did members of the academic community do when they were exposed to this new and important evidence? Unfortunately, they reacted in all-too-human fashion: Rather than opening their minds, they closed their eyes. [...] Tens of thousands of students were therefore sent out into life believing that on every day the price of every stock was "right" (or, more accurately, not demonstrably wrong) and that attempts to evaluate businesses � that is, stocks � were useless. Walter meanwhile went on overperforming, his job made easier by the misguided instructions that had been given to those young minds.
concept: The academics' error: faced with evidence against efficient market theory they closed their eyes, taught that evaluating businesses was useless, and so made the job easier for those who do evaluate them.
evolution_notes: The mistake is the business schools', not Buffett's. The elision skips the Galileo line (lines 1297-1300). After it: "if you are in the shipping business, it's helpful to have all of your potential competitors be taught that the earth is flat" (lines 1305-1306). Related to L1996-036 and the meeting rows on efficient markets (M1995-082, M1998-004).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: This and That

quote_verbatim: We regularly compare the gain in Berkshire's per-share book value to the performance of the S&P 500. Over time, we hope to outpace this yardstick. Otherwise, why do our investors need us?
concept: A manager of other people's money must over time beat what they could get from the index, or they do not need him.
evolution_notes: Principle 15, first printed in this reprint (the FY2005 reprint had "An Added Principle", principle 14 alone). The principle goes on to say the comparison is "less meaningful on a year-to-year basis" because equities are a smaller share of net worth and are counted after tax, so Berkshire expects "to outperform the S&P in lackluster years for the stock market and underperform when the market has a strong year" (lines 5603-5608). Restates the letter rows L1997-002 ("that is the yardstick against which you should measure us") and L2000-001; the question form is new.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: TWO ADDED PRINCIPLES

quote_verbatim: Now, what we really hope over time is more or less to break even on the underwriting of insurance. So when you see a significant profit like last year or underwriting profit this year, just look at that as kind of the good side of what will later be an offset to it in a way of an underwriting loss. But if we break even in insurance on underwriting, we do very, very well because we generate lots of float and we earn money on that float and our float is at an all-time high.
concept: Read an insurer's good underwriting year as the offset to later bad ones; breaking even on underwriting is enough when the float is large and earns money.
evolution_notes: Lead-in: favorable experience "has caused people to lower prices in some areas quite dramatically" and results lag prices (line 51); after it: "about half the years we’ve made money underwriting and half we haven’t" (line 55). Restates the float-cost rows L1993-009, L1997-011 and the letter's "over time" (FY2006 letter lines 375-377, not rowed).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 4. Q1 earnings are “good”

quote_verbatim: Because if you’re running a large private equity fund and you lock up $20 billion for five or longer years and you buy businesses which are not priced daily, as a practical matter, the plug will not — even if you do a poor job, it’s going to take many years before the score is put up on the score board, and it takes many years, in most cases, for people to get out of the private equity fund even if they wished to earlier. [...] And the investors can’t leave and the scorecard is lacking for a long time.
concept: Locked-up money in assets with no daily price does not burst like a market bubble; a poor job goes unscored for years and investors cannot leave.
evolution_notes: Answers whether private equity is a bubble about to burst. What would slow it is a wider spread of junk over high-grade yields, which "won’t cause the investors to get their money back" (lines 75-77). Related to M2006-027 (speculative holdings with no daily price).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 5. Buffett sees no private equity “bubble” about to burst

quote_verbatim: There’s one other aspect, of course, that — of this frenzied activity, you might say, in private equity is that if you have a $20 billion fund and you’re getting a 2 percent fee on it or $400 million a year [...] you can’t start another fund with a straight face until you get that money pretty well invested. It’s very hard to go back to your investors and say, well, I’ve got 18 billion uninvested and I’d like you to give me money for another fund. So there’s a great compulsion to invest very quickly because it’s the way to get another fund and another bunch of fees coming in.
concept: A manager paid on assets must invest fast to raise the next fund, so the fee structure drives deals regardless of price.
evolution_notes: Related to the 2-and-20 rows M2006-045 and M2006-096; the compulsion to deploy in order to raise the next fund is new in this read.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 5. Buffett sees no private equity “bubble” about to burst

quote_verbatim: And those are not competitors for businesses that Charlie and I are going to be particularly effective in competing with. I mean, they — we are going to own anything we buy forever. The math has to make sense to us. We’re not given to optimistic assumptions, and we don’t get paid based on activity.
concept: Buy to own forever, only where the arithmetic works without optimistic assumptions, and with no pay tied to activity.
evolution_notes: Munger closes the answer: "It can continue to go on a long time after you’re in a state of total revulsion" (line 81), an observation not rowed. Restates the letter row L2005-006 ("We buy to keep").
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 5. Buffett sees no private equity “bubble” about to burst

quote_verbatim: It really wouldn’t make any difference to us if Coca-Cola was based in Amsterdam or Munich or Atlanta as long as they had the business they had. [...] We have no bias against buying either marketable securities or entire businesses outside the United States.
concept: Where a company is based does not matter, only the business it has; no bias against buying abroad.
evolution_notes: Buffett faults himself for not doing "the selling job" abroad (line 95). Later, the 3 percent disclosure thresholds in the UK and Germany are "a real minus to us" (line 99), a Berkshire practice not rowed. Related to M2006-021 (buying abroad cheaper than at home).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 6. I didn’t do enough to “sell” Berkshire internationally

quote_verbatim: There are more problems with having the wrong manager than with having the wrong compensation system. I mean, it is enormously important who runs — you name the company — Proctor & Gamble, Coca-Cola, American Express — and any compensation sins are generally of minor importance compared to the sin of having somebody that’s mediocre running a huge company.
concept: Who runs a company matters far more than how he is paid; a mediocre manager is a worse sin than a bad pay plan.
evolution_notes: Restates the letter row L2005-012 ("It's hard to overemphasize the importance of who is CEO of a company").
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 7. CEO compensation is a “joke”

quote_verbatim: That said, Charlie and I think that compensation has — there’s a natural tendency — because of ratcheting, because of the publicity of what other people get, and because of the lack of intensity in the bargaining process. [...] It just doesn’t happen because the CEO cares enormously how he or she is paid, and to the comp committee — and they’re doing, perhaps, a little better job now — but it’s basically play money.
concept: Pay ratchets because the CEO bargains hard for his own money while the committee bargains with play money; look for parity of intensity on the two sides.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the labor-contract comparison (line 115). Later in the answer: "there is not a parity of intensity in the bargaining process. One guy cares enormously and the others don’t" and "what really drives a lot of this ratcheting impact is envy" (line 117). Restates L2005-015 and L2002-031.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 7. CEO compensation is a “joke”

quote_verbatim: The comp committee sits down. The human relations person comes in. The human relations person knows what the CEO thinks of them is going to determine their future, and the human relations department recommends some comp consultant. The comp consultant knows that his recommendation to other firms is dependent on what these people say about him. So under those circumstances, you know, can you imagine that it’s anything like a fair fight? It’s a joke.
concept: Trace the incentives of everyone in the pay process: each adviser depends on the CEO's goodwill, so the process cannot be a fair fight.
evolution_notes: Before it, Munger's point relayed by Buffett that envy is the dumbest of the seven deadly sins and "it does produce this ratcheting effect in pay" (line 119). Munger follows with the compensation-consultant joke (line 123). Related to L2005-017 (consultant layers).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 7. CEO compensation is a “joke”

quote_verbatim: I mean, comp is not rocket science. I mean, we have very simple systems that compensate those people whose pictures you saw during the movie. They’re terrific people. We compensate them based on things that are under their control and that we care about. And we don’t make it complicated, and we don’t pay them for things that are happening that they have nothing to do with. [...] If they have low finding costs, which is under their control, and which is important, I would pay like crazy for that, because a person who finds oil and develops reserves at $6 a barrel is worth a lot more than somebody that finds and develops them at $10 a barrel, assuming they’re similar quality reserves.
concept: Pay simply, on what the person controls and the owner cares about, never on what the market does to the product's price.
evolution_notes: Buffett returns to the previous heading's compensation question here. Restates M2006-004 (pay for controllables only, with copper and oil) and the letter rows L1997-022 and FY2006 letter lines 1147-1154 (not rowed).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 8. Corporate jets can be good

quote_verbatim: If the trappings of power are greatly abused, I think you would find a correlation that some of those companies would be disappointing to investors. And, you know, man has known for a long time that getting too enchanted with the trappings of power is counterproductive. [...] So I think all these things can be abused, and I think the best way to tackle a subject is to provide examples of contrary behavior.
concept: Management enchanted with the trappings of power tends to disappoint investors; the remedy is to set examples of the contrary.
evolution_notes: The elision skips Marcus Aurelius, "totally against the trappings of power even though he had them all". Buffett before it: corporate jets are "a valuable business tool. It can be misused like anything else" (line 137) and "you can abuse any system" (line 139).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 8. Corporate jets can be good

quote_verbatim: Well, we do benefit when others suffer. That doesn’t mean we enjoy their suffering, but times of chaos in financial markets, the situation that existed in junk bonds in 2002, the situation that existed in equities, you know, back in 1974. [...] And that would result in a huge widening of credit spreads, cheaper equity prices, all kinds of things that actually are helpful to Berkshire because we usually have at least some money around to do something at times like that. There will be periods like that.
concept: Keep money on hand, because times of financial chaos, when spreads widen and equities cheapen, are when the prepared buyer benefits.
evolution_notes: The elision skips a forecast that the authorities will not step on the brakes and that an exogenous shock is "much more prone to feed on itself in markets than in most periods in the past". Related to M2006-028 (excess cash beats dumb deals) and L2006-005 (be greedy when others are fearful).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 9. “Extraordinary” things can happen when people panic

quote_verbatim: And that’s rather an interesting example, because that was not a hundred years ago. It was less than ten years ago. You had all kinds of people with high IQs in Wall Street. You had all kinds of people with cash available. And you had some really extraordinary things happen in credit markets simply because people panicked and they felt other people were going to panic. And you get these second- and thirddegree type reactions in markets. We will see that sort of thing again.
concept: High intelligence and ample cash do not stop panics that feed on the fear of others' panic; expect such second- and third-degree reactions again.
evolution_notes: The example is the 1998 seizure when Long-Term Capital Management got into trouble, "people panicked about even the most — even the safest of instruments" (line 163). Followed by Twain's "history doesn’t repeat itself but it rhymes" (line 165). "thirddegree" is as printed. Related to the letter row L2006-012 ("markets will do extraordinary, even bizarre, things").
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 9. “Extraordinary” things can happen when people panic

quote_verbatim: But if you had said to us, in a world of 4 3/4 percent long-term governments, will one major bank after another be earning more than 20 percent on tangible equity, dealing in what is basically a commodity — money — we would have said that that condition just wouldn’t persist. Now, part of that is because the banks are geared up more. [...] And by gearing up more, it does improve the return on equity. But you still would think that would be self-neutralizing.
concept: High returns on equity in a commodity business usually come from leverage and should be competed away; when they persist, ask why.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the arithmetic, 1 1/2 percent on assets at 15 times equity gives 22 1/2 percent. He goes on: "You’d think that after one guy did it, another guy would do it [...] but it hasn’t happened" (line 195). Compare M2003-115, where Buffett also found banks competing "without great competitive advantage" yet earning high returns on tangible capital.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 11. Corporate profits can’t stay at record highs

quote_verbatim: Some of this has come from consumer credit, which I think has been pushed to extremes that we’ve never before seen in the history of this country. Some other countries that pushed consumer credit very hard had enormous collapses. Korea had one, for instance, that caused chaos for, what, two or three years? Maybe longer. So I don’t think this is a time to just swing for the fences.
concept: When profits rest on credit pushed to unprecedented extremes, which elsewhere ended in collapse, it is not the time to swing for the fences.
evolution_notes: Before it, Munger: much of the profit is in the financial sector, which "has, I think, no precedent" (line 191).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 11. Corporate profits can’t stay at record highs

quote_verbatim: I mention in the annual report, in looking for an investment manager to succeed me, that we care enormously about finding somebody who’s not cognizant of everything risky that’s already happened, but that also can envision things that have not yet been experienced. That’s our job in the insurance business, and it’s our job in the investment business. And there are a lot of people that just don’t seem to — they’re not — they’re very smart, but they just — they’re just not wired to think about troubles that they haven’t actually witnessed before.
concept: In insurance and investing the job is to envision troubles not yet experienced; many very smart people are not wired to do it.
evolution_notes: "not cognizant" is as printed; the sense is "not only cognizant". Restates the same year's letter, L2006-012 ("recognize and avoid serious risks, including those never before encountered"). Before it, Korea 1997-98 produced "some of the most ridiculously low stock prices that I’ve ever seen" (line 199).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 11. Corporate profits can’t stay at record highs

quote_verbatim: And the one sure buyer of your stock eventually is somebody who shorted it. [...] I mean, there are more people bowling stocks for phony reasons than there are burying stocks for phony reasons. [...] It’s very easy to spot phony stocks and promoted stocks, but it’s very hard to tell when that will turn around. And somebody that’s promoted a stock to five times what it’s worth, may very well promote it to ten times what it’s worth, and if you’re short, that can get very painful.
concept: Spotting an overvalued promoted stock is easy but timing its fall is not, so shorting is a hard living; and a short seller is a sure future buyer.
evolution_notes: "bowling" is as printed (likely "boosting" or "bulling"), kept per PRIME RULE 1. Also: lending shares to short sellers is "found money", with USG as the case (line 211). Related to M2006-098 (huge short interests often revealed as frauds).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 12. We welcome short-sellers betting against us

quote_verbatim: But those delays in delivering sometimes reflect a tremendous slop in the clearance process, and it is not good for a civilization to have huge slop in the clearance processes for its security trades. [...] It’s not a good idea to have slop that causes a lot of financial exposure that people are ignoring. [...] But a lot of — take derivative trading. There’s a lot of slop in derivative trading. And the clearance problem would be awful if a lot of people wanted to do something at once.
concept: Slop in clearing trades, especially derivatives, creates financial exposure people ignore, and it would be awful if many tried to act at once.
evolution_notes: The second elision crosses Buffett's interjection (line 217, his question about an undelivered General Motors purchase); Munger resumes the same thought. The atomic-power-plant comparison is skipped by the first elision. Related to the derivative rows L2002-018 and L2006-011.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 12. We welcome short-sellers betting against us

quote_verbatim: You know, I would argue that the gambling casinos use clever psychological tricks to cause people to hurt themselves. There is undoubtedly a lot of harmless amusement in the casinos, but there’s also a lot of grievous injury that is deliberately caused by the casinos. It’s a dirty business, and I don’t think you’ll find a casino soon in Berkshire Hathaway.
concept: Do not own a business that profits by deliberately causing its customers grievous injury, however good its prospects.
evolution_notes: Buffett before it: gambling companies "will have a terrific future, if they’re legal" (line 237), and "gambling is a tax on ignorance" with government preying on its citizens (lines 241-243), a political view, not rowed. Munger's line instructs an owner, so it is rowed under the political test.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 13. “Gambling is a tax on ignorance”

quote_verbatim: Well, I think you should read everything you can. [...] But you’ve just got to fill up your mind with various competing thoughts and sort them out as to what really makes sense over time. And then once you’ve done a lot of that, I think you have to jump in the water, because investing on paper and doing — you know, and investing with real money, you know, is like the difference between reading a romance novel and doing something else. (Laughter) [...] So I would say that read and then, on a small scale in a way that can’t hurt you financially, do some of it yourself.
concept: To learn investing, read widely and sort competing ideas, then invest real money on a scale that cannot hurt you.
evolution_notes: Also: "I read a book at age 19 that formed my framework for thinking about investments ever since" (line 259), unnamed here.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 14. How to be a better investor

quote_verbatim: When a young man comes to Sandy, he asks a very simple question, no matter how young the man is. He says, “What do you own and why do you own it?” And if you haven’t been interested enough in the subject to have that involvement already, why, he’d rather you go somewhere else.
concept: Test an aspiring investor by what he owns and why; one not involved enough to have an answer is not suited.
evolution_notes: Sandy Gottesman's practice, a Berkshire director's, related by Munger. Buffett follows with the yellow-pad essay (lines 263-265).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 14. How to be a better investor

quote_verbatim: It’s very — that whole idea that you own a business, you know, is vital to the investment process. [...] It’s the same thing with stocks. I used to always recommend to my students that they take a yellow pad like this and if they’re buying a hundred shares of General Motors at 30 and General Motors has whatever it has out, 600 million shares or a little less, that they say, “I’m going to buy the General Motors company for $18 billion, and here’s why.” And if they can’t give a good essay on that subject, they’ve got no business buying 100 shares or ten shares or one share at $30 per share because they are not subjecting it to business tests.
concept: Before buying any number of shares, write why you would buy the whole company at the implied price; without that essay you have not applied business tests.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the farm example: a quantitative decision "based on pretty solid stuff", not on "what you saw on television that day" (line 263). He ends: questions that made you "defend exactly why you thought that business was cheap at the price at which you are buying it. And any other answer, you’d flunk" (line 265). Restates the share-as-business rows, e.g. R1996-001.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 14. How to be a better investor

quote_verbatim: We favor the businesses where we really think we know the answer. And, therefore, if a business gets to the point where we think the industry in which it operates, the competitive position or anything is so chancy that we can’t really come up with a figure, we don’t really try to compensate for that sort of thing by having some extra large margin of safety. We really want to try to go on to something that we understand better. So if we buy something like — See’s Candy as a business or Coca-Cola as a stock, we don’t think we need a huge margin of safety because we don’t think we’re going to be wrong about our assumptions in any material way.
concept: Do not offset an unpredictable business with a bigger margin of safety; move on to one you understand, where a modest margin suffices because the assumptions will not be materially wrong.
evolution_notes: Compare M2006-039, a greater margin where objectivity is weaker (buying Berkshire's own shares): there the margin widens for a known bias, here it is not used to cover ignorance of the business.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 15. When you don’t need a huge margin of safety

quote_verbatim: What we really want to do is buy a business that’s a great business, which means that business is going to earn a high return on capital employed for a very long period of time, and where we think the management will treat us right.
concept: A great business earns a high return on capital employed for a very long time, under management that will treat the owners right.
evolution_notes: Shares line 273 with the margin-of-safety row on the same line (See's and Coca-Cola needing no huge margin). Followed by "We don’t have to mark those down a lot when we find those factors".
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 15. When you don’t need a huge margin of safety

quote_verbatim: And if we really get to something — you know, when we see a great business, it’s like if you see some — somebody walk in the door, you don’t know whether they weigh 300 pounds or 325 pounds. You still know they’re fat, right, you know? And so if we see something we know it’s fat, financially, we don’t worry about being precise.
concept: A great business is recognized without precise measurement, as one sees a fat man without weighing him.
evolution_notes: Before it: "We’d love to find them when they’re selling at 40 cents on the dollar but we will buy those as much closer to a dollar on the dollar" (line 275). After it: "if we can come in [...] at the equivalent of 270 pounds, we’ll feel good". Related to L1993-017 (approximate rightness).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 15. When you don’t need a huge margin of safety

quote_verbatim: But if we find something where the competitive aspects are — it’s just the nature of the business that you really can’t see out five or 10 or 20 years because that’s what investing is, is seeing out. You don’t get paid for what’s already happened. You only get paid for what’s going to happen in the future. The past is only useful to you in the extent to which it gives you insights into the future, and sometimes the past doesn’t give you any insights into the future.
concept: Investing is seeing five, ten or twenty years out; the past counts only as far as it gives insight into the future, which in some businesses it does not.
evolution_notes: He continues: in "the stable business that you postulated, it probably does give you a pretty good guideline" (line 277). Related to M2006-030 (a long history misleads when conditions change).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 15. When you don’t need a huge margin of safety

quote_verbatim: You should have something that — you always should feel you’re getting a little more than what it’s worth, and there are times when we’ve been able to buy wonderful businesses at a quarter of what they’re worth, but we haven’t seen those — well, we saw it in Korea here recently — but you don’t see those sort of things very often. And does that mean you should sit around and hope they come back for 10 or — you know, wait 10 or 15 years? That’s not the way we do it. If we can buy good businesses at a reasonable valuation, we’re going to keep doing it.
concept: Always get a little more than you pay for, but do not wait years for rare quarter-of-value bargains; keep buying good businesses at reasonable valuations.
evolution_notes: Restates the wonderful-business-at-a-fair-price theme; compare L2006-005 and the letter's "available at a price that will produce a reasonable return" (L2005-006).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 15. When you don’t need a huge margin of safety

quote_verbatim: Yeah. You’re — that margin of safety concept boils down to getting more value than you’re paying. And that value can exist in a lot of different forms. If you’re paid four-to-one on something that’s an even money proposition, why, that’s a value proposition, too. It’s high school algebra.
concept: Margin of safety is getting more value than you pay, in any form, including odds better than the true probability.
evolution_notes: He ends: "people who don’t know how to use high school algebra should take up some other activity". Related to L1993-024 (favorable probability-weighted payoffs) and M1994-046 (Fermat and Pascal).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 15. When you don’t need a huge margin of safety

quote_verbatim: Yeah, we can’t solve that one. We try to look for easy problems because those are the ones we find we have the answers for. And you can do that in investments. We don’t really try tough things. Now, sometimes life hands you a problem, not in the financial area in our case, usually, but it will hand you a problem that is very tough and that you have to wrestle with. But we don’t go around looking for tough problems.
concept: In investing one can choose problems, so choose the easy ones with known answers and do not go looking for tough ones.
evolution_notes: Munger opens the exchange: "Let me try that one. It’s too tough. [...] Warren and I can’t solve that" (lines 291-295). Restates M2006-013 (in, out, too hard).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 16. Health care is too tough for Berkshire

quote_verbatim: You know, if we were to have — if we were looking for a solution through the private sector, we would be looking for something with very, very low distribution costs. I mean, you do not want a lot of the revenue soaked up in frictional costs between the benefits paid and the premiums received.
concept: In an insurance product, look for very low distribution costs, so little of the premium is soaked up between what is received and what is paid in benefits.
evolution_notes: Shares line 297 with the easy-problems row; prefaced "we do very, very little in health insurance". Related to L1995-013 and the letter's GEICO "low-cost producer" (FY2006 letter lines 147-148, not rowed).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 16. Health care is too tough for Berkshire

quote_verbatim: Yeah. Well, the intrinsic value of Berkshire, like any other businesses, is based on the future amount of cash that can be expected to be delivered by the business between now and judgment day, discounted back at the proper rate. Now, that’s pretty nebulous.
concept: Intrinsic value of any business is the cash it can be expected to deliver between now and judgment day, discounted at the proper rate; nebulous but the definition.
evolution_notes: Restates L1994-007 and R1996-018. He later adds that if he and Munger each wrote down Berkshire's intrinsic value "our figures would not be the same. They’d be reasonably close" (line 311), restating R1996-019.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 17. Munger on what’s driven Berkshire’s “extreme” success

quote_verbatim: But since Berkshire retains all of its earnings, it becomes very important to evaluate what will be done with those earnings over time. I mean, it is not only a question what the present businesses are worth. It’s a judgment on the efficiency or the effectiveness with which retained earnings will be used. [...] If we put that to work effectively, each dollar has a greater present value than a dollar has simply in cash or distributed. If we do ineffectively, it has a value of something less.
concept: Where a business retains its earnings, its value depends on a judgment of how effectively the retained dollars will be used, worth more than a dollar if well used and less if not.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the 1965 example, a textile business "probably worth about $12 a share" whose value turned on the plan to use its cash "to try and buy into better businesses" (line 309). Restates R1995-009 and R1996-008.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 17. Munger on what’s driven Berkshire’s “extreme” success

quote_verbatim: I would argue that the young man who was reading everything he could read when he was 10years-old became a learning machine, and he got a lot of power early, and then he got a very long run when he kept learning. If Warren had not been learning all the while, I’m telling you having watched the process closely, the record would be a pale shadow of what it is. And Warren has improved since he passed the retirement age of man. In other words, in this field, at least, you can improve when you’re old. [...] But you get an enormous advantage from practice in this field. And so what happened accidentally in the case of Warren has helped you shareholders greatly because you had this long run with power extremely concentrated, and with the man holding the power being a ferocious learner. Our system ought to be more copied than it is.
concept: An extreme record came from continuous learning over a very long run with power concentrated in a ferocious learner; in investing practice compounds and a manager can improve with age, so routine handovers at retirement age are not necessarily right.
evolution_notes: "10years-old" is as printed. The elision skips "Now, most people don’t even try and create that kind of a record. They pass power from one 65-year-old to one 59-year-old" (lines 313-315). After it: "This idea of passing the power from one old codger to another, in a settled way, is not necessarily the right system at all" (line 315). Compare L2005-022 (self-assessment ebbs with age), which this does not reconcile; see Tensions seen.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 17. Munger on what’s driven Berkshire’s “extreme” success

quote_verbatim: We will need, in capital allocation, to keep doing intelligent things. We won’t get to do brilliant things because you don’t get to do brilliant things with the kind of sums we’re talking about. Maybe once in a blue moon or something, you know, you’ll get a chance. But we will need somebody that never does — basically doesn’t do any dumb things, and occasionally does something that’s reasonably good. [...] It will reject ideas that really are irrational. I’ve been on a lot of boards. Charlie’s been on a lot of boards. You would be amazed at the number of things that are responding to “animal spirits” rather than to rationality that take place.
concept: With large sums the capital allocator's task is to avoid dumb things and occasionally do something reasonably good; an organization should reject decisions driven by animal spirits rather than rationality.
evolution_notes: Lead-in: "We have a very strong culture now of rationality, of being owner-oriented, that will go on long after I’m not around" (line 317). Related to M2006-006 (culture trains managers).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 17. Munger on what’s driven Berkshire’s “extreme” success

quote_verbatim: I mean, there’s nothing evil about a derivative instrument. [...] But they — usage of them on an expanding basis, more and more imaginative ways of using them, introduces, essentially, more and more leverage into the system. And it’s an invisible — or largely invisible — sort of leverage.
concept: A derivative is not evil in itself; the danger is the expanding, largely invisible leverage it puts into the system.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the 60-some Berkshire contracts "we’ll make money out of". He goes on: derivatives and index futures have "totally made any regulation of margin requirements a joke" (line 329). Restates the same year's letter, L2006-011, and L2002-018.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 18. “Deficient” auditing of derivatives will cause problems

quote_verbatim: But you have the same thing existing when you have fund operators operating with billions in aggregate, trillions of dollars, leveraged, who will respond to the same stimulus. They have what we would call a “crowded trade,” but they don’t know it. It’s not a formal crowded trade. It’s just that they’re all ready to sell if a certain given signal or a certain given activity occurs. And when you get that, coupled with extreme leverage which derivatives allow, you will someday get a very, very chaotic situation.
concept: Many leveraged holders who will all sell on the same signal form an unrecognized crowded trade, which with derivative leverage ends in chaos at an unknowable time.
evolution_notes: Before it, portfolio insurance in October 1987, "a bunch of stop-loss orders" that was "a doomsday machine" (lines 331-333), restating M2006-055. After it: "I have no idea when" and the archduke (lines 333-335).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 18. “Deficient” auditing of derivatives will cause problems

quote_verbatim: Yeah. And, of course, the accounting being deficient enormously contributes to the risks. If you get paid enormous bonuses based on reporting profits that don’t exist, you’re going to keep doing whatever causes those phony profits to keep appearing on the books. And what makes that so difficult is that most of the accounting profession doesn’t even recognize how stupidly it is behaving.
concept: Bonuses paid on profits that do not exist drive more of whatever produces them; deficient accounting multiplies the risk.
