evolution_notes: He then recounts telling an accounting standard-setter that mark-to-model lets you "report whatever profit you want as long as you keep expanding the positions", and being told "Well, you just don’t understand accounting" (line 337). Restates L2002-012 and L2002-013.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 18. “Deficient” auditing of derivatives will cause problems

quote_verbatim: I will guarantee you that if you add up the marks on both sides, they don’t equate out to zero. [...] I don’t get paid based on how ours are valued, so I have no reason to want to game the system. But there are people out on the other side that do have reasons to game the system.
concept: Check a derivative mark against the other side's: the two should net to zero, and where the marker is paid on the mark the number will lean his way.
evolution_notes: Before it, Gen Re: every Big Four auditor would have attested the book was marked to market, "I just wish I’d sold the portfolio to the auditors that day. (Laughs) I’d be 400 million better off" (line 339). Restates M2004-026 (opposite marks) and the letter row L2002-013.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 18. “Deficient” auditing of derivatives will cause problems

quote_verbatim: People used to buy bonds to own them and they’d buy bonds to trade them. And there’s nothing evil about that, but it just means that the participants are playing a different game, and that different game can have different consequences than in a buy-andhold environment. And I do think it means that if you’re trying to beat the other fellow on a day-to-day basis, you’re watching news events very carefully or watching the other fellow very carefully.
concept: When most holders can change their minds by the hour and are measured weekly, the market is a different game from buy-and-hold, with different consequences.
evolution_notes: "buy-andhold" is as printed. Before it, the "electronic herd" and turnover rising from 15 or 20 percent to over 100 percent (line 353). Related to L2005-018 (returns fall as motion rises).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 19. Dangers of short-term investing and advanced mathematics

quote_verbatim: Every time — when Charlie and I were at Salomon, they’d always talk to us about five sigma events or six sigma events, and that’s fine if you’re talking about flipping coins, but it doesn’t mean anything when you get human behavior involved. And people do things that — and intelligent people do things — very intelligent, educated people do things — that are totally irrational, and they do them en masse. [...] And you’ll see it — it’s more likely to happen when you have people trying to beat currency, bond, stock markets, day by day. It’s — I think it’s a fool’s game.
concept: Sigma-event probabilities apply to coin flips, not to markets driven by human behavior, where intelligent people act irrationally en masse; trying to beat markets day by day is a fool's game.
evolution_notes: The elision skips "And you saw it in 1998. You saw it in 2002. And you’ll see it again." After it, his partnership practice: "you’ll hear from me once a year" (line 357).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 19. Dangers of short-term investing and advanced mathematics

quote_verbatim: Yeah. When people talk about sigmas, in terms of disaster potentialities in markets, they’re all crazy. They got the idea that bad results in markets would be predicted by Gaussian distributions. And the way they decided on that outcome was it made everything so easy to compute. They don’t follow Gaussian distributions. You have to believe in the Tooth Fairy to believe that. And the disasters are bigger and more irritating than [German mathematician Carl Friedrich] Gauss would have predicted.
concept: Market disasters do not follow Gaussian distributions; the assumption was chosen because it is easy to compute, and real disasters are bigger.
evolution_notes: The bracketed name is the transcript's editorial insertion, kept as printed. Part of an exchange: Buffett "It was easier to teach as well", Munger "It’s easier to teach, too" and the medical professor's obsolete procedure, "It’s so wonderful to teach" (lines 363-369); Buffett's own lesson from the exchange is rowed separately (line 371).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 19. Dangers of short-term investing and advanced mathematics

quote_verbatim: It’s very discouraging to learn advanced mathematics and, you know, how to do things that none but the priesthood can do in your field, and then find out it doesn’t have any meaning, you know. And what you do when confronted with that knowledge, after you’ve invested these years to get your Ph.D., you know, and you’ve maybe written a textbook and a paper or two, having a revelation that that stuff has no utility at all, and really has counter-utility, I’m not sure, you know, too many people can handle it well. And I think they just generally keep on teaching.
concept: Experts who have invested years in a method rarely abandon it when it proves useless; discount teaching that its teachers cannot afford to give up.
evolution_notes: Buffett's lesson from the exchange with Munger on Gaussian models (Munger's row is the one at line 361). Restates in a meeting the same year's letter, L2006-019 (academics "closed their eyes").
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 19. Dangers of short-term investing and advanced mathematics

quote_verbatim: Yeah. When you’re trying to determine something like intrinsic value and margin of safety and so on, there’s no one easy method that could be simply mechanically applied by, say, a computer and make anybody who could punch the buttons rich. By definition, this is going to be a game which you play with multiple techniques and multiple models, and a lot of experience is very helpful.
concept: No mechanical method computes intrinsic value and margin of safety; it is done with multiple techniques and models and much experience.
evolution_notes: He adds: "I don’t think you can become a great investor very rapidly any more than you could become a great bone tumor pathologist very rapidly" (line 381). Buffett had asked Munger to answer first (line 379).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 20. Quantitative approach to intrinsic value and investments

quote_verbatim: So you would be conservative in your assumptions, then. And you might decide that for $70 an acre, you know, you would want a — if you decided you wanted a 7 percent return, you’d pay a thousand dollars an acre. You know, if farmland is selling for 900, you know you’re going to have a buy signal. And if it’s selling for 1200, you’re going to look at something else. That’s what we do in businesses. We are trying to figure out what those corporate farms that we’re looking at are going to produce. And to do that we have to understand their competitive position. We have to understand the dynamics of the business. We have to be able to look out in the future.
concept: Value a business as a farm: estimate on conservative assumptions what it will produce for the owner, set the price that gives the return wanted, buy below it and look elsewhere above it; the estimate needs the competitive position and dynamics.
evolution_notes: The farm figures precede it: 120 bushels of corn, 45 of soybeans, $70 an acre to the owner "using fairly conservative assumptions" (line 383). The farm also appears in heading 14 (M2007-021's notes).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 20. Quantitative approach to intrinsic value and investments

quote_verbatim: But the mathematics of investment were set out by Aesop in 600BC. And he said, “A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.” Now our question is, when do we get the two? How long do we wait? How sure are we that there are two in the bush? Could there be more, you know? What’s the right discount rate? [...] It’s all about evaluating future — the future ability — to distribute cash, or to reinvest cash at high rates if it isn’t distributed. [...] But it’s the ability to distribute cash that gives Berkshire its value.
concept: Value is the future ability to distribute cash, or to reinvest it at high rates: how many birds, how sure, how soon, at what discount rate.
evolution_notes: Restates the letter row L2000-022 (Aesop's axiom) and L2000-021 (three questions of value). Also: "we retain it because we think we can create more than a dollar present value by retaining it" (line 387), restating R1995-009.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 20. Quantitative approach to intrinsic value and investments

quote_verbatim: And that’s all investing is. But you have to know when you know what you’re doing, and you have to know when you’re getting outside of what I call your circle of competency, you don’t have the faintest idea.
concept: Know when you know what you are doing and when you have left your circle of competency.
evolution_notes: Before it, the McDonald's stand: competition, whether McDonald's "could change the franchise arrangement on you", whether people keep eating hamburgers (line 389). Restates M2006-015 (know competency's edge).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 20. Quantitative approach to intrinsic value and investments

quote_verbatim: Yeah. The other thing, you’ve got to recognize that we’ve never had any system for being able to make correct judgments on the values of all businesses. We throw almost all decisions into the too hard pile, and we just sift for a few decisions that we can make that are easy. And that’s a comparative process.
concept: Put almost every decision in the too-hard pile and sift comparatively for the few easy ones; no system values all businesses.
evolution_notes: One row per speaker: Buffett follows with the one-foot bars (line 393), rowed separately. Restates M2006-013.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 20. Quantitative approach to intrinsic value and investments

quote_verbatim: No. We know how to step over one-foot bars. We don’t know how to jump over seven-foot bars. But we do know how to recognize, occasionally, what is a one-foot bar. And we know enough to stay away from the seven-foot bars, too.
concept: Look for the occasional easy problem, a one-foot bar, and stay away from the hard ones.
evolution_notes: Buffett's reply to Munger's too-hard pile (line 391), rowed separately as each states a lesson.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 20. Quantitative approach to intrinsic value and investments

quote_verbatim: We’re not looking for someone to teach. I probably didn’t make that clear enough in the annual report. We’re not — we’re not going to be mentors or teachers or anything of the sort. We’re looking for somebody that we think knows how to do it.
concept: Hire an investment manager who already knows how to do it; do not plan to teach one.
evolution_notes: Restates M2006-007 (Munger: find executives, not train them). Munger's Mozart story closes the answer: "Yes, but I wasn’t asking anybody else for advice how to do it" (lines 407-409).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 21. What Buffett wants as he hires portfolio managers

quote_verbatim: The biggest problem we have is whether they would scale up, because it’s a different job to run a hundred billion than it is to run a hundred million. And incidentally — and you can’t do as well running a hundred billion as a hundred million, in terms of returns. You can’t come close to doing it.
concept: A record on small sums does not show ability to run large ones; returns fall far as the sum grows.
evolution_notes: He goes on: "we do want to find somebody that we think can run large sums of money mildly better than the general performance in securities. And I emphasize mildly" (line 403). Restates L1994-002 ("A fat wallet [...] is the enemy of superior investment results").
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 21. What Buffett wants as he hires portfolio managers

quote_verbatim: But we think maybe we can find somebody or some group, several of them, that can maybe be a couple percentage points better, but we really are interested in being sure that we have somebody that, under conditions that people haven’t even seen yet, will not blow it. You know, anything times zero is zero. And I don’t care how many wonderful figures are in between. evolution_notes: Same answer. Compare L1995-034 (Berkshire has no investor relations department).

heading: ### 7. What an annual report tells you about the CEO

evolution_notes: Same answer, directly after the investor-relations test at lines 689-691; he does not reconcile it with "it makes a difference to us" (line 689) except by the marketable-securities qualifier and the sell-the-stock remedy, so it is listed under Tensions seen, not rowed as a tension. speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 7. What an annual report tells you about the CEO

quote_verbatim: Yeah. I think that’s exactly right. There are two things: the quality of the business and the quality of the management. And if the business is good enough, it will carry a lousy manager. And the converse case, where a really good manager gets in a really lousy business, he’ll ordinarily have a very imperfect record. In other words, it’s a rare person that can take over a textile business, totally doomed, which is what Warren did in his youthful folly — [...] — and turn it into what’s happened here. You should not be looking for other Warrens on the theory they’re under every bush.
concept: Weigh business quality above management quality: a good enough business carries a lousy manager, a good manager in a lousy business ordinarily has an imperfect record, and rare exceptions are not to be expected.

speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 7. What an annual report tells you about the CEO

quote_verbatim: Twenty years, and I finally figured out I was in the wrong business. But there are businesses — if you gave me first draft pick of all the CEOs in America and said it’s your job to run Ford Motor now or, you know, pick a company that’s in a terribly tough business, you know, I wouldn’t do it. I mean, that it’s just too tough. They may get it solved, you know, if they get cooperation from unions and a whole bunch of things, but it will not be solely in the control of the CEO who has that job. He is dependent on too many good things happening outside to say that he alone can get the job, even if he’s the best in the world.

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 7. What an annual report tells you about the CEO

And expectations of the people were bound to be — that they were — people were bound to be disappointed. They simply had an unrealistic view by extrapolation, and that was the main purpose of that article.
concept: Extrapolating a past period's returns produces unrealistic expectations; there is nothing magic about owning equities.

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 8. Stocks over bonds, but with modest expectations

quote_verbatim: Yeah. You really don’t have — in markets you can’t say something terribly important or intelligent every day or every week or every month. But the nice thing about it is you don’t have to have an opinion every day or every week or every month.
concept: You need a view on the market only at the extremes; the gradations in between are too hard, and no opinion is required.

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 8. Stocks over bonds, but with modest expectations

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 8. Stocks over bonds, but with modest expectations

[...] but when they come, just the very things they talk about, what they regard as important and not important, there are a lot of clues that come as to subsequent behavior.

heading: ### 11. Beware when someone says “it’s so easy”

Warren once introduced me to a gentleman promoter who wanted to inveigle us into an insurance program. And he said, “We only write fire insurance on concrete bridges that are covered by water.” He says, “It’s like taking candy from babies.” We are able to filter out propositions like that.
concept: Be deeply suspicious of a proposition too good to be true and of a promoter who calls it like taking candy from babies.

speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 11. Beware when someone says “it’s so easy”

quote_verbatim: Yeah. Anybody that, implicit in their comments or what they kind of laugh about or — all kinds of things in terms of the fact — you know, it’s so easy and — it ain’t that easy, you know, and we get suspicious very quickly. And the truth is, we rule out 90 percent of the times. And we may be wrong about a fair number that we’re ruling out. The important thing is whether the ones we’re ruling in we’re right about. And so we don’t mind — we’re looking for the obvious cases of people you can trust.

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 11. Beware when someone says “it’s so easy”

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 11. Beware when someone says “it’s so easy”

quote_verbatim: Anytime I find somebody with a — what I regard as an unfair fee structure, and saying, “Well, I can get it,” well, you know, I rule them out. And I may rule out some of the wrong people. But the ones that are left in, I feel very good about.
concept: Rule out anyone who charges an unfair fee because he can get it.
evolution_notes: Same turn as the stewardship test on line 763. Compare M2006-096 (Munger, fees as the croupier's rake) and M2007-003 (fees compel fast investing).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 11. Beware when someone says “it’s so easy”

quote_verbatim: Yeah. We don’t formally have discount rates. [...] But we are going to want to get a significantly higher return, obviously — in terms of cash produced relative to the amount we’re outlaying now for a business — than we are from a government bond. I mean, we — you know, we are going to — that has to be the yardstick at a base. And how much more do we want? Well, if government bond rates were 2 percent, we’re not going to buy a business to earn 3 or 3 1/2 percent expectancy over the years. We just don’t want to commit our money that way. We’d rather sit around and wait a little while.
concept: The government bond is the base yardstick: require cash produced well above the bond's yield, and when bonds are very low, wait rather than accept a thin premium.
evolution_notes: Answer to how a discount rate is chosen; the elision skips "Charlie reminds me that I’ve never prepared a spreadsheet. But, in effect, in my mind I do".
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 12. Pay attention to opportunity costs

quote_verbatim: But I can’t tell you that we sit down every morning and I call Charlie in Los Angeles and say, “What’s our hurdle rate today?” I mean, we’ve never used the term. You know, it’s a little bit of the — we want enough so that we feel very comfortable if they closed down on the stock market for a couple of years, if interest rates go up another hundred basis points or 200 basis points, we’re still happy with what we’ve bought. And above that, I really — I know it sounds kind of fuzzy, but it is fuzzy.
concept: Buy only what you would still be happy owning if the market closed for two years and rates rose one or two points; the margin is fuzzy and said to be.
evolution_notes: Same answer as the bond-yardstick row at line 773.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 12. Pay attention to opportunity costs

quote_verbatim: Yeah. The concept of a hurdle rate makes nothing but sense, and yet a lot of terrible errors are made by people who are talking about hurdle rates. Just because you can measure something and guess it, doesn’t mean that it’s the controlling variable in what you’re dealing with in a messy world. And I don’t think there’s any substitute for thinking about a whole lot of investment options and thinking about why one is better than another and what the likely returns are from each, et cetera, et cetera.
concept: A measurable hurdle rate is not necessarily the controlling variable; there is no substitute for comparing many options and why one beats another.
evolution_notes: Munger's turn after Buffett's two rows (lines 773-775).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 12. Pay attention to opportunity costs

quote_verbatim: In other words, if I have something available that I think will give me 8 percent for sure and I can buy all I want of it, and you’ve got a perfectly good investment that I think will earn 7, I don’t have to waste 5 minutes with you. [...] And so this — the concept of opportunity cost is — it’s so little taught in investment. They teach it in the freshman course in economics in all the major universities, but when you get to the corporate finance departments and so forth, it doesn’t lend itself with the kind of mathematics they want to use, so they ignore it. But in the real world, your opportunity costs are what you want to make your decisions based on.
concept: Decide by opportunity cost: an investment that trails your best available, unlimited alternative is not worth five minutes.
evolution_notes: Same turn as the hurdle-rate row on line 777; the elision skips a joke (the mail-order bride, lines 777-779). Restates M2006-074 (opportunity cost as a default option).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 12. Pay attention to opportunity costs

quote_verbatim: Yeah. And even if you had something you were really familiar with and were very sure on the 8 percent, 8 1/2 wouldn’t tempt you if somebody came along, as a practical matter.
concept: A slightly higher return from the less familiar does not displace a sure, well-understood alternative.
evolution_notes: Buffett's addition to Munger's 8-against-7 example (lines 777-779); Munger answers "Sure." (line 783).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 12. Pay attention to opportunity costs

quote_verbatim: I would say that of the presentations I’ve seen — and I’ve seen a lot of them — and every one of them had a calculation of internal rate of return, if they’d burned them all, the boards would have been better off. I mean, there’s so much nonsense presented, because the presenters, essentially, know what the listeners are desirous of hearing, and what is needed in order to get through something the CEO wants to do anyway — you just get nonsense figures.
concept: Distrust internal-rate-of-return figures in board presentations; presenters supply what the CEO and listeners want to hear.
evolution_notes: From his 19 corporate boards (line 785); ends "we may get nonsense figures, too, but they’re ours".
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 12. Pay attention to opportunity costs

quote_verbatim: And there’s no one in the world we think can earn 20 percent with big money. I mean, it just — so anybody making a promise like that, basically, we’re going to write off immediately. It’s amazing to me what — you know, in a sense, how gullible big investors are, pension funds and so on, in that they have people come around and promise them the Holy Grail. And they want it so badly, you know, that they’re willing to believe things that just have to be nonsense.
concept: Write off immediately anyone promising 20 percent on big money; wanting the Holy Grail makes big investors believe nonsense.
evolution_notes: Buffett draws the lesson from Munger's story of the young friend who promised 20 percent because "If I chose any lower number, they wouldn’t give me the money" (line 787); Munger's turn states no lesson and is not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 12. Pay attention to opportunity costs

quote_verbatim: Sure. If you’ve got a child dying of some horrible disease, you have a problem you can’t just put in a “too difficult” pile. So there are lots of things in life that come to you that you — where you have no option to not consider the issue. But where it’s voluntary, like choosing one investment from many, then the “too difficult” pile is a marvelous way of sifting your daily grist.
concept: Where the choice is voluntary, as in choosing one investment from many, put the hard ones in the too-difficult pile; only forced problems must be faced.
evolution_notes: Buffett's next turn (line 805) restates the optional case with his "too hard" file and adds the forced case.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 13. Some problems are too important to be “too difficult”

quote_verbatim: And, as Charlie said, if something is optional and it’s too hard, you just throw it in there. If you’ve got the problems of weapons of mass destruction, it is too hard, but you have to keep wrestling with it. Because if you even reduce the probabilities a tiny bit, you know, you’re doing something. But you’re never going to solve it. You just have to keep working at certain types of problems, and you hope you don’t have too many like that.
concept: Optional problems that are too hard go in the too-hard file; unavoidable ones must be worked at, since even a small cut in probability counts.
evolution_notes: Restates Munger's row at line 803 for the optional case; the forced case is personal conduct and public concern rather than investing, kept for the synthesis to keep or drop.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 13. Some problems are too important to be “too difficult”

quote_verbatim: When I had more ideas than money, I was thinking about everyone all the time because I was thinking about buying the next one and which one I would have to sell in order to buy something even more attractive. So my opportunity cost, as Charlie would put it, then, was the least attractive stock which I would give up to buy something more attractive.
concept: With more ideas than money, the opportunity cost of a new idea is the least attractive holding you would sell to fund it, so every position is under constant review.
evolution_notes: Answer to how often each position is reviewed. Links to Munger's opportunity-cost row under heading 12 (M2007-098).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 14. We’re thinking all the time

quote_verbatim: Now our situation is such that we have more money than ideas, and that means that we really aren’t re-examining something every minute, because the option is cash and not doing something that we really are excited about. [...] So it’s — you know, it is a continuous process, but it’s not a continuous process with the idea that daily activity, or weekly activity, or monthly activity, is going to result. It’s just we want to just keep adding to our thinking and knowledge, refining it further about every business that we’re in.
concept: With more money than ideas the alternative is cash, so review continuously to add knowledge about each business, not to generate activity.
evolution_notes: Same answer as the opportunity-cost definition on line 813; the stored knowledge is used when money must be raised for a big deal (line 815).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 14. We’re thinking all the time

quote_verbatim: Yeah. But even in Warren’s salad days when he had way more ideas than he had money, he did not spend a lot of time thinking about his number one choice. You know, he could put that aside and devote his efforts to other subjects.
concept: Once the best holding is settled, set it aside and spend the effort on other subjects.
evolution_notes: Munger's qualification of Buffett's constant-review answer (lines 813-815); a described habit, rowed as a way of acting.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 14. We’re thinking all the time

quote_verbatim: We like to add to present positions. I mean, those are companies we know, understand, obviously like to some degree. And if the price gets reasonably attractive and we’ve got money around, we will add. If we can find a good business to buy, you know, we will sell the least attractive.
concept: Prefer adding to known, understood positions when price is reasonably attractive; fund a better business by selling the least attractive holding.
evolution_notes: The least-attractive-holding rule restates the opportunity-cost definition given under heading 14 at line 813. Reporting thresholds and the short-swing rule (line 825) are administrative and not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 15. It’s hard to buy billions of dollars of stock

quote_verbatim: So I can just tell you that choosing your heroes is very important. I tell that to the students when they come. Because you are going to gravitate toward the behavior of those around you. I tell people to be sure and associate with people who are better than you are.
concept: Choose your heroes and associates with care, since you will drift toward the behavior of those around you; associate with people better than you.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct. Followed by "Marry up" (line 915), a joke.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 18. “Associate with people who are better than you are”

quote_verbatim: Yeah. I would say that you’re not restricted to living people when picking your mentors. Some of the very best people are dead. (Laughter and applause)
concept: Mentors may be chosen from the dead as well as the living.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct; Munger's addition to Buffett's heroes row at line 915.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 18. “Associate with people who are better than you are”

quote_verbatim: But we are — the best protection for inflation is your own earning power. I mean, somebody that is a first-class surgeon, or lawyer, or teacher, or salesperson, or anything else, whether the currency is seashells, or paper money, or whatever, will do all right in terms of commanding the resources of other people. So your own earning power is your best — is the best hedge against inflation.
concept: The best hedge against inflation is one's own earning power; metals are not necessarily a hedge at all.
evolution_notes: Opens "we would not necessarily look at metals investing as being any protection against inflation at all" (line 953).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 22. Best hedge against inflation

quote_verbatim: The second best hedge is to own a wonderful business, not a metals business, necessarily, not a raw material business, not a minerals business, but a wonderful business. And the truth is, if you own Coca-Cola, if you own Snickers bars, if you own Hershey bars, if you own anything that people are going to want to give a portion of their current income to keep getting, and it has relatively low capital investment attached to it so that you don’t have to keep plowing tremendous amounts of money in just to meet inflationary demands, that’s the best investment you can probably have in an inflationary world.

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 22. Best hedge against inflation

quote_verbatim: So what was a terrible business 30 years ago, and it was operating under regulation — it’s still under — operates under the threat of reregulation, which has a tempering effect on their pricing power — but it’s a better business now. It will never be a sensational business. It’s a very capital-intensive business. And when you put tons of capital out every year, it’s very hard to earn really extraordinary returns on capital. But if they earn a decent return on capital, it can be a good business over time, and it can be a lot better business than it was in the past.

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 23. Railroad business is better but won’t be “sensational”

quote_verbatim: So whatever you can figure out that other people will pay you to do that they don’t want to do themselves or that they’d like done for them — I advise you to look around the neighborhood and talk to your parents, talk to your friends, see what other people have done that have been 10 or 11 or 12 years old that’s worked for them and copy it.

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 24. Best ways a 10-year-old can earn money

speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 24. Best ways a 10-year-old can earn money

concept: Be reliable all your life, faithfully doing whatever you engage to do.

speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 24. Best ways a 10-year-old can earn money

heading: ### 25. Global competitors matter, not global trends

heading: ### 25. Global competitors matter, not global trends

heading: ### 25. Global competitors matter, not global trends

heading: ### 26. It’s all relative with currencies

heading: ### 27. Corporate directors aren’t doing their job

heading: ### 27. Corporate directors aren’t doing their job

quote_verbatim: Most stock deals, they think about what they’re getting and they don’t think about what they’re giving. [...] I’ve heard a lot of discussion about dilution and when dilution will be overcome and all that sort of thing, but that is not the question. The real question is are you — if more value is being created, how is it being whacked up between the two companies? And if not extra value is being created, are you getting more than you’re giving?
concept: In a stock deal weigh what is given against what is got, not dilution: how is any new value split, and if none is created, is more being got than given?
evolution_notes: The first elision skips the point that managers hand away a piece of the business they would not sell at a 20 percent premium (line 1051).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 27. Corporate directors aren’t doing their job

quote_verbatim: When I gave away 2 percent of Berkshire Hathaway to acquire Dexter Shoe, that was one of the dumbest deals in the history of the world. And I did it all by myself. [...] But, you know, it was dumb. I mean, here’s — it wasn’t 2 percent of what I had then at Berkshire, it’s 2 percent of the present Berkshire Hathaway company.
concept: Paying in stock gave away a share of all future Berkshire value for Dexter; the cost of a stock deal is measured in the present company, not the old one.
evolution_notes: The worked case of the giving-against-getting test at lines 1051-1053. Restates L2001-025 and M2002-116; the business misjudgment is this unit's line 675 row.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 27. Corporate directors aren’t doing their job

quote_verbatim: But, you know, the point is that doesn’t show up under conventional accounting at all. You know, it gets brushed under the rug. At Gillette, literally, we had ten deals in a row that never met — came close to meeting — the case that was presented at the time they were presented to the board. Was that ever mentioned to shareholders? Did it show up in our financial report? Never. It never will.
concept: Value given away in acquisitions does not show in conventional accounts; check deals against the case presented, since the report never will.
evolution_notes: Continues the Dexter answer after Munger's "Fortunately, you’ve made some better decisions" (line 1055). Ends that shareholders complain about board diversity "But when you’re blowing away the company, I mean, that, to me, is a whole lot more important."
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 27. Corporate directors aren’t doing their job

quote_verbatim: Yeah. The self-serving delusional nature of even some very good minds, in terms of IQ points, is amazing. I had a friend who sold a business to a government-controlled business in a socialized Scandinavian country. And my friend had a very nice business, and the people on the other side, after they had bought it for stock in their government corporations, said, “This was such a marvelous deal. We got your whole business, and we didn’t have to give anything.”
concept: Even high-IQ buyers delude themselves that paying in stock costs nothing.
evolution_notes: The Scandinavian buyers' mistake, with Munger's lesson stated first. Buffett follows with the Third National Bank story (line 1065), not rowed.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 27. Corporate directors aren’t doing their job

quote_verbatim: There was a local one here called Data Documents that really functioned with everybody on the board thinking about the business, understanding the business, making decisions as owners. Every one of them had a significant percentage of their net worth in the business, and probably the best board I’ve ever been on. [...] We’ve got a board that is in exactly the same position as the shareholders. They don’t have directors’ and officers’ insurance. They’ve got the downside as well as the upside. They bought their stock in the open market, so it hasn’t been given to them. It is a real owners’ board, and I like it that way.
concept: The best board has directors with a significant part of their net worth in stock they bought, no liability insurance, and the downside as well as the upside: an owners' board.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the repeat of the stacked-deck point (lines 1069-1071, named in the line 1045-1047 row). Compare M2004-005 and L2004-014 (shareholders behaving like owners).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 27. Corporate directors aren’t doing their job

quote_verbatim: Yeah. We normally don’t want to do deals with partners. If we like a deal, we want to own it all. And we usually have the money to do it all, so almost — in very few cases would there be a need for a money partner. And then there’s a question for a knowledge partner. And we really wouldn’t want to be going into something, in most cases, where we were relying on somebody else to be the brains of the deal. [...] If we’re going to spend our time on it, we just as soon get a hundred percent of the rewards. We don’t mind taking a hundred percent of the downside. And we ought to understand it well enough so we don’t need a partner.
concept: Own a liked deal outright rather than with partners; never rely on someone else to be the brains, and understand it well enough to need no partner.
evolution_notes: Buffett then names the exception, Leucadia, who "brought us the deal", and managers who own part of their businesses "on the same terms we are" (line 1091).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 28. Why Berkshire avoids deals with partners

quote_verbatim: Yeah. I — and, to my knowledge, Charlie — we’ll hear from him — but we have no opinion on commodities. We — if we were in an oil stock, it’s because we think it offers a lot of value at this price, but it does not mean that we think the price of oil is going up.

quote_verbatim: We, basically, like best the businesses that require very little capital, because they’re the only ones that have a chance of earning really high returns on capital. You can’t have a business that has huge capital expenditures year after year, and end up with a high- return business. It just doesn’t work in this world.

heading: ### 29. No opinion on commodity prices

We’re going to haul them great distances. [...] Well, I don’t think we would be backing him, you know. Now, it happened, you know. The other one came along first, and people’s habits don’t change immediately, and, you know, the world doesn’t turn over. But, in effect, you know, the position of newspapers today still reflects the fact that they have inertia and momentum on their side from the past. And I don’t care how smart you are.
concept: Ask whether you would back the business if it were proposed today against the alternatives; if not, its position rests on inertia and momentum, which no manager's brains will hold.

And it isn’t because the World Book isn’t worth what it sells for. It’s just not worth what it sells to for most people who can go on the internet and get an awful lot of that information free.
concept: A product can be worth its price and still lose most of its buyers when a free substitute arrives.

And once a contract has been made, the idea that you can just stamp your foot and take away the contract strikes me as a — kind of an immature idea.

heading: ### 34. Shareholder proposal to divest PetroChina shares

quote_verbatim: Unfortunately, this wish was promptly granted, as just about all Americans came to believe that house prices would forever rise. That conviction made a borrower's income and cash equity seem unimportant to lenders, who shoveled out money, confident that HPA � house price appreciation � would cure all problems. Today, our country is experiencing widespread pain because of that erroneous belief. As house prices fall, a huge amount of financial folly is being exposed. You only learn who has been swimming naked when the tide goes out � and what we are witnessing at some of our largest financial institutions is an ugly sight.
concept: Lenders who believed prices would rise forever stopped looking at the borrower's income and cash equity; a loan that only appreciation can cure is exposed when prices fall.
evolution_notes: The mistake is the lenders' ("some major financial institutions", line 133), not Buffett's; it follows the "weakened lending practices" of the FY2006 letter (L2006-010). "Swimming naked" restates L2001-018 and L2004-009 (and M1994-048); the borrower's income and equity set aside for appreciation is new in the letters read so far.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: BERKSHIRE HATHAWAY INC.

quote_verbatim: First, most of them have no financial need to work. Many sold us their businesses for large sums and run them because they love doing so, not because they need the money. [...] Conversely, our CEOs' scorecards for success are not whether they obtain my job but instead are the long-term performances of their businesses. Their decisions flow from a here-today, here-forever mindset.
concept: A manager who works for love rather than need, and who has exactly the job he wants for life, judges himself by the business's long-term performance and decides with a here-forever mindset.
evolution_notes: The elision skips "Naturally they wish to be paid fairly" and the contrast with managers elsewhere who see a division as "a way station" and "may well feel like failures" if still there in five years (lines 230-238). Closes: "I think our rare and hard-to-replicate managerial structure gives Berkshire a real advantage" (line 242). Related to the meeting rows on managers who love the business; new in the letters read so far. The yardsticks themselves (lines 164-224) restate L2006-002 and are not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Yardsticks

quote_verbatim: We arrived at a price using only Marmon's financial statements, employing no advisors and engaging in no nit-picking. I knew that the business would be exactly as the Pritzkers represented, and they knew that we would close on the dot, however chaotic financial markets might be. During the past year, many large deals have been renegotiated or killed entirely. With the Pritzkers, as with Berkshire, a deal is a deal.
concept: Price a deal from the financial statements with sellers whose word can be relied on, without advisors or nit-picking, and close as agreed whatever the markets do: a deal is a deal.
evolution_notes: Lead-in: "This deal was done in the way Jay would have liked" (line 276), after the 1954 Rockwood Chocolate story (lines 251-258). New in the letters read so far.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Acquisitions

quote_verbatim: A truly great business must have an enduring "moat" that protects excellent returns on invested capital. The dynamics of capitalism guarantee that competitors will repeatedly assault any business "castle" that is earning high returns. Therefore a formidable barrier such as a company's being the low-cost producer (GEICO, Costco) or possessing a powerful world-wide brand (Coca-Cola, Gillette, American Express) is essential for sustained success. Business history is filled with "Roman Candles," companies whose moats proved illusory and were soon crossed.
concept: A great business has an enduring moat protecting excellent returns on invested capital, because competitors will assault any castle earning high returns; the barrier is typically low cost or a powerful world-wide brand, and many apparent moats prove illusory.
evolution_notes: Before it, the four criteria "a) a business we understand; b) favorable long-term economics; c) able and trustworthy management; and d) a sensible price tag" and the Hope Diamond line (lines 312-316): not rowed, they restate L1994-018 and L1994-006. Earlier moat definitions L1993-021 and L1995-013; the tie of the moat to returns on invested capital and the two named forms (low cost, world-wide brand) are new in the letters read so far.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Businesses � The Great, the Good and the Gruesome

quote_verbatim: Our criterion of "enduring" causes us to rule out companies in industries prone to rapid and continuous change. Though capitalism's "creative destruction" is highly beneficial for society, it precludes investment certainty. A moat that must be continuously rebuilt will eventually be no moat at all.
concept: Rule out industries of rapid and continuous change, since creative destruction precludes certainty; a moat that must be continuously rebuilt is eventually no moat.
evolution_notes: The exclusion of fast-changing industries restates L1996-026 and L1999-020; the sentence on a moat that must be continuously rebuilt is new in the letters read so far.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Businesses � The Great, the Good and the Gruesome

quote_verbatim: Additionally, this criterion eliminates the business whose success depends on having a great manager. [...] But if a business requires a superstar to produce great results, the business itself cannot be deemed great. A medical partnership led by your area's premier brain surgeon may enjoy outsized and growing earnings, but that tells little about its future. The partnership's moat will go when the surgeon goes. You can count, though, on the moat of the Mayo Clinic to endure, even though you can't name its CEO.
concept: A business that needs a superstar to produce great results is not itself great; its moat leaves when the star leaves, whereas a great business endures under managers no one can name.
evolution_notes: The elision skips "a terrific CEO is a huge asset for any enterprise" and Berkshire's abundance of such managers (lines 330-332), so the passage does not belittle managers, only the dependence on one. Compare L1998-006 (great business idea plus great manager) and L2006-006 (eroding fundamentals overwhelm managerial brilliance); the superstar test is new in the letters read so far.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Businesses � The Great, the Good and the Gruesome

quote_verbatim: Long-term competitive advantage in a stable industry is what we seek in a business. If that comes with rapid organic growth, great. But even without organic growth, such a business is rewarding. We will simply take the lush earnings of the business and use them to buy similar businesses elsewhere. There's no rule that you have to invest money where you've earned it. Indeed, it's often a mistake to do so: Truly great businesses, earning huge returns on tangible assets, can't for any extended period reinvest a large portion of their earnings internally at high rates of return.
concept: Seek long-term competitive advantage in a stable industry; growth is welcome but not required, because the earnings need not be reinvested where they were earned, and a truly great business cannot reinvest much of them internally at high returns.
evolution_notes: Followed by See's as "the prototype of a dream business" in an unexciting, non-growing industry (lines 348-352). New in the letters read so far.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Businesses � The Great, the Good and the Gruesome

quote_verbatim: There aren't many See's in Corporate America. Typically, companies that increase their earnings from $5 million to $82 million require, say, $400 million or so of capital investment to finance their growth. [...] A company that needs large increases in capital to engender its growth may well prove to be a satisfactory investment. There is, to follow through on our example, nothing shabby about earning $82 million pre-tax on $400 million of net tangible assets. But that equation for the owner is vastly different from the See's situation. It's far better to have an ever-increasing stream of earnings with virtually no major capital requirements.
concept: Ask how much capital each increment of earnings requires: growth that needs large capital can still be a satisfactory investment, but growing earnings with virtually no capital requirement is far better for the owner.
evolution_notes: The worked See's figures precede it: bought for $25 million, $8 million of capital in 1972 earning 60% pre-tax, $40 million now, only $32 million reinvested against $1.35 billion of pre-tax earnings sent on (lines 360-371); the elision skips the reason, working capital and fixed assets that grow with sales (lines 378-379). Restates L1999-017 (See's needing little added capital); the comparison with a capital-hungry grower that is still satisfactory is new in the letters read so far.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Businesses � The Great, the Good and the Gruesome

quote_verbatim: Now let's move to the gruesome. The worst sort of business is one that grows rapidly, requires significant capital to engender the growth, and then earns little or no money. Think airlines. Here a durable competitive advantage has proven elusive ever since the days of the Wright Brothers. [...] The airline industry's demand for capital ever since that first flight has been insatiable. Investors have poured money into a bottomless pit, attracted by growth when they should have been repelled by it. And I, to my shame, participated in this foolishness when I had Berkshire buy U.S. Air preferred stock in 1989.
concept: The worst business grows rapidly, needs significant capital to grow and earns little or nothing; growth that consumes capital without a durable advantage should repel, not attract.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the Kitty Hawk joke (lines 410-412). Then: "before long our preferred dividend was no longer being paid. But we then got very lucky" and the 1998 sale (lines 418-420). The U.S. Air confession restates L1996-040 and L1997-038; rowed for the test, growth that should repel, which is new in the letters read so far. Between this and the row on lines 376-385, FlightSafety is the "good" case, "excellent but not extraordinary" with a "put-up-more-to-earn-more experience" (lines 403-404), as are the regulated utilities (lines 405-406).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Businesses � The Great, the Good and the Gruesome

quote_verbatim: To sum up, think of three types of "savings accounts." The great one pays an extraordinarily high interest rate that will rise as the years pass. The good one pays an attractive rate of interest that will be earned also on deposits that are added. Finally, the gruesome account both pays an inadequate interest rate and requires you to keep adding money at those disappointing returns.
concept: Businesses as savings accounts: great pays a high and rising rate with no added deposits, good pays an attractive rate on added deposits, gruesome pays an inadequate rate and demands more deposits.
evolution_notes: Sums up See's (great), FlightSafety and the utilities (good) and the airlines (gruesome), lines 348-420. New in the letters read so far.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Businesses � The Great, the Good and the Gruesome

quote_verbatim: And now it's confession time. It should be noted that no consultant, board of directors or investment banker pushed me into the mistakes I will describe. In tennis parlance, they were all unforced errors. To begin with, I almost blew the See's purchase. The seller was asking $30 million, and I was adamant about not going above $25 million. Fortunately, he caved. Otherwise I would have balked, and that $1.35 billion would have gone to somebody else.
concept: Buffett's own near-error: haggling over a few million on a great business nearly cost $1.35 billion of later earnings; price discipline can be misapplied to a great business.
evolution_notes: The lesson is drawn by the contrast he states, $5 million of price against $1.35 billion of earnings, not in a separate sentence. Compare the "one-price" passage at lines 651-663, where he caves on MidAmerican and is "glad I wilted"; listed in the note under Tensions seen.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Businesses � The Great, the Good and the Gruesome

quote_verbatim: I knew that TV stations were See's-like businesses that required virtually no capital investment and had excellent prospects for growth. They were simple to run and showered cash on their owners. [...] In effect Murph whispered "buy" into my ear. But I didn't listen. [...] Why did I say "no"? The only explanation is that my brain had gone on vacation and forgot to notify me.
concept: Buffett's error of omission: he declined a business he knew to be See's-like, offered by an expert friend he trusted, and it earned at least $1 billion; knowing the economics and not acting is itself the mistake.
evolution_notes: The first elision skips Murphy as a close friend and extraordinary manager who "would not have called me unless he felt a purchase was certain to work" (lines 442-444); the second skips the station's $73 million of 2006 pre-tax earnings and $800 million value (lines 449-451). Then the Dexter confession (lines 455-464): not rowed, it restates L2000-034 and L2001-025 with new figures ($3.5 billion, "1.6% of a wonderful business").
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Businesses � The Great, the Good and the Gruesome

quote_verbatim: Now, I'm a "one-price" guy (remember See's?) and for several days the investment bankers representing MidAmerican had no luck in getting me to increase Berkshire's offer. But, finally, they caught me in a moment of weakness, and I caved, telling them I would go to $35.05. [...] And yes, I'm glad I wilted and offered the extra nickel.
