The elision skips "they could tell their client they had wrung the last nickel out of me. At the time, it hurt" and the later purchases and 2007 earnings (lines 654-663). "(remember See's?)" points back to the confession at lines 432-434; the two are listed under the note's Tensions seen.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Regulated Utility Business

quote_verbatim: Though she lacked a managerial background, I did not hesitate to make her CEO in 1994. She's smart, she loves the business, and she loves her associates. That beats having an MBA degree any time. (An aside: Charlie and I are not big fans of resumes. Instead, we focus on brains, passion and integrity.
concept: Judge a manager by brains, passion and integrity, not by resume or credentials.
evolution_notes: Of Susan Jacques, who came to Borsheims "as a $4-an-hour saleswoman" (line 726); then Cathy Baron Tamraz, who "began her career as a cab driver" (lines 730-734). Compare L2001-029 (ability and trustworthiness alone) and M1998-092; the brains-passion-integrity test is new in the letters read so far.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Manufacturing, Service and Retailing Operations

quote_verbatim: P&G and Coke began business in 1837 and 1886 respectively. Start-ups are not our game.
concept: Do not invest in start-ups; the holdings are long-established businesses.
evolution_notes: Said in "the strange world department" after noting that Wells and Fargo organized both American Express (1850) and Wells Fargo (1852), lines 893-894. Related to R1997-001's "Demonstrated consistent earning power"; the start-up exclusion in these words is new in the letters read so far.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Investments

quote_verbatim: I should emphasize that we do not measure the progress of our investments by what their market prices do during any given year. Rather, we evaluate their performance by the two methods we apply to the businesses we own. The first test is improvement in earnings, with our making due allowance for industry conditions. The second test, more subjective, is whether their "moats" � a metaphor for the superiorities they possess that make life difficult for their competitors � have widened during the year.
concept: Judge a holding's year not by its market price but by two tests applied as to a wholly owned business: earnings improvement allowing for industry conditions, and whether its moat widened.
evolution_notes: Then: "All of the "big four" scored positively on that test" (lines 901-902), including Wells Fargo, whose earnings fell but whose intrinsic value "increased, even if only by a minor amount" (lines 890-891). Restates L1993-019 and L1996-024 (monitor the qualities) and defines the moat as in L2005-010; the two named annual tests are new in the letters read so far.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Investments

quote_verbatim: Decades of option-accounting nonsense have now been put to rest, but other accounting choices remain � important among these the investment-return assumption a company uses in calculating pension expense. It will come as no surprise that many companies continue to choose an assumption that allows them to report less-than-solid "earnings." [...] The average holdings of bonds and cash for all pension funds is about 28%, and on these assets returns can be expected to be no more than 5%. Higher yields, of course, are obtainable but they carry with them a risk of commensurate (or greater) loss. This means that the remaining 72% of assets � which are mostly in equities, either held directly or through vehicles such as hedge funds or private-equity investments � must earn 9.2% in order for the fund overall to achieve the postulated 8%. And that return must be delivered after all fees, which are now far higher than they have ever been.
concept: Test a pension return assumption by arithmetic: what the bond and cash portion can earn fixes what the equity portion must earn after fees, and higher yields carry commensurate risk of loss.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the 8% average assumption of the 363 S&P companies with plans (lines 1074-1075). Before it, the option-expensing history and backdating (lines 1048-1069): not rowed, they restate L1998-023 and L2002-039. After it, the Dow from 66 to 11,497 in the 20th century, 5.3% a year, and about 2,000,000 needed by 2099 (lines 1088-1097). L2002-039 named "fanciful" pension assumptions as a warning sign; the arithmetic test is new in the letters read so far. Later: "What is no puzzle, however, is why CEOs opt for a high investment assumption: It lets them report higher earnings" (lines 1134-1135), not rowed, restating the FY2005 and FY2006 letters' point that the chickens come home after the CEO retires.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Fanciful Figures � How Public Companies Juice Earnings

quote_verbatim: Naturally, everyone expects to be above average. And those helpers � bless their hearts � will certainly encourage their clients in this belief. But, as a class, the helper-aided group must be below average. The reason is simple: 1) Investors, overall, will necessarily earn an average return, minus costs they incur; 2) Passive and index investors, through their very inactivity, will earn that average minus costs that are very low; 3) With that group earning average returns, so must the remaining group � the active investors. But this group will incur high transaction, management, and advisory costs. Therefore, the active investors will have their returns diminished by a far greater percentage than will their inactive brethren. That means that the passive group � the "know-nothings" � must win.
concept: As a class, active investors must trail passive ones: all earn the average before costs, and the active pay far higher costs, so the know-nothings must win.
evolution_notes: Restates in substance L2005-016 (owners in aggregate earn what the businesses earn, less frictional costs) and L2005-018 ("returns decrease as motion increases"); the three-step proof that the passive group must beat the helper-aided group is new in the letters read so far. Compare L1993-025 (the know-nothing investor and the index fund).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Fanciful Figures � How Public Companies Juice Earnings

quote_verbatim: I should mention that people who expect to earn 10% annually from equities during this century � envisioning that 2% of that will come from dividends and 8% from price appreciation � are implicitly forecasting a level of about 24,000,000 on the Dow by 2100. If your adviser talks to you about double-digit returns from equities, explain this math to him � not that it will faze him. [...] Beware the glib helper who fills your head with fantasies while he fills his pockets with fees.
concept: Translate an expected return into the index level it implies; a forecast of double-digit equity returns for a century implies an absurd level, so distrust the adviser who offers one.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the Alice in Wonderland line, "six impossible things before breakfast" (lines 1121-1123). The same arithmetic earlier in the section: matching the last century's 5.3% would need the Dow at about 2,000,000 by 2099 (lines 1094-1095), and "does anyone really believe this is the most likely outcome?" (line 1102). Related to L2005-017 on Helpers; the implied-level check is new in the letters read so far.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Fanciful Figures � How Public Companies Juice Earnings

quote_verbatim: Some companies have pension plans in Europe as well as in the U.S. and, in their accounting, almost all assume that the U.S. plans will earn more than the non-U.S. plans. This discrepancy is puzzling: Why should these companies not put their U.S. managers in charge of the non-U.S. pension assets and let them work their magic on these assets as well? I've never seen this puzzle explained. But the auditors and actuaries who are charged with vetting the return assumptions seem to have no problem with it.
concept: Check a company's assumptions for internal consistency: a higher assumed return on one set of plan assets than on another, with no reason given, signals an assumption chosen for the earnings it produces.
evolution_notes: Followed by the reason, CEOs choose a high assumption because "It lets them report higher earnings" (lines 1134-1136). Related to L2002-039; the consistency check is new in the letters read so far.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Fanciful Figures � How Public Companies Juice Earnings

quote_verbatim: After decades of pushing the envelope � or worse � in its attempt to report the highest number possible for current earnings, Corporate America should ease up. It should listen to my partner, Charlie: "If you've hit three balls out of bounds to the left, aim a little to the right on the next swing."
concept: When a pattern of errors leans one way, deliberately correct toward the other side; applied to reporting, stop pushing for the highest possible current earnings.
evolution_notes: Munger's maxim, spoken by Buffett in the letter, so the row is Buffett's. New in the letters read so far.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Fanciful Figures � How Public Companies Juice Earnings

quote_verbatim: And there’s three big lessons in there which relate to your attitude towards stocks generally, which is that you think of them as parts of a business; and your attitude toward the market, which is that you use it to serve you and not to instruct you; and then the idea of a margin of safety, of always leaving some extra room and things. [...] And that’s the way to look at stocks. You’ll never be a lemming if you do that.
concept: Three attitudes keep an investor from following the crowd: a stock is part of a business, the market is there to serve and not to instruct, and always leave a margin of safety.
evolution_notes: From The Intelligent Investor, "particularly Chapters 8 and 20" (line 81); "you can’t get a bad result if you follow the lessons of — Ben Graham taught in that book" (line 83). The elision skips Berkshire holders seeing themselves as owners of the businesses in the exhibition hall. Restates M1997-012, M2003-046 and M2006-077 (the market serves, it does not instruct) and M1996-003 (a share is part of a business); the three named together as the cure for crowd behaviour are new in the read.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 3. How NOT to be a lemming

quote_verbatim: Charlie and I haven’t the faintest idea where the stock market is going to go next week, next month, or next year. We never talk about it. [...] Obviously, if we could guess successfully a high percentage of the time where the stock market was going to go, we would do nothing but play the S&P futures market. There wouldn’t be any reason to look at businesses and stocks. So it’s just not our game.
concept: Do not forecast the market; anyone who could would trade futures and never study businesses, so studying businesses presupposes not knowing where the market is going.
evolution_notes: The elision skips that directors have never heard the market's direction discussed at a board meeting. Then: "we ignore 99.9 percent of what we see, although we run our eyes over them" (line 101). Restates M1996-066, M1997-004 and M1999-002; the futures argument is new in the read.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 5. “Forget about the word ‘stock’”

quote_verbatim: Forget about the word “stock.” So when we buy a stock, we would be happy with that stock if they told us the market was going to close for a couple years. We look to the business. [...] You’d look at what the farm was going to produce over time. You’d look at expected yields. You’d look at expected prices, the taxes, the cost of fertilizer, and you would evaluate the intelligence of your purchase based on what the farm produced relative to your purchase price. Quotes would have nothing to do with it. That’s exactly the way we look at stocks. We look at them as businesses. We make judgments about what the future of those businesses will be. And if we’re right about — in those judgments, the stocks will take care of themselves.
concept: Judge a stock purchase as a farm purchase: by what the business will produce against the price paid, as if the market were closed for years; if the business judgment is right the stock takes care of itself.
evolution_notes: The elision skips "It’s exactly the same way as if you were going to buy a farm a few miles here outside of Omaha. You would not get a price on it every day". Restates M1996-003, M2002-080, M2004-013 and M2007-043. Munger: "Nothing to add" (line 107).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 5. “Forget about the word ‘stock’”

quote_verbatim: I no more could take those hundred and spend a few hours and rank them from number one to a hundred in terms of their future achievements as managers, you know, than I could pick them — you know, it would be impossible for me. But what we do is we buy businesses with great managers in place. We’ve seen those people perform for, in many cases, decades. We’ve seen their record, and they come with the business. Now, our job is not so much to select great managers, because we do have this proven record that they come with. Our job is to retain them.
concept: Managers cannot be ranked from a few hours with candidates; buy businesses whose managers have proven records over decades, and make retaining them the job.
evolution_notes: Opens: "you have to understand that we cheat. (Laughs) We buy businesses with good managers" (line 117). Restates R1997-001's "Management in place (we can’t supply it)" and M1995-079; the admitted inability to rank untried candidates is new in the read.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 6. We don’t cultivate great managers, we keep them

quote_verbatim: And our job is to make sure that they have the same enthusiasm, excitement, passion, for their job after the stock certificate changes hands, than they had before. Now, that requires some judgment on our part as to whether these people love the business or love the money. [...] So we have to see the passion in their eyes, and if we see that, then we have to behave in a way that that passion remains. Can’t be done by contract. We don’t have contracts. It won’t — that doesn’t work.
concept: Ask whether a selling manager loves the business or the money, then behave so the passion survives the sale; contracts cannot secure it.
evolution_notes: The elision skips "They all like money, but many of them — well, our managers in particular — they love their businesses" and the businesses as "a work of art to them". Restates M1998-061, M2000-053, M2000-098, M2003-060 and M2005-002, and the FY2007 letter's L2007-002.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 6. We don’t cultivate great managers, we keep them

quote_verbatim: I would look for the person with passion for the job. I mean, the person that is always doing more than their share. You look for people that are goods communicators and all of that sort of thing. But I like my way better. It’s a lot easier just to take somebody that’s been batting .400 in baseball and say, “I think I’ll stick them in the lineup.”
concept: Without a record to go on, look for passion for the job and the person who always does more than their share; but a long proven record is the easier test.
evolution_notes: Before it: of MBAs, "they sort of learn by that point in life how to fool you, in terms of what answers you want to hear" (line 123). Compare M2003-063 (Munger, passion over brainpower) and the FY2007 letter's L2007-014 (brains, passion and integrity). Munger's reply is the Howard Ahmanson joke (line 127), not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 6. We don’t cultivate great managers, we keep them

quote_verbatim: We would have been better off if we had just bought the stock. Usually, if you want to buy or sell a stock, you should buy or sell the stock. And using an option technique to buy a call on a stock instead of buying the stock outright with the idea that you get it a little cheaper that way means that about four times out of five you’ll be right and the fifth time the stock will have moved earlier and you’ll have missed, you know, the transaction you wanted to have. [...] If we want to buy something, we’ll just start buying it. And if we want to get out of it, we’ll start selling it. And we won’t get involved in any fancy techniques.
concept: To buy or sell a stock, buy or sell the stock; option techniques to get a slightly better price win most times but miss the purchase that mattered.
evolution_notes: Lead-in: the Coca-Cola put once sold, "It didn’t get exercised" (line 135). The elision skips that Berkshire has "virtually never used options as a way to enter a position or exit a position" and that the long-term index puts are "a different sort of thing". New in the read.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 7. Teaching option pricing is “totally nonsense”

quote_verbatim: I mean, you need two courses in a business school: one is how to value a business, and — from the standpoint of investments — how to value a business and how to think about stock market fluctuations. [...] And it really has nothing to do with investment success. Investment success depends on buying into the right businesses at the right price. And you have to know how to value businesses, and you have to have an attitude that divorces you from being influenced by the market. You want the market there, not to influence you, you want it there to serve you.
concept: Investment success needs two things, valuing a business and an attitude that lets market fluctuations serve rather than influence; the formulas of finance teaching have nothing to do with it.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the Biblical-studies analogy and "a great desire of the priesthood in finance to want to teach the things that they know and you don’t know" (line 145). Ends with Chapter 8 of The Intelligent Investor, the same three lessons as the row at line 85. Restates M2001-060 and M2007-041 (experts keep teaching useless methods). Munger, between the two Buffett passages (line 139), on option exchanges as "gambling parlors so the croupiers can make more money": a public-policy view, not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 7. Teaching option pricing is “totally nonsense”

quote_verbatim: In terms of the pitfalls, you know, you can make mistakes in any area. But if you — you should give to things that you personally have an interest in and believe in, and that can be anything. [...] Something you’re involved in. Something you want to give your time to as well as money.
concept: Give to causes you personally believe in and are involved in, with time as well as money.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct. The elision skips "I’m not going to prioritize what should be done with gifts". Before it, his own giving as "excess", against his sister's giving that makes a difference to her life (lines 153-155). Compare M2007-057 and M2007-058 (personal conduct, giving).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 8. Buffett praises sister Doris for her “retail” charity

quote_verbatim: Yeah. Regarding pitfalls, I would predict that, if you have an extreme political ideology, whether of the left or the right, you’re very likely to make a lot of dumb charitable gifts. (Laughter and applause)
concept: Munger: an extreme ideology, of either side, predicts dumb charitable gifts.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct; stated with laughter. Follows Buffett's row on lines 155-157. New in the read.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 8. Buffett praises sister Doris for her “retail” charity

quote_verbatim: We don’t have a shred of reputation more than we need, and we never want to trade away reputation for money. So we give them that same message that was given in the movie, in terms of the Salomon situation, which is that not only do they behave in a way that conforms with the laws, but that they behave in a way where, if a story were written by an unfriendly but intelligent reporter, the next morning, in their local paper, they would have no problem with their neighbors, their family reading it.
concept: Never trade reputation for money; test conduct not only against the law but against how it would read, written by an unfriendly but intelligent reporter, to one's family and neighbors.
evolution_notes: Before it: "we’ve got all the money we need" (line 171) and managers trusted with "the keys, not only to the financial performance of the business, but in terms of how they behave" (line 169). Compare M1999-102 (reputation for trust as an asset); the newspaper test is new in the meeting rows read so far.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 9. We don’t “tell the world how to run their business”

quote_verbatim: There is no pressure from Berkshire’s corporate office to report X dollars per — of earnings in any quarter. They don’t give me budgets, so they don’t — there’s no feeling that they have to come through with given numbers or I’ll be embarrassed in public in terms of publishing earnings or anything of the sort. We have no incentives to cause people to do anything that would go against their conscience or play games or cut corners or anything of the sort.
concept: Remove earnings targets and budgets from above so no incentive pushes managers against their conscience or toward cutting corners.
evolution_notes: Follows the reputation row on line 171. Restates M1995-079, M2005-035 and M2005-036. Then: "It isn’t perfect. You can’t have 250,000 people in the city without having something going on at some point" (line 173).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 9. We don’t “tell the world how to run their business”

quote_verbatim: And we bought that business. And we tried to compete. We had a good brand name. We had great workmanship. And we found out that it just plain wouldn’t work against — competing against — shoes produced in China.
concept: Buffett's own error: a good brand, great workmanship and productive workers did not let a domestic shoe maker compete with far lower-cost foreign production.
evolution_notes: Of Dexter, Maine (not named as Dexter Shoe here, the town is named). The workers "were more productive than workers around the world" (line 177). Restates M2002-116, M2003-077 and M2007-118, and the letter rows L2000-034 and L2001-025.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 9. We don’t “tell the world how to run their business”

quote_verbatim: Generally speaking, if you’re creating a higher value-added product, as ISCAR is doing, from a raw material, there may be three months, six months, of adjustment to changes in raw material prices. And obviously, with some commodities, if it gets high enough you get into substitutes. [...] So I think largely, in our businesses, raw materials get passed through. [...] But over a period of time, our businesses are going to reflect raw material costs.
concept: A higher value-added product passes raw material costs through after months of adjustment, unless a substitute exists; over time prices reflect input costs.
evolution_notes: The first elision skips that there is no substitute for tungsten in cutting tools and the oil substitutes that rose too; the second skips the carpet business's difficulty passing through oil-based costs during the housing slowdown (lines 187-189). Restates M2005-017 and M2005-018. Munger: "we will probably make more money over time because there is inflation" (line 193), a forecast, not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 10. Buffett dismisses higher raw material costs

quote_verbatim: We operate now in a universe of marketable stocks that — where we’re talking about companies with market caps of at least 10 billion but really, in most cases, to have a meaningful impact on Berkshire, we’re talking much bigger than that, maybe 50 billion and up. Well, that universe is not as profitable a universe to operate in as if you have the entire universe of thousands and thousands of companies. [...] I mean, if you’re working with small amounts of money, and you want to put in significant amounts of time, and examine thousands of securities, you will find things that are more intelligent to buy than Berkshire.
concept: Size shrinks the universe of usable investments and with it the returns; a small sum, worked hard across thousands of securities, can find better buys than a giant can.
evolution_notes: The elision crosses Munger's interjections (lines 207 and 211) and resumes the same thought. It skips the arithmetic, 5 percent of a $10 billion company doubling is "less than two-tenths of 1 percent in terms of Berkshire performance" (line 203), and "anyone that expects us to come close to replicating the past should sell their stock" (line 203). Restates M1995-080, M2007-049 and M2007-059. Munger at line 207, "We are very happy making money at a rate in the future that is way less [...] I suggest that you adopt the same attitude", is answered by Buffett, "I wouldn’t condemn them to that"; not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 11. Lots of work to find a better buy than Berkshire

quote_verbatim: What we really like at Berkshire is buying good-sized to very large first-class businesses with first-class management and just sitting there. Because the nice thing about that is you don’t have go from flower to flower. You can just sit there and watch them produce more and more every year and give you capital and you can buy more businesses.
concept: Buy first-class businesses with first-class management and sit, letting them produce more each year and supply capital for more purchases, rather than going from flower to flower.
evolution_notes: Then: "That’s a nice formula. It’s a formula that will work, I think, for us. It won’t produce returns like the past" (line 215). Compare M2000-005 (a few great companies can simply be held) and the FY2007 letter's L2007-007 (use the earnings to buy similar businesses elsewhere).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 11. Lots of work to find a better buy than Berkshire

quote_verbatim: I — there’s just no reason to look at any minuses in life and to focus on that. It would be crazy. So we really do count our blessings because they’ve been many and they continue to come forth, and we’ll enjoy it as long as we can.
concept: Do not dwell on life's minuses; count the blessings.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct. Before it: "we get to do what we love doing every day" and "We’re forced to do virtually nothing we don’t want to" (line 237). New in the read.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 13. Eat what you want and love what you’re doing

quote_verbatim: By the way, this relates to the subject of corporate compensation. You’re in a job which you would pay to have, if that were the only way to get it, and you’re supposed to be an exemplar from other people — for other people. There’s a lot to be said for not paying yourself very well. (Applause.)
concept: Munger: a chief executive in a job he would pay to have, and who is meant to be an exemplar, should not pay himself very well.
evolution_notes: One exchange with Buffett's reply at line 249, which states a separate lesson and is rowed separately (the 2006 convention). Compare M2003-055 (the manager who gets rich with his shareholders).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 13. Eat what you want and love what you’re doing

quote_verbatim: Well, if you think about it, you know, the idea that CEO compensation represents a market system and that you have to pay some guy a $10 million retention bonus or something to stay around in the job that, you know, he’s been fighting to keep and stacking the board and everything so they keep him around. I mean, it’s — I don’t know of a CEO in America — I’m sure there are a few — but I don’t know of any that wouldn’t gladly do the job at half the price or a quarter of the price. And I’ve seen some that have left jobs paying them eight figures and nobody’s offered them anything, you know, a year later or two years later. I wonder where that wonderful market system is that is supposed to have all these bidders for their services.
concept: Test the claim that CEO pay is set by a market: would he do the job for far less, and does anyone bid for him once he leaves?
evolution_notes: Replies to Munger's row on line 247, "He points that out to me regularly. (Laughs)"; one exchange, two rows. Restates M2000-091 (CEO pay is not set by a market).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 13. Eat what you want and love what you’re doing

quote_verbatim: I mean, you have to find out what really — what’s your passion in life? You know, it’s a terrible mistake to kind of sleepwalk through your life, because unless Shirley MacLaine is right, you know, it’s the only one you’re going to have. [...] But when you’re in a position to make choices, you know, I always tell the kids that come visit me, I tell them, “Go to work for an organization you admire or an individual you admire.” [...] The idea — you know, you can’t get a bad result.
concept: Find your passion rather than sleepwalk through life, and when free to choose, work for an organization or a person you admire.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct. The first elision skips how he found his passion in his father's office books, "just plain lucky" (lines 261-263); the second skips "That means many of them become self-employed" (a joke). Then his two years with Ben Graham: "I never asked my salary when I took that job" (line 265). Compare M2000-096 and M2002-038 (qualities admired in others).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 14. Follow your passion and marry the right spouse

quote_verbatim: So just be sure you — and be sure and get the right spouse. That’s enormously important. [...] But it’s enormously important who you marry. I mean, it’s a huge, huge, huge decision. And, you know, if you’re lucky in a couple things like that, you’re going to have a happy life. And you’re going to behave better as you go along.
concept: Choosing a spouse is a huge decision; getting it and one's work right makes for a happy life and better conduct.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct. The elision skips Munger's joke about the perfect woman, retold by Buffett. Then: "it’s a lot easier to behave well when things are going your way and you are enjoying your work" (line 267). New in the read.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 14. Follow your passion and marry the right spouse

quote_verbatim: Well, of course, you’ll do better if you develop a passion for something in which you have a considerable aptitude. I think if Warren had gone into the ballet — (laughter) - nobody would have ever heard of him.
concept: Munger: passion pays best when joined to real aptitude.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct. Qualifies Buffett's row on lines 261-263; Buffett answers "if you find something that turns you on, you probably do have some talent for it" (line 271), which reconciles the two, so no tension row.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 14. Follow your passion and marry the right spouse

quote_verbatim: I think the ability to communicate, both in writing and orally, is of enormous importance, under taught. [...] But if you can communicate well, you have an enormous advantage. And to you, who are talking to the group of introverted people — and, believe me, I was in certain ways quite introverted — it — you know, it’s important to get out there and do it while you’re young. If you wait until you’re 50 it’s probably too late. But if you do it while you’re young, just force yourself into situations where you have to develop those abilities.
concept: Learn to communicate in writing and speech, an under-taught and enormous advantage, by forcing yourself into it while young.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct. The elision skips that business schools would not find an instructor for it. Before it, his own fear and the Dale Carnegie course, the first check stopped (line 279); after it, learning in a group of people with the same problem (lines 281-283). New in the read.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 15. How Buffett overcame his fear of public speaking

quote_verbatim: We follow the dictates of the regulatory bodies that tell us what to do. And in the end they give us a fair return on the assets employed, and we will get that return whatever the assets may be. If they tell us to put in coal assets, we’ll get a return out of that. So from our standpoint, from the standpoint of profitability, it’s neutral.
concept: A regulated utility earns a fair return on whatever assets the regulators direct, so the choice of assets is profit-neutral to the owner.
evolution_notes: The surrounding answer is about public policy tradeoffs (lines 295-297), not rowed. Compare M2007-112 and the FY2007 letter's "good" category, utilities that will "invest many billions" to earn more (lines 405-406, in L2007-009's notes). Dave Sokol's answers at lines 227-229 and 301-303 are another speaker's and not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 16. Klamath River dam economics

quote_verbatim: And he found out it worked modestly — very modestly — well because he was right about four times out of five but the time he was wrong tended to kill him on the other four.
concept: Pair trading, long one security and short another, can be right four times in five and still lose, because the one wrong pair wipes out the other four (Graham's experience).
evolution_notes: The mistake is Ben Graham's hedge fund of the mid-1920s, narrated by Buffett. Restates M2002-089. Compare the "four times out of five" of M2008-007 on options, a different mechanism.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 17. Long-short strategy wasn’t a big money maker

quote_verbatim: And, generally speaking, I think if you’ve got some very good ideas on businesses that are undervalued, it’s really unnecessary to do any shorting out of the market. [...] and now there’s something called 130-30, where you’re long 130 percent long, short 30 percent. That stuff is all basically a bunch of stuff just to try and sell you the idea of the day. It doesn’t really have any great statistical merit. But the fish bite, as Charlie says.
concept: With good ideas on undervalued businesses no market short is needed; packaged long-short formulas are the idea of the day sold to investors, without real statistical merit.
evolution_notes: The elision skips "money managers always have some popular proposal that’s being sold to the potential investors". Before it, the partnership's shorting of the general market with stock borrowed from universities, "probably made some extra money on it in the ’60s" (lines 311-315). "The fish bite" is Munger's line, spoken by Buffett. Restates M2001-039, M2004-111 and M2007-064 on fashionable vehicles.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 17. Long-short strategy wasn’t a big money maker

quote_verbatim: Yeah. We made our money by being long some wonderful businesses. We didn’t make it by a long-short strategy.
concept: Munger: the money was made by owning wonderful businesses, not by long-short strategies.
evolution_notes: Follows Buffett's row on line 315 in the same exchange, a separate statement, so its own row.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 17. Long-short strategy wasn’t a big money maker

quote_verbatim: So you have the same issue with the same broker at the same time being sold at 11.3 percent and 6 percent. Those are marks of extreme dislocation, and you find those occasionally. You found that after the Long-Term Capital Management crisis is 1998. You found the equivalent of it in the stock market in 1974, and so on. And those are great times to make unusual amounts of money.
concept: The same security selling at two very different prices at once marks an extreme dislocation; such times recur occasionally and are the times to make unusual amounts of money.
evolution_notes: The worked case is the tax-exempt auction-rate securities, a museum issue marketed at 3.5 percent one week and 8 percent the next (lines 327-329). Then: "There very well could be some great opportunities out there that Charlie and I will no longer spot because we just can’t be looking at that many things" (line 333), restating M2008-015. Restates M2005-081 (dislocations are where great opportunities lie); the simultaneous-two-prices check is new in the read.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 18. Big opportunities often don’t last long

quote_verbatim: Yeah. What is interesting is that — how brief these opportunities to take advantage of dislocations frequently are. Some idiot hedge fund bought unlimited municipal bonds at, you know, incredible margins. [...] But the dislocation was very brief. [...] So if you can’t think fast and act resolutely, it does you no good. So you’re like a man standing by a stream trying to spear a fish and the fish just comes by once a week or once a month or once every ten years. And you’ve got to be there to throw that spear fast before the fish swims on.
concept: Munger: dislocations are often brief, so they are of use only to someone ready to think fast and act resolutely when the rare fish swims by.
evolution_notes: The second elision crosses Buffett's interjection "But very extreme" and Munger's echo (lines 337-341); Munger resumes the same thought. The hedge fund that borrowed to buy "20 times more municipal bonds than they could afford" (line 335) is the cause named, a third party's error. Then: "It’s a pretty demanding business if you do it right" (line 343), and "It happens about twice a century" (line 347), a quip. Compare M2007-011 (cash ready for chaos); new in the read.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 18. Big opportunities often don’t last long

quote_verbatim: So Charlie and I — you know, we’ve never tried to do in some master stroke — convert Berkshire into something four times as large. People have done that sometimes in business. But we’ve sort of felt that if we kept doing what we understood, and did it consistently, and had fun while we were doing it, that it would be something quite large at some point. [...] And we will have added something. And that’s an automatic formula for getting ahead, but it’s not an automatic formula for galloping ahead.
concept: Build by compounding, not by a master stroke: keep doing what you understand, consistently, keep what you have and add to it; that gets ahead without galloping.
evolution_notes: Opens: "it just takes time. I mean, it’s the nature of compound interest" (line 357). The elision skips "there’s nothing magic" and keeping all present businesses while most do better (lines 357-359). Then the Gypsy Rose Lee joke, businesses "2-inches higher, plus some more businesses" (line 359). Compare M2008-016 (sit with first-class businesses); new in the read as a formula.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 19. “Automatic formula for getting ahead”

quote_verbatim: Yeah. You’ve got to remember that it’s the nature of things that most small businesses will never be big businesses. It’s also in the nature of things that most small — most big businesses — eventually fall into mediocrity or worse. So it’s a tough game out there.
concept: Munger: the base rates are harsh; most small businesses never become big, and most big businesses eventually fall into mediocrity or worse.
evolution_notes: Then: "the players of the game all have to die", and Berkshire has built from scratch only one large business, the reinsurance department, "so we’re a one-trick pony" (lines 361-365). Compare L2006-001 (size makes organizations smug); new in the meeting rows read so far.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 19. “Automatic formula for getting ahead”

quote_verbatim: So they were paying us a fee which was higher to write insurance which would only be paid, not only if the municipality didn’t pay, but the original bond insurer didn’t pay. [...] And they had to pay and they — in fact, the only way we’re going to pay is if they went broke. So it tells you something about the meaning of triple-A in the reinsurance — in the bond insurance — field in the first quarter of 2008.
concept: What buyers will pay for a second guarantee behind a triple-A guarantor shows what the market really thinks the rating is worth.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the rates, about two percent against the original insurer's one percent. Before it, the municipal bond insurance business built from a standing start by Ajit Jain (line 377). New in the read.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 20. Bond insurance business off to strong start

quote_verbatim: In the case you lay out, the first question you’d have to make is do I understand enough about this business so that the financial statements will tell me the information that’s useful to me in making a judgment about what the future financial statements are going to look like. And in many cases, the answer would be no. Probably in a great majority of the cases it would be no.
concept: First ask whether you understand the business well enough that its past financial statements tell you what its future ones will look like; usually the answer is no.
evolution_notes: Lead-in: "what everybody is doing in investment, is they’re laying out money now to get more money back later on" and the farm judged by bushels per acre, not the market (line 389), restating M1999-010 and M2008-003. Compare M2003-092 (knowing what a business does is not knowing its economics).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 21. We prefer “the business which drowns in cash”

quote_verbatim: Now, I couldn’t say the stock was worth X or 105 percent of X or 95 percent of X, but if I could buy it at 40 percent of X, I would feel that I had this margin of safety that Graham would talk about, and I could make a decision. Most times I wouldn’t be able to make it. [...] It could have been a hula hoop business; it could have been a pet rock business. You know, on the other hand it could have been Microsoft early on. So unless I know the nature of the business, the financial statements aren’t going to tell me much, you know.
concept: Value cannot be fixed to within a few percent, but a price near 40 percent of a rough value gives a margin of safety to decide on; and financial statements say little without knowing the nature of the business.
evolution_notes: The elision skips "I wouldn’t know — if you hand me a bunch of financial statements and you don’t tell me what the business is, there’s no way I could make a judgment as to what’s going to happen". The pet rock restates L1993-022 (fad against durable franchise); the margin of safety restates M2008-001 and M2007-027.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 21. We prefer “the business which drowns in cash”

quote_verbatim: The majority of the securities Charlie and I bought, we’ve never met the management and never talked to them, but we have primarily worked off financial statements, our general understanding of business, and some specific understanding of the industry in the business we’re buying.
concept: Most marketable purchases are made without meeting management, from financial statements, general business understanding and specific knowledge of the industry.
evolution_notes: Before it, Wrigley: "if I see the financial statements on Wrigley, I know something about the business" (line 393). Restates M2005-015 and M2007-081.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 21. We prefer “the business which drowns in cash”

quote_verbatim: Yeah. I think there’s one metric that catches a lot of people. We tend to prefer the business which drowns in cash. It just makes so much money that the main — one of the main — principles of owning it is you have all this cash coming in. There are other businesses, like the construction equipment business of my old friend John Anderson. And he used to say about his business “You work hard all year, and at the end of the year there’s your profit sitting in the yard.” There was never any cash. Just more used construction equipment. We tend to hate businesses like that.
concept: Munger: prefer the business that drowns its owner in cash; avoid the one whose profit ends the year as more equipment in the yard and never as cash.
evolution_notes: John Anderson's line is a third party's, spoken by Munger. Restates M1998-085 (seek those that drown you in cash) and M2003-122 (profit that must stay in the business). Buffett's reply at line 397 states a separate lesson and has its own row.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 21. We prefer “the business which drowns in cash”

quote_verbatim: Yeah. It’s a lot easier to understand a business that’s mailing you a check every month. [...] But that’s because it is a business that gives you cash. [...] There are a lot of things that I wouldn’t buy, you know, if I knew the — actually, there are a lot of businesses I wouldn’t buy if I thought the management was the most wonderful in the world because, if they were in the wrong business, it really doesn’t make much difference.
concept: A business that sends its owner cash is easier to understand and value; and a wonderful management in the wrong business makes little difference.
evolution_notes: The first elision skips the apartment house valued from knowledge of its city and its financial statements; the second skips "there can be surprises in that arena as well. But I’ve bought a lot of things off financial statements". Replies to Munger's row on line 395. The wrong-business clause restates L2006-006 and M2007-086; compare the FY2007 letter's L2007-006 (the superstar test), which runs the other way.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 21. We prefer “the business which drowns in cash”

quote_verbatim: You can read the newspapers. You should just sop it up. And you’ll find out what’s the most interesting to you. [...] But you just can’t learn enough in life. And I think the fact — what you’ll find is the more you learn, the more you want to learn.
concept: Read widely and daily, a newspaper first, and let interest find its direction; the more you learn the more you want to learn.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct. Opens: "I would get in the habit [...] of reading a daily newspaper" (line 421). The elision skips his own path from the sports pages to the finance pages. Restates M2007-019 (read widely). Munger: "You’ve got it made" (line 425), a courtesy.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 23. Buffett’s advice to a 12-year-old

quote_verbatim: It really makes no difference to us. We evaluate all kinds of businesses. And what we do want is we want a business with a durable competitive advantage, which both of the companies you named do. And we want something we understand. And we want a management that we like and trust. And then we want a price that makes sense.
concept: Whether high margin with modest growth or global reach with lower margin makes no difference; the tests are a durable competitive advantage, an understood business, management liked and trusted, and a sensible price.
evolution_notes: The question set See's (over 20 percent on sales, "OK" growth) against Lindt (14 percent, global), lines 431-435. Restates M2005-043 and the FY2007 letter's four criteria (lines 312-313, named in L2007-004's notes), and L1994-018.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 24. “We never urge people to sell good businesses”

quote_verbatim: I always tell the manager, the best thing to do if you’ve got a wonderful private business is just keep it. It’s going to be worth more next year and the year after. So there’s no reason to sell a wonderful business except for kind of extraneous factors. [...] But there’s no need — if you’ve got a business worth a billion dollars, you don’t need the billion dollars — you’ve got a business that’s worth a billion dollars — any more than if you’ve got a farm that’s worth a million dollars. You’ve already got the million dollars. You just happen to have it in the farm. And if you like farming, you keep it. So we never urge people to sell good businesses. We urge them to keep them.
concept: An owner of a wonderful business already has its value and need not convert it to cash; keep it unless extraneous factors such as family, taxes or heirs force a sale.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the extraneous factors, "family situations [...] taxes [...] there isn’t another potential heir" (line 437). Then: when they do sell, "they can keep more of the attributes that they love in that business by selling it to Berkshire than they can, by far, selling it to anyone else" (line 439). The owner's side of R1995-011 (good businesses are not sold at any price).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 24. “We never urge people to sell good businesses”

quote_verbatim: But it’s our job to look at hundreds of things and, in terms of marketable securities, buy what we think are the most attractive ones, among the ones we understand and like as a businesses. And then occasionally we get the chance to buy an entire business. We never do that at a bargain price. It just doesn’t happen. People don’t do that. The stock market gives you bargain prices; individual owners won’t. But when we get a chance to do that at a fair price, we like doing it. [...] we aren’t going to look for a given confectionary company and say, “Regardless of price, we’re going to do this,” because we don’t do anything when the phrase “regardless of price” enters into the sentence.
concept: Bargains come from the stock market, never from private owners, so whole businesses are bought at fair prices; and nothing is done once the phrase regardless of price enters the sentence.
evolution_notes: Before it: managers who call their own stock "the most attractive investment in the world" when "There are thousands of possible investments" (lines 441-443). The elision skips "We love building Berkshire with a bunch of businesses with favorable long-term economic characteristics". Compare R1995-011, where "Regardless of price" governs selling good businesses, not buying; the bargains-from-the-market point is new in the meeting rows read so far.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 24. “We never urge people to sell good businesses”

quote_verbatim: Yeah. I watched a man build up a business in southern California, which was a wonderful business. And the time came to sell it — and he devoted his whole life to creating it — he sold it to a known crook who was obviously going to ruin the business just because he could get a slightly higher price. I think that’s an insane way to live a life if you own a prosperous business. I think the better course is to sell to somebody you know is going to be a good steward of what you’ve created.
concept: Munger: an owner selling a life's work should choose a buyer who will be a good steward over a known crook offering a slightly higher price.
evolution_notes: The mistake is an unnamed southern California owner's, narrated by Munger, who draws the lesson. Compare L2000-008 and M2006-003 (the seller who cares where the business goes).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 24. “We never urge people to sell good businesses”

quote_verbatim: So it doesn’t bother me to buy businesses around the world, unhedged in terms of their currency, and have a fair amount of our earnings coming from earnings that originate in other currencies and which I will convert at current rates to dollars at some time in the future. [...] So we are not in the business of hedging currencies, basically. We do not have a lot of hedges set up.
concept: Own businesses earning in other major currencies without hedging, since the harm would come only from a large depreciation of those currencies against one's own.
evolution_notes: The reasoning before it is partly a forecast, "if I had to bet my life one way or another over 10 years, I would probably bet that the dollar would weaken" (line 457), not rowed, and the Mars-currency illustration, "I don’t think I’d put all the billion in U.S. dollars" (line 459). The elision skips Coca-Cola's foreign earnings, "Basically I like that" (line 459). Restates M1994-074 and M1994-075. Munger: "Nothing to add" (line 463).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 25. Dollar will probably weaken over time

quote_verbatim: Well, if I work with small sums of money — and I’d be happy doing that — it would just open up thousands of possibilities to me. And you might very well — certainly we found very mispriced bonds, where we could come nowhere near buying a position of enough size in Berkshire to make a difference, but where it would have made a difference if you were working with a million dollars. [...] An enterprising person can find a lot of different ways to make money. You’ll find most of them will be in small stocks. If you’re working with small money, they’ll be in small stocks or in some specialized bond situations.
concept: With small sums, look across thousands of possibilities, mostly small stocks and specialized bond situations, where mispricings too small for a giant can matter.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the cheap Korean stocks, "It wouldn’t be in currencies with small amounts", and Tom Knapp's friend buying tax liens (line 473). Restates M2007-059, M2006-072 and this session's M2008-015. Munger: "Sure. (Laughter)" (line 477).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 26. Small stocks and mispriced bonds offer opportunities

quote_verbatim: And it gets back to that saying I’ve said many times that you want to buy stock in a business that’s so good that an idiot can run it because sooner or later one will. (Laughter)
concept: Buy a business so good that an idiot could run it, because eventually one will.
evolution_notes: A general rule stated inside a political answer about presidential candidates; the politics are left out of the quote. Restates M2005-080 word for word in substance; compare M1999-106 and M2006-066, and the FY2007 letter's superstar test (L2007-006). | ERRATUM 2026-10-04: "word for word in substance" should read "in substance"; M2005-080's wording was not compared
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 27. Pandering politicians behave better in office

quote_verbatim: I think in any event, when the time comes, they’ll want to pick somebody reasonably young, because I think, on balance, it’s good idea to have a long run at this job, and I think it aids in acquisition and being able to make promises to people about how their businesses will be treated and so on.
concept: Choose a chief executive young enough for a long run, because promises to sellers about how their businesses will be treated need someone who will be there to keep them.
evolution_notes: Berkshire succession, with the general principle stated (a long tenure backs promises to sellers). New in the read.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 28. “There will be no gap after my death”

quote_verbatim: I would still end up making the decisions, and they would probably chafe at the idea of not being able to make the decisions. [...] But in the end, I wanted to make decisions, and I — if Ben Graham made them differently — you know, I actually prefer to make my own decisions. And anybody that manages money well is going to feel that way.
concept: Anyone who manages money well will want to make his own decisions, so a capable investment manager will not sit as an understudy.
evolution_notes: Why the four investment candidates are not hired now (lines 511-513). The elision skips his years with Ben Graham, "I loved the man enormously". Compare L2006-013 (independent thinking) and M2000-134 (a trusted manager runs his portfolio wholly alone). New in the read.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 28. “There will be no gap after my death”

quote_verbatim: There are situations you will see over a long period of time. I mean, you will see things that it would be a mistake — if you’re working with smaller sums — it would be a mistake not to have half your net worth in. I mean, there — you really do, sometimes in securities, see things that are lead-pipe cinches. And you’re not going to see them often and they’re not going to be talking about them on television or anything of the sort, but there will be some extraordinary things happen in a lifetime where you can put 75 percent of your net worth or something like that in a given situation.
concept: A few times in a lifetime an investor with smaller sums sees a near-certainty that no one is talking about; then it is a mistake not to put half or more of net worth in it.
evolution_notes: Before it: "several times I had 75 percent of my net worth in one situation" (line 539), and Munger's "more than a hundred percent of my net worth invested in things" with Buffett's reply "That’s because you had a friendly banker" (lines 537-539), a joke. Restates M2004-041 and L1993-026; the same answer's leverage warning is the next row.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 29. “Diversification is for the know-nothing investor”

quote_verbatim: The problem has been the guys that have put 500 percent of their net worth in. You know, I mean, if you look at — just take LTCM. Very smart guys. Very decent guys. Some friends of mine. High grade. Knew their business. But they put, you know, maybe 25 times their net worth into things that were a cinch, if they hadn’t have gone in that heavily. I mean, they were in things that had to converge, but they didn’t get to play out the hand. But if they’d have had a hundred percent of their net worth in them, it would have worked out fine.
concept: Concentration is not the danger, leverage is: smart, decent people who knew their business were ruined by positions that had to converge because borrowing kept them from playing out the hand.
evolution_notes: The mistake is Long-Term Capital Management's, narrated by Buffett. Then: "If they would have had 200 percent of their net worth in it, it would have worked out fine. But they instead went to, you know, maybe 2500 percent" (line 541). Restates M2007-050 ("anything times zero") and M2004-028; compare M2006-079 (never be where another can force your hand).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 29. “Diversification is for the know-nothing investor”

quote_verbatim: If you could have bought Cap Cities with Tom Murphy running it in the early — in 1974, it was selling at a third or a fourth what the properties were worth and you had the best manager in the world running the place and you had a business that was pretty damn good even if the manager wasn’t. You could have put a hundred percent of your net worth in there and not worry. [...] It would be far more dangerous to do a whole bunch of other things that brokers were recommending to people.
concept: A good business, bought at a third of its worth and run by a superb manager, is safer as a whole net worth than a spread of recommended holdings.
evolution_notes: The elision skips Coca-Cola around the time it was bought, "that would not have been a dangerous position". Before it: "Berkshire was not in a cinch category. It was in the strong probability category, I think" (line 541). Compare M1994-069; the Cap Cities case in these terms is new in the read.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 29. “Diversification is for the know-nothing investor”

quote_verbatim: And some of these people write articles in the newspaper and other places and they say, “Well, the whole secret of investment is diversification.” That’s the mantra. They’ve got it exactly back-ass-ward. The whole secret of investment is to find places where it’s safe and wise to non-diversify. It’s just that simple. Diversification is for the know-nothing investor; it’s not for the professional.
concept: Munger: the secret of investment is not diversification but finding places where it is safe and wise not to diversify; diversification is for the know-nothing investor.
evolution_notes: Lead-in: students at elite schools "learn corporate finance the way it’s now taught" (line 545). Restates M1996-040 and M2004-041. Buffett's reply at line 547 states the other half and has its own row.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 29. “Diversification is for the know-nothing investor”

quote_verbatim: And there’s nothing wrong with the know-nothing investor practicing it. It’s exactly what they should practice. It’s exactly what a good professional investor should not practice. [...] It — a know-nothing investor will get decent results as long as they know they’re a knownothing investor, diversify as to time they purchase their equities, and as to the equities they purchase. That’s crazy for somebody that really knows what they’re doing. And you will find opportunities that, if you put 20 percent of your net worth in it, you’ll have wasted the opportunity of a lifetime, you know, in terms of not really loading up.
concept: The investor who knows he knows nothing should diversify across equities and across purchase dates; one who really knows should load up, since 20 percent in a lifetime opportunity wastes it.
evolution_notes: The elision skips "But that’s — you know, there’s no contradiction in that". Then: "very seldom do we get to buy as much of any good idea as we would like to" (line 549). Replies to Munger's row on line 545; one exchange, two rows. Restates L1993-025, L1993-026, M1994-070 and M2002-011, and the FY2007 letter's L2007-018 (the know-nothings must win).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 29. “Diversification is for the know-nothing investor”

quote_verbatim: And I would — you should — in my view, you should look at your overall financial condition and not worry about where the location of the assets will be. So if you have a net worth of X and you have 20 percent of it in a 401(k) and 30 percent outright and so on like that, just look at the whole picture and decide what mix of assets, what type of assets you want, and don’t treat them as being in separate pots.
concept: Decide the asset mix on the whole financial position, not account by account; money in different accounts is one pot.
evolution_notes: Then Berkshire's own practice, separate insurance portfolios, "I don’t even think about what entity anything is in" (line 573). Munger adds the one exception (line 577), rowed separately. New in the read.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 31. Diversification, IRAs, and brokerage accounts

quote_verbatim: Yeah. Occasionally, you’ll find an investment that is going to produce a huge amount of taxable income. It’s a junk bond paying a high yield that’s taxable or something. So some items are more suitable for those retirement accounts that get tax-deferral benefits. But apart from that, it’s all one pot. Sure.
concept: Munger: place high-taxable-income holdings in tax-deferred accounts; otherwise treat all accounts as one pot.
evolution_notes: Qualifies Buffett's row on line 573 in the same exchange. New in the read.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 31. Diversification, IRAs, and brokerage accounts

quote_verbatim: Well, I’ll be very simple: I — under the conditions you name, I’d probably have it all in a very low-cost index fund, and it would probably be — you know might be Vanguard — somebody I knew was reliable, somebody where the cost was low. And because you postulated that you’re not going to become a professional investor, I would recognize the fact that I’m an amateur investor, and I would feel that a — unless bought during a strong bull market, which this hasn’t been — I would feel that that was going to outperform, to a degree, bonds, under current conditions over a long period of time, and then I’d forget it and go back to work.
concept: An amateur who will not become a professional should put the money in a reliable, very low-cost index fund, avoid buying in a strong bull market, and then forget it.
evolution_notes: The question: $1 million at 30, a full-time job elsewhere (line 633). Restates M1999-065, M2002-010, M2002-011 and M2004-059. The expectation that the index will beat bonds over a long period is a forecast and is kept in the quote only as the reason given.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 35. Amateurs should stick with low-cost index funds

quote_verbatim: Yeah. It’s in the nature of things that you aren’t going to have a whole lot of screamingly successful professional investors. You’ve got a great horde of professionals taking croupiers profits out of the system, most of them by pretending to be professional investors, and that is in the nature of things, too. But if you don’t have any rational prospects of being a very skilled professional investor, of course you should compromise on some simple thing like an index fund.
concept: Munger: very skilled professionals are rare and most professionals take a croupier's cut, so anyone without a rational prospect of real skill should settle for an index fund.
evolution_notes: Between Buffett's rows on lines 635 and 639, a separate statement. Restates M1997-031. Then at line 641, "do not judge stockbrokers generally by the ones you meet at this meeting": a joke, not rowed.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 35. Amateurs should stick with low-cost index funds

quote_verbatim: Yeah. And that — you will not get that advice from anybody because nobody gets paid to give you that advice. So you will have all kinds of people telling you how much better they can do for you than that, and how if you just give them a wrap fee, or give them commissions, or whatever it may be, that they will do better, but they won’t do better. On average, you know, if a thousand other people like you do the same thing, that group of a thousand will do worse if they listen to the people that make pitches at them. And in the end, why should you expect — I mean, you’ve got a very perfectly decent return over a 30- or 40-year period by doing what I suggest. And why should you expect more than that when you don’t bring anything to the party?
concept: Ask who is paid to give advice: no one is paid to recommend the index fund, so the pitches will promise better; as a group those who listen do worse, and one who brings nothing to the party should not expect more.
evolution_notes: Then: "The salesman will tell you that you’ll get it, but you won’t" (line 639). Restates M2004-060 and the FY2007 letter's L2007-018 and L2007-019 (the helper-aided group must be below average).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 35. Amateurs should stick with low-cost index funds

quote_verbatim: Well, Charlie and I have always been big fans of living within your income, and if you do that, you’ll have a whole lot more income later on. [...] So I don’t — I don’t advocate — I may practice — but I don’t advocate extreme frugality. The — and I don’t say that it’s always better to be saving 10 percent of your income instead of 5 percent of your income. I think it’s crazy to be spending 105 percent of your income, and I think that leads to all kinds of problems, and I get letters from people every day that have experienced those problems.
concept: Live within your income; how much to save is a choice, and extreme frugality is not required, but spending more than you make leads to trouble.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct. The elision skips that children follow their parents' example, the warning that too strict a parent gets "the reverse effect", and the case against deferring a family's enjoyment for a bigger boat at 75 (lines 651-653). Compare Munger's M1999-094 ("grossly underspending income"), which goes further than Buffett here; listed under Tensions seen.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 36. No “extreme frugality” but don’t spend more than you make

quote_verbatim: But, you know, in the end you want to have an internal score card. I mean, you are not a better person or a worse person because you live a different kind of life than your neighbor. Live a life that, you know, is true to yourself.
concept: Keep an internal scorecard: judge yourself by your own standards, not by how your life compares with the neighbors'.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct; the answer to keeping up with the Joneses (line 649). The internal scorecard is new in the read.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 36. No “extreme frugality” but don’t spend more than you make

quote_verbatim: Yeah. It’s obviously the best method to train your children to provide the proper example. [...] But of course, even if you do provide the proper example, it’s likely not to work — [...] — some of the time anyway.
concept: Munger: the best way to train children is by example, though even that fails some of the time.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct. The elisions cross Buffett's interjections ("I think we’re hearing a child that didn’t get that advice", line 659, and "It’s noon", line 663); Munger resumes the same thought each time. Agrees with Buffett at line 651 (children follow their parents' example).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 36. No “extreme frugality” but don’t spend more than you make

quote_verbatim:
But I don’t want to have it slim. I want to have it none. So I regard myself as the Chief Risk Officer at Berkshire.

And I think that the discipline, mild as it may be, of telling managements that you’re going to have to value this stuff at market may keep them from doing things that they would otherwise do that would be very stupid if they think they can get away with valuing them at some fictitious — or at cost — which would be fictitious, in terms of markets.

quote_verbatim: But neither Charlie Munger, my partner in running Berkshire, nor I can predict the winning and losing years in advance. (In our usual opinionated view, we don't think anyone else can either.) We're certain, for example, that the economy will be in shambles throughout 2009 � and, for that matter, probably well beyond � but that conclusion does not tell us whether the stock market will rise or fall.
concept: Nobody can call the up and down years in advance, and even a confident view that the economy will be bad says nothing about which way the market will move.
evolution_notes: Restates L1994-004 (ignore macro forecasts) in part; the new point is that a near-certain economic forecast still yields no market forecast. Preceded by the guess that about 75% of years will again be positive (lines 131-132), a forecast, not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: BERKSHIRE HATHAWAY INC.

quote_verbatim: In good years and bad, Charlie and I simply focus on four goals: (1) maintaining Berkshire's Gibraltar-like financial position, which features huge amounts of excess liquidity, near-term obligations that are modest, and dozens of sources of earnings and cash; (2) widening the "moats" around our operating businesses that give them durable competitive advantages; (3) acquiring and developing new and varied streams of earnings; (4) expanding and nurturing the cadre of outstanding operating managers who, over the years, have delivered Berkshire exceptional results.
concept: The owner's standing agenda in every year: an overwhelmingly liquid financial position with modest near-term obligations, wider moats, new and varied earnings streams, and more outstanding managers.
evolution_notes: The list is new as a list in the letters read so far; its parts restate L2002-019 (fortress of financial strength) and L2005-010 (widening the moat daily). Printed as an indented numbered list; the quote joins the items as printed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: BERKSHIRE HATHAWAY INC.

quote_verbatim: During 2008 I did some dumb things in investments. I made at least one major mistake of commission and several lesser ones that also hurt. I will tell you more about these later. Furthermore, I made some errors of omission, sucking my thumb when new facts came in that should have caused me to re-examine my thinking and promptly take action.
concept: When new facts arrive that bear on a held view, failing to re-examine the view and act promptly is itself an error, an error of omission.
evolution_notes: Buffett's own mistake. The commission is named later as ConocoPhillips and two Irish banks (lines 834-844), narrated without a further lesson. "Sucking my thumb" is Munger's phrase per M2001-007; errors of omission as the costliest kind: M2001-004 (both meeting rows). Related to L2005-009 (not moving immediately on Gen Re's trading operation).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Berkshire in 2008

quote_verbatim: Additionally, the market value of the bonds and stocks that we continue to hold suffered a significant decline along with the general market. This does not bother Charlie and me. Indeed, we enjoy such price declines if we have funds available to increase our positions. Long ago, Ben Graham taught me that "Price is what you pay; value is what you get." Whether we're talking about socks or stocks, I like buying quality merchandise when it is marked down.
concept: A fall in the price of holdings is welcome when there is money to add, because price and value are different things and quality bought marked down is the aim.
evolution_notes: The maxim is Graham's, spoken by Buffett, source named in the quote. Restates in substance R1996-002 (short-term price changes meaningless except as a chance to increase ownership), a report row, so rowed here under the letter rule for earlier letters only. Just before it: "When investing, pessimism is your friend, euphoria the enemy" (lines 184-185), not rowed, repeats L1997-035.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Berkshire in 2008

That means we must keep our promises; avoid leveraging up acquired businesses; grant unusual autonomy to our managers; and hold the purchased companies through thick and thin (though we prefer thick and thicker). [...] We have a decided advantage, therefore, when we encounter sellers who truly care about the future of their businesses.

A number of these acquirees, purchased only two to three years ago, are now in mortal danger because of the debt piled on them by their private-equity buyers.

evolution_notes: The danger narrated is the private-equity buyers' doing, not Buffett's. Consequently, our guarantee is far more valuable than theirs"). Related to L1994-026 (certain solvency after a catastrophe is what the buyer pays for).

heading: Insurance

quote_verbatim: This 1997-2000 fiasco should have served as a canary-in-the-coal-mine warning for the far-larger conventional housing market. But investors, government and rating agencies learned exactly nothing from the manufactured-home debacle. Instead, in an eerie rerun of that disaster, the same mistakes were repeated with conventional homes in the 2004-07 period: Lenders happily made loans that borrowers couldn't repay out of their incomes, and borrowers just as happily signed up to meet those payments. Both parties counted on "house-price appreciation" to make this otherwise impossible arrangement work.
concept: A smaller market's disaster is a warning for a larger one built the same way; loans that only rising prices can make good repeat the same error at any scale.
evolution_notes: The mistake is investors', government's and the rating agencies' (and the lenders' and borrowers'), not Buffett's. Restates L2007-001 (lenders counting on appreciation) and adds the failure to learn from the manufactured-housing episode (lines 532-541, "borrowers who shouldn't have borrowed being financed by lenders who shouldn't have lent", which Buffett says he wrote somewhat later about that period). Related to M2003-100.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Finance and Financial Products

quote_verbatim: Our borrowers simply looked at how full-bore mortgage payments would compare with their actual � not hoped-for � income and then decided whether they could live with that commitment. Simply put, they took out a mortgage with the intention of paying it off, whatever the course of home prices. Just as important is what our borrowers did not do. They did not count on making their loan payments by means of refinancing. They did not sign up for "teaser" rates that upon reset were outsized relative to their income. And they did not assume that they could always sell their home at a profit if their mortgage payments became onerous.
concept: A loan is sound when the full payment fits the borrower's actual income and he means to pay it off whatever prices do, not when it counts on refinancing, teaser rates or a profitable sale; credit scores did not decide it.
evolution_notes: Lines 557-562 show Clayton's borrowers had a median FICO of 644 against a national 723, so the test is the payment against income, not the score. Lines 588-593 add that foreclosures follow an unpayable monthly payment, not a house worth less than its mortgage (not rowed separately). Related to L2007-001.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Finance and Financial Products

quote_verbatim: But enjoyment and utility should be the primary motives for purchase, not profit or refi possibilities. And the home purchased ought to fit the income of the purchaser. The present housing debacle should teach home buyers, lenders, brokers and government some simple lessons that will ensure stability in the future. Home purchases should involve an honest-to-God down payment of at least 10% and monthly payments that can be comfortably handled by the borrower's income. That income should be carefully verified.
concept: Buy a home to live in, sized to income, with a real down payment and a payment the income comfortably carries; a lender verifies that income.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct for the home buyer and a lending rule for the lender; it instructs buyers and lenders, so it passes the political test, and the next lines on the country's housing objective (lines 604-605) are a policy view, not rowed. Down payments: M2003-100 and M2007-062 (meeting rows).
speaker: BUFFETT

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Finance and Financial Products

quote_verbatim: The monolines (as the bond insurers are called) initially insured only tax-exempt bonds that were low-risk. Some of these involved the insuring of residential mortgage obligations. When housing prices plummeted, the monoline industry quickly became a basket case.

"Back-tested" models of many kinds are susceptible to this sort of error. Nevertheless, they are frequently touted in financial markets as guides to future action. (If merely looking up past financial data would tell you what the future holds, the Forbes 400 would consist of librarians.)

evolution_notes: Printed after a row of asterisks inside the bond-insurance section, so it takes that heading. Generalises the insured-bond test at lines 707-733 (same batch). New in the letters read so far.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Tax-Exempt Bond Insurance

quote_verbatim: Indeed, the stupefying losses in mortgage-related securities came in large part because of flawed, history-based models used by salesmen, rating agencies and investors. These parties looked at loss experience over periods when home prices rose only moderately and speculation in houses was negligible. They then made this experience a yardstick for evaluating future losses. They blissfully ignored the fact that house prices had recently skyrocketed, loan practices had deteriorated and many buyers had opted for houses they couldn't afford. In short, universe "past" and universe "current" had very different characteristics.
concept: Mortgage-security losses came from measuring future losses against a calm past whose conditions no longer held.
evolution_notes: The mistake is the salesmen's, rating agencies' and investors'. The meeting's Moody's question (heading 10) quotes this passage's "flawed history-based models".
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Tax-Exempt Bond Insurance

quote_verbatim: Investors should be skeptical of history-based models. Constructed by a nerdy-sounding priesthood using esoteric terms such as beta, gamma, sigma and the like, these models tend to look impressive. Too often, though, investors forget to examine the assumptions behind the symbols. Our advice: Beware of geeks bearing formulas.
concept: Distrust history-based models and examine the assumptions under their symbols.
evolution_notes: Related to L1993-017 (beta as precise and wrong) and M2008-082 (Munger on torturing reality into a model).
speaker: BUFFETT
