quote_verbatim: However, I have pledged � to you, the rating agencies and myself � to always run Berkshire with more than ample cash. We never want to count on the kindness of strangers in order to meet tomorrow's obligations. When forced to choose, I will not trade even a night's sleep for the chance of extra profits.

The night's-sleep clause restates R1996-009, a report row, so rowed under the letter rule for earlier letters only; related to L2002-019 and M2008-066.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Investments

quote_verbatim: Clinging to cash equivalents or long-term government bonds at present yields is almost certainly a terrible policy if continued for long. Holders of these instruments, of course, have felt increasingly comfortable � in fact, almost smug � in following this policy as financial turmoil has mounted. They regard their judgment confirmed when they hear commentators proclaim "cash is king," even though that wonderful cash is earning close to nothing and will surely find its purchasing power eroded over time.
concept: The comfort of holding cash or long governments in a panic is not evidence of a good policy; at near-zero yields their purchasing power erodes over time.
evolution_notes: Preceded by "The investment world has gone from underpricing risk to overpricing it" and the "U.S. Treasury bond bubble of late 2008" (lines 856-862), a market description. Sits beside L2008-019 (always more than ample cash): the cash Berkshire keeps is for safety, the cash criticised here is a long-run policy; listed under Tensions seen.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Investments

quote_verbatim: Approval, though, is not the goal of investing. In fact, approval is often counter-productive because it sedates the brain and makes it less receptive to new facts or a re-examination of conclusions formed earlier. Beware the investment activity that produces applause; the great moves are usually greeted by yawns.
concept: Do not seek approval in investing; applause dulls the re-examination of earlier conclusions, and the best moves are usually met with indifference.
evolution_notes: Links to L2008-003 (failing to re-examine on new facts). New in the letters read so far.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Investments

quote_verbatim: Derivatives contracts, in contrast, often go unsettled for years, or even decades, with counterparties building up huge claims against each other. "Paper" assets and liabilities � often hard to quantify � become important parts of financial statements though these items will not be validated for many years. Additionally, a frightening web of mutual dependence develops among huge financial institutions. (Imagine, if you will, getting a quote every day on a farm from a manic-depressive neighbor and then using the volatility calculated from these changing quotes as an important ingredient in an equation that predicts a probability-weighted range of values for the farm a century from now.) And it seems that the higher mathematics, with more false precision, should help you. But it doesn’t. The effects, averaged out, are negative when you try and formalize it to the degree you’re talking about.
concept: Munger: elaborate formal projections and discounting breed belief in false precision and, on average, worse decisions.

speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 9. Higher mathematics can be dangerous for investing

quote_verbatim: So, the false precision that goes into saying that this is a two standard deviation event or this is a three standard deviation event, and therefore we can afford to take this much risk and all that, it’s totally crazy. I mean, you saw it with Long-Term Capital Management in 1998. [...] It’s going to arise much more often than people think, in markets that are made by people that get scared and get greedy. And they don’t observe the laws of flipping coins, it’s — in terms of the distribution of results. And it’s a terrible mistake to think that mathematics will take you a long place in investing. You have to understand certain aspects of mathematics. But you don’t have to understand higher mathematics. And higher mathematics may actually be dangerous and it will lead you down pathways that are better left untrod.
concept: Markets made by frightened and greedy people do not follow coin-flip distributions, so risk sized by standard deviations is false precision; higher mathematics can lead an investor astray.

[...] So I think that we still have got the burden of — we still should have to prove by the fact that Berkshire will sell above the earnings we’ve retained.
concept: The retainer of earnings carries the burden of proving that each retained dollar becomes more than a dollar of market value; the test can fail at a market bottom and is read over time alongside the intrinsic-value record.
evolution_notes: The questioner quotes principle 9 of the Owner's Manual (R-row for the $1 test); Buffett concedes the test failed at the year-end price. The elision skips the claim that no five-year period trailed the S&P on the intrinsic-value measure (line 295).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 19. 2008 was tough, but still no plans for dividend

quote_verbatim: Yeah, I don’t get too excited about these oddball things that happen once every 50 years. If you’re reasonably prepared for them and you’re dented a little on the bottom tick, and other people are suffering a lot more, and unusual opportunities are coming to you that you don’t see under other conditions, I don’t think we deserve any salt tears.
concept: Munger: be prepared for rare extreme events so that they only dent you while bringing opportunities others cannot take.
evolution_notes: Related to L2005-021 (a position that can absorb any outcome) and L2008-019 (ample cash).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 19. 2008 was tough, but still no plans for dividend

quote_verbatim: But you — you know, you have to be prepared. You can’t let somebody else get you in a position where you have to sell out your position. Leverage is what causes people trouble in this world. So you don’t — you never want to be in a position where somebody can pull the rug out from under you. And you also never want to be emotionally in a position where you pull the rug out from under yourself. I mean, you don’t want to have other people force you to sell and you don’t want to let your own fears or emotions to cause you to sell at the wrong time.
concept: Never be where a lender can force a sale, and never let one's own fear force one; leverage and emotion are the two ways a sound holding is sold at the wrong time.
evolution_notes: The heading opens with Munger's forecast that Wells Fargo will come out stronger (line 303). Related to M2008-049 (LTCM, leverage), M2008-066 and L2008-019 (never count on the kindness of strangers).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 20. Wells Fargo’s stock price plunge shouldn’t spark selling

quote_verbatim: If they own a farm like I do, you know, 30 miles from here, they don’t get a price on it every day. [...] And you look to the asset itself to determine whether you made an intelligent investment. You have your expectations about what the asset will produce. But people in stocks tend to look at the price. So they let the price tell them how they should feel or — that’s kind of crazy in our view. We think you should look at the business just like you’d look at the apartment house that you bought or the farm you want. They let the fact that a quote is available every day turn into a liability rather than an asset.
concept: Judge a stock as one judges a farm or an apartment house, by what the asset produces, and do not let the daily quote dictate how one feels.
evolution_notes: Ends by sending the listener to chapter 8 of The Intelligent Investor, "how to think about the market" (line 309), as in M2006-077. The farm comparison restates M1994-047, R1996-001 and M2007-076 among others. | ERRATUM 2026-10-04: M1994-047 is cited in error; it defines investing as paying now for future cash and carries no farm comparison. R1996-001 and M2007-076 stand.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 20. Wells Fargo’s stock price plunge shouldn’t spark selling

quote_verbatim: Yeah, well, as I pointed out in the annual report, we are at a significant disadvantage in any financing-type business where we are competing against people who are getting their funding and their financing with a government guarantee. Our raw material costs us a lot more money. [...] But we don’t have an answer for going head-to-head against a government-sponsored business that gets — can raise money with a government guarantee. We do not have a way of going head-to-head with them at any business, no matter how prudently we conduct our operations.
concept: In a business whose raw material is money, a competitor with government-guaranteed funding cannot be beaten by prudence alone.
evolution_notes: Restates L2008-013 at the meeting. Munger replies (line 341) that Berkshire is not regulated like a bank and "we’d be pretty ungrateful if we took this one disadvantage that has come to us and obsessed on it", not rowed separately.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 22. Hard to compete with government-guaranteed debt

quote_verbatim: But he would probably also say if he saw some that were mispriced, he would act accordingly. But he wouldn’t get himself in a position where the problems of the people who didn’t act prudently could cause him any problems.
concept: Act on a mispriced instrument even in a dangerous field, but never in a way that lets other people's imprudence harm you.
evolution_notes: Attributed to Graham by Buffett's conjecture and spoken by Buffett; restated at line 355 ("if he saw something that looked way out of line and he knew he could handle it himself"). Related to L2006-011 and L2002-017.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 23. Graham would probably agree with us on derivatives

quote_verbatim: So derivatives became a way around regulation of leverage in markets, which like I say, Congress felt was important and the Federal Reserve still has a responsibility for enforcing. Derivatives also meant that settlement dates got pushed out. One of the problems in securities markets comes about when you have a trade today, if you had — didn’t have to settle it for a year, you’d find it very hard sometimes to find the person on the other side. [...] As you extend out periods, you get more and more defaults.
concept: Check how an instrument escapes margin limits and how long it leaves settlement open; unlimited leverage and long settlement multiply defaults.
evolution_notes: Restates L2008-022 (long-unsettled claims) at the meeting; the margin-rule point (total return swaps let one "borrow a hundred percent against what you own", line 353) is new. The elision skips "And derivatives allow these very long settlement periods. Whereas security markets demand them in three days. There’s a reason they demand them in three days."
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 23. Graham would probably agree with us on derivatives

quote_verbatim: I think there’s been a deeper problem in the derivative business. The derivative dealer takes two advantages of the customer. One, there’s croupier-style mathematical advantage equivalent to the house advantage in Las Vegas. And two, the derivative dealer is playing in the same game with his own clients, with the advantage of being a better player. So — [...] — and having knowledge of what the clients are doing. This is basically a dirty business. And you’re really selling things to your clients who trust you, that are bad for the clients.
concept: Munger: a dealer who holds a house edge and also trades against clients with knowledge of their positions is selling them things bad for them; the customer should see both edges.
evolution_notes: The elision crosses Buffett's interjection (line 359, "And having knowledge of what they’re doing."), and Munger resumes the same thought. Ends with a public-policy line, "We don’t need more of this kind of thing in America", left out. Related to M2002-114 and M2008-056 (croupiers).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 23. Graham would probably agree with us on derivatives

quote_verbatim: With U.S. Bancorp or Wells, those are companies making lots of money. There’s lots of equity there. So there’s no reason to go up to senior securities and say that they should give up anything when there’s lots of common equity underneath. [...] If you get into a situation where the common equity is wiped out, then you get into a question of — then you get into the proper allocation of things within the capital structure — who gives up so much, and the senior debt may give up something, and so on.
concept: A senior security is safe while there is ample common equity and earning power beneath it; only when the equity is gone does the allocation of loss reach the seniors.
evolution_notes: Asked inside a political question about bank rescues; the general capital-structure point is rowed and the policy left out. The 70 percent mortgage analogy (line 369) and Chrysler, with no common equity and no competitive advantage (line 371), illustrate it.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 24. Bailouts shouldn’t hurt senior debt holders

quote_verbatim: We would own the half of dozen or so stocks we like best. Their — and it wouldn’t have anything to do with what our cost on them was. It would only have to do with our evaluation of their price versus value. It doesn’t make any difference what the cost is. [...] When Charlie and I ran funds, we didn’t worry about whether something was up or down. We worried about what it was worth compared to what it was selling for. And we tried to have most of our money in a relatively few — very few — positions which we thought we knew very well.
concept: Hold the few stocks liked best on price against value, without regard to cost or to whether they have risen or fallen, concentrated in positions known very well.
evolution_notes: Restates M1997-089 (cost basis) and the concentration rows (M2008-048, M2008-052). Munger: "he’s tactfully suggesting that you adopt a different way of thinking" (line 389), a quip. | ERRATUM 2026-10-04: M1997-089 is cited in error; it filters stocks against the government bond and says nothing of cost basis. No earlier row on ignoring cost basis was found.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 25. Ignore original cost when reviewing your portfolio

quote_verbatim: No, our sustainable competitive advantage is we have a culture and a business model, which people are going to find very, very difficult to copy, even semi-copy. [...] But it is a deeply embedded culture which any CEOs that follow are going to be well-versed in when they come into the job, and dedicated to, and able to continue in the future. [...] Our culture, our managers join that culture. Our shareholders join that culture. It gets reinforced all the time. They see that it works.
concept: A competitive advantage can be a self-reinforcing culture and business model that others cannot copy even in part, and that outlasts its founders.
evolution_notes: The first elision skips the shareholder-turnover figures and the offer to private owners (line 401); the second, the remark that copying it elsewhere is impossible (line 403). The questioner had said the advantage was Buffett and Munger themselves.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 26. Berkshire’s competitive advantage no longer requires us

quote_verbatim: A lot of corporations in America are run stupidly from headquarters, as they try and force the divisions to come up with profits for every quarter that are better than the profits from the same quarter in the previous year. And a lot of terrible decisions and terrible practices creep into those businesses. In the Berkshire model, that doesn’t happen.
concept: Munger: headquarters that demand year-over-year quarterly gains from every division breed terrible decisions and practices; watch for it.
evolution_notes: Ends: "the stupidity of management practice in the rest of the corporate world will likely remain ample enough to give this company some comparative advantage way into the future", a forecast. Related to the earnings-smoothing and guidance rows (L1994-027, R1996 rows).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 26. Berkshire’s competitive advantage no longer requires us

quote_verbatim: Well, the answer is we don’t. You know, and — if we lose confidence in the management, if we lose confidence in the durability of the competitive advantage, if we recognize we made a mistake when we went into it — we sell plenty of times. So it’s not unheard of. On the other hand, if you really get a wonderful business with outstanding management — but mostly the wonderful business part of it — when in doubt, keep holding. But it’s no inviolable rule.
concept: Sell a stock when confidence in management or in the durability of the advantage is lost, or the original analysis proves wrong; with a wonderful business, when in doubt keep holding.
evolution_notes: Restated at line 419 with a fourth reason, "Or if we find something more attractive", and the J&J sale to keep cash above a level, which repeats L2008-019's reason. Related to M2008-040 (keep a wonderful business).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 27. We don’t keep every stock, but we do keep every business

quote_verbatim: Now, among the businesses we own, not just securities we own, we have an attitude, which we express in our economic principles, that when we buy a business it’s for keeps. And we make only two exceptions: when they promise to start losing money indefinitely or if we have major labor problems. But otherwise, we are not going to sell something just ’cause we get offered more money for it, even than it’s worth.
concept: A whole business bought is kept, even against an offer above its worth, unless it will lose money indefinitely or has major labor problems.
evolution_notes: Restates the Owner's Manual principle 11 (R1995-011) at the meeting; the same answer says it "probably helps us in terms of buying businesses over time". Shares the printed line with the stock-selling rule (same batch), which it follows.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 27. We don’t keep every stock, but we do keep every business

quote_verbatim: I frequently ask CEOs of companies what they would do differently if they owned the whole place themselves. [...] “What would you do different if this was a hundred percent owned by you and your family?” And they give me a list of things. There is no list at Berkshire. You know, we basically run this place the same way we’d run if we owned a hundred percent of it.
concept: Ask a chief executive what he would do differently if he owned the whole company; the length of the list measures how far public-company pressures bend his management.
evolution_notes: Related to M1995-114. Line 427 continues: sellers know Berkshire will not spin off, sell or "leverage it up", restating L2008-006. | ERRATUM 2026-10-04: M1995-114 is cited in error; it concerns interest rates and value. No earlier row carries the owned-it-all question.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 28. We run Berkshire as if we owned all of it

quote_verbatim: Yeah, generally, I think it’s quite smart to do what you’re talking about — is to identify some investors you regard as very skilled, and carefully examine everything they’re buying, and copy what you please. I think you have a very good idea.
concept: Munger: studying what very skilled investors buy and copying what one chooses is a sensible way to find ideas.
evolution_notes: Followed by "(Laughter)". Buffett before it (line 443) notes the copier lacks free float but has tax advantages; after it (line 447) he says he got some of his own ideas at 21 from Graham-Newman's semi-annual reports, "there’s nothing wrong with that". The heading answers the first part of the question asked under heading 29.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 30. No “quarrel” with copycats

quote_verbatim: Now, the best protection against inflation is your own earning power. If you’re the best teacher, if you’re the best surgeon, if you’re the best lawyer, you know, whatever it may be, you will command a given part of other people’s production of goods and services no matter what the currency is, whether it’s seashells, or reichsmarks, or dollars. [...] The second best protection is a wonderful business. [...] So those are the — and — those are the great assets, your own earning power first, and then the earning power of a wonderful business that does not require heavy capital investment. If it requires heavy capital investment, you get killed in inflation.
concept: Against inflation the best asset is one's own earning power, the next a wonderful business that needs little capital; a capital-heavy business is ruined by inflation.
evolution_notes: Restates M2007-110, M2005-049 and M2005-050. The second elision skips the Coca-Cola example ("people will give up three minutes of labor ... to enjoy ... 12 ounces", line 465). Lines 459-463 (inflation is certain; fixed-dollar investors will pay for the stimulus) are forecasts and political views, not rowed. Munger: "The young man should become a brain surgeon and invest in Coca-Cola instead of government bonds" (line 469), a joke restating it.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 31. Your best inflation protection

quote_verbatim: So, you don’t want to judge consumer preferences by what we do. The newspaper — no. The answer is, for most newspapers in the United States, we would not buy them at any price. They have the possibility, and in certain places, they’ve already hit it, but they have the possibility of just going to unending losses. [...] So they were a product that had pricing power, that was essential to the customer, essential to the advertiser. And they’ve lost that essential nature. [...] And they were only essential to the advertiser as long as they were essential to the reader.
concept: A business whose pricing power rested on being essential to customers, and through them to advertisers, loses both once it stops being essential; such a business may face unending losses and is not bought at any price.
evolution_notes: Restates L2006-007 and L2006-009 (newspaper economics) at the meeting; "essentiality" is Walter Annenberg's word (line 481). "you don’t want to judge consumer preferences by what we do" refers to Buffett and Munger reading five papers a day.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 32. Newspapers are fading but we’re keeping the Buffalo News

quote_verbatim: And as I put in the annual report, in our economic principles, that as long as we don’t think we face unending losses or have major union problems, we will stick with the businesses, even though it would be a mistake if you were acting as a trustee for, you know, a bunch of crippled children or something of the sort. And that’s just our policy at Berkshire.
concept: Berkshire keeps an owned business short of unending losses or major union trouble, while conceding that a trustee bound to maximise value would sell.
evolution_notes: Restates M2009-041 and R1995-011; new is the concession that the policy would be a mistake for a trustee. Shown by act: Buffett told Stan Lipsey "I agree 100 percent. But we’re not going to do it" about selling the Buffalo News when it could have fetched many hundreds of millions (line 483). "It’s not what they teach you in business school" (line 485).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 32. Newspapers are fading but we’re keeping the Buffalo News

quote_verbatim: The service businesses are generally the better businesses. They require less capital and they can be more specialized in the markets they serve, in general.
concept: Service businesses are usually better than capital-heavy ones because they need less capital and can specialise in the markets they serve.
evolution_notes: Said inside a forecast about retailing, manufacturing and services; the forecasts around it (housing equilibrium, shopping-center cap rates of 5 percent "going to look very silly") are not rowed. Related to the capital point in the inflation answer at line 467 (heading 31, same batch).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 33. Expect weak consumer spending for “quite a bit longer”

quote_verbatim: Because I would say most of the repurchasing done in recent years, I’ve thought has been foolish, because people have been paying too much. [...] Like I say, I don’t — I think, probably 90 percent of the repurchase activity I’ve seen in the last five years, I did not think was serving the cause of the shareholder. I thought it was being done because management thought it was the thing to do, and their investor relations department told them it was the thing to do, and they were actually buying stock at kind of silly prices.
concept: A buyback serves owners only below intrinsic value; one done because it is the fashionable thing or for investor relations, at a high price, destroys value.
evolution_notes: Buffett notes his earlier endorsements of repurchases date from the 1970s and early 1980s, when stocks were cheap (line 513). Restates L1999-033 and the earlier repurchase rows (L1994-013, L1997-010 and others). Line 519: "it’s interesting how many companies were buying in their stock at twice present prices that aren’t buying it now."
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 34. We’ll never buy back Berkshire shares at a “silly” price

quote_verbatim: There’s clearly a point where if we thought it was demonstrably below — conservatively estimated — intrinsic business value and we notified the stock holders we were going to do it, we would do it. [...] We will never buy in our stock at a silly price. We may make a mistake by not buying it at a cheap price. But we’ll never make a mistake, I don’t think, by buying it at a silly price.
concept: Repurchase own shares only when they are demonstrably below conservatively estimated intrinsic value, telling owners first; prefer missing a cheap buyback to making a dear one.
evolution_notes: The elision crosses Munger's "I’ve got nothing to add to that, either" (line 517) and Buffett resumes the same thought. Buffett concedes that announcing it "would largely be self-defeating" (line 515).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 34. We’ll never buy back Berkshire shares at a “silly” price

quote_verbatim: When things are moving very fast, when both prices are moving, and in certain cases, intrinsic business value is moving at a pace that’s far greater than we’ve seen for a long time, it means that in terms of calibrating A versus B, versus C, it’s tougher. [...] I mean, we got a call — we got lots of calls. But, most of them, we ignored. But the calls that we got that we ignored helped us calibrate the calls that we paid attention to, too.
concept: Every opportunity is calibrated against the others available, including those declined; in fast markets the comparison is harder and more profitable.
evolution_notes: Restates the opportunity-cost rows of earlier units and M2009-025 (compare every other bush) in this unit.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 35. Crisis made opportunity cost calculations difficult

quote_verbatim: Because we want to always keep a lot of money around. We have all kinds of levels — extra levels of safety — that we follow at Berkshire. And we will never get so we’re dependent on banks or other people’s money or anything else. [...] Our definition of comfortable is really comfortable. We want to have billions and billions and billions around. And then we’ll think about what we do with the surplus.
concept: Fix the cash cushion first, never depending on banks or others' money, and only then decide what to do with the surplus.
evolution_notes: Restates L2008-019 at the meeting and M2009-030. Shown by act: the J&J sale with a floor price so as not to end up "a couple billion dollars less than comfortable" (line 537). Shares line 531 with the calibration row (same batch), which it follows.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 35. Crisis made opportunity cost calculations difficult

quote_verbatim: Now, it’s harder to sell things in huge quantities than it is to buy things in huge quantities during a period like that. So you have to measure whether you can actually get the offsetting transaction done to move from one to another. We have a much — if we’re going to move billions from one to another, it’s much different than the problem you may have in moving hundreds of thousands or tens of thousands of dollars from one holding to another. We really can have big transactional costs unless we’re careful.
concept: Before switching from one holding to another, check that the sale can actually be done at size in a disordered market; the cost of moving large sums enters the comparison.
evolution_notes: Size point related to M2008-015 (size shrinks the universe). New as a test of switching in the rows read so far.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 35. Crisis made opportunity cost calculations difficult

quote_verbatim: Coca-Cola’s in everybody’s mind around the world. [...] You say Coca-Cola and it means something. And a brand is a promise. We’re getting our — we’re getting that promise in people’s minds that there’s a good chance they can save money if they check with GEICO. And we’ll never stop.
concept: A brand is a promise held in the customer's mind; advertising that plants it can pay off years later when the customer's needs change.
evolution_notes: Restates M2008-075 (a brand is a promise). Earlier in the answer (line 555): "when we get that message in people’s minds, you never know when it’s going to pay off later down the line." The "we waste half of it" line (line 553) is a third party's maxim used as a joke, not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 36. GEICO spends millions on advertising and will “never stop”

quote_verbatim: Yeah, it’s interesting. If GEICO would remain more or less the same size if we didn’t advertise so healthy, and if the new subscribers are worth more than the $800 million we’re spending advertising, then, in an important sense, GEICO is earning $800 million more pre-tax in a way that doesn’t even show. That’s the kind of thing we like to see within Berkshire Hathaway.
concept: Munger: spending that buys customers worth more than its cost is hidden earning power; the reported figure understates such a business.
evolution_notes: Buffett follows (line 561): "The value of GEICO goes up by far more than the earnings every year, if we keep adding these people", and present policyholder counts could be kept for "$100 million a year, maybe less".
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 36. GEICO spends millions on advertising and will “never stop”

quote_verbatim: And if I thought we could get anything like the same return by spending 2 billion next year, we’d spend 2 billion. [...] I mean, we are the low-cost producer. And if you’re the low-cost producer in something people have to buy and is roughly a $1,500 item, I mean, you’ve got a terrific, terrific business. And we have durable competitive advantage there.
concept: Being the low-cost producer of something people must buy, at a meaningful price, is a durable competitive advantage; spend on growth as long as the return holds.
evolution_notes: Restates M2009-027 in this unit and the low-cost-producer rows (M1995-037, L2007-004 and others).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 36. GEICO spends millions on advertising and will “never stop”

quote_verbatim: Well, there’s some you can’t analyze. And on the Irish banks, I couldn’t have been more wrong. But it isn’t a matter of whether they go through $9 or anything like that. It’s really what their business model is and what kind of competitive advantage they have.
concept: Whether a falling stock is a bargain is decided by its business model and competitive advantage, not by how far the price has fallen; some cannot be analysed at all.
evolution_notes: Answers the question "how would you know on the way down?" (line 567). Related to M2009-031 (look at the asset, not the price).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 37. Wells Fargo is better than many other banks

quote_verbatim: But I was wrong on the Irish banks in a very big way. I simply didn’t understand. And I should’ve understood. It was available for me to understand, the incredible exposure they’d got into in more land development-type loans — not property loans, in terms of completed properties — but all kinds of land development loans. It was extraordinary. [...] It was the terrible mistake by me. Nobody lied to me, nobody gave me any bad information. I just plain wasn’t paying attention.
concept: Buffett's own error: the information on the Irish banks' land-development lending was available and he did not pay attention to it; the fault was in his reading, not in the disclosure.
evolution_notes: Buffett's mistake. The FY2008 letter narrates the same purchase (lines 842-844, $244 million written down 89%) without a lesson; listed in this note under the letter, not rowed there. Shares line 571 with the business-model test (same batch), which it follows.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 37. Wells Fargo is better than many other banks

quote_verbatim: You can get in a lot of trouble with leverage. I mean, it’s — you start creating $20 of assets, or something like that. You know, for every dollar of equity, you better be right. And some of those big institutions did some very — what, in retrospect, for certain here — were foolish things, which, if they hadn’t been so highly leveraged, would not have hit them as badly.
concept: At twenty dollars of assets per dollar of equity a financial institution must be right; leverage turns ordinary foolishness into ruin.
evolution_notes: Lead-in: "there were a lot of signs that they were doing things that a highly leveraged institution shouldn’t be doing" if "this model of ever-rising housing prices turned out to be a false model" (line 573). Related to M2009-030 and M2008-049.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 37. Wells Fargo is better than many other banks

quote_verbatim: And I would say most of them, if you read the 10-Ks and 10-Qs and did some checking, you could spot differences in them. [...] It’s like comparing a copper producer whose costs are $2.50 a pound with a copper producer whose costs are $1 a pound. Those are two different kinds of businesses. One is going to go broke at a buck-fifty a pound. And the other one’s going to still be doing fine. And banking has real difference in it. But people don’t — they don’t seem to look at them. The figures are available.
concept: Read the filings and check: within one industry the cost position separates the business that survives a bad price from the one that goes broke, and the figures are public.
evolution_notes: The elision skips "There’s no comparison, if you take Wells Fargo versus a WaMu". Line 575-577 add Wells Fargo's $600 million quarterly amortization of core deposits, "not a real expense", which no commentator mentioned: an example of reading the figures.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 37. Wells Fargo is better than many other banks

quote_verbatim: And I would say that generally speaking, for people that don’t spend a lot of time on their investments, they’re going to have trouble separating financial institutions. I think it’s much easier to come to a conclusion on something like Coca-Cola or Procter & Gamble than it is for a person who is spending only a limited amount of time on investing to make a decision on whether to own bank A, or bank B, or bank C.
concept: An investor with limited time should prefer businesses like consumer brands, whose economics are easy to judge, over financial institutions, which are hard to tell apart.
evolution_notes: Restated after Munger's reply at lines 583-585 (rowed separately in this batch).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 37. Wells Fargo is better than many other banks

quote_verbatim: Yeah, there’s another problem. Generally accepted accounting principles allow a conservative, sensible bank to show vastly increased earnings if it changes its practices to make a lot of extremely dumb loans in large volumes. Generally accepted accounting principles should not be constructed to allow this result. It’s — that what seduces so many of these bankers into this ghastly decision-making.
concept: Munger: accounting that books immediate earnings on large volumes of bad loans tempts bankers into them; reported bank earnings can rise because lending got worse.
evolution_notes: Munger returns to it at line 587 (accountants should be ashamed of their profession), a view of the profession, not rowed. Related to M2009-003 (Munger, own-credit gains).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 37. Wells Fargo is better than many other banks

quote_verbatim: And a black box like that can produce — that’s why managements love them to some degree, they can produce numbers. They don’t necessarily produce cash. And they sure as hell can produce all kinds of problems if you have to start posting collateral and doing things of that sort. And I would say it is tough for, you might say, the passive investor, the one who’s not spending very much time on it. I would say it’s difficult for them to discern when that’s going on. So I — it’s not a bad area to just say, “This one’s too tough,” and go onto something else that’s a lot easier.

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 27. Fight egregious CEO pay with embarrassment, not legislation

quote_verbatim: I mean, right now, every consultant comes in and brings along what the people at so-called pure companies are making. And they — Nobody wants to say their CEO is in the bottom quartile or something. So they just keep comparing themselves to the higher quartiles. And then they ratchet up from there.
concept: Pay set by comparison with peer companies ratchets upward, because no board will place its CEO in the bottom quartile.
evolution_notes: "so-called pure companies" is printed so (a likely mishearing of "peer companies"); flagged, not smoothed. Continues with "I call it the honor system. You know, the shareholders have the honor and the executives have the system" (line 983), a joke, outside the quote.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 27. Fight egregious CEO pay with embarrassment, not legislation

quote_verbatim: Yeah, well, I don’t — I’m not too optimistic about fixing it from the big investor standpoint. The big investor groups contain many an investment manager making $20 million a year for insignificant contributions. He’s like a man in a glass house that starts throwing stones. [...] So, sometimes, the cure is worse than the disease.
concept: Munger: big investors cannot be relied on to police executive pay, because many of their own managers are overpaid; their own incentives are checked before trusting them as a cure.
evolution_notes: The elision leaves out the political part (public pension funds "dominated, in many cases, by left-wing politicians and by labor unions"). Answers Buffett's proposal in the same exchange (lines 979-981); not reconciled. Listed under Tensions seen rather than given a tension row, since both are rowed. Buffett's "on that hopeful note" (line 989) is a joke.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 27. Fight egregious CEO pay with embarrassment, not legislation

quote_verbatim: Well, usually, we hire people that have already proven they’re great managers. [...] And the real question we have to ask ourselves is, you know, will they be with us in the future? Will they keep — will they be feeling the same way after the deal as they did the day before the deal?
concept: Managers are mostly taken on already proven, with the business; the question then is whether they will feel the same after the deal as before it.
evolution_notes: Restates M2008-006 ("take somebody that’s been batting .400") and M2009-072 (the same passion after the stock certificate changes hands). The elision skips the ISCAR example. Followed by "we’ve made occasional mistakes on that" (line 993).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 28. We don’t hire potentially great managers

quote_verbatim:
And, the toughest part is, since we have no retirement age, is when managers lose the abilities that they had at an earlier age. And that — it doesn’t relate to — there’s no yardstick you can use up and down the line for that. [...] CHARLIE MUNGER: By the way, we’ve been slow in those.

WARREN BUFFETT: We’ve been slow every time.

CHARLIE MUNGER: We’ve been slow. If we really love the guy, we’re really slow. (Laughter) We are far from ideal.
concept: With no retirement age, a manager's decline must be judged case by case with no yardstick, and the owners have been slow to act every time, slowest when they love the person.
evolution_notes: A two-speaker exchange carrying one lesson, Buffett first, labels kept; the elision skips "people age ... in very different ways and at different paces" and "we have the responsibility for doing something about it. And we hate it". Buffett's and Munger's own mistake. The example follows: a manager at Wesco with Alzheimer's, "we didn’t want to face it ... it took us probably an extra year, year and a half" (line 1003); "It’s the only part of my job that I don’t like" (line 1007).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 28. We don’t hire potentially great managers

quote_verbatim: We find people who love their businesses, you know? I love Berkshire. I — you know, I go to work every day, and I’m excited about it. And we — you can spot that in people. [...] And, you can’t put that into somebody. But we do recognize it when it’s there. And we do our best to make sure that we don’t do anything that dampens that in any way.
concept: Love of the business can be recognised in a manager but not instilled; find it, then avoid anything that dampens it.
evolution_notes: Restates M2008-005 (see the passion in their eyes, then behave so it remains) and L2007-014 (brains, passion and integrity). The elision skips the example of Tony Nicely handing over GEICO's policyholder count (lines 1007-1009).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 28. We don’t hire potentially great managers

quote_verbatim:
But the cheaper things get, the better I like buying them. I mean, if I was buying hamburgers at McDonald’s, you know, the other day for X, and they reduced the price to 90 percent of X tomorrow — not likely — but if they did, I’m happy.

I don’t think about what I paid yesterday for the hamburger. [...] I’m going to be buying investments the rest of my life. And I would much rather pay half of X than X. And, the fact that I paid X yesterday doesn’t bother me, if I get — as long as I know the values in the business. [...] But I do know when you’re starting to get a lot for your money. And that’s when I believe in buying.
concept: A lifelong buyer welcomes lower prices whatever was paid yesterday, provided he knows the values; buy when the price starts giving a lot for the money, not on a forecast.
evolution_notes: Restates L2008-004 (socks or stocks, quality merchandise marked down). The first elision skips "I think I’m going to be buying hamburgers the rest of my life"; the second skips "I realize that that is not the way all of you feel" and "when I wrote that article in the Times, I did not predict what stocks were going to do. Because I never know what they’re going to do". Earlier (line 1017): 1974 was "the best period I’ve ever seen for buying common equities", though interest rates were far higher then, a comparison, not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 29. Don’t try to time the market

quote_verbatim:
It’s nothing like ’73-4. I knew when that happened that that was my time and my only time. I knew I was never going to get another trip to the buy counter like that one. Unfortunately, I had practically no money available, which is — (Laughter)

WARREN BUFFETT: That’s why it happened.

CHARLIE MUNGER: That’s why those times occur.

WARREN BUFFETT: Yeah.

CHARLIE MUNGER: So, if I were you, I wouldn’t wait for 1973-4.
concept: Munger: the deepest bargains occur precisely because almost nobody has money to buy, so they cannot be counted on; do not wait for the extreme before buying.
evolution_notes: A two-speaker exchange carrying one lesson, Munger first, labels kept. Opens line 1021: "if stocks go off 40 percent on average, they’re obviously closer to an attractive price than they were before". Buffett's own no-bottom-picking row follows at line 1031.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 29. Don’t try to time the market

quote_verbatim: No, we don’t try to pick bottoms or you know — We don’t have an opinion about where the stock market’s going to go tomorrow or next week or next month. So to sit around and not do something that’s sensible because you think there will be something even more attractive, that’s just not our approach to it. Anytime we get a chance to do something that makes sense, we do it. [...] So picking bottoms is basically not our game. Pricing is our game. And that’s not so difficult. Picking bottoms, I think, is probably impossible, but — When you get — when you start getting a lot for your money, you buy it.
concept: Do not hold off a sensible purchase in hope of a lower price; picking bottoms is probably impossible, pricing is not, and the time to buy is when the price gives a lot for the money.
evolution_notes: Continues Buffett's hamburger answer (lines 1017-1019) after the Munger exchange (lines 1021-1029). The elision skips "if it makes even more sense the next day, and if we’ve got money, we may do more". Later in the line: the corporate bond market "got very, very, very disorganized" and Berkshire bought bonds, a description.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 29. Don’t try to time the market

quote_verbatim: And anytime we like to do something, we really like to do it. I mean, our idea is not to tiptoe into anything. So we buy them as fast as we can, when prices are right.
concept: When the price is right, buy decisively and as fast as possible rather than tiptoeing in.
evolution_notes: Answers Munger's question at line 1035 about the life companies full of debt instruments at 10 percent; said of the corporate bonds bought with life-company money "that can’t be used in certain other areas" (line 1037).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 29. Don’t try to time the market

quote_verbatim:
And some of those bonds are up 20, 25 percent. So the opportunities are frequently under shell A, when you’re looking at shell B.

WARREN BUFFETT: Yeah. We try to look at all the shells.

CHARLIE MUNGER: Yeah, we look at all the shells.
concept: Munger: the opportunity is often in a different place from where one is looking, so look at every class of security, not one.
evolution_notes: A two-speaker exchange carrying one lesson, Munger first, labels kept. Said of "perfectly safe bonds that yielded 9 percent or more with very fancy call protection" (line 1043) while the question was about stocks. Bears on M2005-047 (Munger: search for opportunities whatever their category).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 29. Don’t try to time the market

quote_verbatim: So I would say the capital-intensive businesses that scare me more are the ones outside of the utility field, where you just pump in more money without knowing that you’re going, in a general way, to get, more or less — within a range, anyway — a guaranteed return. So I do not have — there’s no way we get rich on our utility investments. But there’s no way we get poor, either.
concept: A capital-intensive business is dangerous when more money must be pumped in with no assurance of a return; a regulated utility's allowed return makes it a decent, never a rich, use of capital.
evolution_notes: Bears on M2007-112 (heavy capital every year under regulation: decent, never extraordinary, returns). Opens: utility earnings come through "a return on equity capital allowed by the jurisdictions", surprises earned back, "you don’t get any bonanzas, either" (line 1059). Then: very high inflation may diminish the value of an 11 or 12 percent return on equity. The question cited Buffett's old warning about utilities overstating profits by understating depreciation; it is not answered directly.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 30. “Decent” rates of return from regulated utilities

quote_verbatim: But the — on balance, if you can find a good business that’s not capital intensive, you’re going to be better off than in a capital-intensive business over time. I mean, the world, they’re hard to find. But the best businesses are the ones that don’t require much capital and, nevertheless, make good money. They’ve got some moat protecting them, other than the capital required as entry in the business that’s protecting them. And if you can find those that are durable, you’ve got a great investment and one that will do the best in inflation, which, as we mentioned earlier, seems fairly likely to come along.
concept: The best business needs little capital yet earns well, behind a moat other than the capital needed to enter; if it is durable it is a great investment and the best one in inflation.
evolution_notes: Restates the morning's M2009-044 (a wonderful business that does not require heavy capital investment, against inflation) and M2009-047 (service businesses need less capital). Munger's moats-filling-with-sand line (1063) follows and is rowed separately.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 30. “Decent” rates of return from regulated utilities

quote_verbatim: Yeah, unfortunately, a lot of moats have been filling up with sand lately, you know, the daily newspaper, the network television station, all these castles with their lovely moats. The moats are filling up.
concept: Munger: moats do not last of themselves; once-great franchises such as daily newspapers and network television stations have seen theirs fill in.
evolution_notes: Stated as an observation about two industries, rowed because it answers Buffett's "if you can find those that are durable" at line 1061 (the definition row just before). Bears on the morning's M2009-045 (newspapers have lost their essential nature). Buffett's "on that cheery note" (line 1067) is a joke.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 30. “Decent” rates of return from regulated utilities

quote_verbatim: From the start, Charlie and I have believed in having a rational and unbending standard for measuring what we have � or have not � accomplished. That keeps us from the temptation of seeing where the arrow of performance lands and then painting the bull's eye around it.
concept: Fix the yardstick for judging one's own results in advance and never change it, so the target is not drawn around wherever the results land.
evolution_notes: The yardstick itself (the S&P 500, lines 103-104, because owners can match it at virtually no cost through an index fund) is not rowed: it repeats L1997-002 and R2006-001. The point rowed here, that the standard must be set beforehand and held, is new in the letters read so far.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: How We Measure Ourselves

quote_verbatim: There are good arguments for simply using the change in our stock price. Over an extended period of time, in fact, that is the best test. But year-to-year market prices can be extraordinarily erratic. Even evaluations covering as long as a decade can be greatly distorted by foolishly high or low prices at the beginning or end of the measurement period.
concept: The stock price is the best test of a management over a long enough period, but even a ten-year record can be distorted by a foolish price at either end, so check the endpoints before judging a record.
evolution_notes: Continues with the CEOs of Microsoft and GE, handed the baton at "nosebleed prices" (lines 110-111), as the example. The distortion of a decade by its endpoints is new in the letters read so far.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: How We Measure Ourselves

quote_verbatim: The ideal standard for measuring our yearly progress would be the change in Berkshire's per-share intrinsic value. Alas, that value cannot be calculated with anything close to precision, so we instead use a crude proxy for it: per-share book value.
concept: Progress is properly measured by the change in per-share intrinsic value; because that cannot be calculated precisely, book value serves only as a crude proxy.
evolution_notes: Earlier v5 rows on the same point are a meeting row and a report row, M1996-008 and R1996-020, so rowed under the convention that the letter restatement rule reaches earlier letters only. Continues: book value at most companies understates intrinsic value, and at Berkshire the gap is huge in insurance (lines 116-118).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: How We Measure Ourselves

quote_verbatim: Long ago, Charlie laid out his strongest ambition: "All I want to know is where I'm going to die, so I'll never go there." That bit of wisdom was inspired by Jacobi, the great Prussian mathematician, who counseled "Invert, always invert" as an aid to solving difficult problems.
concept: Solve hard problems by inversion: work out what would ruin you and stay away from it.
evolution_notes: Munger's dictum is already in L1996-014, where it is applied to borrowing and catastrophe limits; new here is inversion named as a general method (Jacobi's maxim, a third party's, spoken by Buffett), and the letter then lists four applications under this section, rowed separately. Followed by a country-song joke (lines 152-154), not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: What We Don't Do

quote_verbatim: Charlie and I avoid businesses whose futures we can't evaluate, no matter how exciting their products may be. [...] But the future then also included competitive dynamics that would decimate almost all of the companies entering those industries. Even the survivors tended to come away bleeding. Just because Charlie and I can clearly see dramatic growth ahead for an industry does not mean we can judge what its profit margins and returns on capital will be as a host of competitors battle for supremacy. At Berkshire we will stick with businesses whose profit picture for decades to come seems reasonably predictable.
concept: Foreseeing an industry's growth says nothing about its margins and returns once competitors pile in; avoid businesses whose future cannot be evaluated and keep to those whose profits for decades seem reasonably predictable.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the examples: autos in 1910, aircraft in 1930, television sets in 1950 (lines 159-160). Ends "Even then, we will make plenty of mistakes" (line 167). Related to L2007-005 (rule out industries of rapid change) and M2006-016 (prefer businesses whose returns years ahead can be judged); the growth-without-profit argument through competition is new as stated here.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: What We Don't Do

quote_verbatim: We will never become dependent on the kindness of strangers. Too-big-to-fail is not a fallback position at Berkshire. Instead, we will always arrange our affairs so that any requirements for cash we may conceivably have will be dwarfed by our own liquidity. Moreover, that liquidity will be constantly refreshed by a gusher of earnings from our many and diverse businesses. [...] We pay a steep price to maintain our premier financial strength.
concept: Arrange affairs so that one's own liquidity dwarfs any cash requirement that could conceivably arise, never counting on rescue, and accept the cost of that strength.
evolution_notes: Restates L2008-019 (more than ample cash, no kindness of strangers); added here are the measure (liquidity dwarfing any conceivable requirement) and that being too big to fail is not a fallback. The elision skips the September 2008 account of supplying $15.5 billion (lines 174-180) and a printed page number (line 182). Continues: the $20 billion-plus of cash equivalents earns a pittance, "But we sleep well" (lines 184-185).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: What We Don't Do

quote_verbatim: We tend to let our many subsidiaries operate on their own, without our supervising and monitoring them to any degree. That means we are sometimes late in spotting management problems and that both operating and capital decisions are occasionally made with which Charlie and I would have disagreed had we been consulted. [...] We would rather suffer the visible costs of a few bad decisions than incur the many invisible costs that come from decisions made too slowly � or not at all � because of a stifling bureaucracy.
concept: Leave subsidiaries unsupervised and accept the visible cost of some bad decisions and late-spotted problems, rather than the invisible cost of slow or missing decisions under bureaucracy.
evolution_notes: The elision skips that most managers use the independence magnificently with an owner-oriented attitude (lines 190-192). Decentralisation restates M1998-077 and M1999-019 (meeting rows); the stated trade of visible against invisible costs is new. The meeting's heading 24 (NetJets) returns to it.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: What We Don't Do

quote_verbatim: But we will never allow Berkshire to become some monolith that is overrun with committees, budget presentations and multiple layers of management. Instead, we plan to operate as a collection of separately-managed medium-sized and large businesses, most of whose decision-making occurs at the operating level. Charlie and I will limit ourselves to allocating capital, controlling enterprise risk, choosing managers and setting their compensation.
concept: Keep decisions at the operating level with no committees, budget presentations or layers, and confine the centre to four jobs: allocating capital, controlling enterprise risk, choosing managers and setting their pay.
evolution_notes: The four jobs of the centre are new as a list in the letters read so far; capital held at the centre restates M1994-062 and M1998-078, and no budgets sent up M1998-074 (meeting rows). The R-row R1996-024 states the cash half.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: What We Don't Do

quote_verbatim: We make no attempt to woo Wall Street. Investors who buy and sell based upon media or analyst commentary are not for us. Instead we want partners who join us at Berkshire because they wish to make a long-term investment in a business they themselves understand and because it's one that follows policies with which they concur.
concept: Seek owners who invest for the long term in a business they themselves understand and whose policies they agree with, not those who trade on media or analyst commentary.
evolution_notes: Restates M1999-059 (a meeting row, informed owners in sync with objectives) and R1996-001; rowed under the letter rule for earlier letters only. Continues: a small venture with a few partners would seek people in sync, and giant size does not change that (lines 207-210). Lines 212-214, tell owners what we would want to know if positions were reversed, repeat L1995-021 and R1995-012, not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: What We Don't Do

quote_verbatim: And now a painful confession: Last year your chairman closed the book on a very expensive business fiasco entirely of his own making. [...] I reasoned that GEICO policyholders were likely to be good credit risks and, assuming we offered an attractive card, would likely favor us with their business. We got business all right � but of the wrong type. [...] GEICO's managers, it should be emphasized, were never enthusiastic about my idea. [...] I subtly indicated that I was older and wiser. I was just older.
concept: A side product reasoned from the owner's desk, against the warnings of the managers who knew the customers, drew the wrong customers; the owner's seniority was not superior knowledge.
evolution_notes: Buffett's own mistake (the GEICO credit card). The lesson is carried only by the closing line, not stated as a rule. The elisions skip the losses, about $6.3 million plus $44 million on the sold receivables (lines 388-389), and the managers' warning that GEICO would get "the non-cream" (lines 391-393), whose printed dashes I left out.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Insurance

quote_verbatim: Our regulated electric utilities, offering monopoly service in most cases, operate in a symbiotic manner with the customers in their service areas, with those users depending on us to provide first-class service and invest for their future needs. [...] We, in turn, look to our utilities' regulators (acting on behalf of our customers) to allow us an appropriate return on the huge amounts of capital we must deploy to meet future needs. We shouldn't expect our regulators to live up to their end of the bargain unless we live up to ours.
concept: In a regulated monopoly the owner earns an appropriate return on its capital only by first keeping its own side of the bargain with customers and regulators.
evolution_notes: Related to L2008-008 (the regulated owner's record follows him). The letter restates the bargain for BNSF as a "social compact" in which, if either side shirks, both suffer (lines 491-494), and asks for regulators who provide certainty about allowable returns (lines 487-489); both not rowed as restatements of this passage. The meeting's heading 28 answers a question on the allowable return.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Regulated Utility Business

quote_verbatim: In earlier days, Charlie and I shunned capital-intensive businesses such as public utilities. Indeed, the best businesses by far for owners continue to be those that have high returns on capital and that require little incremental investment to grow. [...] Anticipating, however, that Berkshire will generate ever-increasing amounts of cash, we are today quite willing to enter businesses that regularly require large capital expenditures. We expect only that these businesses have reasonable expectations of earning decent returns on the incremental sums they invest.
concept: The best business earns high returns and needs little added capital to grow; an owner with more cash than such businesses can absorb may enter capital-heavy ones, provided the added capital can reasonably be expected to earn decent returns.
evolution_notes: The first half restates M2009-105 and M2001-019 (meeting rows); the change of practice, capital-heavy businesses accepted at decent incremental returns because of the cash to be placed, is new. Continues: the collection should produce above-average, "though certainly not spectacular", returns (lines 478-479). The meeting's heading 15 is a shareholder's question on this passage.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Regulated Utility Business

quote_verbatim: We had a number of companies at which profits improved even as sales contracted, always an exceptional managerial achievement.
concept: Rising profit on falling sales marks an exceptional manager.
evolution_notes: Followed by the list of nine CEOs (lines 558-568). Marmon's cost-conscious management mitigating a 27% sales fall (lines 571-573) is the same point, not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Manufacturing, Service and Retailing Operations

quote_verbatim: Dave and I have the strongest possible personal interest in maintaining these standards because we and our families use NetJets for almost all of our flying, as do many of our directors and managers. None of us are assigned special planes nor crews. We receive exactly the same treatment as any other owner, meaning we pay the same prices as everyone else does when we are using our personal contracts. In short, we eat our own cooking. In the aviation business, no other testimonial means more.
concept: Where safety and service are the product, the strongest guarantee is that the owners and managers use it themselves on the same terms as every customer.
evolution_notes: R1995-002 uses "We eat our own cooking" of directors' wealth held in the company; here the phrase is applied to using one's own product. Just before (lines 592-596) Buffett says "It's clear that I failed you in letting NetJets descend into this condition", a mistake narrated without a lesson, not rowed; the meeting's heading 24 asks what was learned.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Manufacturing, Service and Retailing Operations

quote_verbatim: Before you read further, let me underscore the obvious: Berkshire has a dog in this fight, and you should therefore assess the commentary that follows with special care.
concept: Discount commentary from a party with an interest in the outcome, including one's own.
evolution_notes: Said of his own argument against the mortgage-rate differential for factory-built homes (lines 640-656). Related to M2001-052 (weigh information by the incentives of its source), a meeting row; here applied by the speaker to himself.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Finance and Financial Products

quote_verbatim: We told you last year that very unusual conditions then existed in the corporate and municipal bond markets and that these securities were ridiculously cheap relative to U.S. Treasuries. We backed this view with some purchases, but I should have done far more. Big opportunities come infrequently. When it's raining gold, reach for a bucket, not a thimble.
concept: Seeing a rare bargain and buying too little of it is an error; when big opportunities come, commit on their scale.
evolution_notes: Buffett's own error of omission, in size rather than in seeing. Related to L2008-003 (thumb-sucking on new facts) and M2009-102 (do not tiptoe in).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Investments

quote_verbatim: It's been an ideal period for investors: A climate of fear is their best friend. Those who invest only when commentators are upbeat end up paying a heavy price for meaningless reassurance. In the end, what counts in investing is what you pay for a business � through the purchase of a small piece of it in the stock market � and what that business earns in the succeeding decade or two.
concept: The result of an investment is fixed by the price paid for the business and what it earns over the next ten or twenty years; buying only on upbeat commentary pays for reassurance worth nothing.
evolution_notes: The fear point restates L1997-035 and L1994-004; added is the statement of what alone counts, price against the business's earnings over a decade or two, which I did not find in an earlier letter row.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Investments

quote_verbatim: In my view a board of directors of a huge financial institution is derelict if it does not insist that its CEO bear full responsibility for risk control. If he's incapable of handling that job, he should look for other employment.
concept: A board that does not hold the chief executive of a large financial institution personally responsible for risk control fails its duty, and a CEO who cannot carry that job should go.
evolution_notes: Extends L2008-023 (the CEO must be the Chief Risk Officer) to the board's duty. Lines 847-851, the CEO must not delegate risk control and Buffett initiates and monitors every derivatives contract, repeat L2008-023, not rowed. Lines 857-870, severe consequences for the CEOs and directors of failed institutions, are a policy view, not rowed. Lines 841-845, derivatives bought when mispriced and dangerous when leverage or counterparty risk is extreme, repeat L2006-011 and L2008-022 in substance, not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Investments

quote_verbatim: If we wouldn't dream of selling Berkshire in its entirety at the current market price, why in the world should we "sell" a significant part of the company at that same inadequate price by issuing our stock in a merger? [...] If shares of a prospective acquirer are selling below their intrinsic value, it's impossible for that buyer to make a sensible deal in an all-stock deal. You simply can't exchange an undervalued stock for a fully-valued one without hurting your shareholders.
concept: Issuing shares is selling part of the company; if you would not sell the whole at the market price, do not sell a part at it, and an undervalued acquirer cannot make a sensible all-stock deal.
evolution_notes: The rule of issuing only for equal value is R1995-010 and R1998-001; reluctance to issue is L1997-030; value given against value received is L2005-012. New here is the test of the whole against the part, and the statement that an undervalued acquirer cannot do a sensible all-stock deal. The elision skips the target's expectation of receiving its own intrinsic value (lines 882-884).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: An Inconvenient Truth (Boardroom Overheating)

quote_verbatim: He will neglect to explain, though, that what he is giving will cost his shareholders $125 in intrinsic value. [...] Not everyone at A, it should be noted, is a loser from this nonsensical transaction. Its CEO now runs a company twice as large as his original domain, in a world where size tends to correlate with both prestige and compensation.
concept: In an all-stock deal ask what is given in intrinsic value, not what is received, and ask who gains: the acquiring CEO whose size, prestige and pay grow even as his owners lose.
evolution_notes: The worked example of Company A and Company B, each worth $100 and selling at $80 (lines 888-893); the elision skips the 55.6% and 44.4% ownership arithmetic. Related to R1996-011 (pay never related to size).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: An Inconvenient Truth (Boardroom Overheating)

quote_verbatim: In the end, Charlie and I decided that the disadvantage of paying 30% of the price through stock was offset by the opportunity the acquisition gave us to deploy $22 billion of cash in a business we understood and liked for the long term. [...] But the final decision was a close one. If we had needed to use more stock to make the acquisition, it would in fact have made no sense. We would have then been giving up more than we were getting.
concept: Weigh the undervalued shares given in a deal against what the deal makes possible; past the point where more stock would be needed, more is given than got and the deal makes no sense.
evolution_notes: The test of the row at lines 878-886 applied by Buffett to his own BNSF purchase. The elision skips Matt Rose and further investment at reasonable returns (lines 915-916). Lines 899-905, an overvalued stock used as currency, "counterfeit money", repeat L1997-031 in substance, not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: An Inconvenient Truth (Boardroom Overheating)

quote_verbatim: When stock is the currency being contemplated in an acquisition and when directors are hearing from an advisor, it appears to me that there is only one way to get a rational and balanced discussion. Absent this drastic remedy, our recommendation in respect to the use of advisors remains: "Don't ask the barber whether you need a haircut."

quote_verbatim: I should have written the "five-year rolling basis" sentence differently, an error I didn't realize until I received a question about this subject at the 2009 annual meeting. When the stock market has declined sharply over a five-year stretch, our market-price premium to book value has sometimes shrunk. And when that happens, we fail the test as I improperly formulated it. [...] The five-year test should be: (1) during the period did our book-value gain exceed the performance of the S&P; and (2) did our stock consistently sell at a premium to book, meaning that every $1 of retained earnings was always worth more than $1? If these tests are met, retaining earnings has made sense.
concept: The retention test as first written failed at a market low; restated, retention is justified over five years if book value beat the S&P and the stock always sold above book, so each retained dollar was worth more than a dollar.

quote_verbatim: But you’ve got to treat people fairly. Even though they don’t need the money, everybody wants to be treated fairly. [...] I mean, if you run See’s Candy, to put a cost of capital factor in or something like that, what the consultant would tell you, it’s nonsense. [...] The main thing to do is, in terms of market position and all that sort of thing, the real thing I really want to pay managers for is widening the moat that separates our business from our competitors’ businesses over time. Now, that gets very subjective, so I don’t have any perfect way of doing that.
