heading: ### 14. Why we don’t use bond rating agencies

quote_verbatim: And what happened, of course, is that the cognition faltered. They drifted with the stupidity of their times in a way that was regrettable. Part of it came out of asininity in American business education. They overbelieved in these ridiculous models and so on and so on.
concept: Munger: the rating agencies failed by drifting with the stupidity of their times and overbelieving models taught in business schools.
evolution_notes: A third party's mistake (the rating agencies), lesson drawn by Munger. Before it he calls the agencies, "in their present forum, and structured with their present incentives", a constructive influence for decades; after it, no apology yet from business academia (line 839), a jab, left out.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 14. Why we don’t use bond rating agencies

quote_verbatim: But when they sold the pizza business for $3.7 billion they announced it as selling it for $3.7 billion. They didn’t sell it for $3.7 billion, that’s what the other guy paid. What they got was about $2.5 billion. And that was a terribly tax-inefficient deal when they’d already shown their ability to understand that you could do a tax-efficient deal when they sold the Post cereals business earlier. [...] When they talked about the Cadbury earnings they were buying, they were talking about next year. And when they talked about the pizza earnings they were selling, they talked about last year.
concept: Judge a sale by what the seller keeps after tax, not the headline price the buyer pays, and check that earnings bought and earnings sold are measured over the same year.
evolution_notes: Said of Kraft's sale of its pizza business and purchase of Cadbury. Continues: pizza earned about 340 million pre-tax in 2009 and was growing as fast as Cadbury, "if it’d been me, I would have voted to keep pizza and not buy Cadbury" (line 879). Before it Buffett allows that "the fact I think it’s a dumb deal doesn’t for certain make it a dumb deal" (line 865). Related to L2009-020 (ask what is given in an acquisition, not what is received).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 16. Buffett doesn’t like Kraft’s purchase of Cadbury

quote_verbatim: Yeah, I think generally, at the top of American businesses, people think they know too much about strategy. And they tend to hate the tough competitive conditions in the business they’re in, and to yearn for some business where it’s less difficult. You remember when Xerox bought Crum & Forster, an American insurance company, one of the dumbest acquisitions in all time? The reason Xerox did that is they didn’t have any tough Japanese competing in the insurance business. [...] I think it’s quite typical to dream, if you’re in business, that something that’s a little different, no matter how much you pay for it, will make your troubles less.
concept: Munger: managers tired of hard competition at home buy a different business at any price in the hope it eases their troubles; such a diversifying deal is a warning.
evolution_notes: A third party's mistake (Xerox buying Crum & Forster), lesson drawn by Munger. Munger closes the heading: "We are very stupid in many ways, but we have avoided a slight subset of stupidities. (Laughter) And they’re important." (line 887), not rowed.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 16. Buffett doesn’t like Kraft’s purchase of Cadbury

quote_verbatim: And you will have an absolute army of lawyers, investment advisors, public relations people, all of whom will have a strong economic interest in having you push ahead on deal, after deal, after deal, regardless of how the shareholders come out.
concept: Behind an acquisitive management stand advisers paid by the deal, whose interest is in more deals whatever the shareholders get; weigh their counsel accordingly.
evolution_notes: Follows Munger's point at line 883 (the yearning for an easier business) in the same exchange. Related to L2009-020 (who gains from a nonsensical deal).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 16. Buffett doesn’t like Kraft’s purchase of Cadbury

quote_verbatim: So, integrity’s very important. It’s the safest way to make money, also. [...] And of course everybody mouths the integrity, even when it’s lacking. So it’s difficult to be sure that professing integrity is the same as having it.
concept: Munger: integrity is the safest way to make money, but everyone professes it, so a manager's profession of integrity is no evidence of having it.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the occasional knave who does well, with Pope Urban on Cardinal Richelieu (line 895). The questioner cites "one of your three key questions", whether management loves what they do or loves the money (line 893); cf. M2008-005.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 17. Biggest threat to integrity: “everyone else is doing it”

quote_verbatim: The “everyone else is doing it” is the toughest thing. I think — [...] And I talked to a number of people in that 498 that I would trust to be a trustee of my will, you know, I’d love to have them as a next door neighbor, they could marry my daughter, but in the end they said, “I can’t do it if the other guy isn’t doing it.” It was a variation on the, “I’m doing it because the other guy is doing it.” [...] And the situational ethics problem is huge.
concept: Even trustworthy managers did the wrong thing because the others did: 498 of the S&P 500 chose not to expense options; "everyone else is doing it" is the hardest pressure on integrity.
evolution_notes: A third party's mistake (the 498 companies that chose the non-preferred method after the Accounting Standards Board backed off, line 901), lesson drawn by Buffett. The first elision crosses Munger's "Yeah." (line 899) and the account of the 1993 fight; Buffett resumes the same thought. Restates M2009-013 and M2010-034 (the other fellow doing it is never a reason) and M2008-063.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 17. Biggest threat to integrity: “everyone else is doing it”

quote_verbatim: We try to create as few situations in Berkshire as we can that would induce such behavior. I don’t have the managers submit budgets to me, there is no Berkshire budget, you know. [...] But if they submit them to me, you know, and the temptation becomes, if they’re not quite making it and they think I’m looking at them all the time, the temptation becomes to fudge in some way. And very few would do it, but the more that thought the other ones were doing it, the more that would do it. It’s just human behavior. And you want to try and create a structure that minimizes the weaknesses in human behavior.
concept: Design the organisation so it creates few temptations to fudge: no budgets sent to the top, because watched targets invite fudging and fudging spreads as people think others do it.
evolution_notes: No budget presentations restates L2009-008; new here is the reason, that a budget reported upward invites fudging, and that a structure should minimise the weaknesses in human behaviour.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 17. Biggest threat to integrity: “everyone else is doing it”

quote_verbatim: Yeah, what’s really interesting on this issue is that so much of the bad behavior does not come from malevolence or overweening greed or anything like that. It comes from subconscious poor cognition that justifies a lot of behavior that’s really not justifiable if it’s better understood. And that happens to practically everybody. And the cure is very difficult. The best cure is to have a system where the people who are making the decisions bear the consequences. [...] Systems like that, at a basic level, are irresponsible systems, and it’s deeply immoral to create irresponsible systems like that.
concept: Munger: most bad behaviour comes from subconscious poor cognition, not malice; the best cure is a system in which those who decide bear the consequences.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the example: Wall Street's mortgage system in which nobody owned the mortgages and nobody felt responsible that they be good (line 907). Ends: "There are very few apologies, you’ll note. People think they did fine."
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 17. Biggest threat to integrity: “everyone else is doing it”

quote_verbatim: If you’re of that — if you have a temperament that when others are fearful you’re going to get scared yourself, you know, you are not going to make a lot of money in securities over time, in all probability. [...] And to expect somebody else to tell you when to buy and therefore get your courage back up or something, you know, I could get this fellow’s courage up substantially by saying this is a wonderful time to buy, and then a week from now he’d run into somebody else that tells him the world is coming to an end and he’d sell. I mean, he’s a broker’s friend, but he’s not going to make a lot of money.
concept: An investor who gets scared when others are fearful, or who needs someone else to restore his courage, will not make much money in securities.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the farm and apartment-house passage rowed separately from line 917. Before it: "We’ve seen a few that scream at us ... And 90 percent of the time we’re somewhere in between and we don’t know exactly where we are in between" (line 915). Temperament appears in earlier rows; not cited by id here.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 18. Can’t make money if you’re scared when everyone else is scared

quote_verbatim: If you buy an apartment house, do you get a quote next week or month? No, you look at the apartment house or the farm and you say, “I expect it to produce so many bushels of soy beans and corn, and if it does that, it meets my expectations.” If they buy a stock and they think if it goes up it’s wonderful, and if it goes down it’s bad. We think just the opposite. When it goes down we love it, because we’ll buy more. And if it goes up, it kills us to buy more.
concept: Judge a stock as one judges a farm, by what it produces against expectations, not by quotes; a buyer of more should welcome a falling price.
evolution_notes: Opens at the end of line 915, "think how much more rational investing in a farm is than the way many people buy stocks"; ends "Ben Graham wrote about it" (line 917). The farm comparison recurs in many earlier rows; not checked by id.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 18. Can’t make money if you’re scared when everyone else is scared

quote_verbatim: Yeah, I think I developed more courage after I learned I could handle hardship. So maybe you should get your feet wet with a little more failure. (Laughter and applause)
concept: Munger: courage comes from learning that one can handle hardship, so some failure early helps.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct. Half a joke (the laughter), but the claim about courage is stated plainly. The questioner at heading 25 takes it up (line 1031).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 18. Can’t make money if you’re scared when everyone else is scared

quote_verbatim: They’d be much better off if there were no quotations at all. [...] And in the end, what counts is buying a good business at a decent price, and then forgetting about it for a long, long, long time. And some people can do it and some people can’t.
concept: What counts is buying a good business at a decent price and then forgetting it for a very long time; investors without the temperament would be better off with no daily quotes.
evolution_notes: The elision skips Keynes on quotations and "nobody says, “How liquid is my farm?”" (line 923). Continues the farm passage at line 917 of the same answer.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 18. Can’t make money if you’re scared when everyone else is scared

quote_verbatim: But in terms of immediate business decisions, I think frequently the right answer is counterintuitive, like mine, to say, if you want to put in solar panels, wait. They’re going to get cheaper.
concept: Munger: for a technology whose cost is falling, the right business decision is often the counterintuitive one of waiting to buy.
evolution_notes: Restates his own opening, "I never pass an opportunity to decline to put them in, because I think they’re going to get a lot cheaper and I’d rather wait" (line 931). The rest of his answer (solar is coming, corn ethanol "stunningly stupid", politicians will build a grid) is forecast and political view, not rowed.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 19. Munger is “enormously optimistic” about solar power

quote_verbatim: Of course there are terrible problems, and of course reduced expectations are the rational way. There’s no better way to be happy than getting your expectations down, it’s much easier than — WARREN BUFFETT: Getting your results up. CHARLIE MUNGER: — than getting your results up, yeah. (Laughter)
concept: Munger: lowering expectations is the rational response to hard times and an easier road to contentment than raising results.
evolution_notes: Exchange, Munger first, Buffett finishing his sentence; labels kept as printed. Personal conduct, though Munger ties it at heading 13 to expecting less from investment portfolios (line 821, a forecast, not rowed). Continues: "we never know anything here except the most elementary common sense. It’s amazing that it’s sufficed for us" (line 969), not rowed.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 21. “If I can be optimistic when I’m nearly dead, surely the rest of you can handle a little inflation”

quote_verbatim: I like the idea, whether it’s, you know, in terms of CNBC keeping a record of it or Charlie Rose keeping a record of it, of being judged by my own words rather than somebody writing a few paragraphs trying to summarize some views. [...] So the clearer I can be about what I think, whether writing my own annual report or whether being in broadcast, the better I feel about the accuracy of the reporting.
concept: Speak where a full record of one's own words is kept, so one is judged on them rather than on another's summary or a quote shopped for a storyline.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct. The elision skips the reporter "shopping for a single quote that fits their storyline" (line 981). Before it: Lloyd Blankfein's "God's work" remark (lines 979-981); after it, the Charlie Rose edit that cut the railroad scenes, "So even television isn’t safe" (lines 983-985).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 22. Why Buffett prefers TV interviews

quote_verbatim: Now, if you want a shareholder body that is going to be in sync with you, it’s important — in my view — it’s important that you let them know exactly what sort of institution you plan to run. [...] But what you can’t do is have hamburgers on the outside on the marquee and deliver French food inside.” And so many companies sort of try and promise everything to everybody. [...] It’s our fault if we give out the wrong advertisement. So we try to advertise what we are, and then we try to deliver on that.
concept: A company gets the owners it advertises for: say exactly what kind of institution it will be, deliver that, and do not promise everything to everybody.
evolution_notes: The restaurant passage is Phil Fisher's (a third party's maxim, spoken by Buffett, lines 993-995). Restates L2009-009 and M1999-059 (owners in sync with objectives and horizon); new here are Fisher's marquee and "It’s our fault if we give out the wrong advertisement." The same answer continues at line 1007, rowed separately (catering to expectations by accounting).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 23. How Berkshire gets loyal shareholders

quote_verbatim: And it is really ridiculous, the idea that you go out and try and cater to the expectations of people that are expecting you to do things you can’t do by operations, but maybe you can do by accounting for a short period of time. It leads to the worst behavior. And in the end, somebody’s going to own all your shares, you know. There’s no way that shares remain empty, you know, in the shareholder list. So why not get a bunch of people who are going to stick with you who are in sync? And the way they’re going to be in sync is if you told them rather accurately what you expect, how you expect to do it, and tell them when you make mistakes, all of that.
concept: Catering to holders who expect what operations cannot deliver leads to accounting tricks and the worst behaviour; since someone will own every share, tell owners accurately what to expect and admit mistakes.
evolution_notes: Exchange: follows Munger's "But that was on purpose" (line 1005), said of having no investor relations department to pump the stock (line 1003). Munger: the average institutional investor wants his portfolio to look good the next six months, "you’d find it hard to love your shareholders" (line 999), and "we probably shouldn’t be as critical of people who came up a different way" (line 1009); neither rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 23. How Berkshire gets loyal shareholders

quote_verbatim: The pressure that is exerted by extremely low interest rates — short-term rates — on the value of everything else, it’s hard to overestimate that. [...] But I don’t think you should underestimate the degree to which the last year of stock prices has been a result of the agony that people are being put through that keep their money in short-term money instruments.
concept: Very low short-term rates push up the price of every other asset; check how much of a rise in stock prices comes from money driven out of cash rather than from the businesses.
evolution_notes: Munger states the same just before, "Stocks are up because the return from loaning your money out at interest in a safe way is so lousy, and of course, one answer is that can’t last. In which case, stocks won’t be as pronounced a value, relatively speaking" (line 1023), not rowed separately. Buffett's blame of Congress over the Fed (line 1021) is political, left out.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 24. Low interest rates are hurting people scared out of stocks

quote_verbatim: But you’d be amazed how many businesses I don’t feel that I understand well. The biggest thing is not how big your circle of competence is, but knowing where the perimeter is. You don’t have to be an expert on 90 percent of the businesses, or 80 percent, or 70, or 50. But you do have to know something about the ones that you actually put your money into, and if that’s a very small part of the universe, that still is not a killer.
concept: What matters is knowing where the perimeter of one's competence lies, not its size; one need know only the businesses one actually buys, even if they are a small part of the universe.
evolution_notes: Restates L1999-020 (recognising when one approaches the perimeter). Before it Buffett says Graham taught him a method that "was almost a guarantee against failure" but whose universe of companies dried up, and Munger taught him the value of a durable competitive advantage (line 1037).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 25. Valuing businesses by asking questions

quote_verbatim: Which would you like to buy into? Which do you think you could understand their economics? Which do you think will be around 10 or 20 years from now? Which do you think it would be very tough to compete with? Just keep asking yourself questions about businesses. Talk with other people about them. You will extend your knowledge over time. And always remember that margin of safety.
concept: Learn to value businesses by asking of local ones: would I buy in, can I understand the economics, will it be here in 10 or 20 years, is it very hard to compete with; and always keep the margin of safety.
evolution_notes: Opens with what one would pay for a McDonald's sandwich and the businesses of the questioner's hometown, Olathe (line 1039). Continues: "you recognize your limitations, and that’s enormously important in this business" (line 1039).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 25. Valuing businesses by asking questions

quote_verbatim: But I looked over there, and I could see that there were a number of businesses that met the margin of safety test. And there I diversified, because I didn’t know that much about any specific one, but I knew that a package of 20 was going to work out very well, even if a crook might run one of them, and a couple might run into competition I didn’t anticipate, because they were so cheap. And that was sort of the old Graham approach.
concept: When many stocks are very cheap but none is known well, buy a package and diversify, so that a crook or an unforeseen competitor in a few does not spoil the whole; the old Graham approach.
evolution_notes: Said of Korean stocks bought six or seven years earlier (line 1039). Ends "the beauty of it is you don’t have to find very many of them" (line 1041). Graham named as Buffett names him.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 25. Valuing businesses by asking questions

quote_verbatim: Well obviously, if you want to get good at something which is competitive, you have to think about it a lot, and learn a lot, and practice doing it a lot. And the way the world is constructed in this field, you have to keep learning, because the world keeps changing and your competitors keep learning. So you just have to get up each morning and try and go to bed that night a little wiser than you were when you got up. [...] If you have the right temperament, you may rise slowly but you’re sure to rise.
concept: Munger: in a competitive field one must keep learning because the world and competitors change; go to bed each day a little wiser, and with the right temperament one rises slowly but surely.
evolution_notes: The elision skips that people who do this "almost never fail utterly", though luck may go against them for a while (line 1043).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 25. Valuing businesses by asking questions

quote_verbatim: And he said, “Charlie,” he said, “A business where he enjoys practically no competition. He gathers up and renders dead horses.” That was an example of avoiding competition by one stratagem. And you keep asking questions like that of reality, starting at a young age, you gradually learn.
concept: Munger: learn business by asking of everything one sees how it makes money; the idle prosperous man rendered dead horses, a business with practically no competition.
evolution_notes: Munger's father's answer, a third party's words spoken by Munger. He returns to it after the Kiewit passage: "What was working, what was failing, why was it working, why was it failing? If you have that temperament, you are gradually going to learn" (line 1075).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 25. Valuing businesses by asking questions

quote_verbatim: It’s hard to get anywhere near the top, and it’s hard to hold any position once you’ve attained it. But I think you can predict that Kiewit was likely to win. They cared more about doing it right. They cared more about avoiding trouble. They put more discipline on themselves. [...] I would not have bet on any of the people I knew who were already wealthy. But I would have bet on Pete Kiewit.
concept: Munger: the winner can be predicted from people who care more about doing it right, avoiding trouble and self-discipline, not from present wealth or standing.
evolution_notes: Exchange, Munger first. The elision crosses Buffett's question "if you knew the individual well, you would have bet, right?" (lines 1061-1065); Munger resumes the same thought. Munger returns to Kiewit at heading 28 (line 1159) as the model for BYD.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 25. Valuing businesses by asking questions

quote_verbatim: It’s avoiding the dumb thing. You really don’t have to be brilliant, but, you know, you have to avoid just sort of what almost seem the obvious mistakes.
concept: Success comes from avoiding the obvious mistakes, not from brilliance.
evolution_notes: Said of Pete Kiewit, "you never would have seen him do anything dumb" (line 1077). Restates L2001-017 (results come mainly from avoiding dumb decisions) and M2004-124 (Munger, avoid the really dumb things).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 25. Valuing businesses by asking questions

quote_verbatim: There’s two ways of looking at it. If you talk about the capital necessary to run the business, as opposed to what we might have paid for the business — [...] When we look at what’s a good business, we’re defining it in terms of the capital actually needed in the business. Whether it’s a good investment for us depends on how much we pay for that in the end.
concept: A good business is defined by its return on the capital it actually needs to operate; whether it is a good investment depends separately on the price paid.
evolution_notes: The elision skips Coca-Cola run with no capital but bought for $100 billion (line 1097). Continues with magazines operating on negative capital, subscribers paying in advance (line 1097), and Blue Chip Stamps (line 1099).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 26. Companies with the best return on capital

quote_verbatim: But there are a lot of great businesses that need very, very little capital. Apple doesn’t need that much capital, you know. The best ones, of course, are the ones that can get very large while needing no capital. [...] Generally, the great consumer businesses need relatively little capital. The businesses where people pay you in advance, you know, magazine subscriptions being a case, insurance being a case, you know, you’re using your customer’s capital. And we like those kind of businesses, but of course, so does the rest of the world, so they can become very competitive in buying them.
concept: The best businesses can grow very large with no capital, often consumer or service businesses or ones paid in advance by customers; everyone wants them, so they are hard to buy cheaply.
evolution_notes: The elision skips See's (wonderful, needs little capital, but cannot grow by people eating more chocolate) and crosses Munger's "Except here." (line 1101); Buffett resumes the same thought. Restates M2009-105 (the best businesses need little capital); new here is growth without capital as the mark of the very best and the competition to buy them. Munger: "I’ve got nothing to add, but at any rate, the formula never changes" (line 1105).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 26. Companies with the best return on capital

quote_verbatim: If you name some business that has incredible pricing power, you’re talking about a business that’s a monopoly or a near monopoly.
concept: Munger: incredible pricing power means a monopoly or near monopoly.
evolution_notes: Said to explain why he will not name the business he most admires: "I don’t think it’s very smart for us to sit up here naming our most admired business or something, that other people regard as a monopoly" (line 1121), not rowed.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 26. Companies with the best return on capital

quote_verbatim: And it’s human revulsion that has helped us, because many of the people who sell to us are so smart that they’re revolted by almost everything else. They don’t want to sell into some fee-driven buying system that doesn’t care about their employees or their business. [...] We’ve got a screening device out there that is protecting us, to some extent, from the wrong sort of people.
concept: Munger: a buyer known to care for employees and keep businesses attracts sellers who care, and that reputation screens out the wrong sort of seller.
evolution_notes: Continues: "We get offered things by people who would not sell to anybody else" (line 1133). Buffett then tells of ISCAR and of a seller who rejected a competitor and a buyout firm, not wanting "his place being, basically, a piece of meat that would be resold" (lines 1139-1141); description, not rowed. Cf. M2008-042 (Munger, an owner should sell his life's work to a good steward).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 27. Phone hasn’t been ringing, but we’re still ready to buy

quote_verbatim: But there’s not much we can do to accelerate the process or do anything of the sort. We are ready to act when it happens. I mean, if I get a call, and it’s a $10 billion deal, on Monday, and I like it, I will say yes. (Laughs) And then I’ll figure out how we do it.
concept: Acquisitions cannot be hurried; be ready to say yes at once when the right one calls and work out the means afterwards.
evolution_notes: Earlier in the answer: the criteria published in the annual report, earnings of 75 or 100 million before tax at a minimum, "weeds out a lot of phone calls" (line 1131). Related to M2008-086 (if we cannot decide in five minutes we cannot in five months).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 27. Phone hasn’t been ringing, but we’re still ready to buy

quote_verbatim: I think it is quite interesting that we got into BYD, because BYD is surfing along on the developing edge of new technology, and that has not — we have always bragged about avoiding that. Isn’t that a fair statement? WARREN BUFFETT: That’s fair. CHARLIE MUNGER: And yet here we are. I think it’s because we’ve shown some capability for learning. [...] And we wouldn’t have felt confident enough to go into venture capital, typically with just a bright young man with an idea, no matter how brilliant. [...] But BYD had won its spurs in life by the time we found it. They had accomplished things that struck me as almost impossible to do, and yet they’d done them.
concept: Munger: the BYD purchase breaks the boast of avoiding new technology; his reconciliation is a test, invest not in an idea but in people who have already won their spurs by doing the near impossible.
evolution_notes: Exchange, Munger first, Buffett's "That’s fair." kept as printed. Pulls against L2009-005 (avoid businesses whose futures we can't evaluate, however exciting the products) and L1999-020 (fast-changing industries beyond our competence). The first elision skips BYD working out well and Kiewit's discipline (line 1159); the second crosses Buffett's "Not me." and Munger's "No, I wouldn’t either." (lines 1161-1163), Munger resuming.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 28. Big question for Berkshire’s future

quote_verbatim: And I think the Burlington Northern acquisition — when we did it, we knew it would be better for their shareholders than it was for ours, because, after all, they were getting into Berkshire. (Laughter) But we also thought it was good for our shareholders. And why should we care that it was better for theirs, if it was satisfactory for us?
concept: Munger: a deal that is satisfactory for us is worth doing even if the other side gets more out of it.
evolution_notes: Continues: "I think that will happen again, too. That’s our kind of a culture" (line 1163).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 28. Big question for Berkshire’s future

quote_verbatim: But to answer your question on that, Andrew, I would probably ask the question, you know, “Can you keep using all of the capital you generate, effectively, for a very long time?” [...] There comes a point where the numbers get big enough that it gets extraordinarily hard to do things that add value. [...] And there will come a time when we cannot intelligent — in my view — there will come a time when we cannot intelligently use 100 percent of the capital that we develop internally. And then we’ll do something that’s — whatever is in the most interest — best interest — of the shareholders will be done at that point.
concept: The question to ask of a compounding company is whether it can keep using all the capital it generates effectively; size eventually makes adding more than a dollar of value per dollar extraordinarily hard, and then the surplus must go elsewhere.
evolution_notes: Restates M2010-017 (the morning: huge sums cannot be reinvested at huge returns) and M2010-046 (the retained-dollar test, this session). The elisions skip "we will see more things" and "our history is a curve that approaches that point all the time" (line 1165).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 28. Big question for Berkshire’s future

quote_verbatim: We have managers, you know, they come — some of them went to business school, some of them didn’t, you know. They’re all types. But the common factor in them — they’re successful — the common factor is they love what they do, you know.
concept: Schooling does not mark Berkshire's successful managers; loving what they do is the common factor.
evolution_notes: Related to M2008-005 (does a manager love the business or the money). Buffett's example is Mrs. B, who never went to school, built the largest home furnishings store from $500 of capital and kept price tags on her own furniture (lines 1191-1193).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 29. “Find your passion, and then don’t let anything stop you”

quote_verbatim: So if you find something that turns you on, my guess is you’re going to do very well in it. And the beauty of it is, in a sense, there’s not that much competition. There are not a lot of people out there that are going to be running faster than you in the race that you elect to get into. [...] So find your passion, and then don’t let anything stop you.
concept: Find work that excites you and pursue it without letting anything stop you; few will outrun someone running a race he chose.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct. The elision crosses Munger's "Oh yeah." (line 1189) and the Mrs. B story (lines 1191-1193); Buffett resumes the same thought. Cf. M2010-044 (this session: little competition for one who thinks like an owner).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 29. “Find your passion, and then don’t let anything stop you”

quote_verbatim: It’s pragmatism. Partly, we do things in our different way because it suits us. And partly, we do it — it suits our temperaments and our natures — and partly, we do it because we’ve found through experience that it works better, at least with us sitting where we sit. It’s just that simple. And we’ve had enough good sense when something is working very well to keep doing it. So I’d say we’re demonstrating what might be called the fundamental algorithm of life. Repeat what works.
concept: Munger: the unifying principle is pragmatism; do what suits your temperament and what experience shows works, and keep doing what works.
evolution_notes: Answers a question listing Berkshire's departures from common practice: managers kept after acquisition, no large director pay or options, no earnings guidance, no high tech (lines 1199-1203).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 30. Munger’s fundamental algorithm of life

quote_verbatim: Yeah, I think by its nature, it would be non-economic when it competes with auto and competes with air. We don’t have the point-to-point density and demand that would produce a return on capital. [...] So it will be — if it gets done — unless it’s heavily subsidized in some way, which means it’s public anyway — I don’t think it will happen under private — it won’t meet the test of private economics.
concept: Ask whether a capital project would be funded by money that wants a return: without the density and demand to earn on its capital against cheaper competing modes, it fails the test of private economics.
evolution_notes: Said of high-speed passenger rail; "I made no big study of it" (line 1227). He closes: "if ... it becomes a huge project or something of the government so it isn’t anybody’s math ... I don’t think it’ll ever happen with money that wants a return" (line 1245). A judgment of one kind of project, rowed for the general check it states.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 31. Private high-speed passenger trains aren’t economic

quote_verbatim: That’s what the insurance business is all about. [...] I think in terms of a 250 billion sort of worst case. And my guess is if that came along, and we had a normal year and everything else, Berkshire would still have positive earnings of some substantial amount. So we are prepared.
concept: Size catastrophe exposure against a worst case well beyond any loss yet seen, so that even then the whole company still earns money.
evolution_notes: Implied: Buffett describes Berkshire's position rather than stating a rule; what is shown is a worst case set at 250 billion of industry loss, above Katrina's roughly 70 billion (line 1255). He adds that Berkshire's share would be about 4 percent, $10 billion, less than a year's pre-tax earnings outside insurance (line 1267).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 32. We can handle claims from a major earthquake

quote_verbatim: Berkshire, from any insurance catastrophe — and you’re right that things correlate on the downside — when things are bad in one area, they really do spread to another. But we were built, I think, to withstand anything that — other than a total sort of wipe out of the world.
concept: Risks correlate on the downside, trouble in one area spreading to others; build to withstand everything short of the end of the world.
evolution_notes: Earlier in the answer: "I think Berkshire can withstand anything that any corporation can. And it won’t be our insurance business that causes a problem" (line 1279), and the 2008 bet that the government would act (line 1279), a forecast. Cf. speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 33. “Huge amounts of debt are not going to do us in”

quote_verbatim: Yearly figures, it should be noted, are neither to be ignored nor viewed as all-important. The pace of the earth's movement around the sun is not synchronized with the time required for either investment ideas or operating decisions to bear fruit. At GEICO, for example, we enthusiastically spent $900 million last year on advertising to obtain policyholders who deliver us no immediate profits. If we could spend twice that amount productively, we would happily do so though short-term results would be further penalized.
concept: Judge results over the time an idea or an operating decision needs to bear fruit, not the calendar year, and spend now for customers who pay off later even when short-term results suffer.
evolution_notes: Close to L1998-011 (current results matter but never at the cost of building competitive strength); the point added here is that the calendar year and the payoff period are not synchronized. Lines 167-168 add that large railroad and utility investments are also made for payoffs well down the road. The bull's-eye passage just before (lines 141-143) repeats L2009-001 and is not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Performance

quote_verbatim: There is a third, more subjective, element to an intrinsic value calculation that can be either positive or negative: the efficacy with which retained earnings will be deployed in the future. [...] Some companies will turn these retained dollars into fifty-cent pieces, others into two-dollar bills. This "what-will-they-do-with-the-money" factor must always be evaluated along with the "what-do-we-have-now" calculation in order for us, or anybody, to arrive at a sensible estimate of a company's intrinsic value. That's because an outside investor stands by helplessly as management reinvests his share of the company's earnings. If a CEO can be expected to do this job well, the reinvestment prospects add to the company's current value; if the CEO's talents or motives are suspect, today's value must be discounted.
concept: Intrinsic value includes a judgment of what management will do with retained earnings; add for a capable reinvestor, discount today's value when the CEO's talent or motives are suspect.
evolution_notes: The first two components (investments per share, non-insurance earnings per share, lines 289-346) repeat L2006-002 and are not rowed; this third, subjective element is new in the letters read so far. Related to L1996-008 (retained earnings count fully only when the business can employ capital to advantage), which looks at the business; this looks at the manager. Lines 357-359 give the example: a dollar in the hands of Sears's or Montgomery Ward's CEOs in the late 1960s against a dollar entrusted to Sam Walton.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Intrinsic Value � Today and Tomorrow

quote_verbatim: Our second advantage relates to the allocation of the money our businesses earn. After meeting the needs of those businesses, we have very substantial sums left over. Most companies limit themselves to reinvesting funds within the industry in which they have been operating. That often restricts them, however, to a "universe" for capital allocation that is both tiny and quite inferior to what is available in the wider world. Competition for the few opportunities that are available tends to become fierce. [...] At Berkshire we face no institutional restraints when we deploy capital. Charlie and I are limited only by our ability to understand the likely future of a possible acquisition. If we clear that hurdle � and frequently we can't � we are then able to compare any one opportunity against a host of others.
concept: Do not confine reinvestment to your own industry; the only limit on where capital goes should be the ability to understand a business's likely future, and each opportunity is compared against many others.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the joke of the only girl at a party (lines 388-390). Restates in the letters R1996-024 (the centre has a much wider range of possibilities than an operating manager), a report row, and so is rowed under the 2004-2005 convention. The textile confession (lines 398-402) and the comparison against marketable securities (lines 404-408) follow and are rowed separately; lines 410-412 (money from See's and Business Wire used toward BNSF) illustrate it.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Intrinsic Value � Today and Tomorrow

quote_verbatim: When I took control of Berkshire in 1965, I didn't exploit this advantage. Berkshire was then only in textiles, where it had in the previous decade lost significant money. The dumbest thing I could have done was to pursue "opportunities" to improve and expand the existing textile operation � so for years that's exactly what I did. And then, in a final burst of brilliance, I went out and bought another textile company. Aaaaaaargh! Eventually I came to my senses, heading first into insurance and then into other industries.
concept: Buffett's own error: pouring capital into improving and expanding a money-losing textile business, and buying another, because it was the business he was in; the cure was moving capital into other industries.
evolution_notes: Buffett's own mistake. It is the counter-example to the rule just before it (the capital-allocation universe, lines 384-394). No earlier letter row in the v5 read narrates the textile reinvestment.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Intrinsic Value � Today and Tomorrow

quote_verbatim: There is even a supplement to this world-is-our-oyster advantage: In addition to evaluating the attractions of one business against a host of others, we also measure businesses against opportunities available in marketable securities, a comparison most managements don't make. Often, businesses are priced ridiculously high against what can likely be earned from investments in stocks or bonds. At such moments, we buy securities and bide our time.
concept: Measure the price of a whole business against what the same money can likely earn in stocks or bonds, and buy securities and wait when businesses are priced too high.
evolution_notes: Related to L2000-022 (one discounting formula ranks every use of capital) and L1997-007 (when the favourite commitment is unavailable, park new money short-term); the comparison of whole businesses against marketable securities as a standing test is new in the letters read so far.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Intrinsic Value � Today and Tomorrow

quote_verbatim: Cultures self-propagate. Winston Churchill once said, "You shape your houses and then they shape you." That wisdom applies to businesses as well. Bureaucratic procedures beget more bureaucracy, and imperial corporate palaces induce imperious behavior. [...] As long as Charlie and I treat your money as if it were our own, Berkshire's managers are likely to be careful with it as well. Our compensation programs, our annual meeting and even our annual reports are all designed with an eye to reinforcing the Berkshire culture, and making it one that will repel and expel managers of a different bent.
concept: Culture propagates itself from what the top does: bureaucracy and lavish headquarters breed more of the same, frugality with owners' money at the top is copied below, and pay, meetings and reports should be built to repel managers of a different bent.
evolution_notes: Churchill's line is quoted by Buffett, so the row is his. The elision skips the back-seat joke and the headquarters rent and furniture figures (lines 431-434). Lines 417-422 (directors paid token amounts, no D&O insurance) repeat L2002-035 and are not rowed. Meeting rows on the same theme: M2010-031 (Munger, no imperial headquarters) and M2010-021 (easier to build a culture than to change one).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Intrinsic Value � Today and Tomorrow

quote_verbatim: The excess over tangible net worth of the implied value � $2.7 billion � was what we estimated GEICO's "goodwill" to be worth at that time. That goodwill represented the economic value of the policyholders who were then doing business with GEICO. In 1995, those customers had paid the company $2.8 billion in premiums. Consequently, we were valuing GEICO's customers at about 97% (2.7/2.8) of what they were annually paying the company. By industry standards, that was a very high price. But GEICO was no ordinary insurer: Because of the company's low costs, its policyholders were consistently profitable and unusually loyal.
concept: Economic goodwill is the value of the customers a business holds; it can be priced against what they pay each year, and a high price is justified when low costs make those customers profitable and loyal.
evolution_notes: The section opens (line 447) as a case study of how intrinsic value can far exceed book value. Lines 502-507 apply the same 97%-of-premium yardstick to 2010's $14.3 billion of premium, about $14 billion of economic goodwill against $1.4 billion carried. Related to L1999-010 (economic goodwill often grows) and L1996-015 (GEICO's low-cost circle); line 484 ("get the policyholder's business by deserving his business") restates L1996-015's circle and is not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: GEICO

quote_verbatim: At bottom, a sound insurance operation requires four disciplines: (1) An understanding of all exposures that might cause a policy to incur losses; (2) A conservative evaluation of the likelihood of any exposure actually causing a loss and the probable cost if it does; (3) The setting of a premium that will deliver a profit, on average, after both prospective loss costs and operating expenses are covered; and (4) The willingness to walk away if the appropriate premium can't be obtained. Many insurers pass the first three tests and flunk the fourth. The urgings of Wall Street, pressures from the agency force and brokers, or simply a refusal by a testosterone-driven CEO to accept shrinking volumes has led too many insurers to write business at inadequate prices. "The other guy is doing it so we must as well" spells trouble in any business, but none more so than insurance.
concept: Four tests of an insurance operation (know the exposures, estimate loss conservatively, price for an average profit, walk away when the price cannot be had); the fourth is the one most fail, under pressure from Wall Street, brokers and a CEO who will not shrink.
evolution_notes: A reformulation of the FY2001 letter's three rules (L2001-007, L2001-008, L2001-009), rowed because it names the fourth discipline as the one most insurers fail and the pressures that make them fail it. Related: L1997-018 (Ajit walks away from underpriced business), L2004-004 (managements will not accept a long fall in volume), L1998-030 (everybody's-doing-it reasoning). The float passages (lines 532-570) repeat L1993-009 and L1996-008 and are not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Insurance

quote_verbatim: Unfortunately, a few have very poor returns, a result of some serious mistakes I have made in my job of capital allocation. These errors came about because I misjudged either the competitive strength of the business I was purchasing or the future economics of the industry in which it operated. I try to look out ten or twenty years when making an acquisition, but sometimes my eyesight has been poor.
concept: Buffett's own acquisition errors had two causes: misjudging the bought business's competitive strength, or misjudging its industry's future economics; the judgment must reach ten or twenty years ahead and sometimes fails.
evolution_notes: Buffett's own mistakes, unnamed. Lines 668-670 give the spread of returns on unleveraged net tangible assets across the group (25% to more than 100% after tax for some, 12-20% for others). Related to L2009-017 (what the business earns in the succeeding decade or two) and L2006-006 (the industry, not the manager, decides the outcome).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Manufacturing, Service and Retailing Operations

quote_verbatim: Even though NetJets was consistently a runaway winner with customers, our financial results, since its acquisition in 1998, were a failure. In the 11 years through 2009, the company reported an aggregate pre-tax loss of $157 million, a figure that was far understated since borrowing costs at NetJets were heavily subsidized by its free use of Berkshire's credit. Had NetJets been operating on a stand-alone basis, its loss over the years would have been several hundreds of millions greater. We are now charging NetJets an appropriate fee for Berkshire's guarantee.
concept: A subsidiary's reported results can hide its real losses when it borrows on the parent's credit for free; judge it as if stand-alone and charge it for the guarantee.
evolution_notes: Berkshire's own mistake (the FY2009 letter's "I failed you", not rowed in 2010 AM). The lesson is implied: what was done is the fee now charged for the guarantee ($38 million in 2010, line 718). Applies L2003-020 (every tub on its own bottom; a parent's subsidy breeds sloppy decisions) to NetJets. Meeting row M2010-026 narrates the NetJets aircraft-pricing error.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Manufacturing, Service and Retailing Operations

quote_verbatim: In any event, it is certain to occur at some point. Consequently: (1) At MiTek, we have made, or committed to, five bolt-on acquisitions during the past eleven months; [...] These businesses entered the recession strong and will exit it stronger. At Berkshire, our time horizon is forever.
concept: With a permanent horizon, keep investing in businesses through a slump that is certain to end, even when its timing is not known.
evolution_notes: Implied in part by the acts listed at lines 756-759 (bolt-ons at MiTek, a brick maker bought at Acme, a new Johns Manville plant, $200 million of Shaw capital spending). The sentence before the quote ("A housing recovery will probably begin within a year or so", line 755) is a forecast and is left out. Related to R1996-001 (a share held indefinitely) and L2005-006 (buy to keep, no exit plan).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Manufacturing, Service and Retailing Operations

quote_verbatim: A key characteristic of both companies is the huge investment they have in very long-lived, regulated assets, with these funded by large amounts of long-term debt that is not guaranteed by Berkshire. Our credit is not needed: Both businesses have earning power that, even under very adverse business conditions, amply covers their interest requirements.
concept: Long-lived regulated assets can carry large long-term debt without the parent's guarantee when their earning power covers the interest amply even in very adverse conditions.
evolution_notes: Restates in the letters R2009-001 (debt non-recourse in the capital-heavy subsidiaries), a report row; the coverage test under adverse conditions is the point rowed. Line 772 gives BNSF's 6:1 interest coverage in recessionary 2010. Lines 774-777 (a fair return in exchange for service and investment) repeat L2009-011 and are not rowed. Related: L2005-019 (debt safety depends on diversity of the earnings that service it).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Regulated, Capital-Intensive Businesses

quote_verbatim: Coca-Cola paid us $88 million in 1995, the year after we finished purchasing the stock. Every year since, Coke has increased its dividend. [...] By the end of that period, I wouldn't be surprised to see our share of Coke's annual earnings exceed 100% of what we paid for the investment. Time is the friend of the wonderful business.
concept: A wonderful business shows itself over time: its dividends and earnings keep rising against the fixed price once paid, until a year's earnings can exceed the whole cost.
evolution_notes: The elided lines (1014-1015) carry the 2011 dividend figure and a forecast that it will double within ten years. The sentence "Time is the friend of the wonderful business" has no earlier row in the v5 read. Lines 965-971 (undistributed earnings of investees matched by market gains over time) repeat L1996-038 and L1994-024 and are not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Investments

quote_verbatim: It's easy to identify many investment managers with great recent records. But past results, though important, do not suffice when prospective performance is being judged. How the record has been achieved is crucial, as is the manager's understanding of � and sensitivity to � risk (which in no way should be measured by beta, the choice of too many academics). In respect to the risk criterion, we were looking for someone with a hard-to-evaluate skill: the ability to anticipate the effects of economic scenarios not previously observed. Finally, we wanted someone who would regard working for Berkshire as far more than a job.
concept: Judge an investment manager not by the record alone but by how it was achieved, by his sensitivity to risk (never measured by beta), by his ability to foresee the effects of scenarios never seen, and by whether the work is more than a job to him.
evolution_notes: Restates L2006-012 (an inborn ability to recognize and avoid risks never before encountered) and adds that how the record was achieved is crucial and that the candidate must regard the work as more than a job. Related: L2006-018 (skill against luck in a record), L1993-017 (beta as risk is precisely wrong). Lines 1074-1078 ("a 2-year-old Secretariat, not a 10-year-old Seabiscuit") make a related point about hiring before a name is known, as a joke; not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Investments

quote_verbatim: Todd, as was the case with Lou, will be paid a salary plus a contingent payment based on his performance relative to the S&P. We have arrangements in place for deferrals and carryforwards that will prevent see-saw performance being met by undeserved payments. The hedge-fund world has witnessed some terrible behavior by general partners who have received huge payouts on the upside and who then, when bad results occurred, have walked away rich, with their limited partners losing back their earlier gains. [...] Investors who put money with such managers should be labeled patsies, not partners.
concept: Pay an investment manager on performance against the index only with deferrals and carryforwards, so that a bad stretch claws against earlier good ones; investors who accept upside-only pay are patsies, not partners.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the general partners who restart a fund to escape their past losses (lines 1054-1056). Restates in part L2005-017 (Helpers who take the winnings and leave the losses) and echoes the phrase of L2001-002 (patsies, not partners), which was about managers selling while urging owners to buy; the deferral-and-carryforward structure is the new rule.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Investments

quote_verbatim: Over time, we may add one or two investment managers if we find the right individuals. Should we do that, we will probably have 80% of each manager's performance compensation be dependent on his or her own portfolio and 20% on that of the other manager(s). We want a compensation system that pays off big for individual success but that also fosters cooperation, not competition.
concept: Tie most of each investment manager's incentive pay to his own portfolio and a part to his colleagues', so the system rewards individual success but fosters cooperation.
evolution_notes: Pulls against L1996-020 (foolish to tie an insurer's bonuses to overall results when one side's great work can be neutralized by the other's bad work) and L1997-022 (tie bonuses to each unit's own performance, the direct product of its people): here a fifth of each manager's pay depends on portfolios he does not run. The letter does not reconcile the two. The quote also carries a rule, not a test.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Investments

quote_verbatim: Let's focus here on a number we omitted, but which many in the media feature above all others: net income. Important though that number may be at most companies, it is almost always meaningless at Berkshire. Regardless of how our businesses might be doing, Charlie and I could � quite legally � cause net income in any given period to be almost any number we would like. [...] Operating earnings, despite having some shortcomings, are in general a reasonable guide as to how our businesses are doing. Ignore our net income figure, however.
concept: Where management can choose when to realize gains, net income can be made almost any number and means little; judge the business by operating earnings and the change in book value.
evolution_notes: The elision crosses the mechanism (realized gains counted, unrealized excluded, lines 1161-1166) and the rule on never selling for reported income at lines 1168-1172, rowed in this batch. Lines 1178-1180 add that book value reflects both realized and unrealized gains, so book value and operating earnings together are the right track. Related: R1995-005 (consolidated reported earnings may say little about economic performance).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: On Reporting and Misreporting: The Numbers That Count and Those That Don't

quote_verbatim: If we really thought net income important, we could regularly feed realized gains into it simply because we have a huge amount of unrealized gains upon which to draw. Rest assured, though, that Charlie and I have never sold a security because of the effect a sale would have on the net income we were soon to report. We both have a deep disgust for "game playing" with numbers, a practice that was rampant throughout corporate America in the 1990s and still persists, though it occurs less frequently and less blatantly than it used to.
concept: Never sell a security for the effect the sale will have on the reported income; playing games with numbers is to be shunned.
evolution_notes: Related to R1995-006 (accounting consequences do not influence operating or capital-allocation decisions). The Black-Scholes passage that follows (lines 1184-1207, ending "We would rather be approximately right than precisely wrong") repeats L2008-025, L2008-026 and L1993-017; lines 1209-1214 on academics clinging to efficient markets repeat L2006-019; lines 1218-1221 (value a business, not an option) repeat L1996-036. None of these is rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: On Reporting and Misreporting: The Numbers That Count and Those That Don't

quote_verbatim: The fundamental principle of auto racing is that to finish first, you must first finish. That dictum is equally applicable to business and guides our every action at Berkshire. Unquestionably, some people have become very rich through the use of borrowed money. However, that's also been a way to get very poor. When leverage works, it magnifies your gains. Your spouse thinks you're clever, and your neighbors get envious. But leverage is addictive. Once having profited from its wonders, very few people retreat to more conservative practices. And as we all learned in third grade � and some relearned in 2008 � any series of positive numbers, however impressive the numbers may be, evaporates when multiplied by a single zero. History tells us that leverage all too often produces zeroes, even when it is employed by very smart people.
concept: To finish first you must first finish: leverage magnifies gains but is addictive, and a single zero erases any series of gains, even for very smart people, so survival governs every action.
evolution_notes: The racing maxim appears in R1995-007 (a report row, attributed there to an Indianapolis 500 winner), so the letter passage is rowed under the 2004-2005 convention. Restates L2005-021 (a long record multiplied by one ruinous event is zero) and adds that leverage is addictive once it has paid. Lines 1246-1251 (no activity that could pose the slightest threat; irresponsible to risk what the constituencies need for a few points of return) repeat L2005-020 and are not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Life and Debt

quote_verbatim: Leverage, of course, can be lethal to businesses as well. Companies with large debts often assume that these obligations can be refinanced as they mature. That assumption is usually valid. Occasionally, though, either because of company-specific problems or a worldwide shortage of credit, maturities must actually be met by payment. For that, only cash will do the job. Borrowers then learn that credit is like oxygen. When either is abundant, its presence goes unnoticed. When either is missing, that's all that is noticed. Even a short absence of credit can bring a company to its knees.
concept: Do not count on refinancing: occasionally maturities must be paid, only cash will do, and even a short absence of credit can bring a company down.
evolution_notes: Related to L2008-019 (tomorrow's obligations never depend on others' willingness to lend) and L2002-015 (collateral triggers turn a setback into a liquidity spiral). The refinancing assumption as the hazard is new in the letters read so far. Lines 1265-1271 (Ernest's $1,000, the pledge of at least $10 billion of cash) restate L2008-019 and L2009-006 and are not rowed; the 1939 letter said to be on the facing page is not in the file (lines 1273-1275 carry only page numbers).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Life and Debt

quote_verbatim: We keep our cash largely in U.S. Treasury bills and avoid other short-term securities yielding a few more basis points, a policy we adhered to long before the frailties of commercial paper and money market funds became apparent in September 2008. We agree with investment writer Ray DeVoe's observation, "More money has been lost reaching for yield than at the point of a gun." At Berkshire, we don't rely on bank lines, and we don't enter into contracts that could require postings of collateral except for amounts that are tiny in relation to our liquid assets.
concept: Hold cash in Treasury bills and give up the few extra basis points of other short-term paper; do not rely on bank lines or contracts that can demand collateral.
evolution_notes: Ray DeVoe's maxim, quoted by Buffett, so the row is his. The collateral clause repeats L2008-024; the Treasury-bill and bank-line clauses are new in the letters read so far. Lines 1290-1293 (caution costs a little return, liquidity lets us play offense while others scramble) restate L2009-006 and L2008-002 and are not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Life and Debt

quote_verbatim: Our estimate — we’ve added a little something into their estimate because on balance we feel that most catastrophe losses develop upward. It’s sort of the nature of the business.
concept: Early estimates of catastrophe losses tend to grow, so add to the ceding company's figure rather than accept it.
evolution_notes: Restates L2005-008 (unpleasant reserve surprises far outnumber pleasant ones). The estimate added to is Swiss Re's, under the 20 percent quota-share contract.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 3. Q1 earnings hurt by Asian catastrophes

quote_verbatim: That is added goodwill value, the same sort of goodwill value that a Coca-Cola has, or a Mars has, or any company like that. And people think of it differently when they think of most consumer products. But a policyholder to Berkshire at GEICO has very, very significant value. [...] And it’s something that we do not realize on our balance sheet or income account, but it’s an asset that’s every bit as real as the numbers that we do put on the balance sheet.
concept: A loyal customer base is goodwill as real as a consumer brand's, though the accounts never record its growth.

Line 45 puts the value at about $1,500 per policyholder and the quarter's added policies at nearly $500 million of goodwill; the elision skips the remark that many policyholders have stayed ten years or more.
speaker: BUFFETT

quote_verbatim: the fact that you should ignore gains or losses in securities or derivatives on a quarterly basis, or even an annual basis. The important thing is what the operating earnings of our businesses are doing and what the gain in book value, generally, has been. And then on top of that, you have to make your own estimate for what intrinsic value is, which would include things like the goodwill value that has been developed at GEICO. quote_verbatim: Well, the businesses that will perform the best are the ones that require little capital investment to facilitate inflationary growth and that have strong positions that allow them to increase prices with inflation. [...] So that kind of a business — any business that can — that has enough freedom to price to offset inflation and doesn’t commensurate invest — or huge investment — to support it, will do well. Businesses like our utilities which get, in effect, a bond-like return [...] is not going to do that well in an inflationary period, just because it has certain aspects of a bond-like investment, and bonds generally are not going to do well in inflation.
concept: In inflation the winners need little added capital and can raise prices; businesses earning a fixed, bond-like return on ever costlier plant do poorly.

Munger answers (line 705) that the capital-intensive railroad and utilities are among the best in the world, "it isn’t all bad to be up there, world class, in your main businesses"; Buffett's reply is the next row.

quote_verbatim: Goodwill should not be used in evaluating the fundamental attractiveness of a business. There you should look at return on tangible assets, and even then there’s some minor — some other adjustments you may want to make. But basically, in evaluating the businesses we own, in terms of what the management are doing and what the underlying economics of the business are, forget about goodwill. In terms of evaluating the job we’re doing in allocating capital, you have to include goodwill, because we paid for it.
concept: Judge a business and its operating management on return on tangible assets; judge the buyer's capital allocation on the full price paid, goodwill included.
evolution_notes: Buffett illustrates with Lubrizol (line 775): about 2 1/2 billion of equity employed to earn a billion pretax, against close to 9 billion paid: "You have to judge us based on close to a $9 billion investment. You have to judge James Hambrick in running the business based on the much lower capital that he has employed." Related: L2010-007 (goodwill as the economic value of customers), M2008-074 (good businesses earn good returns on tangible assets).

concept: Goodwill should not be amortized, but written off when a purchase proves wrong because earnings do not cover tangible assets plus goodwill.

quote_verbatim: I don’t think the option price — the original strike price — should be less than if the company were for sale, the assets would bring. So the idea of giving somebody an option during some depressed part of the stock market at the market price, I think, is crazy because you wouldn’t sell your business at that price and why sell part of it on that basis. So I think the base price should be what the business is worth at the time you start, and then I think if, because of the compounding feature of leaving money there — you know, no management at all would produce some gain in value over time — so I think there should be an increase in the base price annually at some rate, and then minus the dividend that’s being paid. [...] But with that kind of a structure, I think you can give a very large option because you — if somebody is creating excess value above a given rate on a very large sum, I think they deserve something quite significant in terms of that excess earned.
concept: Set an option's strike at what the whole business would bring, raise it yearly for the gain retained money produces anyway, less dividends, and then pay generously for value created above that rate.
evolution_notes: Of the next CEO's pay. The elision skips the worked example (a 3 percent dividend, a 7 or 8 percent hurdle, the strike rising 4 or 5 percent). Later in the answer: Berkshire's managers "earn it, and they don’t get it because of any phony targets". Related: L2005-014 (fixed-price ten-year options reward retained earnings alone), L2004-016, L2009-019 (would not sell the whole at that price, so why sell a part).
