heading: ### 20. How to judge if Buffett is doing a good job of allocating capital

quote_verbatim: I was thinking about what else I could do with $2.7 billion, and that’s the way all the decisions are made. So they are not related — they’re not related to each other. They go through a mind that is looking at everything available that day, including the amount of cash we have, the likelihood of being able to do something else next week or next month, what else we can do that day. And past deals we’ve made don’t really make any difference.
concept: Judge each commitment against everything else available that day, the cash on hand and the chance of something better soon; past deals do not set the terms.
evolution_notes: On why five crisis-era deals carried different terms: "Our opportunity costs were different in every single one of those five transactions" (line 901), where Buffett also says "I was early on Goldman and GE". Munger agrees (line 907): "of course, we’re going to make different deals at different times based on different opportunity costs. There’s no other rational way to make deals." Related: M2001-084 (the cost of every deal is the second best deal around), M2003-151 (Munger, everything comes back to opportunity cost).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 21. Don’t compare opportunities now to your best-ever deal

quote_verbatim: one of the errors people make in business — and sometimes it can be a huge error — is that they try and measure every deal against the best deal they’ve ever made. [...] So they, in effect — sometimes they take themselves out of the game. The goal is not to make a better deal than you’ve ever made before. The goal is to make a satisfactory deal that’s the best deal you can make at the time.
concept: Measuring every deal against one's best ever takes one out of the game; aim for the best satisfactory deal available now.
evolution_notes: A mistake Buffett attributes to people in business generally. Opens mid-sentence after "In fact, one of the things —". The elision skips the example of the wonderful past deal setting a bar never to be lowered. Shares line 903 with the opportunity-cost row of this batch. Related: M2010-096 (Munger, a satisfactory deal suffices).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 21. Don’t compare opportunities now to your best-ever deal

quote_verbatim: And it’s a huge advantage to be able to read fast. [...] Obviously, the thing to do is to learn them very young because there really — there’s nothing — there’s hardly anything more pleasurable, you know, than reading and reading and reading and reading. And Charlie and I do a lot of it.
concept: Read a great deal, and learn to read fast young if effective techniques exist.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct. Buffett says he is "not a fast reader" though he reads five papers and many 10-Ks and 10-Qs. The elision skips the Woody Allen speed-reading joke. Munger answers that speed is overestimated (next row); see the note's Tensions seen.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 22. You don’t have to read quickly but you should read

quote_verbatim: Well, I think speed is overestimated. I had a roommate at Caltech who had a very distinguished mind, and I could do problems faster than he could, but he never made a mistake, and I did. (Laughter) So, I wouldn’t be too discouraged if you have to go a little slower.
concept: Accuracy matters more than speed; going slower is no handicap.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct. Exchange: follows Buffett's "it’s a huge advantage to be able to read fast" (lines 915-917), rowed separately; each states a separate lesson. Munger adds "What the hell difference does it make?"
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 22. You don’t have to read quickly but you should read

quote_verbatim: And believe me, when it’s time to pay somebody back, and you have a choice of paying — and you’re forced to pay somebody else’s currency versus paying in your own — it’s entirely a different proposition. [...] And I thought to myself, and Charlie concurred, who the hell knew what they were going to say the value of the dinar was when we went to pay it back. It was not something over which we had a lot of control. So we decided not to borrow the money in dinars even though I kind of wish we’d bought the bank.
concept: Do not borrow in a currency you do not control; repaying in someone else's currency is a different and uncontrollable risk.
evolution_notes: Stated inside a political answer on the debt ceiling; the borrower's rule is rowed, the politics left out (line 939: "The difference between being able to borrow in your own currency and having to borrow in another currency is night and day", said of the United States). The elision skips the euro members and Japan and the Chicago bank story of the late 1960s, when tight money "meant no money" and the only lender found was in Kuwait; it crosses Munger's "Chicago." (line 943) and "Kuwaiti dinars. (Laughter)" (line 947), and Buffett resumes the same thought. Related: M2010-012 (distinguish countries borrowing in their own currency).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 23. Buffett: There shouldn’t even be a debt ceiling

quote_verbatim: Yeah, we can’t be so risk averse that things that have a very tiny chance of making a big dent in one subsidiary are unendurable for us. We have to have a certain reasonable amount of courage in operating this company.
concept: Do not be so risk averse that a tiny chance of a big dent in one part becomes unendurable; operating takes reasonable courage.
evolution_notes: Exchange, Munger first, on whether a MidAmerican nuclear plant risks a mega-catastrophe for Berkshire; Buffett's reply (line 967) states a separate lesson and is rowed separately. Munger adds (line 969) that a new plant "will be a hell of a lot safer than the ones we already have. We are learning as we go along here."
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 24. Nuclear power is “important” and “safe”

quote_verbatim: But we are not bearing any risks, in my view, ever, that threaten the enterprise. I mean, that is one thing I think about all the time. I regard myself as the Chief Risk Officer of Berkshire, and that is not something to be delegated to a committee, in my view, at all.
concept: Never bear a risk that threatens the whole enterprise; the chief executive owns that judgment personally and does not delegate it to a committee.
evolution_notes: Exchange with Munger's courage row (line 965). Before: "you can dream of all kinds of worst-case situations", toxic materials carried by law on the railroad. After: derivatives, leverage, nuclear plants, nothing that "pressing my imagination as far as I can — threatens me losing a night’s sleep over Berkshire’s well-being." Restates M2008-061 (Buffett as Chief Risk Officer); related L2010-019.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 24. Nuclear power is “important” and “safe”

quote_verbatim: CHARLIE MUNGER: We don’t want the parent company involved in distracting arguments about the social issues of the times. WARREN BUFFETT: Well, we certainly don’t want it where it affects — CHARLIE MUNGER: Yeah. WARREN BUFFETT: — people who are just bystanders, basically, who have counted on us over the years to work with them.
concept: Keep the parent company out of distracting social controversies, above all where they hurt bystanders who depend on it.
evolution_notes: Exchange, Munger first, one lesson; Buffett's qualification kept inside the quote. The occasion: the shareholder-designated contributions program, ended when boycotts aimed at it cut the income of Pampered Chef's independent consultants; Buffett (line 989): "it just became apparent to me that it was unfair to continue it". Buffett says he "didn’t mind at all losing some See’s Candy business" (line 987).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 25. Charity program fell victim to pressure groups

quote_verbatim: when we look at a business and we’re looking out in the future, obviously, if we see growth in that picture and it’s growth which is — produces a high return on incremental capital involved, we love it, but we do not rule out companies where we think there will be little or no growth, if the price is attractive relative to the earning power. [...] So it’s a factor in every investment decision because we’re really looking out to the future as to future earning power, but also future capital requirements.
concept: Growth is valuable only when it earns a high return on the added capital; little or no growth is acceptable if the price is attractive against earning power, and future capital needs are weighed with future earnings.
evolution_notes: Opens mid-sentence after "But". The elision skips Lubrizol's modest growth in lubricants. He closes: "we don’t rule out companies that have very slow growth or no-growth possibilities." Related: L2007-007 (a competitive advantage in a stable industry, with or without organic growth).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 26. Why we hate projections

quote_verbatim: I’ve always regarded those projections as doing more harm than good. And Warren has never prepared one that I know of, and where an investment banker prepares one, we tend to throw them aside without reading them. [...] CHARLIE MUNGER: Yeah, yeah. And I think an enormous false precision gets into things when you program computers to make forward projections for a long period of time. We make rough projections in our head all the time. [...] CHARLIE MUNGER: And we don’t do any of those formal projections, because the fact that they’re there on paper and came out of a computer makes some people think they must be significant. I really think they do more damage than they do good.
concept: Formal long-range projections do more harm than good, lending false precision because they are on paper and from a computer; rough projections in the head are enough.
evolution_notes: The elisions cross Buffett's "We them upside down, actually.", Munger's "What?", Buffett's "We turn them upside down." (lines 1019-1023) and Buffett's "Sure." (line 1027); Munger resumes the same thought each time. Opens after the business schools "program these computers to grind these projections out" (line 1017). Restates M1995-049 and M2009-006 (Munger, worst decisions made with formal projections).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 26. Why we hate projections

quote_verbatim: I’ve never seen a projection from an investment banker that didn’t show the earnings going up over time, and believe me, the earnings don’t always go up over time. So, it’s just — you know, it’s the old story: don’t ask the barber whether you need a haircut, you know. You do not want to ask an investment banker what he thinks the earnings are going to be in five years of something he’s trying to sell.
concept: Ignore projections from those paid to sell the business; a seller's banker always shows earnings rising.
evolution_notes: The barber line is an old saying spoken by Buffett. Occasions: Scott Fetzer, where Munger offered to pay First Boston "$2 million if you don’t show me the book" (line 1033), and Lubrizol, whose projections to 2015 Buffett declined to see (line 1035: "I don’t want to look at the other follow’s projections", as printed). Restates M1994-031, M1995-050 and M2003-065; related M2010-068 (advisers paid per deal).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 26. Why we hate projections

quote_verbatim: I mean, when we look at any company to buy, or any stock to buy, we are thinking in our mind, we’ve got a model in our mind, of what that place is likely to look like over some period of years. And then we also have some model in our mind of how far off we can be. I mean there’s some things we can be way off on, there’s other things we’re likely to be in a fairly narrow range on.
concept: Hold a mental model of what the business will look like over years, and a second model of how far off that view could be.
evolution_notes: Just before (line 1035): "we are doing projections in our head, obviously, when we look at a business." After: "we sure don’t want to listen to anybody else’s projections." Munger closes (line 1039) with business-school students: "learn to do it our way, but at least until you’re out of school you have to pretend to do it their way." Related: M2003-138 (what cash can this business generate, how sure do we feel).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 26. Why we hate projections

quote_verbatim: We follow the same principles, but we recognize that we know less about tax laws, about customs, about attitudes towards shareholders, any time we get outside the United States, than we know in the United States. Now, to varying degrees, we weigh in that uncertainty. [...] But the basic principles of trying to value the business, trying to find managements in which we have confidence, in both their ability and integrity, and then finding attractive purchase price, those principles apply wherever in the world we would be investing.
concept: Abroad the same principles apply (value the business, trust management's ability and integrity, pay an attractive price), with an allowance for knowing less about taxes, customs and attitudes to shareholders.
evolution_notes: The elision skips PetroChina against Yukos, both very cheap in 2003, Buffett "more comfortable buying PetroChina" though less so than a domestic company of similar size, and the payout statement rowed next. Related: M2010-061 (advantage, management, price), M2008-069 (PetroChina decided off the figures).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 28. Evaluating a company outside the U.S.

quote_verbatim: For one thing, they said they were going to pay out 45 percent of — as I remember — 45 percent of their earnings in dividends. That’s more than any company — oil company — in the United States would tell me. So I regarded it as a plus and an indication of intent that I thought would be fulfilled, and it has been fulfilled.
concept: A management's stated commitment to pay out earnings can be read as evidence of its intent toward shareholders.
evolution_notes: Of PetroChina's report, which Buffett read: "I was fairly impressed — quite impressed — when I read the report of PetroChina" (line 1075). Same answer as the same-principles-abroad row of this batch.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 28. Evaluating a company outside the U.S.

quote_verbatim: Well, we make so few investments in China that trying to draw general lessons from us would be hard. [...] CHARLIE MUNGER: Well, we only had a couple of things in China. They’re like the one Indian. You can’t draw general lessons from them.
concept: Do not draw general lessons from one or two cases.
evolution_notes: The elision skips Munger's story of the professor who "learned that Indians always walk single file" from seeing one, and Buffett's "How did we get from there to China? (Laughter)" (line 1081); Munger resumes the same thought.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 28. Evaluating a company outside the U.S.

quote_verbatim: the last thing in the world we would do at Berkshire is to try and get 5 or 10 or 20 or 30 basis points more by going into some other things with our short-term money. It is a parking place. It’s an unattractive parking place, but it’s a parking place where we know we’ll get our car back when we want it.
concept: Short-term money is a parking place to be sure of getting back, never a place to reach for extra basis points.
evolution_notes: Opens mid-sentence after "And we get paid virtually nothing now for it, and that’s irritating, but". Before: no commercial paper or money market funds in 2008, "we basically keep it in Treasurys". After (line 1099): the $6.5 billion owed for Wrigley in October 2008, "I had to show up with cash"; later (lines 1107-1109): "our ability to come up with cash when people need it and when the rest of the world is petrified for some reason, has enabled several deals to get done." Restates L2010-021 and L2009-006.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 29. Where Berkshire’s short-term cash goes

quote_verbatim: Well, of course, I’ve watched a lot of people struggle who thought it was their duty in life to get an extra 10 basis points on the short-term money. I think it’s really stupid to try and maximize returns on short-term money if you’re in an opportunist game the way we are, where we want to suddenly deploy money. [...] CHARLIE MUNGER: Why fool around with some dubious instrument when we had sudden needs for money like that?
concept: An opportunist who must deploy money suddenly should not try to maximize returns on short-term money.
evolution_notes: Exchange, Buffett first; Munger adds the opportunist's reason, a separate lesson from Buffett's parking-place rule (line 1097). The elision skips the pipelines that "came for sale on Saturday, and we had to close on Monday" and crosses Buffett's "Yeah." (line 1103); Munger resumes. Related: L2010-021.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 29. Where Berkshire’s short-term cash goes

quote_verbatim: We look at — Berkshire has a lot of different companies, but we feel that it’s one entity and, you know, Moody’s or Standard and Poor’s has to look at each one separately and all of that, but Charlie and I did not — have not been running this business to walk away from some company.
concept: A parent that treats its subsidiaries as one entity stands behind each one and does not walk away from a failing part.
evolution_notes: On whether NetJets was "destined for bankruptcy": only as a standalone, "absent Berkshire’s ownership" (line 1143), where two insurers that would have failed were made whole, "it never crossed our mind that we would let them do it". After: Southern Casualty in Louisiana and another in Chicago, "we didn’t even think about not making them whole."
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 31. We would not have let NetJets go bankrupt

quote_verbatim: anything you do to improve your own skills, you know, you never know where it’s going to pay off later on. [...] There’s nothing like working to improve your own skills, and I would say communications skills are the first area I would work on to enhance your value throughout life, no matter what you do. [...] if you get lucky, you find your passion early on, but you want to work at something you’re passionate about, and then you want to work to improve your skills in that.
concept: Invest in your own skills, communication first, and work at something you are passionate about.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct. Opens mid-sentence after "I mean,". The first elision skips the Dale Carnegie diploma, "it’s incalculable how much value I got from that hundred dollars"; the second skips how he could not have sold securities without learning to talk to people. Restates M2008-023 (communication under taught) and M2010-099 (find what turns you on); related M2007-110 and M2009-044 (one's own earning power as the best inflation protection).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 32. Buffett’s advice: invest in your own skills

quote_verbatim: Yeah, I think economics is a really tough subject, and I think it’s easy to teach the basic microeconomics and certain of the basic ideas, but the minute it gets into the full range of complexity, you have the difficulty that the experts disagree. So, I don’t think I would hurry if I were trying to learn something into the parts of the fields where none of the experts can agree among themselves. I would master the easy stuff first.
concept: Master the basic, agreed parts of a subject first; do not hurry into the parts where the experts disagree.
evolution_notes: Buffett follows (line 1163): "I would not advise taking lots of courses in economics to somebody going to school", his Wharton economics courses not the ones "that pushed me forward in any significant way".
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 32. Buffett’s advice: invest in your own skills

quote_verbatim: We would love to have a lot more attractive reinsurance business on the books, we just — we just can’t find it at prices that we think are commensurate for the risk. But it’s not because of an aversion to risk overall.
concept: Write insurance only at prices commensurate with the risk, even with ample capacity to bear more.
evolution_notes: Before (line 1171): the Munich Re and Swiss Re stakes, under $4 billion, are no constraint, "We’re way below, sort of, capacity, in terms of risk that we will tolerate in insurance." Restates M2010-057 (write only at a fair premium).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 33. Reinsurance is a lot harder than it looks

quote_verbatim: Well, it should be pointed out, we really didn’t succeed at all in the reinsurance business in the first 15 years. [...] It is not an easy business. It looks easy most of the time. I mean — CHARLIE MUNGER: That’s the trouble with it. It looks easier than it is. WARREN BUFFETT: It looks way easier than it is. And, you know, it’s like having a pair of dice, and, you know, accepting bets on boxcars or something like that, and, you know, it’s going to come up once in 36 times, so you can win a lot of bets by giving the wrong odds, but if you keep do it long enough, you lose a lot of money. So these infrequent events, you better have factored in to your pricing, and not fool yourself by whether you make money in a given year or two years or even three or four years. And most people have a little trouble with that, and we had a little trouble with it for about 15 years.
concept: Reinsurance looks easy because rare losses are absent most years; price for the infrequent event and do not be fooled by a few profitable years.
evolution_notes: Buffett's own mistake (Berkshire's first 15 years in reinsurance, from about 1970, until Ajit Jain). Exchange, Buffett first, one lesson; Munger's line 1179 kept inside the quote. The elision skips George Young, "a fellow that I thought the world of", and "net, counting the value of float, it was not a good business for us for 15 years until Ajit came along." Munger before (line 1175): "insurance, and particularly reinsurance, it’s not that easy a business." Related: L2002-002 (megacats are infrequent but must be counted), M2011-001, M2011-051.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 33. Reinsurance is a lot harder than it looks

quote_verbatim: And incidentally, the investment bankers of the world, now that they trade so much for their own account and derivatives, they have sold some of these products where most of the time the customer wins but when the customer loses, he really loses big. In other words, they’re smarter than the customers, and they have caused some of the most horrendous losses to ordinary businessmen. [...] Just beware of the salesman who’s selling a new derivative product. WARREN BUFFETT: Or an old one. An old one, too. CHARLIE MUNGER: Yeah, but new ones are worse.
concept: Beware products sold by a smarter counterparty that usually win small for the customer and occasionally lose big; above all new derivatives.
evolution_notes: Exchange, Munger first, one lesson; Buffett's "Or an old one" kept inside the quote. The elision skips "It happened in Korea, it happened in Mexico, it happened —". Follows the boxcars passage at lines 1177-1181, the same payoff shape seen from the buyer's side.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 33. Reinsurance is a lot harder than it looks

quote_verbatim: And his results will be known over a five-year period or something. I mean, you cannot judge an investor by what they do in six months or a year.
concept: Judge an investment manager over years, never on six months or a year.
evolution_notes: Of Todd Combs, who wrote Munger a letter. Related: L2010-014 (how the record was achieved), L2010-001 (yearly figures neither ignored nor all-important).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 34. How Buffett first met Todd Combs

quote_verbatim: we have to find the right people, and the right people just does not mean a given IQ or a given past record, it means a lot of things.
concept: In choosing people, neither intelligence nor a past record is sufficient.
evolution_notes: Opens mid-sentence after "And it would not be a bad idea, but", on having more than one investment manager. Restates L2010-014 (past results do not suffice) and M2008-078 (good records nowhere near sufficient).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 34. How Buffett first met Todd Combs

quote_verbatim: And when they trade away their present businesses for some other business, they’re either saying their own businesses are pretty fully valued, or they’re saying the guy is making a hell of a mistake that’s selling to them. [...] you can draw the inference that J&J is not valuing its own businesses, you know, as attractively as you might think they should be evaluated.
concept: An acquirer paying in stock signals that it thinks its own businesses fully valued, or the seller mistaken; prefer cash.
evolution_notes: Of Johnson & Johnson's mostly-stock purchase of Synthes; "I have no specific knowledge of the company"; "if it was all for cash, I would like it a lot better." Restates M2011-020 (stock is a currency, a mistake to use unless fully valued) and L1997-031. Munger adds (lines 1215-1219) that neither of them knows much about medical devices, unlike Kraft's businesses.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 35. Acquisitions and stock

quote_verbatim: We are not going to borrow a lot of money. We’re not going to issue shares, except perhaps in some minor amount to make a deal that couldn’t get made otherwise. But — and, obviously, we’ll never sell a business to buy some other business. [...] But we can’t do a really — a really big elephant now, and we won’t — you know, we won’t stretch. We never — we’ve never really taken any risks because we don’t need to, and we will not trade something that we have and need for something that we don’t have and don’t need, even if we’d kind of like to have it.
concept: Do not stretch for a deal: no heavy borrowing, no share issuance, no selling one business to buy another; never risk what you have and need for what you do not need.
evolution_notes: The elision skips cash building month to month, selling some portfolio securities, and deals "roughly similar to Lubrizol" under study. Related: L2010-019 (to finish first, you must first finish), M2011-021 (Munger, businesses too good to part with), L1997-030.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 36. Why we won’t issue stock to make an acquisition

quote_verbatim: companies just couldn’t issue shares fast enough, because they basically were trading confetti for real assets. [...] We hate issuing shares and the idea of selling our — when we issue shares we’re divesting ourselves of a portion of every wonderful business we have, from GEICO to ISCAR to you name it. And we don’t like doing that.
concept: Issuing shares sells a part of every business owned; trading paper for real assets is a game that runs out of gas.
evolution_notes: Opens mid-sentence after "one certainly happened during the internet period —". The elision skips "It usually ends in some kind of a fiasco, but — well, I shouldn’t say it usually does, but it runs out of gas at some point. But, you know, essentially, we’ve never been in that game." Munger before (line 1233): "We are very reluctant to issue shares", and his friend's buyer in a socialist country: "Isn’t this wonderful we’re getting this business for nothing." Restates M2011-034 (the go-go stock-issuance machines) and M2002-053; related L2009-019.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 36. Why we won’t issue stock to make an acquisition

quote_verbatim: When I made the decision to buy the brick company in Alabama, it was not because I thought brick was going to turn in two months or six months or a year. I thought that over time, being a very important brick manufacturer and distributor in Alabama adjacent to our strong operation in Texas, it would be a good investment at the price that we paid. [...] You know, See’s Candy, a wonderful business, loses money roughly eight months of the year. [...] Now, obviously, cyclical businesses, you know, are not going to behave exactly the same as seasonal businesses, but why look at it any differently? I mean, if you take the next 20 years, there will be, you know, three or four terrible years for residential housing, and there will be a lot of them that are pretty good, and there will be a few that are terrific. And I don’t know the order in which they’re going to appear, but I know if I can buy the assets cheap enough to participate in those 20 years, that we’ll do OK over that time.
concept: Buy a cyclical business without timing the turn, as one would a seasonal one: if the assets are cheap enough to share in the whole run of good and bad years, the result will be fine.
evolution_notes: The first elision skips "I won’t feel good about our brick results in the next six months", Munger's reply (line 1251, rowed separately) and "We’ll be there if you need brick in Alabama. (Laughter)"; Buffett resumes the same thought. The second skips the seasonal pattern known, "we don’t worry in July that somehow Christmas won’t come", and the misleading single month or quarter. Before (lines 1245-1247): housing "terrible", a forecast of an upturn "by year-end", "It really isn’t that important to us."
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 37. Housing market is terrible, but we’ll profit on the rebound

quote_verbatim: Well, one advantage of buying these very cyclical businesses is a lot of people don’t like them. And what difference does it make to us if the earnings average, say, 300 million a year, if it comes in in a very lumpy fashion? In the big scheme of things, what do we care if it’s lumpy, as long as it’s a good business? And we have an advantage on that stuff.
concept: Lumpy earnings do not matter if the business is good; the dislike others have for cyclical businesses is an advantage to a buyer who does not care.
evolution_notes: Exchange with Buffett's brick answer (lines 1249-1255), a separate lesson. Munger closes: "Nobody else was bidding for a brick plant in Alabama with no customers to speak of. (Laughter)" Related: M2011-003 (ignore quarterly figures).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 37. Housing market is terrible, but we’ll profit on the rebound

quote_verbatim: The primary job of a Board of Directors is to see that the right people are running the business and to be sure that the next generation of leaders is identified and ready to take over tomorrow.
concept: A board's first job is to see that the right people run the business and that the next generation of leaders is identified and ready.
evolution_notes: The letter's first highlight. Buffett goes on (lines 92-108) to say he has been on 19 corporate boards and Berkshire's directors lead them in time spent on succession, then names Combs and Weschler as able to manage the whole portfolio and says the board admires his successor as CEO. Related: L2006-014 (choose a director by whether he thinks like an intelligent owner).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: BERKSHIRE HATHAWAY INC.

quote_verbatim: A few years back, I spent about $2 billion buying several bond issues of Energy Future Holdings, an electric utility operation serving portions of Texas. That was a mistake � a big mistake. In large measure, the company's prospects were tied to the price of natural gas, which tanked shortly after our purchase and remains depressed. [...] However things turn out, I totally miscalculated the gain/loss probabilities when I purchased the bonds. In tennis parlance, this was a major unforced error by your chairman.
concept: Buffett's own error: bonds whose payment depended on a commodity price; he miscalculated the gain/loss probabilities at purchase.
evolution_notes: Buffett's own mistake. The elision skips the interest received, the write-downs of $1 billion and $390 million and the yearend carrying value (lines 172-178). The "unforced error" phrase recurs from L2007-011. The lesson is stated as the miscalculated probabilities, with the tie to the gas price as the cause; no general rule is drawn in the letter.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: BERKSHIRE HATHAWAY INC.

quote_verbatim: Continuing shareholders are hurt unless shares are purchased below intrinsic value. The first law of capital allocation � whether the money is slated for acquisitions or share repurchases � is that what is smart at one price is dumb at another.
concept: Every use of capital, acquisition or buyback, is right or wrong only according to the price paid; what is smart at one price is dumb at another.
evolution_notes: Just before (lines 267-274): repurchases favoured only when the company has ample funds for its operational and liquidity needs and the stock sells at a material discount to intrinsic value conservatively calculated (repeats L1999-023); offsetting dilution or excess cash does not suffice (repeats L1999-029, L1999-026). The first sentence restates L1999-026; the "first law" is new in a letter and reaches acquisitions as well as buybacks (compare L1994-013). Buffett recommends Jamie Dimon's letter for stressing price/value (lines 276-278).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Share Repurchases

quote_verbatim: And here a confession is in order: In my early days I, too, rejoiced when the market rose. Then I read Chapter Eight of Ben Graham's The Intelligent Investor, the chapter dealing with how investors should view fluctuations in stock prices. Immediately the scales fell from my eyes, and low prices became my friend.
concept: Buffett's own early error: cheering rising prices as a future buyer; Graham's chapter on fluctuations taught him that low prices are a buyer's friend.
evolution_notes: Buffett's own mistake; Graham named as Buffett names him. It closes the IBM illustration (lines 306-337): a long-term holder of a company repurchasing shares should wish its stock to languish, and a future net buyer, directly or through a repurchasing company, "is hurt when stocks rise" (lines 333-335), which repeats L1997-009 and L1999-031 and is not rowed. Related: L1993-018 (the true investor welcomes volatility), L2008-004.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Share Repurchases

quote_verbatim: Our float is deducted in full as a liability in calculating Berkshire's book value, just as if we had to pay it out tomorrow and were unable to replenish it. But that's an incorrect way to view float, which should instead be viewed as a revolving fund. If float is both costless and long-enduring, the true value of this liability is far lower than the accounting liability.
concept: Float is a revolving fund, not a debt due tomorrow; when costless and long-enduring its true value as a liability is far below the accounting figure.
evolution_notes: Restates L1997-013 (cost-free float worth more than equal net worth) and adds the two conditions, costless and long-enduring, and the revolving-fund view. Float defined as before (lines 366-371, repeats L1993-009).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Insurance

quote_verbatim: The cost of the goodwill, however, has no bearing on its true value. If an insurance business produces large and sustained underwriting losses, any goodwill asset attributable to it should be deemed valueless, whatever its original cost. Fortunately, that's not the case at Berkshire. Charlie and I believe the true economic value of our insurance goodwill � what we would pay to purchase float of similar quality � to be far in excess of its historic carrying value.
concept: An insurer's goodwill is worth what one would pay for float of similar quality, regardless of its cost; with sustained underwriting losses it is worth nothing.
evolution_notes: Just before (lines 406-408): the $15.5 billion of insurance goodwill "represents the price we paid for the float-generating capabilities of our insurance operations." Related: L1997-011 (an insurer has value only if its float costs less than market money), L1999-010 and L2010-007 (economic goodwill).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Insurance

quote_verbatim: Please understand, however, that Charlie and I are neither masochists nor Pollyannas. If either of the failings we set forth in Rule 11 is present � if the business will likely be a cash drain over the longer term, or if labor strife is endemic � we will take prompt and decisive action.
concept: A poor business is kept through thick and thin, except when it will likely drain cash over the long term or labor strife is endemic; then act promptly.
evolution_notes: Just before (lines 670-678): Number 11 of the principles describes the reluctance to sell poor performers, which "in most cases, lag because of industry factors rather than managerial shortcomings"; the commitment to sellers to retain businesses "through thick and thin" builds goodwill among prospective sellers (repeats L2008-006). The two exceptions appear earlier in the reprinted principles (R1995-011) and not in an earlier v5 letter row; rowed under the 2004-2005 convention. Such a situation "has happened only a couple of times in our 47-year history" (lines 684-685).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Manufacturing, Service and Retailing Operations

quote_verbatim: "Buy commodities, sell brands" has long been a formula for business success. It has produced enormous and sustained profits for Coca-Cola since 1886 and Wrigley since 1891.
concept: A business that buys commodity inputs and sells a brand has long been a formula for enormous and sustained profits.
evolution_notes: The formula is quoted as a saying; Buffett applies it to See's (lines 762-768): $1.65 billion of pre-tax earnings since a $25 million purchase, with carrying value net of cash below zero. Related: L1993-021 (the moat of brand and distribution).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Manufacturing, Service and Retailing Operations

quote_verbatim: For many of the smaller companies, however, this is not true. I have made more than my share of mistakes buying small companies. Charlie long ago told me, "If something's not worth doing at all, it's not worth doing well," and I should have listened harder.
concept: Buffett's own error: buying small companies whose value does not exceed book; Munger's maxim that what is not worth doing is not worth doing well.
evolution_notes: Buffett's own mistake; the maxim is Munger's, quoted by Buffett. "This" refers to the sector's intrinsic value significantly exceeding book value (lines 801-802). The large purchases "have generally worked well" (lines 804-805). Related: L1994-002 (purchases inconsequential to Berkshire's capital are useless).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Manufacturing, Service and Retailing Operations

quote_verbatim: As was the case with Coca-Cola in 1988 and the railroads in 2006, I was late to the IBM party. I have been reading the company's annual report for more than 50 years, but it wasn't until a Saturday in March last year that my thinking crystallized. As Thoreau said, "It's not what you look at that matters, it's what you see."
concept: Buffett's own lateness: years of reading the same reports without seeing what they showed; what counts is what you see, not what you look at.
evolution_notes: Buffett's own; Thoreau's line quoted by Buffett carries the lesson. The letter does not say what he came to see in IBM beyond the financial management praised at lines 310-313.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Investments

quote_verbatim: They have excellent "business minds" that grasp the economic forces likely to determine the future of a wide variety of businesses. They are aided in their thinking by an understanding of what is predictable and what is unknowable.
concept: A business mind grasps the economic forces that will shape a business's future and knows what is predictable and what is unknowable.
evolution_notes: Said of Combs and Weschler, who will help the next CEO make acquisitions (lines 920-921). Each receives 80% of performance pay from his own results and 20% from his partner's (lines 914-915): the arrangement of L2010-016, not rowed again.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Investments

quote_verbatim: Investing is often described as the process of laying out money now in the expectation of receiving more money in the future. At Berkshire we take a more demanding approach, defining investing as the transfer to others of purchasing power now with the reasoned expectation of receiving more purchasing power � after taxes have been paid on nominal gains � in the future. More succinctly, investing is forgoing consumption now in order to have the ability to consume more at a later date.
concept: Investing is giving up purchasing power now with a reasoned expectation of more purchasing power, after tax on nominal gains, later.
evolution_notes: Opens the letter's essay on the three categories of investment, which the 2011 meeting set out first (M2011-024 to M2011-029). Related: L1993-020 (real risk measured in after-tax purchasing power).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: The Basic Choices for Investors and the One We Strongly Prefer

quote_verbatim: From our definition there flows an important corollary: The riskiness of an investment is not measured by beta (a Wall Street term encompassing volatility and often used in measuring risk) but rather by the probability � the reasoned probability � of that investment causing its owner a loss of purchasing-power over his contemplated holding period. Assets can fluctuate greatly in price and not be risky as long as they are reasonably certain to deliver increased purchasing power over their holding period. And as we will see, a non-fluctuating asset can be laden with risk.
concept: Risk is the reasoned probability of losing purchasing power over the holding period, not volatility; a fluctuating asset can be safe and a stable one risky.
evolution_notes: Restates L1993-020 (real risk in after-tax purchasing power over the holding period) and L1993-017 (beta far off the mark), and adds that a non-fluctuating asset can be laden with risk, which the currency passage at lines 966-980 applies.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: The Basic Choices for Investors and the One We Strongly Prefer

quote_verbatim: Most of these currency-based investments are thought of as "safe." In truth they are among the most dangerous of assets. Their beta may be zero, but their risk is huge. [...] Consequently, a tax-free institution would have needed 4.3% interest annually from bond investments over that period to simply maintain its purchasing power. Its managers would have been kidding themselves if they thought of any portion of that interest as "income."
concept: Currency-based investments thought safe are among the most dangerous; interest that only maintains purchasing power is not income.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the century of purchasing-power destruction, governments determining the value of money, and the dollar's 86% fall since 1965 (lines 970-977). After: the taxable investor in Treasury bills netting nothing after a 25% tax and inflation, the inflation "tax" more than triple the income tax (lines 984-991). Related: L2008-020, M2011-025 (currency investments a bet on government).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: The Basic Choices for Investors and the One We Strongly Prefer

quote_verbatim: High interest rates, of course, can compensate purchasers for the inflation risk they face with currency-based investments � and indeed, rates in the early 1980s did that job nicely. [...] Beyond the requirements that liquidity and regulators impose on us, we will purchase currency-related securities only if they offer the possibility of unusual gain � either because a particular credit is mispriced, as can occur in periodic junk-bond debacles, or because rates rise to a level that offers the possibility of realizing substantial capital gains on high-grade bonds when rates fall.
concept: Hold currency securities beyond liquidity needs only for unusual gain: a mispriced credit, or rates high enough to promise capital gains when they fall.
evolution_notes: The elision skips "Right now bonds should come with a warning label" and the liquidity paragraph: Treasury bills, $20 billion working level, $10 billion absolute minimum (lines 995-1003; repeats L2010-021 and L2009-006). After: Shelby Cullom Davis's "return-free risk" (lines 1010-1011). Related: L2001-026 and L2002-022 (junk bonds bought selectively).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: The Basic Choices for Investors and the One We Strongly Prefer

quote_verbatim: The second major category of investments involves assets that will never produce anything, but that are purchased in the buyer's hope that someone else � who also knows that the assets will be forever unproductive � will pay more for them in the future. [...] This type of investment requires an expanding pool of buyers, who, in turn, are enticed because they believe the buying pool will expand still further.
concept: An unproductive asset is bought only on the hope that another buyer will pay more, and so needs an ever-expanding pool of buyers.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the tulips (lines 1015-1016). Gold follows as the major asset of the class, "neither of much use nor procreative" (lines 1023-1028), and the cube against all U.S. cropland and 16 Exxon Mobils (lines 1044-1068), an illustration not rowed. First letter appearance of the category; restates M2011-026 (unproductive asset, the next buyer's bet).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: The Basic Choices for Investors and the One We Strongly Prefer

quote_verbatim: Beyond that, the rising price has on its own generated additional buying enthusiasm, attracting purchasers who see the rise as validating an investment thesis. As "bandwagon" investors join any party, they create their own truth � for a while. Over the past 15 years, both Internet stocks and houses have demonstrated the extraordinary excesses that can be created by combining an initially sensible thesis with well-publicized rising prices. [...] But bubbles blown large enough inevitably pop.
concept: A rising price breeds its own buyers who take it as proof of the thesis; a sensible thesis plus publicized rising prices makes a bubble, and big bubbles pop.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the skeptics who succumbed to the market's "proof" (lines 1036-1038). After: the proverb "What the wise man does in the beginning, the fool does in the end" (lines 1039-1040), quoted at M2006-018. Restates M2011-028 (rising prices breed excitement) and M2006-018.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: The Basic Choices for Investors and the One We Strongly Prefer

quote_verbatim: Our first two categories enjoy maximum popularity at peaks of fear: Terror over economic collapse drives individuals to currency-based assets, most particularly U.S. obligations, and fear of currency collapse fosters movement to sterile assets such as gold. We heard "cash is king" in late 2008, just when cash should have been deployed rather than held. Similarly, we heard "cash is trash" in the early 1980s just when fixed-dollar investments were at their most attractive level in memory. On those occasions, investors who required a supportive crowd paid dearly for that comfort.
concept: Fear drives the crowd to cash and gold at the worst times; the slogan of the moment marks the opposite opportunity, and needing the crowd's support is costly.
evolution_notes: Related: L2008-020 (the comfort of cash in a panic is no evidence of a good policy).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: The Basic Choices for Investors and the One We Strongly Prefer

quote_verbatim: My own preference � and you knew this was coming � is our third category: investment in productive assets, whether businesses, farms, or real estate. Ideally, these assets should have the ability in inflationary times to deliver output that will retain its purchasing-power value while requiring a minimum of new capital investment. Farms, real estate, and many businesses such as Coca-Cola, IBM and our own See's Candy meet that double-barreled test. Certain other companies � think of our regulated utilities, for example � fail it because inflation places heavy capital requirements on them. To earn more, their owners must invest more.
concept: The best productive asset keeps its output's purchasing power in inflation while needing little new capital; businesses that must invest more to earn more fail that test.
evolution_notes: Next sentence: "Even so, these investments will remain superior to nonproductive or currency-based assets" (lines 1083-1084). Related: L2009-012 (the best businesses need little incremental investment), M2011-027.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: The Basic Choices for Investors and the One We Strongly Prefer

quote_verbatim: Metaphorically, these commercial "cows" will live for centuries and give ever greater quantities of "milk" to boot. Their value will be determined not by the medium of exchange but rather by their capacity to deliver milk. [...] I believe that over any extended period of time this category of investing will prove to be the runaway winner among the three we've examined. More important, it will be by far the safest.
concept: A productive business is valued by its capacity to deliver output, not by the currency; over long periods it is the best and the safest of the three categories.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the compounding of the milk proceeds, the Dow from 66 to 11,497, and Berkshire's goal of owning first-class businesses, whole by preference and also through marketable stocks (lines 1095-1099). Before: people will exchange labor for a Coca-Cola or See's peanut brittle whatever the currency (lines 1086-1090). Restates M2011-027 (value an asset by what it delivers) and M2011-024.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: The Basic Choices for Investors and the One We Strongly Prefer

quote_verbatim: I do believe that the CEO of any large, particularly financialrelated, company should — it really should apply beyond that, but certainly with a financiallyrelated company — should be the chief risk officer. It’s not something to be delegated. [...] So I do — I am the chief risk officer at Berkshire. It’s up to me to understand anything that could really hit us in any catastrophic way. My successor will have the same responsibility, and we would not select anybody for that job that we did not think had that ability. It’s a very important ability. It ranks right up there with allocation of capital and selection of managers for the operating units.
concept: The CEO of a large company, above all a financial one, is its chief risk officer and does not delegate understanding what could hit it catastrophically; successors are chosen for that ability.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the delegated risk committees with "a lot of nice figures lined up" and talk of sigmas, "and the place was just ripe for real trouble". Restates M2008-061, M2011-079 and L2009-018.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 6. Buffett: My successor will also be the “chief risk officer”

quote_verbatim: the person at the top really has to understand whether those three or four people running the big insurance units are correctly assessing their risks, and then also has to be able to aggregate and think how they accumulate over the units. That’s where the real risk is, unless you’re engaging in a lot of leverage in your financial structure, which isn’t going to happen.
concept: The top risk job is judging whether each unit head assesses risk correctly and adding up how the units' risks accumulate; the basic risks are excessive leverage and excessive insurance risk.
evolution_notes: The quote opens mid-sentence after "I mean, it — the basic risks could involve excessive leverage and they — and then the — they could involve excessive insurance risk. Now, we have people in charge of our insurance businesses that themselves worry very much about the risk of their own unit and, therefore," (line 37). Related: L2002-004 (no aggregation of exposures that threatens solvency).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 6. Buffett: My successor will also be the “chief risk officer”

quote_verbatim: Well, not only was it — this risk decision frequently delegated in America, but it was delegated to people who were using a very silly way of judging risk that they’ve been taught in some our leading business schools. (Laughter) So this is a very serious problem this man is raising. The so-called “Value at Risk” and the theories that outcomes in financial markets followed a Gaussian curve, invariably. It was one of the dumbest ideas ever put forward.
concept: Munger: judging risk by Value at Risk and the assumption that market outcomes follow a Gaussian curve is one of the dumbest ideas ever put forward.
evolution_notes: Exchange: Munger answers Buffett's invitation; Buffett follows (line 41) that it is used by people with very high IQs "because everybody knows the properties of that curve", "But the only problem is that curve is not applicable to behavior in markets", a restatement of the same lesson named here and not rowed. Restates M2007-040 and M2007-041.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 6. Buffett: My successor will also be the “chief risk officer”

quote_verbatim: And Sandy Gottesman created one of my favorite risk control examples. One day he fired an associate, and the man said, “How can you be firing me when I’m such an important producer?” And Sandy said, “Yes,” he says. “But I’m a rich old man and you make me nervous.” (Laughter)
concept: Munger: a risk control example: let go of a big producer whose conduct makes you nervous, because a rich owner has more to lose than to gain.
evolution_notes: Implied: the principle is shown by Gottesman's act, which Munger calls a risk control example; no rule is stated. Before it Munger names the Berkshire directors as terrific at risk analysis (Walter Scott at Kiewit). Buffett follows: "We do not have anybody around Berkshire that makes us nervous" (line 51).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 6. Buffett: My successor will also be the “chief risk officer”

quote_verbatim: Getting to the question of how GEICO reserves, how Gen Re reserves, I would say that — it’s described to some extent in our annual report — but I would say that the one overriding principle is that we hope, and our plan is, to reserve conservatively.
concept: The overriding principle of insurance reserving is to reserve conservatively.
evolution_notes: Before it (lines 63-65): the Swiss Re life contract reserved "to the worst case" until it is resolved. After: short-tail auto lines show quickly how you are doing, GEICO's redundancies, Gen Re under-reserved when bought. Restates L2001-023 and L2002-004.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 7. We “reserve conservatively” at insurance operations

quote_verbatim: I would say that we’ve found it almost useless in 60 years of investing to give advice to anybody in business. [...] and we are not in the business of giving them advice. If we thought that the success of our investment depended upon them following our advice, we’d go onto something else. (Laughter)
concept: Do not make an investment whose success depends on management taking your advice; giving advice to businesses is almost useless.
evolution_notes: Exchange with Munger (lines 83-93); each states a separate lesson, and Munger's is its own row. The elision crosses Munger's line 91 and Buffett's own account of talking to the CEOs of the four largest holdings not more than twice a year; Buffett resumes the same thought.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 8. “It’s amazing how little influence we’ve had”

quote_verbatim: It’s amazing how little influence we’ve had when we had 20 percent of the stock. And people have this illusion of mass control at headquarters. The beauty of Berkshire is that we created a system that doesn’t require much control at headquarters.
concept: Munger: even a 20 percent holder has little influence, control from headquarters is an illusion, so build a system that needs little of it.
evolution_notes: Exchange with Buffett (lines 83-93); Buffett's lesson on advice is its own row. Opens after "We have found that we have a lot of control — it’s kind of like controlling affairs by pushing on a noodle."
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 8. “It’s amazing how little influence we’ve had”

quote_verbatim: We have never — I don’t think — certainly never consciously done anything to encourage people to buy our stock at a price we thought was above intrinsic value. [...] I don’t think we’ll ever announce that we think the stock is selling considerably above intrinsic business value, but we will certainly do nothing to indicate that we think the stock is attractively priced, if that comes about.
concept: Never encourage anyone to buy your own stock above intrinsic value; when it is overpriced, say nothing that suggests it is attractive.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the 1996 B-share prospectus saying neither would buy at the price, and the repurchase disclosure rowed next from line 103. Before: they would like the stock to trade at a fair value once a year, and announcing overvaluation would have to reach every holder at once. Related: M1995-118 (stock should track intrinsic value).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 9. No warnings when Berkshire shares are overvalued

quote_verbatim: We think that if we are going to repurchase shares from people, that we ought to let them know what — that we think we’re buying it too cheap. I mean, we wouldn’t buy out — if we had two or three partners and somebody wanted to sell out — but we’d probably try to arrive at a fair price — but if it was established by a market and they were going to sell too cheap, we’d tell them we thought they were selling it too cheap.
concept: When buying back stock, tell the sellers you think they are selling too cheap, as you would a partner.
evolution_notes: Restates L1999-032 and the FY2011 letter's "we want those exiting partners to be fully informed" (letter lines 284-286, not rowed as a repeat). Related: M2004-085.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 9. No warnings when Berkshire shares are overvalued

quote_verbatim: we wanted to be dramatically — or very significantly — undervalued to do buybacks, and we want to be very sure that every shareholder that sells to us knows that we think that it’s dramatically — or significantly — undervalued when we do it. [...] And if we get the chance to do it, as long as we don’t take our cash position below 20 billion, we will — we would buy very aggressively at that price.
concept: Buy back only when the stock is significantly undervalued and sellers know it, never taking cash below a set floor, and then buy aggressively.
evolution_notes: The quote opens mid-sentence after "The 1.1 is a figure that we feel very comfortable with. So, we would probably feel comfortable with a figure somewhat higher than that, but" (line 115). The elision skips the businesses worth far more than carried and "we would love to buy ... tens of billions ... at 110 percent of book". Restates M2011-019 and the letter's two conditions (L1999-023); the cash floor is the letter's $20 billion (letter line 292).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 10. We’ll buy “significantly” undervalued Berkshire shares

quote_verbatim: CHARLIE MUNGER: Well, some people buy their own stock back regardless of price. That’s not our system. WARREN BUFFETT: Well, we think it’s — we think a lot of the share repurchases are idiotic. [...] I mean, it’s for ego. I’ve been in a lot of board rooms where share repurchase authorizations have been voted, and I will guarantee you it’s not because the CEO is thinking the way we think at all. They like buying their stock better at higher prices, and they like issuing options at lower prices. You know, it’s just exactly the opposite than the way we would think. We will only do it for one reason, and that’s to increase the per-share value the day after we’ve done it.
concept: Many buybacks are made for ego, buying high and issuing options low; buy back only to raise per-share value the day after.
evolution_notes: Exchange, Munger first; Buffett states the lesson, so the row is his under the 2010 PM to 2011 PM convention. The elision crosses Munger's "I was trying to say that more gently" (line 123) and Buffett's "You’ve never done it before. (Laughter) The — it’s —"; Buffett resumes the same thought. After: Munger, "We hope the opportunity never comes" (line 127). Restates M2011-019, L1999-026 and L1999-028.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 10. We’ll buy “significantly” undervalued Berkshire shares

quote_verbatim: If you look at the Bank of America or Wells Fargo, they get an enormous amount of money from a natural customer base. European banks tended to get much more of it on a wholesale basis, and that money can run pretty fast.

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 11. U.S. banks are in better shape European banks

They need to be operated efficiently in order to achieve their rate of return, but if they are operated efficiently and in the public interest, whether coal or labor, whatever it is, may go up or down, really doesn’t affect them, although it affects their customers.
concept: A regulated utility passes its fuel and labor costs through to customers; its return depends on operating efficiently and in the public interest, not on input prices.

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 12. Munger: “Idiotic” to use natural gas instead of coal

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 13. GEICO has no plans to use driver tracking technology

quote_verbatim: I mean, it is astounding to me how the schools have focused on sort of one fad after another in finance theory, and it’s usually been very mathematically based. When it’s become very popular, it’s almost impossible to resist if you’re — if you hope to make progress in faculty advancement. Going against the revealed wisdom of your elders can be very dangerous to your career path at major business schools.
concept: Finance teaching follows mathematical fads because a teacher's career depends on not contradicting his elders; discount it accordingly.
