speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 14. Business schools are improving but still teach “nonsense”

quote_verbatim: And you know, really, investing is not that complicated. I would have — you know, a couple of the courses. I would have a course on how to value a business, and I would have a course on how to think about markets. [...] If you buy businesses for less than they’re worth, you’re going to make money. And if you know the difference between the businesses that you can value and the ones that you can’t value, you know, which is key, you’re going to make money.
concept: Investing needs two things taught: how to value a business and how to think about markets; buy below value, and know which businesses you can value and which you cannot.
evolution_notes: The elision skips modern portfolio theory and option pricing, Ray Kroc thinking about whether people would buy hamburgers, not the option value of McDonald's stock, and the textbooks with "really nothing in there about valuing businesses, and that’s what investing is all about". After: the high priests must "convince the laity that the priests have to be listened to" (lines 197-199). Restates M2009-018 and M2008-008.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 14. Business schools are improving but still teach “nonsense”

quote_verbatim: The folly creeps into the accounting, too. A very long-term option on a big business you understand — the stock of a big business that you understand — or even a stock market index — should not be — the optimal way to price it is not by using Black Scholes, and yet the accounting profession does that. They want some kind of a standardized solution that requires them not to think too hard, and they have one. (Laughter)
concept: Munger: Black-Scholes is the wrong way to price a very long-term option on a business you understand; a standard formula is adopted because it spares thought.
evolution_notes: Munger's reply to Buffett's invitation in the same answer. Restates L2008-025, L2008-026 and L2010-018 (Black-Scholes absurd over long periods).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 14. Business schools are improving but still teach “nonsense”

quote_verbatim: It’s very hard, because of the random nature of quakes and hurricanes and that sort of thing, very hard to know when you really have had a trend. [...] We tend to sort of assume the worst. I mean, if we see more earthquakes in New Zealand than have existed, you know, in the last few years than existed over the last 100 years, we don’t say that we’ll extrapolate the last couple of years and say that’s going to be the case, this huge explosion of quakes. But we also don’t take the 100-year figure anymore.
concept: When random events may hide a trend, assume the worst: do not extrapolate the last few years, but no longer rely on the long-run record either.
evolution_notes: The elision skips global warming and the recent warm and cold spells: "separating out the random from new trends is really — is not easy to do." Related: L2008-017 (losses from measuring the future against a calm past).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 16. Catastrophe insurance: “nobody knows for sure what the right rate is”

quote_verbatim: But nobody knows for sure what the right rate is. I mean, we can tell you how many 6.0 or greater quakes have happened in California in the last hundred years and how many Category 3 hurricanes have hit, you know, both sides of Florida, whatever. There’s all kinds of data available on that, but the question is, how much does it tell you about the next 50 years? And so we — if we think we’re getting a rate that — if a fairly negative hypothesis would indicate — then we move ahead [...] Now, we don’t want that 10 billion to correlate with anything else, and we want to be sure we get the right price.
concept: Past catastrophe data says little about the next 50 years; write only at a rate a fairly negative hypothesis supports, and take large limits only when uncorrelated with other exposures.
evolution_notes: The elision skips Christchurch's $12 billion of insured damage ("ten Katrinas" for its size), the Thai floods, and "we are perfectly willing to take on very big limits if we think we’re getting the right price. We have propositions out for as much as 10 billion of coverage". Related: L2006-005 (any risk properly paid for), M2010-103 (risks correlate on the downside).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 16. Catastrophe insurance: “nobody knows for sure what the right rate is”

quote_verbatim: I don’t know what her politics are, and, you know, I don’t know what her religion is. She’s got all kinds of personal views, I’m sure, that probably are better than mine, but it doesn’t make any difference. I just want to know how she runs the business. [...] And if you start selecting your investments, or your friends, or your neighbors, based on trying to get people that agree with you totally, you’re going to live a pretty peculiar life, I think.
concept: Judge a manager by how the business is run, not by personal or political views; do not select investments by agreement with your opinions.
evolution_notes: Said of IBM's CEO, with $11 or $12 billion invested. A political question; the rule is rowed and the politics left out (the FOX joke, line 279, and the citizenship remarks, line 277). The elision crosses Munger's country-club jokes (lines 281-285) and Buffett's own "we’ve never had an argument in 53 years" and "it’s irrelevant"; Buffett resumes the same thought.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 18. Political views shouldn’t affect investing decisions

quote_verbatim: We used stock in the Burlington Northern acquisition, and we felt that it was a mistake, but we were using it for what, in effect, turned out to be about 30 percent of the deal, and we felt that we were doing well enough with the cash that overall that the mix was OK. But we would not use our stock now, and we wouldn’t even use it for 30 or 40 percent of some deal.
concept: Buffett's own: issuing stock for part of BNSF was a mistake, tolerable only because the cash part was a good deal; now no stock at all, even for part of a deal.
evolution_notes: Buffett's own mistake. Against L2009-021 (the FY2009 letter weighed the 30% in undervalued shares against what the deal made possible and accepted it); reconciled in the same answer ("overall that the mix was OK"), so listed under Tensions seen. Restates M2011-020 (stock a currency only when fully valued). Munger: "It’s hard to imagine, but it could be conceivably happen" (line 297).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 19. Size of potential deals limited by commitment to not use stock

quote_verbatim: But it would have stretched us, but we would not have pushed it to the point where it would have taken our cash below 20 billion. We would have sold securities, we would have done whatever was necessary to have a $20 billion cash balance when we got done with the deal. [...] Now, if that had been 40 billion, I don’t think we, you know, no matter how well I liked it, I don’t think I would have wanted to peel off 25 billion or so of marketable securities trying to get it done, and I certainly wouldn’t want to be in limbo not knowing exactly where the money was going to come from, and therefore, be subject to some terrible shock in the world, in the market.
concept: Size an acquisition so the cash floor survives it, and never be left mid-deal not knowing where the money will come from, exposed to a shock.
evolution_notes: On a deal of about $22 or $23 billion considered a month or two before. The elision skips "But I would have had to sell some securities I didn’t want to sell. I liked the deal well enough so I would have done it." Related: L2009-006 (own liquidity dwarfing any requirement), the letter's $20 billion working level (letter line 1003).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 19. Size of potential deals limited by commitment to not use stock

quote_verbatim: The problem is there, we’re not going to assume anything much better than the risk-free rate in making a bid for that sort of thing. I mean, we do not like the idea of taking on long-term liabilities and paying 150 basis points, you know, above Treasuries or something, to do that. And there are people that will do that. They may not be quite as likely to fulfill those promises in the years to come as we would. But we want to get money on the liability side at attractive rates. Now, the most attractive is if we can write property-casualty business at an underwriting profit and get it for nothing.
concept: Take on long-term liabilities only at attractive rates, assuming little above the risk-free rate when bidding; the cheapest liability is float written at an underwriting profit.
evolution_notes: On runoff annuity books. Related: L1997-011 and L1994-025 (float judged against the market cost of money), L2011-005.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 22. We’ll take on runoff annuity liabilities at the right price

quote_verbatim: I would try to attract some money, and then when I’d build up a fair amount of money out of investing, I would try to get into something much more interesting, which would be buying businesses to keep. You mentioned private equity, which very often is buying businesses to sell. I don’t want to be buying and selling businesses. I mean, if I establish relationships with people that come to me with their business, and they want to join Berkshire, I want it to be for keeps.
concept: Build capital by investing, then buy businesses to keep rather than to sell, so that sellers who join know it is for keeps.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct in part: what he would do over, starting earlier, building an audited record and aggregating money faster (line 365). Related: L2008-006 (deserve to be the buyer of choice), M2009-074, L2011-007.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 23. What Buffett would have done differently

quote_verbatim: But that — stocks — the beauty of stocks is they do sell at silly prices from time to time. That’s how Charlie and I have gotten rich. [...] And Chapter 8 says that in the market you’re going to have a partner named “Mr. Market,” and the beauty of him as your partner is that he’s kind of a psychotic drunk — (laughter) — and he will do very weird things over time and your job is to remember that he’s there to serve you and not to advise you.
concept: Stocks sell at silly prices from time to time; treat the market as a partner there to serve you, not to advise you.
evolution_notes: Graham named as Buffett names him: "Chapters 8 and Chapters 20 are really all you need to do to get rich in this world" (line 381). Before (line 379): any business run long enough will at times be over- and undervalued; Capital Cities at a third of its properties' value in the early 1970s. Restates L1993-018 and M1997-012; the letter's confession is L2011-004.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 24. Take advantage when “Mr. Market” acts like a “psychotic drunk”

quote_verbatim: But the important thing is that you make your decisions based on what you think the business is worth. And if you make your buy and sell decisions based on what you think a business is worth, and you stick with businesses that you think — you’ve got good reason to think — you can value, you simply have to do well in stocks. The stock market is the most obliging, money-making place in the world because you don’t have to do anything. [...] The rules are stacked in your favor, if you don’t turn those rules upside down and start behaving like the drunken psychotic instead of the guy that’s there to take advantage of it.
concept: Buy and sell on what the business is worth, stay with businesses you have good reason to think you can value, and act only when prices oblige; the rules favour you unless you behave like the market.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the farm neighbour who will not name a price every day (line 385). Before (line 383): Berkshire will someday be significantly overvalued and at other times significantly undervalued, as will Coca-Cola, Wells Fargo and IBM. Restates M2012-016's "know the difference between the businesses that you can value and the ones that you can’t value" (line 197) and M2009-018.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 24. Take advantage when “Mr. Market” acts like a “psychotic drunk”

quote_verbatim: Well, what’s interesting about this place is I think we’ve had a lot more fun and we got rich enough so we bought businesses and stocks to hold instead of to resell. It’s an enormously more constructive life.
concept: Munger: buying businesses and stocks to hold rather than to resell makes an enormously more constructive life.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct. Munger's reply to Buffett's invitation; it echoes Buffett's "buying businesses to keep" at line 365 under the previous heading. After: "So as fast as you can work yourself into our position, the better off you’ll be. (Laughter)".
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 24. Take advantage when “Mr. Market” acts like a “psychotic drunk”

quote_verbatim: Charlie and I, to my memory, in 53 years, I don’t think we’ve ever had a discussion about buying a stock or a business, or selling a stock or a business, that has been — where we’ve talked about macro affairs. I mean, if we find a business that we think we understand and we like the price at which it’s being offered, we buy it. And it doesn’t make any difference what the headlines are, it doesn’t make any difference what the Federal Reserve is doing, it doesn’t make any difference what’s going on in Europe. We buy it.
concept: Buy a business you understand at a price you like whatever the headlines or the macro picture; macro views play no part in buying or selling.
evolution_notes: After (lines 397-399): his first stock in June 1942 while the war was being lost, "But stocks were cheap"; the October 2008 article, "I should have written it a few months later"; "we look to value, and we don’t look to headlines at all." Restates M2009-015 and M2010-014.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 25. We ignore headlines and macro factors

quote_verbatim: CHARLIE MUNGER: Yeah, but we did keep liquid reserves at the bottom of the panic that, if we’d known it was not going to get any worse, we would have spent, but we didn’t know that. WARREN BUFFETT: Yeah. We know what we don’t know. We all — we know we don’t want to go broke. I mean, we start with that. And we know you can’t go broke if you’ve got a fair amount of liquid reserves around and you don’t have any near-term debts and so on. So our first rule is always to play it tomorrow, no matter what happens. But if we’ve got that covered, and we can find things that are attractive, we buy it.
concept: Not knowing whether a panic will worsen, keep liquid reserves and no near-term debt so you can never go broke; with that covered, buy what is attractive.
evolution_notes: Exchange, Munger first; Buffett states the lesson, so the row is his. After: Munger's Daily Journal sat on cash and bought stocks in 2008, "that was the time to use the money, not to sit on it" (line 403). Restates L2009-006, L2010-019 and M2010-018's concern with not going broke.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 25. We ignore headlines and macro factors

quote_verbatim: But the railroad business for very fundamental reasons, which I should have figured out earlier, has improved its position dramatically over the last, really, 15 or 20 years, but it continues to this day. I mean, it is an extremely efficient and environmentally-friendly way of moving a whole lot of things that have to be moved. And it’s an asset that couldn’t be duplicated for, you name it, three, four, five, six times, you know, what it’s selling for.
concept: A business whose asset could not be duplicated for several times its price, and which moves what must be moved efficiently, has a strengthening position; Buffett should have seen it earlier.
evolution_notes: "which I should have figured out earlier" is a confession of lateness with no lesson stated beyond the test itself; compare the letter's lateness to the railroads in 2006 (L2011-010). Related: M2011-055 (replacement cost of a capital-heavy asset the country will always need).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 26. Big Berkshire subsidiaries have “done well” over past 5 years

quote_verbatim: And the mistakes have been made in the purchasing. I mean, it’s where I misgauged the competitive position of the business. It isn’t because of the faults of management. It’s because I just — either because I had too much money around or because I was — been drinking too much Cherry Coke or whatever it was — I assessed the future competitive position in a way that was really inappropriate. But it wasn’t because it really changed on me so much.
concept: Buffett's own: the poor purchases came from misjudging the business's future competitive position at the time of buying, not from management's faults or later change.
evolution_notes: Buffett's own mistake; "too much money around" is named as one cause. Before: Munger, 80 percent or more of the businesses by value have increased their market strength, "We’re never going to get the rate to 100 percent" (lines 415-423). Restates L2010-009 and the FY2011 letter's lines 660-663 (a repeat of L2010-009, not rowed).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 26. Big Berkshire subsidiaries have “done well” over past 5 years

quote_verbatim: But the rules have changed in relation to collateralizing, and I don’t like ever exposing us to anything that would cause me to worry about Berkshire’s financial condition if the Federal Reserve were hit by a nuclear bomb tomorrow, or anything of the sort, or Europe, you know, something terrible happened. We just — we think about worst cases all of the time around Berkshire. Charlie and I probably think about worst cases more than any two managers you’ll ever find, and we are never going to expose ourselves to a worst case. And a requirement to collateralize things means that you are putting yourself in a position where you may have to come up with some cash tomorrow morning, and we’re never going to do that on any significant scale, because we don’t know what tomorrow morning will bring.
concept: Think about worst cases constantly and never take a position, such as a collateral requirement, that could demand cash tomorrow morning on any significant scale.
evolution_notes: Munger follows (line 443): "We never would have entered if we’d had to sign normal contracts", the same lesson from his side, named here and not rowed. Earlier (line 439): the successors are unlikely to use derivatives, "although I wouldn’t restrict them from doing it because they’re smart people and sometimes derivatives get mispriced". Restates L2008-024 and the FY2011 letter's lines 929-933 (not rowed as a repeat).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 27. Derivatives are “not going to be a huge factor at Berkshire”

quote_verbatim: But basically, I would say that GEICO is worth — has an intrinsic value — that’s greater — significantly greater — than the sum of its net worth and its float. Now, I wouldn’t say that about some of our other insurance businesses. But that’s for two reasons. One is, I think it’s quite rational to assume a significant underwriting profit at GEICO over the next decade or two decades, and I think it’s likely that it will have significant growth. And both of those are value — items of enormous value.
concept: An insurer is worth more than net worth plus float only when a sustained underwriting profit and growth can rationally be assumed; otherwise not.
evolution_notes: Answer to the analyst's view that Berkshire values insurance at cash plus investments. Related: L2011-006 (insurance goodwill worth what similar float would cost), L1997-011.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 28. Different valuation methods for different companies

quote_verbatim: I’m not talking about EBITDA or anything like that, which is nonsense. I’m talking about regular pretax earnings. If they have similar characteristics, we’d probably pay a little more than that, because we know so much more about them than we might know about some other businesses. [...] It’s nonsense. I mean, if you compare a business that, you know, leases pencils or something like that where they all get depreciated in a two-year period and then compare that to some business that uses virtually no capital, you know, like See’s Candies, it’s just nonsense. But it works for the people that sell businesses.
concept: Price a business on regular pretax earnings, never EBITDA, which ignores how much capital a business consumes; pay a little more for what is better known.
evolution_notes: Exchange with Munger (lines 453-463); Munger's lesson is its own row. The elision crosses Munger's line 455, Buffett's "We prefer EBE, which is earnings before everything" and Munger's "Right." (lines 457-459); Buffett resumes the same thought. Before (line 453): he would love to buy businesses of similar competitive position at nine or ten times pretax earnings "Under today’s conditions", a price view. Restates R1996-023 and L2002-040.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 28. Different valuation methods for different companies

quote_verbatim: When you used the word EBITDA, I thought to myself, I don’t even like hearing the word. (Laughter) There’s so much nutcase thinking involving EBITDA. Earnings before what really counts in costs. (Laughter)
concept: Munger: EBITDA leaves out the costs that really count and breeds nutcase thinking.
evolution_notes: Exchange with Buffett (lines 453-463); Buffett's lesson is its own row. After (line 463), on Buffett's remark that EBITDA works for sellers of businesses: "They don’t sell these lures to fish."
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 28. Different valuation methods for different companies

quote_verbatim: It’s very hard for an unproductive investment to beat productive investments over any long period of time, and I recognize that — It’s very interesting. [...] But if you say anything negative about gold, I mean, it arouses passions with people, which is kind of fascinating, because usually if you thought through something intellectually, it shouldn’t really make much difference what people say. It should be that, well, you know, the question is whether your facts are right and your reasoning is right.
concept: Unproductive investments rarely beat productive ones over long periods; a thought-through view is judged by whether the facts and reasoning are right, not by what people say.
evolution_notes: The elision skips "I can say bonds are no good and [Federal Reserve Chairman Ben] Bernanke still smiles at me". Before (line 471): over 50 years Berkshire, stocks as a group and probably farmland will beat gold; the ounce caressed for a hundred years against the farmland's crops. Restates L2011-016, L2011-020 and M2011-026. Munger (line 475): "I have never had the slightest interest in owning gold. It’s a much better life to work with businesses and people engaged in business", a preference, not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 29. Buffett’s negativity on gold “arouses passions”

quote_verbatim: we bought, and we’re buying, Wells Fargo stock, and that takes me out of the business of buying Wells Fargo. So therefore, I go into something that I don’t like quite as well but that I still like very much. And that’s one of the problems I have, is that I can’t be buying what Berkshire is buying, and I’ve got some money around, and therefore, I go into my second choices, or into tiny little companies like I did with Korean companies and that sort of thing. But my best ideas are all in Berkshire.
concept: A fiduciary does not buy for himself what the company he runs is buying; his best ideas go to the company, his own account takes second choices.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct. The quote opens mid-sentence after "The truth is I like Wells Fargo better than I like J.P. Morgan but I — but I also —". After (line 487): with 98 1/2 percent of his money in Berkshire, thinking about the other 1 1/2 percent would be "a little bit crazy"; (line 491) "I know Wells better. It’s easier to understand."
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 30. Buffett: “my best ideas are all in Berkshire”

quote_verbatim: Yeah. But basically the Munger family is in two or three things only. Diversification is my idea of — not something I have practically no interest in, except as it happens automatically in a big place like Berkshire. I rejoiced the day I got rid of a quote — you know, a stock quoting machine. And I like this buy and hold investing. It’s a lovely way to live a life and you deal with a better class of people, and it’s worked pretty well for all of us.
concept: Munger: concentrate in two or three things, ignore the quotation machine, and buy and hold.
evolution_notes: Partly personal conduct. The printed sentence on diversification is garbled ("Diversification is my idea of — not something I have practically no interest in") and is kept as printed. Related: M2004-041 (wide diversification for skilled investors is madness), M2012-027.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 30. Buffett: “my best ideas are all in Berkshire”

quote_verbatim: We’ll never have anything that can come up, remotely, that would cause me to lose any sleep as long as I start with the 20 billion. That’s probably considerably more than we need, but it just leaves us comfortable, and it makes us feel we can do other things aggressively, as long as we know the downside is protected. [...] If we were to make a big acquisition, it might require shifting some funds from one place to another, but we’ll always leave every place more than adequately capitalized.
concept: Hold more liquidity than needed so the downside is protected and other things can be done aggressively; leave every unit more than adequately capitalized.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the railroad placed in National Indemnity and the rating agency's refusal to credit it. Before (line 499): money in the life companies has less utility than in the property-casualty companies, and the holding company is the best place for money. Munger (line 505) and Buffett (line 507): the railroad's earnings inside the casualty company are "like having a royalty": descriptions, not rowed. Restates L2009-006 and M2012-022.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 31. Why is BNSF a subsidiary of National Indemnity?

quote_verbatim: So the idea of paying out money, which we think is worth at least 110 cents on the dollar within the place, and have it turn into 100 cents on the dollar when paid out, just is not very attractive to us, unless we find we can’t do things in the future that make sense.
concept: Retain earnings while a dollar kept is worth more than a dollar paid out; pay out only when sensible uses run out.
evolution_notes: Before (line 521): a dividend would not help the stock sell at intrinsic value, "I think it might be just the opposite". Restates M2008-104 and M2004-089.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 32. We don’t want Berkshire’s stock to be too high or too low

quote_verbatim: We’d still prefer using cash, though. Cash is our favorite medium of purchase just because we’re going to generate a lot of it. And we hate giving out shares. We do not like the idea of trading away part of See’s Candies or GEICO or ISCAR or BNSF. The idea of leaving you with a lower percentage interest in those companies because of any acquisition ambitions of ours is anathema to us.
concept: Pay for acquisitions in cash; issuing shares trades away part of every business already owned, which acquisition ambition does not justify.
evolution_notes: Before (line 523): stock might be used when it trades at or above intrinsic business value. Restates M2011-020 and the BNSF mistake under heading 19 (line 295). Munger (line 527): the questioner's dividend is "a very conventional approach", a view.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 32. We don’t want Berkshire’s stock to be too high or too low

quote_verbatim: And we think if we perform reasonably well, in terms of running the business, and if we tell the truth about the business, and explain to a selected group of shareholders who are interested in that aspect of investing, that over time, it will average that. And that’s happened over the years, but it doesn’t happen every year.
concept: To have a stock average its intrinsic value, run the business well, tell the truth about it, and explain it to shareholders who care about value.
evolution_notes: "that" is fair value (line 529): Buffett, giving his stock away yearly, has more interest than anyone in its selling at a fair rather than a discount value. Restates M1995-118 and principle 14 of the reprinted manual (report lines 6037-6045).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 32. We don’t want Berkshire’s stock to be too high or too low

quote_verbatim: Newspapers — you know, news is what you don’t know that you want to know. [...] So newspapers have to be primary about something of interest to a significant percentage of the people that live within their distribution area.
concept: News is what you do not know and want to know; a newspaper survives only by staying the primary source for something many local people care about.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the areas where the paper was once primary, apartments, jobs, the price of bananas, box scores, stock prices, now found elsewhere "on a more timely, often cost-free, basis". After (lines 543-549): the World-Herald still primary on local matters; obituaries; papers bought only where there is a strong sense of community and the product is not given away. Related: L2006-009 (free substitutes a click away).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 33. Buffett sees value in local newspapers

quote_verbatim: Now, I don’t know of any business plan that has sustained itself for a long time, maybe you can think of — maybe Charlie can think of one — but that has charged significantly in one version and offers the same version free to people, that had a business model that would work over time.
concept: A business that charges for one version of its product while giving the same version away free has no model that lasts.
evolution_notes: Said of newspapers putting the delivered product on the web free. Before: the papers are expensive to distribute and their number has fallen from 1700 to about 1400 (line 543). Munger (lines 551-559): World Book about 80 percent destroyed by software given away, still selling at a reasonable profit, "They’re not going to be our great lollapaloozas": a fact and an expectation, not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 33. Buffett sees value in local newspapers

quote_verbatim: Going back to Amazon, though, in terms — GEICO was very affected by the internet, and at first, we missed that. [...] And then the internet came along, and I thought, originally, that only young people would look for quotes on the internet and that — you know, I mean, I never would have done it. [...] So, things do change very significantly, and if the consumer finds something they like to do better in some new way — and Amazon has been an incredible success.
concept: Buffett's own: he missed the internet's effect on GEICO by judging from his own habits; when consumers find a way they like better, things change very significantly.
evolution_notes: Buffett's own mistake. The first elision skips GEICO's history from mail to television; the second skips the rotary-dial joke. The sentence at line 573 runs on into Amazon's success and is cut where Amazon is named.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 34. Buffett: Amazon won’t affect Nebraska Furniture Mart

quote_verbatim: It’s very hard to find people who have done business with Amazon that are unhappy about the transaction. They have happy customers. And a business that has millions and millions of happy customers can introduce them to new items and then, you know, and it will be a powerhouse, and I think it could affect a lot of businesses.
concept: A business with millions of happy customers can introduce them to new items and become a powerhouse that reaches into other businesses.
evolution_notes: After: "It’s hard for me to figure out." Before (line 569): Amazon could affect retailing businesses that do not think they will be affected, but not Nebraska Furniture Mart, a view not explained.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 34. Buffett: Amazon won’t affect Nebraska Furniture Mart

quote_verbatim: WARREN BUFFETT: Which ones do you think it will hurt the most, Charlie? CHARLIE MUNGER: Well, anything that can be easily bought by using a home computer, or an iPad, for that matter. [...] But I think it will hugely affect a lot of people. I think it’s terrible for most retailers. Not slightly terrible, really terrible.
concept: Munger: whatever can easily be bought from a home computer is exposed to online selling, which is really terrible for most retailers.
evolution_notes: Exchange, Buffett first; Munger states the lesson, so the row is his. The elision crosses Buffett's "Which of our businesses do you think it can hurt?" (line 581) and Munger's "I won’t be buying the stuff because I’m habit bound. Besides, I almost never buy anything. (Laughter)"; Munger resumes the same thought. Before (line 575): "I think it’s almost sure to hurt a lot of businesses a lot."
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 34. Buffett: Amazon won’t affect Nebraska Furniture Mart

quote_verbatim: Besides, I mean, it’s taken a long, long time to get here. It’s taken a great amount of consistency, and that consistency has been allowed because, basically, we’ve had a controlling shareholder during that time. So we’ve not had to bow to any of the urgings of Wall Street or, you know, whatever may be the fad of the day. But we have had a culture that — where we could write out 13 or 14 principles more than 30 years ago, and we’ve been able to stick with them. And that’s very hard to do for most American corporations, and I think it’s very hard to do when managers come and go and they have small shareholdings.
concept: Sticking to stated principles for decades needs owners who can ignore Wall Street's fads, which is hard when managers come and go with small shareholdings.
evolution_notes: Before: Munger, "we have a very peculiar model ... very hard for other people to get the same result" (line 593). The 13 or 14 principles are the reprinted owner-related principles (report lines 5807-6054).

heading: ### 35. “Almost impossible” to copy Berkshire

I mean, if somebody’s only interest is to get the top price for their business, you know, seldom we’ll get one. [...] But the big private acquisitions are going to come to Berkshire because they want to come to Berkshire. And that’s a significant competitive edge, and I don’t see how anybody really challenges us on that.

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 35. “Almost impossible” to copy Berkshire

quote_verbatim: but our general feeling is that when we’re a large shareholder of a company that we certainly generally like the business, we generally like the management. We realize that they’re not going to subscribe to our views 100 percent, in many cases 90 percent or 80 percent. [...] But that doesn’t rule out owning a big piece of the business. We are not in the business of trying to change people. We don’t try and change people when we buy the entire business. We think it’s like marrying somebody to change them. It just doesn’t work very well.
concept: Own a business whose management you like as it is; do not buy expecting to change the people, which works no better than marrying to change someone.

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 36. Rarely try to change companies in our stock portfolio

heading: ### 1. Gen Re improving after “major fix-up operation”

And my successor will understand that just as well as I do. And there would be a lot of people that might very well manage other companies that, I think if stuck in my position, would lose a fair number of managers. They just have a different style.

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 2. Threats to Berkshire’s culture after Buffett

heading: ### 3. Buffett OK with 12 percent return for cash-consuming businesses

heading: ### 4. Berkshire’s float growth rate likely to slow

concept: A declining business is worth much less than a growing one, but can still be valuable if much cash will come out of it.

heading: ### 5. Past mistakes buying declining businesses

quote_verbatim: Yeah. Generally speaking, it pays to stay away from declining businesses. It’s very hard. You’d be amazed at the offerings of businesses we get where they say, you know, it’s — I don’t want to upset Charlie, but they say, you know, it’s only six times EBITDA, and then they project some future that doesn’t have any meaning whatsoever. If you really think a business is declining, most of the time you should avoid it. [...] The real money is going to be made by being in growing businesses, and that’s where the focus should be.

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 5. Past mistakes buying declining businesses

It just isn’t — the same amount of energy and intelligence brought to other types of businesses is just going to work out better.
concept: Time spent valuing a declining business for one last puff is better spent on other kinds of business; the same effort pays more there.
evolution_notes: After (line 773): "our general reaction, unless there’s some special case, is to avoid new ones." Related: M2001-114 (the cigar butt defined, one free puff).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 5. Past mistakes buying declining businesses

quote_verbatim: If you think what came out of those three declining businesses, all of which failed, it’s so many billions you — it’s hard to imagine how much came out of it. We’re not looking for an opportunity to do it again.
concept: Berkshire began with three declining businesses that all failed (textiles, a Baltimore department store, trading stamps); though billions were built from them, they will not repeat the start.
evolution_notes: Their own mistake, narrated together: Buffett lists textiles, U.S.-made shoes, the department store at Howard and Lexington, Blue Chip Stamps (lines 773-801); "So we were sort of masochistic in the early days." Munger: "Ignorant, too." (lines 801-803). Buffett on the $6 million in Diversified Retailing that "has turned into about $30 billion" and Munger's "— failed business." (lines 797-799). Related: the cigar-butt rule at line 773.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 5. Past mistakes buying declining businesses

quote_verbatim: I think I would describe it as we try to stay away from the things, to start with, that we don’t understand. And when I say don’t understand, it isn’t that I don’t understand, you know, what a certain business does. But when I say understand, it means that I think I have a reasonably — a reasonable fix on about what the earning power and competitive position will look like in five or 10 years. So I’ve got some notion of how the industry will develop and where the company will stand within the industry. Well, that eliminates a whole bunch of things. And then, beyond that, if the price is crazy, even though I understand it, that eliminates another bunch.
concept: To understand a business is not to know what it does but to have a reasonable fix on its earning power and competitive position, and on its industry, five or ten years out; that filter comes first, a crazy price is the second.
evolution_notes: Answer to a question asking what to avoid, by inversion. After (line 813): the universe gets very small, especially with large sums. Related: M1997-053 (filters screen out businesses whose value in ten or twenty years cannot be guessed).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 6. Stay away from IPOs and big commissions

quote_verbatim: I mean, the idea, that somebody is bringing something to market today, a seller who has a choice of when to come to market, and that that security, where there’s going to be a lot of hoopla connected with it, is going to be the single cheapest thing to buy out of thousands and thousands and thousands of businesses in the world is nonsense, you know. [...] you know, it just doesn’t make any sense to spend five seconds thinking about new issues, so we don’t think about them.
concept: A new issue is brought when the seller chooses, with promotion attached, so it is almost never the cheapest of thousands of choices; new issues are not considered at all.
evolution_notes: Before (line 813): no new issue bought in at least 30 years; Munger "I can’t think of one." The elision crosses Munger's line 819 ("And then when it carries a 7 percent commission, or higher. It’s ridiculous."), and Buffett resumes the same thought: thousands of opportunities not promoted, "when the seller picks the time to bring it, as opposed to just this auction market". Restates M2004-100 (an IPO is a sale timed by an informed seller).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 6. Stay away from IPOs and big commissions

quote_verbatim: And we also — you know, there’s industries we know that may have a wonderful future, but we don’t have the faintest idea who the winners will be, so we don’t think about those, either. So there’s a whole lot of things we don’t think about. And we have a — Charlie and I have a number of filters that things have to get through very quickly before we’re willing to think about them.
concept: An industry with a wonderful future is not considered when the winners cannot be identified; ideas must pass quick filters before any thought is given.
evolution_notes: After (line 823): callers are cut off politely when an idea fails the first filter or two, "we don’t want to have you finish the sentence." Related: M1999-064 (missing big winners accepted for few big losers).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 6. Stay away from IPOs and big commissions

quote_verbatim: We don’t have to do very many things that work. I mean, that’s the beauty of this business. [...] You just have to do one or two things every now and then that — where you don’t make a big mistake and where every now and then one works out real well. And the solution — you know, you’ll get a good result. You can’t have a big disaster. You just — that is what we try to avoid. We do not ever want to lose a significant percentage of Berkshire’s net worth, and so far we haven’t.
concept: Investing needs only a few good decisions now and then, provided no big mistake is made; a loss of a significant share of net worth is what is avoided above all.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the spelling-bee comparison ("You don’t have to be able, you know, to spell 500 words").
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 6. Stay away from IPOs and big commissions

quote_verbatim: CHARLIE MUNGER: I think there are a couple little rules of thumb. If it’s got a really large commission in it — WARREN BUFFETT: Forget it. CHARLIE MUNGER: — don’t read it. Because the chance of somebody who is paying a very high commission to give you a big advantage is very low.
concept: Do not even read an offering that carries a large commission; whoever pays a high commission is unlikely to be handing you an advantage.
evolution_notes: Exchange, Munger first and Munger states the rule; Buffett's "Forget it." interjects. Buffett closes the heading (line 843): "Don’t go into things with big commissions." Munger earlier (line 819): a new issue that "carries a 7 percent commission, or higher. It’s ridiculous." Related: M2008-057 (ask who is paid to give the advice).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 6. Stay away from IPOs and big commissions

quote_verbatim: And the other thing that is, I think, helpful in reverse, is — as a place to look, looking at things that other smart people are buying. That is not a crazy search method as a sorting device for opportunities to consider.
concept: What other able investors are buying is a sensible place to look for ideas, as a sorting device, not as a decision.
evolution_notes: Buffett follows (lines 835-839): he "grabbed the Graham-Newman reports as fast as they would come out", "if Graham Newman was doing something, it was certainly worth my time to look at it." Munger (line 841): "Warren has made a lot of people rich he doesn’t even know. Just copied him."
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 6. Stay away from IPOs and big commissions

quote_verbatim: They earn fantastic returns on capital. They look very tough to dislodge, where they have their strengths. You know, I would not be at all surprised to see them be worth a lot more money 10 years from now, but I wouldn’t want to buy either one of them. I do not get to the level of conviction that would cause me to buy them. But I sure as hell wouldn’t short them, either.
concept: Fine returns and a strong position do not justify a purchase without the level of conviction needed to buy; lacking it is no reason to bet against the business either.
evolution_notes: On Google and Apple, asked whether they are "inevitable" like Coke and Gillette.

heading: ### 9. Won’t invest in Apple or Google, but wouldn’t bet against them

concept: Where others will always understand a company better, one has the reverse of an edge, and such a position is not sought.
evolution_notes: After (line 901): "I think IBM is easier to understand." Later (line 905): "And what do we know about computer science?"
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 9. Won’t invest in Apple or Google, but wouldn’t bet against them

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 9. Won’t invest in Apple or Google, but wouldn’t bet against them

quote_verbatim: But there’s no question that railroads, utilities, insurance companies, are all very much affected by the political process. Fortunately, I think, in the railroad industry, you know, we’ve got economics on our side. And economics usually win out.

Railroad employment from 1,700,000 to under 200,000 (line 927).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 10. Strong freight railroad economics will overcome politics

speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 10. Strong freight railroad economics will overcome politics

quote_verbatim: We want our businesses to run very autonomously, and we want the managers of those businesses to feel like they’re their own business. That’s enormously important at Berkshire. [...] any gains we would get from doing that, by selling incremental units, I think would be far offset by the change in the feeling of the manager as to whether they’re really running their own business. [...] And the moment we start telling them how to change the way they operate, or to coordinate with this guy, or get this person’s approval, or anything like that, you know, that just erodes that advantage, which we think is very substantial, that they have this proprietary feeling about their business.

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 13. We don’t even try to coordinate our subsidiaries

We’ve looked at forest products companies, but we don’t think about them in terms of how they may divert their products to some other subsidiaries of ours, or how other subsidiaries might benefit from selling them something. To date, we’ve looked at several. To date, we’ve never really found any that met our test for returns against purchase price. I mean, it’s a business that’s easy — or reasonably easy — to understand, I mean, in terms of the economics and its permanence and all that sort of thing. But the math has escaped us, in terms of being compelling.
concept: An acquisition is judged on its own returns against purchase price, never on what it could sell to or buy from other subsidiaries; an understandable business still fails if the math is not compelling.

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 14. Acquisition of a forest products company unlikely

evolution_notes: Munger states it first for forests (line 993): forest companies convert into flow-through partnerships, "Berkshire is actually organized so that we’d be a disadvantage — we’d be at a disadvantage — in bidding for forests." Buffett generalises; the exchange carries one lesson, rowed under Buffett, who states it generally. The elision skips REITs and Plum Creek Timber as examples.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 14. Acquisition of a forest products company unlikely

quote_verbatim: Yeah. Well, it isn’t the magic number, and there is no magic number. I would get very worried about somebody that walked in every morning and told us precisely how many dollars of cash we needed to be, you know, secured at three sigma or something like that.
concept: The cash a business needs for safety has no precise formula; a sigma-calibrated figure is a reason for worry, not comfort.
evolution_notes: After (line 1003): "we saw a lot of problems develop in an organization that expressed their risks in sigma"; Munger "It was truly horrible." (line 1005). Later (line 1009): "if you’re calibrating it in some mathematical way, I would say it’s really dangerous." Related: M2007-039 (sigma events and human behavior).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 15. No magic formula for calculating risk

quote_verbatim: But we both have the same bend of mind whereby we think about worst cases all the time, and then we add on a big margin of safety, and we don’t want to go back to go. [...] And I’m just not interested in explaining to them that we went broke because there was a onehundredth of 1 percent chance that we would go broke and there was a — the remaining probability was filled by the chance of doubling our money, and I decided that that was just a good gamble to take. We’re not going to do that.
concept: Think about worst cases always and add a big margin of safety; no tiny chance of ruin is accepted, however large the reward that fills the rest of the odds.
evolution_notes: The elision skips "I enjoy tossing those papers in the other room, but I don’t want to do it for a living again", the layers of safety others may call foolish, and the 600,000 shareholders and family members with "80 or 90 percent of their net worth in the company." "onehundredth" is printed as one word, kept. Related: M2012-032 (worst cases all of the time).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 15. No magic formula for calculating risk

quote_verbatim: We are never going to risk what we have and need for what we don’t have and don’t need. We’ll still find things to do where we can make money, but we don’t have to stretch to do it. [...] But it’s our job to figure out what can really go wrong with this place and, you know, we’ve seen September 11th, and we’ve seen September of 2008, and we’ll see other things of a different nature but similar impact in the future.

evolution_notes: The elision skips "And it’s my job — and Charlie thinks the same way. We don’t have to talk about it much." After: "we not only want to sleep well all those nights, we want to be thinking about things to do with some excess money". Restates M2011-099 (never risk what you have and need) and M2011-079 (no risk that threatens the enterprise).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 15. No magic formula for calculating risk

quote_verbatim: So it’s at the top of the mind, always, around Berkshire, and your returns in 99 years out of 100 will probably be penalized by us being excessively conservative, and one year out of a hundred, we’ll survive when some other people won’t.

evolution_notes: Before (line 1011): "some really great organizations have had dozens of people with advanced mathematical training [...] and they don’t really get at the problem."
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 15. No magic formula for calculating risk

quote_verbatim: Yeah, how do these super-smart people with all these degrees in higher mathematics end up doing these dumb things? I think it’s explainable by the old proverb that, “To a man with a hammer, every problem looks pretty much like a nail.” They’ve learned these techniques and they just twist the problem so they fit the solution, which is not the way to do it.
concept: Mathematically trained risk managers fail by bending the problem to fit the techniques they know; the problem must come first.
evolution_notes: A third party's mistake: the mathematically trained risk managers of large organizations. The proverb is old and unattributed. Restates M2009-012 (rating agencies, the same proverb) and M1998-059.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 15. No magic formula for calculating risk

quote_verbatim: And they have a lack of understanding of history, I would say. [...] And to me, the lesson — that fellow probably understood sigmas and everything and knew how impossible it was that in one day a stock could go from 170 to 1,000 to cause margin calls on everything else. And he ended up in a vat of hot beer, and I’ve never wanted to end up in a vat of hot beer. (Laughter) So those seven days that I put up on the wall — life in financial markets has got no relation to sigmas.
concept: Financial history shows the impossible happening in a day; a borrower on margin who trusted the odds was ruined, so markets are read through history, not sigmas.
evolution_notes: A third party's mistake: a Troy, New York brewer on margin during the Northern Pacific corner of May 1901, which Buffett keeps among seven pages of financial history on his office wall since 1962. The elision skips the corner's story and crosses Munger's "To the shorts." (line 1017); Buffett resumes. After (line 1019): "if everybody that operated in financial markets had never had any concept of standard errors and so on, they would be a lot better off." Munger afterward (lines 1025-1037): sigma thinking "created a lot of false confidence", "We always knew there were fat tails."
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 15. No magic formula for calculating risk

quote_verbatim: But the fact that that expires and our premium volume will go down by multiple billions does not cause us to do one thing differently than we would do otherwise. [...] We regard every decision, you know, as independent. We don’t do — if money comes in, that doesn’t cause us to want to think about doing something today that we weren’t thinking about doing the day before.
concept: Each decision stands alone: losing volume does not prompt replacing it, and new money does not prompt doing what was not wanted the day before.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the capacity to write billions and "we don’t want to write any dumb business when we lose that contract. It’s just — it’s a nonevent, in terms of future strategy." After (line 1047): "Every decision is sort of independent."
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 16. Swiss Re contract expiration is “nonevent”

quote_verbatim: I don’t think there’s another large insurance operation in the world that is more cheerful about losing volume than we are. If it doesn’t make sense — WARREN BUFFETT: We don’t want it. CHARLIE MUNGER: — if the business has to shrink, we let it shrink.
concept: An insurer should accept losing volume cheerfully; when business does not make sense, let it shrink.
evolution_notes: Exchange with Buffett; two separate lessons in one exchange, one row per speaker, the other being Buffett's measure-by-value passage at lines 1055-1059. Related: M2004-077 (do not worry about premium volume).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 16. Swiss Re contract expiration is “nonevent”

quote_verbatim: WARREN BUFFETT: We don’t measure ourselves in any way — CHARLIE MUNGER: By size. WARREN BUFFETT: — by size, except by the growth in value over time.
concept: Size is not a measure of success; only growth in value over time is.
evolution_notes: Exchange with Munger, whose "By size." completes the phrase; Buffett states the lesson. The other row from this exchange is Munger's let-it-shrink passage at lines 1049-1053.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 16. Swiss Re contract expiration is “nonevent”

quote_verbatim: WARREN BUFFETT: Charlie, we resigned from the Savings and Loan League a good many years ago just because we thought such nutty stuff was going on and — CHARLIE MUNGER: It was disgraceful.
concept: Implied: leave an industry association, and in the end the industry, when its common practice is unsound, rather than conform to it.
evolution_notes: Implied: what was done was resigning from the League and (Munger, line 1103) "We left the savings and loan business." Exchange, Buffett first and Buffett states it. Between (lines 1093-1095): Munger refused a regulator's demand that the savings and loan make "a lot of dumb loans because we’re telling you to." The rest of the heading (Fannie and Freddie, Munger on the government's duty to step on booms, Greenspan) is political view, not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 17. Housing problems after Fannie and Freddie “left the tracks”

quote_verbatim: Well, we’ve always been more concerned about how our record is achieved than the precise record itself. And with both Todd and Ted, Charlie and I were struck by, not only a good record, but intellectual integrity and qualities of character, a real commitment to Berkshire, a lifelong-type commitment. And we’ve seen hundreds and hundreds of good records in our lifetimes; we haven’t seen very many people we want to have join Berkshire.
concept: In judging an investment manager, how the record was achieved matters more than the record; good records are common, integrity, character and lifelong commitment are rare.
evolution_notes: Restates M2011-097 (not IQ, not past record). Munger after (line 1127): "they’ll be terrific for the long pull for Berkshire."
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 18. How Todd Combs and Ted Weschler are compensated — and taxed

quote_verbatim: But these two are perfect, and we pay them each a salary of a million dollars a year, and we give them 10 percent of the amount by which their portfolios beat the S&P. [...] But we do it on a three-year rolling basis so you don’t get the seesaw effect. And each one gets paid 80 percent based on their own efforts and 20 percent based on the other person’s, so that they have every incentive to operate in a collaborative way rather than sit there jealously guarding their own ideas and hoping the other guy doesn’t do very well.
concept: Pay an investment manager a share only of performance above the index, measured over rolling years to avoid the seesaw, and partly on a colleague's results so that ideas are shared rather than guarded.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the worked example (10 points over the S&P earns one point). After (lines 1117, 1121): the same structure as Lou Simpson's for 20-some years; people they hire come out of their own record; two-thirds of a year's gain deferred and lost back on underperformance. Munger (line 1123): "at least 90 percent of the investment management business of the United States would starve to death on our formula." Related: the record-and-character passage on the same line.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 18. How Todd Combs and Ted Weschler are compensated — and taxed

quote_verbatim: Well, in terms of what’s a good investment, you know, we try to look at every aspect, everything we can that will tell us how the world is going to develop for both that industry and the company in the future. And sometimes we feel a lot of confidence about that. If we’re looking at Coca-Cola, we think we know a lot about how the world will look with the Coca-Cola Company over the next five or 10 or 20 years. If we’re looking at some retail business or something, we would not have the same degree of conviction at all. [...] We just look at the dynamics of the specific industry and company.
concept: A good investment is judged by how the world will develop for the industry and the company over five to twenty years; confidence is high for some businesses and low for others, such as retail.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the rail-versus-truck fuel comparison and "there’s no magazine we go to or books we go to". Restates M2012-065 (understanding means a reasonable fix five or ten years out).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 20. Environmental benefits of freight railroads

quote_verbatim: If that works for us, why shouldn’t it work for a bunch of other people who have long been doing what they like to do and now, in many cases, have all the money they possibly need? [...] So we give them the paint brush, let them keep the paint brush, and we don’t go around and tell them to use more red paint than blue paint or something of the sort. And we applaud and we try to compensate them fairly, because though they aren’t primarily doing it for the money in many cases, nobody likes to be taken advantage of.
concept: Managers who already have all the money they need are kept by leaving them in charge, applauding them and paying fairly, since nobody likes to be taken advantage of.
evolution_notes: Before (line 1171): Buffett and Munger themselves "get the opportunity to paint our own painting every day" and would resent being told "use more red paint than blue paint". The elision skips sellers who sell for family or tax reasons and still love the work. Restates M2012-056 (managers stay for the environment).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 21. Berkshire lets managers paint their own pictures

quote_verbatim: So I can’t put passion into somebody about their jobs, but I can certainly create a structure that will take that passion away from them. And Berkshire is a negative art in that way. We focus on not messing up something that’s already good, and that’s my job.
concept: An owner cannot instill a manager's passion but can destroy it; the owner's job is the negative art of not messing up what is already good.
evolution_notes: Before (lines 1175-1177): a manager from England spends his time talking to investors, "which does him no good. I mean, he ought to be talking to customers"; managers are freed from lawyers, bankers and investors. After (line 1177): "we have a bunch of managers nobody else can hire". Related: M2003-063 (Munger, passion more important than brainpower).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 21. Berkshire lets managers paint their own pictures

quote_verbatim: And every incentive arrangement with a key executive is different from every other, so we can’t help you with a standard formula. We don’t have one.
concept: Each key executive's incentive is designed for that business; there is no standard formula or weighted scorecard.
evolution_notes: Before (line 1181): no formulas "where X percent is on diversity and Y percent is on something else" run through a human resources department. Buffett's restatement (line 1183): "Our businesses are all so different. It would be crazy to try and have some master arrangement", some use no capital.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 21. Berkshire lets managers paint their own pictures

quote_verbatim: And, you know, who does a human relations VP want to — whose approval do they want? The CEO’s. Whose approval does the compensation consultant want? Well, they want to get recommended elsewhere by the CEO and the human relations VP. So what kind of a system do you get? You get what I call ratchet, ratchet, and bingo, you know. We’re not going to have any of that at Berkshire, and like I say it’s worked very well. [...] But it does relate to logical measures of performance in practically all cases.
concept: Ask whose approval each party to a pay decision wants: the HR officer and the compensation consultant both want the CEO's, so pay ratchets; pay should relate to logical measures of performance.
evolution_notes: Before (lines 1183-1187): compensation consultants "would want to please the people they were working for and get referred elsewhere"; Munger "We never have." (line 1185). The elision skips the page and a half of managers earning a million dollars and over. Related: M2009-094 and M2007-007 (pay ratchets).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 21. Berkshire lets managers paint their own pictures

quote_verbatim: You get your expectations too high. When you think that 4 percent is what the world ought to provide, you’re asking for trouble. [...] That’s what happened in the housing boom. People got these foolish dreams, and they just started doing foolish things to try and reach unattainable objectives.
concept: Expectations set too high invite trouble: in the housing boom people chased unattainable objectives with foolish acts.
evolution_notes: A third party's mistake: those who took part in the housing boom. The elision crosses Buffett's "It won’t do it." (line 1225); Munger resumes the same thought. Before (line 1219): 1 percent real growth per capita "would be a sensational result." The rest of the heading is a growth forecast, not rowed.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 22. Modest GDP growth creates “staggering” increases over time

quote_verbatim: Well, I’d say no, but I’d say it’s in the nature of things that the market is not going to do exactly what you want when you want it. I think over time, “Mr. Market” will treat the Berkshire shareholders fine, and I wouldn’t worry too much about what happens over this six months or this 12 months.
concept: The market will not move when one wants; a price that lags the business over six or twelve months is not a worry for a long-term owner.
evolution_notes: After (line 1273): "I don’t think you’re really all that welcome in this room if the short-term orientation is what turns you on."
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 24. Don’t worry about Berkshire’s short-term stock moves

quote_verbatim: WARREN BUFFETT: I think you’d agree, though, probably, that Berkshire is somewhat cheaper relative to its price than it was a year ago. CHARLIE MUNGER: Yes, absolutely, if that’s your test. Should you feel better about the margin of safety in Berkshire? Yes, it’s fine.
concept: When the business grows and the price stands still, the stock is cheaper and the margin of safety larger.
evolution_notes: Exchange, Buffett first; Munger states the lesson in terms of margin of safety. Buffett's "cheaper relative to its price" is printed so; the sense appears to be relative to value, which the question framed ("intrinsic value, as a multiple of book value, should be increasing"). Kept as printed.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 24. Don’t worry about Berkshire’s short-term stock moves

quote_verbatim: Yeah. By and large, we feel, perhaps unjustifiably, but so far justified, that we can create more than a dollar of present value by investing. Sometimes, if the stock is cheap, we can create more than a dollar of present value by simply repurchasing shares. But even if that option isn’t available, we feel that by every dollar we retain, we can — overall — we can turn that into a greater than a dollar of present value. [...] So, if somebody wanted to create their own income stream out of it, they were much better off selling a little bit of stock every year than they were by getting a dividend out of it.
concept: Retain earnings while each dollar retained becomes more than a dollar of present value; an owner wanting income does better selling a little stock each year than receiving a dividend.
evolution_notes: The elision skips "And for 47 years, that’s worked." After (line 1285): more money stays working per share if an owner sells 2 percent than if 2 percent is paid out; "the question is whether we can keep doing that in the future." Munger (line 1289): dividends "will come in due course because eventually we’ll find it difficult to multiply the rabbits". Restates M2012-040 (110 cents within, 100 cents paid out) and M2010-017.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 25. Why Berkshire hasn’t paid a dividend

quote_verbatim: But so far, at any point in our history, if we had paid out dividends — and I paid out 10 cents a share back in the 1960s which was a big mistake, but — we won’t repeat that. If we paid out dividends, our shareholders, net, would be worth less money than they are by having left it in
concept: Buffett calls the one ten-cent dividend of the 1960s a big mistake not to be repeated, since every payout would have left shareholders worth less.
evolution_notes: Buffett's own mistake. The quote stops mid-sentence before ", and I think that will continue to be the case, but who knows?" Related: the retain-or-pay test at line 1285.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 25. Why Berkshire hasn’t paid a dividend

quote_verbatim: Berkshire’s record would have been terrible compared to the way it turned out if Warren hadn’t kept learning and learning and learning all the way. I mean, each decade, to make the record decent, he had to learn to do some things he didn’t know how to do at the start of the decade. And I think that’s pretty much the human condition
concept: A long record needs continuous learning: each decade demands skills not held at its start.
evolution_notes: Before (line 1329): "There’s enough craziness out there. If you have endless time and only a very small amount of money, I think you could find ways to do pretty well." Buffett (lines 1323, 1331): they could do better with $1 million now than then, "we would know more places to look". Restates M2010-028 (the old men continuing to learn).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 26. “Learning and learning and learning”

quote_verbatim: we think in terms of not exposing ourselves to any mistakes that could really hurt our ability to play tomorrow. And so we are always thinking about, you know, worst-case situations and there are — on the other hand, we have a natural instinct to do things big, both of us. So we have to think about whether we’re doing anything really big that could have really terrible consequences.
concept: Mistakes are accepted, but never one that could stop you playing tomorrow; an instinct to do things big must be checked against really terrible consequences.
evolution_notes: Asked for techniques to minimise mistakes. Opens: "we made mistakes; we’ll make more mistakes. We do — we think not so much —". Restates the worst-case passages at heading 15 (M2012-080, M2012-081).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 27. Learning from the follies of others

quote_verbatim: And, I would say this, that A) I don’t worry much about mistakes, I mean, the idea of learning from mistakes. The next mistake is something different. So I do not sit around and think about my mistakes and things I’m going to do differently in the future or anything of the sort. [...] I haven’t learned more about a basic investment philosophy. I got that when I was 19 and I still — I think I’ve learned more about people over the years.
concept: Buffett does not dwell on his past mistakes because the next one will differ; the investment philosophy was fixed at 19, and what improves is judgment of people.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct. After (line 1345): "I’ll recognize the extraordinary ones better than I would have 40 or 50 years ago", not by "conscious sitting around and focusing on what mistake did I make". Same answer as the not-exposing passage on line 1343. See the note's Tensions seen (Munger at line 1333).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 27. Learning from the follies of others

quote_verbatim: Warren, I would argue that what you’ve done, and what I’ve done to a lesser extent, is to learn a lot from other people’s mistakes. That is really a much more pleasant way to learn hard lessons. (Laughter) And we have really worked at that over the years, partly because we find it so interesting, the great variety of human mistakes and their causes. And I think this constant study of other people’s disasters and other people’s errors has helped us enormously
concept: Study other people's mistakes and disasters and their causes; it is the pleasanter way to learn hard lessons.
evolution_notes: Buffett agrees (line 1349): "I’ve always been absolutely absorbed with reading about disasters", the high-IQ mathematicians "really just didn’t have an understanding of how human beings behave", "we have been a student of other people’s folly, and its served us well." ("its" as printed). Related: the hot-beer passage at heading 15 (M2012-084).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 27. Learning from the follies of others

quote_verbatim: Yeah. We sort of buy barriers; we don’t build them. (Laughter)
concept: Barriers to entry are bought, not built.
evolution_notes: Buffett answers (line 1369): "Yeah. Well, think about that because it’s true." Munger restates (line 1371): "our great brands we bought, we didn’t create."
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 28. We don’t build strong barriers to entries, we buy them

quote_verbatim: It’s very — there are some industries that are just never going to have barriers to entry. And in those industries, you better be running very fast because there are a lot of other people that are going to be running and looking at what you’re doing and trying to figure out, you know, what your weakness is or what they can do a little bit better. You really — you know, a great barrier to entry, you know, is something like this. If you gave me 10, 20, $30 billion and told me to go in and try and knock off the Coca-Cola Company with some new cola drink, I wouldn’t have the faintest idea how to do it.
concept: Test a barrier to entry by asking whether tens of billions would let you knock off the leader; without a barrier a business must run very fast against rivals probing its weakness.
evolution_notes: After (line 1369): "billions of people around the world that have something in their mind about Coca-Cola". After (line 1373): Virgin Cola, hundreds of failed colas; Lipitor, where "the time runs out and what was an absolute gold mine still is a pretty good mine". Related: L2007-004 (the moat and the castle).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 28. We don’t build strong barriers to entries, we buy them

quote_verbatim: But if you’re buying something at a huge discount from replacement cost and it’s an essential sort of activity, you’ve certainly got a barrier to new competition.
concept: An essential activity bought far below its replacement cost has a barrier to new competition.
evolution_notes: Before (line 1373): "nobody’s going to build another railroad". After (line 1375): "But the UP is out there fighting for every bit of business every day". Related: M2011-055 (replacement value of a capital-heavy asset).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 28. We don’t build strong barriers to entries, we buy them

quote_verbatim: Yeah. We have found in a long life that one competitor is frequently enough to ruin a business.
concept: A single competitor is often enough to ruin a business's economics.
evolution_notes: Buffett's gas-station story follows at line 1379.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 28. We don’t build strong barriers to entries, we buy them

quote_verbatim: Well, I did find that out. I started with a gas station out at 30th and Redick here in Omaha, and we had a Phillips station next to it. I had a Sinclair station. And you know, whatever he charged for gas was my price. (Laughs) I didn’t have much choice. You don’t like to be in a business like that.
concept: Buffett's own gas station took its price from the station next door; avoid a business whose price is set by a competitor.
evolution_notes: Buffett's own mistake, told to confirm Munger's one-competitor passage on line 1377.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 28. We don’t build strong barriers to entries, we buy them

quote_verbatim: Well, the economic value comes from the ability to utilize float if obtained at a bargain rate. Now, if interest rates were 7 or 8 percent and float even cost you 2 percent to obtain, it still would be very valuable.
concept: An insurer's economic value comes from using float obtained at a bargain rate; float that costs something can still be valuable when it costs well below prevailing interest rates.
evolution_notes: Asked how to value the different insurance businesses. Closing the same answer (line 1411): "It does relate in the end to a combination of growing a large float, and extremely low-cost float, and in our case, the cost of float has been negative". Related: L1993-009 (cost of float is the underwriting result).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 30. Berkshire’s insurance float and low interest rates

quote_verbatim: But the economic — at GEICO, for example, I think it’s quite reasonable to expect a fairly substantial underwriting profit, on average, for as far as the eye can see, and growth for as far as the eye can see. And then coupled with that is a growing float, because float grows with the premium volume. Well, that’s the most — you know, that is a very attractive combination of factors that comes about because GEICO is a low-cost producer. [...] It’s always good, though, to own a low-cost producer in any business, but it’s very, very nice in the insurance business.
concept: The most attractive insurer combines lasting underwriting profit, growth and growing float, and that combination comes from being the low-cost producer, which is good in any business and especially in insurance.
evolution_notes: The elision skips GEICO's scale and method of operation, "very hard for other companies to duplicate their cost structure." After (line 1411): Tony Nicely took GEICO from 2 percent of the market and "quintupled, virtually, our share". Restates M2012-033 (GEICO worth more than net worth plus float); the bargain-float definition earlier on line 1407.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 30. Berkshire’s insurance float and low interest rates

quote_verbatim: In Ajit’s business, he has to be smart on each deal, because something comes along and somebody wants to buy coverage for events causing the loss of more than $10 billion in Japan in the next year. That is not — you can’t look it up in any book, and you can’t do enough transactions just like that one to even know whether your calculation was right on that specific deal. Now, if you make 100 calculations on 100 of these type of deals, you’ll soon find out whether you have the right person making those calculations or not. But the economic goodwill with Ajit’s operation is based much more on the skill to price individual transactions and the ability to find the people even that want those transactions.
concept: A statistical insurance business is valued on its machine and its costs; a one-off reinsurance business is valued on one person's skill in pricing single deals, which can be judged only across many deals, never on one.
evolution_notes: Before (line 1409): GEICO's well over 10 million policies, "a statistical-type business"; after (line 1411): "Whereas at GEICO, it’s based basically on a machine. But it’s enormously important how that machine is run". Buffett later (line 1417): low rates on 36 or 37 billion of cash mean "our normal earning power is being depressed", not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 30. Berkshire’s insurance float and low interest rates

quote_verbatim: I’m a puritan. I always want to suffer now to make the future better, because I think that’s the way grown-ups should behave.
concept: Munger: accept present sacrifice to make the future better; that is how grown-ups behave.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct, stated inside a political answer (use other nations' oil and conserve our own; energy independence "one of the stupidest ideas"); the politics is left out of the quote. Buffett (line 1443): "This is Charlie’s version of saving up sex for your old age."
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 31. Munger: Energy independence is a “stupid idea”

quote_verbatim: Well, the nice thing about sovereign debt is they can not pay you in the end and you can’t grab anything from them, unlike other kinds of debts. And, you know, the truth is that the world has seen many, many failures of sovereign debt. I remember when Walt Wriston, back in the early 1980s, said sovereigns don’t default. Well, the truth is they’ve defaulted many, many times over history.
concept: Sovereign debt gives the lender no recourse, and history shows sovereigns default many times; the claim that they do not is false.
evolution_notes: "the nice thing" is ironic, as the rest of the sentence shows. Walt Wriston's claim is a third party's error corrected by history.
