After (line 1511): in default the wealth is reallocated, it "doesn’t go away". The rest of the heading (the ECB, fiscal stimulus, Munger on "fiscal virtue") is political and economic view, not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 33. Sovereign debt and “fiscal virtue”

quote_verbatim: I would avoid — I would — certainly at these rates, I would totally avoid buying medium-term or long-term government bonds. I think that’s the obvious answer. [...] But in terms of your own situation, I would stay away from medium- or long-term government bonds, our own, or those of other countries.
concept: At the yields of the day, an investor should avoid medium- and long-term government bonds of any country.
evolution_notes: Instruction to an investor inside a political answer on sovereign debt; the politics is left out. Tied to "these rates". Restates L2008-020 (long governments at present yields a terrible policy if continued).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 33. Sovereign debt and “fiscal virtue”

quote_verbatim: We regard it — and I speak for all the directors — we regard it as the number one obligation of the board to have a successor, and one that we’re very happy with, as to both ability and integrity, and that we know well, to step in tomorrow morning if I should die tonight. And we spend more time on that subject than any other subject that might come before the board.
concept: A board's first obligation is a successor it knows well, of proven ability and integrity, ready to step in the next morning.
evolution_notes: Reply to the AFL-CIO motion for a written succession policy. After (line 1609): naming the candidates has "obvious disadvantages"; (line 1611) a formal item in the proxy statement would add nothing. Related: M2012-001 (successors chosen for risk judgment).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 37. Shareholder proposal for written CEO succession planning policy

quote_verbatim: Since the basic game is so favorable, Charlie and I believe it's a terrible mistake to try to dance in and out of it based upon the turn of tarot cards, the predictions of "experts," or the ebb and flow of business activity. The risks of being out of the game are huge compared to the risks of being in it.
concept: Because owning American business is a game stacked in the owner's favour, moving in and out on forecasts or the business cycle is a mistake; the risk of being out exceeds the risk of being in.
evolution_notes: Just before (lines 229-231), addressed to CEOs: people sometimes focus on the myriad of uncertainties that always exist and at other times ignore them, usually because the recent past has been uneventful; and (lines 235-237) stocks will do well because their fate is tied to business performance, a game "heavily stacked in their favor." Just after: his first purchase in spring 1942 amid wartime losses. Related: M1996-066 (never try to predict markets), M1999-078 (do not trade in and out of the best holdings), M2012-028 (no macro). No earlier letter row states the asymmetry of the risk of being out.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: BERKSHIRE HATHAWAY INC.

quote_verbatim: In last year's tepid economy, for example, BNSF's interest coverage was 9.6x. (Our definition of coverage is pre-tax earnings/interest, not EBITDA/interest, a commonly-used measure we view as deeply flawed.)
concept: Interest coverage is measured as pre-tax earnings over interest, never EBITDA over interest, which is deeply flawed.
evolution_notes: Inside the passage restating L2010-012 (long-lived regulated assets carrying debt not guaranteed by Berkshire because earning power covers interest even under terrible conditions, lines 463-466; not rowed). Earlier rows against EBITDA: R1996-023, L2000-036, L2001-019, M2012-034 (price on pretax earnings, never EBITDA). New in a letter as the definition of the coverage test.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Regulated, Capital-Intensive Businesses

quote_verbatim: I won't explain all of the adjustments � some are small and arcane � but serious investors should understand the disparate nature of intangible assets: Some truly deplete over time while others never lose value. With software, for example, amortization charges are very real expenses. Charges against other intangibles such as the amortization of customer relationships, however, arise through purchase-accounting rules and are clearly not real expenses. GAAP accounting draws no distinction between the two types of charges.
concept: Sort intangible amortization by whether the asset truly depletes: software amortization is a real expense, purchase-accounting charges on customer relationships are not, though GAAP treats both alike.
evolution_notes: Buffett goes on (lines 617-620): of $600 million of amortization in the segment he calls about 20% real; IBM's adjusted operating earnings exclude such charges and analysts rightly focus on them (lines 622-624); Wells Fargo's "amortization of core deposits" charge of about $1.5 billion is in no sense, except GAAP, an expense, since core deposits regularly increase (lines 628-632). Related: M1998-048 and M1998-127 (add back intangible amortization), M1999-037 (some goodwill does waste), M2011-061.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Manufacturing, Service and Retailing Operations

quote_verbatim: More than 50 years ago, Charlie told me that it was far better to buy a wonderful business at a fair price than to buy a fair business at a wonderful price. Despite the compelling logic of his position, I have sometimes reverted to my old habit of bargain-hunting, with results ranging from tolerable to terrible. Fortunately, my mistakes have usually occurred when I made smaller purchases.
concept: Buffett's own error: reverting to bargain-hunting against Munger's rule that a wonderful business at a fair price beats a fair business at a wonderful price, with results from tolerable to terrible.
evolution_notes: Buffett's own mistake; Munger's maxim spoken by Buffett. Just before (lines 637-640): some businesses earn 25% to over 100% after tax on unleveraged net tangible assets, a few very poor returns from "serious mistakes I made in my job of capital allocation" (repeats L2010-009). Just after (line 651): "a business with terrific economics can be a bad investment if the price paid is excessive" (repeats L2011-003 in substance, not rowed). Related: M2003-040 (the maxim at a meeting), M1997-003.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Manufacturing, Service and Retailing Operations

quote_verbatim: Charlie and I believe in operating with many redundant layers of liquidity, and we avoid any sort of obligation that could drain our cash in a material way. That reduces our returns in 99 years out of 100. But we will survive in the 100th while many others fail. And we will sleep well in all 100.
concept: Hold redundant liquidity and avoid any obligation that could drain cash materially, accepting lower returns in ninety-nine years to survive the hundredth.
evolution_notes: Just before (lines 810-815): new derivative commitments would require posting collateral, which Berkshire with minor exceptions will not do, since markets can behave in extraordinary ways and an out-of-the-blue event might require posting mountains of cash on a moment's notice (repeats L2008-024 and L2010-021). Related: L2008-019 (keep more than ample cash), M2012-029 and M2012-032. New in a letter: the stated cost, lower returns in 99 years of 100.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Investments

quote_verbatim: News, to put it simply, is what people don't know that they want to know. And people will seek their news � what's important to them � from whatever sources provide the best combination of immediacy, ease of access, reliability, comprehensiveness and low cost.
concept: News is what people do not know and want to know, and they take it from whichever source best combines immediacy, ease of access, reliability, comprehensiveness and low cost.
evolution_notes: The letter's first statement of the definition given at the 2012 meeting (M2012-043); the letter adds the five factors by which a source is chosen. Just after (lines 860-888): the paper's old primacy, advertisers' need for a megaphone, a monopoly paper's certain profits whether managed well or poorly, and "survival of the fattest" (the last repeats L2006-007, not rowed).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: We Buy Some Newspapers . . . Newspapers?

quote_verbatim: Newspapers continue to reign supreme, however, in the delivery of local news. [...] Wherever there is a pervasive sense of community, a paper that serves the special informational needs of that community will remain indispensable to a significant portion of its residents.
concept: A newspaper keeps its place only where it is still primary: local news for a community with a pervasive sense of itself.
evolution_notes: Just before (lines 890-895): papers have lost their primacy in quotes, sports, jobs, homes and national news, and help-wanted revenue has fallen more than 90% in twelve years. Restates in a letter M2012-043 (a paper must be primary about something of interest to many in its area). Related: M1996-050, L1995-023.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: We Buy Some Newspapers . . . Newspapers?

quote_verbatim: Even a valuable product, however, can self-destruct from a faulty business strategy. And that process has been underway during the past decade at almost all papers of size. Publishers � including Berkshire in Buffalo � have offered their paper free on the Internet while charging meaningful sums for the physical specimen. How could this lead to anything other than a sharp and steady drop in sales of the printed product?
concept: A valuable product can destroy itself by strategy: giving the product away free in one form while charging for it in another drives down the paid form and reverses the virtuous circle.
evolution_notes: Buffett names Berkshire's own Buffalo paper among those that did it. Just after (lines 907-915): falling circulation makes a paper less essential to advertisers, the virtuous circle reverses, and the Wall Street Journal and Walter Hussman's Arkansas Democrat-Gazette went to pay models early. Restates in a letter M2012-044 (charging for one version while giving the same away free does not last).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: We Buy Some Newspapers . . . Newspapers?

quote_verbatim: We do not believe that success will come from cutting either the news content or frequency of publication. Indeed, skimpy news coverage will almost certainly lead to skimpy readership. And the less-than-daily publication that is now being tried in some large towns or cities � while it may improve profits in the short term � seems certain to diminish the papers' relevance over time.
concept: Do not cut a product's content or frequency to lift short-term profit when what keeps it alive is its relevance to its customers.
evolution_notes: Just before (lines 918-919): papers delivering comprehensive and reliable information to tightly-bound communities, with a sensible Internet strategy, will remain viable for a long time. Just after (lines 923-924): the goal is to keep the papers loaded with content and be paid appropriately by those who find them useful, in print or on the Internet.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: We Buy Some Newspapers . . . Newspapers?

quote_verbatim: Berkshire's cash earnings from its papers will almost certainly trend downward over time. Even a sensible Internet strategy will not be able to prevent modest erosion. At our cost, however, I believe these papers will meet or exceed our economic test for acquisitions. [...] At appropriate prices � and that means at a very low multiple of current earnings � we will purchase more papers of the type we like.
concept: A business whose earnings will trend down can still be bought, but only at a very low multiple of current earnings that meets the acquisition test at that cost.
evolution_notes: Pulls against M2012-062 (Buffett at the 2012 meeting: "it pays to stay away from declining businesses" and "If you really think a business is declining, most of the time you should avoid it", against offers at "only six times EBITDA"). The letter does not reconcile the two; "most of the time" in the earlier row leaves room. Carries a rule. The elision skips lines 948-953: economic principle 11, no business doomed to unending losses is kept, and one unprofitable daily bought in the Media General bulk purchase was shut down (repeats L2011-007 and R1996-014). Also at lines 848-852: the papers fall far short of the size requirements, and "if their economics make sense" newspapers are bought even so.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: We Buy Some Newspapers . . . Newspapers?

quote_verbatim: A profitable company can allocate its earnings in various ways (which are not mutually exclusive). A company's management should first examine reinvestment possibilities offered by its current business � projects to become more efficient, expand territorially, extend and improve product lines or to otherwise widen the economic moat separating the company from its competitors.
concept: The first use of a profitable company's earnings is reinvestment in its current business, efficiency, territory, product lines or anything that widens its moat.
evolution_notes: The first of four uses of funds in order. The letter continues (lines 1004-1008): Berkshire's first priority will always be to examine whether funds can be intelligently deployed in its businesses, where its range of choices lets it "water the flowers and skip over the weeds"; second (lines 1010-1013), acquisitions, tested by whether shareholders are left "wealthier on a per-share basis" (repeats L1994-013 and R1996-011, not rowed); third (lines 1028-1038), repurchases at a meaningful discount to conservatively calculated intrinsic value, "price is all-important" (repeat L1999-023 and L1999-026, not rowed); last, dividends. Related meeting rows: M1995-054, M1996-014, M2000-018 (managers asked to widen the moat yearly).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Dividends

quote_verbatim: But sometimes our managers misfire. The usual cause of failure is that they start with the answer they want and then work backwards to find a supporting rationale. Of course, the process is subconscious; that's what makes it so dangerous. Your chairman has not been free of this sin. [...] I wanted the business to succeed and wished my way into a series of bad decisions. (I even bought another New England textile company.) But wishing makes dreams come true only in Disney movies; it's poison in business.
concept: Reinvestment fails when managers start from the answer they want and work back to a rationale, unconsciously; Buffett's own textile years show wishing is poison in business.
evolution_notes: Buffett's own mistake, and carries a test of managers' reinvestment proposals. The elision skips lines 999-1001: the 1986 annual report described twenty years of effort and capital in the textile business as an exercise in futility. The textile error itself repeats L2010-004; new here is its cause, wishing, and the general form, the answer chosen first and the rationale worked backwards. Related: M1996-045 (capital rationalized as smart), M2005-007.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Dividends

quote_verbatim: There is an alternative approach, however, that would leave us even happier. Under this scenario, we would leave all earnings in the company and each sell 3.2% of our shares annually. [...] Voila! � you would have both more cash to spend annually and more capital value. This calculation, of course, assumes that our hypothetical company can earn an average of 12% annually on net worth and that its shareholders can sell their shares for an average of 125% of book value.
concept: When a company earns well on retained net worth and its shares sell above book, owners who sell a slice of shares each year get more cash and more capital than a dividend gives; the conclusion rests on both assumptions.
evolution_notes: The worked example runs from line 1045: a $2 million business earning 12% on net worth, shares at 125% of book; paying out a third grows everything at 8%, while the sell-off leaves the owner after ten years with shares about 4% more valuable and cash receipts 4% higher (lines 1066-1076). Just after (lines 1080-1086): the S&P 500 earns more than 12% on net worth and sells far above 125% of it, and if the assumptions are exceeded the case strengthens. Lines 1138-1141 make the policy conditional: "We will stick with this policy as long as we believe our assumptions about the book-value buildup and the market-price premium seem reasonable." Related: M2000-049, M1997-091 (retain a dollar only if it becomes more than a dollar).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Dividends

quote_verbatim: First, dividends impose a specific cash-out policy upon all shareholders. If, say, 40% of earnings is the policy, those who wish 30% or 50% will be thwarted. [...] The sell-off alternative, on the other hand, lets each shareholder make his own choice between cash receipts and capital build-up. [...] The second disadvantage of the dividend approach is of equal importance: The tax consequences for all taxpaying shareholders are inferior � usually far inferior � to those under the sell-off program. Under the dividend program, all of the cash received by shareholders each year is taxed whereas the sell-off program results in tax on only the gain portion of the cash receipts.
concept: Weigh a dividend against owners' own share sales on two further counts: a dividend imposes one cash-out rate on every owner, and it is taxed in full where a sale is taxed only on the gain.
evolution_notes: Continues the sell-off example at lines 1062-1079. The first elision skips lines 1090-1092 (most shareholders are in a net-savings mode and logically should prefer no payment); the second skips lines 1097-1101 (a shareholder reinvesting a dividend pays taxes and a 25% premium). Lines 1108-1121: Buffett's own case, giving away about 4 1/4% of his shares a year for seven years while the book value of his interest rose from $28.2 billion to $40.2 billion.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Dividends

quote_verbatim: Above all, dividend policy should always be clear, consistent and rational. A capricious policy will confuse owners and drive away would-be investors. [...] Phil explained that you can successfully run a restaurant that serves hamburgers or, alternatively, one that features Chinese food. But you can't switch capriciously between the two and retain the fans of either.
concept: Whatever the dividend policy, keep it clear, consistent and rational; switching capriciously loses both sets of owners.
evolution_notes: Phil Fisher's restaurant illustration, from Chapter 7 of Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits, spoken by Buffett; the elision skips the book's ranking behind The Intelligent Investor and the 1940 Security Analysis (lines 1125-1127). Just after (lines 1131-1136): most companies, the Big Four among them, pay consistent and rising dividends, which Buffett applauds, "We like increased dividends, and we love repurchases at appropriate prices." Related: M2000-051 (a fixed payout ratio has no logic), which pulls slightly against the praise of consistent dividends; listed under Tensions seen.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Dividends

quote_verbatim: I should point out, incidentally, that we use book value because it’s a calculable figure, and it does serve as a reasonable proxy of the yearto-year change in the intrinsic value of Berkshire. [...] But in the end, we have to do better for you than you would do in an index fund. And if we don’t, we aren’t earning our pay.
concept: Book value is used only because it is calculable and tracks the yearly change in intrinsic value; the real test is beating what owners would get from an index fund.
evolution_notes: "yearto-year" as printed. The elision skips lines 51 (part): a million new GEICO policyholders add about $1.5 billion to intrinsic value and nothing to book value, which is why stock is bought at 120% of book; buying the last ISCAR stake took about $1 billion off book value for a satisfactory purchase. Just before (line 49): the first five-year shortfall against the S&P is likely, in a market up every year; Berkshire does relatively better in down years. Restates L2009-003, R2006-001 and L2012 letter's lines 102-107 (not rowed). Munger (line 55): returns will slow because past returns were "almost unbelievable", a forecast.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 8. Berkshire lagging the S&P 500

quote_verbatim: Sandvik is a very good company, and ISCAR is a much better company. The advantage it has is brains and incredible passion for the business. [...] And there’s no other answer you can give to your question when you see that result than to say that you have had some incredibly talented people who never stopped working, never stopped trying to improve the product, never stopped trying to make customers happy, and that continues to this day.
concept: When a newcomer with no locational or raw-material advantage beats entrenched, well-financed rivals, the advantage can only be its people: talent and unceasing effort on product and customer.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the history (lines 73-75): Stef Wertheimer at 25 in Israel in about 1951, tungsten from China, customers thousands of miles away, against Sandvik and Kennametal. Munger (line 77): "it’s a particular achievement to really do a little better in the competitive market, as ISCAR has done"; (lines 85, 89) nothing but robots and engineers. Related: L2007-014 (brains, passion, integrity), M2003-063, M2011-063.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 10. ISCAR vs Sandvik

quote_verbatim: And that’s why the culture is all important, the businesses we own are all important, because those trains will keep running and people will keep calling GEICO the day after I die. [...] I think that anything that came in — any foreign-type behavior would be cast out because people have self-selected into this group, into the company, and it would be rejected like a foreign tissue if we got the wrong sort of person in there.
concept: What carries a company past its founder is its businesses and its culture; a culture that owners, directors and managers have self-selected into rejects foreign behavior like foreign tissue.
evolution_notes: The elision skips (line 103): the key is a successor with more brains, energy and passion, the board's first subject at every meeting, and the culture built over time as everyone who joined bought into it. Just after (line 105): directors are not held by large pay, and owners brought companies to Berkshire to be part of it, as ISCAR did. Munger (line 107) and Buffett (line 109): their families should not sell, a joke. Related: M2004-074 (policies select which shareholders a company attracts), M2000-111.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 11. Preserving Berkshire’s culture after Buffett

quote_verbatim: Now, we actually, Charlie and I, probably paid a little more than we would have paid if we had been doing the deal ourselves, because we think that Jorge Paulo and his associates are extraordinary managers. They’re both classy, and they’re unusually good, and so we stretched a little because of that fact.
concept: Pay somewhat more to be in a deal run by extraordinary managers than one would pay doing it alone.
evolution_notes: Just before (lines 117-119): the deal came from Jorge Paulo Lemann with a term sheet and governance terms Buffett did not change a word of, "an absolutely fair deal". Just after (lines 119-121): the partners took more leverage and will likely earn a higher return on their $4 billion; Berkshire has more money than operating ability at the parent level and took $8 billion of preferred plus common on fair terms; "If anybody thinks that the common is dead money ... they’re making a mistake" (an expectation).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 12. Partnering with 3G Capital for $23B Heinz deal

quote_verbatim: Well, generally speaking, I don’t think the reinsurance business is a very good business for most people. And I think it’s a very desirable part of Berkshire’s business, the way it’s run, but it’s different from something like the other businesses, which would work pretty well if somebody else owned them. I think our reinsurance business under Ajit is very peculiar, and other people who think it’s easy are going to find out that it isn’t.
concept: Munger: reinsurance is a poor business for most who enter it; it works at Berkshire only because of how it is run, unlike businesses that would do well under any owner.
evolution_notes: Answering Cliff Gallant on the Aon participation and the AIG hires for commercial insurance. Buffett before (lines 133-137): the goal is a greater share, entered because the profit possibilities are reasonable, with capital like nobody else; after (line 141): primary commercial risks offer "a lot of chances to make mistakes" and he would rather have this group oversee it than any other. Related: M1994-048, M2011-094 (reinsurance looks easy because rare losses are absent most years).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 13. Moving into commercial insurance

quote_verbatim: I would say that our ability to sell insurance at a price that’s considerably lower than most of our competitors, evidenced by the fact that when people call us, they shift to us, and, at the same time, earn a significant underwriting profit, indicates that our selection process is working quite well. I mean, if your selection process is wrong, if you treat a 16-year-old male and give him the same rate that you’d give a 40-year-old that’s driving their car 3 or 4,000 miles a year, you know, you’re going to get terrible underwriting results.
concept: An insurer's risk selection is proved by selling below most competitors while still earning an underwriting profit; wrong selection shows up as terrible underwriting results.
evolution_notes: Just before (lines 153-155): underwriting is an attempt to figure the propensity of an applicant to have an accident from a number of variables. Just after (line 157): GEICO's criteria were built over decades on a huge number of policyholders, making its underwriting cells credible; Progressive's Snapshot is watched with interest. Munger (line 159): nothing to add. Related: M2012-014 (adopt better predictors), and heading 31 of this session returns to Snapshot.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 14. GEICO vs Progressive’s Snapshot

quote_verbatim: But the key to disclosure is accuracy and simultaneity. I mean, if we own stocks, or are thinking about owning stocks, we want to be very sure that we get accurate information and we get it exactly at the same time as all other people.
concept: Good disclosure is accurate and reaches every holder at exactly the same time.
evolution_notes: Buffett calls the SEC's new allowance of social-media announcements "a mistake" (line 167), a view. Just after (line 169): Berkshire puts out information after the market closes because "it’s a terrible mistake to have people try and figure it all out in reading a one- or two-page announcement", and anything important comes out on Business Wire. Restates L1995-034 and L1997-040 (all owners hear the same thing at once). Munger (line 171) avoids Twitter, a joke.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 15. Business Wire and new rule allowing internet disclosures

quote_verbatim: So we have paid up — partly at Charlie’s urging — we’ve paid up for good businesses more than we would have 30 or 40 years ago. [...] But even with some diminution from returns of the past, they still can be satisfactory and we are willing — there’s companies we should of bought 30 or 40 years ago that looked higher priced then, but we now realize that paying up for an extraordinary business is not a mistake.
concept: Buffett's own error: passing on extraordinary businesses decades ago because they looked high-priced; the lesson is that paying up for an extraordinary business is not a mistake.
evolution_notes: Buffett's own mistake, the companies unnamed. "should of" as printed. Answering Doug Kass, the short seller, on paying higher multiples (IBM, BNSF, Heinz, Lubrizol). Just before (line 189): size means Berkshire cannot do as well as in the past, though in bad markets size can be an advantage, as in 2008; GEICO cost 20 times earnings. The elision skips "But it’s tougher as we get bigger, I we’ve always known that would be the case." Related: L2012-004 (reverting to bargain-hunting), M1997-003 (too price-conscious, missed great businesses), M2003-040.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 16. As Berkshire grows, it’s paying more for bigger acquisitions

quote_verbatim: If you look at the oil companies that got really big in the past history of the world, the record is not all that good. If you stop to think about it, Rockefeller’s Standard Oil is practically the only one, after it got monstrous, continued to do monstrously well. So, when we think we’re going to do pretty well in spite of getting very big, we’re telling you we think we’ll do a little better than the giants of the past.
concept: Munger: companies that become giants rarely keep compounding; expecting to do well while very big is a claim to beat nearly every giant of the past.
evolution_notes: Munger says he will make the short seller's argument better than he did. Just before (line 193): "we can’t do as well in percentage terms per annum in the future as we did in our early days." Just after: "We think we’ve got a better system." Related: M1998-071 (size is a handicap).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 16. As Berkshire grows, it’s paying more for bigger acquisitions

quote_verbatim: Well, I think, of course, it would be unwieldy to have so many businesses, a lot of them small, if we were trying to run them through an imperial headquarters that dominated all the details. But our system is totally different. If your system is decentralization, almost to the point of abdication, what difference does it make how many subsidiaries you have?
concept: Munger: the number of subsidiaries matters only to a headquarters that runs the details; under decentralization almost to abdication it does not.
evolution_notes: Buffett states the narrower form in his own answer (line 247): "we’ll certainly never leave the principle of our CEOs running their businesses in virtually all important ways except, perhaps — except for capital allocation"; named here, not rowed (2012 convention: the general statement is rowed). Munger again (lines 261, 265): if it were that difficult, what is being done now would be impossible, with a staff of ten in Omaha. Restates M1998-077 (decentralize almost to abdication).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 19. Too many subsidiaries for Buffett’s successor to manage?

quote_verbatim: Incidentally, the best acquisitions — to some extent, the best acquisitions — certainly from my standpoint makes it easier — is the one — is these bolt-ons that I talked about in the annual report, in which we did, I think, 2-and-a-half billion worth of last year, because they fall under the purview of managers that we’ve got terrific confidence in and they add really nothing to what happens at headquarters. And, of course, the best bolt-ons out of all are when we do buy a — buy out — a minority interest. [...] Those are the ultimate in bolt-on acquisitions, getting more of a good thing.
concept: The best acquisitions are bolt-ons under managers already trusted, adding nothing at headquarters, and best of all is buying out the minority in a business already owned.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the ISCAR ($2 billion) and Marmon purchases (line 259). Just before (line 257): the successor will not do things identically, "It’d be a mistake", but the culture and the preeminence of the operating managers will remain; acquisitions are sought at $75 million pretax or more. The FY2012 letter (lines 159-160) calls bolt-ons low-risk, no burden on headquarters, expanding the scope of proven managers (not rowed there).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 19. Too many subsidiaries for Buffett’s successor to manage?

quote_verbatim: You know it— interest rates are to asset prices, you know, sort of like gravity is to the apple. And when there are very low interest rates, there’s a very small gravitational pull on asset prices. [...] So, interest rates power everything in the economic universe, and they have some effect on the decisions we make.
concept: Interest rates act on asset prices as gravity on an apple: very low rates exert little pull, and rates drive every valuation decision.
evolution_notes: The elision skips borrowing at near zero against 1981-82's 15% government bonds. Just after (lines 309-311): the Heinz money was borrowed cheaper, which affects what people pay; low rates kept down make houses more attractive; unwinding the Fed's buying will be far more difficult than buying. Related: M1994-047 (every asset's value moves fully with interest rates), M2000-002, M2002-076.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 21. Effects of low interest rates

quote_verbatim: We do not — we never stretch for yield in terms of commercial paper that brings ten basis points more than Treasury. Our money— we don’t count on anybody else, so we keep it in Treasurys, basically, and so we’re earning nothing on that.
concept: Keep cash in Treasurys and never reach for a few basis points of yield, so the cash depends on no one else, even when it earns nothing.
evolution_notes: Just before (line 317): $48 or $49 billion in short-term securities at the end of the quarter earning basically nothing; at 5% short rates that would be a couple of billion a year pretax. Restates L2010-021 (Treasury bills, not other short-term paper) and L2012-005 (redundant liquidity). Munger (line 315): incremental float is worth less while huge cash is carried at low rates, a fact about Berkshire, not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 21. Effects of low interest rates

quote_verbatim: But the prices would be probably far higher than what we think we might be able to develop a comparable operation for. I mean, we — in effect — I think we’re going to build a very large commercial operation, and essentially we’ve built it at book value. And we pick up no bad habits of other companies, at least we hope we don’t. And so, it’s really better to build than buy, if you can find the right people with the right mindset, and everything, in the business.
concept: Where an operation can be built at book value with the right people, building beats buying at a higher price, and it imports no other company's bad habits.
evolution_notes: Just before (line 337): few big commercial insurers are worth acquiring, some not wanted at all. Just after (line 339): "if there were certain commercial operations, and we could’ve bought them at the right price, we’d have done it"; the people sought out Ajit. Related: M2013-005 and the commercial hires at heading 13 of this session.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 22. Building, not buying, commercial insurance growth

quote_verbatim: But, I think the key, obviously, is whether a direct marketing operation is really based on selling product to would-be distributors of one sort, and loading them up, instead of sell— in effect — selling it to end users. [...] I think that should be the distinguishing characteristic.
concept: Tell a sound direct-selling business from a scheme by whether its money comes from end users of the product or from loading recruits with product they never sell.
evolution_notes: Buffett says he has never read Herbalife's 10-K and does not judge it. The elision skips Pampered Chef's parties selling to people who use the product (lines 363-365). Just after (line 365): a regulator should look hard at operations where thousands invested savings in product they did not need on a dream not fulfilled. Munger follows with a check stated as a joke (line 367), rowed separately.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 24. Pampered Chef isn’t a pyramid scheme

quote_verbatim: Well, there’s likely to be more flimflam in selling magic potions than pots and pans. (Laughter)
concept: Munger: the nature of the product predicts the likelihood of flimflam; expect more of it in miracle cures than in ordinary goods.
evolution_notes: Stated as a joke. Follows Buffett's end-user test at lines 363-365 of the same heading; a separate lesson in one exchange, so one row per speaker (2006 convention). Buffett's reply (line 369), that at their age they are in the market for magic potions, is a joke.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 24. Pampered Chef isn’t a pyramid scheme

quote_verbatim: And at those times, very few people — few people have the capital, and a lot fewer people have the willingness, to commit. But I have no question that my successor will have unusual capital at times when — at turbulent times when — the ability to say “yes” very quickly with very large sums sets you apart from virtually anybody in the investing universe.
concept: In a panic few have capital and fewer the willingness to commit; having large sums and saying yes at once is what sets an investor apart.
evolution_notes: Answering Doug Kass on whether the successor's imprimatur will match Buffett's. Just after (lines 383-385): Berkshire is "the 800 number" in a panic, not its main business; when the tide goes out the naked swimmers will call; the reputation becomes the Berkshire brand, not one person's. Buffett again (line 393): others "don’t have the money and they don’t have the willingness to act immediately." Related: M2010-094 (be ready to say yes at once), M2008-073, L2012-005.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 25. “Lender of last resort” after Buffett?

quote_verbatim: Well, I would argue that in the early days, Warren had huge success as a value investor in little-owned companies because his competition was so small. If he stayed in that field, he would have to be in bigger companies, and his competition would be way more intense. He’s gotten into a field, being a good home for a big companies that don’t want to be controlled in meticulous detail by headquarters, where there isn’t much competition.
concept: Munger: success came from fields with little competition; as size closes one such field, move to another where competition is thin rather than stay where it has grown intense.
evolution_notes: "a good home for a big companies" as printed. Just after: "it’s ridiculous to think that the past is the thing he should have stayed in." Munger (line 391): "other people are not getting the calls"; Buffett (line 393): "the area we occupy becomes more and more our own as we get even bigger." Munger returns to the theme at heading 27 (line 425).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 25. “Lender of last resort” after Buffett?

quote_verbatim: Yeah. We didn’t buy anything from any unwilling sellers.
concept: Munger: buy only from willing sellers; do not persuade owners to sell.
evolution_notes: Exchange: Buffett states the facts around it (lines 407, 411-413): See's was put up for sale by the family after Larry See's death and "Charlie persuaded me to buy it. We didn’t persuade them to sell it"; the Berkshire blocks from Otis Stanton and the Chace relatives came from people happy to sell, with no sales talk; "we were not out convincing anybody to sell their stock." The one time he talked to a holder (Betty Peters, Wesco) it was to avoid a dumb merger. Buffett's line is the narrower factual statement, named here (2012 convention). Related: M2012-049 (no auctions).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 26. We only buy from willing sellers

quote_verbatim: We’ve always tried to stay sane, and other people, a lot of them, like to go crazy. That’s a competitive advantage. (Laughter and applause) Number two: as we’ve gotten bigger, we’ve used this sort of golden rule that we want to treat the subsidiaries the way we would want to be treated if we were in the subsidiaries. And that, again, is a very rare attitude in corporate America, and it causes people to come to us who don’t want to come to anybody else. That is a long-term competitive advantage. [...] And so, we are leaving behind a field that’s very competitive and getting into a place where we’re more unusual. This was a very good idea. I wish we had done it on purpose. (Laughter)
concept: Munger: lasting advantages can be behavioral: staying sane while others go crazy, treating subsidiaries as one would want to be treated, and moving to where one is unusual rather than in a crowded field.
evolution_notes: Munger's "two-minute monologue" for a 13-year-old, as Buffett hands him the question. The elision skips "We’ve tried to be a good partner to people who come to us and need a partner with more money. That is a competitive advantage." Continues his answer at line 387 of heading 25. "I wish we had done it on purpose" admits the move was not planned. Related: M2000-111, M2012-049.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 27. Berkshire’s edge for acquisitions

quote_verbatim: We’re not — we very seldom buy businesses from people who want to retire. [...] If he sold it to a competitor, they would come in and basically they would put their people in charge. They would have all these ideas about synergy, and synergy would mean that the people that had helped him build the business over 30 years would all get sacked [...] And he figured that if he sold it to them, they’d load it up with debt, which he didn’t like, and then they’d resell it later on. [...] Well, that company has turned out to be a wonderful acquisition for Berkshire, and our competitive advantage is we had no competitors.
concept: Seek sellers who want to keep running the business and secure its future, not to retire; to such an owner a competitor means synergy firings and private equity means debt and resale, so a permanent home has no competitors.
evolution_notes: The story of an unnamed owner in his sixties who loved his work and wanted to protect the business, family and employees after his death. The elisions skip his year of thought and the logical buyer being a competitor (line 429), and his words "You’re the only guy left standing" and the promise of a permanent home (line 431). Just after (line 433): shareholders looked on as partners, "not something a public relations firm wrote for us" (repeats the first owner-related principle). Related: M2012-024, L2008-007 (judge a buyer by what it does to the bought company's equity), M2005-002.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 27. Berkshire’s edge for acquisitions

quote_verbatim: We won’t see anything like that for a while, but we’ll see similar things at some point in the future. I mean, the world is given to excesses, and they have consequences, and we are always willing to act. I mean, we did not think Harley-Davidson was going to go broke. I mean, it was that simple.
concept: Excesses recur and have consequences; be always willing to act when they come, on a simple judgment such as that the borrower will not go broke.
evolution_notes: Just before (line 459): the 2009 private deals came when the corporate bond market was frozen, on the best terms those companies could get; "I wish the five-year deals had been ten-year deals"; "that’s a depleting asset." The tattoo line (line 461) is a joke. Related: the willingness to commit in a panic stated at heading 25 of this session (line 383), and M2010-094.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 29. Sorry to see Harley-Davidson notes expire

quote_verbatim: And when I managed money, you know, I wanted to be a free agent. If he wanted to give me — they could make the decision on whether they wanted to give me the money, but once they gave me the money, and I had the responsibility for managing it, I wanted free reign to do what I wanted. And I did not want to be held responsible for things with my hands tied. And that’s exactly the position we have with Todd and Ted now. It takes a lot of — it’s an unusual person that we will give that kind of responsibility to.
concept: Once money is entrusted to a manager, give full freedom with full responsibility, never responsibility with hands tied; so entrust it only to an unusual person.
evolution_notes: "free reign" as printed. Just before (line 469): Combs and Weschler do not check with Buffett before buying, have no limits on what they buy or how much they diversify beyond legal restrictions, and have bought things he would not. Just after: "we thought they deserved the trust when we hired them, and we believe that more than ever after watching them in action." Munger (line 473): nothing to add. Related: L2010-015 (pay an investment manager on performance).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 30. Todd Combs and Ted Weschler’s stock-picking independence

quote_verbatim: Well now, obviously, we’re not going to immediately copy the oddball thing that every single competitor does in the world, particularly when we’ve got an operation that’s working so well.
concept: Munger: do not copy every competitor's novelty when one's own operation is working well; let results decide.
evolution_notes: Buffett states the narrower form in his answer (line 483): "we continue, always, to look for further ways, obviously, to refine the selection technique. But we don’t do any of it lightly because what we’re doing now is working very well"; and (line 485) invites comparing Progressive's results with GEICO's over two or three years, promising to admit it if wrong. Named here, not rowed (2012 convention). Buffett after (line 489): a newcomer to direct auto insurance should copy GEICO, "It wouldn’t work, but it would offer you the best chance." Related: M2013-006, M2012-014 (adopt better predictors, drop weak ones), which pulls slightly against this; listed under Tensions seen.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 31. Why GEICO isn’t copying Progressive’s Snapshot

quote_verbatim: We didn’t know, when we started out, this modern psychological evidence to the effect that you shouldn’t make a lot of important decisions when you’re tired and that making a lot of difficult decisions is tiring. [...] And what happens, of course, is that both Warren and I live entirely on autopilot, in terms of the ordinary decisions in life, which is totally habitual, so we don’t work — waste — any decision making industry — I mean energy — on that stuff
concept: Munger: do not make important decisions tired; put ordinary life on habit so no decision energy is spent on it.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct. Partly stated as a joke: the elision skips the caffeine-and-sugar line ("how helpful it is to be consuming caffeine and sugar when you’re making important decisions. (Laughter)"). "decision making industry — I mean energy" as printed, Munger's own correction. Munger again (line 503): "I cannot remember an important decision that Warren has made when he was tired", his style "absolutely ideal for human cognition", stumbled into. Buffett (line 497): he has never made lists, a personal fact.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 32. We rely on sugar and caffeine, not to-do lists

quote_verbatim: We are buying the papers at very, very low prices compared to current earnings, and we must do that because the earnings will go down. Now, the interesting thing is, of course, is that we see books from investment bankers on all kinds of businesses, and always the projected earnings go up in the book. A lot of times they don’t — you know, in reality — they don’t go up. The difference is that we expect them to go down in the newspapers, and whatever the investment salesmen expect, they certainly don’t project that any business they sell will have declining earnings.
concept: A business whose earnings will decline must be bought at a very low price to current earnings; sellers' books always project rising earnings, so the honest projection of decline is the buyer's own.
evolution_notes: Restates L2012-010 (declining papers bought only at a very low multiple of current earnings). Just before (lines 513-515): at least 10 percent after tax with declining earnings, helped by writing off intangibles bought from S corporations, about $100 million pretax that does not move the needle, and "we wouldn’t have done it in any other business. I mean, there’s no question — the questioner is right about that", which treats newspapers as an exception and so reconciles in this answer the pull of L2012-010 against M2012-062. Munger (line 519): "it’s an exception and you like doing it" (a joke). Related: M2006-056 (sale books' projections are silly), M1995-050.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 33. Buffett defends buying newspaper companies

quote_verbatim: WARREN BUFFETT: And he was incredible in that, and he made a fortune for shareholders that stayed with him. But he was — to some extent, he looked at the shareholder group as somebody to be taken advantage of, and he issued stock like crazy. [...] WARREN BUFFETT: He wanted to use a very fancy price stock. He was playing the game of the ’60s, and we actually have never wanted to get in that game. I mean, he promoted the stock. [...] and it was a game that worked wonderfully if you didn’t care about how it ended up. And so we have not played that game.
concept: Issuing overpriced stock and later buying it back cheap made money for those who stayed, but it treats the shareholder group as someone to take advantage of; refuse that game.
evolution_notes: Pulls against M2011-034, where Buffett at the 2011 meeting drew from Teledyne the lesson to issue stock when overpriced and buy it back when underpriced; here he calls the same cycle taking advantage of shareholders and a game Berkshire never wanted to play. Carries a test (does a manager treat the shareholder group as partners or as a mark). Exchange with Munger, a third party's conduct (Henry Singleton's). The first elision crosses Munger's "Yes." (line 551) and Buffett resumes the same thought; the second skips the Litton Industries background (line 553). Just after (lines 553-555): the third stage, selling Teledyne to Berkshire for its stock, completed by Munger as "sell it to us for more than it was worth." Munger before (line 537): Singleton bought in stock "relentlessly and very logically" on the way down and managed far more centrally than Berkshire; Berkshire refused to issue its stock for his businesses. Munger (line 559): "that cool rationality was to be admired. I like our system better." Buffett (line 535): breaking up Berkshire "would produce a poorer result", a view.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 34. Follow Teledyne CEO Henry Singleton’s lead

quote_verbatim: Yeah, it’s a — we really don’t want to try and control it out of headquarters. We like that kind of decision being made near the firing line.
concept: Munger: keep operating decisions, even large cost questions like health care, near the firing line rather than at headquarters.
evolution_notes: Buffett before (lines 587-589): health costs are huge; the companies will try to learn what is in store, "we do very few things with ... on a centralized basis", and "it’s not something we try to control out of headquarters" (the same rule, named here). Restates M2013-010 and M1998-077.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 36. Obamacare’s effect on Berkshire?

quote_verbatim: CHARLIE MUNGER: Well, the competition was very weak in your early days, and I don’t think the competition is as weak now. So I think, sure, we got advantages from timing. And I don’t think that means there’s nothing to be done ahead. [...] CHARLIE MUNGER: But I sat for a lot of years before I did it. WARREN BUFFETT: But it still became available.
concept: Munger: early success owed much to weak competition, yet opportunity still comes even among thousands of able professionals; the price is sitting for years until it does.
evolution_notes: Exchange. The elision crosses Buffett's lines 623-631: in 2008 and 2009, with thousands of high-IQ, experienced professionals, Munger bought equities for the Daily Journal now worth three or four times cost; Munger resumes the same thought at line 633. Buffett's closing line kept inside the quote. Buffett before (lines 615-619): luck of being born in the U.S., male, and in 1930; a passionate investor born today is likely to do very well, a forecast. Munger after (line 637): "you were drowning in opportunities when I first knew you", Buffett (line 643): "now we’ve got money and no ideas", a joke. Related: M2013-018 (move where competition is thin), M2008-029.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 38. Luck, timing, and success

quote_verbatim: CHARLIE MUNGER: Yeah, we’re basically so old-fashioned that we’re boringly trite. We think you ought to keep plugging along and stay rational and stay energetic and just all the old virtues still work, and— WARREN BUFFETT: But find what turns you on. CHARLIE MUNGER: You’ve got to work where you’re turned on. I don’t know about Warren, but I have never succeeded to any great extent in something I didn’t like doing.
concept: Munger: keep plugging, stay rational and energetic, and work where you are turned on; he never succeeded much at what he did not like.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct. Exchange with one lesson; Buffett's one-line "But find what turns you on" is kept inside the quote and is the same lesson. Buffett after (line 667): they were lucky to find what they liked very early and pushed hard while enjoying it; "We have had so much fun running Berkshire, I mean, it’s almost sinful." Related: M2008-020, M2008-022 (passion pays best when joined to aptitude), M2010-099.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 39. You have to like what you’re doing

quote_verbatim: So, you know, insurance should be conducted as a rational activity. And one of the problems that some insurers have had is that they would have a pressure for increasing premium volume every year, brought upon by Wall Street, you know— very few— We actually contracted the business written by National Indemnity, formerly our main business, its traditional business, I think we contracted it, probably, by 80 percent or something of the sort when the business became less attractive. I’m not sure any manager of a public company that was answering to quarterly earnings calls and that sort of thing, I’m not sure whether they could’ve really stood up to the kind of pressure that they would receive if they followed a similar policy.
concept: Ask whether an insurer's managers are free of pressure for yearly premium growth; one answering to quarterly earnings calls can hardly shrink volume by 80 percent when business turns unattractive.
evolution_notes: Just before (line 685): Berkshire is "an unusually rational place", helped by a very long run and controlling shareholders, so no outside influences pushed it where it did not want to go. Just after (line 687): "if we do something stupid, it’s because we did something stupid ... no external factors are pressing on us"; a holder of half of one percent finds it very hard to resist doing what Wall Street applauds. Related: L2010-008 (the fourth discipline, walking away), L2004-005, M2004-078.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 40. Rational insurance pricing

quote_verbatim: We were major writers of catastrophe — natural catastrophe — insurance in the United States some years ago when the prices were right. We don’t think the prices are right now, so we don’t write it. We haven’t left the market, the market left us, and — but we are not about to do something where we get paid 90 cents for running the — running a probabilistic loss of a dollar. It just doesn’t make any sense and we won’t do it. And we don’t put any pressure on anybody to do it, and their incomes are not dependent on doing it.
concept: Write a line only while its price exceeds the probable loss; when the market price falls below it, stop writing, and pay no one in a way that depends on writing it.
evolution_notes: Continues the answer whose test is rowed from line 685. Restates M2011-093 (write only at prices commensurate with the risk) and L1995-019; new here is the pay link: "their incomes are not dependent on doing it." Buffett ends (line 689): "So it’s not hard to be rational at Berkshire."
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 40. Rational insurance pricing

quote_verbatim: Yeah. There are pressures on other people that we don’t want and therefore don’t have. It is very hard to shrink an insurance operation by 80 percent when the people who come in every day don’t have enough to do, and it’s just — it’s a counter-intuitive thing to do. But it’s absolutely required that you do it in a place where people go as crazy as they do in insurance.
concept: Munger: in a business where competitors periodically go crazy, shrinking hard when prices fail is counter-intuitive and painful for idle staff but absolutely required.
evolution_notes: Follows Buffett's lines 685-689 of the same heading, a separate statement of the lesson as a requirement. Related: M2004-078 (accept a high expense ratio in slow years), L2004-005.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 40. Rational insurance pricing

quote_verbatim: Well, it’s like buying Internet stocks, you know, in the late 1990s. I mean, the — all around you, you have these people that have high IQs and they’re doing it and they’re being successful in it. [...] And, of course, it creates this social proof where it works for a while. That’s the great danger period in all of these bubbles, is that what starts out with skepticism ends up with your neighbor getting richer than you are because he went along and you didn’t. And that sort of thing — the bandwagon effect and everything — those things are very hard to resist. [...] We just think we don’t understand what it’s all about. And if they can make a lot of money, you know, day trading or whatever it may be, you know, good luck to them. But we’re not envious of them, but we certainly are not going to do it just because they’re doing it.
concept: The great danger in a bubble is social proof: skepticism gives way as neighbors get richer by going along; refuse to act merely because others are succeeding at what one does not understand.
evolution_notes: The first elision skips spouse, employer and press asking "how come you think you’re so smart" (line 693); the second skips "But we don’t have any pressures to do that sort of thing. I mean, we just don’t give a damn, you know, and if — We don’t necessarily think we’re smarter than the other person on that." (lines 693-695). Related: L2011-017 (rising prices breed their own buyers), M2006-018, L2000-031. Munger follows on envy (line 697), rowed separately.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 40. Rational insurance pricing

quote_verbatim: Oh, I always say there’s a reason why all that stuff is in the Bible. You can’t covet your neighbor’s ass or — (Laughter) I mean, they were having trouble with envy a long time ago. And it’s a perfectly terrible thing to do, and how much fun can you have being envious? We always say it’s the one sin there’s no fun in.
concept: Munger: envy is a perfectly terrible thing and the one sin with no fun in it; do not let it drive conduct.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct, partly stated as a joke. Follows Buffett's "we’re not envious of them" (line 695). Restates M2008-112 (rule out envy). Buffett (line 699): gluttony and lust, a joke.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 40. Rational insurance pricing

quote_verbatim: And people talk about it, you know, being an uncorrelated type of operation and all of that. Anything Wall Street can sell, it will sell. I mean, you can count on that.
concept: Expect Wall Street to sell anything that can be sold; a product's salability, such as reinsurance as an uncorrelated asset, says nothing about its merit.
evolution_notes: Just before (line 707): "We hate dumb competition"; hedge funds entered reinsurance in part as "a beard" to operate in low-tax Bermuda and defer U.S. taxes. Munger (line 709): "They like big words, too." Restates L2000-031 (Wall Street will sell whatever investors will buy) and M2004-111.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 41. “Dumb” competition from hedge funds in reinsurance

quote_verbatim: And in the end, you know, we know what we’re willing to do, we know what we think the prices should be, and we will do insurance business where we think that the odds favor us earning an underwriting profit. And if we can’t do it, we’ll watch for a while. You can’t afford, you know, to go along with the crowd in investment, insurance, or a whole lot of other things. [...] But insurance, it’s — nice thing about it is— the standby costs are not huge, so it’s not like idling steel plants or something. So we were perfectly willing in the 1980s to have our expense ratio go up significantly because our volume went down so dramatically.
concept: Against dumb competition, write only where the odds favor a profit and otherwise watch; this is affordable where standby costs are small, as in insurance, unlike idle steel plants or a gas station facing below-cost pricing.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the gas station across the street selling below cost, "you’ve got a terrible problem. That’s why I got out of the gas station business a long time ago" (line 711), the contrast case of a business with no way to wait. Just after (line 713): the higher expense ratio was a real standby cost but not back-breaking, "and we just waited for better days, and they came along." Munger (lines 715, 719): the "cranky, wait-it-out methods" produced "the best large-scale causality insurance operation in the world" ("causality" as printed), "So why would we change?" Buffett (lines 721, 725): it was not anticipated, it evolved, and managers like an environment without pressures to do dumb things. Related: M1998-035 (hold price when competitors misprice risk), M2004-078, M2013-024.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 41. “Dumb” competition from hedge funds in reinsurance

quote_verbatim: I mean, we will have bubbles in capitalism. Capitalism goes to excess, and it’s because of the humans that operate it. And we will have that again, but usually you don’t get it the same way as you got it before. I don’t think it will be a housing boom next time.
concept: Excess recurs because people run capitalism, but the next bubble usually takes a different form from the last; do not watch only for a repeat.
evolution_notes: Just before (lines 753-755): the banking system is stronger than in 25 years, "the higher the capital ratio, the lower the return on equity will be", and "I do not worry about the banking system being the cause of the next bubble." Just after: Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank and M&T should be decent investments with lower returns on tangible equity under thicker equity rules. Related: M2013-022 (excesses recur, always willing to act), M2005-022, M1997-063.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 43. Berkshire is not “too big to fail”

quote_verbatim: The more bankers want to be like investment bankers instead of bankers, the worse I like it. (Applause) I don’t want to say more.
concept: Munger: judge a bank worse the more its bankers want to act like investment bankers.
evolution_notes: The rule is rowed and the politics left out (section 5): just before (line 759) Munger would limit bank activities further and does not see "why massive derivative books should be mixed up with insured — deposits that are insured — by the country", a policy view Buffett joins (line 761). Munger is less optimistic than Buffett about the banking system long-term (line 759). Related: M2002-114 (the old bankers screened issuers), M2004-109.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 43. Berkshire is not “too big to fail”

quote_verbatim: The investment world has been very good at extracting a very significant percentage of the returns that investors get for themselves. So I offered to bet anyone that wanted to step up to the plate that a group of hedge funds would not beat an unmanaged no-load index over a ten-year period. [...] But there’s two levels of fees involved. There’s the standard fees of the hedge funds, which probably many times are “2 and 20,“ but can be other things, and then there’s the fee of the fund of funds on top of it.
concept: Fees take a large share of what investors earn; layered fees, as in funds of hedge funds, make it unlikely the managers beat an unmanaged low-cost index over ten years.
evolution_notes: The quotation mark printed after "2 and 20," is a left quote, kept as printed. The elision skips the bet's terms, Ted Seides as taker, the zero-coupon Treasurys sold and Berkshire bought with the proceeds, and the hedge funds' fast start, 13 points ahead after year one, behind over the last four (lines 773-775). Just after (lines 777-779): longbets.org and its other wagers, jokes. Related: L1996-034 (minimal-fee index fund), M2006-096 (fee terms as a house edge), M2008-056, L2007-017.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 44. Buffett updates his bet against hedge funds

quote_verbatim: I think, actually, you have to love something to do well at it. There may be exceptions on that, but it is an enormous, enormous advantage if you absolutely love what you’re doing, every minute of it. And the nature of it is that that intensity adds to your productivity.
concept: Doing well at something requires loving it; love of the work brings intensity, and intensity raises productivity.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct. Answer to Doug Kass's question whether Buffett's intensity has faded. Same answer: the scorecard is part of the game, the proceeds unimportant, and he would not feel the same about Berkshire if he did not own a share or get paid (lines 793-795). Related: M2011-056 (love of the work as an important part of doing well at any activity, said of a manager), M2013-030 (Munger, work where you are turned on), M2008-020 (find your passion).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 2. Buffett: I haven’t lost any intensity

quote_verbatim: what I learned sitting with Lorimer Davidson on a Saturday at GEICO in January of 1951 is still — is useful to me, and I don’t have to learn it a second time. I can build on it. But that’s one of the great things about investing. I mean, the universe, there’s enough in it so that you can finds lots of opportunities, but there — it’s not like it’s changing dramatically all the time. There’s some things that may change, and we just don’t play in that part of the game if we don’t understand them.
concept: Knowledge of businesses accumulates because most of the investing universe does not change fast; the parts that do change, and are not understood, are left alone.
evolution_notes: Exchange: Munger says the first American Express purchase needed deep digging and the second was easy, "the first one was hard, and the second was easy" (line 801); Buffett: "It’s all cumulative." (line 803); Munger: "Yeah, it’s cumulative, eventually." (line 805). Buffett's lines here follow and state the general lesson. "you can finds lots of opportunities" is printed so; kept. Related: M2012-103 (the philosophy was fixed at 19; what improves is judgment).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 2. Buffett: I haven’t lost any intensity

quote_verbatim: he was telling me that there was no way in the world that he could get rid of American Express, or even get them to cut their fees. That was my kind of business.
concept: A business whose large customers cannot drop it and cannot even negotiate its fees down has the kind of position worth buying.
evolution_notes: Buffett on Frank Olson of Hertz, met on the golf course, before the second American Express purchase; Munger told the same story first (lines 797-801). Same answer: companies repurchasing their own shares raise Berkshire's interest each year, "a double play" (line 809), a fact about the holdings. Related: M2008-076 (whether a buyer would switch to a substitute for a penny less).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 2. Buffett: I haven’t lost any intensity

quote_verbatim: we aren’t looking at the aspects of the stock, we’re looking at the aspects of a business. It’s very important to have that mindset, that we are buying businesses, whether we’re buying 100 shares of something or whether we’re buying the entire company. We always think of them as businesses. [...] And different numbers are of different importance — or various numbers are of different importance — depending on the kind of business.
concept: Whether buying a hundred shares or the whole company, the object is a business, not a stock; and which figures matter depends on the kind of business.

heading: ### 3. We don’t buy anything just “by the numbers”

quote_verbatim: And it’s not because I calculate some price — precise — P/E ratio or price-book value ratio or whatever it might be. It is because I have some idea of what the company might look like in five or ten years, and I have a reasonable amount of confidence in that judgment, and there’s a disparity in price and value, and it’s big. [...] We are looking at businesses exactly like we’d look at them if somebody came in and offered us the entire business, and then we try to think, what is this place going to look like in five or ten years, and how sure are we of it.

[...] I have not found any aspect of that bedrock philosophy that has flaws in it. You have to learn how to apply it in different ways.

heading: ### 6. Influential books and early investments

quote_verbatim: And in some businesses, you can have only two competitors and they’re still terrible businesses, they beat each other’s brains out. [...] So it’s very industry specific. The airline industry, you know, has this situation where they have very, very, very low incremental costs per seat, you know, with enormous fixed costs, and the temptation to sell that last seat at a very low price is very high and it’s very — and sometimes it can be very difficult to distinguish between the last seat and other seats. So it’s a labor-intensive, capital-intensive, largely commodity-type business

heading: ### 7. Buffett remains bearish on airlines

[...] It goes into my too hard pile. (Scattered laughter)

heading: ### 12. Reluctantly paying more for a great business

In negotiated purchase of a business, you’re almost always dealing with someone that has the option of either selling or not selling, and can sort of pick the time when they decide to sell, and all of that sort of thing. In stock markets, it’s an auction market. Crazy things can happen.
concept: Expect bargains in the auction market of stocks, where crazy things happen, not in negotiated purchases, where the seller chooses whether and when to sell.
evolution_notes: After: a technological blip can trip a flash crash while "the world really hasn’t changed at all" (line 1071). The rule on holding great businesses forever follows in the same paragraph and is a separate row. heading: ### 18. How should a young money manager attract investors?

quote_verbatim: And it had that aspect to it, which bubbles do, where year after year for three or four or five years, whatever it might be, that the skeptics looked like idiots and that the people who jumped on the bandwagon were the ones that were refinancing their houses at ever higher prices and people who were speculating on other houses. So it just looked all so wonderful. And people are really susceptible to that sort of bandwagon effect where they see their neighbors making easy money, everybody’s making easy money but them, and they finally succumb. [...] And, you know, it’s happened many times in history, it’ll happen again, and you can use that very much to your profit.
concept: A bubble is marked by years in which skeptics look like idiots and neighbors make easy money until people succumb; it recurs, and can be used for profit.
