heading: Some Thoughts About Investing

quote_verbatim: If you instead focus on the prospective price change of a contemplated purchase, you are speculating. There is nothing improper about that. I know, however, that I am unable to speculate successfully, and I am skeptical of those who claim sustained success at doing so. [...] And the fact that a given asset has appreciated in the recent past is never a reason to buy it.
concept: Buying on an expected change in price rather than on what the asset produces is speculation; a recent rise in price is never a reason to buy.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the coin-flippers line (lines 972-973). The passage also carries a rule (a recent rise never a reason to buy). Earlier: L2000-027 (speculation as focus on what the next fellow will pay rather than on what the asset produces; Berkshire does not play). New here: the recent-appreciation rule and Buffett's skepticism of claimed sustained success at speculating.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Some Thoughts About Investing

quote_verbatim: With my two small investments, I thought only of what the properties would produce and cared not at all about their daily valuations. Games are won by players who focus on the playing field � not by those whose eyes are glued to the scoreboard.
concept: Watch what the holding produces, not its daily price.
evolution_notes: Just after (lines 978-979): "If you can enjoy Saturdays and Sundays without looking at stock prices, give it a try on weekdays." Related: R1996-002 (success measured by the long-term progress of the companies, not month-to-month movements of their stocks).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Some Thoughts About Investing

quote_verbatim: Forming macro opinions or listening to the macro or market predictions of others is a waste of time. Indeed, it is dangerous because it may blur your vision of the facts that are truly important.
concept: Do not form or listen to macro or market forecasts; beyond wasting time they cloud the facts that matter.
evolution_notes: Just after (lines 988-991): what the economy, interest rates or the market might do in 1987 and 1994 was of no importance to the farm and NYU purchases, "corn would keep growing in Nebraska and students would flock to NYU." Related: L2008-001 (no one can predict the winning and losing years), L2012-001 (dancing in and out on experts' predictions a terrible mistake), M2012-028 (macro never discussed in a purchase). New in a letter: macro opinion as a danger that blurs the important facts, not only as useless.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Some Thoughts About Investing

quote_verbatim: Owners of stocks, however, too often let the capricious and often irrational behavior of their fellow owners cause them to behave irrationally as well. [...] Those people who can sit quietly for decades when they own a farm or apartment house too often become frenetic when they are exposed to a stream of stock quotations and accompanying commentators delivering an implied message of "Don't just sit there, do something." For these investors, liquidity is transformed from the unqualified benefit it should be to a curse.
concept: Stock owners err by letting other owners' irrational prices and the commentary around them move them to act, turning liquidity from a pure benefit into a harm.
evolution_notes: The mistake is other investors', with Buffett drawing the lesson. The elision skips the chatter about markets and pundits (lines 1005-1007). Just before (lines 997-1002): the moody neighbour who yells a daily price for the farm, from whose erratic behaviour Buffett can only benefit (repeats L1993-018 in substance, not rowed). Just after (lines 1014-1017): tumbling markets help the true investor with cash, "A climate of fear is your friend when investing; a euphoric world is your enemy" (repeats L2009-017 and L2008-004, not rowed).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Some Thoughts About Investing

quote_verbatim: And, if I had owned 100% of a solid business with good long-term prospects, it would have been foolish for me to even consider dumping it. So why would I have sold my stocks that were small participations in wonderful businesses? True, any one of them might eventually disappoint, but as a group they were certain to do well.
concept: In a panic, ask whether one would sell the whole of a solid business with good prospects; if not, there is no reason to sell small participations in wonderful businesses.
evolution_notes: Just before (lines 1019-1020): in the 2008 panic he never thought of selling the farm or the New York property though a severe recession was brewing. Just after (lines 1023-1024): the earth would not swallow America's productive assets and human ingenuity. Related: L2012-001 (the risk of being out exceeds the risk of being in).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Some Thoughts About Investing

quote_verbatim: When Charlie and I buy stocks � which we think of as small portions of businesses � our analysis is very similar to that which we use in buying entire businesses. We first have to decide whether we can sensibly estimate an earnings range for five years out, or more. If the answer is yes, we will buy the stock (or business) if it sells at a reasonable price in relation to the bottom boundary of our estimate. If, however, we lack the ability to estimate future earnings � which is usually the case � we simply move on to other prospects.
concept: A stock or a whole business is bought only if an earnings range five or more years out can sensibly be estimated, and then only at a reasonable price against the low end of that range; usually it cannot, and they move on.
evolution_notes: Just after (lines 1032-1034): in 54 years they have never foregone an attractive purchase because of the macro or political environment or others' views (repeats M2012-028, not rowed); (lines 1036-1039) recognise the perimeter of the circle of competence and stay well inside it (repeats L1999-020, not rowed), so mistakes will not be the disasters of buying on anticipated price behaviour in a long-rising market. Related: M1998-163 (no purchase without knowing who wins five years out). New in a letter: the price set against the bottom boundary of the estimated range.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Some Thoughts About Investing

quote_verbatim: The main danger is that the timid or beginning investor will enter the market at a time of extreme exuberance and then become disillusioned when paper losses occur. [...] The antidote to that kind of mistiming is for an investor to accumulate shares over a long period and never to sell when the news is bad and stocks are well off their highs. Following those rules, the "know-nothing" investor who both diversifies and keeps his costs minimal is virtually certain to get satisfactory results. Indeed, the unsophisticated investor who is realistic about his shortcomings is likely to obtain better long-term results than the knowledgeable professional who is blind to even a single weakness.
concept: For the non-professional the timing rule is to buy over a long period and never sell on bad news after a fall; with diversification and minimal cost that is nearly sure to work, and realism about one's weaknesses beats knowledge blind to one.
evolution_notes: The elision skips Barton Biggs's line (lines 1056-1057), a joke quoted by Buffett. Just before (lines 1043-1052): non-professionals should not try to pick winners but own a cross-section through a low-cost S&P 500 index fund (repeats L1993-025 and L2007-018, not rowed). Just after (lines 1063-1071): frenetic trading of farmland would only cut the owners' earnings by the costs; ignore the chatter, keep costs minimal, invest in stocks as in a farm (repeats L2005-016, L2005-018, L2004-001, not rowed). L1993-025 already says to space out purchases; new here: never selling on bad news, and realism about one's weaknesses as the edge.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Some Thoughts About Investing

quote_verbatim: My advice to the trustee could not be more simple: Put 10% of the cash in short-term government bonds and 90% in a very low-cost S&P 500 index fund. (I suggest Vanguard's.) I believe the trust's long-term results from this policy will be superior to those attained by most investors � whether pension funds, institutions or individuals � who employ high-fee managers.
concept: Buffett's instruction for his wife's trust: ten percent short-term government bonds, ninety percent a very low-cost S&P 500 index fund, expected to beat most investors who pay high fees.
evolution_notes: Just before (lines 1073-1076): "My money, I should add, is where my mouth is"; the bequest must be in cash because all his Berkshire shares go to philanthropies. Related: L1993-025, L2007-018 (index investing for those who cannot judge businesses). New: the advice embodied in his own will, with the split stated.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Some Thoughts About Investing

quote_verbatim: And if we even break even, that $77 billion, which is subtracted from net worth, I mean, it’s a liability on the balance sheet, but if it’s cost free, it really does us about as much good as net worth itself does.
concept: Float carried as a liability is, if it costs nothing, worth about as much to the owner as equity itself; its cost is set by whether underwriting makes a profit.
evolution_notes: Just before (line 21): quarter-to-quarter underwriting means little and is affected by foreign exchange; the float of $77 billion is Berkshire's to invest and whether it costs anything is determined by underwriting profit. Related: L1993-009 (cost of float is the underwriting loss or profit). The FY2013 letter's revolving-fund passage (letter lines 368-374) is in this unit's note as a repeat.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 4. Berkshire’s Q1 earnings summary

quote_verbatim: We always advise you to pay little — pay no attention, really — to quarterly or even annual realized gains or losses in securities because we make no attempt to time the sales of securities to produce earnings in any given quarter. We just try to manage the money as well as we can. And we let the chips fall where they may, in terms of whether those actions produce gains or losses in the short term.
concept: Sales of securities are never timed to produce reported earnings, so realized gains or losses in a quarter or year say nothing about performance and are ignored in reading short-term results.
evolution_notes: Earlier: L2010-018 (never sell a security for the effect on reported income). Just before (line 19): earnings released after Friday's close so owners have the weekend to read the 10-Q, not just the summary figures.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 4. Berkshire’s Q1 earnings summary

quote_verbatim: We made a very clear statement about the excessiveness of the plan. And at the same time, we, in no way, went to war with Coca-Cola. [...] I don’t think going to war is a very good idea in most situations. And I think if you’re going to join forces in going to war with somebody, you’d better be very sure about what that alliance might mean.
concept: An owner who objects to a management's plan states the objection plainly but avoids open war, and joins no campaign whose allies and arguments it has not checked.
evolution_notes: The occasion: Berkshire abstained on Coca-Cola's option plan, told Muhtar Kent beforehand that it thought the plan excessive and announced the reason right after the vote (line 45); the shareholder campaigning against it used dilution figures "wildly off" and Berkshire did not want to endorse them (lines 45-47). Munger: "I think you handled the whole situation very well" (line 49). Buffett adds he talked it over only with Munger beforehand (line 51). Related: the dilution arithmetic rowed from lines 51-55.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 7. Buffett defends abstaining on “excessive” Coca-Cola compensation

quote_verbatim: But for those of you who would really — would like to know how to think about calculating dilution, Coca-Cola has regularly repurchased the shares that are issued through options. [...] So the dilution — assuming all the proceeds from the option exercise and the tax refund were used to buy shares — the dilution would be 108 million shares on 4.4 billion, or about 2 1/2 percent. And I don’t like dilution and I don’t like 2 1/2 percent dilution. But it’s a far cry from the numbers that were getting tossed around.
concept: Measure option dilution net: the transfer of value at exercise, less the exercise proceeds and the tax deduction, as if both were used to buy back stock at the exercise-date price.
evolution_notes: The elided arithmetic (lines 51-53): 500 million option shares over about four years, issued at $40 and exercised at $60, a $10 billion transfer of value; $20 billion of exercise proceeds plus $3 1/2 billion of tax savings buys 391,666,666 shares at $60, leaving the company out about 108 million shares. He adds (line 55) that changing the assumed price to 55 or 65 does not change things much, and that he has never seen the math written about. Related: M2002-087 (Munger: an option is both an expense and a dilution).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 7. Buffett defends abstaining on “excessive” Coca-Cola compensation

quote_verbatim: But the — but we have not enforced, or attempted to enforce, nor would wish to enforce, a strong discipline on every subsidiary as to whether they have a few too many people or not. [...] We encourage — I mean, we encourage, just by example. But we do not encourage it by edicts, particularly.
concept: The parent does not impose cost discipline on its subsidiaries by edict; it encourages leanness by its own example.
evolution_notes: An exchange with Munger, who states the companion lesson in his own words (row from line 71). Just before (line 63): 3G runs businesses magnificently with a different, hands-on style, and "I don’t think it would pay to try and blend the two"; (line 65) managers joining Berkshire find no other home like it, "a huge corporate asset"; (line 69) no overstaffing at the home office, most subsidiaries lean but not all.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 8. Berkshire likely to team with 3G again despite different styles

quote_verbatim: I think a lot of great businesses spill a little just because they don’t want to be fanatic. And that’s all right. I don’t think you have to have the last nickel out of the staffing cost.
concept: Munger: a great business can tolerate a little slack rather than become fanatical about cost; the last nickel of staffing cost need not be squeezed out.
evolution_notes: An exchange with Buffett, whose lesson (no edicts, example only, line 69) is rowed separately. Munger had opened (line 67): "I don’t think we’ve ever had a policy that loved overstaffing."
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 8. Berkshire likely to team with 3G again despite different styles

quote_verbatim: And American business earnings on net tangible assets, which is the way to measure profitability overall, you know, it’s basically the envy of the world.
concept: Profitability is measured by earnings on net tangible assets.
evolution_notes: A general measure stated inside a political answer (on the President, Obamacare and corporate tax rates as a share of GDP, lines 83-85); the politics is left out of the quote. Munger declined to comment (line 87). Related: the FY2013 letter measures its manufacturing group the same way (letter lines 722-735, on unleveraged net tangible assets).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 9. Corporate taxes aren’t holding back businesses

quote_verbatim: We only believe in repurchasing shares when we can do so at a significant discount from intrinsic value. Some companies talk about — Coca-Cola does — they talk about buying in shares to cover options. That actually isn’t the best reason to buy in shares. I mean, the stock could be overpriced, and even though you issued on options, you shouldn’t be buying it in. [...] But again, if you buy shares — if you buy a dollar bill for 90 cents, you’re doing your shareholders a favor. And if you buy it for $1.10, you are doing them no favor at all.
concept: Repurchase only at a significant discount to intrinsic value; buying in stock to offset option issuance is no reason to buy if the stock is overpriced.
evolution_notes: Earlier: M2013-055 (repurchase price set by intrinsic value, not book), L1999-026 (a buyback above intrinsic value harms continuing owners), L2011-003. Just before (lines 121-123): eager to buy at 120% of book, about $45 billion over book being a bargain; no exact intrinsic value given because it changes and because Buffett and Munger would be within 5 percent of each other but probably not within 1 percent. The letter's 120% passage (letter lines 98-102) is in the note as a repeat.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 11. “Eager” to buy back shares at 120% of book value

quote_verbatim: Well, I don’t believe we’ve ever wanted to get the stock way over intrinsic value so that we can issue it to other people and get an advantage for ourselves and a disadvantage for them. And, I think the people that want the stock up very close to intrinsic value, or higher, really want egg in their beer. It’s okay if it’s a little below.
concept: Munger: do not push one's stock above intrinsic value to issue it at others' expense; a price a little below value is acceptable.
evolution_notes: An exchange: Munger's line follows Buffett's buyback rule (lines 125-127) and precedes Buffett's account of managers who overprice their stock (line 131), each rowed separately. Munger goes on: "we’re not in the game of ballooning our stock up as high as we can get it so we can issue it more at a profit to ourselves", and the stock will eventually go above intrinsic value whether they like it or not.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 11. “Eager” to buy back shares at 120% of book value

quote_verbatim: because if you’re trying to get your stock to be overpriced, you’re very likely to cheat on your earnings and cheat on projections. Cheat on everything. And it works, incidentally. It doesn’t work indefinitely, but it works. [...] That’s a game that we not only don’t want to play, we really found it very distasteful, because we saw a lot of these people in action.
concept: A management trying to get its stock overpriced, to use as currency, is very likely to cheat on earnings and projections; the effort itself is a warning sign.
evolution_notes: The quote begins mid-sentence. Just before (line 131): managers getting their stock to sell for far more than it was worth to trade for other companies was "all the rage in the late ’60s" and one reason he wound up the partnership. Elided: some companies were built on that principle. Just after (line 133): "we don’t want to come close to playing it." Earlier: M2011-034 (the go-go conglomerates as stock issuance machines), M2001-092 (an overvalued stock lets promoters issue shares). Related: the Munger row from line 129.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 11. “Eager” to buy back shares at 120% of book value

quote_verbatim: Well, we’ve kept our word to them. And now we have to be very careful about what we promise, because we can’t promise, for example, never to have a layoff in a business we buy, because who knows what the world holds. But we can promise that we won’t sell their business, for example, if it turns out to be disappointing, as long as it doesn’t run into the prospect of continuing losses or having significant labor problems. [...] And if we behave differently, you know, the word would get around.
concept: Promise a seller only what can surely be kept, then keep it; the reputation for kept promises is what wins owner-founders' trust.
evolution_notes: Elided: some kept businesses would not get a passing grade at business school, and the promise is printed in the economic principles at the back of the annual report so sellers can count on it. Just after (lines 147-149): kept for 49 years, it puts Berkshire in a class hard to compete with for sellers who care where their business goes; a private equity firm is unimpressed and "there’s nothing wrong with that". Munger (line 151): they behave this way because they like it and it has worked. Earlier: L2008-006 (be the buyer of choice by deserving it), M2009-041 (a business bought is kept unless it will lose money indefinitely or has major labor problems), M2013-063, R1995-011.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 12. Why sellers trust Berkshire with the companies they’ve built

quote_verbatim: because the nature of boards is such that they’re part business organizations and part social organizations. And people behave in some ways with their business brain and they behave to some extent with their social brain. [...] Now bear in mind that the so-called independent directors on such a board are probably receiving maybe $200,000 a year, maybe $300,000 a year. Believe me, they are not independent.
concept: Judge a board's oversight by its social dynamics: delegated committee reports go unquestioned, and directors whose fees matter to them are not independent whatever the rules say.
evolution_notes: The quote begins mid-sentence. Elided (lines 165-167): in 55 years on 19 boards he never saw a compensation committee report get a dissenting vote, because the board delegates to the committee and questioning it is almost unheard of. Just after (line 169): "They do not look for Dobermans. (Laughter) They look for cocker spaniels." Earlier: M2009-086 (a director whose fees matter is not independent), M2009-085 (Munger, liberally paid directors reciprocate), M2013-071 (a board as a social institution).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 13. “Social dynamics” weaken oversight by corporate boards

quote_verbatim: And I think the general idea that a person should just shout disapproval all day long of everything he disapproves of is very suspect. In the world in which we inhabit, people accomplish more if they pick their spots for public disapproval.
concept: Munger: an owner or director accomplishes more by choosing where to disapprove publicly than by objecting to everything.
evolution_notes: An exchange: Buffett's answer on boards (lines 165-171) is rowed separately. Munger begins with Buffett being voted down on compensation at Salomon. Buffett adds (line 177): "you not only have to pick your spots, you have to pick how you do it", and that changing others' behaviour "is not helped by shouting a lot"; named here, not rowed. Applies to the Coca-Cola abstention rowed under heading 7.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 13. “Social dynamics” weaken oversight by corporate boards

quote_verbatim: In terms of cost of capital, Charlie and I always figure that our cost of capital is the — is what could be produced by our second best idea. And then our best idea has to exceed that. [...] The real test, you know, over time, is whether the capital we retain produces more than a dollar of market value as we go along.
concept: Cost of capital is what the second-best idea would produce, which the best idea must beat; the test over time is whether each retained dollar creates more than a dollar of market value.
evolution_notes: An exchange: Munger interjects "I’ve never heard an intelligent one" (line 193), elided; Buffett resumes. Elided (line 195): CFOs always claim a deal exceeds the cost of capital without knowing what it is. Just after (line 197): "we are constantly measuring that opportunity cost". Munger (line 199) restates: the phrase means silly things in business schools, "we just don’t use it", and Warren's dollar-retained standard is the best description of cost of capital; named here, not rowed. Earlier: M2001-084 (cost of a deal is the second best deal around), M2003-116 (no cost-of-capital figure used), M2001-081 (Munger, opportunity cost), M2000-050 (the dollar-retained test).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 14. Everyone else is wrong on cost of capital

quote_verbatim: So, it was not a bargain purchase. It was a great business. It was a wonderful opportunity to join as fine a family as I’ve ever met. [...] And I never asked her for an audit. I just asked her if she owed any money. And I asked her if she owned the building. And she said yes. And we made the deal.
concept: A great business with an exceptional family is worth a full price; where the owner's word is trusted, the checks can be as few as whether the business owes money and owns its premises.
evolution_notes: Implied: Buffett shows the checks by what he did at the 1983 purchase rather than stating them as a rule. Just before (line 209): the price was about 11 or 12 times after-tax earnings for 80% on a $60 million valuation, more than book, not the 85% of book the questioner computed. Elided (line 211): a German company was also bidding. Related: the FY2013 letter tells the same purchase, "her word was good enough for me" (letter lines 765-769, not rowed).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 15. Buying Nebraska Furniture Mart from the Blumkins

quote_verbatim: In terms of my wife’s situation, you know, that is not a question of maximizing capital. It’s just a question of total, 100 percent peace of mind on something that cannot get a bad result.
concept: Fit the investment to the purpose of the money: where the aim is certainty of an adequate result rather than the largest result, choose what cannot turn out badly.
evolution_notes: Explains L2013-014 (the 90/10 instruction in the will). Just before (line 227): all his Berkshire shares go to five foundations over about 12 years after his death, and he tells the trustees "Don’t sell any Berkshire shares until they have to be sold"; just after (line 229) the same instruction for the part he cares about maximizing. Munger (lines 231, 235): Buffett is entitled to distribute his money as he pleases, a meritocrat returning it to the civilization that produced it; personal, not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 16. Why Buffett recommends an index fund for his wife’s inheritance

quote_verbatim: Berkshire is better off because the two of us have worked together than if either one of us had been working individually, there’s no question about that. [...] And I think that in both cases that I just named, I think that they accomplished far more because they had two incredible people running them who admired and worked well with the other. And they were complimentary, in terms of the talents they brought. In many ways, it’s a great way to operate. You can’t will it to somebody.
concept: A company run by two able people who admire each other and bring complementary talents tends to accomplish more than either alone; such a partnership cannot be bequeathed.
evolution_notes: The elision crosses "(Applause)" and the two examples, Roberto Goizueta and Don Keough at Coca-Cola and Tom Murphy and Dan Burke at Cap Cities (line 285). "complimentary" is printed for complementary and kept. Just before (line 283): whoever succeeds him as CEO will probably develop someone to work with very closely. Munger's reply (line 287) is a joke.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 19. Two heads running Berkshire are better than one

quote_verbatim: They were disappointed because they looked at somebody else in the place and it drove them crazy. [...] I think it’s very seldom that publishing compensation accomplishes much for the shareholders. [...] It is only human to look at a whole bunch of proxy statements and say, “Well, I’m worth more than that guy,” and negotiate that way. And a comp committee is going to respond to that.
concept: Pay is driven by comparison with others' pay, so publishing compensation tends to ratchet it upward rather than restrain it.
evolution_notes: Elided (lines 331-333): at Salomon virtually everybody was dissatisfied with enormous pay, and the management's secret deal with John Meriwether's arbitrage group made compensation "an even greater problem because of the jealousy"; corporate CEOs as a group would be paid much less had proxy statements not revealed others' pay. Just after (line 333): "American shareholders are paying a significant price" for seeing the top five officers' pay every year. Just before (lines 329-331): publishing subsidiary salaries would hurt shareholders in negotiating with others. Related: Munger's envy row from lines 335-347.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 22. Shareholders aren’t helped by rule requiring CEO pay disclosure

quote_verbatim: We’re way better off without adding to the culture of envy in America. [...] I would say that envy is doing the country a lot of harm. And our practices are envy dampeners.
concept: Munger: arrange a company's practices, such as what pay it discloses, to damp envy rather than feed it.
evolution_notes: The elision crosses Buffett's interjections (lines 337-345: no CEO ever reads other proxy statements and concludes he should be paid less) and Munger's short replies; Munger resumes the same thought at line 347. Munger began (line 335): "In the spirit of transparency, you’re asking for something that wouldn’t be good for the shareholders." Earlier: M1997-048 (envy spreads pay excess), M2008-112, M2013-035 (Munger, envy no fun). Related: Buffett's row from lines 331-333.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 22. Shareholders aren’t helped by rule requiring CEO pay disclosure

quote_verbatim: We always will have $20 billion around Berkshire. We will never be dependent on the kindness of strangers. [...] There will be some time in the next 100 years, and it may be tomorrow and it may be 100 years from now, and nobody knows, you know, where we cannot depend on anybody else to keep our own strength and to maintain our operations. And we spent too long building Berkshire to have that one moment destroy us. [...] I’ve always said that, you know, cash is — available cash or credit — is a lot like oxygen: that you don’t notice it — the lack of it — 99.9 percent of the time. But if it’s absent, it’s the only thing you notice. [...] We never feel a compulsion to use it though, just because it’s there.
concept: Keep a fixed cash floor and never rely on others, since at some unknowable moment only one's own cash will serve; and never feel compelled to spend cash because it is there.
evolution_notes: Elided: Blanche DuBois; no reliance on bank lines; loans in the panic to Harley-Davidson at 15%, Goldman Sachs, General Electric and Tiffany's, "when you need cash ... it’s the only thing you need" because others are not providing it (lines 359-361); above $20 billion they try to invest intelligently. Restates L2013-002 (this unit's letter: at least $20 billion, no material short-term obligations). Earlier: L2009-006, L2008-019, M2012-022. Just before (line 355): BNSF distributes cash since it buys no businesses, while BH Energy retains earnings for acquisitions. Munger (line 363): lucky to own businesses that can employ new capital at very respectable rates; named, not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 23. Why Berkshire maintains $20B cash cushion

quote_verbatim: I know where the cash is. [...] And I know when we’re going to need cash and I know what I’m thinking about doing, or may possibly do in the next few months, that maybe something’s a 50/50 probability of happening. And anything I am committing to do, I know where the cash is coming from.
concept: Never commit to anything without knowing where the cash for it will come from, including for deals that are only possible.
evolution_notes: Just before (line 399): the $20 billion minimum counts only cash obtainable by a phone call, not money in the energy business or the railroad; subsidiaries hold more cash than a conglomerate with sweep accounts would allow. Just after (lines 401-403): "we’re not big disciplinarians of our subsidiaries day by day". Earlier: M2012-022 (never be mid-deal not knowing where the money will come from). Related: the cash-floor row from lines 359-361.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 25. Berkshire’s cash cushion is partially held by subsidiaries

quote_verbatim: Now, we think that giving our managers the degree of freedom that they enjoy will also accomplish a lot. [...] And they’ll be right. But what they won’t be able to measure is how much on the positive side we have achieved with dozens and dozens of people because we gave them that same sort of leeway. [...] And we’re not saying that’s a 100 percent benefit in all ways. We think — but we think on balance, it’s a benefit.
concept: Accept that light supervision will occasionally miss something, because the unmeasurable gain from giving many managers freedom outweighs it on balance.

quote_verbatim: I would ask them if they had to put all of their money into any coal company except their own and go away for ten years and couldn’t change it, which one would it be and why? And then I would say, after I got an answer to that, I would say, and if as part of that deal they had to sell short in the equivalent amount of money — in one coal company — which would it be and why? And if I went around and talked to everybody in the coal business about that, I would know more about the coal companies from an economic standpoint than any one of those managers probably would.
concept: Learn an industry's economics by asking each manager which competitor he would own for ten years and which he would sell short, and why.

heading: ### 10. How to find what you love and do it

quote_verbatim: You do have to have — you have to have a real curiosity about it. I mean, you — I don’t think you can do it because your mother’s telling you to do it, or something of the sort. (Laughs) I think you — it really has to turn you on. [...] If you just keep learning things, something will come along that you’ll find extremely useful to do. I mean, it — but you’ve got to be open to it.

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 10. How to find what you love and do it

quote_verbatim: So I called in eight people and I said, you know, “Who besides you would be the ideal person to run this, and why?” One guy told me that there was nobody compared to him. (Laughter) He was gone from the firm within a few months. (Laughter) But — the — it’s not a bad system to use. You can really learn a lot just by asking.
concept: To choose who should run a business, ask each candidate who besides himself would be the ideal person and why.
evolution_notes: An exchange: Munger first tells Larry Bird's trick (line 845), asking every agent whom he would recommend if not himself and hiring the common second choice, "there are a lot of tricks that people use" (line 849); Buffett applies it to his Saturday at Salomon, printed "Solomon" at line 851. concept: Munger: avoid a very competitive field that plainly requires qualities one lacks, and keep eliminating fields until one or two remain.

heading: ### 12. Will GEICO eventually overtake State Farm?

[...] It’s easy to talk the game, but living the game is something else. I mean, it’s against the human nature of many entrepreneurial people to try and get the price down and the service quality up all the time. I mean, it’s like wearing the ultimate hair shirt and yet it works.

heading: ### 15. Try for Mexico’s rail freight market?

quote_verbatim: But intrinsic value has come to be equated with, and I think quite properly, with what you might call private business value. [...] But the intrinsic value of any business, if you could foresee the future perfectly, is the present value of all cash that will be ever distributed for that business between now and judgment day. And we’re not perfect at estimating that, obviously. (Laughs) But that’s what an investment or a business is all about. You put money in and you take money out.
concept: Intrinsic value is private business value: the present value of all the cash a business will distribute until judgment day, never perfectly estimated; an investment is money in and money out.
evolution_notes: Opens by saying Graham "didn’t get too specific about intrinsic value in terms of precise calculations"; Graham named as Buffett names him. Restates L1993-001 (a present-value estimate of the cash that can be taken out of a business).

heading: ### 16. Intrinsic value and the Berkshire model

quote_verbatim: Aesop said, “A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.” [...] Now the question is, you know, how sure are you that there are two in the bush, you know? How far away is the bush? There are all kinds of things. What are interest rates? [...] the real question is, A) are you going to have to put more cash into after you buy it? But it’s really cash in, cash out? When? What discount rate? All the standard stuff.
concept: To value any purchase ask how sure the future cash is, how far away it is, what interest rates are, whether more cash must go in after buying, and at what discount rate.
evolution_notes: Aesop's maxim, spoken by Buffett, belongs to him (2005 convention). Follows the definition at line 979 in the same answer. The second elision crosses the Graham and Fisher passage at line 981, rowed separately.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 16. Intrinsic value and the Berkshire model

quote_verbatim: One emphasized quantitative factors and one emphasized qualitative factors, but neither one would have disagreed with the math. And I started out very influenced by Graham, so I emphasized quantitative factors. Charlie came along and said I was all wrong, and that he’d learned more in law than I’d learned in financial studies and everything, and that I should think more about qualitative factors, and he was right. And Phil Fisher said the same thing.
concept: Buffett's own error: starting with Graham's emphasis on quantitative factors; Munger, and Fisher, taught him to weigh the qualitative factors more, within the same arithmetic.
evolution_notes: Buffett's own. Graham and Fisher named as Buffett names them. Just before (line 981): Fisher "would want to look a lot harder at the qualitative factors of the business in making that estimate of how many birds were in the bush. Graham would say he would want to see the bush — you know, $2 worth of cash in the bush, you know, and to pay a dollar for it now." Compare M2013-051 (Fisher telling him what Munger was telling him).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 16. Intrinsic value and the Berkshire model

quote_verbatim: I see private equity buying lots of businesses and having an advantage in that they’ll leverage up when we won’t, and also that presently they can borrow money very cheap and all of that. [...] But I don’t see anybody that’s got a model, or trying to build a model, that will essentially go after what we’re trying to achieve, which is to buy wonderful businesses from people that care about where their business goes, and who generally want to keep on running them.
concept: Concede leverage to private-equity buyers; aim instead to buy wonderful businesses from owners who care where the business goes and want to keep running it.
evolution_notes: Restates M2014-050 (founder families the best bet). Answers the questioner's "which company do you fear the most?".
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 16. Intrinsic value and the Berkshire model

quote_verbatim: If you stop to think about it, all the great big businesses of yesteryear, how few of them have really gotten big and stayed big. Of the really old businesses, only one stayed big and that was Rockefeller’s Standard Oil.
concept: Munger: few great businesses stay big over long periods; the base rate of lasting greatness is low.
evolution_notes: Around it, a forecast for Berkshire, not rowed: "the Berkshire model as now constructed will have — as said in show business, with legs" and "we’ll keep learning from our mistakes." and "The momentum’s in place, the ethos is in place." Line 989: "Don’t be too quick to sell the stock." Compare his Union Tank Car remark at line 825: "It’s amazing how some of these good businesses have lasted."
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 16. Intrinsic value and the Berkshire model

quote_verbatim: But essentially, you don’t create wealth by inflation or by having — you can move it around, but you don’t create it by inflation, and you don’t — a firm like Berkshire, you know, our earnings per share would go up. The intrinsic value of our business, measured in dollars, would go up. But under lots of inflation, unless we had leveraged those businesses, the value of your investment, in real terms, would go down.
concept: Inflation moves wealth but does not create it; an unleveraged business's dollar earnings and value may rise while the owner's real value falls, so judge value in real terms.
evolution_notes: Line 1017: "inflation would hurt us, but it would hurt most businesses", with only highly leveraged assets benefiting, and the thought experiment of a million dollars dropped on every household. Line 1023: a home with a very large mortgage survives inflation that wipes out the mortgage.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 17. Positive and negative effects of inflation

quote_verbatim: Well, we had a test of hyperinflation in Weimar Germany, and the people who owned stocks in places like Berkshire got through. And they didn’t prosper joyously, but they got through. And everybody else, practically, life insurance policies, bank deposits, you name it, got wiped out.
concept: Munger: in hyperinflation, owners of stock in businesses like Berkshire got through, while holders of claims fixed in money, such as policies and deposits, were wiped out.
evolution_notes: The rest of the line, on printing money, Hitler and "crazy politicians", is a political view left out of the quote (section 5).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 17. Positive and negative effects of inflation

quote_verbatim: It’s in the nature of corporations that are prosperous to be talked into dumb deals, and bureaucracy tends to feed on itself and create unnecessary costs. So I think the history of acquisitions is that it’s not an enormous way to wealth. Now, it has been for us, but we’re very peculiar, and luckily a lot of people don’t want to be peculiar in our way.
concept: Munger: prosperous corporations are talked into dumb deals and bureaucracy breeds cost, so acquisitions in aggregate are not a path to wealth.
evolution_notes: Opens "Well, let me summarize. I think the sum total of all acquisitions done by American industry will be lousy." Buffett follows at line 1043: "When we read that a company we don’t control is going to make an acquisition, I’m much more inclined to cry than to smile." and most of the hundreds of acquisition discussions he sat in on as a director "have been bad ideas".
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 18. Why companies make “dumb” deals

quote_verbatim: after it got back on the tracks, it made a couple of acquisitions. And they weren’t disasters, but they certainly weren’t successes, and they tended to take people’s — I think they took their eyes off the ball in terms of the potential of GEICO itself. [...] But if you look to secondary effects, it was huge. I mean, there were a dozen years there or so where all kinds of gains could have been made that weren’t. And you don’t get those years back.
concept: GEICO's error after its recovery: two acquisitions of modest accounting cost took management's eyes off GEICO's own potential; the secondary effect, a dozen lost years, is the real cost.
evolution_notes: GEICO management's mistake; Buffett draws the lesson. The elided text: the accounting cost of the two acquisitions "was poor, but it wasn’t disastrous". Line 1049: it was probably a net plus for Berkshire, which got to buy the other half.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 18. Why companies make “dumb” deals

quote_verbatim: And they have animal spirits, as Keynes talked about, and they like to do things. And the supporting staff certainly senses that they like to do things. I mean, they often have people in charge of strategy or acquisitions, or all of those things. What do you think those people are going to do? Sit around and suck their thumbs? No, they’re going keep coming up with deals. And the investment bankers will be, you know, calling on them daily. So there are all these forces that push toward deals, and if you try to push toward deals, you’re going to get a lot of dumb deals.
concept: Look for the forces pushing a company toward deals: a CEO with animal spirits, a staff that senses it, strategy and acquisition departments, and bankers calling daily; pushing toward deals yields dumb deals.
evolution_notes: Keynes's phrase spoken by Buffett belongs to him (2005 convention). Just before: "normally the people who get to be CEOs are not shrinking violets, you know."
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 18. Why companies make “dumb” deals

quote_verbatim: We try very hard, Charlie and I, not to get eager to do a deal. We’re just eager to do a deal that makes sense. And that would be a lot harder if we had directors, strategy departments, whatever it might be, all pushing us toward, you know, what have you done in the last three months, or something of the sort. So the setting in which you operate really can be very important.
concept: Be eager only for a deal that makes sense, never for a deal; keep a setting free of directors or departments pressing for activity.
evolution_notes: Follows the forces toward deals at line 1049 in the same answer.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 18. Why companies make “dumb” deals

quote_verbatim: Somebody is doing something wrong now, I mean, that — you know, you cannot have a city of 300,000 people and not have somebody behaving badly. [...] The disaster is if somebody is doing something wrong that, you know, that actually reflects badly on the whole organization. And I know that’s, to a degree, out of my hands. I can tell the managers, and they can tell the people that work for them that reputation is more important than anything else. And that’s going to have an effect, and I think it’s going to have more of an effect than having them — giving them some 200-page manual. But it’s not going cure everything. And what we hope is when there is something wrong that we find it out early, and then it’s up to us to do something about it.
concept: In a large organization someone is always behaving badly; tell managers reputation matters more than anything, which works better than a long manual, and aim to find wrongdoing early and act on it.
evolution_notes: The elided text says he does not worry about making money, and "But it won’t be a disaster, ever." The rest of the answer, on prosecuting individuals rather than corporations (lines 1077-1079, 1085), is a policy view and is not rowed; it carries the incentive point that behaviour changes when the fear comes home to the individual.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 19. Prosecute individuals or corporations?

quote_verbatim: The companies have insurance, but they don’t like — they’re not going talk about the amounts that they have or anything of the sort because that becomes a honey pot sometimes, and it’s not advisable to discuss your insurance limits publicly.
concept: Do not disclose one's insurance limits publicly; a known limit becomes a honey pot for claimants.
evolution_notes: Same answer: the four major railroads can pay even a very large award, and a common carrier is not paid enough per carload for hazardous materials (lines 1091, 1105).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 20. Effect of major railroad accident on BNSF and Berkshire

quote_verbatim: Nobody in their wildest dreams believed that a major oil company, from an accident in one well, would have a loss in so many tens of billions of dollars. And, of course, that’s gotten a lot of attention. I don’t know about Warren, but after that happened, I would have less enthusiasm for drilling in the Gulf. It was just such a big loss compared to anything. [...] And gain — possible gain. And that was a big oil field they tapped into, but it wouldn’t remotely pay for this accident.
concept: Munger: weigh a venture's possible accident loss against its possible gain; BP's one-well loss dwarfed what the field could ever pay.

heading: ### 20. Effect of major railroad accident on BNSF and Berkshire

heading: ### 21. Is commercial property-casualty insurance expansion too late?

heading: ### 22. Buy a sports team or sports equipment company?

quote_verbatim: we love the math that you just described, as long as we are going to get returns on the added capital investment. [...] And the return is not measured by the cash minus the increased capital investment we’re making. It’s measured by the operating earnings after depreciation. And there will be times in our businesses where no net investment may be required. But we actually prefer the ones where net — in the utility business — where net investment is required because we like the idea of getting more capital out at reasonable returns.

"getting more capital out at reasonable returns" as printed; the sense suggests "in", kept per the 2012 convention. Compare L2009-012 (the best businesses need little incremental investment; capital-heavy regulated businesses accepted for decent returns on added capital).

And we’ve got every reason to believe that’s true in the jurisdictions in which we operate. And one of the reasons we believe it’s true is because we’ve done so much better than, really, the great majority of utilities in delivering electricity at lower rates than are charged by most utilities. heading: ### 26. MidAmerican energy return on assets

It’s an old-fashioned way of getting ahead. And the interesting about it is it still works in these modern times. Nothing changes, if you just behave yourself correctly, it’s amazing how well it works.

quote_verbatim: there’s no question that at some point we will have more cash than we can intelligently deploy. And then — in the business — and then the question is what do we do with the excess? And that will depend on circumstances at the time. I mean, if the stock can be bought in at a price that makes sense for continuing shareholders, in other words that their value is enhanced by the repurchase, you know, if I were around at that time I would probably be very aggressive about repurchasing shares. [...] All I can tell you is that whatever is done will be done in the interest of the shareholder. That, you know, that is what every decision starts from, from that principle.
concept: When cash outgrows intelligent deployment, repurchase aggressively if the price enhances continuing shareholders' value; every decision starts from the shareholders' interest.

quote_verbatim: You know, when anybody’s threatened, or any business is threatened, it tries to fight back. [...] And you’ll see that, and in the end the better mouse trap usually wins. But the people with the second or third-best mouse trap will try to keep that from happening.

evolution_notes: The elided example: the agency system in insurance, sacrosanct when State Farm arrived around 1920 with "a better mouse trap" and GEICO "with a better mouse trap yet", and the incumbents' state laws on what could be done without agents (lines 1423-1425).

quote_verbatim: The ones you name, I don’t know anything about. And we try to stick with businesses where we know the winners. [...] And then there’s other fields where we can’t pick the winners, and so we just sit and watch. We find them interesting but we don’t get tempted.

concept: Build good financial habits as early as possible; habits are powerful and the holes dug by financial illiteracy can take a lifetime to climb out of.

Munger (line 1451): "the most powerful example (applause) is the behavior of the parent"; Buffett agrees (line 1453), "but not everybody gets the right parents."

heading: ### 33. Teach financial literacy to children in school?

quote_verbatim: there’s not a way to deliver a dividend to a few shareholders and not to others, although — whereas there is a way to — for shareholders to maintain an even and greater dollar investment in Berkshire, in terms of the underlying assets, and still cash out annually some portion of their investment, just like they would with a partnership, and incur fairly little tax in the matter.

quote_verbatim: Larry and his dad, Cecil, spent 62 years building the group, following a strategy that made owner-partners of all local managers. Creating this mutuality of interests proved over and over to be a winner.
concept: Making the local managers owner-partners creates a mutuality of interests between owner and manager, and that alignment repeatedly works.
evolution_notes: The Van Tuyls' practice, stated and endorsed by Buffett in describing the Van Tuyl Automotive purchase (lines 205-219). Just after (lines 216-219): manufacturer approval governs every dealership transfer, so Berkshire's job is to perform so that manufacturers welcome further purchases. Related: R1995-001 (shareholders as owner-partners, Berkshire's own form). New in a letter: owner-partnership of the operating managers credited as the winning strategy of an acquired business.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: The Year at Berkshire

quote_verbatim: I've mentioned in the past that my experience in business helps me as an investor and that my investment experience has made me a better businessman. Each pursuit teaches lessons that are applicable to the other. And some truths can only be fully learned through experience. [...] Among Arno's "certain things," I would include two separate skills, the evaluation of investments and the management of businesses. I therefore think it's worthwhile for Todd Combs and Ted Weschler, our two investment managers, to each have oversight of at least one of our businesses.
concept: Investing and running businesses are separate skills that teach each other and are learned fully only by doing, so an investor gains by having oversight of an operating business.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the Fred Schwed book and the Peter Arno cartoon, "There are certain things that cannot be adequately explained to a virgin either by words or pictures" (lines 272-276), and the printed page number (line 278). Just after (lines 282-290): two small companies earning $100 million on about $125 million of net tangible assets, each to be chaired by Combs or Weschler in Buffett's very limited way, to make them better investors. Related: M2003-070 (the way to a reputation as a good businessman is to buy a good business). New in a letter: the two skills named as separate, and operating oversight given to investment managers on purpose.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: The Year at Berkshire

quote_verbatim: An attentive investor, I'm embarrassed to report, would have sold Tesco shares earlier. I made a big mistake with this investment by dawdling. [...] In 2013, I soured somewhat on the company's then-management and sold 114 million shares, realizing a profit of $43 million. My leisurely pace in making sales would prove expensive. [...] In the world of business, bad news often surfaces serially: You see a cockroach in your kitchen; as the days go by, you meet his relatives.
concept: Buffett's own error: having soured on Tesco's management he sold slowly, and the delay was costly; bad news in a business tends to arrive in a series, so once it shows, act.
evolution_notes: Buffett's own mistake. The first elision skips the position's size and cost, $2.3 billion for 415 million shares (lines 908-910), and a page number (line 912); the second skips "Charlie calls this sort of behavior "thumb-sucking." (Considering what my delay cost us, he is being kind.)" (lines 915-916) and "During 2014, Tesco's problems worsened by the month. The company's market share fell, its margins contracted and accounting problems surfaced." (lines 918-919). Just after (lines 922-927): out of the position at a $444 million after-tax loss, about 1/5 of 1% of net worth; only one realized loss in 50 years cost 2% of net worth and two cost 1%, all in 1974-1975 when cheap stocks were sold to buy cheaper ones. Related: L2005-009 (Gen Re's trading operation, "Fault me for dithering. (Charlie calls it thumb-sucking.)", the time to act is now) and L2002-039 ("There is seldom just one cockroach in the kitchen", said there of weak accounting). New here: the same failing in a marketable stock rather than an operation, and the cockroach line turned from accounting to a business's news in general.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Investments

quote_verbatim: It is true, of course, that owning equities for a day or a week or a year is far riskier (in both nominal and purchasing-power terms) than leaving funds in cash-equivalents. That is relevant to certain investors � say, investment banks � whose viability can be threatened by declines in asset prices and which might be forced to sell securities during depressed markets. Additionally, any party that might have meaningful near-term needs for funds should keep appropriate sums in Treasuries or insured bank deposits. For the great majority of investors, however, who can � and should � invest with a multi-decade horizon, quotational declines are unimportant.
concept: Whether price declines are a risk depends on the holder: one who may be forced to sell or has near-term needs for funds should hold those sums in Treasuries or insured deposits, while a multi-decade investor can ignore quotational declines.
evolution_notes: Just before (lines 941-952): the unconventional conclusion that over fifty years it was far safer to own a diversified collection of American businesses than securities tied to the currency (repeats L2011-014 in substance, not rowed), and "Volatility is far from synonymous with risk" (line 951, repeats L2011-013 and L1993-020, not rowed). Just after (lines 961-974): for them a diversified equity portfolio bought over time is far less risky than dollar-based securities; investors who fled to Treasury bills in 2009 out of fear of meaningless volatility now earn a pittance. Related: L2011-013 (risk as the reasoned probability of loss of purchasing power over the contemplated holding period). New in a letter: the exception stated as a rule, near-term needs kept in Treasuries or insured deposits, and the forced seller named as the one for whom short-term declines are real risk.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Investments

quote_verbatim: Investors, of course, can, by their own behavior, make stock ownership highly risky. And many do. Active trading, attempts to "time" market movements, inadequate diversification, the payment of high and unnecessary fees to managers and advisors, and the use of borrowed money can destroy the decent returns that a life-long owner of equities would otherwise enjoy. Indeed, borrowed money has no place in the investor's tool kit: Anything can happen anytime in markets.
concept: The investor's own conduct (trading, timing, too little diversification, high fees, borrowing) is what makes owning stocks risky, and borrowed money should never be used because anything can happen in markets at any time.
evolution_notes: Just after (lines 980-981): no advisor, economist or TV commentator, "and definitely not Charlie nor I", can tell when chaos will occur; "Market forecasters will fill your ear but will never fill your wallet." Then (lines 983-992): institutions as a group underperform the index-fund investor, largely through fees paid to consultants who recommend high-fee managers, "a fool's game"; in the short run it is hard to tell luck from talent; most advisors' core competence is salesmanship (repeats L2005-017, L2005-018 and L2007-018 in substance, not rowed). Related: L2010-019 (to finish first you must first finish), M1999-005 (bright people go broke through leverage). New in a letter: the list of investor sins as the source of stock risk, and the flat bar on borrowed money for the investor.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Investments

quote_verbatim: If you look back at the housing bubble in — well, ending more or less in 2008, one of the great problems, in fact, maybe the greatest cause, was the fact that the mortgage holder became totally divorced from the mortgage originator and from the home builder. [...] And the mortgage originator suffered no loss if the loan went bad. [...] Now, when a mortgage goes bad, two people lose: the person that owns the house loses, and the person that owns the mortgage loses. And in our case, we have this identity of interest.
concept: When the party that makes a loan bears no loss if it goes bad, lending standards fail; keeping the loan aligns the lender's interest with the borrower's.
evolution_notes: The mistake is the mortgage industry's before 2008 (builders, originators and securitizers), with Buffett drawing the lesson; the answer is a defence of Clayton against a newspaper story, and the defence of Clayton's practices is left out. The first elision skips the builder who sold and took his profit and the originator who securitized loans sold around the world (line 55); the second skips Clayton offering mortgages to all buyers and retaining about $12 billion on 300,000 homes (line 57). Just after (lines 57-59): talk of rules making originators keep some skin in the game, maybe 3 percent, while Clayton keeps 100 percent in about half the cases, "so we have exactly the same interest as society has, and as the home buyer has"; (line 63) "if we make a mistake, it hurts them and it hurts us." Later in the answer (lines 63-67): gross profit is not profit, the story's arithmetic error. Munger's lesson in the same exchange is rowed separately (the foreclosure rate, line 85).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 9. Defending Clayton Homes from predatory lending accusations

quote_verbatim: So, Clayton is a very productive part of the economy, but we can’t make lending to poor people who buy houses 100 percent successful for everybody. We wouldn’t be running the business right if the foreclosure rate was zero. Too many people would deserve credit that wouldn’t get it.
concept: A lender with no losses at all is lending too tightly; some defaults are the price of extending credit to everyone who deserves it.
evolution_notes: An exchange with Buffett, whose lesson on the lender bearing the loss (lines 55-57) is rowed separately. Just before (line 81): Munger has wondered why manufactured houses do not have a bigger share, "such an efficient way of creating quite usable houses." Just after (line 87), Buffett: the big causes of default are loss of a job, death and divorce, and "I don’t think that’s a reason to deny them a house"; Clayton's default rates far below those of securitized deals on costlier houses in 2008-2009.

quote_verbatim: And I hope our Berkshire companies are not being run with more people than they need, either. They usually aren’t when we buy them, and, you know, we look for those companies that are well managed. 3G is — will — if they find out that 100 people are doing what 50 people can do, they’ll get it to where 50 people are doing it. And I think that actually makes sense throughout American business. [...] Efficiency is required over time in capitalism, and I really tip my hat to what the 3G people have done.
concept: A business should carry only the people it needs; Berkshire looks for well-managed companies that already do, and efficiency is what capitalism demands over time.
evolution_notes: The elision crosses Munger's interjection (line 97: the alternative to right-sizing is Russia, where "they pretend to pay us and we pretend to work"; "Of course, we want the right number of people in the jobs", a one-line restatement of the same lesson, not rowed) and Buffett's own railroad history, 1.6 million workers after World War II against fewer than 200,000 now carrying more freight more safely (line 99); Buffett resumes the same thought. Just before (line 93): no statement by Buffett or Munger ever said a company should have more people than needed; 3G's companies did extremely well after cutting to the number needed, with fair severance. Related: M2014-005 (no edicts on staffing at subsidiaries, example only) and M2014-006 (Munger: no need for the last nickel of staffing cost); see the note's Tensions seen.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 10. Defending 3G from accusations of excessive job cuts

quote_verbatim: We don’t have a one-size-fits-all system for buying businesses. They’re all different, every industry is different, and we also keep learning. So what we did ten years ago, we hopefully are doing better now. But we can’t give you a formula that will help you.
concept: There is no single checklist for buying businesses; each industry differs and the method itself keeps improving with learning.
evolution_notes: An exchange with Buffett, who states a separate lesson (the filters, lines 129-131), rowed separately. The question asked for five characteristics that give confidence to predict earnings ten years out, with IBM as a case. Related: M2004-057 (no one-size-fits-all arrangement), M2004-015 (no one formula across the businesses), M2002-020 (people always want a formula), M1995-115 (a general framework but no specifics). New here: the method itself said to improve over time.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 12. Company characteristics for predictable earnings

quote_verbatim: And most of the things that go through our minds are things that will stop us from going further. I mean, there’s — the filters are there. [...] We are looking for things where we do think we’ve got some reasonable fix on how it’s going to look in five or ten years, and that does eliminate a great many businesses. [...] Certainly, when we’re buying a business where we’re going to have somebody that’s selling it to us continue to run it for us, you know, a very big question is, you know, do we really want to be in partnership with this person and count on them to behave in the future when they don’t own the business, as they behaved in the past when they do own the business. And that stops a fair number of deals.
concept: Evaluation works mostly as a set of filters that stop a deal: a reasonable fix on how the business looks in five or ten years, and whether a selling owner who stays on will behave as well when he no longer owns it.
evolution_notes: An exchange with Munger, whose separate lesson (no one-size-fits-all system, line 127) is rowed separately. The first elision skips "there are a lot of things that, if we see it in a business, including, maybe, who we’re dealing with, will stop us from going on to the next layer. But it’s very different in different businesses" (line 129); the second skips "But it’s not the same — it’s not the same five questions at all" (line 129). Just after (line 131): "we don’t have a list of five. Or if we do, Charlie has kept it from me." Related: L2013-012 (an earnings range five years out or move on), L1995-005 (owners who care what happens to their companies and people), L1995-003 (the seller knows more and picks the time). New here: the seller-manager test put as behaviour after he no longer owns the business.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 12. Company characteristics for predictable earnings

quote_verbatim: We have no interest in encouraging other people to buy what — the investments we own. I mean, we are better off, because either we or the company is likely to be buying stock in the future. Why would we want the stock to go up if we’re going to be a buyer next year, and the year after, and the year after that? [...] If we talked our book, from our standpoint, we would say pessimistic things about all four of the biggest holdings we have, because all four of them are repurchasing their shares, and, obviously, the cheaper they repurchase their shares, the better off we are.
concept: A continuing buyer, or the owner of a company that keeps buying back its own shares, gains from lower prices, so there is no reason to talk up what one owns.
evolution_notes: The elision skips Wall Street's mentality that one is better off if a stock goes up the next day, and "talking your book" (line 153). Just after (line 157), Munger: "Warren, if people weren’t so often wrong, we wouldn’t be so rich" (a joke, not rowed). Related: L1997-009 (only those who will be sellers in the near future should be happy at rising stocks), R1995 principle 13 in practice (no talk of specific stocks). New here: the investee's buybacks as the reason a holder should prefer lower prices for what it already owns.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 14. Why we don’t “talk up” our investments

quote_verbatim: But the whole — the whole thing in business is being open to ideas as they come along, and insurance happened to be something that I could understand. I mean, that was in my sweet spot. [...] And that’s — there’s an awful lot of accident in life, but if you keep yourself open to having good accidents happen, and kind of get past the bad accidents, you know, some good things will happen.
concept: Stay open to opportunities as they arrive, act on the ones inside one's own understanding, and get past the bad accidents; chance then delivers some good ones.
evolution_notes: Just before (lines 167-169): the three pieces of luck, Lorimer Davidson's four hours with a 20-year-old, Jack Ringwalt's five minutes a year of wanting to sell National Indemnity, and Ajit Jain walking in on a Saturday; the odds of a trifecta like that again are very much against it. The elision skips "If Lorimer Davidson had talked to me about some other business, you know, it wouldn’t have done any good" and that he could understand National Indemnity when Jack had it for sale (line 171). Munger (line 173): "mostly we bought wonderful businesses and nourished them", but reinsurance was created out of whole cloth; insurance has been different for them. The question cited Munger's anniversary letter (letter file lines 2108-2111, read not rowed). Related: L1995-004 (no strategic plan, free to go where the opportunity is).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 15. “Three extraordinary pieces of luck” with insurance

quote_verbatim: So it does — it’s a vital part of Berkshire to have a clearly defined, deeply embedded culture that pervades the parent company, the subsidiary companies. [...] So we — it’s — we try to make clear and define that culture in every way possible, and it’s gotten reinforced over the years to an extreme degree. People who join us believe in it; people who shun us don’t believe in it, so we — it’s self-reinforcing.
concept: Define the culture clearly and act on it consistently everywhere; it then selects the people who join and repels those who do not, and so reinforces itself.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the evidence offered: 97 percent of shareholders voting against a dividend, and directors who see stewardship and buy their shares in the market rather than taking $2- or $300,000 a year (line 183). Just after (line 185): once he and Munger are gone it will be clear the culture is institutionalized, not the force of personality. The question asked how outside investors can judge the culture after they depart. Related: L2010-006 (cultures self-propagate), M2006-006 (managers who believe in the sort of operation Berkshire has), M2009-038 (culture and business model as the sustainable advantage). Buffett's anniversary letter says the same (letter file lines 1891-1892, read not rowed).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 16. Berkshire’s culture “runs deep”

quote_verbatim: I should say culture is everything at Berkshire. And if you run into a terrible culture, it’s — you know, the Salomon thing was up there on the screen, and it would be hard to turn Salomon into a Berkshire. I don’t think we could have done it, Charlie.
concept: A terrible culture cannot be turned into a good one even by the best owners, so the culture found in a business is close to fixed.
evolution_notes: Munger's reply (line 195), "I don’t think anybody’s ever done it on Wall Street", is a one-line restatement, not rowed. Just after (line 197): Berkshire is no monastery, but he, Munger and many managers care more about getting a good job done for Berkshire than what they get out of it. Restates M2010-021 (easier to build a new organization around a culture than to change an existing one's) in substance.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 16. Berkshire’s culture “runs deep”

quote_verbatim: Well, I think it’s an enormously wide moat, but I think it’s also true that the trends you described are happening. [...] I think you will see all food and beverage companies adjust to the expressed preferences of the consumers as they go along. No company ever does well ignoring its consumers. [...] There, obviously, are some shifts in preferences, although it’s remarkable how durable items are in this field. [...] Coca-Cola dates to 1886. It’s a pretty good bet that an awful lot of people are going to like the same thing.
concept: A durable brand's moat survives shifts in taste so long as the company adjusts to what consumers say they want; long-lived preferences are a good bet, ignoring consumers never is.
evolution_notes: The elisions skip the 1.9 billion daily servings (line 205), the forecast of more Coca-Cola cases in 20 years and the 1930s Fortune article (line 205), Buffett's one-quarter-Coca-Cola diet and the broccoli joke (lines 205-207), Munger's sugar joke (line 209, crossed; Buffett resumes the same thought at line 211), and the General Foods brands surviving Philip Morris and the Kraft split, Heinz from 1869 (line 211). Just after (line 213): the Whole Foods joke; "So I like the brands we’re buying." The question asked whether Coca-Cola's moat is narrowing and what news would convince him. Related: M1998-105 (products that travel well), L2011-008 (buy commodities, sell brands).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 17. Health concerns about sugar won’t stop Coca-Cola’s growth

quote_verbatim: There are not any huge advantages of scale, at least that I’m aware of, in owning lots of dealerships. But running dealerships well is a very good business. It’s a local business. [...] We don’t see the finance business, in dealers — we don’t bring anything to that party. [...] And we can’t come up with money as cheap as the banks can, and they’re the natural lenders for loans, so we’re not going to be in the finance business.
concept: Ask where an advantage actually lies: in a local business more units do not widen margins, and one should stay out of an adjacent line, such as auto finance, where others have the cheaper money and one brings nothing.
evolution_notes: The first elision skips the 17,000 dealers known by local names and "I don’t think that you widen profit margins, particularly, by having a thousand dealers versus having a hundred or even having one very good dealer" (line 221); the second skips Wells Fargo's cost-of-funds advantage, perhaps 12 basis points (lines 221-223). Just after (line 223): no buying advantage from manufacturers; margins widen only where a local dealer can be run better. Munger states a separate lesson in the same exchange (Van Tuyl's meritocracy, line 225), rowed separately.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 18. Why Buffett likes local auto dealerships

quote_verbatim: And Van Tuyl has a system of meritocracy where the right people get the power and get some ownership. [...] Those are very successful cultures, and I think they’ve got a very good thing going for them. The right people are prospering in Van Tuyl.
concept: A culture in which the right people get both authority and a share of ownership is a mark of a very successful business.
evolution_notes: An exchange with Buffett, whose separate lesson on scale and finance (lines 221-223) is rowed separately. The elision skips the comparison with Kiewit, Berkshire's Omaha landlord, "kissing cousins" (line 225). Related: L2014-001 (the FY2014 letter on Van Tuyl's owner-partner managers and the mutuality of interests).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 18. Why Buffett likes local auto dealerships

quote_verbatim: Yeah, well I think culture has to come from the top, it has to be consistent, it has to be part of written communications, it has to be — you know, has to be lived, and it has to be rewarded when followed, and punished when not. And then it takes a very, very long time to really become solid. [...] And people — just like your child, you know, sees what you do rather than what you say, it’s the same thing in a business, that people see how those above them behave and they move in that direction. [...] So there’s all — you’ve got to protect a brand. You’ve got to enhance it in every way. You’ve got to get a promise in people’s minds that gets delivered that way. But that’s the question Charlie and I faced in 1972 when we looked at See’s. quote_verbatim: I certainly think investment principles do not stop at borders. So if I were investing in China or any place else — India, UK, Germany — I would apply exactly the same sort of principles that I learned from “The Intelligent Investor.” I would think of stocks as a small piece of a business. I would think of investment fluctuations being there to benefit me, rather than to hurt me. And I would try to focus my attention on businesses where I thought I understood the competitive advantage they had and where they would — what they would — look like in five or ten years.
concept: The same principles hold in every market: a stock is a small piece of a business, price fluctuations are there to be used, and attention goes to businesses whose competitive advantage and shape in five or ten years one understands.
evolution_notes: The book is Graham's, named by Buffett. The question asked whether value investing applies in China, where the market had doubled in six months. Related: M2008-001 and M1997-135 (the three basic ideas from Graham), M2002-042, M2015-005 (a reasonable fix five or ten years out, this session). New here: the principles said to be the same across borders.

quote_verbatim: There’s a certain irony, in that we will — we would — do the best, over decades, if we operated in a market where people operated very foolishly. [...] I mean, if you’re a young investor, and you can sort of stand back and value stocks as businesses and invest when things are very cheap, no matter what anybody is saying on television or what you’re reading, and perhaps, if you wish, sell when people get terribly enthused, it is really not a very tough intellectual game. It’s an easy game, if you can control your emotions.
concept: Value stocks as businesses, buy when very cheap whatever is being said, and perhaps sell into enthusiasm; the intellect required is modest, the emotional control is the whole difficulty.
evolution_notes: The elision skips that wild enthusiasm and depression let people make money in securities though it is not the greatest thing for a society, and 1973-74, when stocks were cheaper than in 2008-2009, "humans behave the way humans behave" (line 597). quote_verbatim: I don’t think that value investing will ever go out of style. Who in the hell doesn’t want value when you buy something? How can there be anything else that makes any sense except value investing? [...] People are looking for an easier way. [...] And that’s a mistake. It looks easier, but, in fact, it’s harder. And there’s a lot of misery to be obtained by misusing stocks.
concept: Value investing is simply wanting value for what one pays, so nothing else makes sense; the apparently easier alternatives are harder and bring misery.
evolution_notes: The quote opens partway into Munger's line 601, which begins "Yeah. But there’s great opportunities for excess and nasty contractions after unnatural booms" and that China is wise to dampen speculative booms (a view on China, left out).
