quote_verbatim: Nobody buys a farm to make a lot of money next week or next month, or they buy, you know, an apartment house. They buy it based on what they think the longterm future is. And if they get a — if they make a reasoned calculation of that and the purchase price looks attractive, they buy it and then they don’t get a quote on it every day or every week or every month or even every year, and that’s probably a better way to look at stocks.
concept: Buy a stock as one buys a farm or apartment house, on a reasoned estimate of its long-term future at an attractive price, and then ignore the quotations.

I’ve seen a lot of businesses run by people that really don’t understand the math of investing or capital allocation very well.

quote_verbatim: I purchased BPL's first shares of Berkshire in December 1962, anticipating more closings and more repurchases. The stock was then selling for $7.50, a wide discount from per-share working capital of $10.25 and book value of $20.20. Buying the stock at that price was like picking up a discarded cigar butt that had one puff remaining in it. Though the stub might be ugly and soggy, the puff would be free. Once that momentary pleasure was enjoyed, however, no more could be expected.
concept: A cigar butt is a poor business bought so far below its working capital and book value that one last gain is free, after which nothing more can be expected.
evolution_notes: From Buffett's signed "Berkshire � Past, Present and Future" (letter file lines 1207-1915), printed after the FY2014 letter's signature and rowed by the parent session's ruling of 2026-10-04 (supplement to this unit). Just before (lines 1238-1239): the company closed nine plants, sometimes using the proceeds to repurchase shares, "And that pattern caught my attention." Related: M1998-006 (the cigar-butt approach, one good free puff, given up; meeting row). First letter row for the term.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: In the Beginning

quote_verbatim: Shortly before the tender offer was mailed, Stanton had asked me at what price BPL would sell its holdings. I answered $11.50, and he said, "Fine, we have a deal." Then came Berkshire's letter, offering an eighth of a point less. I bristled at Stanton's behavior and didn't tender. That was a monumentally stupid decision. [...] Instead, irritated by Stanton's chiseling, I ignored his offer and began to aggressively buy more Berkshire shares. [...] Through Seabury's and my childish behavior � after all, what was an eighth of a point to either of us? � he lost his job, and I found myself with more than 25% of BPL's capital invested in a terrible business about which I knew very little. I became the dog who caught the car.
concept: Buffett's own error: pique over an eighth of a point made him refuse the free gain he had planned for and buy control of a terrible business he knew little about.
evolution_notes: Buffett's own mistake. The first elision skips the textile industry's long-understood decline, the 1955 merger as "a suicide pact", the cigar-butt passage (lines 1241-1245, rowed separately in this batch) and the tender at 50% above BPL's cost, "my free puff" (lines 1223-1250); the second skips a page number (line 1255) and BPL's 392,633 shares and control in May 1965 (line 1257). Just after (lines 1262-1273): net worth down to $22 million, two lucky tax-free years, then 18 years of struggle until the textile operation closed in 1985, "But stubbornness � stupidity? � has its limits." Related: L2010-004 (the dumbest thing was to expand the existing textile operation) and M2000-116 (the original purchase of Berkshire a terrible mistake; meeting row). New in a letter: the purchase traced to an emotional reaction over a trivial sum.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: In the Beginning

quote_verbatim: Undeterred by my first mistake of committing much of BPL's resources to a dying business, I quickly compounded the error. Indeed, my second blunder was far more serious than the first, eventually becoming the most costly in my career. [...] So why did I purchase NICO for Berkshire rather than for BPL? I've had 48 years to think about that question, and I've yet to come up with a good answer. I simply made a colossal mistake. [...] Despite these facts staring me in the face, I opted to marry 100% of an excellent business (NICO) to a 61%-owned terrible business (Berkshire Hathaway), a decision that eventually diverted $100 billion or so from BPL partners to a collection of strangers.
concept: Buffett's own costliest error: putting an excellent business into a vehicle that was a partly-owned terrible business, so its value and the capital it threw off were shared with owners he owed nothing and tied to a dying operation.
evolution_notes: Buffett's own mistake. The first elision skips the $8.6 million purchase of National Indemnity in 1967, "Insurance was in my sweet spot: I understood and liked the industry", and Jack Ringwalt's wish to sell to Buffett personally (lines 1280-1285); the second skips the three costs counted (100% ownership lost, growth impeded for nearly two decades by "the unproductive funds imprisoned in the textile operation", later acquisitions 39%-owned by legacy holders, lines 1289-1293). Just after (lines 1298-1301): the 1975 Waumbec purchase, a "bargain" on assets and projected synergies, a disaster (read, not rowed: repeats L2010-004 and L2012-012). No earlier v5 row names this mistake.

quote_verbatim: But a major weakness in this approach gradually became apparent: Cigar-butt investing was scalable only to a point. With large sums, it would never work well. In addition, though marginal businesses purchased at cheap prices may be attractive as short-term investments, they are the wrong foundation on which to build a large and enduring enterprise. Selecting a marriage partner clearly requires more demanding criteria than does dating.
concept: Cheap marginal businesses can serve as short-term investments but fail at size and cannot be the foundation of a lasting enterprise; a permanent holding needs more demanding criteria than a temporary one.
evolution_notes: Just before (lines 1310-1318): the many free puffs of the 1950s made that decade his best; GEICO the main exception, 65% of his $9,800 net worth; most early gains from mediocre companies at bargain prices, the technique Ben Graham taught (Graham named by Buffett, not rowed). Just after (lines 1325-1327): Berkshire would have been a "date" at about 40% a year had BPL taken Stanton's offer. Then (lines 1348-1350) Munger's blueprint, "Forget what you know about buying fair businesses at wonderful prices; instead, buy wonderful businesses at fair prices" (read, not rowed: repeats L2012-004). Related: M1998-006 (cigar butts do not work with big money; meeting row). New in a letter: the marriage-and-dating test, permanence demanding stricter criteria.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Charlie Straightens Me Out

quote_verbatim: Moreover, the company had a huge asset that did not appear on its balance sheet: a broad and durable competitive advantage that gave it significant pricing power. That strength was virtually certain to give See's major gains in earnings over time. Better yet, these would materialize with only minor amounts of incremental investment. [...] But I didn't want to pay more than $25 million and wasn't all that enthusiastic even at that figure. (A price that was three times net tangible assets made me gulp.) My misguided caution could have scuttled a terrific purchase. [...] Additionally, through watching See's in action, I gained a business education about the value of powerful brands that opened my eyes to many other profitable investments.
concept: Buffett's own near-error: a durable competitive advantage with pricing power is an asset the balance sheet omits, and balking at a multiple of tangible assets nearly cost him the business that taught him the value of brands.
evolution_notes: Buffett's own mistake, narrowly escaped. The first elision skips "In other words, See's could be expected to gush cash for decades to come" and the family's $30 million ask, "Charlie rightly said it was worth that much" (lines 1368-1372); the second skips the sellers taking the $25 million bid and See's $1.9 billion of pre-tax earnings on $40 million of added investment, distributed to buy other businesses, "(Envision rabbits breeding.)" (lines 1374-1378). speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Charlie Straightens Me Out

quote_verbatim: Even with Charlie's blueprint, I have made plenty of mistakes since Waumbec. The most gruesome was Dexter Shoe. [...] The fact is that I gave Berkshire stock to the sellers of Dexter rather than cash, and the shares I used for the purchase are now worth about $5.7 billion. [...] Several of my subsequent errors also involved the use of Berkshire shares to purchase businesses whose earnings were destined to simply limp along. Mistakes of that kind are deadly. Trading shares of a wonderful business � which Berkshire most certainly is � for ownership of a so-so business irreparably destroys value.
concept: Buffett's own repeated error: paying for so-so businesses with shares of a wonderful one destroys value permanently, a cost far beyond what accounting records.

The first elision skips Dexter's terrific record, competitive strengths soon to evaporate under foreign competition "And I simply didn't see that coming", $433 million paid, value to zero, GAAP not recording the magnitude (lines 1385-1390); the second skips "As a financial disaster, this one deserves a spot in the Guinness Book of World Records" (line 1392). speaker: BUFFETT

quote_verbatim: Too often CEOs seem blind to an elementary reality: The intrinsic value of the shares you give in an acquisition must not be greater than the intrinsic value of the business you receive. [...] I can promise you that long after I'm gone, Berkshire's CEO and Board will carefully make intrinsic value calculations before issuing shares in any acquisitions. You can't get rich trading a hundred-dollar bill for eight tens (even if your advisor has handed you an expensive "fairness" opinion endorsing that swap).
concept: In any acquisition paid in stock, compare the intrinsic value of the shares given with the intrinsic value of the business received, and do not give more.

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Charlie Straightens Me Out

quote_verbatim: I've yet to see an investment banker quantify this all-important math when he is presenting a stock-for-stock deal to the board of a potential acquirer. Instead, the banker's focus will be on describing "customary" premiums-to-market-price that are currently being paid for acquisitions � an absolutely asinine way to evaluate the attractiveness of an acquisition � or whether the deal will increase the acquirer's earnings-per-share (which in itself should be far from determinative). [...] Post mortems of acquisitions, in which reality is honestly compared to the original projections, are rare in American boardrooms. They should instead be standard practice.
concept: Judge an acquisition by the values exchanged, not by customary premiums or per-share earnings accretion, and afterwards compare the result honestly with the original projections.
evolution_notes: The elision skips "In striving to achieve the desired per-share number, a panting CEO and his "helpers" will often conjure up fanciful "synergies." (As a director of 19 companies over the years, I've never heard "dis-synergies" mentioned, though I've witnessed plenty of these once deals have closed.)" (lines 1409-1411). speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Charlie Straightens Me Out

quote_verbatim: Since the per-share earnings gains of an expanding conglomerate came from exploiting p/e differences, its CEO had to search for businesses selling at low multiples of earnings. These, of course, were characteristically mediocre businesses with poor long-term prospects. This incentive to bottom-fish usually led to a conglomerate's collection of underlying businesses becoming more and more junky. [...] Eventually, however, the clock struck twelve, and everything turned to pumpkins and mice. Once again, it became evident that business models based on the serial issuances of overpriced shares � just like chain-letter models � most assuredly redistribute wealth, but in no way create it.
concept: Growth by issuing high-multiple shares for low-multiple businesses pushes the buyer toward ever worse businesses and, like a chain letter, moves wealth around without creating any.

quote_verbatim: At both BPL and Berkshire, we have never invested in companies that are hell-bent on issuing shares. That behavior is one of the surest indicators of a promotion-minded management, weak accounting, a stock that is overpriced and � all too often � outright dishonesty.

evolution_notes: Follows directly the conglomerate passage (lines 1468-1473, rowed in this batch). speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Berkshire Today

quote_verbatim: Nevertheless, there are often obstacles to the rational movement of capital. As those 1954 Berkshire minutes made clear, capital withdrawals within the textile industry that should have been obvious were delayed for decades because of the vain hopes and self-interest of managements. Indeed, I myself delayed abandoning our obsolete textile mills for far too long. A CEO with capital employed in a declining operation seldom elects to massively redeploy that capital into unrelated activities. A move of that kind would usually require that long-time associates be fired and mistakes be admitted. Moreover, it's unlikely that CEO would be the manager you would wish to handle the redeployment job even if he or she was inclined to undertake it.
concept: Expect a manager of a declining business to keep capital in it: vain hope, self-interest, loyalty to associates and reluctance to admit mistakes block redeployment, and he is seldom the right person to redeploy it anyway.
evolution_notes: Includes Buffett's own delay (line 1490-1491). Just before (lines 1484-1486): market-driven allocation of capital "is usually far superior to any alternative." Just after (lines 1498-1512): taxes and frictional costs on shareholders' reallocation, "Money-shufflers don't come cheap"; Berkshire can move huge sums without tax and is "free of historical biases created by lifelong association with a given industry", "If horses had controlled investment decisions, there would have been no auto industry" (read, not rowed: the advantage repeats L2010-003 in substance). Related: L2010-004 and L2012-012 (his own textile delay), L1994-016 (capital allocation skill). New in a letter: the reasons a declining operation's capital stays put, stated as a general expectation of CEOs.

heading: Berkshire Today

quote_verbatim: Families that own successful businesses have multiple options when they contemplate sale. Frequently, the best decision is to do nothing. There are worse things in life than having a prosperous business that one understands well. But sitting tight is seldom recommended by Wall Street. (Don't ask the barber whether you need a haircut.)
concept: An owner of a prosperous business he understands often does best to keep it, and should discount advice to sell from those paid for transactions.
evolution_notes: Just after (lines 1545-1578): a public offering when part of a family wishes to sell; otherwise a competitor wringing "synergies" by dismissing the seller's associates, or a private-equity buyer piling on debt, "In effect, the business becomes a piece of merchandise" (read, not rowed: repeats L2008-007); Berkshire's permanent home as the third choice (a description). Related: L2009-022 (the barber line said of advisors on stock acquisitions). New in a letter: doing nothing named as frequently the best decision for an owner.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Berkshire Today

quote_verbatim: Investment bankers, being paid as they are for action, constantly urge acquirers to pay 20% to 50% premiums over market price for publicly-held businesses. [...] A few years later, bankers � bearing straight faces � again appear and just as earnestly urge spinning off the earlier acquisition in order to "unlock shareholder value." [...] (Mental "flexibility" of this sort by the banking fraternity has prompted the saying that fees too often lead to transactions rather than transactions leading to fees.)
concept: Advisors paid for action will argue one way and then the reverse, buy at a control premium and later spin off to unlock value; their advice follows the fee, not the merits.
evolution_notes: The first elision skips the "control value" justification and "(What acquisition-hungry manager will challenge that assertion?)" (lines 1594-1596); the second skips that spin-offs strip control value without payment, the entrepreneurial-management story "(So much for that talented CEO we met earlier.)", and a later reacquisition at a fresh control premium (lines 1599-1605). Just before (lines 1581-1591) and after (lines 1609-1619): voluntary spin-offs make no sense for Berkshire, losing control value, capital-allocation flexibility and tax advantages (a description of Berkshire's case, not rowed). The saying is quoted by Buffett without a named source. Related: L2009-022 (don't ask the barber), L1997-033 (advisors supply the projections the CEO wants), L2007-018 (helpers).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Berkshire Today

quote_verbatim: Ling, it should be noted, had never displayed any managerial skills. But Charlie told me long ago to never underestimate the man who overestimates himself. And Ling had no peer in that respect.
concept: A promoter's overconfidence can carry him and his company a long way regardless of skill, so do not dismiss him; it is a force in the market, not a sign of ability.
evolution_notes: Munger's maxim, spoken by Buffett here (the 2004-2005 convention). Just before (lines 1623-1628): LTV from $36 million of sales in 1965 to number 14 on the Fortune 500 two years later through "a lot of corporate razzle-dazzle"; the D Magazine piece of October 1982. Just after (lines 1632-1643): "project redeployment", acquisitions to meet "the test of the 2 plus 2 equals 5 (or 6) formula" (Ling's words), Meatball, Golf Ball and Goof Ball, Ling himself "spun off from LTV . . . that is, fired" (the lesson drawn at lines 1645-1650, rowed in this batch). No earlier v5 row carries the maxim.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Berkshire Today

quote_verbatim: Periodically, financial markets will become divorced from reality � you can count on that. More Jimmy Lings will appear. They will look and sound authoritative. The press will hang on their every word. Bankers will fight for their business. What they are saying will recently have "worked." Their early followers will be feeling very clever. Our suggestion: Whatever their line, never forget that 2+2 will always equal 4. And when someone tells you how old-fashioned that math is --- zip up your wallet, take a vacation and come back in a few years to buy stocks at cheap prices.
concept: When promoters with recent success claim that combinations create value beyond the arithmetic, hold to the arithmetic, stay out, and return later when stocks are cheap.
evolution_notes: The lesson Buffett draws from Jimmy Ling and LTV (lines 1623-1643; Ling's maxim on the man who overestimates himself rowed in this batch at lines 1628-1630). "---" is printed so at line 1649. Related: L1997-033 (projected synergies prove illusory), L2014-013 (fanciful synergies and no dis-synergies, this supplement). New in a letter: the recurring promoter described trait by trait, and the response, stand aside and buy later.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Berkshire Today

quote_verbatim: This cheery prediction comes, however, with an important caution: If an investor's entry point into Berkshire stock is unusually high � at a price, say, approaching double book value, which Berkshire shares have occasionally reached � it may well be many years before the investor can realize a profit. In other words, a sound investment can morph into a rash speculation if it is bought at an elevated price. Berkshire is not exempt from this truth.
concept: The price paid decides whether a purchase is an investment or a speculation; even a sound business bought at an elevated price can take many years to show a profit.
evolution_notes: Just before (lines 1672-1674): the chance of permanent capital loss for patient Berkshire holders is as low as any single-company investment because per-share intrinsic value is almost certain to advance (a forecast). Just after (lines 1682-1685): purchases modestly above the level at which Berkshire would repurchase should produce gains in reasonable time; repurchases only "at a price they believe to be well below intrinsic value" (read, not rowed: repeats L1999-032; the same at lines 1791-1792). Related: L2014-012 (value given versus value received, this supplement). New in a letter: the same business called investment or speculation according to the entry price, applied by Buffett to Berkshire's own stock.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: The Next 50 Years at Berkshire

quote_verbatim: For those investors who plan to sell within a year or two after their purchase, I can offer no assurances, whatever the entry price. Movements of the general stock market during such abbreviated periods will likely be far more important in determining your results than the concomitant change in the intrinsic value of your Berkshire shares. [...] Since I know of no way to reliably predict market movements, I recommend that you purchase Berkshire shares only if you expect to hold them for at least five years. Those who seek short-term profits should look elsewhere.
concept: Over a year or two the market's swings outweigh the change in a business's value, which no one can predict, so buy only with a holding period of at least five years.
evolution_notes: The elision skips Ben Graham's "In the short-term the market is a voting machine; in the long-run it acts as a weighing machine" and "Occasionally, the voting decisions of investors � amateurs and professionals alike � border on lunacy" (lines 1690-1692); Graham is off the shelf and his line is left out of the quote. Just after (lines 1698-1702): "Berkshire shares should not be purchased with borrowed money", three falls of about 50% since 1965 (read, not rowed: repeats L2010-019 and L2005-020 in substance, and L2014-005 in this letter). Related: L2014-004 (multi-decade horizon, this letter), L1995-030 (market price outrunning intrinsic value cannot persist). New in a letter: a minimum holding period stated in years.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: The Next 50 Years at Berkshire

quote_verbatim: We will always be prepared for the thousand-year flood; in fact, if it occurs we will be selling life jackets to the unprepared. [...] Financial staying power requires a company to maintain three strengths under all circumstances: (1) a large and reliable stream of earnings; (2) massive liquid assets and (3) no significant near-term cash requirements. Ignoring that last necessity is what usually leads companies to experience unexpected problems: Too often, CEOs of profitable companies feel they will always be able to refund maturing obligations, however large these are. In 2008-2009, many managements learned how perilous that mindset can be.
concept: A company survives anything only if it has, at all times, large and reliable earnings, massive liquid assets and no significant near-term cash requirements; the third is the one profitable companies neglect, assuming maturities can always be refinanced.
evolution_notes: The elision skips Berkshire as "first responder" in 2008-2009, the balance sheet more than doubled, "the Gibraltar of American business" (lines 1706-1708). Just after (lines 1717-1739): earnings from a vast array of businesses with durable competitive advantages; "Cash, though, is to a business as oxygen is to an individual: never thought about when it is present, the only thing in mind when it is absent"; at least $20 billion in U.S. Treasury bills, "When bills come due, only cash is legal tender" (read, not rowed: repeats L2010-020, L2010-021 and L2013-002). Related: L2010-020 (companies assume debts can be refinanced; credit like oxygen), L2010-019, L2002-019 (a fortress of financial strength). New in a letter: the three strengths named together as the test of staying power.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: The Next 50 Years at Berkshire

quote_verbatim: Finally � getting to our third point � we will never engage in operating or investment practices that can result in sudden demands for large sums. That means we will not expose Berkshire to short-term debt maturities of size nor enter into derivative contracts or other business arrangements that could require large collateral calls. [...] Moreover, we will not write insurance contracts that give policyholders the right to cash out at their option. Many life insurance products contain redemption features that make them susceptible to a "run" in times of extreme panic.
concept: Never take on any arrangement, debt, derivative or insurance contract, that lets others demand large sums suddenly, because those demands come in a panic.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the earlier derivative contracts, mispriced and with minor collateral, "quite profitable", and full collateralization on newly-written contracts that "ended our interest in derivatives, regardless of what profit potential they might offer" (lines 1746-1750). Just after (lines 1754-1755): property-casualty contracts carry no such feature, so shrinking premiums reduce float only slowly. Repeats in part L2013-002 (no material short-term obligations), L2010-021 (no contracts requiring collateral postings) and L2008-024 (the lethal threat of posting requirements); new here and rowed for it: the principle stated generally as "sudden demands for large sums", and the bar on insurance policies with a cash-out right.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: The Next 50 Years at Berkshire

quote_verbatim: The reason for our conservatism, which may impress some people as extreme, is that it is entirely predictable that people will occasionally panic, but not at all predictable when this will happen. [...] And if you can't predict what tomorrow will bring, you must be prepared for whatever it does. A CEO who is 64 and plans to retire at 65 may have his own special calculus in evaluating risks that have only a tiny chance of happening in a given year. He may, in fact, be "right" 99% of the time. Those odds, however, hold no appeal for us. We will never play financial Russian roulette with the funds you've entrusted to us, even if the metaphorical gun has 100 chambers and only one bullet. In our view, it is madness to risk losing what you need in pursuing what you simply desire.
concept: Panics are certain but their timing is not, so refuse any risk of ruin however small, and never risk what you need to gain what you merely want; a manager near retirement has an incentive to take such odds.
evolution_notes: The elision skips "Though practically all days are relatively uneventful, tomorrow is always uncertain. (I felt no special apprehension on December 6, 1941 or September 10, 2001.)" (lines 1758-1760). Related: M1999-007 (Russian roulette, 99 percent not good enough when there is no gain to offset the risk; meeting row), M2015-027 (a hundred times too cautious, this unit's meeting), L2010-019 (to finish first you must first finish). New in a letter: the retiring CEO's calculus named, and the need-against-desire rule.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: The Next 50 Years at Berkshire

quote_verbatim: To further ensure continuation of our culture, I have suggested that my son, Howard, succeed me as a non-executive Chairman. My only reason for this wish is to make change easier if the wrong CEO should ever be employed and there occurs a need for the Chairman to move forcefully. [...] In my service on the boards of nineteen public companies, however, I've seen how hard it is to replace a mediocre CEO if that person is also Chairman. (The deed usually gets done, but almost always very late.)
concept: Separate the chairman from the CEO so that a wrong or mediocre CEO can be replaced promptly; when one person holds both posts, removal comes very late.
evolution_notes: The elision skips "I can assure you that this problem has a very low probability of arising at Berkshire � likely as low as at any public company" (lines 1811-1812). Just after (lines 1816-1819): Howard to take no pay, a safety valve to whom any director can go with concerns about the CEO. Just before (lines 1799-1807): directors paid token fees, shares bought in the market, no D&O insurance, "At Berkshire, directors walk in your shoes" (read, not rowed: repeats L2002-035). No earlier v5 row on separating the chairman from the CEO.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: The Next 50 Years at Berkshire

quote_verbatim: Choosing the right CEO is all-important and is a subject that commands much time at Berkshire board meetings. Managing Berkshire is primarily a job of capital allocation, coupled with the selection and retention of outstanding managers to captain our operating subsidiaries. [...] These duties require Berkshire's CEO to be a rational, calm and decisive individual who has a broad understanding of business and good insights into human behavior. It's important as well that he knows his limits. (As Tom Watson, Sr. of IBM said, "I'm no genius, but I'm smart in spots and I stay around those spots.")
concept: A capital allocator who picks managers should be rational, calm, decisive, broad in business understanding, perceptive about people, and aware of the limits of his competence.
evolution_notes: The elision skips "Obviously, the job also requires the replacement of a subsidiary's CEO when that is called for" (lines 1823-1824). The duties repeat L2009-008 (Charlie and I will limit ourselves to allocating capital, controlling enterprise risk, choosing managers and setting their compensation); the qualities are new in a letter and are why the row is written. Tom Watson, Sr.'s line is a third party's maxim spoken by Buffett; related M2006-014 (the same line, circle of competence; meeting row), L1999-020. Related: M2015-044 (the CEO needs both investing and operating experience, this unit's meeting).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: The Next 50 Years at Berkshire

quote_verbatim: Character is crucial: A Berkshire CEO must be "all in" for the company, not for himself. [...] But it's important that neither ego nor avarice motivate him to reach for pay matching his most lavishly-compensated peers, even if his achievements far exceed theirs. A CEO's behavior has a huge impact on managers down the line: If it's clear to them that shareholders' interests are paramount to him, they will, with few exceptions, also embrace that way of thinking.
concept: Judge a CEO's character by whether he works for the company rather than himself and resists pay set by peers; managers below copy the priority he shows.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the note on male pronouns, "gender should never decide who becomes CEO", and "He can't help but earn money far in excess of any possible need for it" (lines 1830-1831). Related: M2015-033 and M2015-034 (a CEO's messages shape what subordinates do, this unit's meeting), M2015-045 (character over record), L2010-006 (cultures self-propagate). New in a letter: the successor's character tested by his restraint on pay and his example to managers.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: The Next 50 Years at Berkshire

quote_verbatim: My successor will need one other particular strength: the ability to fight off the ABCs of business decay, which are arrogance, bureaucracy and complacency. When these corporate cancers metastasize, even the strongest of companies can falter. [...] Their one-time financial strength and their historical earning power proved no defense. Only a vigilant and determined CEO can ward off such debilitating forces as Berkshire grows ever larger. [...] If our non-economic values were to be lost, much of Berkshire's economic value would collapse as well. "Tone at the top" will be key to maintaining Berkshire's special culture.
concept: Arrogance, bureaucracy and complacency bring down even dominant companies whatever their past strength and earnings; a company's economic value rests on its non-economic values, kept by the tone at the top.
evolution_notes: The first elision skips "The examples available to prove the point are legion, but to maintain friendships I will exhume only cases from the distant past" and General Motors, IBM, Sears Roebuck and U.S. Steel, which "sat atop huge industries" and fell to depths their CEOs and directors had thought impossible (lines 1841-1846); the second skips "He must never forget Charlie's plea: "Tell me where I'm going to die, so I'll never go there."" (lines 1850-1851, repeats L2009-004). Just after (lines 1854-1866): delegation as the antidote to bureaucracy, no committees, no required budgets, trust over "streams of directives, endless reviews and layers of bureaucracy" (read, not rowed: repeats L2009-007 and L2009-008). Related: L2010-006 (bureaucratic procedures beget more bureaucracy), M2014-074 (prosperous corporations; meeting row). New in a letter: the three named causes of decay, and past financial strength named as no defense against them.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: The Next 50 Years at Berkshire

quote_verbatim: Our directors believe that our future CEOs should come from internal candidates whom the Berkshire board has grown to know well. Our directors also believe that an incoming CEO should be relatively young, so that he or she can have a long run in the job. Berkshire will operate best if its CEOs average well over ten years at the helm. (It's hard to teach a new dog old tricks.)
concept: Choose a CEO from insiders the board knows well and young enough to serve well over ten years, because a long tenure is what lets the job be learned and relationships be built.
evolution_notes: A Berkshire practice rowed because it states a general principle (the 2004-2005 convention). Just after (lines 1871-1876): "And they are not likely to retire at 65 either"; counterparties in acquisitions and large tailored investments must know and feel comfortable with the CEO, which takes time, "The payoff, though, can be huge." Then (lines 1878-1894): a successor in place; investments handled by specialists reporting to the CEO; "To a large degree, both good and bad cultures self-select to perpetuate themselves" (read, not rowed: repeats L2010-006). Munger's signed text (letter file lines 2169-2171) contrasts the typical CEO who comes in at about 59 and is forced out by a fixed retirement age.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: The Next 50 Years at Berkshire

quote_verbatim: The management system and policies of Berkshire under Buffett (herein together called "the Berkshire system") were fixed early and are described below: (1) Berkshire would be a diffuse conglomerate, averse only to activities about which it could not make useful predictions. (2) Its top company would do almost all business through separately incorporated subsidiaries whose CEOs would operate with very extreme autonomy. (3) There would be almost nothing at conglomerate headquarters except a tiny office suite containing a Chairman, a CFO, and a few assistants who mostly helped the CFO with auditing, internal control, etc.
concept: Range across any business except those whose future cannot usefully be predicted, run them through autonomous subsidiaries, and keep headquarters almost empty.
evolution_notes: From Munger's signed "Vice Chairman's Thoughts � Past and Future" (letter file lines 1919-2178), printed after the FY2014 letter's signature and rowed by the parent session's ruling of 2026-10-04; the first L-rows under MUNGER. Elements (1) to (3) of the fifteen Munger lists (lines 1939-2010); the others are rowed in this batch by line span. Just after the list (lines 2012-2013): "No other large corporation I know of has half of such elements in place." Buffett's letters state the same in substance: L2009-007 and L2009-008 (subsidiaries on their own, no monolith), L1999-020 (circle of competence); rowed here as Munger's own statement of the system.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: Vice Chairman's Thoughts � Past and Future

quote_verbatim: (4) Berkshire subsidiaries would always prominently include casualty insurers. Those insurers as a group would be expected to produce, in due course, dependable underwriting gains while also producing substantial "float" (from unpaid insurance liabilities) for investment.
concept: Hold casualty insurers as a core, expecting them both to make underwriting profits and to supply float for investment.
evolution_notes: Element (4) of the Berkshire system. Munger returns to it at lines 2085-2111: "Marvelously well", and "Ordinarily, a casualty insurance business is a producer of mediocre results, even when very well managed" (rowed in the next batch); he reconciles the two in the same text ("Berkshire's marvelous outcome in insurance was not a natural result"), so no tension row. Related: Buffett's FY2014 letter on float and underwriting discipline (lines 353-561, read, not rowed as repeats; see this note's earlier Rows).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: Vice Chairman's Thoughts � Past and Future

quote_verbatim: (5) There would be no significant system-wide personnel system, stock option system, other incentive system, retirement system, or the like, because the subsidiaries would have their own systems, often different.
concept: Impose no uniform personnel, option, incentive or retirement scheme on owned businesses; let each keep its own.
evolution_notes: Element (5) of the Berkshire system (lines 1939-2010). Related: L1996-018 (the GEICO plan as Berkshire's incentive principles, a subsidiary's own scheme). No earlier v5 row states the absence of a system-wide scheme as a policy.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: Vice Chairman's Thoughts � Past and Future

quote_verbatim: (6) Berkshire's Chairman would reserve only a few activities for himself. [...] (ii) He would choose all CEOs of important subsidiaries, and he would fix their compensation and obtain from each a private recommendation for a successor in case one was suddenly needed. (iii) He would deploy most cash not needed in subsidiaries after they had increased their competitive advantage, with the ideal deployment being the use of that cash to acquire new subsidiaries. [...] (v) He would write a long, logical, and useful letter for inclusion in his annual report, designed as he would wish it to be if he were only a passive shareholder, and he would be available for hours of answering questions at annual shareholders' meetings. [...] (vii) His first priority would be reservation of much time for quiet reading and thinking, particularly that which might advance his determined learning, no matter how old he became
concept: The head of a holding company keeps only a few jobs: choosing and paying subsidiary CEOs with a successor named for each, deploying cash the subsidiaries do not need after strengthening their advantage, reporting as he would want if a passive owner, and above all reserving time to read, think and keep learning.
evolution_notes: Element (6) of the Berkshire system. The first elision skips (i), managing almost all security investments, normally held in the casualty insurers (lines 1960-1961); the second skips (iv), prompt availability to any subsidiary CEO and almost no required contact (lines 1969-1970); the third skips (vi), being an exemplar in a culture that works for customers, shareholders and others before and after his departure (lines 1976-1977). The quote ends before "; and" (line 1979). Just after (line 1984): (viii) "He would also spend much time in enthusiastically admiring what others were accomplishing" (personal conduct, not rowed). Related: L2009-008 (Buffett: allocating capital, controlling enterprise risk, choosing managers, setting compensation), R1996-007 (telling shareholders how we think), M2015-014 (Munger: never satisfied, kept learning, this unit's meeting). Cash deployed only after subsidiaries have increased their competitive advantage is new in a letter.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: Vice Chairman's Thoughts � Past and Future

quote_verbatim: (7) New subsidiaries would usually be bought with cash, not newly issued stock. (8) Berkshire would not pay dividends so long as more than one dollar of market value for shareholders was being created by each dollar of retained earnings.
concept: Pay for acquisitions in cash rather than new stock, and retain earnings only while each retained dollar creates more than a dollar of market value.
evolution_notes: Elements (7) and (8) of the Berkshire system. Munger restates (7) at lines 2116-2117: "Why did Berkshire prefer to buy companies with cash, instead of its own stock? Well, it was hard to get anything in exchange for Berkshire stock that was as valuable as what was given up" (the same lesson, named here, not rowed). Related: R1995-009 (the $1 of market value for each $1 retained test; report row), R1998-001 (prefer to buy for cash), L2014-011 and L2014-012 (Buffett's anniversary text on paying with shares, this supplement).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: Vice Chairman's Thoughts � Past and Future

quote_verbatim: (9) In buying a new subsidiary, Berkshire would seek to pay a fair price for a good business that the Chairman could pretty well understand. Berkshire would also want a good CEO in place, one expected to remain for a long time and to manage well without need for help from headquarters. (10) In choosing CEOs of subsidiaries, Berkshire would try to secure trustworthiness, skill, energy, and love for the business and circumstances the CEO was in.
concept: Buy a good business the buyer can understand at a fair price, with a good long-staying CEO who needs no help; choose CEOs for trustworthiness, skill, energy and love of the business.
evolution_notes: Elements (9) and (10) of the Berkshire system. Related: R1995-014 (Acquisition Criteria: management in place, businesses we understand), L2012-004 (a wonderful business at a fair price; Buffett's anniversary text repeats the blueprint at lines 1348-1350), L1999-016 (skills, energy and devotion of managers). New in a letter: Munger's four qualities for a CEO, love of the business among them.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: Vice Chairman's Thoughts � Past and Future

quote_verbatim: (11) As an important matter of preferred conduct, Berkshire would almost never sell a subsidiary. (12) Berkshire would almost never transfer a subsidiary's CEO to another unrelated subsidiary. (13) Berkshire would never force the CEO of a subsidiary to retire on account of mere age.
concept: Keep what is bought, leave each CEO in the business he knows, and never retire a capable CEO for age alone.
evolution_notes: Elements (11) to (13) of the Berkshire system. Related: R1996-014 (Berkshire's reluctance to sell businesses; report row). Munger's closing (lines 2169-2171) sets the typical CEO forced out "by a fixed retirement age" against this; Buffett's anniversary text (L2014-030) on long-serving CEOs "not likely to retire at 65 either". The CEO-transfer and age elements are new in a letter.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: Vice Chairman's Thoughts � Past and Future

quote_verbatim: (14) Berkshire would have little debt outstanding as it tried to maintain (i) virtually perfect creditworthiness under all conditions and (ii) easy availability of cash and credit for deployment in times presenting unusual opportunities.
concept: Carry little debt, both to stay creditworthy in all conditions and to have cash and credit ready when unusual opportunities appear.
evolution_notes: Element (14) of the Berkshire system. Related: L2005-020 (no significant debt), L2013-002 (supreme financial strength), L2014-023 and L2014-024 (Buffett's anniversary text on staying power and sudden demands, this supplement). New in a letter: low debt justified also as readiness to seize opportunity.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: Vice Chairman's Thoughts � Past and Future

quote_verbatim: (15) Berkshire would always be user-friendly to a prospective seller of a large business. An offer of such a business would get prompt attention. No one but the Chairman and one or two others at Berkshire would ever know about the offer if it did not lead to a transaction. And they would never tell outsiders about it.
concept: Treat a prospective seller with prompt attention and complete confidentiality, so that offers keep coming.
evolution_notes: Element (15) of the Berkshire system, the last. Repeats R1998-001 (complete confidentiality and a very fast answer; report row) in substance; rowed as Munger's statement in his own signed text. Just after (lines 2012-2024): the system's size unusual; Buffett, controlling about 45% at 34, "could install whatever system he wanted"; each element chosen to work under him, not "a one-type-fits-all system for other corporations", and some subsidiaries flourished with different systems (read, not rowed: a history).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: Vice Chairman's Thoughts � Past and Future

quote_verbatim: (1) He particularly wanted continuous maximization of the rationality, skills, and devotion of the most important people in the system, starting with himself. (2) He wanted win/win results everywhere--in gaining loyalty by giving it, for instance. (3) He wanted decisions that maximized long-term results, seeking these from decision makers who usually stayed long enough in place to bear the consequences of decisions. (4) He wanted to minimize the bad effects that would almost inevitably come from a large bureaucracy at headquarters. [...] But, when he saw useful consequences, he strengthened their causes.
concept: Design an organisation to keep raising the rationality, skill and devotion of its key people, to give loyalty to get it, to leave decision makers in place long enough to bear the consequences, and to avoid headquarters bureaucracy; then reinforce whatever turns out to work.
evolution_notes: Munger's diagnosis of Buffett's aims ("over the years I diagnosed several important themes", line 2028). The elision skips (5), the wish "like Professor Ben Graham" to spread wisdom attained (line 2040, Graham named by Munger), and "When Buffett developed the Berkshire system, did he foresee all the benefits that followed? No. Buffett stumbled into some benefits through practice evolution" (lines 2042-2043). Related: L2014-031 to L2014-039 (the elements, this supplement), L2010-006 (cultures self-propagate). New: decision makers kept long enough to bear the consequences, and strengthening the causes of useful consequences found in practice.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: Vice Chairman's Thoughts � Past and Future

quote_verbatim: In particular, Buffett's decision to limit his activities to a few kinds and to maximize his attention to them, and to keep doing so for 50 years, was a lollapalooza. [...] Buffett was, in effect, using the winning method of the famous basketball coach, John Wooden, who won most regularly after he had learned to assign virtually all playing time to his seven best players. That way, opponents always faced his best players, instead of his second best. And, with the extra playing time, the best players improved more than was normal.
concept: Confine effort to a few kinds of activity and give them nearly all attention for a long time; the best capacity is always in play and improves faster with use.
evolution_notes: The elision skips "Buffett succeeded for the same reason Roger Federer became good at tennis" (lines 2062-2063). Just after (lines 2070-2072): Buffett "much out-Woodened Wooden", skill concentrated in one person and improving with age over 50 years. Just before (lines 2047-2059): "Only four large factors occur to me: (1) The constructive peculiarities of Buffett, (2) The constructive peculiarities of the Berkshire system, (3) Good luck, and (4) The weirdly intense, contagious devotion of some shareholders and other admirers", "the heavy freight was carried by the constructive peculiarities, the weird devotion, and their interactions" (read, not rowed: an account of causes, not one of the five kinds; listed in the note for the operator). John Wooden is a third party whose method Munger draws the lesson from. Related: M2006-014 (stay around the spots where you are smart; meeting row).

heading: Vice Chairman's Thoughts � Past and Future

quote_verbatim: Moreover, by concentrating so much power and authority in the often-long-serving CEOs of important subsidiaries, Buffett was also creating strong Wooden-type effects there. And such effects enhanced the skills of the CEOs and the achievements of the subsidiaries. Then, as the Berkshire system bestowed much-desired autonomy on many subsidiaries and their CEOs, and Berkshire became successful and well known, these outcomes attracted both more and better subsidiaries into Berkshire, and better CEOs as well. And the better subsidiaries and CEOs then required less attention from headquarters, creating what is often called a "virtuous circle."
concept: Giving long-serving subsidiary CEOs real power improves them, and the autonomy draws better businesses and managers, who need still less oversight: a self-reinforcing circle.
evolution_notes: Continues the Wooden passage (lines 2061-2072, rowed in this batch). Related: L2009-007 (subsidiaries operate on their own), L2010-006 (cultures self-propagate and repel managers of a different bent), M2013-003 (people have self-selected into the group; meeting row), L2014-030 (Buffett on long-serving CEOs, this supplement). New in a letter: autonomy described as the engine that both improves managers and attracts better ones.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: Vice Chairman's Thoughts � Past and Future

quote_verbatim: Berkshire's marvelous outcome in insurance was not a natural result. Ordinarily, a casualty insurance business is a producer of mediocre results, even when very well managed. And such results are of little use.
concept: Expect a casualty insurer, however well run, to produce mediocre and nearly useless results unless something unusual sets it apart.
evolution_notes: Just before (lines 2085-2106): insurers holding stocks about equal to equity rode the S&P's roughly 10% a year; Ajit Jain's reinsurance, GEICO's quadrupled share, the rest improved "largely by dint of reputational advantage, underwriting discipline, finding and staying within good niches, and recruiting and holding outstanding people"; privately issued securities offered only to Berkshire. Just after (lines 2109-2111): Buffett "would now fail to recreate it if he returned to a small base while retaining his smarts and regaining his youth." Munger's element (4), always to include casualty insurers (L2014-032), is reconciled in this same passage. Related: Buffett's FY2014 letter on the industry's subnormal returns (lines 405-411, read, not rowed; see this note's earlier Rows).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: Vice Chairman's Thoughts � Past and Future

quote_verbatim: Well, Berkshire, by design, had methodological advantages to supplement its better opportunities. It never had the equivalent of a "department of acquisitions" under pressure to buy. And it never relied on advice from "helpers" sure to be prejudiced in favor of transactions. And Buffett held self-delusion at bay as he underclaimed expertise while he knew better than most corporate executives what worked and what didn't in business, aided by his long experience as a passive investor. And, finally, even when Berkshire was getting much better opportunities than most others, Buffett often displayed almost inhuman patience and seldom bought.
concept: Acquisitions go better when no one in the buyer is under pressure to buy, no advisor is paid for deals, the buyer underclaims his expertise, and he waits with extreme patience, buying seldom.
evolution_notes: Answers Munger's own question (lines 2119-2120): why Berkshire's acquisitions outside insurance worked when "the normal result in such acquisitions is bad for shareholders of the acquirer". Just after (lines 2127-2129): in Buffett's first ten years in control, one business near death and two new ones in, "for a net gain of one". Related: L1997-033 (advisors produce whatever projections the CEO wants), L2007-018 (helpers), L2014-018 (bankers paid for action, this supplement), M2014-076 and M2014-077 (strategy and acquisition staff push toward deals; eager only for a deal that makes sense; meeting rows). New in a letter: the four methods stated together, underclaimed expertise among them.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: Vice Chairman's Thoughts � Past and Future

quote_verbatim: What were the big mistakes made by Berkshire under Buffett? Well, while mistakes of commission were common, almost all huge errors were in not making a purchase, including not purchasing Walmart stock when that was sure to work out enormously well. The errors of omission were of much importance. Berkshire's net worth would now be at least $50 billion higher if it had seized several opportunities it was not quite smart enough to recognize as virtually sure things.
concept: The costliest errors are purchases not made; count opportunities missed, not only bad purchases.
evolution_notes: Berkshire's and Buffett's mistake, Munger's lesson. Related: M2001-004 (Munger: the most extreme mistakes are of omission and show up in opportunity costs; meeting row), M2001-006, M1997-083, M2004-039 (Buffett's Walmart purchase stopped for a little more in price; meeting row), L2008-003. New in a letter: the errors of omission put at $50 billion or more.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: Vice Chairman's Thoughts � Past and Future

quote_verbatim: In its early Buffett years, Berkshire had a big task ahead: turning a tiny stash into a large and useful company. And it solved that problem by avoiding bureaucracy and relying much on one thoughtful leader for a long, long time as he kept improving and brought in more people like himself. Compare this to a typical big-corporation system with much bureaucracy at headquarters and a long succession of CEOs who come in at about age 59, pause little thereafter for quiet thought, and are soon forced out by a fixed retirement age. I believe that versions of the Berkshire system should be tried more often elsewhere and that the worst attributes of bureaucracy should much more often be treated like the cancers they so much resemble.
concept: A company is better served by one thoughtful, improving leader over a long tenure and by treating bureaucracy as a cancer than by short-tenure CEOs under fixed retirement ages and a heavy headquarters.
evolution_notes: Munger's answer to his fifth task, whether the results have implications elsewhere: "The answer is plainly yes" (line 2166). Just after (lines 2173-2175): George Marshall won from Congress the right to ignore seniority in choosing generals, "A good example of bureaucracy fixing". Just before (lines 2137-2163): a prediction that results would stay better than normal if Buffett left, Jain and Abel "World-leading" (a forecast, not rowed). Related: L2014-029 (Buffett: arrogance, bureaucracy and complacency) and L2014-030 (internal, young, long-serving CEOs), both this supplement; L2010-006, L2009-008.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: Vice Chairman's Thoughts � Past and Future

quote_verbatim: Well, the best businesses during inflation are usually the best — they’re the businesses that you buy once and then you don’t have to keep making capital investments subsequently. So you get — you do not face the problem of continuous reinvestment involving greater and greater dollars because of inflation. [...] Now, if you’re in a business such as the utility business or the railroad business, it just keeps eating up more and more money, and your depreciation charges are inadequate and you’re kidding yourself as to your real economic profits. So, any business with heavy capital investment tends to be a poor business to be in in inflation and often it’s a poor business to be in generally. And the business where you buy something once — a brand is a wonderful thing to own during inflation.
concept: The business that does best in inflation is bought once and needs no continuing reinvestment; a capital-heavy business under-depreciates, overstates its real profit in inflation, and is often poor in any season, while a brand gains in value.
evolution_notes: Restates M2011-054 (inflation winners need little added capital and can raise prices). Around it: real estate as a one-time outlay priced at replacement value (line 705); See's brand nourished but gaining value in inflation, and Gillette's 1939 World Series radio rights bought in 1939 dollars and paid off in 1960 to 1980 dollars, "So that’s the kind of business you want to own" (lines 707-709). Munger's reply (line 711) on Weimar inflation and Hitler is a political view, not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 2. Businesses that do best in high inflation

quote_verbatim: it’s almost certain we will not take over a large commercial insurance company. [...] And if we bought a big operation, we would have paid a very substantial nondeductible acquisition premium, and this way we’ve actually made money while we’re in the building stage.
concept: Where the right people and capital are in hand, building an operation avoids paying a large, nondeductible acquisition premium and can earn money even while it is being built.
evolution_notes: Restates M2013-014 (building at book value beats buying at a higher price), on the same Berkshire Hathaway Specialty operation. Between the elided parts: the right people, Ajit overseeing, more capital than any commercial insurer so the policies are better than anyone else's. Munger: "Well, I certainly agree with you." (line 731).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 3. Organic growth vs. acquisitions

quote_verbatim: Well, of course, reputation you get over a long period of time. [...] Most of us have to acquire one very slowly, and that was true in Berkshire’s case. And any individual you just have to get the best reputation you can in the years you’re allotted and the time available. And it may work out well, it may work out poorly. But it’s a wise investment. I see, all the time, opportunities come to people where it’s the credibility they’ve gotten in the past that causes them to have the new opportunity. So, I think hardly anything is more important than behaving well as you go through life.
concept: Munger: reputation is acquired slowly and is a wise investment, because past credibility is what brings new opportunities; nothing matters more than behaving well throughout life.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct. Same line, just after: "I think we actually try to behave better as we got more prosperous, and I think you’d be crazy if you didn’t." Then (line 751) no way to guarantee a powerhouse brand. Exchange with Buffett's Agnelli reply at line 757, rowed separately as a separate lesson (2006 convention). Related: M2010-032 (reputation cannot be bought back).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 4. Munger on reputation and behaving well

quote_verbatim: “When you get to be my age,” he said, “Whatever reputation you have, it’s probably the one you deserve.” And I think the same is true of companies. And, frankly, you know, it has helped Berkshire a whole lot that it has gotten a reputation to be a somewhat different sort of company.
concept: Over time a company, like a person, ends up with the reputation it deserves; for a while one can fool people, but not at the end, and a distinct reputation has helped Berkshire.
evolution_notes: Third party's maxim: Gianni Agnelli of Fiat at dinner about 1988 (line 753), spoken by Buffett. Munger supplies "Fool people." at line 755 inside the maxim. Exchange with Munger's reputation answer at line 749, rowed separately. Buffett adds he did not set out to build that reputation exactly.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 4. Munger on reputation and behaving well

quote_verbatim: Would you change the rate for tomorrow on insurance because — from the rate today — for global warming? I doubt it very much. Now, you know, would you change it for 50 years? Might very well. But I think that one year is much closer to one day than it is to 50 years, in terms of focusing on that factor. So, I do not want our underwriters to sit there thinking a lot about — in terms of writing a risk or the price at which to write that risk — I do not want them thinking about global warming. I want them thinking about whether there’s a moral risk involved and who owns the property. I mean, that can be very significant.
concept: Match the factors weighed to the term of the contract: a one-year policy is priced on what can change in a year, so underwriters attend to moral risk and who owns the property, not to slow long-term trends.
evolution_notes: Earlier in the answer (lines 765-767): property-casualty prices are set one year at a time, unlike life contracts priced decades out; on a one-year policy on a $1 billion plant he cares about fire protection and what is adjacent, and a 50-year Florida windstorm policy would need thought about global warming. Moral risk restates L2001-009. The "Marvin the Torch" story follows as a joke. Munger's ideology line (779) rowed separately.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 5. Climate change risk for insurance subsidiaries

quote_verbatim: A lot of people get very invested. It’s like a crazy ideology. [...] It’s just that you can get so excited about it you make all kinds of crazy extrapolations that aren’t necessarily correct.
concept: Munger: people who become emotionally invested in an idea make crazy extrapolations from it; excitement is a warning about one's own forecasts.
evolution_notes: A general principle about behaviour stated inside a policy answer, rowed with the policy left out (the elided sentence is "It’s not that global warming isn’t happening."). Before it (line 771): a lot of guesswork in the field, people "howling about calamities that are by no means sure"; at line 775 he agrees the one-year rate would not change.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 5. Climate change risk for insurance subsidiaries

quote_verbatim: I was at $35, and I don’t change my prices [...] And I said, “Well, in that case, we’ll pay $35.05 and you can say you got the last nickel out of me.”
concept: Set a price for a purchase and hold to it; a seller's advisers get a token nickel at most, not a renegotiation.
evolution_notes: Told as a story with laughter: the 1999 MidAmerican purchase, investment bankers spent a week in Omaha "doing nothing" and asked for something to justify their bill. Buffett's stated ambition since: that the company earn $35.05 per share (line 793).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 6. More oil & gas investments possible despite poor record

quote_verbatim: In the end, we look at the cash, we look at available opportunities, both in investments and businesses, and we make decisions, occasionally, on buying something and sometimes we change our mind.
concept: Capital is allocated by comparing cash on hand against all available opportunities, marketable investments and whole businesses together, and decisions may be reversed.
evolution_notes: Context: ConocoPhillips written down at the auditors' requirement but ended with some profit; "we will not be buying, very often, oil and gas stocks". Line 795: "we have not distinguished ourselves, at all, in the oil and gas field [...] we passed up one or two where we could have made a lot of money", an admission with no lesson stated, not rowed. Line 799: "There were other things we could have done a lot better, but that’s always been true and will continue to be true." Munger's cash-substitute line (797) rowed separately.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 6. More oil & gas investments possible despite poor record

quote_verbatim: And with interest rates being so low and the dividend on ExxonMobil being the size it was, it was not a bad cash substitute, if you think only in those terms.
concept: Munger: when interest rates are very low, a large company's sizeable dividend can make its stock a tolerable substitute for cash, judged only on those terms.
evolution_notes: Munger's justification of the ExxonMobil position; Buffett: "It worked out OK." (line 799).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 6. More oil & gas investments possible despite poor record

quote_verbatim: the idea that you let other people do what they’re best at and stick with what you’re best at, I’ve carried from mowing my lawn to philanthropy, and it’s a wonderful thing to just shove off everything and say somebody else is better than I am at that, and then work in the field that’s most productive for you.
concept: Let others do what they are best at, hand off everything someone else does better, and work only in the field most productive for you.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct. Adam Smith's specialization of labour (the pin makers), named by Buffett as the source, applied to his own philanthropy. Earlier in the answer (line 845) he says the book did not shape his investment philosophy but taught him economics, and recommends Fred Schwed's "Where Are the Customers’ Yachts?". Munger (line 853): "You didn’t do your own bowel surgery, either."
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 8. Buffett on Adam Smith’s “Wealth of Nations”

quote_verbatim: And, you know, if we tell them to think about 100 years, we mean think about 100 years, and I think they know we mean it. They certainly know we run Berkshire, you know, in terms of our own decisions that way. So, I think we set the right example, and I think we use the words to convey that belief as strongly as we can [...] We believe in sort of hammering the same message out there over and over again. Now, we don’t ignore yearly results at all, it’s just we don’t live by them. [...] And I think what really counts, you know, is where we’re going to be three years, five years, or 10 years from now. But I also — I wouldn’t — if we’re subpar in some area, I wouldn’t accept the fact that we’re working to maximize things in 10 years mean that we should be throwing away money, or anything like that, in the short run, or not paying attention to the business.
concept: Tell managers to think in decades, set the example in one's own decisions, and repeat the message constantly; watch yearly results without living by them, but never let a long horizon excuse short-run waste or inattention.
evolution_notes: The questioner asked whether formerly public subsidiaries chase calendar-year earnings; Buffett (line 863) and Munger (lines 865, 869) reject the premise. Between the elisions: he gets monthly figures on virtually every business and reads them with great interest. The compensation part of the question (12-month or multiyear) is not answered.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 9. Subsidiaries aren’t too focused on short term

quote_verbatim: There’s a lot of money that’s come into reinsurance, not because they want to reinsure people, but because it’s become either a fashionable asset class for people that are looking for so-called noncorrelated investments and may not know what they’re doing, but it’s something you can sell people [...] So when you get a whole lot of people that are bringing money in and they sort of need your facade of reinsurance to cover up what their real motivations are, you’re likely to get less attractive prices in reinsurance.
concept: Ask why capital is entering an industry: money that comes for reasons other than the business itself (a saleable asset class, a tax or asset-management facade) drives prices down for everyone.
evolution_notes: Restates M1996-045 (capital brought into an industry gets employed, a warning). Between the elisions: reinsurance as a beard for running an offshore hedge fund without tax. After: the business is "not as good as it was" for the next ten years industry-wide, but "There are certain things that only Berkshire can do", all eight contracts with premiums of a billion dollars or more (line 917). Munger's narrative line (921) and Buffett's refusal (923) rowed separately.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 12. Reinsurance business getting worse due to “facades”

quote_verbatim: They’re searching for a robust narrative. We’re not searching for a robust narrative so we can sell something. We’re playing the game for the long pull and other people just pretend to be doing so.
concept: Munger: promotional capital looks for a story that sells; play for the long pull instead of building a narrative to sell something.
evolution_notes: Just before, same line: "this competition from promotional finance is getting more and more intense and they’re more optimistic." Exchange with Buffett's facade test at lines 915-917 and his refusal at line 923, each rowed separately.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 12. Reinsurance business getting worse due to “facades”

quote_verbatim: We could — we’ve had the opportunity over — for a long period of time — to go out and promote reinsurance-type money, and really take advantage, you know, of people on it, because we would have the best reputation in the field, and we could attract a ton of money, and we could get a big overwrite on it. But it’s not our game.
concept: Do not use a reputation to gather and promote other people's money for fees, even where it would attract a great deal; that game is refused.
evolution_notes: Munger (line 925): "And we don’t particularly admire the way it’s being played." Exchange with Munger's line 921.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 12. Reinsurance business getting worse due to “facades”

quote_verbatim: I mean, I have looked at other people during my lifetime and at these wonderful teachers. They weren’t teachers in the standard definition, but they were people I admired and I thought to myself, “Why do I admire these people?” And if I want to be admired myself, you know, why shouldn’t I take on some of their qualities? [...] If you look around you at the people you like in your school, write down three or four things they do that make you like them, and then look around at the three or four people that turn you off, and write down those qualities, and decide that you’re going to be a person you, yourself, would like, that you’d take on the qualities of the person on the left.
concept: Study why you admire the people you admire, list their qualities and those of the people who repel you, then adopt the first and get rid of the second in yourself.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct, answered to a seventh grader. Restates M2008-115 (study what makes admired people effective and copy it). Buffett lists the qualities after: generous, friendly, good humour, not claiming credit for things you don't do; and to remove: always late, claiming credit, negative on everything (line 939). Munger's opening (line 935) is a joke about getting rich and generous; his marriage line (941) rowed separately.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 13. How to win friends and influence people

quote_verbatim: And it really works in marriage. If you can change yourself instead of trying to change your spouse, that’s a good idea.
concept: Munger: change yourself rather than trying to change the other person.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct; said for a laugh, extending Buffett's answer at lines 937-939. Buffett follows (line 943) with Munger's joke about looking for a partner with low expectations, not rowed.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 13. How to win friends and influence people

quote_verbatim: I’m flying on NetJets. My kids are all flying on NetJets. Our managers, in many cases, are flying on it, so nobody cares more about safety. This is not a company where the CEO flies on his own jet and other people fly in other ways.
concept: Check whether those who run a business use its product on the same terms as the customers; owners and managers who share the customers' exposure care most about its quality.
evolution_notes: Same line, after: "I get the same planes that the other people get and the same pilots. I mean, there’s no special arrangements." Earlier (line 951): judging NetJets by return on the billions in aircraft orders "is not really the right way to look at it" because the planes are resold to owners and the core investment is held largely by the owners themselves; a point about whose capital is employed, named here, not rowed. Labour relations (lines 951-957): hundreds of unions, three strikes in 50 years, "we have no anti-union agenda whatsoever": facts.
