speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 14. NetJets wasn’t a mistake despite labor problems

quote_verbatim: As to the declining business part, the battery business will be a declining business, but it will be around for a very, very, very long time on a worldwide basis. And Duracell has a very strong position. It’s a very good business. [...] it will have unit declines over a period of time, but I think we’ll do fine with the Duracell investment.
concept: A business in a declining industry can still be a good purchase if the industry will last a very long time and the business holds a very strong position in it.
evolution_notes: The tax answer (lines 969-973): neither P&G nor Berkshire would have done the deal at that price without the exchange's tax benefits; Berkshire keeps the old low tax basis, as in a real estate exchange. A fact about the deal, not rowed. Buffett knew Duracell from the Gillette board.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 15. Tax code helped Duracell-P&G deal

quote_verbatim: So the question is, where does it do the most good? [...] So, here these things are that have no utility to me and they have enormous utility to some people in other parts of the world. [...] Charlie and I both like fairly simple lives. But the one thing we do know is we know what we like and what we don’t like, and we don’t judge it by what other people like.
concept: Decide where surplus wealth does the most good, since beyond one's needs it has no utility to the owner; and judge what one likes by one's own standard, not by what other people like.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct. Around it: leave children enough to do real good (line 989); "There’s no Forbes 400, you know, in the graveyard" (line 987); "I don’t have too much advice for anybody, but I would say start thinking about it" (line 991); to a 70-year-old who would wait, "Are you going to make a better decision when you’re 95 with some blond on your lap?" (line 993), a joke. Munger (line 995) on the estate tax change: a political view, not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 16. Why I’m giving away most of my wealth

quote_verbatim: I am much more of a believer, however, in individual philanthropy than corporate philanthropy. I really feel that I’ve got everything I need, but I do also feel that I’m working for the shareholders and they should determine their own philanthropic activities, that it’s their money. [...] I really look at this as a partnership. [...] If they’re not — if they won’t put up their own money, why should they write checks on behalf of all their shareholders? So I’ve got real reservations about corporate philanthropy for the personal reasons, to some extent, of the CEO, or the directors.
concept: Corporate money belongs to the shareholders, who should choose their own giving; a CEO or director who will not give his own money has no business giving theirs, though acquired companies may keep their local community giving.
evolution_notes: Restates M1999-069 (corporate money belongs to the owners; owners designate gifts). The last elision crosses Munger's line 1053 ("my taste for giving away somebody else’s money is also quite restrained"), Munger's one-line restatement of the same lesson, named here, not rowed; Buffett resumes the same thought at line 1055 with the story of being asked to solicit only corporate money from corporate chieftains, and refusing. Between the elisions: subsidiaries are encouraged to continue the giving they did before acquisition, to help the entities that help their employees and customers; the shareholder-designated contributions program, given up "for reasons that" are not stated (lines 1049-1051).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 19. Why individual over corporate philanthropy?

quote_verbatim: You can’t form a business partnership with your frivolous, drunken brother-in-law, you know. (Laughter) I mean, you have to make your partnerships with somebody else.
concept: Munger: choose partners for their soundness; a partnership with a frivolous, unreliable party will strain however noble the design.
evolution_notes: A general principle inside a policy answer on the euro, rowed with the policy left out. The same line goes on: "And I think they lowered their standards a little and it’s caused strains", said of admitting countries that should not have been in the euro. Buffett's euro answer (lines 1071, 1079, 1091) is a political view and forecast, not rowed; his aside at line 1079 rowed separately.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 20. Euro can survive eurozone changes

quote_verbatim: And so — he loves to name names. (Laughter) Praise by name; criticize by category. (Laughter)
concept: Praise individuals by name; criticize only by category.
evolution_notes: Restates M2003-049. Said for a laugh, after Munger names Argentina (line 1077) as a country that could not share a currency.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 20. Euro can survive eurozone changes

quote_verbatim: You always have these things that the investment banker will tell you will produce synergy and all that. Most times that doesn’t work. [...] I think that those two companies will do better if run as two independent businesses than if we try to push through something. We — Charlie and I have seen a lot of things on paper that involve that sort of a proposition and very, very few succeed.
concept: Distrust synergies promised on paper; most fail, and two businesses usually do better run independently than forced together.
evolution_notes: Related: M2010-043 (subsidiaries are not told to trade with each other). Between the elisions: selling auto insurance through dealerships has not been effective historically; paying dealership staff for insurance sales would add cost to GEICO's low-cost model, whose success "depends on delivering first-class insurance at a better price than other people can get". Munger (line 1107): "It’s a very dumb idea, and we’re not going to do it."
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 21. Munger: GEICO synergies are “dumb idea”

quote_verbatim: the interesting thing about silver is that there are some pure silver mines, but overwhelmingly, silver is produced as a by-product, you know, in terms of copper mining and that. So it — it doesn’t respond as much to its own supply and demand characteristics — that’s still a factor — as it does in terms of the supply and demand characteristics of the things of which it’s a by-product, like copper.
concept: For a commodity produced mainly as a by-product, supply follows the main product's economics more than its own price; analyse the host product.
evolution_notes: Buffett no longer follows silver; Berkshire once owned over 100 million ounces (line 1115). Munger: "We didn’t do that well." (line 1117); Buffett: "We made a little money." (line 1119).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 22. Buffett doesn’t follow silver market anymore

quote_verbatim: Well, if it’s run right, there won’t be a premium in breaking it up. It may look like it. I mean, people will say there’s subsidiary A that would sell at 20 times earnings and the whole place would sell, like, at 15. But the whole place won’t sell at 15 if you spin off the one at 20. [...] The best defense against activism is performance.
concept: A well-run conglomerate yields no real break-up premium, since removing the highest-valued part lowers the rest; the defence against activists is performance.
evolution_notes: Between the elisions: the benefit of the subsidiaries filing in one corporate tax return, so the parts are unlikely to be worth more than the whole. After (lines 1135-1137): money pours into activist funds because they have recently been easy to raise money for, and "people are really reaching"; restates M2014-084 (activists seek an event that moves the price). [...] If you had a partnership and the partner wanted to sell out to you at 120 percent of what the business is worth, you’d say forget it. And if he’d want to sell out to you for 80 percent of what it’s worth, you’d take it. It’s not complicated. [...] I’ve been around a lot of managements that announce they’re going to buy X worth and then they buy it regardless of price. And a lot of times the price makes sense. But if it doesn’t, they don’t seem to stop, and nobody tries to — seems to want to stop them.

quote_verbatim: But when profits are good, we want to pay a lower multiple. I mean, because, if we’re going to be in the car business forever, we’re going to have some good years and we’re going to have some bad years. And we would rather buy at a 10 or 12 times multiple of a bad year than buy at an eight times multiple of a good year. And that’s not necessarily the way that sellers think, although they probably understand it, but they don’t want to think that way.
concept: In a cyclical business owned forever, price a purchase against a bad year's earnings, not a good year's; a low multiple of peak profits can cost more than a higher multiple of trough profits.

You’re talking about two different universes. And to attribute the entire difference to the one variable, that they went to college as opposed to the difference between the people who want to go to college and have the ability to get into college —

quote_verbatim: What I noticed that was very interesting is that when the Great Recession came, every successful university in America was horribly overstaffed and they all behaved just like 3G. They all, with a shortage of money, laid off a lot of people. And the net result was they all worked better when it was all over with the people gone. And so this right-sizing is not all bad.
concept: Munger: prosperous institutions become overstaffed unnoticed; forced cuts in a downturn left them working better, so right-sizing is not all bad.

quote_verbatim: But we basically looked for companies where we thought we could understand what the future would look like 5 or 10 or 15 years hence. And that didn’t mean we had to do it to four decimal places or anything of the sort, but we had to have a feel for it, and we had to know our limitations. So we stayed away from a lot of things.
concept: Buy only where one can see roughly what the business will look like 5 to 15 years out; precision is not needed, but a feel for it and knowledge of one's limits are, and much is left alone.

quote_verbatim: We just kept reading and we kept thinking and we kept looking at things that came along, as Charlie described it in the movie, and you know, comparing Opportunity A with Opportunity B. [...] And that always makes for — you know, that’s the — an interesting challenge, always, when you’re measuring something you hold against something that has come along and to see which is more attractive. And we probably leaned very much toward things where we felt we were certain to get a decent result than where we were hopeful of getting a brilliant result.
concept: Keep reading and compare each new opportunity with what is already held; prefer the near-certain decent result over the hoped-for brilliant one.

What’s really admired around Berkshire is somebody who sees it the way it is. [...] But that goes beyond a technique for amassing wealth. To me that’s a moral principle. I think if you have some easily removable ignorance and keep it, it’s dishonorable. I don’t think it’s just a mistake or a lack of diligence. I think it’s dishonorable to stay stupider than you have to be, and so that’s my ethos.
concept: Munger: rationality, seeing things as they are, is a moral duty; keeping ignorance that could easily be removed is dishonorable, not merely a mistake.

[...] We can lose money on individual things, obviously. We can have bad years in the economy, and we can have years the stock market goes down a lot. That doesn’t bother me in the least. What bothers me is if I do something that actually costs Berkshire, in terms of its long-term value, and then I feel, you know, I do not feel good about life on that day.
concept: Judge a year by whether the business built is better than the year before; losses on single items, bad economic years and market falls do not matter, an act that costs long-term value does.

[...] It’s actually a pretty easy game, and it does require a certain emotional stability. [...] between ages seven and about 19, I had that same enthusiasm, but I didn’t really have any guiding principle. And then I ran into “The Intelligent Investor” and Ben Graham. And then at that point, I was able to take all this energy and everything, and enthusiasm for it, and now I had a philosophy that made a lot of sense — total sense — and I found that I could employ, and so the game became even more fun.

[...] If you wrest a fortune from life by being shrewder than other people and buying little pieces of paper, I don’t think that’s an adequate contribution in exchange for what you’re taking.

quote_verbatim: We did not do that when we initially introduced Berkshire's two quantitative pillars of valuation because our insurance results were then heavily influenced by catastrophe coverages. If the wind didn't blow and the earth didn't shake, we made large profits. But a mega-catastrophe would produce red ink. In order to be conservative then in stating our business earnings, we consistently assumed that underwriting would break even over time and ignored any of its gains or losses in our annual calculation of the second factor of value.
concept: In valuing a business, an earnings stream that swings on catastrophes is stated conservatively at break-even, and counted only once it has become steadier.

quote_verbatim: I suggest that you ignore a portion of GAAP amortization costs. But it is with some trepidation that I do that, knowing that it has become common for managers to tell their owners to ignore certain expense items that are all too real. "Stock-based compensation" is the most egregious example. [...] Wall Street analysts often play their part in this charade, too, parroting the phony, compensation-ignoring "earnings" figures fed them by managements. Maybe the offending analysts don't know any better. Or maybe they fear losing "access" to management. Or maybe they are cynical, telling themselves that since everyone else is playing the game, why shouldn't they go along with it. Whatever their reasoning, these analysts are guilty of propagating misleading numbers that can deceive investors.

And, if real and recurring expenses don't belong in the calculation of earnings, where in the world do they belong?", which restates L1998-028. heading: Manufacturing, Service and Retailing Operations

quote_verbatim: Depreciation charges are a more complicated subject but are almost always true costs. Certainly they are at Berkshire. I wish we could keep our businesses competitive while spending less than our depreciation charge, but in 51 years I've yet to figure out how to do so. Indeed, the depreciation charge we record in our railroad business falls far short of the capital outlays needed to merely keep the railroad running properly, a mismatch that leads to GAAP earnings that are higher than true economic earnings. (This overstatement of earnings exists at all railroads.) [...] To embrace reality, however, you should remember to add back most of the amortization charges we report. You should also subtract something to reflect BNSF's inadequate depreciation charge.

(the FY2014 letter said "wire them up for a polygraph test"), restating R1996-023 and L2002-040. heading: Manufacturing, Service and Retailing Operations

quote_verbatim: Both the originator and the packager of these financings had no skin in the game and were driven by volume and mark-ups. Many housing borrowers joined the party as well, blatantly lying on their loan applications while mortgage originators looked the other way. Naturally, the gamiest credits generated the most profits. [...] At Clayton, our risk retention was, and is, 100%. When we originate a mortgage we keep it (leaving aside the few that qualify for a government guarantee). When we make mistakes in granting credit, we therefore pay a price � a hefty price that dwarfs any profit we realized upon the original sale of the home.
concept: The pre-2008 mortgage chain failed because originators and packagers kept none of the risk and were paid on volume; the lender who keeps every loan he makes pays for his own credit mistakes and so makes fewer.
evolution_notes: The mortgage industry's mistake (originators, packagers, Wall Street salesmen), Buffett's lesson. Elided: the salesmen and the rating agencies (lines 876-879) and Barney Frank on Dodd-Frank and proposed 1%-to-5% retention (lines 881-885), a policy passage left out under the political test. Before (line 870): "(When Wall Street gets "innovative," watch out!)". Restates M2015-001 (originator bears no loss), a meeting row; no earlier letter row.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Finance and Financial Products

quote_verbatim: Normally, it is risky business to lend long at fixed rates and borrow short as we have been doing at Clayton. Over the years, some important financial institutions have gone broke doing that. At Berkshire, however, we possess a natural offset in that our businesses always maintain at least $20 billion in cash-equivalents that earn short-term rates.
concept: Lending long at fixed rates on short borrowings has broken important institutions; it is tolerable only with an offsetting holding that gains when short rates rise.
evolution_notes: Before (lines 905-909): Clayton's fixed-rate mortgages financed with floating-rate or short-term debt, "(Incidentally, we would have enjoyed similar margins had we simply bought long-term bonds and financed the position in some short-term manner.)" After (lines 916-919): with $60 billion at 1/4% or less, higher short rates would bring benefits "far exceeding the higher financing costs"; Berkshire "heavily asset-sensitive".
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Finance and Financial Products

quote_verbatim: Historically, the survival of a local electric company did not depend on its efficiency. In fact, a "sloppy" operation could do just fine financially. [...] That's all changing. [...] Those tax credits, or other government-mandated help for renewables, may eventually erode the economics of the incumbent utility, particularly if it is a high-cost operator. BHE's long-established emphasis on efficiency � even when the company didn't need it to attain authorized earnings � leaves us particularly competitive in today's market (and, more important, in tomorrow's as well).
concept: A protected business whose returns never depended on efficiency is exposed when the protection erodes, the high-cost operator first; efficiency kept up when it was not needed is the defence.
evolution_notes: Between the elisions (lines 1134-1137): utilities priced for a prescribed return, "the only business that would automatically earn more money by redecorating the boss's office. And some CEOs ran things accordingly."; and (lines 1139-1141) society's decision to subsidize wind and solar through federal tax credits, left out as policy. After (lines 1147-1150): the Iowa utility's output up with fewer employees and no rate increase for 16 years. Restates M2015-025 (low cost the best defence against distributed energy), a meeting row; related L1997-021 (a low-cost operator welcomes a tough market).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Productivity and Prosperity

quote_verbatim: I can't remember, however, an instance when reading a 10-K's "risk" section has helped me in evaluating a business. That's not because the identified risks aren't real. The truly important risks, however, are usually well known. Beyond that, a 10-K's catalog of risks is seldom of aid in assessing: (1) the probability of the threatening event actually occurring; (2) the range of costs if it does occur; and (3) the timing of the possible loss. A threat that will only surface 50 years from now may be a problem for society, but it is not a financial problem for today's investor.
concept: A list of risks is of little use; what must be judged for each threat is its probability, the range of its cost and its timing, and a threat far in the future is not today's investor's financial problem.
evolution_notes: After (lines 1217-1220): such possibilities are "easy to list but hard to evaluate: Charlie, I and our various CEOs often differ in a very major way in our calculation of the likelihood, the timing and the cost (or benefit)". Lines 1222-1234 list Berkshire's own threats (coal volume, driverless cars, print circulation, storage, online retailing) and end: "We simply adapted. And we will continue to do so."
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Important Risks

quote_verbatim: Nevertheless, what's a small probability in a short period approaches certainty in the longer run. (If there is only one chance in thirty of an event occurring in a given year, the likelihood of it occurring at least once in a century is 96.6%.)
concept: A small yearly probability compounds toward certainty over a long horizon, so a rare event must be planned for as one that will happen.
evolution_notes: Said of a "successful" cyber, biological, nuclear or chemical attack on the United States (lines 1244-1247), "one clear, present and enduring danger to Berkshire against which Charlie and I are powerless"; after (line 1260): "There is no way for American corporations or their investors to shed this risk." Restates M2015-020 (small probabilities recur), a meeting row; no earlier letter row found.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Important Risks

quote_verbatim: It would be foolish, however, for me or anyone to demand 100% proof of huge forthcoming damage to the world if that outcome seemed at all possible and if prompt action had even a small chance of thwarting the danger. [...] Call this Noah's Law: If an ark may be essential for survival, begin building it today, no matter how cloudless the skies appear.
concept: Do not wait for proof of a possible catastrophe when early action might prevent it; prepare for what survival may require while conditions still look calm.
evolution_notes: Said of climate change, in reply to a proxy proposal; the general form is Buffett's own ("Noah's Law"), so it is rowed under the political test with the climate passage left out. Elided (lines 1279-1283): Pascal's Wager (Pascal named as Buffett names him), and "Likewise, if there is only a 1% chance the planet is heading toward a truly major disaster and delay means passing a point of no return, inaction now is foolhardy." Before (lines 1273-1275): climate change "highly likely" a major problem; he has "no scientific aptitude" and remembers the Y2K experts.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Important Risks

quote_verbatim: And such worries might, in fact, be warranted if we wrote ten- or twenty-year policies at fixed prices. But insurance policies are customarily written for one year and repriced annually to reflect changing exposures. Increased possibilities of loss translate promptly into increased premiums. [...] But these increased costs have been promptly matched by increased premiums. So, paradoxically, the upward march in loss costs has made insurance companies far more valuable.
concept: Judge a threat to an insurer by whether its prices can be reset as the exposure changes; rising loss costs passed through each year enlarge an insurer rather than ruin it.
evolution_notes: The example elided (lines 1294-1298): GEICO's loss per policy from about $30 in 1951 to about $1,000 in 2015, driven by inflation in repair costs. After (lines 1301-1311): with unchanged costs GEICO would do $600 million rather than $23 billion; costlier super-cats would likely make the business "larger and more profitable"; "when you are thinking only as a shareholder of a major insurer, climate change should not be on your list of worries."
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Important Risks

quote_verbatim: These two were the best managerial duo � both in what they accomplished and how they did it � that Charlie and I ever witnessed. Much of what you become in life depends on whom you choose to admire and copy. Start with Tom Murphy, and you'll never need a second exemplar.
concept: Choose carefully whom to admire and copy, since much of what one becomes follows from it; Tom Murphy as the exemplar.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct. "These two" are Tom Murphy and Dan Burke of Capital Cities, in a note on Phil Beuth's book (lines 1407-1408). Restates M2007-108 (choosing your heroes) and M2015-085 (Munger: Berkshire copies the right people), meeting rows; no earlier letter row found.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: The Annual Meeting

quote_verbatim: At Berkshire we have hired some wonderful people � and they have stayed with us. Moreover, no one is hired unless he or she is truly needed. That's why you've never read about "restructuring" charges at Berkshire.
concept: Hire no one who is not truly needed, so that there is never a later restructuring to undo the excess.
evolution_notes: Said of the 25-person home office, unchanged through 2015 while revenues rose $16 billion (lines 1523-1527). Restates M1996-043 (no one taken on who is not needed, so no layoffs), M2015-003 and M2015-037, meeting rows; the letter rows on restructuring (L1998-031) are about the accounting charge, not hiring.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: The Annual Meeting

quote_verbatim: They will bounce around from quarter to quarter, and we make no attempt to manage earnings in any way, to have them be smoother. We could do that very easily, but it’d be ridiculous. We make investment decisions solely on the basis of what we think the best investment decision is, not on the basis of how it will affect earnings in any quarter or in any year.
concept: Never manage reported earnings for smoothness; make each investment decision on its merits, without regard to its effect on any quarter's or year's earnings.
evolution_notes: Said of the figures below operating earnings (line 27: "And we always urge you to pay no attention to the figures below operating earnings."), with the euro borrowings' currency swings and the Procter and Gamble exchange for Duracell as examples. Restates R1996-015 (no big baths, no smoothing) and the Owner's Manual's sixth principle (accounting consequences do not influence decisions), reprinted in the FY2015 report (report lines 6496-6501, read, not rowed).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 5. Q1 earnings

quote_verbatim: But we don’t manage, as you know, we don’t manage to try to get any given number from quarter to quarter. We never make a forecast on earnings. We don’t give out earnings guidance. We think it’s silly. We do not have budgets at the parent company level. [...] We just focus, day after day, year after year, decade after decade, on trying to add earning power, sustainable and growing earning power, to Berkshire.
concept: Aim at adding sustainable and growing earning power over decades, not at any quarterly number; no earnings forecasts, no guidance, no parent-level budgets.
evolution_notes: The elision skips "Most of our subsidiaries have budgets, but they don’t submit them, or they’re not required to submit them, to headquarters." (line 39). Earlier (line 33): shares outstanding up only 8.2 percent in the 17 years since the Gen Re merger, against more than 50 percent in the 30-some years before; (line 37) $32 billion of after-tax gains "not important in any given year" except as money to buy businesses. Restates R1996-016 (no guidance) and M2015-033 (eliminate hidden ego incentives, the forecasting CEO).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 6. Share count and earnings

quote_verbatim: The ideal business is one that takes no capital, but yet grows, and there are a few businesses like that, and we own some. [...] because, obviously, if you have a business that grows and gives you a lot of money every year and doesn’t take it — it isn’t required in its growth — you know, you get a double-barreled effect from the earnings growth that occurs internally without the use of capital, and then you get the capital it produces to go and buy other businesses. [...] But capital — increasing capital — acts as an anchor on returns in many ways. And one of the ways is that it drives us into — just in terms of availability — it drives us into businesses that are much more capital intensive.
concept: The ideal business grows without needing capital, so its owner gets both the internal growth and the cash to buy other businesses; a growing capital base drags returns down by forcing the owner into capital-intensive businesses.
evolution_notes: The question quoted the 1987 letter on businesses needing little capital. The first elision skips the wish for a $10 to $30 billion business that is not capital intensive and "that does hurt us, in terms of compounding earnings growth"; the second skips See's and the Buffalo News ($40 million a year, "no capital requirement"). After (lines 49-51): BHE and BNSF take "lots of money", BHE earns 11 or 12 percent, "a very decent return", against a few businesses earning 100 percent on true invested capital. Related: L2009-012 (the best business needs little added capital to grow). Munger's reply rowed separately.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 7. “One of the problems of prosperity”

quote_verbatim: Well, when our circumstances changed, we changed our minds. [...] In the early days, quite a few times we bought a business that was soon producing 100 percent per annum on what we paid for it and didn’t require much reinvestment. If we’d been able to continue doing that, we would have loved to do it, but when we couldn’t, we got to plan B. And plan B is working pretty well. In many ways, I’ve gotten so I sort of prefer it.
concept: Munger: when circumstances change, change the method; when the best course is no longer available, move to the next-best plan and make it work.
evolution_notes: An exchange with Buffett on the same question; Buffett's lesson on capital intensity rowed separately. The elision crosses Buffett's interjection "Slowly and reluctantly. (Laughs)" (line 55); Munger resumes the same thought at line 57. Buffett's reply (line 59), the same lesson in his words, named here, not rowed: "the question is, does it lead you from what looks like a sensational result to a satisfactory result. And we don’t — we’re quite happy with a satisfactory result. The alternative would be to go back to working with very tiny sums of money".
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 7. “One of the problems of prosperity”

quote_verbatim: And Warren would say we buy a business an idiot can manage, because sooner or later, an idiot will. And we did buy some businesses like that in the early days, and they were widely available. Of course we’d prefer to do that, but the world has gotten harder, and we had to learn new and more powerful ways of operating. A business like Precision Castparts requires a very superior management that’s going to stay superior for a long time. And we gradually have done more and more and more of that, and it’s simply amazing how well it works. I think, to some extent, we’ve gotten almost as good at picking the superior managers as we were in the old days at picking the no-brainer businesses.
concept: Munger: businesses so good an idiot could run them are preferred but now scarce; the harder alternative is to buy businesses that need a superior management that will stay superior, which makes judging managers the central skill.
evolution_notes: Buffett's old maxim, quoted by Munger, belongs to Munger at this meeting. The line opens: "Well, in the early days, we used to make wiseass remarks." Heading printed "Precisions Castparts", kept. Buffett before (lines 71-75): Mark Donegan freed from explaining quarterly earnings to analysts and negotiating bank lines; "running a public company, you do waste your time on quite a bit of stuff that isn’t productive". Buffett's separate test that follows (line 79) rowed separately. Related: M2016 heading 7 exchange above (plan B), described rather than cited by id.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 8. Precisions Castparts acquisition

quote_verbatim: but we would love to find another three or four of a similar type to Precision Castparts, where they, forever, are going to be producing something that — where quality is enormously important, where the customers depend very heavily on them, when there’s contracts that extend over many years, and where people don’t simply just take the low bid in order to get this gadget of one sort or another. It’s very important that you have somebody there that has enormous skill running the business, and their reputation, among aircraft manufacturers, engine manufacturers, you know, is absolutely unparalleled.
concept: A supplier worth owning makes something where quality matters enormously, customers depend heavily on it, contracts run many years and buyers do not simply take the low bid, and it is run by someone of unparalleled skill and reputation.
evolution_notes: The line opens: "Yeah, we would love to find — we won’t be able to find them because they’re very rare birds —". Follows Munger's line 77 (the need for superior management), rowed separately. Munger returns to the point under heading 10 (line 107): customers "would be totally crazy to hire some other supplier".
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 8. Precisions Castparts acquisition

quote_verbatim: Well, looking back, I don’t regret that I didn’t make more money, or become better known, or any of those things. I do regret that I didn’t wise up as fast as I could have and — But there’s a blessing in that, too. Now that I’m 92, I still have a lot of ignorance left to work on. (Laughter and applause)
concept: Munger: his one regret is not wising up faster; the work of removing one's own ignorance never ends.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct; Munger's own mistake. Asked what they would have done differently in the search for happiness. Buffett before (lines 87-89): "I did decide, fairly early in life, that my favorite employer was myself", "It’s more fun doing things as a partnership", and "I don’t think I would have started with a textile company". Restates M2014-026 (ignorance removal) and M2015-093 (dishonorable to stay stupider than you have to be).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 9. “Can’t imagine anybody any happier”

quote_verbatim: They’re fine companies. They’re well-managed companies. I like the people that run them. I think their business — the business of the reinsurance companies generally — is less attractive for the next 10 years than it has been for the last 10 years. In part, that’s because what’s happened to interest rates. A significant portion of what you earn in insurance comes from investment of the float. [...] So it was not a negative judgment, in any way, on those two companies. It was not a negative judgment on their managements. But it was a — at least — a mildly negative judgment on the reinsurance business.
concept: A holding in a fine, well-managed company may be sold on a judgment that its industry's economics will be worse for the next decade, when the company is tied to one business model and cannot redeploy.
evolution_notes: On the sale of all of Berkshire's Munich Re and Swiss Re. The elision skips that the reinsurers are more restricted in investing float, lacking Berkshire's capital cushion and unrelated earning power. After (lines 101-103): "all the major reinsurance companies, except for us, is pretty well tied to a given type of business model. They don’t really have as many options"; "The whole idea of float is it’s supposed to be invested at a positive rate", and with negative yields "that game has been over for a while". Before (line 99): the FY2015 letter's forecast that reinsurance will not be as good in the next ten years. Related: L2015-006 and L2013-003 on float.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 10. Reinsurance outlook a factor in Munich Re and Swiss Re sales

quote_verbatim: But, you know, there’s a lot of new capacity in reinsurance and there’s a lot of very heavy competition. A lot of people from finance have come over into reinsurance, and all the old competitors remained, too. That’s different from Precision Castparts, where most of the customers would be totally crazy to hire some other supplier, because Precision Castparts is so much more reliable and so much better. Of course, we like the place with more competitive advantage. We’re learning.
concept: Munger: compare businesses by competitive advantage: one where new capacity floods in and old rivals stay is worse than one whose customers would be crazy to switch suppliers.
evolution_notes: An exchange with Buffett, each stating a separate lesson; Buffett's two rows on reinsurance under this heading are rowed separately. Refers back to Buffett's Precision Castparts test under heading 8 (line 79).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 10. Reinsurance outlook a factor in Munich Re and Swiss Re sales

quote_verbatim: The — to put it in terms of Economics 101 — basically, in reinsurance, supply has gone up and demand has not gone up. And some of the supply is driven by investment managers who would like to establish something offshore where they don’t have to pay taxes, and reinsurance is sort of the easiest beard — what you might call beard — behind which to actually engage in money management in a friendly tax jurisdiction. [...] But that becomes supply in the reinsurance field, and supply has gone up relative to demand, and it looks to me like that will continue to be the case. And couple that with the poor returns on float, and it’s not as good a business as it was.
concept: Judge an industry's prospects by supply against demand, including capacity that enters for reasons other than the business itself (here tax-driven money management), which keeps pricing poor.
evolution_notes: Follows Munger's line 107 in the same exchange. The elision skips "And you can set up a reinsurance operation with very few people, by taking large chunks of what brokers may offer. It’s not the greatest reinsurance in the world, and a couple of the operations that have done that have proven that statement to be right. But nevertheless, it is a very, very easy way to have a disguised investment operation in a friendly tax jurisdiction." Related: L1997-017 (volume follows price), L2010-008 (walk away when the price cannot be had).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 10. Reinsurance outlook a factor in Munich Re and Swiss Re sales

quote_verbatim: Well, I don’t think it’s a tragedy that some competitor got a little better ratio from one period. GEICO’s quadrupled its market share since we bought all of it. [...] I don’t think we should worry about the fact that somebody else had a good quarter.
concept: Munger: judge a competitive position by long-run gains in share, not by a rival's better result in one period.
evolution_notes: Asked whether Progressive's growth and better combined ratio meant GEICO was losing. The elision crosses Buffett's "Quintupled." (line 125) and Munger's own "Yeah, quintupled, all right. (Laughter)" (line 127). Buffett before (lines 117-121): frequency and severity rose suddenly, GEICO adjusted its rates, and "I made a bet a long time ago on — a mental one — on the GEICO model versus the Progressive model."
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 11. Rise in auto death rate hurt GEICO

quote_verbatim: We don’t make any decision involving even the manufacturing of goods, the retailing, whatever it is, without thinking long and hard about what the world will look like in five or 10 or 20 years with that powerful trend — really hugely powerful trend — that you just described. So, we’re not — we don’t look at that as something where we’re going to try and beat them at their own game, you know. They’re better than we are at that. And so, Charlie and I are not going to out-Bezos Bezos, by a long shot. But we are going to think about that.
concept: Test every decision against what a powerful trend will make the world look like in five to twenty years, and do not try to beat a stronger competitor at its own game.
evolution_notes: The question: the shift from push to pull marketing with Amazon. After (line 147): "if I owned a bunch of shopping malls, or something like that, that would be — I’d be thinking plenty hard about what they might look like 10 or 20 years from now." Related: M2000-010 (keep asking whether new technology threatens the businesses owned), M2014-048 (keep asking whether the business can be done better).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 12. Amazon has “disrupted plenty of people”

quote_verbatim: GEICO’s a good example of a company in an industry that had to adjust to change, and some people made the change better than others. We were slow on the internet. The phone had worked so well for us, you know, this traditional advertising, and the phone had worked so well, you know, there’s always a resistance to think about new possibilities. When we saw what was happening on the internet, we jumped in with both feet and you know, with mobile and whatever. But — but there are — capital — the nature of capitalism is somebody’s always trying to figure — if you’ve got some good business — they’re always trying to figure out how to take it away from you and improve on it.
concept: GEICO was slow to the internet because the old method had worked so well; success breeds resistance to new possibilities, while competitors are always trying to take a good business away.
evolution_notes: GEICO's mistake ("We were slow"), Buffett's lesson. Before (line 143): the trend "20 years ago, was not on anybody’s radar screen" and many, "including us, in a few areas", have not figured how to participate or counter it. Related: L2007-004 (competitors will assault any castle earning high returns), L2005-010 (widening the moat daily).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 12. Amazon has “disrupted plenty of people”

quote_verbatim: For one thing, one big advantage we have is we didn’t ever see ourselves as starting out in one industry. [...] So we’ve thought of ourselves as having capital to allocate. If you start with a given industry focus and you spend your whole time working on a way to make a better tire, or whatever it may be, I think it’s hard to have the flexibility of mind that you have if you just think you have a large — hopefully large — and growing pile of capital, and trying to figure out what is the best — next — best next move that you can make with that capital.
concept: Think of oneself as an allocator of capital rather than a member of any industry; an industry identity narrows the mind, while a pile of capital seeking its best next use keeps it flexible.
evolution_notes: The elision skips "I mean, we didn’t go into — we went into department stores — but we didn’t think of ourselves as department store guys, or we didn’t think of ourselves as steel guys, or tire guys, or anything of that sort." Restates L2013-001 (the two-sided appetite widens the field) in a new form; the FY2015 letter makes the same point against one-industry companies (letter lines 1238-1241, not rowed).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 12. Amazon has “disrupted plenty of people”

quote_verbatim: Well, I would say that we failed so thoroughly in retailing when we were young that we pretty well avoided the worst troubles when we were old.
concept: Munger: early and thorough failure in a field teaches what to avoid there later.
evolution_notes: Munger's and Buffett's own retailing failures (in the 2015 PM session Buffett named the Baltimore department store and trading stamps). Same line, after: Berkshire, net, helped by the internet, at GEICO enormously; "our biggest retailers are so strong that they’re — they’ll be among the last people to have troubles from Amazon." Related: M2015 PM row on the Baltimore department store (bad businesses teach the worth of good ones), described rather than cited.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 12. Amazon has “disrupted plenty of people”

quote_verbatim: I think the people who ask questions like that one always make one ghastly error that’s really inexcusable. They measure the detriment without considering the advantage. Well, that’s really stupid. That’s like saying we should give up air travel through airlines because 100 people die a year in air crashes or something. That would be crazy. The benefit is worth the risk.
concept: Munger: never weigh a product's harm without weighing its benefit; judge the two together.
evolution_notes: Asked why owners should be proud to own Coca-Cola given studies linking sugary drinks to deaths. Same line, after: water with flavour, stimulation and calories gives "huge benefits to humanity" and "it’s worth having some disadvantage"; the line ends with a remark on a law for editorials and "I’m sounding like Donald Trump", left out. Buffett's answer before (lines 161-169), on his own calories and longevity, is a personal view and a joke, not rowed.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 13. Defending Coca-Cola from sugar health worries

quote_verbatim: But the great danger in derivatives is if there’s a discontinuity. If there’s not discontinuities, you probably don’t have much of a problem, assuming they get marked to market, and collateralized, and so on. [...] But you will also — when things reopen — you will find there can be enormous gaps in things that you thought were fully protected by collateral, and that sort of thing, or netting arrangements, and that type of thing. So I regard very large derivative positions as dangerous.
concept: Judge derivative exposure by what happens if markets stop: collateral and netting that protect in continuous markets can leave enormous gaps after a discontinuity.
evolution_notes: The elision skips markets that stopped (after 9/11, in World War One, nearly on October 20, 1987) and "if you have a major cyber, nuclear, chemical, biological, attack on the country — which will certainly happen at some point", which restates L2015-009. After (line 207): Gen Re's inherited position lost about $400 million unwinding "in a benign market" "with no pressure on us whatsoever". Line 215: "anything where discontinuities can exist, can be real poison in markets", with Kuwait's delayed settlement as the example. Related: L2002-016 (exposures that look diversified fail together).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 15. Derivatives still a “danger to the system”

quote_verbatim: And you can only come to the conclusion that some trader got somehow — influenced whoever did mark it, or marked it himself, heaven forbid, and probably just influenced someone. Or they didn’t know enough. Some of these things get so complicated, they are very hard to evaluate. That’s the kind that have the most profit in them, usually, so they were quite enthusiastic about those when we were at Solomon. [...] And, you know, the auditors, I don’t think, are necessarily capable of holding that behavior in check.
concept: Distrust the marks on complex derivatives: those hardest to value carry the most profit for the trader, who influences the mark, and auditors cannot be relied on to check it.
evolution_notes: "Solomon" printed for Salomon, kept. Before (line 211): Munger found a position mismarked by $20 million on Salomon's audit committee; Buffett knows of one "incredibly mismarked" position. Munger (line 209): "the accountants blessed that big derivative position as being worth a lot of money. They were only off, what, many hundreds of millions.", the same lesson, named here, not rowed. After (line 213): the same auditor may attest to different marks on the two sides of one transaction. Restates L2002-013 and L2002-014 (estimation errors lean toward whoever is paid on the estimate).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 15. Derivatives still a “danger to the system”

quote_verbatim: Derivatives are still dangerous, in large quantities, and we have — we would not do them, on a collateralized basis, because if there was a discontinuity, I don’t know exactly where we would end up, and I’m never going to get us in a position where we could have money demanded of us and not be able to fulfill it with ease, and with me sleeping well. So we won’t engage in it.
concept: Never enter a position under which money can be demanded that could not be paid with ease; so no collateralized derivatives.
evolution_notes: After (line 215): profitable runoff contracts "does not entice me, at all, into doing any derivative transactions that would involve collateral, when collateral is not required." Restates L2008-024 (no contracts requiring collateral when markets move), L2014-024 (no sudden demands) and L2013-003. Line 217: "If you take the 50 largest banks in the world, we wouldn’t even think about probably 45 of them." Munger (line 219): Berkshire will make about $20 billion from derivatives but would have preferred them illegal for it to buy, "better for our country": a view on policy, not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 15. Derivatives still a “danger to the system”

quote_verbatim: Float is not worth as much to insurance companies now as it was 10 years ago or 15 years ago. And that’s true at Berkshire. I think it’s worth considerably more to us than it is to the typical insurance company, because I think we have a broader range of options as to what to do with it. [...] It’s shown as a liability, but it’s actually a huge asset.
concept: The worth of float depends on what it can earn and on the holder's range of uses for it; at low rates it is worth less to every insurer, but more to one with wider options, and it remains an asset though booked as a liability.
evolution_notes: Asked how negative rates would affect Berkshire. Before (lines 227-229): about $60 billion in short-term governments at a quarter of 1 percent, "almost as painful" as a negative rate. The elision skips that low rates are also a problem for retirees and anyone in fixed-dollar investments, and "We love the idea, however, of increasing our float." Restates L2013-003 and the FY2015 letter's float as revolving fund (letter lines 473-484, not rowed); related M2016-008 (the reinsurers' float).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 16. Float still “useful” despite low interest rates

quote_verbatim: But the decline in coal, for sure, is secular. [...] We don’t — we love the fact we own BNSF. We think we bought it at an attractive price. We’d love to be able to buy a second thing exactly like it at that price. [...] But we don’t mark up, and down, our wholly-owned businesses, based on stock market valuations. Obviously, stock market valuations are some factor in our thinking, but we are not marking our wholly-owned businesses to market because we know we’re going to hold them forever.
concept: Separate a secular decline from a cyclical one, and do not revalue a business held forever on the stock market's swings in comparable companies.
evolution_notes: Asked whether BNSF's value fell with the other western railroad's 30-35 percent fall in market capitalization. The first elision skips the mild winter and utilities' coal stocks, a temporary factor, and "the market, generally, got very enthused about railroad stocks a year or two ago"; the second skips "We’d do it in a second. We’d even pay a little bit more, probably." After (line 247): BNSF "will lose coal volume" and "may lose in other areas, but it will gain in other areas". Related: L2007-016 (judge a holding by earnings, not its price), M2014-048 (a real industry threat no reason to sell).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 17. We still love BNSF despite falling coal shipments

quote_verbatim: Just, all you have to do is figure out what makes sense. And you don’t — you look at buying — when you — when you buy a stock, you get yourself in the mental frame of mind that you’re buying a business, and if you don’t look at a quote on it for five years, that’s fine. You don’t get a quote on your farm every day or every week or every month. [...] You know, you want to look at your stocks as businesses, and think about their performance as businesses. Think about what you pay for them, as you would think about buying a business. And let the rest of the world go its own way. You don’t want to get into a stupid game just because it’s available.
concept: Buy a stock in the frame of mind of buying a business: judge it by the business's performance and the price paid, need no quotation for years, and stay out of games merely because they are available.
evolution_notes: Asked how children should look at stocks when unprofitable companies go public every day. The elision skips the apartment house and the McDonald's franchise, which get no daily quote either. Restates L1993-019 (a part-owner needs no daily quote), M2015-043 (buy stocks like a farm) and the FY2013 letter's farm and building (L2013-005 onward). The envy passage under the same heading (line 279) rowed separately.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 18. Don’t envy people making money from risky behavior

quote_verbatim: Yeah, well, I think that your children are right to look for people they can trust in dealing with stocks and bonds. Unfortunately, more than half the time, they will fail, in a conventional answer. So you — they really have to — they have a hard problem. If you just listen to your elders, they’ll lie to you and make — spread — a lot of folly.
concept: Munger: an investor must find advisers who can be trusted, and conventional sources fail more than half the time and spread folly.
evolution_notes: An exchange with Buffett, each stating a separate lesson; Buffett's two rows under this heading are rowed separately. Buffett replies (line 271): "But they really have an easy problem, in the sense that American business, as a whole, is going to do fine over time." Munger (line 273): "But not the average client of a stock broker." Buffett defers the point to heading 29 (line 279: "I’d rather address that just a little later"); see the note's Tensions seen.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 18. Don’t envy people making money from risky behavior

quote_verbatim: But — just — you don’t want to worry — you don’t want to be — a lot of problems are, as Charlie would say, are caused by envy. You don’t want to get envious of somebody who’s won the lottery, or bought an IPO that went up. You have to figure out what makes sense and follow your own course.
concept: Do not envy others' lucky gains from lotteries or hot offerings; work out what makes sense and follow your own course.
evolution_notes: Munger's view on envy, quoted by Buffett, belongs to Buffett here. Buffett earlier (line 263): "People win lotteries every day, but there’s no reason to have that effect you at all. You shouldn’t be jealous about it." ("have that effect you" as printed). Line 265: those who "do mathematically unsound things" and "one of them occasionally gets lucky" are put on television. Personal conduct as well as investing.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 18. Don’t envy people making money from risky behavior

quote_verbatim: We don’t think we can predict commodity prices. We don’t hedge cocoa or sugar (inaudible). We do some forward buying of chocolate coatings or something of the sort. But basically, we are not two fellows who think we can predict the price of soybeans or corn or oil or anything else. So, anything you have seen in our investment transactions — some of those securities you mentioned there were bought by Todd or Ted, and one was bought by me — but neither they nor I bought those, or if we sell them, sell them, based on commodity price predictions. We don’t know how to do it.
concept: No purchase or sale is made on a forecast of commodity prices, which cannot be predicted.
evolution_notes: Asked whether buying Phillips 66 and Kinder Morgan was a statement about oil. Before (line 317): "We haven’t the faintest idea what the long-term price of oil was"; a forward purchase of oil made once, Munger (line 319): "Cashed it in too soon, too." After: "And we’re thinking about other things when we make those decisions." Munger (line 323): "I’m even more ignorant than you are." Restates L2013-009 (no macro or market forecasts) and M2015-016 (no macro).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 20. We don’t buy or sell based on commodity price predictions

quote_verbatim: But I was the trustee of a college that saw the endowment go from $8 million to over a billion. And I didn’t see the tuition come down. And I didn’t see the number of students go up. [...] But when you read the figures on endowment of the big schools, you know, and some of them have really got up in the big numbers, the main objective of the people running the endowment is to have the endowment grow larger. And that will be ever thus. That is the way humans operate.
concept: Expect the people who run a pool of money to aim at making the pool larger rather than at the purpose it serves; that is how humans operate.
evolution_notes: The elision crosses Munger's "Nothing went up, except the professors’ salaries." (line 355) and Buffett's "Yeah. From 8 million to a billion. I mean — and very, very decent people running the place." (line 357). Munger earlier (line 349): "Monopoly has kind of — and bureaucracy — have kind of pernicious effects everywhere, and the universities aren’t exempted from it.", a related general line, named here, not rowed. Buffett's K-12 spending as an entitlement for the young (line 351) is a political view, left out. Related: M2015-033 (hidden ego incentives).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 21. Don’t expect efficiency in higher education

quote_verbatim: You can change the math of banking, and the attractiveness of banking, totally, by capital requirements. Obviously, if you said every bank had to be 100 percent equity, it would be a terrible business. You couldn’t possibly earn any money that was significant on capital. And if you let people operate with 1 percent capital ratios, they can make a lot of money and they will cause the system all kinds of trouble. [...] And that just means returns on equity go down, but returns on equity were awfully high prior to that. So it doesn’t — it hasn’t turned it into a bad business, it’s turned it into a less attractive business than earlier.
concept: A bank's attractiveness turns on the capital it must hold: more required equity lowers returns on equity, too little produces large profits and systemic trouble.
evolution_notes: The elision skips "So, since 2009, the rules have been tilted against the larger banks by — primarily — through capital requirements.", and the line opens with public policy since 2008-9 designed to make very large banks less profitable: the policy left out under the political test, the general form being Buffett's own. After (lines 415-419): Wells Fargo bought as "a very well run bank", "weighted for upside and downside", not for investment banking. Munger (line 423): "No, I think, generally, we fear the genre more than we love it.", of investment banks, a view, named here, not rowed.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 24. Berkshire indifferent to Wells Fargo’s investment banking

quote_verbatim: I think the more important factor would be that Berkshire will always be in a position to repurchase very significant amounts of stock, and as long as it’s willing to buy that stock at some price — and it should be — close to intrinsic value, there should not be a large margin, in terms of anybody that might come along and think there’d be a lot money to be made by breaking up. There would be money lost by breaking it up, in terms of we’d lose — there’d be certain advantages lost. MidAmerican Energy could not have done what it has done in renewables without Berkshire being the parent. I mean, if it had been split off, it would have been worth — the parts would have been worth — less than the whole.
concept: A company willing to repurchase its stock at a price close to intrinsic value keeps the discount too small for anyone to profit by breaking it up, which matters where the parts are worth less than the whole.
evolution_notes: Asked whether activists will target Berkshire at a discount to intrinsic value and whether defences are needed. The line opens: "Yeah, I used to worry more about that than I do now. Partly, size is one factor." After (line 433): in 1973-74 good companies such as Cap Cities sold at huge discounts with little activity, "when the discounts are huge, money is hard to get". Related: L1999-032 (buy back only well below conservative value), L2011-003. Munger (lines 437-441): Berkshire is the strong ally others would pick against attackers: a view.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 25. “Very, very unlikely” activists could break up Berkshire

quote_verbatim: Leasing, generally, isn’t something that will — we have to bring something to the party. [...] But pure leasing — leasing of new cars, which is a huge business — the math is not that attractive for us. The banks have an advantage over us because their cost of funds is so low now. [...] So, pure money-type leasing is not an attractive business for us when we’ve got other people with a lower cost of funds. I mean, they’ve got the edge. [...] And some people have done well in it by, in recent years, by using short-term money to finance longer-term assets which have big residual risks, and that just isn’t for us.
concept: Enter a business only where one brings something to the party; a pure financing business belongs to whoever has the lowest cost of funds, and financing long assets with big residual risk on short money is to be avoided.
evolution_notes: The first elision skips XTRA's service advantages, "much more than just handing people a trailer and taking a check every month"; the second, Wells Fargo's funds at about 10 basis points; the third, railcar repair and servicing, and "aircraft leasing doesn’t interest me in the least [...] And that’s a scary business." Restates M2015-011 (no finance edge against the banks) and L2015-006 (lend long, borrow short). Munger (line 455): "I don’t agree that we have huge opportunities."
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 26. No interest in “pure” leasing businesses

quote_verbatim: And — and the real — what we want our managers to be doing, you know, is thinking every day about how to achieve a stronger competitive position. We call it “widening the moat.” But, we want to turn out better products, we want to keep our costs down to a minimum, you know, we want to be thinking about what our customer’s likely to be wanting from us, you know, a month, a year, 10 years from now. And, generally, if you take care of your customer, the customer takes care of you.
concept: Managers should work every day to widen the moat: better products, costs at a minimum, and anticipating what customers will want a month to ten years out.
evolution_notes: Asked which competitor he would take out with a silver bullet. Restates L2005-010 (widening the moat by daily acts). Munger (line 475): "We’re not targeting competitors for destruction. We’re just trying to do the best we can everywhere.", the same lesson, named here, not rowed. The rest of the line (an unanswerable force, the Baltimore store) rowed separately.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 27. “We’re not targeting competitors for destruction”

quote_verbatim: But there are cases where there is some force coming along that really is — you may not have the answer for it. And then, you know, you get out of that business. We had that department store in Baltimore in 1966, and if we’d kept it, we would have gone out of business. So, recognizing reality is also important. I mean, you do not want to try and fix something that’s unfixable.
concept: When a force arrives that a business has no answer to, recognize it and get out rather than try to fix the unfixable; the Baltimore department store would have failed had it been kept.
evolution_notes: Buffett's own mistake (buying the Baltimore store in 1966), with the lesson drawn from having sold it. Follows the moat passage on the same line, rowed separately. Related: the Owner's Manual's eleventh principle, reprinted this year (report lines 6579-6594, read, not rowed): textiles closed only when "doomed to run never-ending operating losses"; M2016-012 (do not out-Bezos Bezos).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 27. “We’re not targeting competitors for destruction”

quote_verbatim: And we said there were two people that we admired enormously in the investment business, not simply because they were terrific investors, but they were terrific people. And they would be the kind of people that you’d make trustee of your will.
concept: Recommend a money manager for character as well as skill: someone one would make trustee of one's will.
evolution_notes: On the advice given his partners in 1969, naming Sandy Gottesman and Bill Ruane. Line 487: Sequoia let partners with small sums reach "an outstanding investment manager, like I say, both for ability and for integrity". Restates M2015-045 (character over record).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 28. Sequoia Fund was “overly entranced” by Valeant

quote_verbatim: So, I think it was a very unfortunate period when the manager got overly entranced with a business model, which, [...] In my view, the business model of Valeant was enormously flawed. [...] But it illustrated a principle that Pete Kiewit, I think, said many, many years ago. He said if you’re looking for a manager, find somebody that’s intelligent, energetic, and has integrity. And he said that if they don’t have the last, be sure they don’t have the first two. If you’ve got somebody that lacks integrity, you want them to be dumb and lazy. You know — and if you get an intelligent, energetic guy, or woman, who is pursuing a course of action which, if put on the front page, you know, would make you very unhappy, you can get in a lot of trouble. It may take a while.
concept: Sequoia's manager was taken with Valeant's business model and its managers; the lesson is the old one: look for intelligence, energy and integrity, and without integrity the first two only make a manager more dangerous.
evolution_notes: The Sequoia manager's mistake (an unusually large position in Valeant, maintained and increased despite board doubts, lines 489-491), Buffett's lesson. Pete Kiewit's maxim belongs to Buffett here. The first elision skips the Senate hearings, "it was not a pretty picture"; the second, "It had been touted to us. We had several people who urged us, strongly, to buy Valeant, and wanted us to meet Pearson, and all that sort of thing." Restates M1997-115 and M2005-003 (brains, energy, integrity) and M2008-011 (the front-page test). Munger (line 501): "Valeant, of course, was a sewer": a view.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 28. Sequoia Fund was “overly entranced” by Valeant

quote_verbatim: You get — pattern recognition gets very important in evaluating humans and businesses. And, the pattern recognition isn’t 100 percent, and none of the patterns exactly repeat themselves, but there’re certain things in business and securities markets that we’ve seen over and over, and that frequently come to a bad end, but frequently look extremely good in the short run. [...] You’re going to see chain letters the rest of your life. Nobody calls them chain letters because that has a connotation that will scare you off. But they’re disguised chain letters. And many of the schemes in Wall Street that are designed to fool people have that particular aspect to it.
concept: Judge people and businesses by recognizing patterns seen before that look very good in the short run and end badly, above all the disguised chain letter.
evolution_notes: The elision skips "One, which I talked about last year — I’m not referring to Valeant in this regard — is the chain letter scheme, the disguised chain letter." After (line 495): "there were patterns at Valeant that I think [...] really should have been picked up on". Restates M2000-006 and M2000-008 (chain-letter mathematics) and L2014-014 (serial issuance like a chain letter).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 28. Sequoia Fund was “overly entranced” by Valeant

quote_verbatim: Now what’s their result going to be? Their result is going to be exactly average, as how America business does, because they own half of all of it. They have no expenses, no nothing. [...] This half is going to have the same gross results — you’re going to have the same results as the low-energy — no-energy people, and they’re also going to have terrific expenses, because they’re all going to be moving around, hiring hedge funds, hiring consultants, paying lots of commissions and everything. And that half, as a group, has to do worse than this half. The people who don’t do anything have to do better than the people that are trying to do better. It’s that simple.
concept: As a group, active investors earn the same gross result as passive ones and pay far more in costs, so the passive must do better than those trying to do better.
evolution_notes: Reporting the ten-year bet against Ted Seides's five funds of funds: after eight years the Vanguard S&P index is "40some points ahead" (line 509, as printed). Line 511: two managers each running $9 billion for Berkshire would get "$180 million each, you know, merely for breathing" on 2-and-20, "a compensation scheme that is unbelievable to me, and that’s one reason I made this bet". The elision skips the "hyperactives", whose gross result "is also going to be half". Restates L2007-018 (active investors must trail passive ones), M1997-031 and L2005-018. Buffett calls this (line 15) "probably the most important investment lesson in the world".
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 29. Buffett leads in wager against hedge funds

quote_verbatim: But I will guarantee you that no endowment fund, no public pension fund, no extremely rich person, wants to sit in that part of the auditorium. They just can’t believe that because they have billions of dollars to invest that they can’t go out and hire somebody who will do better than average. [...] and no consultant in the world is going to tell you, just buy an S&P index fund and sit for the next 50 years. You don’t get to be a consultant that way. And you certainly don’t get an annual fee that way. So the consultant’s got every motivation in the world to tell you, this year I think we should concentrate more on international stocks, or this year this manager is particularly good on the short side.
concept: Large and rich investors cannot believe their money cannot buy above-average results, and the consultants they hire are paid to recommend activity, never the index fund.
evolution_notes: The elision skips "I hear from them all the time. So this group over here, supposedly sophisticated people, generally richer people, hire consultants," (line 517). After (lines 517-519): consultants recommend managers who charge fees that "cumulatively eat up capital like crazy", and "always change the recommendations a little bit from year to year. They can’t change them 100 percent, because then it didn’t look like they knew what they were doing the year before"; pension funds taken through the math still hire consultants. Restates M2008-057 (no one is paid to recommend the index fund) and L2005-017.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 29. Buffett leads in wager against hedge funds

quote_verbatim: So I hope you realize that for most — for the population as a whole — American business has done wonderfully, and the net result of hiring professional management, you know, is a huge minus. [...] It’s so obvious, and yet all the commercial push is behind telling you that you ought to think about doing something today that’s different than you did yesterday. You don’t have to do that. You just have to sit back and let American industry do its job for you.
concept: For the population as a whole, hiring professional investment management is a large net minus; resist the commercial push to act and simply own American business.
evolution_notes: The elision skips Fred Schwed's "Where Are the Customer’s Yachts?" (as printed), read at about ten, whose lesson "is told in that book from 1940". Before (line 521): "the flow of money from the hyperactive to what I call the helpers is dramatic". Restates L1996-034 and L2013-014 (the index fund) and L2005-018 (sit still). Answers Munger's "hard problem" under heading 18 (M2016-023).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 29. Buffett leads in wager against hedge funds

quote_verbatim: Well, you’re talking to a bunch of people who have solved their problem by buying Berkshire Hathaway. (Laughter) That worked even better. And there have been a few of these managers, the managers — [...] — who’ve actually succeeded. They are a few in the universities who are really good. But it’s a tiny group of people. It’s like looking for a needle in a haystack.
concept: Munger: a few professional managers really do succeed, but finding one is like finding a needle in a haystack.
evolution_notes: The elision crosses Buffett's "Sure." (line 525); Munger resumes the same sentence at line 527. An exchange with Buffett, who states a separate lesson after (line 529), rowed separately. Restates M2008-056 (very skilled professionals are rare).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 29. Buffett leads in wager against hedge funds

quote_verbatim: But the — the people — there’s been far, far, far more money made by Wall — by people in Wall Street — through salesmanship abilities than through investment abilities. There are a few people out there who are going to have an outstanding investment record. But there are very few of them, and the people you pay to have identify them don’t know how to identify them. And — and they do know how to sell you.
concept: Wall Street earns more by salesmanship than by investment skill; the rare outstanding managers exist, but those paid to find them cannot identify them and can only sell.
evolution_notes: Before (line 529): in 1969 he could name only two managers (Ruane and Gottesman), Walter Schloss "would not scale up well", and those who stayed with Sequoia "have been well-served". "have identify them" as printed. After: "That’s my message." The morning session ends here (line 531 begins the Afternoon Session). Related: M2004-060 (brokers' advice does worse than an index fund).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 29. Buffett leads in wager against hedge funds

quote_verbatim: When you look at what has happened, you know, just take Amazon, you have to — you want to try a lot of things, and it amazed me how fast the inquiries on personal auto migrated from phone to the internet [...] So the answer is, we’ll try various things and we’ll make some mistakes, and my guess is that 10 and 20 and 30 years from now, it’ll be a lot different.
concept: Where a channel of selling may shift, try various things and accept some mistakes, since customers adapt faster than expected and the channel will look very different in decades.
evolution_notes: Asked whether commercial insurance can go direct as GEICO did in personal auto. Before (line 539): two online arrangements, one run by Applied Underwriters and one by Ajit, plus some commercial auto through GEICO, "we will be experimenting more with various insurance lines." Restates M2015-036 (experiment with channels).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 1. Sell commercial insurance on the internet?

quote_verbatim: The main — by far, the main factor in keeping Berkshire’s culture is that you have a board and you’ll have successor board members. You have managers and you’ll have successor managers. And you have shareholders that clearly recognize the special nature of the culture, that have embraced the culture. When they sold their businesses to us, they wanted to join that culture. It’s a — it thrusts out people that really aren’t in tune with it, and there are very few of them.
concept: A culture lasts when its board, managers and shareholders have each chosen it and successors are drawn from those who embraced it; such a culture expels those not in tune with it.
evolution_notes: Asked how the culture survives once Howard Buffett no longer serves as non-executive chairman. Before (line 549): a non-executive chairman makes it easier to correct a mistake in selecting a successor, "a 1-in-100 or 1-maybe-in-500 probability, but there’s no sense ignoring it totally. It’s not a key factor." Munger (line 557): "I really think the culture is going to surprise everybody — how well it lasts". Restates M2013-003 (a self-selected culture rejects foreign behaviour).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 2. Our culture will endure for “many, many decades”

quote_verbatim: I think that the main problem that Berkshire will have will be size, and I’ve always — I thought that when I was managing money, when I first started managing money. Size is the enemy of performance to a significant degree.
concept: Size works against investment performance to a significant degree, a view held since the first days of managing money.
evolution_notes: Same answer as the culture passage at line 549. After: "But I do think that the culture of Berkshire adds significantly to the value of the individual components viewed individually." Related: M2014-043 and M2014-085 (what Berkshire's size forces it to buy).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 2. Our culture will endure for “many, many decades”

quote_verbatim: You know, without a retirement age, and I tend to bring that up at every meeting to reinforce the idea, the — but without a retirement age and with people working because they love their jobs — and they like the money as well — but their primary motive is that they really like accomplishing what they do in their jobs. And that means that we get long tenure out of our managers. So the turnover is low, the directors are not here for the money, and so we have great tenure among the directors, and I would argue that’s a huge plus.
concept: With no retirement age and managers and directors who work for the accomplishment rather than the money, tenure is long and turnover low, which is a large advantage.
evolution_notes: Same answer. Before (line 567): "the number of managers that have been needed, that we’ve had to replace in the last ten years, are very few." The other side of the same practice is M2009-097 (with no retirement age, decline must be judged case by case and the owners have been slow to act).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 2. Our culture will endure for “many, many decades”

quote_verbatim:
We are looking for people who are business savvy, shareholder oriented, and have a special interest in Berkshire. [...] So I think we’ve got — we will continue to apply that test: business savvy, shareholder oriented, and with a strong personal interest in Berkshire. And every share of Berkshire that our shareholders own, they bought just like everybody else in this room. [...] We want our shareholders to walk in the shoes — I mean, our directors to walk in the shoes of shareholders.

We want them to care a lot about the business, and we want them to be smart enough so that they know enough about business that they know what they should get involved in and what they shouldn’t get involved in.
concept: Choose directors by three tests, business savvy, shareholder orientation and a strong personal interest in the company, with shares bought like any owner's, so that they walk in the shareholders' shoes and know what to get involved in.
evolution_notes: Asked whether diversity should be considered for leadership and board roles and in valuing a company; Buffett answers no to the last part. The policy question is left out of the quote. The first elision crosses Munger's one-word interjection (line 585, "Yeah.") and the passage on Theranos's big-name board and directors who serve for $2-300,000 a year or prestige; Buffett resumes the same thought. "every share of Berkshire that our shareholders own" is printed so and the context (directors given stock "for breathing") shows directors are meant; kept as printed.
