Restates L2006-014 (does he think like an intelligent owner) and M2007-127 (an owners' board, stock they bought).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 3. Diversity isn’t a factor in choosing Berkshire directors

quote_verbatim: And the archbishop looked at him like he was an idiot and said, “Mr. Peeler,” he says,” last year I had some very serious surgery, and I did not look around for the leading Catholic surgeon.” That’s the way I feel about board members.
concept: Munger: board members, like surgeons, are chosen for competence at the work, not for belonging to a category.
evolution_notes: Stated as a story, in the same diversity answer; the policy question is left out and the general form is Munger's own ("That’s the way I feel about board members"). Before: years ago he worked for the Roman Catholic Archbishop of Los Angeles, and his senior partner said there were plenty of good Catholic tax lawyers. The quotation marks around the archbishop's words are printed unbalanced ("he says,” last year"); kept as printed.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 3. Diversity isn’t a factor in choosing Berkshire directors

quote_verbatim: I mean, if you can buy dollar bills for anything less than a dollar, you know, there’s no more certain way of making money. On the other hand, I don’t particularly like — enjoy the actual act of buying out people who are my partners at a price that is below — well below what I think the stock is worth. [...] But we would do it in a manner where we were not propping the stock at any given level. And if it happens, it will be very good for the stockholders who continue.
concept: Repurchasing below value is the surest way to make money per share for continuing owners, though it means buying out partners below worth; it is done without propping the price.
evolution_notes: Asked whether to raise the 1.2 times book threshold. Before (line 605): the stock has come close to but not hit 1.2, "or we would’ve done it"; the threshold was raised from 1.1 because acquired businesses widened the gap between carrying value and intrinsic value. Elided: "So — but we will buy stock, almost certainly. We don’t make it a 100 percent pledge [...]". After (line 609): the threshold acts as a backstop making a no-dividend policy return at least $1.20 for each dollar left in. Restates M2004-086 (prop the price or serve continuing owners) and M2015-074 (a partner buying out a partner).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 4. Buffett’s “mixed emotions” on Berkshire buybacks

quote_verbatim: you don’t want to keep accumulating so much money that it burns a hole in your pocket. And it’s been said, actually, that — you know, that a full wallet is a little like a full bladder, that you may get an urge fairly quickly to pee it away, and we don’t want that to happen.
concept: Accumulated cash creates an urge to spend it, so do not let it pile up to that point; if capital cannot be used well inside the company, raising the repurchase threshold is the outlet.
evolution_notes: Same answer. Before (line 611): "if it really becomes apparent that we can’t use capital effectively within the company, in the quantities with which it’s being generated, then at some point the threshold might be moved up a little because it could still be attractive to buy it." The full-wallet saying is attributed to no one ("it’s been said"). The demonstrable-margin passage later on the same line is a separate row in this batch.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 4. Buffett’s “mixed emotions” on Berkshire buybacks

quote_verbatim:
Anytime you can buy stock in for less than it’s worth, it’s advantageous to the continuing shareholders, and — but it should be by a demonstrable margin.

You can’t — intrinsic value can’t be that finely calculated that you can figure it out to four decimal places or anything of the sort.
concept: A buyback below worth helps continuing owners, but the discount must be demonstrable, because intrinsic value cannot be calculated finely.
evolution_notes: Same answer, closing it; the full-wallet passage earlier on line 611 is a separate row in this batch. Restates M2009-049 (repurchase only when demonstrably below conservatively estimated intrinsic value).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 4. Buffett’s “mixed emotions” on Berkshire buybacks

quote_verbatim: Can you imagine somebody going out and saying, we’re going to buy a business and we don’t care what the price is? You know, we’re going to spend $5 billion this year buying a business, we don’t care what the price is. But that’s what companies do when they don’t attach some kind of a metric to what they’re doing on their buybacks. [...] It’s got nothing to do with preventing dilution. I mean, if you’re — dilution by itself is a negative and buying back your stock at too high a price is another negative. So it has to be related to valuation.
concept: A buyback is a purchase and must carry a price metric tied to valuation; buying back to offset dilution adds a second negative to the first.
evolution_notes: Exchange. Munger (line 615): "it’s gotten quite common to buy back stock at very high prices that really don’t do the shareholders any good at all. I don’t know why people exactly are doing it. I think it gets to be fashionable." Buffett (line 617): "It’s fashionable and they get sold on it by advisors." Elided (line 621): companies should say they will buy back "if it’s advantageous", and Jamie Dimon is explicit about buying below intrinsic value; (line 623) he has sat on boards that voted buybacks "to prevent dilution or something like that." After: "you will not find a lot of press releases about buybacks that say a word about valuation." Restates M2006-042 and M2009-048 (fashionable buybacks at any price).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 4. Buffett’s “mixed emotions” on Berkshire buybacks

quote_verbatim: So we really had to take our foot off the gas pedal because the last thing in the world we want to do, you know, is make first impressions with delivery problems — accompanied by delivery problems.
concept: Slow a new operation's growth rather than let poor service shape customers' first impressions; expand once service meets the standard.
evolution_notes: Asked how the Dallas Furniture Mart is doing. Before (line 641): the store generated so much initial volume that it had a delivery problem, as Kansas City had. After: deliveries now meet the Omaha standards, "But that wasn’t the case for some months"; (line 643) "We’re getting ready to step on the gas."
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 5. New Nebraska Furniture Mart store in Dallas doing big business

quote_verbatim: But I just don’t know — the offense can be ahead of the defense, and that’s — you can win the game 99.99 percent of the time, but eventually anything that has any probability of happening, you know, will happen.
concept: Anything with any probability of happening eventually will happen, however often the defense wins.
evolution_notes: Asked whether he would fund lobbying on cyber, nuclear, chemical and biological attack; the policy and philanthropy are left out of the quote. Before (line 653): "As I put in the annual report, it’s the only real threat to Berkshire’s economic — external threat to Berkshire’s economic well-being over time." (line 659): "being in the insurance business [...] you know that someday somebody will pull off something on a very, very, very big scale". Restates L2015-009 (a small probability compounds toward certainty), M2004-062 and M2015-020.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 6. Buffett’s concerns about weapons of mass destruction

quote_verbatim: In terms of the businesses we buy, and we — when we buy stocks, we look at it as buying businesses, so they’re very similar decisions — we try to know all, or as many as we can know, of the microeconomic factors.
concept: A stock purchase is a business purchase, and for either the aim is to know as many of the business's microeconomic factors as can be known.
evolution_notes: Exchange. Buffett first answered about macroeconomic factors (line 703: "That doesn’t mean we know where they’re going to lead") until Munger corrected him (line 709, "It says microeconomic factors"). After (line 733): at See's in 1972 "We’ll look at numbers on each one, and we’ll watch them over time, and we’ll see how third-year shops behave in the second year — we really like understanding businesses", and "who knows when some little fact stored in the back of your mind pops up and really does make a difference." Related: M2006-038 and M2012-028 (decide on the specific business, not macro views).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 8. “We like to look at micro factors”

quote_verbatim:
Well, there hardly could be anything more important than the microeconomics. That is business. Business and microeconomics is sort of the same term.

AUDIENCE MEMBER: I guess —

CHARLIE MUNGER: Microeconomics is what we do, and macroeconomics is what we put up with.
concept: Munger: microeconomics is the business itself and the work; macroeconomics is something endured, not something known better than others.
evolution_notes: Exchange; the audience member's interjection (line 723) is kept as printed. Before (line 717): "If you talk about macro, we don’t know any more than anybody else." Related: M2005-082 and M2015-029 (Munger: do not predict macro factors).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 8. “We like to look at micro factors”

quote_verbatim: We try and avoid the worst anchoring effect, which is always your previous conclusion. We really try and destroy our previous ideas.
concept: Munger: the worst anchor is one's own previous conclusion, so try to destroy one's previous ideas.
evolution_notes: Asked how they control the anchoring effect of known stock prices. Before (line 729): "Well, we’re not anchored to what we’re ignoring." Related: M1997-127 and M1998-004 (Buffett: examine evidence against a cherished belief at once). The disagreement rule that follows (lines 739-745) is a separate row in this batch.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 8. “We like to look at micro factors”

quote_verbatim:
WARREN BUFFETT: Charlie says that if you disagree with somebody, you want to be able to state their case better than they can.

CHARLIE MUNGER: Absolutely.

WARREN BUFFETT: And at that point, you’ve earned the right to disagree with them.

CHARLIE MUNGER: Otherwise, you should just keep quiet.
concept: Disagree only after being able to state the other side's case better than its holder can; otherwise keep quiet.
evolution_notes: Exchange carrying one lesson, Munger's view quoted by Buffett (the convention: it belongs to the speaker who says it at this meeting); Munger completes it. Line 745 continues "It would do wonders for our politics if everybody followed my system. (Laughter and applause)", a political aside left out. Follows Munger's anchoring rule at line 737 (a separate row in this batch).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 8. “We like to look at micro factors”

quote_verbatim: As a practical matter, you know, my best ideas are — I hope they’re my best ideas —are offlimits for me because they go to Berkshire, if they’re sizable enough to have a significance to Berkshire. [...] But I try to stay away from anything that could conflict with Berkshire.
concept: A manager's best ideas go to the company he runs; his own account takes only what is too small for it, and he stays away from anything that could conflict.
evolution_notes: Asked how he decides between personal and Berkshire investments (Seritage). Before (line 757): about 1 percent of his net worth is outside Berkshire, "I can’t be doing things that Berkshire does", and a $2 billion REIT is not of Berkshire size. "—are offlimits" is printed without a space and "offlimits" without a hyphen; kept as printed. Restates M2012-037. Munger's general statement (line 763) is the next row.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 9. I’d “much rather make money for Berkshire than for myself”

quote_verbatim: Well, part of being in a position like that we occupy, is you really don’t want conflict of interest or even the appearance of it.
concept: Munger: a fiduciary avoids conflict of interest and even its appearance.
evolution_notes: Same exchange as Buffett's best-ideas passage at line 759 (the previous row in this batch). After: "Both of us have practically nothing of significance, in the total picture, outside of Berkshire. I’ve got some Costco stock, because I’m director of Costco."
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 9. I’d “much rather make money for Berkshire than for myself”

quote_verbatim: There’s a lot of deferred tax that’s attributable to unrealized appreciation in securities. [...] That isn’t really cash that’s available. It’s just an absence of cash that’s going to be paid out until we sell the securities. [...] But overall, I think of, primarily, the cash flow of Berkshire as a practical matter relating to our net income plus our increase in float, assuming we have an increase.
concept: Deferred tax on unrealized gains is not cash available but tax not yet paid; the company's real new cash is its earnings plus any increase in float.
evolution_notes: Asked about free cash flow running above earnings less capex because of deferred taxes. Elided: an illustration (60 billion of appreciation, 21 billion of deferred tax), and "Some arises through bonus depreciation." After (line 775): the railroad and Berkshire Hathaway Energy will spend more than depreciation "for a long, long, long, long time"; earnings plus change in float "is the net new available cash." Related: M2015-030 (deferred taxes from accelerated depreciation not hidden equity).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 10. Berkshire’s cash flow outlook

quote_verbatim: The big thing, the goal, what Charlie and I think about, we want to add, every year, something to the normalized — you know, the normalized earning power per share of the company.
concept: The goal is to add something every year to normalized earning power per share, knowing ahead of time neither which year nor how much.
evolution_notes: Same answer as the deferred-tax passage on line 773. After (line 777): "We have retained earnings to work with every year to get that job done. Sometimes it doesn’t look like we’ve accomplished much, and we haven’t accomplished much." Restates M2016-002 (sustainable and growing earning power, not a quarterly number).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 10. Berkshire’s cash flow outlook

quote_verbatim:
American business has been good enough that you don’t have to be — you don’t have to really be smart to get a decent result. And if you can bring a little bit of intellect, you know, then you should get a pretty good result.

CHARLIE MUNGER: What you’ve got to do is be aversive to the standard stupidities. You just keep those out. You don’t have to be smart.
concept: Munger: a good result needs no brilliance, only steady aversion to the standard stupidities; American business has been good enough to allow many mistakes.
evolution_notes: Exchange carrying one lesson, stated as a rule by Munger; the quote opens partway into Buffett's paragraph, which begins at line 785 "No. And it’s allowed for a lot of mistakes. I mean, that’s the interesting thing." Before (line 779), Munger: "we’ve lived in a torrent of money, and we were constantly deploying it [...] and we were wising up as we went along." Related: M2007-033 (with large sums, avoid dumb things).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 10. Berkshire’s cash flow outlook

quote_verbatim: and I would say it’s important to recognize what you can’t do. So we have — we may have tried the department store business and a few things, but we’ve — we’ve generally tried to only swing at things in the strike zone, and our particular strike zone. And it really hasn’t been much more complicated than that.
concept: Recognize what you cannot do and swing only at pitches in your own strike zone.
evolution_notes: Asked what obvious truth let him think ahead of the crowd. Before (line 801): he owes Ben Graham for investing and Munger for business, has spent a lifetime looking at why some businesses work and some do not, "as Yogi Berra said, you can see a lot just by observing", and "I mentioned pattern recognition earlier". The department store is named as the exception tried. Related: M2014-051 (being realistic about one's talents) and L1997-006 (wait for the fat pitch).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 11. We’ve “avoided the self-destructive behavior”

quote_verbatim: You do not need — you don’t need the IQ in the investment business that you need in certain activities in life. But you do have — you do have to have emotional control. I mean, we see very smart people do very stupid things, and it’s fascinating how humans do that. Just take the people that get very rich and then leverage themselves up in some way that they lose everything. I mean, they are risking something that’s important to them for something that isn’t important to them.
concept: Investing needs emotional control more than IQ; the self-destructive error is to leverage up wealth and risk what is important for what is not.
evolution_notes: The mistake is other people's (the very rich who leverage and lose everything); Buffett draws the lesson. After: "you could figure that one out in first grade, but people do it time after time [...] I think we’ve sort of avoided the selfdestructive behavior." Restates M2009-020 (emotional stability over IQ), M2005-029 and L2014-025 (never risk what you need for what you do not).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 11. We’ve “avoided the self-destructive behavior”

quote_verbatim: Well, there’s just a few simple tricks that work — work well, and particularly if you’ve got a temperament that has a combination of patience and opportunism in it. And I think that’s largely inherited, although I suppose it can be learned to some extent.
concept: Munger: a few simple tricks work, best in a temperament combining patience with opportunism, largely inherited though partly learnable.
evolution_notes: Same question, Munger's part. Related: M2005-041 (Munger: success needs intelligence and temperament, partly inherited). His fairly-won passage later on line 805 is a separate row in this batch.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 11. We’ve “avoided the self-destructive behavior”

quote_verbatim:
Then I think there’s another factor that accounts for the fact that Berkshire has done as well as it has, is that we’re really trying to behave well. And I had a great-grandfather. When he died, the preacher gave the talk, and he said none envied this man’s success, so fairly won and wisely used. [...] And we’ve turned down businesses, including a big tobacco business.

So, I don’t think Berkshire would work as well if we were just terribly shrewd, but didn’t have a little bit of what the preacher said about my grandfather, Ingham. We want to have people think of us as having won fairly and used wisely. It works.
concept: Munger: behaving well is part of why the company works; aim for success fairly won and wisely used, and turn down businesses whose way of earning money is not admired.
evolution_notes: Same answer as Munger's temperament passage earlier on line 805. Elided: "That’s a very simple idea, but it’s exactly what Berkshire’s trying to do. There are a lot of people who make a lot of money and everybody hates them, and they don’t admire the way they earned the money. And I’m not particularly admirable of making money running gambling casinos. And, you know, we don’t own any." The turned-down tobacco business is a refusal shown, not a rule stated. The preacher's words are named as the source. "great-grandfather" and "my grandfather, Ingham" both printed; kept. Restates M2010-036 and M2011-037 (fairly won and wisely used).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 11. We’ve “avoided the self-destructive behavior”

quote_verbatim:
We’ve made plenty of mistakes in acquisitions. Plenty. And we made mistakes in not making acquisitions, but the mistakes are always about making an improper assessment of the economic conditions in the future of the industry of the company. They’re not a bad lease. They’re not a specific labor contract. They’re not a questionable patent. They’re not the things that are on the checklist, you know, for every acquisition by every major corporation in America. Those are not the things that count. What counts is whether you’re wrong about — whether you’ve really got a fix on the basic economics and how the industry’s likely to develop, or whether Amazon’s likely to kill them, you know, in a few years, or that sort of thing.

We have not found a due diligence list that gets at what we think are the real risks when we buy a business. [...] But none of those would have been cured by a lot more due diligence. They might have been cured by us being a little smarter.
concept: Acquisition mistakes, of commission and omission, come from misjudging the future economics of the industry, not from items on a due-diligence checklist; more diligence would not have cured them.
evolution_notes: Asked whether fast, handshake diligence puts Berkshire at risk. Before (line 845): lawyers ask why they do not do more due diligence, "which we would have paid them by the hour for." Elided (line 847): "And like I say, we’ve made — we’ve certainly made at least — oh, at least a half a dozen mistakes and probably a lot more if you get into mistakes of omission." Buffett's own mistakes. Restates M1997-037, M1998-175 and M2008-072.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 12. Due diligence doesn’t find the real risks of buying a company

quote_verbatim: Assessing whether a manager, who I’m going to hand a billion dollars to, for his business, and he is going to hand me a stock certificate, assessing whether he’s going to behave differently in the future in running that business than he has in the past when he owned it, that’s incredibly important, but there’s no checklist in the world that’s going to answer that.
concept: The vital judgment in buying a business is whether the seller, now paid in cash, will run it as he did when he owned it; no checklist answers that.
evolution_notes: Same answer as the mistakes passage at lines 845-847. After (lines 847-849): a few items do get covered, "you want to make sure that they don’t have twice as many shares out as you’re buying"; 150 leases at See's and 170 plants at Precision Castparts are not what decides a $32 billion acquisition. Buffett returns to it at line 855: "You really have to size up whether that person who’s getting a lot of cash from you is going — how they’re going to behave in the future, because we’re counting on them."
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 12. Due diligence doesn’t find the real risks of buying a company

quote_verbatim: Well, if you stop to think about it, business quality usually counts on something more than whether you cross the T in some old lease or something. And the human quality of the management who are going to stay are very important. And how are you going to check that as — by due diligence, you know?
concept: Munger: what decides an acquisition is business quality and the human quality of the managers who stay, neither of which due diligence checks.
evolution_notes: Same question. After: "I don’t know anybody who’s had a generally better record than Berkshire in judging business quality and the human quality of the people." Later (line 859), stated as a joke: "How many people who, in this room, are happily married, carefully checked their spouse’s birth certificate and so on?"
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 12. Due diligence doesn’t find the real risks of buying a company

quote_verbatim: Negotiations that drag out have a tendency — they’re more likely to blow up for some reason. [...] I like to keep things moving. I like to show a certain amount of trust in the other person, because usually trust comes back to you. [...] If I have the deal on the right terms, I don’t believe in — in making a — and Tom Murphy taught me this — I mean, you know, you just don’t try and win every point. It’s a terrible mistake. You make a decent deal, and if you find something that bends a little different someway, that’s OK. If you think it’s bad faith and gives an indication of the character of the person you’re dealing with, then you got another problem, and you’re lucky if you find that out early.
concept: Keep a negotiation moving and show trust, which usually returns; with the deal on the right terms do not try to win every point, but treat bad faith as a sign of character.
evolution_notes: Same question. "you just don’t try and win every point" is credited to Tom Murphy (the convention: it belongs to the speaker who says it). Elided: "I mean, people — they can get obstinate about very small points, and it’s silly to be obstinate, but people get silly sometimes." and "But the — you know, the truth is there’s some bad apples out there, and spotting them is not going to come from looking at documents. [...] And I’m perfectly willing to lose small points here and then on a deal." Related: M1995-084 (no good deal with a bad person).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 12. Due diligence doesn’t find the real risks of buying a company

quote_verbatim:
Well, and there’s an obverse side of that. Not only can the able people usually do a lot more, but the unable people by and large you can’t fix. So —

WARREN BUFFETT: That is for sure.

CHARLIE MUNGER: I think you’re forced to use our system if you have your wits about you.
concept: Munger: able people can handle far more than expected and unable people mostly cannot be fixed, so give the able more to do.
evolution_notes: Exchange; Munger's is the general form (the 2012 convention). Buffett's narrower line before (line 871): "I have found with really able people, they can handle so much. [...] So there’s just no limit to what talented people can accomplish. And if I had something else in insurance tomorrow that needed doing, I’d probably call Ajit on that, too." Asked about Ajit Jain taking over General Re's reinsurance.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 13. “We don’t pay any attention to titles”

quote_verbatim: And we don’t feel the need to follow any kind of organizational common view as to, you know, you do this and you have — only so many people can report to you or any of this sort of thing. Berkshire — every decision that comes up, you know, we just try and figure out the most logical thing to do at that time. But we don’t have some grand design in mind of, you know, like an army organizational chart or something of the sort, and we never will.
concept: Decide each organizational question by the most logical answer at the time, not by conventional rules such as spans of control or a grand design.
evolution_notes: Same answer, following Munger's line 879. Before (line 873): no successor names are announced because "five years from now, something different could make sense."
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 13. “We don’t pay any attention to titles”

quote_verbatim:
Warren and I once reached a decision we wouldn’t pay more than X dollars for something, and the man who was subordinate to both of us who was working on it just said, you guys are out of your minds. This is really stupid. This is a quality operation, you ought to pay up for it. We just looked at one another, and did it his way.

WARREN BUFFETT: Yeah.

CHARLIE MUNGER: We don’t pay any attention to titles or — [...] If a charwoman gave us a good idea, we’d accept it cheerfully.
concept: Munger: judge an idea by its merit, not by the rank of the person offering it; a subordinate once rightly overruled their price limit on a quality business.
evolution_notes: Exchange; the elision crosses Buffett's interjections (line 889, "He was right, too."; line 893, "OK. I’m sorry. Have you got —?") and Munger's line 891 ("He was right, yeah, of course. (Laughs)"); Munger resumes the same thought. The story is their own error (a price limit set too low on a quality operation), corrected by the subordinate.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 13. “We don’t pay any attention to titles”

quote_verbatim: Tom Murphy had the best approach. I mean, he never hired a person that he didn’t need, and therefore, they never had layoffs. [...] but the idea that you give up your staff, whatever it may be, economists or something like that, because business has slowed down — if you didn’t need them — if you don’t need them now, you didn’t need them in the first place, you know.
concept: Hire no one not needed and there are no layoffs; outside a genuinely cyclical cut in direct work, staff shed when business slows were never needed in the first place.
evolution_notes: Asked how to judge whether cost cutting at Kraft Heinz cuts muscle as well as fat. Before: "sometimes you can cut costs that are a mistake to cut, and you can — and sometimes you can keep costs that are a mistake to keep." Elided: Berkshire headquarters follows a similar approach, and a cyclical business "may have to cut a workforce because there aren’t as many carloads of freight moving". Murphy's practice named as the source. Restates L2015-013 (hire only the truly needed) and L2004-006.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 15. 3G’s cost cutting hasn’t hurt Kraft Heinz

quote_verbatim: You know, you get people — you get a department going and they’re always going to want to expand. The ideal method is not to do it in the first place. But there are all kinds of American companies that are loaded with people that aren’t really doing anything or are doing the wrong thing. And if you cut that out, it should not really have any significant effect on volume. On the other hand, if you cut out the wrong things, you could have a big effect. I mean, it can be done in a dumb way or a smart way.
concept: A department once started always wants to expand, so the best course is not to start it; cutting people who do nothing should not hurt volume, but cutting the wrong things can, so ask whether cuts are smart or dumb.
evolution_notes: Same answer, following Murphy's practice on line 931. Before (line 933): investor relations departments are named, "since we’ve forgotten to insult this group so far". After: 3G's cuts "have been extremely intelligent about it, and have not done things that will cut volume." Related: L2015-001 (buy lean businesses).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 15. 3G’s cost cutting hasn’t hurt Kraft Heinz

quote_verbatim: And the test will be over time — you know, three, five years — are the operations which have had their costs cut, do they do poor, in terms of volume, than the ones, that in my judgment, look very fat? So far I see no evidence of that whatsoever. [...] But believe me, I look at those figures every month, and I look at everybody else’s figures every month, and I try to — I’m always looking for any signs of underperformance because of any decisions made, and I’ve seen none.
concept: Judge whether cost cuts cut muscle by comparing, over three to five years and month by month, the volume of the cut operations against that of fat competitors in the same industry.
evolution_notes: Same answer. Before (line 935): in packaged goods "volume trends for everybody — whether they’re fat or lean in their operation — volume trends are not good." Elided: Kraft Heinz lines will rise and fall, the industry will not grow in physical volume, "I’ve never seen anybody run anything more sensibly than 3G has". "do they do poor" printed so; kept.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 15. 3G’s cost cutting hasn’t hurt Kraft Heinz

quote_verbatim: Yeah. And sometimes when you reduce volume, it’s very intelligent, because you’re losing money on the volume you’re discarding. It’s quite common for a business, not only to have more employees than it needs, but sometimes it has two or three customers that it would be better off without. And so it’s hard to judge from outside whether things are good or bad just because volume is going up or down a little. Generally speaking, I think the leanly-staffed companies do better at everything than the ones that are overstaffed.
concept: Munger: falling volume is not by itself bad, since discarding money-losing volume or customers can be intelligent; lean companies do better at everything than overstaffed ones.
evolution_notes: Same question. After: "I think overstaffing is like getting to weigh 400 pounds when you’re a normal person. It’s not a plus." Related: M2015-083 (Munger: prosperous institutions become overstaffed unnoticed).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 15. 3G’s cost cutting hasn’t hurt Kraft Heinz

quote_verbatim: Yeah. Sloppy thinking in one area probably indicates there may well be sloppy thinking elsewhere. And I have been a director of 19 public corporations, and I’ve seen some very sloppy operations, and I’ve seen a few really outstanding business operators. And there’s a huge, huge difference. If you have a wonderful business, you can get away with being sloppy. [...] But it’s the really prosperous companies that — you know, some — well, the classic case I think were the tobacco companies many years ago. I mean, they, you know, they went off into this thing and that thing and — and it was practically play money because it was so easy to make, and it didn’t require, you know — it didn’t require good management, and they took advantage of that fact.
concept: Sloppy thinking in one area suggests it elsewhere; a wonderful business lets management be sloppy unnoticed, as the prosperous tobacco companies showed by spending easy money on diversions.
evolution_notes: Follows Munger's line 939. The elision crosses Munger's interjection (line 943, "I would.") and Buffett's own lines on wasting a billion dollars a year at Berkshire, 4 percent of earnings, "maybe you wouldn’t notice it" and "— it grows. (Laughter) Charlie would notice it, so I —"; Buffett resumes the same thought. The tobacco companies' mistake is a third party's, Buffett's lesson. After: "You can read about some of that in “Barbarians at the Gate.”" Related: L2015-007 (a protected business whose returns never depended on efficiency).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 15. 3G’s cost cutting hasn’t hurt Kraft Heinz

quote_verbatim: And I think to a small degree, that’s because people think we paid more for Van Tuyl than we did. They’re not seeing certain factors in it, so they think we paid X, and therefore they’re entitled to X, and we didn’t pay X, so we haven’t made — we’ve bought very little so far. I hope that changes in the future. But we’re not going to change — we’re not going to change our metrics, in terms of how we value auto dealerships.
concept: Keep the valuation metrics fixed even when sellers, misreading what was paid before, expect more and few purchases follow.
evolution_notes: Asked why Van Tuyl contributed less than expected. Before (line 957): about a billion dollars of securities came with the $4.1 billion price, and acquisition accounting charges and allowable amortization make the real price lower than it appears; "if I had [laid out a projection], it would look very much like things have turned out." Restates M2015-079 (price auto dealers against a bad year).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 16. We paid less for Van Tuyl than it appears

quote_verbatim:
The nature of it is that you’ll pay more for a business when interest rates are zero than if they were, like, 15 percent when [former Federal Reserve Chairman Paul] Volcker was around, and you can take that up and down the line.

I mean, we don’t get too exact about it, because it isn’t that exact a science, but very cheap money makes me pay a little more for businesses than when money was at what we previously thought was normal rates. And very tight money would cause me to pay somewhat less. [...] And if you ask me whether I paid a little more for Precision Castparts because interest rates were around zero, than if they’d been 6 percent, the answer is yes. I try not to pay too much more, but it has an effect.
concept: The price paid for a business moves with interest rates, a little more when money is very cheap and somewhat less when it is tight, inexactly and without paying too much more.
evolution_notes: Asked how negative rates change valuation. Before (line 967): going from zero to minus a half "is really no different than going from 4 to 3 and a half"; what is dramatic is rates near zero for so long. Elided (line 969): Aesop's bird in the hand "is worth about nine- tenths of a bird in the bush in Europe [...] it depends on how far out the bush". The bracketed editorial insertion is printed in the transcript. After (line 971): if people start thinking this is normal, "that will have an enormous effect on asset values" (a forecast). Related: M2013-012 (rates act on asset prices as gravity), M2014-068 and M2015-015. See Tensions seen for M2003-149.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 17. “Very cheap money makes me pay a little more”

quote_verbatim:
No. Our advantage is that we know we don’t understand it.

WARREN BUFFETT: It’s interesting, though. I mean, we are — you know, it’s — it makes for an interesting movie. And it does modestly affect what we pay for businesses. Whether — I don’t think anybody expected it to last this long, do you Charlie, personally?

CHARLIE MUNGER: I don’t think — if you’re not confused, you haven’t thought about it correctly.
concept: Munger: on something no one understands, such as negative rates, the advantage lies in knowing one does not understand it; confusion is the correct state.
evolution_notes: Exchange carrying one lesson, stated by Munger; Buffett's question at line 979 is kept inside the quote. Before (line 973): "I don’t think anybody really knows much about negative interest rates. We never had them before. [...] And none of the great economists who have studied this stuff, and taught it to our children, understand it, either. So we just do the best we can." Buffett (line 975): "And they still don’t understand it."
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 17. “Very cheap money makes me pay a little more”

quote_verbatim: A lot of great businesses aren’t quite so great as they used to be. The packaged good business, the Procter & Gambles and so forth of the world — General Mills — they’re all weaker than they used to be at their peak and — [...] When I was young, General Motors loomed over the economy like a colossus. It looked totally invincible. Torrents of cash. Torrents of everything. [...] And so the world changes, and we can’t change — make a portfolio change — every time something is a little less advantaged than it used to be.
concept: Munger: great businesses weaken and even an invincible-looking giant can wipe out its owners, yet a portfolio cannot be changed every time a holding is a little less advantaged.
evolution_notes: Exchange about American Express. The elisions cross Buffett's lines 1015 ("And the auto companies.") and 1019 ("Trying to hold down market share."), and Munger's own lines 1017 ("they wiped out all the shareholders — I would no more have predicted that.") and 1021 (GM afraid of being too monopolistic); Munger resumes the same thought. Buffett's completion is the next row.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 19. American Express faces tough competition

quote_verbatim:
WARREN BUFFETT: But you have to be —

CHARLIE MUNGER: Alert.

WARREN BUFFETT: — you have to be thinking all the time and alert to whether there’s been something that really changes the game in a big way. And that’s not only true for American Express, that’s true for other things we own, including things we own 100 percent of. And we’ll be wrong sometimes. We’ll be late sometimes, we’ll be wrong sometimes. But we’ll be right sometimes, too. But it’s not that we’re not cognizant of threats. Assessing the probabilities of those threats being a minor problem, or a major problem, or a life-threatening problem, you know, it’s a tough game, but that’s what makes our job interesting.
concept: Reassess every holding, wholly owned or not, by staying alert to anything that changes the game and judging whether each threat is minor, major or life-threatening, accepting being late or wrong at times.
evolution_notes: Exchange; Munger supplies "Alert." (line 1025). Before (line 1007): "we reassess our reasons for owning all investments on almost a continuous basis"; (line 1011) American Express has been under attack for decades "and it will continue to be under attack", too attractive a business for able people to ignore. Munger (line 1029): an established player in payments with an old method "has more danger than used to exist". Related: L2015-008 (probability, range of cost, timing of a threat) and M2016-008 (a fine company sold on its industry's next decade).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 19. American Express faces tough competition

quote_verbatim:
I think it’s one of the worst businesses I can imagine for somebody like us. (Laughter)

WARREN BUFFETT: There’s nothing personal about this.

CHARLIE MUNGER: Yeah. Not only is it a bad business, but we have no aptitude for it.
concept: Munger: two separate reasons rule a business out, that it is a bad business and that one has no aptitude for it.
evolution_notes: Asked whether investing in cattle is wise given a growing world population. Stated partly as a joke. After (line 1051): "They have one good year every 20 years or something." (line 1057): "But not owning cattle." (line 1061): "Somebody has to occupy the tough niches in the economy. We need you." Buffett (line 1059): people who did well in cattle "usually own banks on the side", a joke.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 20. We like steak but aren’t interested in owning cattle

quote_verbatim: But the — when it comes to assess — our incentive systems are different and what they try and adapt to is the reality of each situation. And the basic rule on incentives is you get what you reward for. So, if you have a dumb incentive system, you get dumb outcomes.
concept: Munger: you get what you reward, so a dumb incentive system gives dumb outcomes; each system is adapted to the reality of its business.
evolution_notes: Asked how incentives are designed at Berkshire and how the next CEO should be paid. Before: "I’ll let Warren worry about the next CEO." After: GEICO's system has no normal profits-type incentive, which Buffett explains (line 1077). Related: M2009-083 (reward doing right, discourage doing wrong).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 21. Don’t reward profits in compensation plans

quote_verbatim:
And those two variables are very simple. I care about growing the business, and I care about growing it with a profitable business. So we have a grid, which consists of growth and policies in force on one axis — not gross in dollars, because that’s reflected by average premiums, which are outside their control — but growth in policies in force. And then on the other grid, we have the profitability of seasoned business. It costs a lot of money to put business on the books.

I mean, we spend a lot of money on advertising and all of that. So the first year, any business we put on the books is going to reduce profits significantly. And I don’t want people to be worried about the profit if it’s going — that comes — that might be impaired by growing the business fast. So, profit of seasoned business, growth of policies in force. Very simple. [...] And it totally aligns the goals of the organization, in terms of compensation, with the goals of the owner.
concept: Pay on simple variables the employees control that match what the owner wants: at GEICO, growth in policies in force and profit on seasoned business, so that costly new business is not discouraged.
evolution_notes: Before (line 1077): the two variables apply to well over 20,000 people with a multiplier up the ladder. Elided: used since 1995 with a tweak or two, everybody understands it, and February's announcement day. Premium dollars are excluded because average premiums are outside employees' control.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 21. Don’t reward profits in compensation plans

quote_verbatim: you don’t want to award profits, alone. It’d be the dumbest thing you could do. You just quit advertising, and, you know, start shrinking the business a little. That’s a — and like I said, that — people there know that the very top person is getting paid based on those same two variables. So that they — they don’t think that the guys at the top have got a cushy deal compared to them, and all of that.
concept: Rewarding current profit alone invites cutting advertising and shrinking the business; paying the top person on the same variables as everyone keeps the plan credible.
evolution_notes: Exchange. Munger before (line 1081): "It’s simple, but other people might reward something like just profits, and so the people don’t take on new business, they should take it on, because it hurts profits. So you’ve got to think these things through". The GEICO grid it follows is at lines 1077-1079.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 21. Don’t reward profits in compensation plans

quote_verbatim: The — you know, the idea of having a — sort of — a coordinated arrangement for incentive compensation across 70 or 80 businesses, or whatever, is just totally nuts. [...] We try to figure out what makes sense in each business we’re in. There’s some businesses where the top person is enormously important, or some businesses where the business itself dominates the nature — the result. [...] I mean, you just go up and down the line, and to think that you’ll have a simple formula that can be sort of stamped out for the whole place, and then with some overall stuff for corporate results on top of it, you’d be wasting a lot of money, and you’d be misdirecting incentives. So we think it through one at a time, and it seems to work out pretty well.
concept: Design incentive pay business by business, according to whether the top person or the business itself drives the result; one formula across many businesses wastes money and misdirects incentives.
evolution_notes: Before (line 1083): a compensation consultant "would start coming up with plans that would be designed for all of Berkshire"; Munger (line 1085): "Maybe an undertaking parlor." The elisions skip Buffett's own lines on the consultant's master plan and the seller asked to set his own plan (rowed separately in this batch). Restates M2010-029 (pay as a sole owner would, for each business's own economics) and M2003-127.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 21. Don’t reward profits in compensation plans

quote_verbatim: I said, I don’t want a guy working for me that has a plan that he thinks doesn’t make sense, or that he’s unhappy with, or chewing at him, or he’s complaining to his wife about it, whatever it may be. You tell me what makes sense. And he told me what made sense, and it made sense, and we’ve been using it ever since. Never changed a word.
concept: Let a manager propose the pay plan he thinks makes sense; a plan he is unhappy with keeps chewing at him.
evolution_notes: Before (line 1091): a seller who wanted to keep running his business was asked what the plan should be, "And he said, well, he said, I thought you told me that. (Laughs) I said no." The tailoring passage on the same lines is a separate row in this batch.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 21. Don’t reward profits in compensation plans

quote_verbatim: And if you reward somebody with some share of the profits, and the profits are being reported using accounting practices that cause the profit to exist on paper that are not really happening in terms of underlying economics, then people are doing the wrong thing, and it’s endangering the bank and hurting the country and everything else. [...] The accounting allowed, for a long time, a lender to use his bad — as his bad debt provision — his previous historical loss rate. So an idiot could make a lot of money by just making waygamier loans at high interest, and accruing a lot of interest, and saying, “I’m not going to lose any more money on these, because I didn’t lose money on different loans in the past.”
concept: Munger: paying a share of profits that exist only on paper rewards the wrong conduct; loss provisions set by past loss rates let riskier, higher-rate loans show profits that are not real.
evolution_notes: The mistake is the banks' and the accountants' ("a major part of the cause of the great financial crisis"), Munger's lesson. Before: "A lot of the bad examples of incentives come from banking and investment banking." After: "That was insane for the accountants to allow that. [...] I’ve never met an accountant that’s ashamed of it." "waygamier" printed so; kept.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 21. Don’t reward profits in compensation plans

quote_verbatim: The other — another thing that — possibility is when you get the very greedy chief executive who wants an enormous payoff for himself, and to justify it, designs a pyramid, so that a whole bunch of other people down the line get overpaid in some relation — or get paid — in relation to something they have no control over, just so it doesn’t look like he’s all by himself, in terms of that fantastic payoff he’s arranged for himself. [...] Well, if you’ve got people interested in having options issued at a terribly low price, they may occasionally do something that might cause that. And it certainly — what could be dumber than a company looking for a way to issue shares at the lowest price?
concept: Look for pay pyramids built to justify a greedy chief executive's payoff, paying many on things they do not control, and for managers who want options issued at a low price, which gives them a motive to depress it.
evolution_notes: Same answer. Elided: "There’s a lot of misbehavior. [...] I literally would hear conversations in a board room where they hoped they were issuing the options, you know, at a terribly low price." Related: M2012-011 (buybacks for ego, options issued low).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 21. Don’t reward profits in compensation plans

quote_verbatim: Compensation isn’t as complicated as the world would like to make it, but that’s — if you were a consultant, you would want to make people think it’s very complicated, and that only you could solve this terrible problem for them that they couldn’t solve.
concept: Compensation is simpler than it is made to look; the consultant's incentive is to make it seem complicated.
evolution_notes: Same answer, closing Buffett's part. Restates M2004-096 (a consultant's income favours complex plans) and M2003-127. Munger's closing line follows (line 1105), a separate row.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 21. Don’t reward profits in compensation plans

quote_verbatim: We want it simple and right, and we don’t want it to reward what we don’t want. If you have — those of you with children — just imagine how your household would work if you constantly rewarded every child for bad behavior. The house would be ungovernable in short order.
concept: Munger: keep pay simple and right, and never reward what is not wanted.
evolution_notes: Closes heading 21, following Buffett's line 1103. Restates his opening at line 1075 (you get what you reward).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 21. Don’t reward profits in compensation plans

quote_verbatim: As I mentioned in the annual report, in the case of all railroads, merely spending their depreciation expense will not keep them in the same place. So depreciation is an inadequate measure of the actual steady state of capital expenditure needs of a railroad, even in these fairly noninflationary ways. And that’s an important consideration in buying the business. [...] I would say that the true maintenance capex, if you’re looking at 4.3 billion, is higher than 60 percent of that number, when you really evaluate keeping the railroad in competitive shape to do just the same volume as it would be doing the year before.
concept: Depreciation can understate the steady-state capital spending needed just to keep a business competitive at the same volume; measure true maintenance spending that way, and weigh it in buying.
evolution_notes: Asked about BNSF's capital spending beyond maintenance. Elided: "We knew that going in, and it’s been reinforced since. We spent a lot of money in 2015 because we had a lot of problems to correct." After: some intangible amortization elsewhere is not a real expense, so "Berkshire’s figures actually are on the conservative side, in relation to real economic earnings. But that’s not true at any railroad"; (line 1115) "we will spend more than depreciation [...] to stay in the same place for a long, long time [...] that’s a negative in the picture." Restates L2015-004, the letter the meeting names.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 22. BNSF’s capital expenditures

quote_verbatim: Yeah. I think it’s hard to do that, brutally, when you’re rich and your supplier isn’t, and think that your supplier is going to love you. And so I think there’s something to be said for leaning over backward to have a win-win relationship with both suppliers and customers, always.
concept: Munger: do not squeeze poorer suppliers for working capital; lean over backward for win-win relations with suppliers and customers.
evolution_notes: Asked why the operating businesses hold so much working capital. Munger raised (line 1161) whether to pay suppliers more slowly, as others do. Buffett (line 1165): "the desire for — great relations with suppliers is — would probably overcome, in most of our managers’ minds, any desire to start extending terms." After (line 1171), Munger: "we don’t need it. Let somebody else set the record on that one."
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 24. No need to sweep cash from subsidiaries

quote_verbatim: We don’t do it. We’re not interested in manipulating those numbers, and we haven’t had a restructuring charge ever, and I don’t think we’re about to start.
concept: Munger: do not separate out restructuring charges to flatter operating earnings; never manipulate the numbers.
evolution_notes: Asked how much higher operating earnings would be if Berkshire separated out one-time restructuring costs as others do. Before: "That’s a question like asking, why don’t you kill your mother to get the insurance money? (Laughter)". Related: L1998-031 (treat restructuring charges with suspicion) and R1996-015 (no big baths).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 25. “We don’t need to inflate the figures”

quote_verbatim: I never want to report one of these things where I have the whole adjusted earnings set out and say, this is what you’re supposed to pay attention to, because every one of those I’ve seen virtually results in some inflation of figures. Things are good enough at Berkshire. We don’t need to inflate the figures.
concept: Do not present an adjusted-earnings figure as the one owners should watch; nearly every one seen inflates the figures.
evolution_notes: Same question. Before (line 1181): the numbers would not be huge, they are more conservatively stated than most, and railroad depreciation "is inadequate as a measure of true operating earnings"; Munger (line 1183): "we like to advertise our defects." Before, in this line: more amortization of intangibles "which reduce earnings and reported earnings, but which, in reality, are not expenses" than some companies, "And I’ve pointed that out." Related: L2015-003 (managers telling owners to ignore real expenses).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 25. “We don’t need to inflate the figures”

quote_verbatim: Well, the truth of the matter is that we don’t pay much attention to trying to get an extra two basis points by being gamey on our short-term things.
concept: Munger: do not reach for a few extra basis points by gamey handling of short-term money.
evolution_notes: Asked whether Berkshire would unwind its municipal-bond protection or trade its own CDS. After: "that credit default position is a weird, historical accident"; (line 1205) "we don’t fool around with our own credit defaults." Buffett (line 1199): "They didn’t get collateral from us and we wouldn’t have given it to them", restating M2016-019 (no collateral). Related: M2011-089 (Munger: do not maximize returns on short-term money).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 26. Berkshire Hathaway’s credit default swaps

quote_verbatim: It’s — having a fantastic manager that has a large business — potential business — available to them, and who makes the most of it, you know, it’s huge over time. You don’t see it necessarily in a week or a month or anything of the sort. [...] So, really outstanding managers, they’re invaluable, and we want to — Charlie and I can’t do it ourselves, but we want to align ourselves with them and then, you know, have them feel about Berkshire the way we feel about it.
concept: An outstanding manager with a large potential business is worth an enormous sum over time, unseen in any short period; align with such managers and make them feel about the company as the owners do.
evolution_notes: Asked about losing Ajit Jain. Before (line 1227): losing him "would be very significant", and many managers have created billions for Berkshire. Elided (line 1229): Jeff Bezos at Amazon, and Tom Murphy and Dan Burke building from "a bankrupt UHF station in Albany. It wasn’t that they were — they didn’t invent television or anything of the sort, they just managed it so well." Restates M1997-045 (an outstanding manager can hardly be overpaid).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 27. A fantastic manager makes a huge difference

quote_verbatim:
And so we do not — we are not measuring it against, you know, double-A corporates, or anything of the sort.

We’re measuring it in the potential utility, to us with our really pretty unusual flexibility, in respect to the deployment of funds, and this long period when we’ll have an opportunity, perhaps, to come up with one or two things that — where we can deploy money at a rate that may be quite a bit higher than other people.
concept: Float bought at an underwriting loss is valued not against a bond yield but by its utility over a long period to a holder able to deploy it at unusually high rates when chances come.
evolution_notes: Asked how to value float from retroactive reinsurance booked at an underwriting loss. Before (line 1241): "we don’t expect these rates, but we could be wrong", and occasional chances come even when rates are low. After: "Assume now the money can be deployed." Restates M2016-020 (float's worth depends on rates and the holder's options). Munger's option-cost line follows (line 1245), a separate row.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 28. Paying a little money now to have a lot of money later

quote_verbatim:
Yeah, we’re willing to pay a little money now to have just a certainty of having a lot of money available in case something really attractive comes up in a difficult time.

WARREN BUFFETT: Yeah. It’s an option cost.

CHARLIE MUNGER: It’s an option cost, right.
concept: Munger: paying a small cost now for the certainty of large funds in a difficult time is an option worth buying.
evolution_notes: Exchange carrying one lesson, stated by Munger; Buffett names it an option cost. After (line 1251), Buffett: "And that option came in handy in 2008 and ’9, for example." Munger: "Did it ever."
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 28. Paying a little money now to have a lot of money later

quote_verbatim: The — you know, we’re not particularly better at predicting real estate markets than we are stock markets, or interest rate markets, but there’s certainly — and it’s driven to some extent by these low interest rates — but there’s certainly properties that are being sold at very, very low cap rates that strike me as having more potential for loss than gain. But again, if you can borrow money for very, very little, and you think you’re getting into some very safe asset, 100 basis points or 150 basis points higher, there’s a great temptation to do it. I think it’s a mistake to do that, but, you know, I could be wrong.
concept: Without predicting markets, judge an asset by its potential for loss against gain; borrowing very cheaply to buy a supposedly safe asset at a thin spread above the borrowing cost is a tempting mistake.
evolution_notes: Asked whether real estate is frothy. Before: "It’s not as attractive as it was in 2012. (Laughs)". After: no nationwide bubble in residential real estate, and the next problem will not be a replica of 2008 (forecasts). Related: L2015-006 (lend long on short money only with an offset).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 29. No nationwide bubble in residential real estate now

quote_verbatim: But their approach to investing, I mean, they’re looking for businesses that they understand and that are going to — and through the stocks of those businesses — that they can buy at a sensible price and that they think will be earning significantly more money five or ten years from now. So it’s very similar to what I’m thinking about, except I’d probably add another zero to it.
concept: The approach in one line: through stocks, buy businesses one understands, at a sensible price, that will earn significantly more five or ten years out.
evolution_notes: Asked how Todd Combs and Ted Weschler think differently from Buffett. Before: they have a bigger universe, ideas for $500 million against his billions, and more knowledge of industries developed in the last ten or fifteen years. Restates L1994-001 (sensible prices, good economics, honest and able people) and M2013-045 (a view of the business five or ten years out).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 30. Praise for portfolio managers Ted Weschler and Todd Combs

quote_verbatim: We don’t — we are not forced — we don’t write policies for a long period of time. We’re not forced to write a policy on anything, so we are — our judgment is made as propositions are presented to us, usually as to whether, for one year, we are willing to accept a given risk for a given price.
concept: An insurer that writes one-year policies and is never forced to write any judges each risk afresh at its price, so a slowly rising hazard is repriced rather than borne.
evolution_notes: On the shareholder proposal for a report on climate risk to the insurance business; the climate policy is left out of the quote. Before: "we respectfully disagree with them [the Bank of England] in terms of — not in terms of the importance of climate change — but in terms of the risk to our insurance business." Restates L2015-011 (annual repricing).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 37. Shareholder proposal on climate change risks

quote_verbatim: But it — we will not write — if we lose a customer because they want us to do something stupid, we lose the customer, and there is not a — in our business — I’m not speaking for other reinsurers, but in our business, and I believe with most other reinsurers, they are not going to do something that they think is terribly disadvantageous to them just to maintain a relationship. That’s not really a relationship. It’d be a subsidy. [...] But we have not written business — catastrophe business — in Florida during that period, because we didn’t think the rates were adequate. They were adequate, we just were wrong about it. So the — and incidentally, that does not — the fact that we walked away from cat business in Florida that we thought was mispriced — does not hurt us in the business.
concept: Never write business one judges terribly disadvantageous to keep a relationship, which would be a subsidy; walking away from what one thinks mispriced costs nothing in a transactional business, even when the judgment proves wrong.
evolution_notes: Answering Jim Jones (another speaker, not rowed), who argued reinsurance customers expect long-term protection. Before (line 1383): "we have not been asked, ever, to my knowledge, to write long-term contracts. [...] It’s much more a transactional business." Elided: after Katrina rates went up and Florida's hurricane experience has been the best since before 1850, "That’s been a surprise to us". The Florida passage is Buffett's own error of omission, kept inside the rule it illustrates. After: "And no one expects you to do something that’s very stupid. You know, if they do, it’s the wrong kind of a relationship."
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 37. Shareholder proposal on climate change risks

quote_verbatim: I think you’ll have a reasonable time to move, but I would say, if you’re making a 50-year investment in low-lying properties, it’s probably a mistake. [...] And I would say that if you expect to be there for ten years or so, I don’t think I would consider moving. But if I thought I was making a 100-year investment, I don’t think I would make it.
concept: Weigh a slow-building hazard against the holding period: negligible over ten years, decisive for a fifty- or hundred-year commitment.
evolution_notes: Answering Jane Kleeb (another speaker), who quoted his report's advice to homeowners in low-lying areas. It is puzzling, therefore, that corporate repurchase announcements almost never refer to a price above which repurchases will be eschewed. That certainly wouldn't be the case if a management was buying an outside business. There, price would always factor into a buy-or-pass decision. When CEOs or boards are buying a small part of their own company, though, they all too often seem oblivious to price. Would they behave similarly if they were managing a private company with just a few owners and were evaluating the wisdom of buying out one of them? Of course not.
concept: Check whether a buyback program names a price above which it stops, and judge buying back shares as one would judge buying out a partner in a private company; a buyback with no price discipline is suspect.

quote_verbatim: It is important to remember that there are two occasions in which repurchases should not take place, even if the company's shares are underpriced. One is when a business both needs all its available money to protect or expand its own operations and is also uncomfortable adding further debt. Here, the internal need for funds should take priority. This exception assumes, of course, that the business has a decent future awaiting it after the needed expenditures are made. The second exception, less common, materializes when a business acquisition (or some other investment opportunity) offers far greater value than do the undervalued shares of the potential repurchaser.
concept: Even below value, do not buy back stock when the business needs the money to protect or expand itself (and has a decent future after spending it), or when another investment offers far more value.
evolution_notes: The first exception restates in part L1999-023 (repurchase only with funds beyond the business's needs); the second is named as a reason for missed buybacks in L1999-030. quote_verbatim: Finally, there are three connected realities that cause investing success to breed failure. First, a good record quickly attracts a torrent of money. And they might even wish to perhaps set an example by engaging for something far lower than actually what you could say their true market value is.

quote_verbatim: would probably pay them a very modest amount and then have an option which increased in value by — or increased in striking price — annually. Nobody does this, hardly. [...] but would increase because it’s assuming that there were substantial retained earnings every year. Because why should somebody retain a bunch of earnings and then claim they’ve actually improved the value, simply because they withheld the money from shareholders? [...] But they might have a very substantial one that could be exercised, but where the shareholder’s — the shares had to be held for a couple years after retirement, so that they really got the result over time that the majority of the stockholders would be able to get, and not be able to pick their spots, as to when they exercised and sold a lot of stock.

heading: ### 31. “If the board hires a compensation consultant after I go, I will come back”

quote_verbatim: And the human relations department, you know, who work for the CEO, come in and suggest a consultant. What consultant is ever going to get another assignment if he says, “You should pay your CEO below the — down in the fourth quartile because you’re getting a fourth quartile result?” It — I mean, it just, you know — it isn’t that the people are evil or anything. It’s just the nature of the situation just — it produces a result that is not consistent with how representatives of the owners should behave.
concept: A pay consultant hired through the CEO's own staff cannot recommend below-median pay for below-median results and keep getting work; the arrangement, not malice, pushes pay up against the owners' interest.

[...] And there they are, you know, making decisions on who should be CEO and how they should be paid and all that sort of thing. But, you know, they never felt like shelling out a dollar themselves. Now they’d been given a lot of stock. And it’s, you know, we’re dealing with human nature here, folks. (Laughs) And that — what you want is to have a system that works well in spite of how human nature’s going to drive it.

quote_verbatim: So you need a very sensible capital allocator in the job of being CEO of Berkshire. And we will have one. It would be a terrible mistake to have someone in this job where, really, capital allocation might be — might even be their main talent. It probably should be very close to their main talent. [...] And if they’ve come from a different background or haven’t done it, it’s a little bit, as I put in one of my letters, I think — it’s like getting to Carnegie Hall playing the violin, and then you walk out on the stage and they hand you a piano.
concept: A chief executive who will allocate large sums needs capital allocation as close to his main talent; one who rose by sales, law or operations and has not done it is unprepared for the job's central task.
evolution_notes: "It would be a terrible mistake to have someone in this job where, really, capital allocation might be — might even be their main talent" is kept as printed; the sense (from the next sentence) appears to be "might not be", a doubt recorded, not resolved. speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 33. Berkshire’s next CEO needs a “money mind”

quote_verbatim: I’ve talked about it as being something I call a “money mind.” I mean, people can have 120 IQs or 140 IQs or whatever it may be, very similar scoring abilities in terms of intelligence tests. And some of them have minds that are good at one kind of thing and some of them another. I’ve known very bright people that do not have money minds, and they can make very unintelligent decisions. [...] And I’ve known other people that really would not do that brilliantly. They do fine, but on an SAT test or something like that. But they’ve never made a dumb money decision in their life.
concept: A money mind is a distinct aptitude for financial decisions, separate from measured intelligence; very bright people can lack it and make unintelligent money decisions.
evolution_notes: Related: M2015-046 and M2016-062 (intelligence does not prevent self-destruction or substitute for emotional control) and L2016-004 (soundness over IQ).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 33. Berkshire’s next CEO needs a “money mind”

quote_verbatim: And a money mind will recognize when it makes sense to buy in stock and doesn’t. You know, and — In fact, it’s a pretty good test for some people, in terms of managements, how they think about something like buying in stock, because it’s not a very complicated equation if you sort of think straight about that sort of a subject. But some people think that way and some don’t, and they’re probably miles better at something else. But they say some very silly things when you get to something that seems so clear as whether, say, buying in stock makes sense.
concept: Test a management's money mind by how it reasons about buying in its own stock, a simple equation that some able people get badly wrong.
evolution_notes: Answers Munger (line 711): "there’s also the option of buying in stock, which — so, it isn’t like it’s some hopeless problem." Related: L2016-002 (buyback price discipline) and L1999-028.

quote_verbatim: And if you go to a dentist, if you hire a plumber, in all of the professions, there is value added by the professionals as a group, compared to doing it yourself or just randomly picking laymen. In the investment world, it isn’t true. I mean, they, the active group, the people that are professionals, in aggregate, are not, cannot do better than the aggregate of the people who just sit tight. And if you say, “Well, in the active group there’s some person that’s terrific,” I will agree with you. But the passive people can’t all pick that person. And they wouldn’t — they don’t know how to identify them.
concept: Unlike other professions, investment professionals as a group cannot add value over those who sit tight, and the few superior ones cannot be picked by everyone or identified.

[...] CHARLIE MUNGER: And so you’ll find the person who has a long career at “2 and 20,” and if you analyze it, net, all the people who’ve lost money because some of the early people have had a good record but more money coming in later and they lose it. So, the investing world is just, it’s a morass of wrong incentives, crazy reporting, and I’d say a fair amount of delusion.

Because you do not want a plane that — or an engine — that’s 99 percent complete while somebody’s dealing with a problem of faulty parts or anything else that would delay delivery. heading: ### 10. Online competition hasn’t yet affected Berkshire retailers

quote_verbatim: Well, it’s got some relevance, but it’s got a whole lot less relevance than it used to. [...] But I think the best method, of course, is just to calculate intrinsic business value. But it can’t be precise. [...] But as the businesses have evolved, as we built in unrecognized value at the operating businesses — unrecognized for accounting purposes — I think it still has some use as being kind of the base figure we use. If it were a private company and 10 of us here owned it, instead we’d just sit down annually and calculate the businesses one by one and use that as a base value.
concept: Book value loses relevance as value builds up in operating businesses that accounting does not mark up; the better measure is intrinsic value, estimated business by business as private owners would, though never precisely.
evolution_notes: Answers a question on book value per share. Compare L1994-008 (book value says nothing about intrinsic value) and M2014-067 (intrinsic value as private business value). Ends: "I think the easiest thing is to use the standards we’re using now, recognizing the limitations in them."

And so I, basically, like it when our marketable securities go down and our own businesses go up. [...] CHARLIE MUNGER: We have a lot of — we’ve replaced a lot of marketable securities with unmarketable securities that are worth a lot more.
concept: Munger: stocks held inside a taxed corporation are worth less than their market value because the tax is embedded; owning operating businesses outright is better.

heading: ### 12. I don’t know tech, but I know consumer behavior

quote_verbatim: This table offers the strongest argument I can muster against ever using borrowed money to own stocks. There is simply no telling how far stocks can fall in a short period. Even if your borrowings are small and your positions aren't immediately threatened by the plunging market, your mind may well become rattled by scary headlines and breathless commentary. And an unsettled mind will not make good decisions. [...] When major declines occur, however, they offer extraordinary opportunities to those who are not handicapped by debt.

quote_verbatim: The bet illuminated another important investment lesson: Though markets are generally rational, they occasionally do crazy things. Seizing the opportunities then offered does not require great intelligence, a degree in economics or a familiarity with Wall Street jargon such as alpha and beta. What investors then need instead is an ability to both disregard mob fears or enthusiasms and to focus on a few simple fundamentals. A willingness to look unimaginative for a sustained period � or even to look foolish � is also essential.
concept: To use the market's occasional craziness one needs not brilliance but the ability to ignore the crowd, hold to a few fundamentals, and look unimaginative or foolish for a long time.
evolution_notes: Restates L2016-001 and L2011-018 on the crowd; rowed for the new element, the willingness to look unimaginative or foolish for a sustained period.

heading: "The Bet" is Over and Has Delivered an Unforeseen Investment Lesson

quote_verbatim: I want to quickly acknowledge that in any upcoming day, week or even year, stocks will be riskier � far riskier � than short-term U.S. bonds. As an investor's investment horizon lengthens, however, a diversified portfolio of U.S. equities becomes progressively less risky than bonds, assuming that the stocks are purchased at a sensible multiple of earnings relative to then-prevailing interest rates. It is a terrible mistake for investors with long-term horizons � among them, pension funds, college endowments and savings-minded individuals � to measure their investment "risk" by their portfolio's ratio of bonds to stocks. Often, high-grade bonds in an investment portfolio increase its risk.
concept: For a long horizon, do not measure risk by the bond share of a portfolio; diversified stocks bought at a sensible multiple relative to interest rates grow less risky than bonds as the horizon lengthens.
evolution_notes: Before (lines 672-673): "Investing is an activity in which consumption today is foregone in an attempt to allow greater consumption at a later date. "Risk" is the possibility that this objective won't be attained." (restates L2011-012 and L2011-013, not rowed). The horizon point restates L2014-004 and the danger of currency investments L2011-014; new here are the condition (a sensible multiple of earnings relative to prevailing interest rates) and the named mistake of the bond-to-stock ratio.

When you buy something because you’re hoping tomorrow morning you’re going to wake up, you know, and the price will be higher, the only reason, you know, you need more people coming into it than are leaving. quote_verbatim: Well, what people do generally with that is they take what they want to be the answer for them and then they hire — or they just attach themselves to some economist that gives them a more complicated way of saying it’s all going to be wonderful because it’s happened. [...] It’s very, very, very difficult in economics to measure the impact of single variables. You cannot just do one thing in economics. People kind of learn that in physics and talk about butterflies in China and all that sort of thing. But the — every question you get in economics the next, any statement, you should say “and then what?”
concept: Distrust the economic answer people choose because it suits them; no single variable acts alone, so ask "and then what?" of every economic statement.
evolution_notes: Said of the 2017 corporate tax cut; the political matter and the utility pass-through are left out of the quote (the 2014 PM and 2015 convention). The elision skips the utility rate-base explanation and Buffett's "I think it’s human nature if you’re getting a break to say it’s going to work wonderfully for everybody else" (lines 875-877).
