heading: ### 13. Shareholders will get a lot of the corporate tax cut benefit

quote_verbatim: But generally I think people make more money if they’re very narrowly specialized, like the proctologist. (Laughter) And it’s much harder to make a lot of money for most people if you try to imitate Warren and me.
concept: Munger: most people earn more by narrow specialization than by imitating a generalist approach such as his and Buffett's.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct (a career rule), for the synthesis to keep or drop. Before (line 897): "you’ve got to get near that interface to benefit from being bilingual and so on." Buffett's advice to learn the other country's language (lines 889, 893) is advice to one student, not rowed.

heading: ### 14. Utilizing multicultural backgrounds to improve international economies, and the benefits of multiculturality

quote_verbatim: The only thing we — I think we have asked the companies to have a limit on the percentage, I think, that they might put in Berkshire’s stock through the 401(k). We don’t want people to lose jobs who are tied to Berkshire. We certainly don’t want to be in the position of encouraging to put 100 percent or something of their savings in Berkshire itself.
concept: Do not encourage employees to put all their savings in the employer's own stock; limit it.
evolution_notes: "We don’t want people to lose jobs who are tied to Berkshire" is as printed (the sense appears to be that employees should not lose both job and savings; the doubt is recorded, not resolved). After (line 925): "I don’t think even there we’ve insisted on any company doing that."
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 15. Subsidiaries encouraged to offer low-cost 401(k) options

quote_verbatim: But the managers will run the companies. [...] We’ve got a wide variety of managers that run our businesses. And we’re not going to start trying to run them from Omaha.
concept: Leave operating decisions, even ones the owner disagrees with, to the subsidiaries' managers rather than run them from headquarters.
evolution_notes: Said of the subsidiaries' 401(k) plans, where Buffett's own view favours an index option (line 923: "our managers know what I think about the attractiveness of having an index fund option"). The elision skips the employees making their views known to managers. Restates M2002-127 and M2013-010 (decentralization). Munger's lines 927-931 draw the cost of this delegation (rowed separately); the exchange ends (lines 939-941) "No, it’s up to the managers. But we wouldn’t object to a little different viewpoint." / "And we have made it very clear what we think."
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 15. Subsidiaries encouraged to offer low-cost 401(k) options

quote_verbatim: That business of the high-fee choices, because we’ve delegated the whole subject to the managers of the subsidiaries. And so no attention at all is being given to the employee choices at headquarters. And what you’re pointing out is that a lot of the employees in the subsidiaries would do better if they indexed instead of choosing what they did choose. [...] And if there are any people, managers, in the business today, I hope we’ll do a little better at encouraging better choices.
concept: Munger: delegating a whole subject means headquarters gives it no attention, and here employees were left in high-fee choices; the remedy is encouragement, not control.
evolution_notes: Berkshire's own lapse, Munger's lesson. Opens after "Well, you’re right. That has happened." (line 927). The elision crosses "My guess is you’re absolutely right about that. You know." and Buffett's "Yeah." (lines 927-929); Munger resumes the same thought. Same exchange as Buffett's row at line 925; reconciled in the exchange, listed under Tensions seen.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 15. Subsidiaries encouraged to offer low-cost 401(k) options

quote_verbatim: We’re happy to have public shareholders. And we like having individual shareholders. And we don’t favor institutions. And we’re not going to, you know, give guidance and talk especially to them on investor calls and all that sort of thing. We want our — we want it to be directly with — we want shareholders who are partners, basically.
concept: Treat shareholders as partners, favour no institution, and give no guidance or special investor-call access to any group.
evolution_notes: Before (line 949): the culture "gets reinforced by the shareholders we have". Restates the morning's M2018-032 (shareholders as partners).

heading: ### 16. Berkshire’s culture will continue because “it works”

quote_verbatim: It’s a group of owner-oriented, Berkshire-conscious, business-savvy owners. And we don’t have anybody on the board because they’re a leading, you know, educator or whatever it may be. We want people who, basically, think about how to run a business well for themselves and for their partners.
concept: Choose directors who are owner-oriented and business-savvy, thinking how to run the business well for themselves and their partners, not for their eminence elsewhere.
evolution_notes: Before (lines 949-951): directors "who represent, in many cases, lots of shares themselves. They didn’t gets special deals." ("gets" as printed). Restates L2006-014 (the director who thinks like an intelligent owner).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 16. Berkshire’s culture will continue because “it works”

quote_verbatim: Cultures get passed along. You do things that are consistent with the culture, so you do — what you talk about is what you do. And you don’t find people saying, you know, “We’re a wonderful partnership,” and then voting themselves, you know, huge options. [...] And we will keep — we will try to keep behaving in a way that reinforces it and doesn’t dilute it.
concept: A culture is passed on by acting consistently with what is said; a test of it is whether those who speak of partnership vote themselves huge options.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the options "beneath them" and an unnamed deal paying "many, many, many billions", and "We have a few people all of the time that really don’t buy into it entirely". Munger after (line 957): the culture will last because "it’s not that damned easy to duplicate", a forecast, not rowed. Near M2017-003 (govern by a culture).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 16. Berkshire’s culture will continue because “it works”

quote_verbatim: if you buy a company that has a million dollars’ worth of net worth and you pay a billion for it, it still only had the million dollars’ of net worth. I mean you just paid more for it. So the basic profitability of the company is huge, even though your investment may be at a significantly higher price.
concept: Separate the business's return on its own tangible net worth from the investor's return on the price paid; a high price does not change the first.
evolution_notes: The quote opens mid-sentence ("the earnings as a percent of net tangible assets, and the rest is just, you know,"). Said of the S&P 500's rising earnings on tangible net worth and the asset-light giants. After (line 999): "I didn’t see that coming in 1999 when I wrote whatever I wrote there." Near the morning's M2018-047 (returns on tangible assets).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 18. “Amazing” earnings in the new “asset-light economy”

quote_verbatim: And you know, while Warren may have predicted a little wrong when he wrote that very scholarly article, he didn’t invest wrong. And so it just shows that it’s hard to make these economic predictions.
concept: Munger: a wrong economic prediction need not mean a wrong investment; such predictions are hard, and investing need not rest on them.
evolution_notes: Buffett's error (the 1999 Fortune article's view that profits would not hold much above 6 percent of GDP), Munger's lesson. Buffett (line 1011): "Being right for the wrong reason or something. (Laughs) Or wrong for the right reasons." Near M2013-047 (macro forecasts play no part).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 18. “Amazing” earnings in the new “asset-light economy”

quote_verbatim: I mean, the amount of enjoyment per real — in terms of the real — of what you pay for this, has gone dramatically down in inflation-adjusted money. So it is a bargain product. You know, you have to look at — See’s Candy, you know, if you live in California and you were a teenage boy, and you went to your girlfriend’s house and you gave the box of candy to her or to her mother or father and she kissed you, you know, you lose price sensitivity at that point. (Laughter) So we really want products where people feel like kissing you, you know — (laughs) — rather than slapping you.
concept: Look for products whose buyers lose price sensitivity because of what the product means to them, and whose real cost per unit of enjoyment has fallen, so they remain a bargain at a premium.
evolution_notes: In answer to how one forecasts the success of American Express and Coca-Cola rather than Diners Club or RC Cola. Before (line 1037): offered RC Cola at half the price, "in terms of drinking it", he would not switch; Coke "sold for a nickel in 1900". Near M2005-020 (the agony of a price increase).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 20. “We really want products where people feel like kissing you”

quote_verbatim: American Express had this huge salad oil scandal in 1960 happen — in ’63, November, right around the time [President John] Kennedy was shot. And there was really worry about whether the company would survive. But nobody quit using the card. Nobody quit using the traveler’s checks. And they charged a premium price for their traveler’s checks. So there are things you can see around consumer products that sometimes can give you a pretty good insight into the future. And then sometimes we make mistakes.
concept: When a company is in trouble, watch whether customers keep using the product and paying a premium; consumer behavior can give insight into the future that the headlines do not.
evolution_notes: Before (line 1039): "in effect we’re betting on the ecosystem of Apple products ... But I may be wrong." Restates the morning's M2018-013 (a scandal at a sound company) and M2017-078 (infer from consumer behavior).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 20. “We really want products where people feel like kissing you”

quote_verbatim: No, he’s right. I mean, we don’t foresee things that we haven’t got a lot of evidence in on. [...] We want to see a lot of — if we’re talking about a consumer product — we want to see how a consumer product behaves under a lot of different circumstances, and then we want to use something — [...] And it talks about the “scuttlebutt method” of investing, which was quite a ways from what Ben Graham taught me in terms of figures. But it’s a very, very good book. And you can learn a lot, you know, just by going out and using some shoe leather. [...] you can get a feel for some products, and then there are others you can’t. And then sometimes you’re wrong. But it is a good technique. It’s an important investing technique, I would say that.
concept: Do not foresee what there is little evidence on: watch how a consumer product behaves under many circumstances, and gather it by scuttlebutt, going out and asking, accepting that some products cannot be read.
evolution_notes: Agrees with Munger (lines 1041-1045): "if we’d been offered a chance to go into Coca-Cola right after it was invented, we probably would have said no." The first elision crosses Munger's "No." (line 1049) and Buffett resumes the same thought; the second skips the naming of Phil Fisher's "Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits" (the method is Fisher's, named by Buffett); the third skips "Now they call them channel checks now or something like that. But it’s —". Restates M1998-144 (talk to competitors, customers, suppliers).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 20. “We really want products where people feel like kissing you”

quote_verbatim: They delight — they surprise and delight their customers. And there is nothing like that in business. You have delighted customers, you’re a long way home.
concept: A business that surprises and delights its customers is a long way toward success; there is nothing like it.
evolution_notes: Said of Costco, whose virtues Munger keeps finding (line 1053). Near L2005-010 (delighting customers widens the moat).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 20. “We really want products where people feel like kissing you”

quote_verbatim: Well, we will not make hostile tenders ourselves. I do not believe that there’s anything fundamentally wrong with the idea. [...] We like being liked by the managements that we join, because we’re counting on them to run the company, and we’re not bringing in a whole bunch of people that know how to change businesses. [...] We don’t think every management is entitled to be — you know, they don’t have a lifetime hold on their business. [...] But we don’t think it’s evil for the shareholders, in some cases, to have different opinions about who should run the company, or whether compensation’s appropriate, or matters of that sort. The stockholders still own the company.
concept: Make no hostile bids, because the method depends on being welcomed by managers who will keep running the business; yet no management has a lifetime hold, and the stockholders, who own the company, may rightly challenge it.
evolution_notes: The first elision skips the Fortune 500 not all being "managed by the best"; the second, "We seldom take a position opposite the management — very seldom — on anything involving a proxy, but — contest of sorts. But we don’t rule it out."; the third, the votes against option proposals and the withheld vote at Coca-Cola (line 1063). Munger (line 1065): "I don’t envy these people that are in these unfriendly uproars all the time."
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 21. Hostile bids aren’t “evil” but Berkshire doesn’t do them

quote_verbatim: And we’re so — there’s so much craziness in price from our viewpoint. Of course, it’s very hard for us to do it. The people in the leveraged buyout game, who love massive leverage and don’t mind high prices, even they are getting nosebleeds. It’s hard. And it’s not an environment that means that — that allows Berkshire just to go out and buy a whole lot of companies. [...] We have to wait.
concept: Munger: when buyers using heavy leverage set crazy prices, do not compete; wait.
evolution_notes: Before (line 1097): the acquisition game "is so driven by the leveraged buyout and the so-called, whatever they call them, strategic, yes, strategic. I usually translate that into barnyard language." The elision crosses Buffett's question (line 1099), and Munger resumes the same thought. After (line 1109), to Buffett's question whether they ever made a strategic deal: "We’ve never had a strategic plan unless you’ve hidden it from me. (Laughter)", a joke. Restates the morning's M2018-005 (doing nothing when there is nothing to do).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 22. Berkshire still not on radar screen of international business sellers

quote_verbatim: And I would rather have a person — if I could hire somebody among the top five graduates of number one, two or three of the business schools, and my choice was somebody that had — was bright — but had chapter eight of “The Intelligent Investor” absolutely — it just was natural to them — they had it in their bones, basically — I’d take the person from chapter eight. This is not — what we do is not a complicated business. It’s got to be a disciplined business, but it is — it does not require a super IQ or anything of the sort. And there are a few fundamentals that are incredibly important, and you do have to understand accounting. And it helps to get out and talk to consumers and start thinking like a consumer in many ways in certain — and all of that. But it just doesn’t require advanced learning.
concept: Hire for the right attitude to the market held in the bones over academic rank; investing needs discipline, a few fundamentals and accounting, not a super IQ or advanced learning.
evolution_notes: Before (line 1135): the efficient-market "priesthood ... strayed pretty far, in our view, from the reality of investing." Chapter eight is the market chapter, as Buffett glosses it at line 1151 ("in terms of looking at stocks as a business"). Near M1996-085 (the three ideas).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 23. Investing “doesn’t require advanced learning”

quote_verbatim: Before he died, Bill Graham — I mean, Ben Graham — recognized that the exact way he sought undervalued companies wouldn’t necessarily work for all times under all conditions. And that’s certainly the way it worked for us. We gradually morphed into trying to buy the better companies when they were underpriced, instead of the lousy companies when they were underpriced. [...] So we’ve had to learn a different game. And that’s a lesson for all the young people in the room. If you’re going to live a long time, you have to keep learning. [...] What you formerly knew is never enough. So if you don’t learn to constantly revise your earlier conclusions and get better (inaudible), you are — I always use the same metaphor. You’re like a one-legged man in an ass-kicking contest. (Laughter)
concept: Munger: a method that worked will not work for all times; move from cheap lousy companies to better companies bought underpriced, keep learning and constantly revise earlier conclusions.
evolution_notes: "Bill Graham — I mean, Ben Graham" is as printed, a self-corrected slip. The first elision skips Graham outliving his game and net-net stocks too small for Berkshire; the second crosses Buffett's "Yeah." (line 1147), and Munger resumes the same thought. Restates M2010-086 and M2017-092 (keep learning) and M2014-069 (from Graham's quantitative emphasis).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 23. Investing “doesn’t require advanced learning”

quote_verbatim: And so the utility of chapter eight, in terms of looking at stocks as a business, is of enormous value. The utility of chapter 20 about a margin of safety is of enormous value. But that’s not complicated stuff.
concept: Two simple ideas carry enormous value: look at stocks as businesses, and keep a margin of safety.
evolution_notes: Before (line 1151): "Graham was not scalable"; Graham-Newman worked with about $12 million and Graham "really wasn’t interested in making a lot of money for himself." Restates M1996-085 (a stock is part of a business; a margin of safety). Shares the heading with the hiring test at lines 1135-1137.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 23. Investing “doesn’t require advanced learning”

quote_verbatim: Yeah, whenever you hear a theory described as elegant, watch out, you know. (Laughter)
concept: Distrust a theory praised for being elegant.
evolution_notes: Stated as a joke, to laughter. The general form of Munger's point (line 1153): corporate-finance teachers teach formulas because "it’s a fine teaching experience", like the famous eye doctor's obsolete cataract operation, "such a wonderful operation to teach"; "It’s all balderdash." Under the 2012 convention the general statement is rowed and Munger's line named here.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 23. Investing “doesn’t require advanced learning”

quote_verbatim: Generally speaking, we’re always trying to get the best — to get something that’s worth buying. [...] So people want to find some formula. It’s what I call “physics envy.” These people want the world to be like physics. But the world isn’t like physics, outside of physics. And that false precision just does nothing but get you in trouble. So I would say you’ve got to master the general ideas, and you’ve got to work to improve your judgment slowly, the way all the rest of us had.
concept: Munger: capital allocation is getting something worth buying; formulas give false precision, so master the general ideas and improve judgment slowly.
evolution_notes: In answer to "what is the first principle of capital allocation". The elision skips academia's rejection of a one-sentence answer. Restates M2018-050 (heading 5 of this session, no formula) and adds the false-precision warning and the slow improvement of judgment. Buffett (line 1221): machines do not "bring much to the table in terms of capital allocation or investing"; Munger (line 1223): "very remunerative, fee-earning twaddle".
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 26. Munger: “I don’t think the world is going to be changed that much by machine intelligence”

quote_verbatim: American investors are missing China. And they’re missing it because it’s a long way away, it looks different, they’re not used to it, it’s complicated, the headlines confuse them. In other words, it just looks too hard, sitting in Omaha, to outsmart the Chinese market. But I think you’re absolutely right. It’s where they should be looking.
concept: Munger: investors neglect markets that are distant, unfamiliar and confusing, and that neglect is why one should look there.
evolution_notes: Restates M2017-085 (fish where the fish are) and the morning's M2018-031 (young markets better hunting grounds). Buffett after (lines 1233-1235): accumulating "a 6 or 8 or $10 billion position" abroad is hard, with 3 percent reporting in the U.K. and Europe, "Some of the problems are, just by the nature of our size"; a fact of size, not rowed.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 27. Munger: “American investors are missing China”

quote_verbatim: We are looking for things when we do get into the durability of the competitive advantage, and whether we think that our opinion might be better than other people’s opinion in assessing the probability of the durability, so to speak.
concept: The test is the durability of the competitive advantage, and whether one's own judgment of that durability is likely better than other people's; not whether the business is labelled tech.
evolution_notes: Before (line 1249): "we don’t think of whether we should be in tech companies or not, or that sort of thing." Near M2009-040 (durability of the advantage).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 28. “What Jeff Bezos has done is something close to a miracle”

quote_verbatim: And the problem is, if I think something will be a miracle, I tend not to bet on it. (Laughs)
concept: Do not bet on an outcome that would take a miracle, even from an exceptional manager.
evolution_notes: Said with a laugh, of Amazon. Before (line 1249): "I think what Jeff Bezos has done is something close to a miracle." Buffett later (line 1263): "I had a very, very, very high opinion of Jeff’s ability when I first met him. And I underestimated him." The rule and the admission sit in the same answer; listed under Tensions seen.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 28. “What Jeff Bezos has done is something close to a miracle”

quote_verbatim: And I didn’t go into Apple because it was a tech stock in the least. I mean, I went into Apple because I made certain — came to certain conclusions about both the intelligence with which the capital would be employed, but more important, about the value of an ecosystem and how permanent that ecosystem could be, and what the threats were to it, and a whole bunch of things. [...] It’s much more the nature of consumer behavior. And some things strike me as having a lot more permanence than others.
concept: Judge a technology company as any other: by how intelligently capital will be employed and, more, by how permanent its customer ecosystem is and what threatens it, read from consumer behavior rather than the product's components.
evolution_notes: The elision skips "And that didn’t — I don’t think that required me to, you know, take apart an iPhone or something and figure out what all the components were or anything." speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 28. “What Jeff Bezos has done is something close to a miracle”

quote_verbatim: We’ve looked at it, and you know, I made a mistake in not being able to come to a conclusion where I really felt that at the present prices that the prospects were far better than the prices indicated. [...] But the answer is, we’ll miss a lot of things that — or I’ll miss a lot of things — that I don’t feel I understand well enough. And there is no penalty in investing if you don’t swing at a ball that’s in the strike zone, as long as you swing at something at some point, then you know, eventually that you find the pitches you like. And that’s the way we’ll continue to do it. We’ll try to stay within our circle of competence.
concept: Buffett's own error: not reaching a conclusion on Amazon and Google at their prices; the lesson he keeps is that missing what one does not understand carries no penalty, so long as one swings eventually, and one stays within the circle of competence.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the Apple passage rowed at line 1251. After (line 1253): "Charlie and I generally agree on sort of where that circle ends". Later (line 1263): "But I made the wrong decision on Google." Restates M2016-061 and L1997-006 (the strike zone and the fat pitch).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 28. “What Jeff Bezos has done is something close to a miracle”

quote_verbatim: The mystery was how much competition would come along, and how effective they would be, and whether it would be a game where four or five people were slugging it out without making as much money as they could if one company dominated. Those are tough decisions to make. You can have industries where there’s only two people in it, and they still don’t (inaudible) very good because they beat each other’s brains out.
concept: Understanding what a company does is not the question; the question is how much competition will come and whether competitors will fight away the profits, which can happen even with two players.
evolution_notes: Said of Google. Before (line 1261): "it wasn’t like what they were doing was a mystery to me." After (line 1263): the airlines, "a better business now than it used to be, but it used to be suicide". Restates M2013-052 (only two competitors and still terrible businesses).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 28. “What Jeff Bezos has done is something close to a miracle”

quote_verbatim: Usually if businesses get much larger, everybody from the CEO down expects to earn more money for something that — where they really bring the same amount of intensity and work and (inaudible) to it. It is really a tough question. I think that if you engage compensation consultants at public companies, which they all do, they’re going to recommend things that cause them to have CEOs recommend them to other companies. (Laughs) It’s just, you’re working against human nature when you have an arrangement like that.
concept: Pay that scales with size rewards the same effort more as a business grows, and a compensation consultant recommends what makes CEOs recommend him; both work against human nature.
evolution_notes: Before (line 1295): "trying to come to the right answer when you have different degrees of capital intensity ... and how much you scale up based on size, because there is an incentive to grow businesses." Restates M2004-096 (the consultant's own income).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 30. No “precise formulas” on Berkshire’s incentive plans

quote_verbatim: And I think people do like — they do like to make their own decisions. They do like recognition. You know, they — most people respond — they like doing a good job, and they like the fact that we understand it. And compensation’s part of that. But it’s not the whole thing.
concept: Managers are kept by making their own decisions, recognition and an owner who understands good work; pay is part of it, not the whole.
evolution_notes: Before (lines 1295-1297): "we have obviously kept a very, very, very high percentage of the managers that we hoped to have stay with us. In fact, just about a hundred percent." After (line 1297): "I wish I could give you some precise formulas, but there aren’t any".
speaker: BUFFETT

concept: Munger: keep individual managers' pay arrangements private; publishing them gains nothing.

And he keeps them all private.", a joke; Buffett (line 1309): "We publish what the directors are paid." Munger (line 1311): "We publish what we have to, yes." Near the morning's note on Todd's and Ted's individual performance never being reported.
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 30. No “precise formulas” on Berkshire’s incentive plans

quote_verbatim: The fact is that the annual change in Berkshire's book value � which makes its farewell appearance on page 2 � is a metric that has lost the relevance it once had. [...] Second, while our equity holdings are valued at market prices, accounting rules require our collection of operating companies to be included in book value at an amount far below their current value, a mismark that has grown in recent years. [...] The math of such purchases is simple: Each transaction makes per-share intrinsic value go up, while per-share book value goes down. That combination causes the book-value scorecard to become increasingly out of touch with economic reality. [...] Over time, however, Berkshire's stock price will provide the best measure of business performance.
concept: Book value stops being a usable yardstick once most value sits in operating businesses carried far below worth and buybacks are made above book but below value; over time the stock price measures performance better.
evolution_notes: The first elision skips the first circumstance (the shift from marketable stocks to operating businesses, lines 115-117); the second skips the third circumstance's opening, that Berkshire will likely repurchase "at prices above book value but below our estimate of intrinsic value" (lines 119-121); the third skips a page number (line 125) and "In future tabulations of our financial results, we expect to focus on Berkshire's market price. Markets can be extremely capricious" (lines 127-128). Reverses the measure set out in L2009-003 (book value as "a crude proxy" for per-share intrinsic value) and qualifies L1996-001, L1997-003 and R1996-020 (book value tracking the change in intrinsic value); the letter itself gives the reasons for the change, so it is listed under the note's Tensions seen rather than rowed as a tension.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: BERKSHIRE HATHAWAY INC.

quote_verbatim: Fortunately, it's not necessary to evaluate each tree individually to make a rough estimate of Berkshire's intrinsic business value. [...] I believe Berkshire's intrinsic value can be approximated by summing the values of our four asset-laden groves and then subtracting an appropriate amount for taxes eventually payable on the sale of marketable securities. [...] Forget that thought: It would be foolish for us to sell any of our wonderful companies even if no tax would be payable on its sale. Truly good businesses are exceptionally hard to find. Selling any you are lucky enough to own makes no sense at all.
concept: Value a many-business company roughly by its few major groups, each appraised whole, deducting the tax that will fall due on securities that will be sold but none on businesses that will never be sold, because truly good businesses are too hard to find to sell.
evolution_notes: The first elision runs from the five groves (line 148) through the four groves' description to line 265: the operating subsidiaries, the equities, the shared-control quartet, the cash, and the paragraphs listed in the note as repeats. The second skips the question it answers, whether an allowance should be made "for the major tax costs Berkshire would incur if we were to sell certain of our wholly-owned businesses" (lines 269-270). speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Focus on the Forest � Forget the Trees

quote_verbatim: For 54 years our managerial decisions at Berkshire have been made from the viewpoint of the shareholders who are staying, not those who are leaving. Consequently, Charlie and I have never focused on current-quarter results. [...] Our lack of such an instrument means that the parent company has never had a quarterly "number" to hit. Shunning the use of this bogey sends an important message to our many managers, reinforcing the culture we prize.
concept: Decide for the owners who stay, not those who leave; so set no quarterly number at the top, because having none tells managers what the culture values.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the absence of monthly earnings reports at the parent (lines 321-323) and "Furthermore, Berkshire has no company-wide budget (though many of our subsidiaries find one useful)." (line 325). Next (lines 329-334), not rowed: the "innocent" fudge to meet Wall Street expectations becoming "the first step toward full-fledged fraud", and "if it's okay for the boss to cheat a little, it's easy for subordinates to rationalize similar behavior", which repeat L2000-039 (fudging into fraud) and L2016-006 (bad behaviour contagious to subordinates). speaker: BUFFETT
heading: Repurchases and Reporting

quote_verbatim: Those who regularly preach doom because of government budget deficits (as I regularly did myself for many years) might note that our country's national debt has increased roughly 400-fold during the last of my 77-year periods. That's 40,000%! Suppose you had foreseen this increase and panicked at the prospect of runaway deficits and a worthless currency. To "protect" yourself, you might have eschewed stocks and opted instead to buy 3 1/4 ounces of gold with your $114.75. And what would that supposed protection have delivered? You would now have an asset worth about $4,200, less than 1% of what would have been realized from a simple unmanaged investment in American business.
concept: Buffett's own long habit of preaching doom over deficits: even a correct forecast of the debt's growth, acted on by fleeing stocks for gold, would have kept less than 1% of what owning American business returned.
evolution_notes: Buffett's own error, admitted in the parenthesis; the lesson is drawn from the hypothetical investor who acted on the same view. The passage continues "The magical metal was no match for the American mettle." (lines 664-665). Restates the meeting row M2018-003 (productive over nonproductive gold) and is near L2011-018 (fear of currency collapse driving money to gold) and L1994-004 (ignore macro and political forecasts); new in the letters is that a correct macro forecast would still have misled. The deficit as a political matter is not quoted beyond the passage's own words.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: The American Tailwind

quote_verbatim: So, I encourage you now, and I encourage all the press that’s here, focus on what we call our operating earnings, which were up a bit. And forget about the capital gains or losses in any given period. Now, they’re enormously important over time. [...] They are an important part of Berkshire, but they have absolutely no predictive value or analytical value on a quarterly basis or an annual basis.

(the first "future" kept as printed in the skipped words). Restates M2018-001 and M2011-003 at earlier meetings, and the FY2018 letter's "Our advice? Focus on operating earnings" (letter line 105, not rowed, which repeats L2017-001).

heading: ### 3. Berkshire’s Q1: Pay attention to operating earnings

quote_verbatim: We repurchase shares — we used to have a policy of tying it to book value. But that became — really became obsolete. It did not — The real thing is to buy stock — repurchase shares — only when you think you’re doing it at a price where the remaining shareholders have had — are worth more the moment after you repurchased it than they were the moment before. [...] Most companies adopt repurchase programs and they just say, “We’re going to spend so much.” That’s like saying, you know, “We’re going to buy XYZ stock, and we’re going to spend so much here.” [...] We will buy stock when we think it is selling below a conservative estimate of its intrinsic value. [...] And you will — you could easily see periods where we would spend very substantial sums if we thought the stock was selling at, say, 25 or 30 percent less than it was worth, and we didn’t have something else that was even better.
concept: Repurchase only when the remaining owners are worth more per share the moment after; a program set as an amount to spend is like buying any stock regardless of price; spend heavily only at a wide discount and when nothing better is available.
evolution_notes: The first elision skips the three-partner illustration (a $3 million business, the departing partner's offers at $1.1 million, $1 million and $900,000, lines 51-53); the second skips "“We’re going to buy a company.” “We’re going to spend whatever it takes.”" (line 53); the third skips the intrinsic-value band (rowed separately from lines 53-55) and the first quarter's purchases of "something over a billion", "we don’t salivate over buying it" (line 55). Charlie would have a band in his mind, and it would probably be 10 percent. And ours would not be identical, but they’d be very close. And sometimes he might figure a bit higher than I do, a bit lower.

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 7. Munger: “I predict we’ll get a little more liberal in repurchasing shares”

But we don’t have to do it today or tomorrow, but we do have to find something that gets at least equal, and hopefully better, customer satisfaction and that makes our railroad more efficient.
concept: Copy whatever competitors prove successful, but only where it keeps or improves customer satisfaction while raising efficiency, and without haste.

quote_verbatim: it looks like to me like Wells made some big mistakes in what they incentivized. And as Charlie says, there’s nothing like incentives, but they can incentivize the wrong behavior. [...] but when you find a problem, you have to do something about it. And I think that’s where they probably made a mistake at Wells Fargo. They made it at Salomon. [...] But when he heard about it, he didn’t immediately notify the Federal Reserve. [...] Because, essentially, he heard about a pyromaniac, and he let him keep the box of matches.
concept: Incentives can reward the wrong behaviour; the fatal error at Wells Fargo and at Salomon was not acting at once on a problem once it was known, leaving the wrongdoer in place.

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 10. Bank CEOS who make bad mistakes should lose all their net worth

quote_verbatim: There’s no way to have a city of 390,000 people and not need a policeman or a court system. And some people don’t follow the rules. And you can incentivize the wrong behavior. You’ve got to do something about it when it happens. [...] And I don’t have any advice for anybody running a business except, when you find out something is leading to bad results or bad behavior, you know, you — if you’re in the top job, you’ve got to take action fast. And that’s why we have hotlines. That’s why we get — when we get certain anonymous letters, we turn them over to the audit committee or to outside investigators.
concept: Any large organization will have people breaking rules; the person in the top job must act fast when he learns of bad results or behaviour, with hotlines and outside investigation as the means of hearing.
evolution_notes: Lines 101 and 103 are consecutive paragraphs; the elision skips the banks whose shareholders "paid a price" and the absence of jail sentences (line 103). speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 10. Bank CEOS who make bad mistakes should lose all their net worth

quote_verbatim: We do feel, if shareholders — if we’re going to be repurchasing shares from shareholders who are partners, and we think it’s cheap, we ought to be very sure that they have the facts available to evaluate what they own. I mean, just as if we had a partnership, it would not be good if there were three partners and two of them decided that they would sort of freeze out the third, maybe in terms of giving him material information that they knew that that third party didn’t know.

evolution_notes: Next (line 123): disclosure "the same sort of disclosure that I would give to my sisters", and "if you’re going to sell your stock, should have the same information that’s important, that’s available to me and to Charlie." speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 11. “We will spend a lot of money” on buybacks if price is right

quote_verbatim: Yeah, we will be good at it. We don’t have any trouble being decisive. We don’t say yes very often. But if it’s something obvious — I mean, Jay, if you and I are partners, you know, and our business is worth a million dollars and you say you’ll sell your half to me for 300,000, you’ll have your 300,000 very quickly.
concept: Say yes rarely, but when a bargain is obvious, act decisively and fast.
evolution_notes: Exchange: Munger (lines 125 and 129), "When it gets really obvious, we’ll be very good at it.", said of buybacks; Buffett's line gives the general form (2012 convention, the general statement rowed under its speaker). speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 11. “We will spend a lot of money” on buybacks if price is right

quote_verbatim: I have said that you do not put your citizenship in a blind trust. But you also don’t speak on behalf of your company. You do speak as a citizen if you speak. And therefore, you have to be careful about when you do speak, because it’s going to be assumed you’re speaking on behalf of your company. [...] But — the general — well, the rule is, I mean, that people do not pursue their own political interests with your money here. We’ve had one or two managers over the years, for example, that would do some fundraising where they were fundraising from people who were suppliers of them or something of the sort. And if I ever find out about it, that ends promptly. My position, at Berkshire, is not to be used to further my own political beliefs.
concept: A chief speaks on politics only as a citizen and with care, since he will be taken to speak for the company; no one pursues his own political interests with the owners' money or leans on suppliers for his causes.
evolution_notes: A rule about how a company conducts itself in politics, rowed with the policy matter left out (2016 convention). The elision skips Berkshire's record of no contributions to candidates and the regulated subsidiaries' political action committees, kept "simply to achieve the same access as their competitors" (lines 165-167). speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 13. Buffett speaks for himself on politics, not for Berkshire

quote_verbatim: We can’t do that. But that’s — we don’t want the stock to be either significantly underpriced or significantly overpriced. And we’re probably unique on the overpriced part of it. But we don’t want it. I do not want the stock selling at twice what’s it worth because I’m going to disappoint people, you know. [...] But ideally, we would hope the stock would sell in a range that more or less is its intrinsic business value. We have no desire to hype it in any way. And we have no desire to depress it so we can repurchase it cheap.
concept: A company should want its stock to sell near intrinsic value, neither hyped above it, which disappoints buyers, nor depressed below it to repurchase cheap.
evolution_notes: "We can’t do that" refers to the ideal just described (line 191): a yearly fair price, as in a private company, at which leaving owners could get out. The elision skips "there’s no magic formula to make a stock worth what it’s selling for, if it sells for way too much" and the commercial liking for a cheap repurchase (lines 191-193). Earlier in the heading (line 187): "There’s no master plan on that other than to buy aggressively when we like the price"; Munger (line 189): "I don’t think we care much which class we buy."
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 15. We don’t try to push Berkshire stock higher or lower

quote_verbatim: And we count on our managers to anticipate what is coming in their business. And sometimes they talk to us about it. But we do not run that on a centralized basis. [...] But we don’t try to run those from headquarters. And that may mean — that may have certain weaknesses at certain times. I think, net, it’s been a terrific benefit for Berkshire. Our managers, to a great degree, own their businesses. And we want them to feel a sense of ownership. We don’t want them to be lost in some massive conglomerate, where they get directions from this group, which is a subgroup of that group.
concept: Leave each business's managers to anticipate change in their own field rather than direct it from the centre, accepting some weaknesses for the sense of ownership it gives them.
evolution_notes: The elision crosses Buffett's turn to Munger, Munger's reply (line 203, "I know very little about 5G. But I do know a little about China", not rowed) and Buffett's resumption of the same thought (line 205), as the 2004-2005 convention allows. Restates L2014-031 (autonomous subsidiaries, almost nothing at headquarters) and L2009-008 (decisions at the operating level); new here is the admitted cost, "certain weaknesses at certain times".
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 16. We welcome change, but we won’t always adapt to it

quote_verbatim: And some of those changes hurt us. They hurt us in textiles. They hurt us in shoes. They hurt us in the department store business. Hurt us in the trading stamp business. These were the founding businesses of this operation. But we do adjust. [...] So, we welcome change. And we certainly want to have managers that can anticipate and adapt to it. But sometimes, we’ll be wrong. And those businesses will wither and die. And we’d better use the money someplace else.
concept: Change will kill some owned businesses despite able managers; accept it and move the money elsewhere rather than keep feeding them.
evolution_notes: The elision skips Buffett's "card-carrying capitalist" and the farm-employment illustration (80 percent on farms in 1800). Same answer as the row on lines 201-205 (managers anticipating change); this row carries the separate lesson about withering businesses. Near R1995-011 (poor businesses kept only while they produce some cash), which this qualifies by naming redeployment.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 16. We welcome change, but we won’t always adapt to it

quote_verbatim: We paid too much money for Kraft. To some extent, our own actions had driven up the prices. Now, Kraft Heinz, the profits of that business, 6 billion — we’ll say very, very, very roughly, I’m not making forecasts — but 6 billion pretax on 7 billion of tangible assets, is a wonderful business. But you can pay too much for a wonderful business. [...] So, the business does not know how much you paid for it. I mean, it’s going to earn based on its fundamentals.
concept: Buffett's own error at Kraft: a wonderful business earning highly on tangible assets was still bought at too high a price, partly pushed up by Berkshire's own actions; the business earns on its fundamentals regardless of what was paid.
evolution_notes: The elision skips the See's illustration: "there’s some price at which we could’ve bought even See’s Candy, and it wouldn’t have worked." Restates L2014-021 (a sound investment bought at an elevated price becomes a speculation). The general rule follows at lines 217-219 (the row on paying too much and cigar butts in this batch). Munger (line 221): "it’s not a tragedy that, out of two transactions, one worked wonderfully, and the other didn’t work so well. That happens."
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 17. Kraft Heinz is a good business, but we paid too much

quote_verbatim: And that brand moves from product to product, which is terrific, if a brand travels. [...] So, brands — the retailer and the brands have always struggled as to who gets the upper hand in moving a product to the consumers. [...] But basically, retailers — certain retailers — the retail system — has gained some power. And particularly in the case of Amazon and Walmart and their reaction to it, and Costco — and Aldi and some others I can name — has gained in power relative to brands.
concept: For a consumer brand, ask who holds the upper hand between brand and retailer; a retailer's own brand that travels across products, like Kirkland, shifts power from the makers' brands.
evolution_notes: Said of Kraft Heinz against Kirkland ($39 billion against Kraft Heinz's $26 billion, line 215). The elisions skip the Coca-Cola and Kirkland comparison (line 215) and the private-label shares of 35 to 40 percent in soft drinks abroad (line 217). Restates M2001-090 (brand value moves to the trusted retailer), M2006-091 (brand makers and retailers contend for the margin) and M2015-038 (a brand holds against retailer pressure only as a promise in the customer's mind).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 17. Kraft Heinz is a good business, but we paid too much

quote_verbatim: You can turn any investment into a bad deal by paying too much. What you can’t do is turn any investment into a good deal by paying little, which is sort of how I started out in this world. But the idea of buying the cigar butts that are declining or poor businesses for a bargain price is not something that we try to do anymore. We try to buy good businesses at a decent price. And we made a mistake on the Kraft part of Kraft Heinz.
concept: Overpaying spoils any purchase, but a low price cannot rescue a poor or declining business; buy good businesses at a decent price, not cigar butts.
evolution_notes: Follows the Kraft overpayment narrated at line 213 (the mistake-and-lesson row in this batch). Restates L2014-006 (the cigar-butt method defined and left behind) and L2017-002 (a sensible purchase price among the checks); Buffett names his own start as the cigar-butt method.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 17. Kraft Heinz is a good business, but we paid too much

quote_verbatim: The reduction of costs, you know — there can always be mistakes made, when you’ve got places, and you’re reorganizing them to do more business with the same number of people. And we like buying businesses that are efficient to start with.
concept: Prefer businesses already efficient when bought over ones whose value depends on reorganising for cost cuts, where mistakes come easily.
evolution_notes: Said after Munger's line 221, of Kraft Heinz's cost reductions; continues "But the management — the operations — of Kraft Heinz have been improved over the present management overall." Near M2015-037 and M2018-037 (profitable businesses carrying people they do not need).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 17. Kraft Heinz is a good business, but we paid too much

quote_verbatim: So, a leveraged investment in a business is going to beat an unleveraged investment in a good business a good bit of the time. [...] It’s not something that interests us at all. We are not going to leverage up Berkshire. If we’d leveraged up Berkshire, we’d have made a whole lot more money, obviously, over the years. But both Charlie and I, probably, have seen some more high-IQ people — really extraordinarily high-IQ people — destroyed by leverage. [...] And then we saw some of those same people, after that happened to them once, go on and do the same thing again.
concept: Leverage beats an unleveraged holding most of the time, yet it destroys even extraordinarily able people, and some repeat it after being ruined once; so do not lever up.
evolution_notes: The first elision skips deteriorated covenants, low rates and an up-market for businesses, and "you’re going to have some bankruptcies. But you’re going to also have better results in many cases" (lines 249-251); the second skips Long-Term Capital Management in 1998, "it all turned to pumpkins and mice" (line 251). Restates M1997-125 (leverage would have raised returns; never risk what you need), M1999-005 (ruin for the able runs through borrowed money) and L2017-008.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 19. Pension funds should avoid “alternative” investments

quote_verbatim: And I’m sure it doesn’t happen with your Winnipeg operation, but we have seen a number of proposals from private equity funds, where the returns are really not calculated in a manner than — well, they’re not calculated in a manner that I would regard as honest. And so I — it’s not something — if I were running a pension fund, I would be very careful about what was being offered to me. If you have a choice in Wall Street between being a great analyst or being a great salesperson, salesperson is the way to make it.
concept: Scrutinise private-equity offers, whose stated returns are often not honestly calculated; Wall Street pays the salesman more than the analyst.
evolution_notes: "than" kept as printed ("in a manner than"). Next (line 255): a $10 billion fund at 1 1/2 percent locked up for ten years enriches the manager "if you are the dumbest investor in the world". Restates M2004-111 (judge a fund by the fees it collects) and L2016-012 (fees reward gathering assets). Earlier (line 253): about a trillion dollars, perhaps three trillion levered, chasing private businesses, so "the supply-demand situation ... has changed dramatically".
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 19. Pension funds should avoid “alternative” investments

quote_verbatim: It’s not a fair fight, actually, usually, when a bunch of public officials are listening to people who are motivated to really just get paid for raising the money. Everything else is gravy after that. But if you run a fund, and you get even 1 percent of a billion, you’re getting $10 million a year coming in. And if you’ve got the money locked up for a long time, it’s a very one-sided deal.
concept: When a fiduciary is pitched by someone paid for raising money, with fees on locked-up capital, the incentive makes it a one-sided contest.
evolution_notes: Next (line 267): the manager asked why he charged 2-and-20 without evidence of beating an index fund, "Well, that’s because I can’t get 3-and-30". Preceded (line 259) by the Omaha Public Schools' retirement fund, which "were doing fine until the manager started going in a different direction", interrupted by Munger. speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 19. Pension funds should avoid “alternative” investments

concept: Munger: buying an asset because its accounting need not be marked down in a panic is a silly reason to buy it.
evolution_notes: Munger in the exchange on private equity in pension funds; his later line (273), "Warren, all they’re doing is lying a little bit to make the money come in", sums up Buffett's line 271 (rowed separately).
speaker: MUNGER
heading: ### 19. Pension funds should avoid “alternative” investments

quote_verbatim: And when you commit the money — in the case of private equity often — you — they don’t take the money, but you pay a fee on the money that you’ve committed. And of course, you really have to have that money to come up with at any time. And of course, it makes their return look better, if you sit there for a long time in Treasury bills, which you have to hold, because they can call you up and demand the money, and they don’t count that. They count it in terms of getting a fee on it. But they don’t count it in terms of what the socalled internal rate of return is. It’s not as good as it looks.
concept: A private-equity internal rate of return leaves out committed money the investor must hold idle in Treasury bills while still paying a fee on it, so the true return is lower than stated.
evolution_notes: "socalled" kept as printed. Munger answers (line 273): "Warren, all they’re doing is lying a little bit to make the money come in." Gives the mechanism behind "not calculated in a manner that I would regard as honest" (the row on lines 253-255).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 19. Pension funds should avoid “alternative” investments

quote_verbatim: The idea that value is somehow connected to book value or low price/earnings ratios or anything — as Charlie has said, all investing is value investing. I mean, you’re putting out some money now to get more later on. And you’re making a calculation as to the probabilities of getting that money and when you’ll get it and what interest rates will be in between. And all the same calculation goes into it, whether you’re buying some bank at 70 percent of book value, or you’re buying Amazon at some very high multiple of reported earnings.
concept: Value is not tied to low book or earnings multiples: all investing lays out money now for more later, weighing the probability, timing and interest rates, the same calculation for a cheap bank or a high-multiple growth company.
evolution_notes: "as Charlie has said": Munger's maxim spoken by Buffett. Said in defence of the Amazon purchase by one of the two investment managers. Restates M2000-005 and M2015-042 (value investing as getting value for what one pays), M2000-002 and M2009-004 (cash now for more cash later).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 20. Amazon buy doesn’t mean portfolio managers aren’t “value” investors

quote_verbatim: But they are looking for things that they feel they understand what will be developed by that business between now and Judgement Day, in cash. And it’s not — current sales can make some difference. Current profit margins can make some difference. Tangible assets, excess cash, excess debt, all of those things go into making a calculation as to whether they should buy A versus B versus C. [...] tries to figure out whether there’s three or four or five in the bush and how long it’ll take to get to the bush, how certain he is that he’s going to get to the bush, you know, and then who else is going to come and try and take the bush away and all of that sort of thing. [...] And your success in investing depends on how well you were able to figure out how certain that bush is, how far away it is, and what the worst case is, instead of two birds being there, and only one being there, and the possibilities of four or five or ten or 20 being there.

quote_verbatim: Tom Murphy, a valued director of Berkshire and an all-time great among business managers, long ago gave me some important advice about acquisitions: "To achieve a reputation as a good manager, just be sure you buy good businesses." [...] Applying those images to corporate acquisitions, I'd have to say it is usually the buyer who encounters unpleasant surprises. It's easy to get dreamy-eyed during corporate courtships. [...] Fortunately, the fallout from many of my errors has been reduced by a characteristic shared by most businesses that disappoint: As the years pass, the "poor" business tends to stagnate, thereupon entering a state in which its operations require an ever-smaller percentage of Berkshire's capital. Meanwhile, our "good" businesses often tend to grow and find opportunities for investing additional capital at attractive rates.

quote_verbatim: But it is hard to think about things that haven’t happened yet. So, we can experience when something like the current pandemic happens — it’s just — it’s hard to factor that in. And that’s why you never want to use borrowed money, at least in my view, buy on margin to buy into investments. And we run Berkshire that way. We’ve run it so that we literally try to think of the worst case of not only just one thing going wrong, but other things going wrong at the same time, maybe partly caused by the first, but maybe independent even of the first. [...] you can have any series of numbers times zero, and just need one zero in there, and the answer is zero. There’s no reason to use borrowed money to participate in the American tailwind, but there’s every other reason to participate.
concept: Because the unprecedented is hard to factor in, never invest on borrowed money; plan for several things going wrong at once, since one zero in a series of multiplied outcomes makes the whole product zero.

In 1965, the company did not pay a dime of income tax, an embarrassment that had generally prevailed at the company for a decade. quote_verbatim: With marketable equities, it is easier to change course when I make a mistake. Berkshire's present size, it should be underscored, diminishes this valuable option. With controlled companies, we can dictate these decisions, but we have far less flexibility in the disposition of mistakes.
