Other people have figured out ways to make money in hyperinflationary situations, but that’s not our game, and I don’t think I’d play it well.
concept: Stay out of countries with a real chance of runaway inflation; it is too hard to figure and outside one's game.
evolution_notes: Answer to a question from Mongolia; the line opens with advice to that government ("develop a reputation for having a solid currency over time"), left out. Line 315: Berkshire would not likely find anything there to fit its size. Near M2014-073 (Munger: in hyperinflation stockholders got through, holders of fixed claims were wiped out) and the currency test at lines 281-287 of this session, rowed in this batch.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 13. Question from audience

quote_verbatim: As long as the economy is good and credit spreads are low, they will make money – they’ll make a lot of money because of leverage. However, there is always the danger that at some point the regulators might get cranky and say they’re taking too much risk on behalf of their policyholders, and that could end in tears. We do not like the risk-reward that these situations offer, and therefore we put up the white flag and said we can’t compete in this segment right now.
concept: When rivals win a segment with leverage and credit risk that pays only while conditions stay good, withdraw rather than match them.
evolution_notes: Said of private equity firms in the life end of insurance (lines 325-327): "in the last 3-4 years, I don’t think we’ve done a single deal." Buffett's own lesson in the same exchange (lines 333-335) is rowed separately in this batch. Near M2014-070 (concede leverage to private-equity buyers) and M2019-070 (Munger: do not match prices set by rivals spending others' money).
speaker: JAIN
heading: ### 14. Question from Becky

quote_verbatim: I think there are people that want to copy Berkshire’s model, but usually they don’t want to copy it by also copying the model of the CEO having all of his money in the company forever. They have a different equation – they’re interested in something else. [...] If it doesn’t work, they go on to other things. If what we do at Berkshire doesn’t work, I spend the end of my life regretting what I’ve created. So it’s just a whole different personal equation.
concept: Judge an imitator of a model by whether its chief has all his money in it for good; one who can walk away has a different equation and a different fiduciary feeling.
evolution_notes: The exchange with Ajit Jain on private equity in insurance (lines 325-337); Jain's lesson is rowed separately in this batch. The elision skips "That’s capitalism, but they have a whole different situation and probably a somewhat different fiduciary feeling about what they’re doing. Sometimes it works and sometimes it doesn’t work." Near L2024-008 (owners' stake far above pay) and L2022-007 (future CEOs' net worth in the shares).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 14. Question from Becky

quote_verbatim: Who you associate with is just enormously important. Don’t expect that you’ll make every decision right on that, but you are going to have your life progress in the general direction of the people that you work with, that you admire, that become your friends. [...] You want to hang out with people that are better than you are and that you feel are better than you are because you’re going to go in the direction of the people you associate with.
concept: Choose associates who are better than you, since your life moves in the direction of the people you work with, admire and befriend.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct. Widens M2025-014 (careful who you work for; you take on their habits) from employers to friends and associates. Restates M2019-082 (seek out people better than yourself) and M2024-024. Lines 347-351: Tom Murphy, Sandy Gottesman and Walter Scott, who "always did more than their share and never sought more than their share of the credit"; line 361: "If you wanted to become a better person, you’d want to work for Tom Murphy."
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 15. Question from audience

quote_verbatim: And of course, if somebody’s going to be helpful to you, you want to try to figure out ways to be helpful to them. So you get a compounding of good intentions and good behavior. Unfortunately, you can get the reverse of that in life, too.
concept: Return help to those who help you, so that good intentions and good behaviour compound.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct. Said of Lorimer Davidson at GEICO in 1951 ("in 10 minutes, I found that I had a man that was going to be just wonderfully helpful to me"). The reader's searches found no earlier v5 row in these words.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 15. Question from audience

quote_verbatim: You don’t want to associate with people or enterprises that ask you to do something that you shouldn’t be doing.
concept: Avoid people and enterprises that ask you to do what you should not.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct. The same line continues: "Different professions select for different types of people. It’s interesting to me that in the investment business, so many people get out of it after they’ve made a pile of money. You really want something that you’ll stick around for whether you need the money or not." (restating line 349 and M2024-024, not rowed separately). Same answer as the row at lines 343-345.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 15. Question from audience

quote_verbatim: But if it makes a difference to you whether your stocks are down 15% or not, you need to get a somewhat different investment philosophy because the world is not going to adapt to you. You’re going to have to adapt to the world. [...] That’s part of the stock market, and that’s what makes it a good place to focus your efforts if you’ve got the proper temperament for it and a terrible place to get involved if you get frightened by markets that decline and get excited when stock markets go up. I don’t mean to sound particularly critical – I know people have emotions, but you’ve got to check them at the door when you invest.
concept: An investor bothered by a 15% fall needs a different philosophy; the market rewards only those whose temperament leaves emotion out of investing.
evolution_notes: The elision skips line 379 ("You will see a period in the next 20 years that will be a “hair curler” ... The more sophisticated the system gets, the more the surprises can come out of left field."). Line 373: Berkshire has fallen 50% three times in a short period and "Nothing was fundamentally wrong with the company at any time." Restates M2020-022 (be prepared to sit through a fall of 50 percent), M2020-010 (the right temperament is a requirement) and M2023-005 (decisions without emotion).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 16. Question from Becky

quote_verbatim: So I would focus on the things that have been good in your life rather than the bad things that happen, because bad things do happen. It can often be a wonderful life even with some bad breaks.
concept: Setbacks come to everyone; dwell on what has been good rather than on the bad breaks.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct. Line 389: "Usually the people who get good luck don’t really think it was so much luck as themselves"; line 401 restates it ("Look at the bright side of things to the extent that you can."). Near M2022-030.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 17. Question from audience

quote_verbatim: So the car has become incredibly safer, and it costs 50 times as much to buy an insurance policy. When people talk about developments in car driving, it’s a lot easier to look at the Buck Rogers aspect of it, but they don’t actually think about what really happens to the math of the business.
concept: Judge a technological change by what it does to the economics of the business, not by its spectacle.
evolution_notes: Line 433: a GEICO policy cost about $40 a year in 1951 and can now reach $2,000, while deaths fell from about six per 100 million miles to a little over one. Ajit Jain's lines 429-431 (fewer accidents but a far higher cost per repair, "How those two variables interact ... is still an open issue") make the particular case and are not rowed; Buffett's sentence gives the general form.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 18. Question from Becky

quote_verbatim: So it’s very hard to predict what these big changes mean. You just have to keep thinking all the time. But you don’t want to read some research report that says the world’s coming to an end or the world’s going to be wonderful because of this or that – there are about 50 other developments going on at the same time that you need to think about and keep observing as you go along. You never reach a final answer in this business – you reach a point of action that you take. We try to get into high probability things and play the game in the same way. But it will be different than you think, and you should wake up every morning and think about that if you’re in the business of managing businesses.
concept: Big changes cannot be predicted from a single report; keep observing the many developments at once, act on high probabilities, and expect the outcome to differ from your view.
evolution_notes: Lines 411-413 open the answer: "We expect change in all our businesses. If I’d settled for being in New England textiles – even though it worked well for 70 years or so prior – the world changes."; near M2019-012 (change will kill some owned businesses), not rowed separately. Line 427: "You deal with the world as it develops".
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 18. Question from Becky

quote_verbatim: If you get real opportunities every five or six years, you have to be patient. Charlie always pointed out that we made most of our money out of about eight or nine ideas over 50 years. We talked about it every day and read every report and did everything else. But if you think you can get an idea a day from listening to your broker or reading financial information, forget it. Every now and then you get extraordinary opportunities, and most of the time you don’t have much of an edge.
concept: Real opportunities come every few years and most of the record comes from a handful of ideas; most of the time there is no edge, and a daily idea from a broker is an illusion.
evolution_notes: Restates M2025-005 (opportunistic, a few big decisions, heading 4 of this session) and adds that most of the time one has little edge and that ideas do not come daily from brokers or financial reading. Munger's count (eight or nine ideas over 50 years) reported by Buffett. Near M2024-034 (swing only at pitches one likes).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 18. Question from Becky

quote_verbatim: That is money that, as long as we’re writing at an underwriting profit, is absolutely free money. We would expect that over a 50 or 100-year period that we would be able to say the same thing. But there will be years when you have a very bad underwriting record, and it’ll eat into the float earnings.
concept: Float is free money only while underwriting makes a profit; bad underwriting years eat into its earnings.
evolution_notes: Ajit Jain's interjections (line 467 and line 471, a cost of float of "negative 2.2%" across all lines including life) are facts, not rowed; Buffett line 473: "It’s like running a bank where people leave their money with you and you pay a minus 2.2%". Restates M2014-001 (float's cost set by whether underwriting makes a profit).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 18. Question from Becky

quote_verbatim: We will only buy in our shares if we think that they are almost certainly underpriced as valued very conservatively.
concept: Repurchase only when the shares are almost certainly below a very conservative value.
evolution_notes: Lines 475-481: the 1% repurchase tax makes Berkshire pay more than an outside buyer and hurts investees such as Apple; the policy matter is left out. Near M2022-082 (large profitable repurchases need a market that misprices the stock).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 18. Question from Becky

quote_verbatim: I spend more time looking at balance sheets than I do income statements. Wall Street doesn’t pay much attention to balance sheets, but I like to look at balance sheets over an 8 or 10 year period before I even look at the income account because there are certain things it’s harder to hide or play games with on the balance sheet than with the income statement. Neither one gives you the total answer on anything, but you should understand what the figures are saying and what they don’t say and what they can’t say and what the management would like them to say that the auditors wouldn’t like them to say.
concept: Read a company's balance sheets over eight or ten years before the income account, since they are harder to manipulate, and know what the figures do not and cannot say.
evolution_notes: The quote opens mid-sentence: line 503 begins "It’s one thing we’ve really never talked about here, but". Abel's particular case precedes it (lines 497-501: at the MidAmerican purchase Buffett went first to the balance sheet's derivative contracts and their underlying risk), named here under the 2012 rule; Buffett's lines are the general form.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 1. Question from audience

quote_verbatim: Charlie was never satisfied with just superficial things about any subject. He really wanted to understand it and he always would tell me that you shouldn’t take a position on anything until you can describe the arguments against it better than the person who is arguing with you – that you should be able to argue their case better than they can.
concept: Take no position until you can state the case against it better than its advocates can.
evolution_notes: Munger's maxim reported by Buffett; belongs to the speaker who says it at this meeting. Near M2016-054 (Munger: try to destroy one's previous ideas).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 1. Question from audience

quote_verbatim: Make the most of the people you meet that are going to make you a better person and probably forget about the rest to quite an extent.
concept: Spend yourself on the people who make you better and largely ignore the rest.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct. Restates the morning's M2025-022 (associate with people better than you) and M2025-012 (make the most of a person who can change your life). Shares line 509 with the row on Munger's argue-the-other-side maxim in this batch.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 1. Question from audience

quote_verbatim: When I think of our values, a couple are absolutely critical. One: we will maintain the reputation of Berkshire and that of our company. [...] Looking at our balance sheet, as Warren commented, we will have a fortress of a balance sheet. [...] We recognize it as a strategic asset that allows us to weather difficult times and not be dependent on anybody. We will remain Berkshire and will never be dependent on a bank or some other party for Berkshire to be successful.
concept: Allocating capital starts from two values: protect the reputation, and keep a balance sheet strong enough never to depend on a bank or anyone else.
evolution_notes: Abel on capital allocation as incoming CEO. Near M2020-016 (prepare as if no rescuer will act) and M2025-015 (never risk what has been built).
speaker: ABEL
heading: ### 2. Question from Becky

quote_verbatim: But the value relative to the risk have to be right. If it’s right, we want to own it. If it’s not the time, there’ll be another time to own assets like that. Then there’s the opportunity to own pieces of companies through equity. But as Warren’s always highlighted, though we own a piece of a company, we own a piece of that cash flow, a piece of their balance sheet. It’s not just a share certificate. We’ll approach it with the thought that we’re going to own this company for the long term.
concept: Buy a whole business only when value against risk is right, otherwise wait for another time; treat a stock as a piece of the business's cash flow and balance sheet, held for the long term.
evolution_notes: Part of Abel's order of deployment (lines 527-531): first the capital needs of the owned businesses, then whole businesses, then pieces through equities. Restates the morning's M2025-004 in Abel's words, and the stock-as-business theme of many earlier rows.
speaker: ABEL
heading: ### 2. Question from Becky

quote_verbatim: We need to thoroughly understand what the economic prospects of those companies will look like – as Warren said earlier – 5 years from now, 10 years from now, 20 years from now. If we don’t have a view of that, we won’t be investing, be it 100% or 2% of a company through equities. We have to thoroughly understand what those prospects look like and the underlying risks of the businesses.
concept: No investment, whole or partial, without a view of the business's economics five, ten and twenty years out and of its underlying risks.
evolution_notes: Abel cites Warren's morning remark. Restates M2025-004 (commit only to what is understood).
speaker: ABEL
heading: ### 2. Question from Becky

quote_verbatim: Hard work takes all of us a long way in life, and I would never diminish that. There’s a lot of things that matter in life, but if you start with a great work ethic and have that attitude that you want to contribute, you’re going to go a long way in life.
concept: Start with a work ethic and a wish to contribute.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct, said to a 14-year-old asking how to join Berkshire. Buffett's separate lesson at line 559 is rowed separately in this batch (one exchange, two lessons, the 2006 rule).
speaker: ABEL
heading: ### 3. Question from audience

quote_verbatim: Keep a lot of curiosity and read a lot, as Charlie would say.
concept: Stay curious and read widely.
evolution_notes: Personal conduct; Munger's advice reported by Buffett. Abel's lesson at line 557 is rowed separately in this batch (the 2006 rule). Near M2014-058 (real curiosity) and M2015-088 (Munger: curiosity).
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 3. Question from audience

quote_verbatim: You earn a very set return for taking on a very defined risk associated with that asset, and this has gone well beyond that. We don’t earn the type of returns nor can you earn a large enough return to take on these risks. So it’s not just solving the return side. We really have to solve the risk side, which means we work with our regulators and state legislators to get to the right answer.
concept: A fixed return is priced for a defined risk; when the risk grows beyond what was agreed, no return is large enough, and the risk itself must be bounded.
evolution_notes: Said of utility wildfire liability. Abel restates it at lines 599 and 605 ("we can’t just become the insurer of last resort"), named here, not rowed. Near L2023-011 (the regulatory bargain behind a utility's fixed return can break) and M2017-094.
speaker: ABEL
heading: ### 4. Question from Becky

quote_verbatim: There’s some problems that can’t be solved, and we shouldn’t be in the business of taking investors’ money and tackling things that we don’t know the solution for. [...] If you’re in something where you’re going to lose, the big thing to do is quit. You present your case as well as you can, but if you don’t hold the pen in the end, we don’t have any business taking your money and doing dumb things with it. [...] The problem you have, of course, is that the people that work for you – that’s their job. So they want to have reasons to keep going.
concept: Do not spend owners' money on problems you cannot solve or on a game you will lose where others hold the pen; quit, knowing the people who work in it will want reasons to go on.
evolution_notes: Said of utilities facing politically decided wildfire liability. The first elision skips line 591's political sentence and the second skips line 595, which restates line 591 ("we are not in the business of trying to solve insolvable problems"). Earlier in the heading (line 565) Buffett names the PacifiCorp purchase's mistake, not carving it into the seven states, without a stated lesson. Near M2001-107 and M2020-026.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 4. Question from Becky

quote_verbatim: If we want to do it with our own money, we can do it, but we’re not going to do things with your money that we think are stupid. You ought to get rid of us if we do. It’s easier to do stupid things with other people’s money than it is with your own.
concept: Spending other people's money makes stupid acts easier; owners should remove managers who do with their money what they think stupid.
evolution_notes: Same answer as the quit passage at lines 591-597, adding the mechanism. The rest of line 607 applies it to government and is left out. Near M2019-073 (treat shareholders' money as one's own) and M2021-025.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 4. Question from Becky

quote_verbatim: you just ask them one question: if they were to be stuck on a desert island and they had to own only one of their competitors’ stock during the 10 years they were going to be on that island, which one would it be, and why? And then after they give you that answer, you ask the same thing if they were to short one of their competitors’ stock, which would it be and why? Because every manager likes to talk about their competitors. They’re like little school kids when they get into talking about their competitors. I probably learned more about various industries by just making sure that they didn’t think I’d stay too long and that in the meantime they would have the floor and talk about their competitors.
concept: Ask a manager which competitor he would own for ten years and which he would short, and why; managers talk freely about competitors, and the answers teach an industry.
evolution_notes: The quote opens mid-sentence: line 631 begins "But once you have that, if they’re in the coal business, which happened to be one that I was interested in 70 years ago or so,". Line 629 adds the tactic of an hourglass on the desk to promise a ten-minute visit. Restates M1999-130 and M2017-091.
speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 5. Question from audience

quote_verbatim: But do a little of your own work your own way. Berkshire Hathaway has got plenty of material out there for you to read. And when you get through reading it all, you’ll know way more than most the people that work at Berkshire. So, you don’t need a personal interview.
concept: Do your own work from the published material; reading it all teaches more than a personal meeting.
evolution_notes: Said in declining a request for an hour in his office. Restates the morning's M2025-003 (read through everything yourself). heading: ### 5. Question from audience

quote_verbatim: we also know that certain of the attitudes demonstrated by that particular example have analogues throughout the utility system. [...] So it wasn’t just a direct question of what was involved at PacifiCorp. It was an extrapolation of a societal trend. Secondly, we also had a decision we didn’t expect at all in the real estate business. Those kind of things can change values, and courts can change values. It’s a lot easier to make those decisions when you just own marketable securities than when you own businesses. [...] But that’s the explanation – values change and they don’t always change upward.

Explains the lower price paid for the last Berkshire Hathaway Energy shares. heading: ### 6. Question from Becky

quote_verbatim: And it’s particularly dramatic in public utilities because they are going to need lots of money. So, if you’re going to need lots of money, you probably ought to behave in a way that encourages people to give you lots of money.

heading: ### 6. Question from Becky

quote_verbatim: We will make our best deals when people are the most pessimistic. [...] Over my lifetime I’ve had fabulous opportunities sometimes, and they happen because humans are human. I don’t get fearful by things that other people are afraid of in a financial way. The idea that if Berkshire went down 50% next week – I would regard that as a fantastic opportunity and it wouldn’t bother me in the least. [...] It’s not that I don’t have emotions, but I don’t have emotions about the prices of stocks. [...] the investment business is that everything isn’t properly appraised, and the more fearful other people get, the better your opportunities get.

heading: ### 7. Question from audience

heading: ### 8. Question from Becky

You can buy Apple and have it support that business. That can be a pretty good business and it’s one of the reasons we’ve done well over time.

speaker: BUFFETT
heading: ### 8. Question from Becky

So we really did share the losses with our own capital, but we got an override on other people’s capital. People have made advances where they get the override on other people’s capital without putting up any of their own capital to speak of. That’s a very good business, but it can lead to a lot of abuse.

heading: ### 8. Question from Becky

heading: ### 9. Question from audience

heading: ### 11. Question from audience

But if there’s opportunities to see where maybe I’ve seen something in another business or an opportunity I may see in their industry, we’re going to discuss it and see if that’s something we should pursue or if we are properly addressing the risk. [...] We want to make sure the right folks are talking and figuring out how we can benefit from the prior experiences.

heading: ### 12. Question from Becky

heading: ### 12. Question from Becky
